documents.title: Overview
documents.html: ModernBASIC is a native 64-bit BASIC programming environment, available as a Linux application and as an integrated Linux distribution. Use its workspace to write programs, make graphics, play music and explore the program catalog. Linux provides the drivers, networking and system services underneath it.
documents.text:
## Overview

ModernBASIC is a native 64-bit BASIC programming environment, available as a Linux application and as an integrated Linux distribution. Use its workspace to write programs, make graphics, play music and explore the program catalog. Linux provides the drivers, networking and system services underneath it.

documents.title: Meet your workspace
documents.html:
The system hub is your starting point. Use it to open programs, switch tasks, change display settings and shut down. Each program opens in its own window with a READY. prompt, its own code and its own working memory. Hub commands and BASIC program statements serve different purposes.

In the system hubWhat it does
DIRBrowse the program directory
CLS or Ctrl+LClear command output while keeping the working directory and open tasks
LOAD "examples/hello.bas"Open an existing program (choose a path shown by DIR)
NEW "hello.bas"Create a new program file and open its window
TASKSList open tasks
FOCUS 1Focus the indicated task
STOP 1Interrupt the indicated task
CLOSE 1Close the indicated task
SETTINGSOpen sound/display/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth settings and hardware status
SETUPReopen the first-run checklist
DISPLAYChange resolution with automatic rollback
HELP or F1Read the built-in manual
BASH or F12Open the Bash terminal

In the native Linux application, the Bash terminal runs as your normal Linux user. In the integrated distribution, its administration terminal uses the configured appliance policy.

Use Alt+Tab to switch windows. Drag a title bar to move a window and its edges to resize it. Double-click a title bar to maximize or restore. Super+D shows the hub. Task numbers come from TASKS; use the number actually shown on your computer.
documents.text:
## Meet your workspace

The system hub is your starting point. Use it to open programs, switch tasks, change display settings and shut down. Each program opens in its own window with a `READY.` prompt, its own code and its own working memory. Hub commands and BASIC program statements serve different purposes.

| In the system hub | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `DIR` | Browse the program directory |
| `CLS` or Ctrl+L | Clear command output while keeping the working directory and open tasks |
| `LOAD "examples/hello.bas"` | Open an existing program (choose a path shown by DIR) |
| `NEW "hello.bas"` | Create a new program file and open its window |
| `TASKS` | List open tasks |
| `FOCUS 1` | Focus the indicated task |
| `STOP 1` | Interrupt the indicated task |
| `CLOSE 1` | Close the indicated task |
| `SETTINGS` | Open sound/display/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth settings and hardware status |
| `SETUP` | Reopen the first-run checklist |
| `DISPLAY` | Change resolution with automatic rollback |
| `HELP` or F1 | Read the built-in manual |
| `BASH` or F12 | Open the Bash terminal |

In the native Linux application, the Bash terminal runs as your normal Linux user. In the integrated distribution, its administration terminal uses the configured appliance policy.

Use Alt+Tab to switch windows. Drag a title bar to move a window and its edges to resize it. Double-click a title bar to maximize or restore. Super+D shows the hub. Task numbers come from `TASKS`; use the number actually shown on your computer.

documents.title: Your first program
documents.html:
In the hub, enter NEW "hello.bas". If that name already exists, load it or choose a different name. In the new window, type each of these lines and press Enter:

10 FOR I = 1 TO 5
20 PRINT "HELLO, WORLD!"
30 NEXT I
40 END

Type RUN to see the greeting five times. Type LIST to see your code. Change line 20 by typing a replacement with the same line number. A line number alone deletes that line.

20 PRINT "I MADE THIS!"
RUN
SAVE "hello.bas"

SAVE writes your source to a file. Changes in a live session are temporary unless copied to persistent storage. On an installed system, saved files survive reboot. Closing a program window discards unsaved changes and its working memory.
documents.text:
## Your first program

In the hub, enter `NEW "hello.bas"`. If that name already exists, load it or choose a different name. In the new window, type each of these lines and press Enter:

```basic
10 FOR I = 1 TO 5
20 PRINT "HELLO, WORLD!"
30 NEXT I
40 END
```

Type `RUN` to see the greeting five times. Type `LIST` to see your code. Change line 20 by typing a replacement with the same line number. A line number alone deletes that line.

```basic
20 PRINT "I MADE THIS!"
RUN
SAVE "hello.bas"
```

`SAVE` writes your source to a file. Changes in a live session are temporary unless copied to persistent storage. On an installed system, saved files survive reboot. Closing a program window discards unsaved changes and its working memory.

documents.title: Files and editing
documents.html:
PWD shows your current BASIC directory. DIR lists folders and files. CD "examples" enters a folder and CD / returns to the BASIC program root. Use paths from your actual directory listing.

At a program's READY. prompt, use LOAD, SAVE, LIST, NEW, RUN, STEP and CONT to manage and run code. READY NEW clears the stored program; hub NEW "name.bas" creates a file and opens a window.

F2 lists the program for editing. Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down select stored lines. Edit the selected line and press Enter to replace it. Ctrl+U switches between uppercase and mixed-case input.

Ctrl+Escape interrupts a running program and keeps its window and working state available. Closing the window ends the task. Plain Escape cancels editing or an input operation; it is not the general program interrupt.

In the Debian appliance, user programs are stored under /home/modernbasic/programs and generated output under /home/modernbasic/output. Back up both directories from Linux before reinstalling or replacing a disk. The initial catalog is copied on first boot; updates do not overwrite your edited copies.

## Files and editing

`PWD` shows your current BASIC directory. `DIR` lists folders and files. `CD "examples"` enters a folder and `CD /` returns to the BASIC program root. Use paths from your actual directory listing.

At a program's `READY.` prompt, use `LOAD`, `SAVE`, `LIST`, `NEW`, `RUN`, `STEP` and `CONT` to manage and run code. READY `NEW` clears the stored program; hub `NEW "name.bas"` creates a file and opens a window.

F2 lists the program for editing. Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down select stored lines. Edit the selected line and press Enter to replace it. Ctrl+U switches between uppercase and mixed-case input.

Ctrl+Escape interrupts a running program and keeps its window and working state available. Closing the window ends the task. Plain Escape cancels editing or an input operation; it is not the general program interrupt.

In the Debian appliance, user programs are stored under `/home/modernbasic/programs` and generated output under `/home/modernbasic/output`. Back up both directories from Linux before reinstalling or replacing a disk. The initial catalog is copied on first boot; updates do not overwrite your edited copies.

documents.title: Appearance and display
documents.html:
Use DISPLAY in the hub to select a display mode. Change the default background and text with names:

COLORS
SCREEN COLOR = navy
TEXT COLOR = white

COLORS lists the 32 supported names. Names ignore case, and #rrggbb values also work. Preferences save automatically. New text uses the new default; previously printed text retains its original colors. BASIC drawing colors and the TEXTCOLOR statement are separate programming controls.
documents.text:
## Appearance and display

Use `DISPLAY` in the hub to select a display mode. Change the default background and text with names:

```text
COLORS
SCREEN COLOR = navy
TEXT COLOR = white
```

`COLORS` lists the 32 supported names. Names ignore case, and `#rrggbb` values also work. Preferences save automatically. New text uses the new default; previously printed text retains its original colors. BASIC drawing colors and the `TEXTCOLOR` statement are separate programming controls.

documents.title: Sound and first-run setup
documents.html:
Open SETTINGS, choose Sound, then select your speakers, headphones, or TV. Choose Use for new playback to make that output the default. Adjust its volume, unmute if necessary, and use the left/right test. The test does not change the volume or default output. If sound is still quiet, check the speaker or TV volume. Restart already playing programs after changing outputs.

On the first appliance startup, a welcome checklist offers sound, display, and network checks. Finish setup records completion; Later postpones it until next startup. Use SETUP to revisit it. Live-session settings are temporary; installed systems retain saved network profiles and Bluetooth pairings. Bluetooth radio power follows the adapter’s boot policy.
documents.text:
## Sound and first-run setup

Open `SETTINGS`, choose Sound, then select your speakers, headphones, or TV.
Choose **Use for new playback** to make that output the default. Adjust its volume,
unmute if necessary, and use the left/right test. The test does not change the
volume or default output. If sound is still quiet, check the speaker or TV volume.
Restart already playing programs after changing outputs.

On the first appliance startup, a welcome checklist offers sound, display, and
network checks. **Finish setup** records completion; **Later** postpones it until
next startup. Use `SETUP` to revisit it. Live-session settings are temporary;
installed systems retain saved network profiles and Bluetooth pairings. Bluetooth
radio power follows the adapter’s boot policy.

documents.title: Bluetooth devices
documents.html:
Open SETTINGS → Bluetooth, select an adapter, turn it on, and choose Find nearby devices. Put the accessory in pairing mode and select it by name and address. Choose Pair this device. Compare any displayed code on both devices before confirming; PIN entry is masked. Some keyboards require typing the displayed code on the keyboard itself and pressing Enter there.

Choose Connect after pairing. For speakers/headphones, then use Sound to select the output and test it. Allow this device to reconnect explicitly trusts it, allowing future connections/services without another prompt; use this only for your devices. Actual reconnection depends on device power, range and profile. Disconnect retains pairing; Forget removes the saved pairing keys. Have another input device available before disconnecting a Bluetooth keyboard or mouse.

Scanning stops after 12 seconds or when you choose Show devices. Canceling an operation asks BlueZ to cancel pairing or disconnect the attempted connection; refresh to see its current state. Completed pairings are removed only by Forget. If no adapter is found, check the hardware switch, firmware or USB connection. Saved pairings persist on installed systems; live sessions remain temporary.
documents.text:
## Bluetooth devices

Open `SETTINGS` → **Bluetooth**, select an adapter, turn it on, and choose
**Find nearby devices**. Put the accessory in pairing mode and select it by name
and address. Choose **Pair this device**. Compare any displayed code on both
devices before confirming; PIN entry is masked. Some keyboards require typing
the displayed code on the keyboard itself and pressing Enter there.

Choose **Connect** after pairing. For speakers/headphones, then use **Sound** to
select the output and test it. **Allow this device to reconnect** explicitly trusts
it, allowing future connections/services without another prompt; use this only
for your devices. Actual reconnection depends on device power, range and profile.
**Disconnect** retains pairing; **Forget** removes the saved pairing keys. Have
another input device available before disconnecting a Bluetooth keyboard or mouse.

Scanning stops after 12 seconds or when you choose **Show devices**. Canceling an
operation asks BlueZ to cancel pairing or disconnect the attempted connection;
refresh to see its current state. Completed pairings are removed only by **Forget**.
If no adapter is found, check the hardware switch, firmware or USB connection.
Saved pairings persist on installed systems; live sessions remain temporary.

documents.title: Networking and Linux tools
documents.html:
Open SETTINGS → Wi-Fi to find a network or connect to a hidden network. Enter credentials in the masked-password dialog, then choose Remember or Connect once. Remember saves the profile and password in NetworkManager’s root-owned connection storage and enables automatic reconnection; Connect once forgets the new profile on disconnect. The live medium remains temporary.

The page also offers saved-network reconnection/removal, disconnect, and Wi-Fi on/off controls. Canceling connection attempts restores the previous connection on that adapter. If BASIC closes during an attempt, allow up to three minutes for network recovery. A connection does not guarantee Internet access; captive portals may require a browser login.

Use BASH then nmtui for administrator or advanced network setup. Network access by BASIC programs is a separate capability and is disabled by default in the appliance.

Linux commandPurpose
filesOpen the file manager
edit FILEOpen the supplied Linux text editor
softwareOpen the package manager
backend audioShow the audio backend and devices
backend storageShow storage devices
backend printersShow printer status
backend helpList available Linux backend tools
exitClose the Bash terminal

The appliance's BASH terminal is a trusted-console administration tool with full machine access. Use BASIC program windows for ordinary programming; BASIC's file restrictions do not apply to Linux administration commands.

## Networking and Linux tools

Open `SETTINGS` → Wi-Fi to find a network or connect to a hidden network. Enter
credentials in the masked-password dialog, then choose **Remember** or **Connect
once**. Remember saves the profile and password in NetworkManager’s root-owned
connection storage and enables automatic reconnection; Connect once forgets the
new profile on disconnect. The live medium remains temporary.

The page also offers saved-network reconnection/removal, disconnect, and Wi-Fi
on/off controls. Canceling connection attempts restores the previous connection on
that adapter. If BASIC closes during an attempt, allow up to three minutes for
network recovery. A connection does not guarantee Internet access; captive portals
may require a browser login.

Use `BASH` then `nmtui` for administrator or advanced network setup. Network access
by BASIC programs is a separate capability and is disabled by default in the appliance.

| Linux command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `files` | Open the file manager |
| `edit FILE` | Open the supplied Linux text editor |
| `software` | Open the package manager |
| `backend audio` | Show the audio backend and devices |
| `backend storage` | Show storage devices |
| `backend printers` | Show printer status |
| `backend help` | List available Linux backend tools |
| `exit` | Close the Bash terminal |

The appliance's BASH terminal is a trusted-console administration tool with full machine access. Use BASIC program windows for ordinary programming; BASIC's file restrictions do not apply to Linux administration commands.

documents.title: Updates and shutdown
documents.html:
On an installed system, the distribution configures daily Debian security updates when networking is available. It does not automatically reboot. Live-session updates are disabled; the live overlay is temporary. Use Linux administration tools to review other package updates and restart when required.

The development distribution now stages modernbasic-update for offline ModernBASIC package updates. It checks trusted package checksums, architecture, profile and dependencies, retains the exact installed package, and restores it if installation or desktop health checks fail. Save your work and keep an independent backup before applying an update. Use F12 and modernbasic-update --help; modernbasic-update status also appears on the Settings update page. This is package recovery, not kernel or whole-disk rollback. Public signed release downloads are still pending.

At the system hub, SHUTDOWN followed by Y requests a clean operating-system power-off. RESTART restarts the BASIC environment. QUIT or EXIT at a program prompt closes that program window.

Save your programs before closing their windows or shutting down. Keep backups independently of the installation disk.

On an installed system, the distribution configures daily Debian security updates when networking is available. It does not automatically reboot. Live-session updates are disabled; the live overlay is temporary. Use Linux administration tools to review other package updates and restart when required.

The development distribution now stages `modernbasic-update` for offline
ModernBASIC package updates. It checks trusted package checksums, architecture,
profile and dependencies, retains the exact installed package, and restores it
if installation or desktop health checks fail. Save your work and keep an
independent backup before applying an update. Use F12 and
`modernbasic-update --help`; `modernbasic-update status` also appears on the
Settings update page. This is package recovery, not kernel or whole-disk rollback.
Public signed release downloads are still pending.

At the system hub, `SHUTDOWN` followed by `Y` requests a clean operating-system power-off. `RESTART` restarts the BASIC environment. `QUIT` or `EXIT` at a program prompt closes that program window.

Save your programs before closing their windows or shutting down. Keep backups independently of the installation disk.

documents.title: If something goes wrong
documents.html:
Start by checking the matching manual chapter. For an unresponsive program, use Ctrl+Escape. For audio trouble, start with Sound in SETTINGS. Network status and administration instructions are also available there. A service crash may restart the affected desktop component.

Internal failure reports are saved locally. Once reporting is configured and the desktop is available, a reporting prompt lets you review a report and choose whether to send it to the configured project website. Sending requires an explicit consent checkbox and button. Canceling, closing the dialog, or letting it expire keeps the report locally without uploading. An offline upload failure also keeps the local copy; it does not silently retry later.

A report can include kernel/build versions, service states, recent logs, memory and storage information. Common credentials are redacted, but logs can still identify hardware or contain private text. Read the preview before agreeing to send. No source programs or home files are automatically attached.

From BASH, you can create a report yourself:

diagnostics report --category basic --reason "Describe what went wrong"
diagnostics list

Use the returned report path with diagnostics preview REPORT or diagnostics send REPORT. The terminal sender also asks before uploading. Categories are kernel, basic, integration and unsure. The website keeps these queues separate and developers can reclassify reports.

A machine that cannot boot or display a dialog cannot ask for consent immediately. Reports that were successfully saved can be reviewed after recovery. Hard crashes or power loss can prevent evidence from being written at all.

## Overview

This guide is built into F1 help and MANUAL, followed by the full language

documents.title: Your first program
documents.html:
At the graphical system hub, type NEW "hello.bas" to create a new file and open its program window. If that file already exists, use LOAD "hello.bas" instead. Click the program window and enter the commands below at its READY prompt, including each line number. Press Enter after each line. The terminal REPL accepts the same program and editor commands.

10 PRINT "HELLO, BASIC"
20 FOR I=1 TO 5
30 PRINT I; " SQUARED IS "; I*I
40 NEXT I
50 END
CHECK
RUN

CHECK validates control structures and DATA without running the program. It is not a complete expression or type checker: RUN can still report runtime errors. A completed run returns to READY. In a graphical window, Ctrl+Escape stops a runaway program; plain Escape does not stop execution.

documents.title: Keep your work
documents.html:
Start in your BASIC programs directory. DIR shows examples and folders; PWD shows where you are. Make your own folder once, then save there:

CD /
MKDIR "mywork"
CD "mywork"
SAVE "hello.bas"
VERIFY "hello.bas"

On later visits use CD "mywork" without repeating MKDIR. SAVE replaces an existing file, so use a new name or COPY "hello.bas" AS "hello-backup.bas" before substantial changes. VERIFY compares the saved bytes with your current source. NEW clears the editor; OLD restores the previous program retained by NEW or LOAD. OLD is an in-session recovery aid, not a disk backup.

On an installed distro, user source lives in /home/modernbasic/programs and exports in /home/modernbasic/output. The live image has no persistent overlay: copy work to external storage before shutting it down. Use the storage settings and administrator Bash for storage/backup operations outside the BASIC file root. Keep a backup on a separate device. Bundled originals remain in /usr/share/modernbasic/programs; provisioning only adds missing files and never replaces existing user files. A filename you delete may be restored on boot.

documents.title: Edit and organize source
documents.html:
LIST shows stored source. In the graphical editor, F2 lists it and Ctrl+Up or Ctrl+Down selects a line to edit. Left/Right, Home/End, Backspace and Delete edit the input row; Enter stores it. Up/Down recall command history. Ctrl+U toggles uppercase input. EDIT 20 prompts for a replacement line body in either UI.

Type a line number alone to delete it. DELETE 20-40 deletes a range. RENUM 100,10,10 renumbers from 100 in steps of 10, starting at old line 10, and adjusts recognized branch references. AUTO 10,10 supplies line numbers; an empty input line ends AUTO mode.

Unfinished SUB, FUNCTION, TYPE and other structured blocks remain editable. Complete their closing statements before RUN. CHECK reports structural errors without throwing your source away. SAVE also works on unfinished drafts. EDIT "draft.bas" reopens a source draft even if a block is incomplete; LIST then shows it for repair. LOAD and LOADB retain their stricter structure checks and leave the previous program in place on failure. Lexically malformed source (such as an unterminated quoted string) needs correction in a text editor before it can be opened as numbered BASIC. MERGE "part.bas" adds or replaces numbered lines; save a backup first when line numbers overlap.

Recover command-interface drafts

With an explicit file workspace, the BASIC prompt automatically checkpoints a changed, nonempty program before accepting the next command. These are separate session copies in .modernbasic-recovery, not writes to the original source. This includes unfinished structured blocks. Text still being typed, before Enter, and unsaved Microsoft Edit buffers are outside this mechanism.

After a restart, use RECOVER to list snapshots. Enter one of the displayed EDIT "/.modernbasic-recovery/session-....bas" commands to open that draft, then use LIST, repair it, and SAVE "my-program.bas". Recovery never runs a program or replaces the current draft automatically. NEW does not erase the last nonempty checkpoint. Copies remain available after normal exit as well.

AUTOSAVE reports its status; AUTOSAVE OFF disables checkpoints without deleting copies, and AUTOSAVE ON enables or retries them. Sessions without an explicit workspace default to off. There is one atomic snapshot per editing session, with a 4 MiB source limit and room for 32 session files. Remove unneeded copies using Files or KILL after saving anything you want to keep. A full, unwritable, or linked recovery folder pauses autosave and reports the problem; editing and explicit SAVE remain available. Recovery on a nonpersistent live image cannot survive destruction of that image's temporary filesystem.

Understand runtime errors

Unhandled stored-program errors show the failing statement, not merely its physical line. For example, 10 A=4:PRINT A/0 reports PRINT A / 0 at line 10, with a hint about the divisor. Procedure context includes up to eight active procedure frames and eight GOSUB/event callers. Imported procedures identify the original library filename and source line. Excerpts are bounded, canonical listings rather than exact source-column highlights. BASIC's ON ERROR behavior and error codes are unchanged. Structure-check and source-loading errors may still have only their existing diagnostic; this is not a complete parser diagnostic or graphical debugger redesign.

documents.title: Learn with the supplied lessons
documents.html:
The tutorials directory contains small programs with no external asset needs:

  • 01_loops.bas: arithmetic, variables, FOR and IF.
  • 02_procedures.bas: reusable FUNCTION and SUB blocks with parameters.
  • 03_files.bas: save a data file, read it back, and close its channel.
  • 04_debugging.bas: pause with STOP, inspect values, and continue.

Copy a lesson into your own folder before changing it. At READY:

CD /
COPY "tutorials/01_loops.bas" AS "mywork/loops.bas"
LOAD "mywork/loops.bas"
LIST
RUN

The file lesson writes tutorial-values.txt in the current BASIC directory and replaces that file on each run. The full catalog also includes graphics, games, audio, sprite/font editors, networking and dialect examples. Examples needing input, devices, permission or external services describe those requirements; not every example finishes unattended.
documents.text:
## Learn with the supplied lessons

The tutorials directory contains small programs with no external asset needs:

- 01_loops.bas: arithmetic, variables, FOR and IF.
- 02_procedures.bas: reusable FUNCTION and SUB blocks with parameters.
- 03_files.bas: save a data file, read it back, and close its channel.
- 04_debugging.bas: pause with STOP, inspect values, and continue.

Copy a lesson into your own folder before changing it. At READY:

```basic
CD /
COPY "tutorials/01_loops.bas" AS "mywork/loops.bas"
LOAD "mywork/loops.bas"
LIST
RUN
```

The file lesson writes tutorial-values.txt in the current BASIC directory and
replaces that file on each run. The full catalog also includes graphics, games,
audio, sprite/font editors, networking and dialect examples. Examples needing
input, devices, permission or external services describe those requirements;
not every example finishes unattended.

documents.title: Debug step by step
documents.html:
Load tutorials/04_debugging.bas and use STEP to execute one statement. STEP 3 executes up to three statements before pausing. The prompt identifies the next line; colon-separated statements are stepped individually. At STOP or STEP:

INSPECT TOTAL
INSPECT A(1)
CHECK
CONT

INSPECT reads a scalar, scalar record field or existing array element without changing variables, random state, storage or continuation. Use literal nonnegative integer subscripts, such as A(1) or GRID(2,3); expressions, function calls and record-array field expressions are not accepted. Missing scalars show their BASIC default; missing arrays report an error without being created. Strings are shown quoted, with control characters escaped.

Inside a procedure, inspection uses its local, STATIC, SHARED and BYREF scope. CONT resumes; RUN restarts the program. Editing source invalidates the old continuation. Direct statements and EVAL are available when not paused; use INSPECT during a pause. TRON and TROFF enable and disable line tracing.

documents.title: Files, graphics and sound
documents.html:
BASIC file commands stay within the configured programs root. Open and close channels explicitly; the file lesson demonstrates OPEN, PRINT#, INPUT# and CLOSE. Use separate names for source (.bas), tokenized programs (.m64b) and data. SAVEB stores a tokenized program, not a machine-code executable. LOADB reads it.

SCREEN and drawing statements provide graphics; SOUND and PLAY provide audio. The language and audio references explain device options, soundfonts and exports. Missing audio hardware does not prevent text programming. Images, fonts, soundfonts and media are opened on first use, so CHECK cannot prove that those files or devices will be available when the program runs.

documents.title: Create a native executable
documents.html:
The Debian distribution supplies the shared runtime source, Rust compiler, Cargo, GCC and X11 development files for local COMPILE. At READY, after loading and checking a complete program:

COMPILE "hello"

COMPILE packages the BASIC program with the shared native runtime; it does not translate each BASIC statement into machine code. It builds for the current machine's architecture, requires writable build space, and may take time on small devices. It uses the locally bundled Rust dependencies and builds without contacting package registries. The generated executable and build files use the configured output directory. Keep referenced external assets with your deployment and test it on its target system. ARM64, AMD64 and RISC-V executables differ, while all profiles use the same maintained source and BASIC behavior.

Export mode follows graphics statements in the stored program. A plain assignment such as VIEW=LOOKAT(...), a graphics-like variable name in an expression, a comment, or DATA text does not request a window. Actual drawing/window commands, including those after colons, in inline IF/ELSE branches, or in subroutines, select the graphical wrapper. LINE INPUT, VIEW PRINT and file GET #/PUT # remain console operations. A graphical export accepts --headless for noninteractive tests and file rendering. This selection is static: it considers stored commands even in branches that will not run, and cannot predict commands introduced later by dynamically loaded programs.

The desktop editor offers New BASIC program and Build / install. Source stays under Programs/; builds go to Binaries/. After a successful build, choose Software application (Applications/) or BASIC system component (Components/), or keep the binary without installing it. Components belong to the BASIC environment and do not automatically start as Linux services. See Editor and files for the workflow.

For a development checkout, enable compilation with --native-compile when launching the REPL or graphical shell. Ordinary runs require no compiler. Use the administrator terminal to run exported executables; BASIC file paths and host paths have different roots. A failed COMPILE reports the compiler diagnostic and keeps the source program available for correction.

documents.title: AI programming paths
documents.html:
programs/ai/basic_chatbot.bas implements softmax training, inference and weight save/reload entirely in BASIC. Run it with a writable file root; -- SELFTEST checks training and checkpoint reload without interactive input. Its three-intent bag-of-words classifier is an educational model, not a generative LLM. programs/ai/local_chat.bas is a single-turn local LLM client using TASK AIMODELS and TASK AICHAT. Run it with --local-ai; use Up/Down to select an installed local completion model and Enter to start chatting. Escape cancels. Home/End and Page Up/Down navigate longer lists, and /model returns to the chooser. Each prompt is independent (no conversation history). The compiled client opens a BASIC window by default. For terminal or piped input, run target/ai/local-chat --headless --local-ai --file-root /path/to/workspace -- TERMINAL and choose a model by its displayed number; no model name needs to be typed. Both can be packaged with COMPILE, installed as applications or components, and run as native executables. Compilation preserves runtime semantics rather than turning training loops into optimized machine code.

The editor's Review with Ollama action uses TASK AIREVIEW and leaves source unchanged. See Editor and files for limits and capabilities, and Foundation review for the language and desktop audit.

save/reload entirely in BASIC. Run it with a writable file root; `-- SELFTEST`

local completion model and Enter to start chatting. Escape cancels. Home/End and

and choose a model by its displayed number; no model name needs to be typed.

run as native executables. Compilation preserves runtime semantics rather than

documents.html: This document summarizes the current 0.8.2 implementation. It is a guide to ModernBASIC, not a claim that every historical dialect manual is reproduced page for page.

## Overview

This document summarizes the current 0.8.2 implementation. It is a guide to
ModernBASIC, not a claim that every historical dialect manual is reproduced
page for page.

documents.title: Program model
documents.html:
• Stored source uses line numbers from 0 through 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. The bundled catalog uses numbers no larger than 65,529 for readability.
  • A line number followed by text inserts or replaces a line.
  • A line number alone deletes that line.
  • Text and binary programs share limits of 100,000 stored lines, 1,000,000 tokens and 64 MiB of token objects/string payload. Text input additionally permits at most 1 MiB per line and 64 MiB per load. Rejected edits, merges and loads preserve the previous program.
  • Colons separate statements without splitting strings, comments, or DATA.
  • Immediate statements use the same tokenizer and execution engine as stored statements, including compact forms such as PRINT42. A direct GOSUB resumes the remaining immediate statements after the matching RETURN.
  • Direct READ and subroutine calls share the active program's DATA cursor, including before its first RUN. Successful source replacement resets that cursor to the new program's data; a failed replacement leaves it unchanged.
  • STOP retains an exact statement-level continuation point for READY CONT. CONT is a session command, not an executable statement inside a stored program.
  • READY STEP [count] executes exact statements rather than whole physical lines; colon-separated statements, GOTO/GOSUB targets, and RETURN addresses remain individually observable. RUN always starts a fresh session.
documents.text:
## Program model

- Stored source uses line numbers from 0 through 9,223,372,036,854,775,807.
  The bundled catalog uses numbers no larger than 65,529 for readability.
- A line number followed by text inserts or replaces a line.
- A line number alone deletes that line.
- Text and binary programs share limits of 100,000 stored lines, 1,000,000
  tokens and 64 MiB of token objects/string payload. Text input additionally
  permits at most 1 MiB per line and 64 MiB per load. Rejected edits, merges
  and loads preserve the previous program.
- Colons separate statements without splitting strings, comments, or `DATA`.
- Immediate statements use the same tokenizer and execution engine as stored
  statements, including compact forms such as `PRINT42`. A direct `GOSUB`
  resumes the remaining immediate statements after the matching `RETURN`.
- Direct `READ` and subroutine calls share the active program's `DATA` cursor,
  including before its first `RUN`. Successful source replacement resets that
  cursor to the new program's data; a failed replacement leaves it unchanged.
- `STOP` retains an exact statement-level continuation point for READY
  `CONT`. `CONT` is a session command, not an executable statement inside a
  stored program.
- READY `STEP [count]` executes exact statements rather than whole physical
  lines; colon-separated statements, GOTO/GOSUB targets, and RETURN addresses
  remain individually observable. `RUN` always starts a fresh session.

documents.title: Values and expressions
documents.html:
Expression nesting is limited to 32 levels, including raw numerical arguments and PIECEWISE branches. Nested evaluators share a ten-million-entry work allowance and check BREAK when entering a nested expression or numerical sample. The statement-step limit is separate from this expression-work allowance.

Retained images, media and SoundFonts share a conservative asset reservation budget of 1 GiB per program and 1 GiB across the process. Reservations include decode/copy headroom; they are not a measurement of total process RAM. Asset names are limited to 4,096 per program. Equivalent resolved local image/media paths reuse retained data. Assets still used by playback or rendering retain their charges until their last owner releases them. Over-budget operations return an error; close unused programs, replace a program with NEW, or reduce the assets. These limits are separate from FRE's retained-variable payload budget and the appliance's final OS memory limit.

SoundFont loading validates chunk bounds before reserving sample storage and decodes directly into an exactly sized sample vector. Metadata and decoder working space have separate headroom within the same reservation.

ModernBASIC uses checked signed 64-bit integers, finite binary64 reals, owned UTF-8 strings, complex numbers, and lists. Traditional suffix typing is accepted. Arithmetic overflow, invalid conversion, non-finite results, and illegal quantities are errors rather than host-language wraparound.

Implemented expression areas include:

  • ordinary arithmetic and comparison, checked MOD, integer DIV/\, and boolean/bitwise NOT, AND, OR, XOR, and BBC EOR; modern BITXNOR(left,right) and BITIMPLIES(left,right) provide one-operation equivalents for classic Microsoft EQV and IMP without adding dialect operators or changing expression precedence;
  • classic bare and argument-taking RND, plus checked FACT/FACTORIAL;
  • string slicing, ASCII case conversion, search, formatting, DEC, and BIN$/OCT$/HEX$;
  • trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, rounding, and special functions;
  • number theory, probability, statistics, regression, and finance;
  • polynomial, numerical, signal, geometry, and linear-algebra functions;
  • complex arithmetic and list-oriented analysis;
  • LBOUND(array[,dimension]) and UBOUND(array[,dimension]), including OPTION BASE, resized, record-field, local, STATIC, and BYREF arrays;
  • host-local seconds-since-midnight TIMER, local/session DATE$ and TIME$, logical text-row CSRLIN/CSRLIN(), nonblocking INKEY$/INKEY$(), and live PCOLLISION(sprite[,sprite]);
  • bounded host-approved COMMAND$ and ENVIRON$(name-or-index) process context.

Reproducible random streams

Each BASIC program run owns a deterministic CPU RND stream. RANDOMIZE seed chooses an explicit starting seed; without a seed it uses host time. Positive RND arguments advance the stream, zero repeats the cached result, and a negative argument deterministically reseeds before advancing. RNGSTATE$() returns a versioned MBRNG1 text checkpoint for the exact stream position, and RNGRESTORE(checkpoint$) restores it and returns BASIC true. A checkpoint includes the cached value used by RND(0), so restoring replays subsequent draws exactly. The text has a checksum and contains data only; unknown versions, corruption or impossible state are rejected without changing the active stream. This saves the random stream only, not program variables, tensors or scheduler state, and the generator is for reproducible simulation rather than cryptographic secrets.

10 S$=RNGSTATE$():A=RND(1)
20 C=RNGRESTORE(S$):PRINT RND(1)=A

Keep S$ or persist its text with normal BASIC file commands when a run must resume later. The checksum detects accidental changes; it is not an authentication mechanism.

FRE(0) reports the remaining retained-value payload budget. The runtime's fixed numeric graph-window cells (XMIN, XMAX, XSCL, YMIN, YMAX, YSCL) and error-status cells (ERR, ERL) do not consume that budget. Non-numeric values assigned to those cells are charged normally and release their payload when replaced or reset.

PI() is the unambiguous built-in constant. Bare PI remains an assignable classic numeric variable, which preserves Microsoft-family variable semantics but differs from dialects that reserve bare PI as a constant.

COMMAND$ and COMMAND$() return the command tail approved by the host. ENVIRON$(name$) performs an ASCII-case-insensitive lookup, while ENVIRON$(n) returns the one-based nth NAME=VALUE entry. A missing name or an index beyond the supplied entries returns an empty string; a nonpositive index is an illegal quantity. Duplicate names retain their original position but use the final spelling and value.

Both sources are empty by default. Library hosts opt in with RunOptions::with_command_line, with_environment, or with_environment_variable. The CLI accepts repeatable --env NAME=VALUE options and joins arguments following -- with one space for COMMAND$, for example modernbasic run --env MODE=production program.bas -- input.dat -v. ModernBASIC never imports ambient process variables implicitly. At most 255 environment entries are accepted, and the command plus normalized environment must fit the configured string-byte budget.

documents.title: Statement index
documents.html:
This index describes the executable statement surface. Built-in expression functions such as ABS(), SIN(), SPRITEX(), and OBJECTZ() are not statements and are therefore not repeated here. Canonical spellings appear in the main lists; accepted compatibility aliases are collected separately so an alias is not mistaken for a second implementation.

Statements are case-insensitive. A colon separates statements on one source line. REM and apostrophe introduce comments, and ? tokenizes as PRINT. Traditional suffixes are $ for string, % for integer, & for long, ! for single precision, and # for double precision. Longer variable names with keyword prefixes remain whole in scalar and indexed assignment targets, for example ORIGINS(I)={0,0,1}. Exact reserved names and compact IF, FOR, LET and ON control forms retain their existing meaning.

Assignment, declarations, and data

[LET] target = expression
MID$(string$,start[,length]) = replacement$
expression -> variable                 Unicode → is also accepted

CONST name=expression[,name=expression...]
DIM declaration[,declaration...]
REDIM [PRESERVE] declaration[,declaration...]
ERASE array[,array...]
OPTION BASE 0|1
SWAP variable,variable
CHANGE source TO destination
RANDOMIZE [seed]
CLEAR
SHARED name[,name...]
STATIC declaration[,declaration...]
COMMON name[,name...]

DATA values
READ target[,target...]
RESTORE [line]

DIM accepts ordinary arrays, typed primitive scalars and arrays, and user-defined record scalars and arrays. CLEAR has the accepted CLR alias.

Records and procedures

TYPE name
    field AS INTEGER|LONG|SINGLE|DOUBLE|STRING [* bytes]|record-type
END TYPE

SUB name[([BYVAL|BYREF] parameter,...)]
END SUB
EXIT SUB

FUNCTION name[([BYVAL|BYREF] parameter,...)]
END FUNCTION
EXIT FUNCTION

CALL name[(arguments)]
DEF FNname(parameter[,parameter...])=expression
DEF SEG [= expression]
DEF USR[n]=service-address
DEFINT letter-range
DEFSNG letter-range
DEFDBL letter-range
DEFSTR letter-range

The spaced default-type forms such as DEF INT A-Z are accepted too. The standalone spelling DEFTYPE is reserved by the tokenizer but has no executable statement form; programs should use DEFINT, DEFSNG, DEFDBL, or DEFSTR. Comma-separated letter ranges are validated and committed as one declaration; a malformed range or storage failure leaves the previous default types unchanged. Explicit type suffixes override these defaults even for values that have not been assigned yet.

Input and output

PRINT [items]
PRINT USING format$;items
WRITE [items]
INPUT [prompt;]variable[,variable...]
LINE INPUT [prompt;]string-variable
GET variable

WIDTH columns
LOCATE row[,column[,cursor-visible]]
VIEW PRINT [top TO bottom]
HOME
HTAB column
VTAB row
TEXTCOLOR [foreground[,background]]
LPRINT [items]
LLIST [range]
NULL count
TRON
TROFF

GET variable is the console/key-input form. File-channel GET # is listed with the file statements below. LINEINPUT is accepted as the compact spelling of LINE INPUT.

Text rows are one-based 1 through 25 and columns are one-based 1 through 80; explicit out-of-range LOCATE, HTAB, VTAB, or VIEW PRINT coordinates raise IllegalQuantity. VIEW PRINT with no bounds restores the full screen. HOME clears through the text backend and moves to column 1 at the active region's top. TEXTCOLOR accepts zero through 0xFFFFFF; one argument changes the foreground, two change both colors, and no arguments restore defaults. TEXTCELL(row,column[,field]) queries the same bounded logical cells in batch, terminal, and graphical sessions. The default field 0 returns the Unicode codepoint, field 1 returns the foreground color, and field 2 returns the background color. Blank cells return codepoint 32. Invalid coordinates or field selectors raise IllegalQuantity. These identifier-encoded names remain ordinary assignable variables when immediately followed by =.

PRINT column tracking and WIDTH wrapping count Unicode characters rather than UTF-8 bytes. Numeric PRINT USING fields accept only integer and real values; strings, complex values, and lists report TypeMismatch.

LPRINT and LPRINT USING append to modernbasic_print.spool beneath the configured output root (or file root when no separate output root is supplied). The spool obeys the per-file byte ceiling and rejects symlink targets. It does not discover a physical printer or write to a shared temporary path. An embedding host may approve one explicit spool path through RunOptions.

Control flow

END
STOP
SLEEP [seconds]

GOTO line                         GO TO line is accepted
GOSUB line                        GO SUB line is accepted
RETURN

IF condition THEN statement-or-line [ELSE statement-or-line]
IF condition GOTO line
IF condition THEN
    block
[ELSE
    block]
END IF

FOR variable=start TO limit [STEP increment]
NEXT [variable]
WHILE condition
WEND
DO [WHILE|UNTIL condition]
LOOP [WHILE|UNTIL condition]
REPEAT
UNTIL condition

EXIT FOR
EXIT WHILE
EXIT DO
EXIT REPEAT

SLEEP uses seconds and accepts fractional durations. A queued keypress ends both timed and indefinite sleep; Ctrl+Escape/BREAK remains interruptible.

RETURN has no destination argument. It resumes at the exact statement after the corresponding GOSUB. Block-IF endings ENDIF, IFEND, and IF END are accepted aliases for END IF.

Selection supports both the standard and BBC-family structured forms:

SELECT CASE expression
CASE value[,value...]
CASE low TO high
CASE IS comparison value
CASE ELSE
END SELECT

CASE expression OF
WHEN value-or-range
OTHERWISE
ENDCASE

ENDSELECT, ENDCASE, END CASE, and CEND are accepted compact endings. Errors while evaluating branch values, ranges, or comparisons use the active ON ERROR handler. ERL identifies the enclosing selection statement; RESUME retries selection and RESUME NEXT skips to its next statement (normally the first branch marker, which skips the remaining selection).

Computed branches, errors, and events

ON expression GOTO line[,line...]
ON expression GOSUB line[,line...]

ON ERROR GOTO line
ERROR code
RESUME
RESUME NEXT
RESUME line

ON TIMER(seconds) GOSUB line
TIMER ON|OFF|STOP

ON COLLISION GOSUB line
COLLISION ON|OFF|STOP

Files, memory, and host-approved services

OPEN path$ FOR INPUT|OUTPUT|APPEND|RANDOM|BINARY AS #channel [LEN=record-size]
OPEN mode$,#channel,path$
OPEN #channel,path$,mode$

PRINT#, WRITE#, INPUT#, LINE INPUT#, and GET# are accepted compact file-channel spellings. PEEK, INP, and USR are expression functions, not statements. Memory, ports, and callable services are bounded virtual or host-approved resources; these forms never expose unrestricted host hardware.

INPUT# consumes comma- or line-separated fields until every requested destination has a value. Fields left on the same line remain available to the next read; LINE INPUT# and GET# continue at that same byte position. A trailing comma contributes an empty field. Quoted fields may contain commas and newlines; doubled quotes decode to one quote, matching WRITE# output. The total raw field bytes collected by one INPUT# statement must fit the configured input-byte limit. Conversion or storage failure leaves all destination values unchanged.

During execution, MERGE installs the combined program immediately and continues after the executing statement's line and colon position. Saved loop, subroutine, procedure, and error-resume positions retain their line and colon positions when inserted lines shift the executable layout. If a replacement line has fewer statements, a removed position continues at the end of that line. MERGE rebuilds the DATA cursor without clearing variables or default type declarations.

CHAIN starts the loaded program with COMMON values, arrays, and their declared types retained. Non-COMMON declarations and prior error-handler/resume state are cleared; the new program installs its own ON ERROR handler if needed.

Networking and host web services

WEB OPEN url$
WEB GET url$,response$
WEB POST url$,body$,response$[,content-type$]
WEB DOWNLOAD url$,path$

PLAY AUDIO source$
PLAY VIDEO source$

Network access is a host capability and is disabled by default. Start a CLI session with --network, or set RunOptions::network_enabled through the library API. WEB OPEN hands an HTTP(S) address to the operating system's default browser; on Linux this uses xdg-open. The browser remains responsible for HTML, JavaScript, logins, cookies, accessibility, downloads initiated by a page, and licensed/DRM playback. For an owned graphical Chromium surface controlled from BASIC, use the optional WEB VIEW interface described in Browser. WEB VIEW OPEN also requires the host network grant; it is separate from the external WEB OPEN handoff.

WEB GET returns one UTF-8 response in a string variable. WEB POST sends a string body and returns a UTF-8 response; its default content type is application/json, and an optional fourth argument selects another content type. Use WEB DOWNLOAD for binary data: it performs an HTTP(S) GET and writes the response beneath the output sandbox. The host curl executable performs HTTP, redirects, and TLS through fixed arguments. URLs are limited to HTTP and HTTPS; embedded credentials are rejected. Requests starting with HTTPS keep every redirect on HTTPS; HTTP entry points may redirect to HTTP or HTTPS. POST redirects use GET after 301/302/303, while 307/308 retain the method and body. Transfers honor interruption during request writes, response reads and process exit, have a 30-second deadline, and responses are bounded by --max-network-bytes (16 MiB by default). Downloads must also fit the configured file limit.

PLAY AUDIO and PLAY VIDEO accept either an existing sandboxed local path or a direct HTTP(S) media URL when the capability is enabled. For a stored program, the loader reads or fetches the complete bounded source before READY.; FFmpeg later decodes those retained bytes through fixed arguments and the existing 30-minute media-duration ceiling. A normal YouTube, Netflix, or other web-page URL is not a direct media source; pass that page to WEB OPEN so the installed browser can handle its site logic and any licensed playback.
