Exact symbolic polynomial mathematics

The polynomial functions in this section accept expression strings and return exact results for polynomials over rational numbers, including multiple variables. Integer literals, variable names, parentheses, unary signs, +, -, *, division by a nonzero constant, and nonnegative integer literal powers are supported. Multiplication must be explicit. Decimals, functions such as SIN, and variable denominators are rejected. Write 3/2, not 1.5. Variable names are ASCII alphanumeric, start with a letter, and are case-insensitive; output names are uppercase. Calculus selects X unless another variable is supplied.

FunctionExact result
SYMSIMPLIFY$(expr$[,variable$])Expanded polynomial with reduced rational coefficients, ordered by descending total degree and then lexicographic powers with alphabetically ordered variables.
SYMDIFF$(expr$[,variable$])Partial derivative with respect to the selected variable; all other variables are held constant.
SYMINT$(expr$[,variable$])Polynomial antiderivative with the term independent of the selected variable set to zero. The general answer adds an arbitrary function of the other variables, or a constant in the univariate case.
SYMPROVE(left$,right$[,variable$])-1 if canonical coefficients prove a polynomial identity in all variables; 0 if the polynomials differ. Unsupported statements raise errors.
SYMVARS(expr$)Alphabetically ordered list of variable-name strings remaining after simplification. A constant returns an empty list.
SYMGRAD(expr$,variables)List of partial-derivative strings in the explicitly requested variable order.
SYMHESSIAN(expr$,variables)Nested list of second-partial-derivative strings. Entry (i,j) differentiates with respect to the requested variables i and j.
SYMSUBST$(expr$,variable$,replacement$)Exact substitution of one polynomial for the selected variable, followed by expansion. Inserted expressions are not recursively substituted again.
SYMDIV(dividend$,divisor$[,variable$])Univariate only: two strings {quotient$,remainder$} satisfying the polynomial division identity.
SYMGCD$(left$,right$[,variable$])Univariate only: monic polynomial GCD; GCD(0,0) returns 0.
SYMMIN(expr$,lower$,upper$[,variable$])Univariate only: two exact constant-expression strings {location$,value$} for the global minimum of a degree-at-most-two polynomial on a closed rational interval.
SYMMAX(expr$,lower$,upper$[,variable$])Corresponding global maximum.

For gradients and Hessians, variables is a comma-separated string such as "Y,X,Z", or the string list returned by SYMVARS. A nonempty set of distinct names is required; duplicates are rejected case-insensitively. An absent variable has zero derivative. BASIC brace literals remain numeric, so use a string to specify variable order. Returned derivative strings can be indexed, printed, and passed directly to other symbolic functions. For existing calls, the optional identifier on SYMSIMPLIFY$ and SYMPROVE remains accepted and validated; it does not restrict the variable set or change the canonical ordering.

Division, GCD, and the univariate SYMMIN/SYMMAX optimizers require every input expression to use only the selected variable. Optimization bounds must be constant rational expressions. Equal bounds are allowed; reversed bounds are rejected. Endpoints and any interior stationary point are compared exactly; ties retain the lower endpoint. These univariate calls accept either curvature. For convex multivariable problems with box constraints, use the separate calls below. General linear constraints, integer and nonlinear optimization are not supplied by these symbolic functions.

SYMPROVE is a decision procedure for polynomial identities, not a general purpose theorem prover. A false result means the expressions are not identical, not that they differ at every point. No floating-point samples are used as proof. Division by a variable expression is rejected even when cancellation seems possible: X/X must not silently become an everywhere-defined constant. Powers are polynomial powers (P^0 is the constant polynomial 1).

Exact rational coefficients use dynamically allocated arbitrary-precision integers with a 4096-bit limit on each normalized numerator and positive denominator (about 1233 decimal digits). Small coefficients keep an inline signed-integer fast path. Each addition, multiplication and division reduces its result before applying the size limit; temporary cross-products can exceed it. An intermediate *normalized* result beyond the limit fails even if a later expression would cancel it. Zero denominators always raise an error.

Total degree is limited to 64, input and individual output expressions to 8192 bytes, variable names to 32 characters, and parser recursion to 32 levels. Sparse multivariable operations allow at most eight distinct input/requested variable names per call, 2048 intermediate terms, and one million charged algebra steps. A separate per-call budget of 32 million coefficient-work units charges rational arithmetic by squared 64-bit limb width and checks BREAK. Existing certificate, term, recursion and output limits still apply; arbitrary precision is bounded, not unlimited computation. Every returned expression fits its parser's input limit and can be used in another symbolic call.

SYMEVAL converts exact rational constants directly to binary64 with one rounding (ties to even), including subnormal values. It does not divide two independently rounded floating-point coefficients. Finite binary64 variable bindings can all be represented exactly for symbolic domain checks. Rational subexpressions and guard signs are evaluated exactly before conversion where the coefficient limits permit it. BASIC retains its canonical single zero representation. Ordinary BASIC numeric variables, tensor kernels and transcendental function evaluation still use their existing machine-number types; this does not add arbitrary-precision floats.

Polynomial degrees retain their existing limits. General constant integer-power evaluation and some integration searches use signed 128-bit exponents. Exhaustive integer-divisor/Kronecker factor searches use exact big integers for primitive coefficients, divisors, sampled values and interpolated factors. Primitive coefficients, common denominators and integer Horner intermediates have a 4096-bit limit. Prime powers are stripped before generating complete divisor lists; large smooth integers can therefore finish without scanning up to their square roots. Difficult remaining integer factors can still exhaust the search budget. These bounded searches fail explicitly rather than return unfinished factors. The big-integer implementation is vendored in src/vendor, compiled into ModernBASIC, and available to standalone compiled BASIC programs without a Python or external big-integer runtime.

10 P$="X^2*Y+Y^3"
20 PRINT SYMDIFF$(P$,"Y")
30 G=SYMGRAD(P$,"X,Y"):PRINT G(1),G(2)
40 H=SYMHESSIAN(P$,SYMVARS(P$)):PRINT H(1,2)
50 PRINT SYMSUBST$(P$,"X","Y+1")
60 PRINT SYMPROVE("(X+Y)*(X-Y)","X^2-Y^2")

Elementary symbolic calculus with domain conditions

A separate expression-tree API supports real elementary functions and general powers while retaining domain conditions through simplification and repeated differentiation. Bounded antiderivative rules use the same guarded result format. The polynomial APIs above retain their exact polynomial grammar.

FunctionResult
SYMDERIV(expression[,variable$]){formula$,{condition$...}} for a partial derivative, with sufficient real smooth-domain conditions. Defaults to variable X. Accepts a source string or a complete guarded symbolic result.
SYMREFINE(expression[,assumptions]){formula$,{condition$...}} simplified using bounded exact sign deductions and real identities. Accepts a string or guarded result; optional assumptions are one condition string or a list of condition strings. Assumptions remain attached to the result.
SYMANTIDERIV(expression[,variable$]){formula$,{condition$...}} for one antiderivative on its stated real domain. Defaults to X. Accepts a string or complete guarded result. Unsupported integrands raise an explicit error.
SYMPARTFRAC(expression[,variable$]){formula$,{condition$...}} for an exact univariate rational partial-fraction decomposition. Defaults to X; accepts a string or guarded result. Original domain restrictions survive cancellation.
SYMDEFINTEGRAL(expression,start,finish[,variable$])Exact symbolic proper integral of a supported rational function, after proving its source domain covers the closed interval. Returns a guarded pair usable with SYMEVAL.
SYMLIMIT(expression,point[,variable$[,side$]])Exact finite or infinite rational-function limit, with an algebraic witness and local domain flags. See below for the result format.
SYMLIMITCHECK(expression,point,result[,variable$[,side$]])Checks the limit witness and domain classification using exact polynomial identities.
SYMSERIES(expression,point,order[,variable$[,side$]])Rational Taylor/Laurent expansion, including an exact remainder and reusable guarded approximation.
SYMSERIESCHECK(expression,point,order,result[,variable$[,side$]])Checks all series coefficients together by polynomial multiplication and validates the returned approximation, remainder and guards.
SYMTAYLOR(expression,point,order[,variable$])Elementary-function Taylor polynomial with symbolic coefficients and retained source/center conditions.
SYMFACTOR(expression[,variable$]){formula$,{condition$...}} containing a complete factorization of a univariate rational-coefficient polynomial over the rationals, when the bounded exact algorithm finishes. Defaults to X; accepts a string or guarded result.
SYMDOMAIN(expression)List of conditions sufficient for evaluating a source string or guarded calculus result. These describe the supported real branches, not a solved set of intervals.
SYMEVAL(expression[,variables,values])Finite binary64 evaluation after checking its conditions. Pass a source string or a complete guarded symbolic result. With no bindings, every variable still needed by the formula or conditions must be absent.

Expressions accept integer literals, rational expressions such as 1/3, names, parentheses, unary signs, and + - * / ^. Multiplication must be explicit; decimal and exponent-format literals inside these symbolic expression strings are unsupported. The separate HPEVAL/HPBOUNDS interface below accepts them exactly. Powers associate to the right; -X^2 means -(X^2). Variable denominators and variable exponents are supported. PI and E are reserved constants in this API. Names are case-insensitive, ASCII alphanumeric, start with a letter, and have at most 32 characters. All trigonometric arguments are radians.

Supported functions are SIN, COS, TAN, EXP, LN, SQRT, SINH, COSH, TANH, ASIN, ACOS, ATAN, ASINH, ACOSH, ATANH, and ABS. LOG aliases natural logarithm LN, and SQR aliases SQRT. Differentiation uses chain, product, quotient, and general power rules. Rational coefficients stay exact; functions remain symbolic. SYMINT$ retains its polynomial-only contract; SYMANTIDERIV supplies the separate elementary integration rules below. The elementary rules follow the NIST DLMF formulas, including its trigonometric and inverse-function derivatives.

For bindings, variables is a comma-separated string such as "Y,X" or a list of name strings. values is a numeric list in that order; a scalar is accepted for a single variable. An empty string/list with an empty value list is allowed. Names must be distinct, and PI/E cannot be rebound. Unknown variables and mismatched lengths are errors. Integer bindings use the runtime's checked real conversion; real-valued bindings can contain decimal/exponent literals.

Conditions form a conjunction. They are expression strings ending in >0, >=0, or <>0. Inputs also accept <0, <=0, and =0; these are normalized to conditions on the subject or its negative. The right-hand side must be literal zero: write X-1>0 for a bound at one. The API keeps the original expression's restrictions even when simplification removes the restricted operation: the derivative of X/X has formula 0 and condition X<>0, and the derivative of 0*LN(X) retains X>0. Pass the entire result to SYMEVAL, SYMDERIV, or SYMANTIDERIV to preserve these conditions. Extracting only D(1) discards the original conditions.

OperationValue-domain conditionSufficient derivative-domain condition
a/u, negative integer powers of uu<>0Same
LN(u)u>0Same
SQRT(u)u>=0u>0
TAN(u)COS(u)<>0Same
ASIN(u), ACOS(u)1-u^2>=01-u^2>0
ACOSH(u)u-1>=0u-1>0
ATANH(u)1-u^2>0Same
ABS(u)None beyond the argument's domainu<>0
Noninteger or variable powers u^vu>0Same

Nonnegative constant integer powers allow any real base, with u^0=1, including 0^0. The domain of the original base and exponent expressions is still kept. Negative bases with noninteger or variable exponents are outside this real branch convention, even when a particular rational exponent could have a real root. All other operations retain the conditions of their arguments.

Derivative conditions are sufficient, not necessarily maximal. For example, SQRT(X^4) is differentiable at zero, but the conservative rule excludes that point; partial derivatives can also be restricted by an independent variable's boundary. The basic calculus rules do not solve inequalities, prove all conditions jointly satisfiable, or infer removable singularities. SYMREFINE adds the bounded reasoning described below. A condition that simplifies to a false rational constant is rejected; other conditions are checked on evaluation.

SYMEVAL and numerical condition checks use binary64 arithmetic, not formal proofs of domain membership near singularities. Intermediate overflow or an unrepresentable result raises an error; underflow may round to zero. The engine recognizes integer/half-integer multiples of PI built by rational arithmetic, including representable bound values, so known poles such as TAN(PI/2) and TAN(PI*(X+1)/2) at X=0 are rejected rather than evaluated at a rounded angle. This recognition does not cover every algebraically equivalent expression.

Each source/output expression is limited to 8192 bytes, each tree to 4096 nodes and 64 levels, parser nesting to 128 levels, and a call to eight variable names. There are at most 128 conditions and 65536 bytes of serialized conditions. Bounded arbitrary-precision rational coefficients and the shared one-million-step work budget apply to construction, simplification, differentiation, integration, and evaluation. Output is reparsed before return to ensure it remains usable within these limits. Resource failures and BREAK interrupt the operation without a partial result.

10 D=SYMDERIV("EXP(SIN(X^2))")
20 PRINT D(1),D(2)
30 PRINT SYMEVAL(D,"X",1)
40 L=SYMDERIV("LN(X)")
50 PRINT L
60 D2=SYMDERIV(L)
70 PRINT SYMEVAL(D2,"X",2)
80 PRINT SYMDOMAIN("SQRT(X)")

L contains formula (1/X) and condition X>0. Its second derivative evaluates to -0.25 at X=2; evaluating that complete result at a negative X is an error.

Exact limits and local series

SYMLIMIT and SYMSERIES accept univariate rational functions, as strings or guarded expression pairs. Their coefficients and conditions must reduce to rational expressions in the selected variable. The variable defaults to X. Parameters requiring additional assumptions, nonrational functions, oscillatory limits and fractional-power series are outside these two calls.

point is a BASIC integer, an exact rational constant string such as "1/3", or "+INF"/"-INF" ("INF" also means positive infinity). BASIC real values are rejected here to avoid silently rounding an exact center. At a finite point, side$ is "LEFT", "RIGHT", or the default "BOTH". At infinity use "BOTH"; the sign of infinity already selects the direction.

The limit result is:

{status$, value$, {numeratorCoefficients...}, {denominatorCoefficients...},
 {leftAllowed,rightAllowed}}

Coefficients and finite values are exact rational strings. Coefficients are in ascending powers of a local coordinate T: T=X-point at finite points and T=1/X at infinity. The two flags are BASIC booleans (-1 or 0) for small negative and positive T, respectively. The denominator witness is nonzero.

StatusMeaning
FINITEvalue$ is the exact rational limit.
+INF, -INFDivergence to the stated infinity. value$ is empty.
DNEBoth sides are allowed but their infinite limits disagree. value$ is empty.
OUTSIDE_DOMAINAt least one requested side has no allowed punctured neighborhood. value$ is empty.

BOTH requires both neighborhoods, even for a source restricted to one side. Use RIGHT for a right boundary or LEFT for a left boundary. Conditions are classified by the sign and parity of the first nonzero local rational coefficient. An equality that holds only at the center does not supply a neighborhood. Contradictions already reduced to false constants can raise a domain error during input validation. Other unsupported conditions raise an error instead of an undecided claim being labeled as a limit.

A limit can exist at an excluded point: (X^2-1)/(X-1) has limit 2 at 1. This operation does not change the original expression's domain. No numerical samples or floating-point comparisons decide these results. SYMLIMITCHECK verifies the witness by exact cross multiplication, checks the local conditions, and replays the leading-coefficient classification. Rational rescalings of a valid witness are accepted; a well-formed false claim returns 0.

SYMSERIES returns:

{approximation, firstExponent, order, {coefficients...}, exactRemainder,
 {leftAllowed,rightAllowed}}

approximation and exactRemainder are ordinary guarded expression pairs for use with SYMEVAL and other expression APIs. The series coefficients are exact rational strings, in ascending exponents from firstExponent through order. Negative exponents form the Laurent principal part. At infinity this is an expansion in 1/X. If the first nonzero term has exponent greater than order, the coefficient list is empty and the approximation is zero. The identically zero function uses first exponent zero and zero coefficients.

On the retained source domain, source = approximation + exactRemainder. The remainder has local order at least order+1. Rational functions have a convergent Laurent expansion in some sufficiently small punctured neighborhood; these calls do not calculate its convergence radius. The exact remainder can be evaluated directly when assessing approximation error. It retains source poles and is itself evaluated using ordinary binary64 arithmetic. A series is not a global identity between the source and its truncated approximation.

SYMSERIESCHECK checks the low coefficients of A-B*H, without repeating the producer's division recurrence, then verifies the canonical approximation, remainder, order and guard fields. Edited or incorrect records return 0; malformed data and resource exhaustion raise errors. Series construction requires every requested side to be allowed and raises an error otherwise.

The rational input layer retains its degree-32 intermediate bound. Series order is an integer from 0 through 32, with at most 65 Laurent coefficients. Exact remainder and certificate products may have degree up to 96. Records contain at most 65536 text bytes, individual strings at most 8192 bytes, and existing coefficient, expression-tree, guard and work budgets apply. A resource failure never returns a partial series, guessed limit or successful certificate.

10 L=SYMLIMIT("(X^2-1)/(X-1)",1)
20 PRINT L(1),L(2)
30 PRINT SYMLIMITCHECK("(X^2-1)/(X-1)",1,L)
40 PRINT SYMLIMIT("1/X",0,"X","LEFT")
50 S=SYMSERIES("1/(X^2*(1-X))",0,3)
60 PRINT S(2),S(4)
70 PRINT SYMEVAL(S(1),"X",0.1),SYMEVAL(S(5),"X",0.1)
80 PRINT SYMSERIESCHECK("1/(X^2*(1-X))",0,3,S)
90 PRINT SYMSERIES("(X^2+1)/(X-1)","+INF",3)

SYMTAYLOR additionally handles the supported real elementary functions and independent parameters, using exact symbolic differentiation and substitution. Its finite center must be an integer or rational string, and order is 0 through

  1. It returns {approximation,{coefficientExpressions...},center$,order}.

Coefficient k+1 is f^(k)(center)/k!, as an expression string; constants such as EXP(1/3) remain symbolic. The approximation is a guarded expression pair. This API provides a local Taylor polynomial, without an automatic error bound or convergence-radius claim. Use SYMSERIES for rational poles and exact remainders.

Taylor construction retains source restrictions, sufficient smooth-domain conditions, and those conditions evaluated at the center. For example, the expansion of LN(X+Y) at zero requires Y>0. Rationally false center conditions raise domain errors. Unresolved parameter or elementary-constant conditions stay attached and are checked by SYMEVAL; construction does not prove their joint satisfiability. An isolated equality in the selected variable cannot justify a Taylor expansion. Nonsmooth centers such as ABS(X) at zero are rejected by the conservative domain rules. Refinement may establish a wider smooth domain first. Existing expression/work limits can be reached before order 16 on complex compositions. Total result text is bounded to 65536 bytes.

10 T=SYMTAYLOR("SIN(X)",0,7)
20 PRINT T(2)
30 PRINT SYMEVAL(T(1),"X",0.2)
40 U=SYMTAYLOR("X^Y",1,3)
50 PRINT U(2)
60 PRINT SYMEVAL(U(1),"X,Y",{1.1,2.5})

Assumptions and real-expression refinement

SYMREFINE combines exact sign information from constants, sums, products, quotients, integer powers and selected elementary functions. It propagates conditions through negation, absolute values, powers, products/quotients with a known factor sign, and sign-preserving functions. Contradictions established by these deductions are errors; a successful result does not prove that every remaining condition can hold simultaneously. Unresolved expressions stay symbolic.

Examples:

InputRefined formulaRetained restriction
SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^2)")ABS(X)None
SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^4)")X^2None
SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^2)","X<0")-XX<0
SYMREFINE("ABS(X+Y)",{"X>=0","Y>=0"})X+YBoth assumptions
SYMREFINE("LN(EXP(X))")XNone
SYMREFINE("EXP(LN(X))")XX>0
SYMREFINE("X","X=0")0X=0

The identities include exact rational square roots, square roots of even powers, even powers of square roots/absolute values, and forward functions applied to their real inverse (SIN(ASIN(X)), for example). Reverse compositions such as ASIN(SIN(X)) are not generally identities. Square-root products split only when both factors are known nonnegative. Refinement retains source poles and function domains, even after cancellation. Only conditions proved structurally true without using the assumptions are discarded; a condition cannot prove itself away.

Calculus requires a neighborhood in the selected variable. When differentiating or integrating a guarded result, variable-dependent >=0 conditions become >0 unless structural sign reasoning already proves them everywhere nonnegative. This conservatively excludes uncertain boundaries. An equality such as X=0 cannot justify replacing X by zero and then reporting its derivative as zero: that calculus call is rejected. To obtain a derivative at a point, differentiate first, then refine/evaluate. Assumptions on independent parameters remain valid when differentiating another variable.

For example, SYMDERIV(SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^4)")) gives 2*X and is evaluable at zero. Refining an already guarded derivative preserves its stored exclusions. SYMDERIV(SYMREFINE("ABS(X)","X>=0")) excludes zero; it does not claim that ABS(X) is differentiable there.

This is conditional real algebra, not a general inequality/feasibility solver or complex branch engine. Numerical evaluation still has binary64 rounding, underflow and overflow limits; identities may avoid intermediate overflow that the original spelling would encounter. Refinement shares the expression, guard, variable, coefficient and work limits above, with at most 1024 internal sign facts. It uses the shared bounded arbitrary-precision coefficient arithmetic.

10 F=SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^2)","X<0")
20 PRINT F
30 PRINT SYMEVAL(F,"X",-3)
40 D=SYMDERIV(SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^4)"))
50 PRINT SYMEVAL(D,"X",0)
60 P=SYMREFINE(SYMDERIV("X"),"X=0")
70 PRINT SYMEVAL(P,"X",0)

Bounded real antiderivatives

SYMANTIDERIV returns one primitive F, with sufficient conditions under which its partial derivative equals the input integrand. It omits the arbitrary integration constant; in multiple variables this constant may be any function independent of the selected variable, separately on each connected domain component. It accepts and returns the same guarded pairs as SYMDERIV, allowing integration and differentiation to be composed without dropping restrictions.

Supported rules include:

PatternScope
Constants, sums, differences, polynomial expressionsConstants may be expressions in other variables. Products of polynomial sums can be expanded within limits.
Powers u^nConstant rational or parameter exponents independent of the integration variable. Uses u^(n+1)/(n+1); literal exponent -1 uses LN(ABS(u)).
a^uBase independent of the integration variable, on the existing positive-base branch, with LN(a)<>0.
Elementary functions of uAll 16 functions listed above, including inverse functions, logarithm and absolute value.
Reciprocal kernels1/(1+u^2), 1/(1-u^2), 1/(u^2-1), reciprocals of their square roots, 1/COS(u)^2, and 1/COSH(u)^2. Even integer powers can supply the squared inner expression.
SubstitutionThe remaining product must be an exact constant multiple of du/dx. Affine arguments are a special case.
Integration by partsA polynomial times EXP(a*x+b), SIN(a*x+b), or COS(a*x+b), where a and b are independent of x and a<>0.
Finite harmonic productsA polynomial times products of nonnegative integer powers of SIN(a*x+b) and COS(c*x+d), optionally multiplied by affine exponentials. Arguments may have different slopes and offsets. Integer powers and reciprocals of affine exponentials are combined exactly.

Rational combinations of SIN(u), COS(u) and TAN(u) with a common affine argument also use T=TAN(u/2). Rational combinations of EXP(u), SINH(u), COSH(u) and TANH(u) with a common affine argument use T=EXP(u). The transformed rational integrand includes the exact Jacobian and passes through the same bounded partial-fraction integrator. Its coefficients must be rational, and its denominator must have supported linear/quadratic rational factors. Negative function powers and denominators such as 2+COS(X) are supported.

Affine slopes and offsets may contain independent parameters. A symbolic slope is retained as a nonzero condition; a zero-slope parameter case requires separate simplification. Different recognized affine arguments, non-affine arguments, mixed circular/exponential kernels and unsupported transformed factors are rejected. Circular results retain the additional chart restriction COS(u/2)<>0. The primitive is valid separately on the resulting connected components; it is not claimed to be a single continuous global primitive across chart boundaries. Original integrand poles remain excluded after cancellation.

Here u can be a composite expression. The matcher combines rational coefficients and commutative products with integer powers. Sums and function arguments remain structural atoms in the substitution matcher. The harmonic product rule uses exact finite exponential identities for sine and cosine; it does not search arbitrary trigonometric identities or decide general equivalence. A mathematically equivalent spelling can therefore fall outside the supported patterns. No numerical sampling is used to choose an integration rule.

Examples include 2*X*COS(X^2), COS(X)*EXP(SIN(X)), X/(1+X^2), X/(1+X^4), (X+1)*(X+2), X^2*SIN(2*X), EXP(X)*SIN(X), X^2*EXP(-X)*COS(3*X), and SIN(X)^4*COS(2*X)^2. Bounded rational partial fractions extend these rules as described below. Arbitrary elementary products, special-function primitives, and general integration algorithms are not implemented: EXP(X^2), SIN(X^2), X^X, and 1/(X^3+X+1) produce an unsupported-integral error. This error does not assert that an antiderivative fails to exist.

Source smooth-domain conditions are collected before simplification, and the primitive's smooth-domain conditions are added afterward. These conditions are conservative, just as for SYMDERIV: boundary points may be excluded even when a primitive exists there. Generated parameter denominators must be nonzero. For example, SIN(Y*X) produces a primitive restricted to Y<>0; substitute a literal zero into the source to integrate that exceptional branch. X^Y excludes Y=-1, which is handled by the explicit source X^(-1). Numerical evaluation retains the binary64 accuracy and intermediate-overflow limitations above.

The harmonic rule uses exact rational coefficients, checks conjugate pairing, and solves the polynomial coefficient equations for each real sine/cosine pair. Zero rates and frequencies recognized by exact structural algebra use a separate polynomial primitive. For symbolic exponential rate a and harmonic frequency b, a nonconstant pair requires a^2+b^2<>0. Either rate may individually be zero. If parameter values make both zero, substitute those values into the source and integrate that branch separately. The result does not automatically contain piecewise parameter cases. Rate normalization combines rational multiples of identical products; it is not a general assumption solver.

The primitive of 1/X uses LN(ABS(X)), valid on either side of zero. Integrating the guarded derivative of LN(X) retains its original condition X>0. SYMANTIDERIV does not check continuity over an interval; subtracting endpoint values alone does not check for intervening poles or domain gaps. Use SYMDEFINTEGRAL for supported proper rational integrals as described below. Improper integrals remain unsupported.

The additional limits are 128 distinct multiplicative atoms, degree 64 for polynomial expansion, and degree 16 for the integration-by-parts or harmonic polynomial. Harmonic expansion additionally limits the total sine/cosine power to 16 and intermediate complex harmonic terms to 128. Trigonometric reciprocals, fractional powers and non-affine arguments are outside this additional rule; some remain supported by the earlier substitution/reciprocal rules. The shared expression-size, output, coefficient and work limits still apply and can be reached before those degree limits. All-or-error behavior applies to sums as well: no partially integrated result is returned.

The elementary primitives can be checked by differentiation; references include the NIST DLMF sections on logarithmic and exponential integrals, trigonometric integrals, and hyperbolic integrals.

10 F=SYMANTIDERIV("2*X*EXP(X^2)")
20 PRINT F
30 PRINT SYMEVAL(SYMDERIV(F),"X",1)
40 L=SYMANTIDERIV("1/X")
50 PRINT SYMEVAL(L,"X",-2)
60 PRINT SYMANTIDERIV("X^2*SIN(2*X)")

Rational functions and partial fractions

SYMPARTFRAC decomposes a rational function into a polynomial part and proper fractions with linear or quadratic denominators, including repeated factors. After elementary simplification, the formula must use only rational coefficients, the selected variable, + - * /, and constant integer powers. Other variables are not treated as symbolic coefficients by this rational layer. Existing conditions in a guarded input are retained even if they involve other variables.

For example, (X^2+3*X+5)/(X+1) decomposes into X+2+3/(X+1). All coefficients, GCDs, divisions and the coefficient-system solve use checked exact rational arithmetic. The implementation recombines the result and checks the exact numerator identity before returning it. This follows the usual partial-fraction method, with polynomial division first for improper fractions.

Denominator discovery uses square-free decomposition, written linear/quadratic subexpressions checked by exact GCDs, bounded rational-root search, and exact quadratic-factor discovery over the rationals. The quadratic search specializes the Kronecker divisibility/interpolation method: it clears denominators and content, enumerates possible integer leading coefficients and values at two integer points, interpolates candidates, and checks divisibility by exact polynomial division. All factor multiplicities are verified by multiplying the factors back together before partial fractions. Quadratics with rational roots are split into linear factors; other quadratics remain intact, including those with irrational real roots.

Thus 1/(X^4+5*X^2+4) and 1/((X^2+1)*(X^2+4)) are both supported, as are expanded products with nonmonic rational factors and repeated factors. Subject to the limits below, discovery covers denominators whose irreducible factors over the rationals all have degree one or two. Factors of higher degree remain unsupported: for example, 1/(X^4+1) cannot be decomposed by this layer, even though it has quadratic factors over an algebraic extension of the rationals. Output grouping can depend on the written factors.

SYMANTIDERIV automatically uses this rational layer when the earlier elementary rules do not apply. It integrates repeated linear factors using powers and LN(ABS(...)). Quadratic fractions split into a logarithmic derivative and a reciprocal-quadratic primitive, using ATAN or real logarithms according to the exact discriminant sign. Higher powers of quadratics use a finite recurrence. Square roots of rational constants remain symbolic where needed; no approximate root finding chooses a factor or an integration formula.

Original restrictions are collected before rational cancellation. Thus the decomposition of (X^2-1)/(X-1) has formula equivalent to X+1 but still rejects X=1. Keep the complete guarded result when composing SYMPARTFRAC, SYMANTIDERIV, SYMDERIV, and SYMEVAL. Rational identity does not imply that two original expressions have identical domains. Numerical evaluation retains the binary64 limitations above, particularly near poles and when large terms cancel; the exact decomposition does not promise uniformly accurate evaluation.

This layer limits intermediate numerator/denominator degree to 32, reduced denominator degree to 16, and the magnitude of integer powers to 32. It stores at most 64 distinct small-factor hints and 2048 divisors per integer coefficient or sampled value used by factor search. Integer factorization uses exact trial division with repeated prime-power removal; primality is never assumed from a probabilistic test. Trial division, interpolation, candidate evaluation, GCDs and coefficient solving share the one-million-step work budget. Big-integer operations also consume the shared 32-million-unit coefficient budget. Large coefficient factor searches can exhaust either budget even at small degree. The existing 4096-bit coefficient, expression-size and guard limits apply. These additional limits belong to the rational layer; previously supported elementary rules retain their own limits. Unsupported factors and resource exhaustion return errors; an exhausted search is not reported as proof of irreducibility. Explicitly writing factors can avoid expensive discovery even when the expanded spelling exhausts the budget.

10 A=SYMPARTFRAC("(3*X+2)/(X^3-X^2-2*X)")
20 PRINT A
30 F=SYMANTIDERIV("(X+2)/(X^2+2*X+3)^3")
40 PRINT F
50 PRINT SYMEVAL(SYMDERIV(F),"X",1)
60 PRINT SYMPARTFRAC("(X^2-1)/(X-1)")

Exact polynomial factorization over the rationals

SYMFACTOR factors a polynomial into its rational leading coefficient and monic irreducible factors over Q, with repeated factors represented by integer powers. Factor order is unspecified. Zero and constant inputs return their constant formula; zero is not assigned an irreducible factorization. For example, X^8+3*X^4+2 factors into (X^4+1)*(X^4+2). Both quartics are irreducible over Q. Likewise X^2-2 stays quadratic: factorization over real, complex, or algebraic-number coefficient domains is outside this call.

After elementary simplification and exact rational cancellation, the input must be a polynomial in the selected variable with rational coefficients. Other variables are not symbolic coefficients. The complete guarded result can be stored in a BASIC variable and passed to SYMEVAL, SYMDERIV, SYMANTIDERIV, or SYMFACTOR again. Original and inherited conditions survive cancellation: factoring (X^6-1)/(X^3-1) still excludes X=1. Preserve the complete result when composing calls; extracting just F(1) discards its conditions.

The algorithm uses exact square-free decomposition, small-factor discovery, and bounded Kronecker interpolation/divisibility search through every possible proper factor degree. A successful Rabin finite-field irreducibility test at one of the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, or 13 can prove a factor irreducible over Q without exhaustive search or a potentially expensive square-free GCD. Reductions that lose degree are skipped; inconclusive modular tests fall back to exact search. Every returned product, including its multiplicities, is checked against the original monic polynomial by exact multiplication. Euclidean GCD remainders are normalized to reduce intermediate coefficient growth.

This API limits the polynomial degree after cancellation to 16, intermediate rational-polynomial degree to 32, and remaining integer power magnitudes to 32. It shares the bounded arbitrary-precision rational arithmetic, 64 small-factor hints, 2048 divisors per sampled integer, one-million-step work budget, and expression/guard limits described above. Search can be expensive even at modest degree; degree 16 is a ceiling, not a promise that every input up to that degree succeeds. Coefficient overflow, work exhaustion, and other limits raise errors, without returning a partial product or asserting that an unsearched residual is irreducible. These limits also apply to explicitly written products.

Factoring a denominator into higher-degree irreducibles does not extend the linear/quadratic denominator restriction of SYMPARTFRAC or the rational antiderivative rules.

10 F=SYMFACTOR("X^8+3*X^4+2")
20 PRINT F
30 PRINT SYMEVAL(F,"X",2)
40 PRINT SYMEVAL(SYMDERIV(F),"X",2)
50 PRINT SYMFACTOR("(Y^3+Y+1)^3","Y")

Exact multivariate division, ideals, and proof certificates

These calls work over rational-coefficient polynomials with the same fixed graded lexicographic order as SYMSIMPLIFY$: total degree first, then powers of alphabetically ordered variable names. For lexicographic elimination use the separate SYMELIMINATE family below. These calls do not solve for numerical roots.

FunctionResult
SYMDIVMULTI(expr$,divisors){{quotient$...},remainder$} satisfying expr = sum(quotient(i)*divisor(i)) + remainder. Uses divisors in the supplied order; zero divisors are errors.
SYMGROEBNER(generators)List of strings forming the monic reduced Gröbner basis, ordered by descending leading monomial. Zero and redundant generators are removed.
SYMREDUCE$(expr$,generators)Canonical normal form after completing the generators to a Gröbner basis.
SYMIDEALMEMBER(expr$,generators)-1 when the polynomial belongs to the generated ideal, otherwise 0, after a successful exact computation.
SYMIDEALCERT(expr$,generators){{multiplier$...},remainder$} expressing the input as a combination of the original generators plus its canonical normal form. Multipliers retain the original generator order, including zero and duplicate entries.
SYMIDEALCHECK(expr$,generators,multipliers)-1 exactly when expr = sum(multiplier(i)*generator(i)). A valid but incorrect certificate returns 0; malformed input, mismatched counts, or exceeded limits raise errors.

generators, divisors, and multipliers accept a semicolon-separated string, such as "X*Y-1;Y^2-1", or a list of polynomial strings returned by another call. An empty string or empty list denotes an empty collection. Empty entries inside a nonempty string are errors. BASIC brace literals also accept polynomial strings, for example {"X*Y-1","Y^2-1"}, and nested certificate lists. A relation such as X=Y is supplied as the polynomial X-Y, whose value is assumed to be zero.

Multivariate division by an arbitrary list has an order-dependent remainder. A nonzero remainder from SYMDIVMULTI does not establish nonmembership. Use SYMREDUCE$ or SYMIDEALMEMBER for that decision; both complete the basis first. The zero ideal has an empty basis and leaves every input unchanged. A basis containing a nonzero constant reduces to {1} and every polynomial belongs to that ideal. These conventions also apply to empty and all-zero generator lists.

Basis construction uses bounded Buchberger completion and reduced-basis normalization, with polynomial witnesses propagated back to the original input. The certificate checker is separate: it only multiplies, adds, and compares exact coefficients. It neither constructs a Gröbner basis nor trusts the search's membership decision. The certificate remainder must be zero to prove membership; for a nonzero remainder, the multipliers prove membership of expr-remainder. See the algebraic basis and membership criterion.

This proves polynomial-combination identities, not arbitrary mathematical statements or all consequences of equations. For example, X does not belong to the ideal generated by X^2, even though X^2=0 implies X=0 over the real or complex numbers. A negative ideal-membership result is not a counterexample to such a logical implication. Radical ideals, inequalities, integer arithmetic, factorization, and general theorem proving are outside these calls. Use the separate radical-membership functions below for polynomial consequences over all complex solutions.

In addition to the shared symbolic limits, collections and retained intermediate bases allow at most 32 polynomials. Input collections and retained basis/proof collections are limited to 8192 terms; polynomial string collections are limited to 65536 bytes, with the usual 8192-byte limit on each expression. Intermediate bases count before redundant elements are removed. Certificate growth can reach a limit even when the final reduced basis would be small. The one-million-step budget includes proof construction, and every long reduction checks BREAK. Any arithmetic, degree, storage, or work-limit failure raises an error; no partial basis or unverified membership answer is returned.

10 G$="X*Y-1;Y^2-1"
20 B=SYMGROEBNER(G$):PRINT B
30 PRINT SYMREDUCE$("X^2-1",B)
40 C=SYMIDEALCERT("X^2-1",G$)
50 PRINT C(1),C(2)
60 PRINT SYMIDEALCHECK("X^2-1",G$,C(1))
70 PRINT SYMIDEALCHECK("X^2",G$,C(1))

The basis is {Y^2-1,X-Y}. The normal form and certificate remainder are zero. The original certificate checks successfully (-1); changing the target to X^2 makes that same certificate fail (0).

Exact polynomial elimination and completeness certificates

These functions remove selected variables from an ideal of rational polynomials. They return a monic reduced basis for the elimination ideal: every polynomial combination of the input equations that contains only retained variables. generators accepts a semicolon-separated string or a list of polynomial strings, as above. eliminateVariables accepts a comma-separated string or a list of distinct variable names. Names are case-insensitive and follow the multivariate polynomial identifier rules. An empty string or {} removes no variables. Names absent from the generators are allowed and count toward the variable limit.

FunctionResult
SYMELIMINATE(generators,eliminateVariables)List of polynomial strings forming the reduced elimination basis.
SYMELIMCERT(generators,eliminateVariables){eliminationBasis,fullLexBasis,{proofRow...}}. Each row contains one polynomial multiplier per original generator and proves fullLexBasis(i) = sum(proofRow(i,j)*generator(j)). Zero and duplicate generator slots are retained.
SYMELIMCHECK(generators,eliminateVariables,certificate)-1 for a verified complete certificate, 0 for a well-formed incorrect claim. Malformed shape, mismatched dimensions, arithmetic overflow and exceeded resource limits raise errors.

The order is pure lexicographic, with eliminated variables first in the supplied order, then all remaining generator variables alphabetically. Basis entries are sorted by descending leading monomial in this order. Text within each polynomial retains the usual graded-lex rendering, so its first printed term need not be its lexicographic leading term. For example, eliminating X from X^2-Y;X-Z returns {-Z^2+Y}; the lexicographic leading term is Y. Passing no elimination variables returns the complete lexicographic basis. The order and signatures of SYMGROEBNER and the existing ideal functions are unchanged.

The checker first requires a nonzero, monic, sorted, reduced full basis. Exact proof identities show that each basis polynomial belongs to the original ideal. It then reduces every original generator to zero, establishing the reverse inclusion, and verifies that every required S-polynomial reduces to zero by Buchberger's criterion. The product criterion skips pairs with relatively prime leading monomials. Finally, the elimination list must equal precisely the full basis entries free of eliminated variables. This verifies completeness using bounded division and exact arithmetic; it does not run basis completion or trust a partial list of consequences. See the elimination theorem. Both producing functions perform this check before returning a result.

This is elimination of polynomial ideals, not real quantifier elimination or a decision about whether every projected point lifts to a solution. For example, eliminating X from X*Y-1 returns {}, although Y=0 has no corresponding solution. Eliminating X from X^2+1 also returns {}, without asserting that a real root exists. Removing an unrelated variable from X^2 leaves {X^2}; the operation does not take radicals. A unit ideal returns {1}, even when all variables are removed; an empty or all-zero ideal returns {}.

Limits are degree 64, eight variables, 2048 terms per polynomial, 32 input and retained intermediate basis polynomials, 8192 aggregate terms in a retained basis/proof collection or complete certificate, 8192 bytes per polynomial, and 65536 bytes across the entire certificate. Coefficients use checked signed bounded arbitrary-precision rational arithmetic. The one-million-step budget includes construction and verification, with BREAK checkpoints. Lexicographic reduction can increase total degree, so inputs below the degree ceiling can still exceed an intermediate limit. Both producers enforce complete-certificate bounds, even when only the elimination list is requested. An exceeded limit raises an error and never returns a partial basis. The checker rejects nonzero polynomial variables outside the input ring (generator variables together with the elimination variables).

10 G={"X-T^2","Y-T^3"}
20 C=SYMELIMCERT(G,"T")
30 PRINT C(1)
40 PRINT SYMELIMCHECK(G,"T",C)
50 P={{"Y-Z^2"},{"X-Z","Y-Z^2"},{{"0","1"},{"-1","X+Z"}}}
60 PRINT SYMELIMCHECK("X^2-Y;X-Z","X",P)

The curve basis is {X^3-Y^2}. Both the generated certificate and the separately written certificate verify as -1.

Exact radical membership and algebraic consequences

SYMRADICALMEMBER(expr$,generators) decides whether some positive integer power of the query polynomial belongs to the ideal generated by the supplied polynomials. For rational coefficients, this is equivalent to the query vanishing at every common complex zero of the generators. Each generator is interpreted as an equation with value zero. Collections use the same semicolon-string or polynomial-string-list format as the ideal APIs above.

FunctionResult
SYMRADICALMEMBER(expr$,generators)-1 for radical membership and 0 for nonmembership after a completed, verified computation.
SYMRADICALCERT(expr$,generators){status$,auxiliary$,fullLexBasis,{proofRow...}}, where status is "MEMBER" or "NONMEMBER".
SYMRADICALCHECK(expr$,generators,certificate)-1 if the supplied certificate correctly proves its stated status, including "NONMEMBER"; 0 for a well-formed incorrect claim. Malformed input and exceeded limits raise errors.

For example, SYMIDEALMEMBER("X","X^2") returns 0, whereas SYMRADICALMEMBER("X","X^2") returns -1: X^2=0 forces X=0 over the complex numbers. The zero polynomial always belongs to the radical, the zero ideal contains no nonzero query, and inconsistent equations whose ideal contains 1 imply every query polynomial vanishes on their empty solution set.

This is the ordinary algebraic radical, not the real radical. For example, SYMRADICALMEMBER("X","X^2+Y^2") returns 0, although the real equation X^2+Y^2=0 forces X=Y=0. Also, SYMRADICALMEMBER("1","X^2+1") returns 0: there are complex solutions even though there are no real ones. A negative result does not assert a real counterexample, provide counterexample coordinates, or decide inequalities. These functions decide membership of a query; they do not return generators for the radical ideal or prove arbitrary logical statements.

Certificates use the Rabinowitsch criterion. For a fresh auxiliary variable T, extend the original generators F by the single polynomial 1-T*expr. The query belongs to the radical exactly when this augmented ideal has the reduced basis {1}. Every proof row supplies multipliers for the original generators in their original order, including zero/duplicate slots, followed by one multiplier for 1-T*expr. The row must reproduce its full basis polynomial exactly. Thus a positive certificate directly proves an identity 1 = sum(multiplier(j)*F(j)) + lastMultiplier*(1-T*expr).

The complete basis uses pure lexicographic order with the auxiliary variable first, followed by original/query variables alphabetically. Polynomial text retains the usual graded-lex rendering. Generated auxiliary names are MBRAD, MBRAD1, etc., choosing the first unused name. A supplied certificate may use any valid fresh variable name; names are case-insensitive. Even names canceled out of the original expressions count as used. Proof polynomials cannot introduce additional nonzero variables outside this fixed ring.

The checker verifies monic sorted reduced form, exact proof identities, reverse ideal inclusion and Buchberger's criterion, without running completion. It then requires {1} for "MEMBER" and a nonunit complete basis for "NONMEMBER". An incomplete set of valid consequences cannot certify nonmembership. Both producing APIs verify the complete certificate before returning a decision.

There are at most seven distinct input variables and 31 original generators, reserving one variable and one generator for the criterion. These reservations apply even for constant queries and unit ideals. Nonzero query degree is at most 63 so 1-T*expr fits degree 64; original generators and all intermediates have degree at most 64. Proof growth can exceed this limit even for small inputs. The remaining limits are bounded arbitrary-precision rationals, 2048 terms per polynomial, 32 retained basis polynomials, 8192 aggregate terms in a retained basis/proof collection, 8192 bytes per polynomial, 65536 bytes across the complete certificate (including status/name), and one million work steps shared by construction and verification, with BREAK checkpoints. No output is returned when a limit is exceeded, and a failed search is never interpreted as nonmembership. The boolean API enforces the same certificate limits.

10 PRINT SYMRADICALMEMBER("X","X^2")
20 C=SYMRADICALCERT("X+Y","X^2;Y^3")
30 PRINT C(1)
40 PRINT SYMRADICALCHECK("X+Y","X^2;Y^3",C)
50 P={"MEMBER","T",{"1"},{{"T^2","1+T*X"}}}
60 PRINT SYMRADICALCHECK("X","X^2",P)
70 N={"NONMEMBER","T",{"T*Y-1","X^2"},{{"0","-1"},{"1","0"}}}
80 PRINT SYMRADICALCHECK("Y","X^2",N)

The membership decision is -1, the generated status is MEMBER, and all three certificate checks return -1. The separately written positive certificate uses 1 = T^2*X^2 + (1+T*X)*(1-T*X).

Polynomial implications with nonzero assumptions

These calls decide whether a rational polynomial query must vanish whenever a list of polynomial equations holds and every supplied nonzero condition holds. The domain is complex numbers, as with radical membership. equations and nonzero each accept a semicolon-separated string or a list of polynomial strings. Equations mean F(i)=0; conditions mean H(i)<>0. Empty strings or lists impose no conditions of that type. Supply the query X-Y to ask whether X=Y follows; comparison operators are not part of the polynomial grammar.

FunctionResult
SYMIMPLIES(expr$,equations,nonzero)-1 when the query is zero at every complex point satisfying the assumptions; 0 otherwise, after a completed verified computation.
SYMIMPLYCERT(expr$,equations,nonzero){status$,auxiliary$,fullLexBasis,{proofRow...}}, with status "IMPLIED" or "NOTIMPLIED".
SYMIMPLYCHECK(expr$,equations,nonzero,certificate)-1 if the supplied certificate correctly proves its status, including "NOTIMPLIED"; 0 for a well-formed incorrect claim. Malformed input or exceeded limits raise errors.

For example, SYMIMPLIES("X","X*Y","Y") returns -1: if X*Y=0 and Y<>0, then X=0. Removing the nonzero assumption returns 0, because the equation also permits Y=0 with nonzero X. Conditions are conjoined, so "Y;Z" requires both Y<>0 and Z<>0. Repeated factors, constant conditions, zero/duplicate equations, and rational coefficients are supported. With an empty nonzero list the decision agrees with SYMRADICALMEMBER within the documented resource limits.

An implication is true when its assumptions have no solutions. In particular, a zero polynomial in nonzero makes every query vacuously implied. So do contradictions such as X=0 together with X<>0. An IMPLIED certificate does not assert that the assumptions are consistent. To test inconsistency over the complex numbers, use the query "1": a successful -1 means the assumptions have no complex solution; 0 means at least one complex solution exists. The API does not return solution coordinates. It does not decide implications restricted to real numbers: SYMIMPLIES("X","X^2+Y^2","Y") returns 0, even though those assumptions have no real solution. Strict signs, ordered inequalities, disjunctions, integer domains and arbitrary quantified logic are unsupported.

The implementation forms P = expr * product(nonzero), where the empty product is 1, then applies the radical criterion above to P. This is valid because over a field a product is nonzero exactly when each factor is nonzero. The certificate proves completeness of the augmented ideal <equations, 1-T*P>, using a fresh auxiliary variable T. A proof row contains one multiplier for each original equation, including zero and duplicate slots, followed by one multiplier for 1-T*P. Nonzero assumptions are incorporated into P; they do not have individual multiplier slots. Every row must reproduce its corresponding full-basis polynomial exactly.

The independent checker verifies both ideal inclusions, monic sorted reduced form and Buchberger's criterion without completing a basis. It requires the unit basis {1} for IMPLIED and a complete nonunit basis for NOTIMPLIED. A partial set of valid consequences cannot certify a negative result. Both producing APIs perform the same check before returning. A negative decision establishes a complex counterexample exists, without asserting a real counterexample exists.

The auxiliary name is generated as MBIMPL, MBIMPL1, etc., avoiding all names in the query, equations and conditions, including canceled names. Supplied certificates may choose any valid fresh name. The lexicographic variable order places that name first and all remaining names alphabetically. Polynomial text retains graded-lex rendering. Certificates can be reused for condition permutations when the product is unchanged; equivalent assumptions do not necessarily produce identical certificates.

Limits are seven distinct input variables, 31 equations and 32 nonzero conditions. The parsed query/equation/condition collection has at most 8192 terms in total. Each input and intermediate polynomial is limited to degree 64 and 2048 terms; the nonzero combined polynomial P must have degree at most 63 to leave room for T. Thus individually small factors may still exceed the product limit. Every input is parsed and counted before handling a zero query or zero condition; such a zero avoids unnecessary multiplication of the other factors. One auxiliary variable and one equation slot remain reserved even in these cases. The existing 32-polynomial basis limit, bounded arbitrary-precision rationals, 8192 retained certificate terms, 8192 bytes per polynomial, 65536 total certificate text bytes and shared one-million-step budget apply. Product construction and verification both consume the budget and check BREAK. Failures raise errors and never return NOTIMPLIED or a partial proof. The boolean API enforces complete-certificate output limits.

10 PRINT SYMIMPLIES("X","X*Y","Y")
20 PRINT SYMIMPLIES("X","X*Y",{})
30 C=SYMIMPLYCERT("X-Y","(X-Y)^2*Z","Z")
40 PRINT C(1)
50 PRINT SYMIMPLYCHECK("X-Y","(X-Y)^2*Z","Z",C)
60 P={"IMPLIED","T",{"1"},{{"T","1"}}}
70 PRINT SYMIMPLYCHECK("X","X*Y","Y",P)
80 PRINT SYMIMPLIES("1","X*Y","X;Y")

The decisions on lines 10 and 20 are -1 and 0. Both certificates verify as -1. The final decision is -1 because its assumptions are inconsistent.

Exact sums of squares and real polynomial certificates

These functions use exact rational polynomial strings in up to eight real variables. They provide global nonnegativity witnesses and check polynomial inequalities under real assumptions. Comparison operators, elementary functions, variable denominators and complex coefficients are outside the grammar.

FunctionResult
SYMSOS(expr$)Constructs a weighted sum-of-squares certificate for a globally nonnegative polynomial of total degree at most two, subject to resource limits. Raises an error for a quadratic that takes negative values, higher degree, or exhausted limits.
SYMSOSCHECK(expr$,certificate)-1 if the supplied weighted squares reproduce the target exactly and every weight is nonnegative; 0 for a well-formed invalid proof. Supports higher-degree supplied proofs.
SYMREALCHECK(expr$,inequalities,equations,certificate)-1 if the supplied certificate proves expr>=0 whenever every inequality G(i)>=0 and equation F(j)=0 holds. Returns 0 for a well-formed invalid proof.

An SOS certificate is a list of pairs {{weight$,polynomial$},...} representing sum(weight(i)*polynomial(i)^2). Both entries are strings; weights must be exact rational constant expressions with no variable tokens, even canceled ones. Nonnegative rational weights avoid introducing irrational square roots. Zero weights are accepted, but their polynomial entries are still parsed and counted. The empty certificate {} represents zero. Supplied proofs can use repeated squares and need not match the constructor's choice of decomposition. A negative weight invalidates a proof even when its polynomial is zero or another row would cancel it.

SYMSOS builds the augmented Gram matrix on 1 and the variables, then completes squares with exact rational Schur complements. Zero pivots require a zero remaining row, so singular nonnegative forms are supported. The constant and linear terms participate in the test: a positive-semidefinite Hessian by itself does not establish global nonnegativity. The returned proof is expanded and checked before return; the separate checker only expands supplied identities and does not rerun construction. No floating-point tolerance or sampling is used. Construction is limited to quadratics, even for obvious higher-degree squares.

For SYMREALCHECK, each assumption collection is a semicolon-separated string or list of polynomial strings; an empty string or list means no assumptions of that type. Inequalities are always interpreted as greater than or equal to zero. Preserve zero, duplicate and original-order constraint slots. The certificate has three elements:

{freeSOS,{inequalitySOS1,...},{equationMultiplier1$,...}}

The checker verifies the exact identity

expr = freeSOS + sum(inequalitySOS(i)*G(i)) + sum(equationMultiplier(j)*F(j)).

Here each SOS denotes its expanded weighted squares. There must be one SOS certificate per original inequality and one arbitrary polynomial multiplier string per original equation. Equation multipliers may have either sign. No assumptions are silently added or removed. This is a sufficient proof format; the checker does not search for a certificate or decide whether every true inequality has a certificate in this form. The underlying SOS/Gram and real algebraic certificate constructions are described in Parrilo's Sum of Squares Programs and Polynomial Inequalities.

Use the target objective-bound to certify a lower bound, or bound-objective for an upper bound. This proves a bound only; it does not produce a feasible optimizer or prove attainment. An accepted target -1 proves the assumptions have no real solution. Other accepted targets may hold vacuously on an empty feasible set. A rejected certificate says nothing about whether the target is actually nonnegative. Nonnegative multivariate polynomials need not be sums of squares; there is no general SDP search, real quantifier elimination, strict-sign reasoning, integer-domain reasoning or completeness claim here.

Limits apply to the whole request: eight distinct variable tokens (including canceled variables), 32 inequalities, 32 equations, 128 square rows across all SOS groups, 8192 parsed terms across target/assumptions/certificate and 65536 combined input text bytes. Each polynomial string is limited to 8192 bytes and each polynomial/intermediate to 2048 terms and total degree 64. Square bases have degree at most 32, including bases with zero weight. Products with nonlinear constraints can exceed the degree or intermediate limits even when each input fits. Bounded arbitrary-precision rational arithmetic and one shared million-step work budget apply to parsing, construction, expansion and checking, with BREAK checkpoints. Malformed shapes, wrong slot counts, unsupported input, coefficient overflow or exceeded limits raise errors. A false checker result is never used to report an exhausted computation. All supplied entries are parsed and counted before rejecting negative weights; invalid weights need not be expanded.

10 P$="(X-Y+1)^2+Y^2/3"
20 S=SYMSOS(P$)
30 PRINT SYMSOSCHECK(P$,S)
40 H={{"1/3","X^2-Y^2"},{"2","X*Y-1"}}
50 PRINT SYMSOSCHECK("(X^2-Y^2)^2/3+2*(X*Y-1)^2",H)
60 C={SYMSOS("Y^2"),{SYMSOS("1")},{}}
70 PRINT SYMREALCHECK("1-X^2","1-X^2-Y^2",{},C)
80 D={SYMSOS("X^2"),{},{"-1"}}
90 PRINT SYMREALCHECK("-1",{},"X^2+1",D)

All four checks return -1. Line 70 proves X^2<=1 on the unit disk; line 90 proves X^2+1=0 has no real solution.

Proper definite integrals of rational functions

SYMDEFINTEGRAL(expression,start,finish[,variable$]) returns the guarded pair {valueExpression$,conditions}. The integrand is a univariate rational expression or an existing guarded pair; coefficients are exact rationals. Endpoints are BASIC integers or exact rational-expression strings, such as "1/3". The variable defaults to "X". Other free parameters, binary64 endpoint values, algebraic endpoints and infinite endpoints are unsupported.

Before constructing the result, the engine proves that every original domain condition holds on the entire closed interval between the endpoints. This includes denominator conditions collected before cancellation and any supplied rational inequalities/equalities. Exact Sturm root counts handle endpoint, interior, repeated and irrational roots. Square-free sign certificates establish nonnegative conditions, including conditions that touch zero. Each internal certificate is checked by polynomial identities. No sampling or floating-point root estimates establish the domain.

Only then does the bounded rational integrator produce a real primitive and subtract its endpoint values. Its denominator factors must be supported rational linear/quadratic factors; logarithms use absolute values, and quadratic terms use real arctangents or logarithms. The rational primitive's variable singularities are roots already excluded by the domain check. Circular half-angle substitution primitives are not used here because their extra chart boundaries need separate handling. Constant radical/logarithm conditions from the final expression remain in its guarded pair. SYMEVAL produces the ordinary binary64 approximation.

10 A=SYMDEFINTEGRAL("X^2",0,1)
20 PRINT A(1)
30 B=SYMDEFINTEGRAL("1/(X^2+1)",-1,1)
40 PRINT SYMEVAL(B)
50 C=SYMDEFINTEGRAL("1/X",1,2)
60 PRINT C(1)

The first result is exact 1/3, the second evaluates to PI/2, and the third is an exact logarithmic expression. Reversing endpoints negates the integral. Equal endpoints return zero only after validating the source domain at that point; no factor search is required in this case.

SYMDEFINTEGRAL("1/X",-1,1) is an error, even though subtracting the finite endpoint values of LN(ABS(X)) would produce zero. Likewise, 1/(X^2-2) on [1,2] is rejected because of the irrational pole, and (X^2-1)/(X-1) on [0,2] is rejected because its original source excludes X=1. The latter has an integrable continuous extension, but choosing that extension is a separate explicit operation. This API does not compute improper integrals, principal values, removable-hole extensions, elementary nonrational integrals or piecewise/parameter case splits. Domain failure, unsupported input and resource exhaustion are errors; none returns a partial integral.

The existing degree-32 rational input, degree-16 factorized denominator, 4096-bit normalized coefficient, expression, guard, output and shared work limits apply. Exact symbolic output does not remove binary64 cancellation or conditioning limitations when evaluating it. See programs/examples/symbolic_definite_integrals.bas and tools/check-symbolic-definite.py for executable checks.

Exact real algebraic numbers

These calls retain a real polynomial root exactly and calculate rational functions of that root. They do not round the root to a BASIC real before doing arithmetic. This is useful for exact geometry, polynomial equilibria, irrational ratios and checking identities that would otherwise have numerical residuals.

FunctionResult
SYMALGROOT(poly$,lower,upper[,variable$])Exact selected root, requiring precisely one distinct root in the closed rational interval.
SYMALGROOTS(poly$,lower,upper[,tolerance[,variable$]])Sorted list of all distinct real roots in the closed interval. Each isolating interval has width at most the positive rational tolerance, default 1/1000000000000. Repeated roots appear once.
SYMALGADD(a,b), SYMALGSUB(a,b), SYMALGMUL(a,b), SYMALGDIV(a,b)Exact arithmetic with real algebraic records or rational scalars, including independently selected roots within the degree/work limits below. Division by an exactly zero value is an error.
SYMALGPOW(a,integer)Exact integer power, from -64 through 64. Negative powers require a nonzero value; exponent zero returns one after input validation.
SYMALGSIGN(a)Exact sign: -1, 0, or 1. These are sign codes, not BASIC Boolean values.
SYMALGCMP(a,b)Exact sign of a-b, including independently selected roots within the same degree/work limits as arithmetic.
SYMALGEVAL(expression,a[,variable$])Substitutes the exact algebraic value into a univariate rational expression or guarded pair, checking its original rational domain conditions exactly.
SYMALGENCLOSE(a[,tolerance])Two exact rational-expression strings {lower$,upper$} enclosing the value, with width at most the positive tolerance. The default is 1/1000000000000.

Endpoints, tolerances and rational scalar operands are BASIC integers or exact rational-expression strings. Binary64 inputs are rejected; use "1/10" instead of 0.1. The selected input variable defaults to "X"; internal record polynomials always use X. Polynomial coefficients are rational, with no other free variables. The inherited polynomial parser and exponent limits apply to constant expressions too; large decimal integer literals avoid its exponent limit.

An algebraic result is an ordinary serializable six-field BASIC list:

{"ALGEBRAIC", polynomial$, lower$, upper$, numerator$, denominator$}

It means numerator(alpha)/denominator(alpha), where alpha is the unique root of polynomial in [lower,upper]. The polynomial is normalized to monic, square-free form. Equal endpoints select an exact rational root. If an input interval selects a root at one endpoint, the constructor tightens it to that point. Numerator and denominator are reduced modulo the defining polynomial; the denominator must be nonzero at the selected root, even for reducible defining polynomials. Each public operation validates the record anew. A malformed or ambiguous record, or a removable denominator hole in a supplied record, produces an error. Rational-only arithmetic also returns this record format; SYMALGENCLOSE can expose its exact singleton rational value.

10 A=SYMALGROOT("X^2-2",1,2)
20 PRINT SYMALGCMP(SYMALGMUL(A,A),2)
30 B=SYMALGEVAL("(X+1)/(X-1)",A)
40 PRINT SYMALGCMP(B,SYMALGADD(3,SYMALGMUL(2,A)))
50 PRINT SYMALGENCLOSE(A,"1/100000000000000000000")
60 Q=SYMALGROOT("X^5-X-1",1,2)
70 PRINT SYMALGSIGN(SYMALGEVAL("X^5-X-1",Q))

The comparison/sign results in this example are exact zeros. The enclosure is a pair of rational bounds, not an arbitrary-precision floating-point value. SYMEVAL(bound$) converts an individual bound to ordinary binary64 when needed for rendering or simulation. Further floating-point calculations retain their usual rounding and conditioning limits.

Arithmetic accepts independently constructed real roots. The same BASIC calls work for sqrt(2)+sqrt(3), opposite roots, and dependent values such as sqrt(8)-2*sqrt(2). A common selected root still uses the smaller polynomial arithmetic path. Otherwise, exact multiplication matrices construct a polynomial for the result; rational interval arithmetic and Sturm counts select its real root. No numerical equality threshold is used.

10 W=SYMALGROOT("X^2-2",1,2)
20 H=SYMALGROOT("X^2-3",1,2)
30 AREA=SYMALGMUL(W,H)
40 PRINT SYMALGCMP(SYMALGPOW(AREA,2),6)
50 PERIMETER=SYMALGMUL(2,SYMALGADD(W,H))
60 PRINT SYMALGENCLOSE(PERIMETER,"1/1000000000000")

The first result is exactly zero. All values remain BASIC lists, and programs can save, pass and reuse the resulting records with the existing SYMALG calls. See programs/examples/symbolic_combinations.bas for the complete geometry demo.

The independent-root path first expresses each operand as a selected root of its own square-free annihilating polynomial. Denominator factors at other roots are removed before modular inversion; division by zero at the selected value remains an error. A multiplication-matrix characteristic polynomial removes repeated conjugate values, so (root(X^16-2))^8 can use a quadratic polynomial. The product of the resulting operand dimensions must be at most 16 before constructing the combined matrix. This is a construction bound, even if a later cancellation could give a lower-degree answer. The polynomials need not be minimal; irrelevant factors and successive combinations can exhaust the bound.

The engine checks modular inverses, quotient identities, the characteristic recurrence's zero-matrix identity and each rebased polynomial's annihilation identity. Characteristic-polynomial trace identities are described in Haber's notes. The test oracle separately uses exact biquadratic arithmetic and optional SymPy Sylvester resultants. Neither reference package is needed by BASIC.

Guaranteed minimal-polynomial construction and algebraic coefficients for all existing symbolic solvers remain unsupported. Exact complex values assembled from real algebraic components use the separate SYMC functions below. Expressions such as SIN(alpha) and SQRT(alpha) are outside SYMALGEVAL; it accepts rational functions and rational guards.

Sturm sequences establish root counts and are checked by polynomial identities. A GCD detects exact zero at the selected root before any inconclusive interval refinement. Nonzero signs and value bounds use exact rational interval Horner arithmetic and bisection. Thus failure to separate a difficult case within the resource budget raises an error rather than returning an approximate equality or incomplete root list. This polynomial-plus-isolating-interval representation is also described in the CGAL algebraic kernel manual; ModernBASIC uses its existing Sturm machinery and has no CGAL runtime dependency.

Defining polynomials have degree 1 through 16 before square-free reduction; rational expressions and record numerator/denominator inputs retain the existing degree-32 bound. Each call permits at most 2048 interval-refinement or isolation-subdivision steps in total, plus the shared coefficient/work budgets. The 4096-bit normalized coefficient cap, 8192-byte individual string cap and 65536-byte output-record cap also apply. These limits may be reached before a requested tolerance or nominal degree; there is no guarantee that every input within the size limits will finish. See programs/examples/symbolic_algebraic.bas, programs/examples/symbolic_combinations.bas, tools/check-symbolic-algebraic.py and tools/check-symbolic-combinations.py for executable checks.

Exact complex algebraic values

SYMCOMPLEX(real,imaginary) constructs an exact value real + i*imaginary from rational scalars or SYMALG records. Each component may use independently selected real roots. Values remain ordinary BASIC lists:

{"COMPLEX_ALGEBRAIC", realRecord, imaginaryRecord}

The component records use the six-field ALGEBRAIC format above. A manually constructed complex record may also contain exact integer or rational-string components. Every public operation validates both components, including when projecting one part or taking the zeroth power. Complex components cannot be nested inside one another. Floating-point and native numeric complex values are rejected; "1/10" supplies an exact tenth. Arithmetic accepts an exact real scalar or SYMALG record wherever a complex operand is expected, promoting it to a zero imaginary part.

FunctionResult

SYMCADD(a,b), SYMCSUB(a,b)Exact complex sum or difference.
SYMCMUL(a,b), SYMCDIV(a,b)Exact product or quotient. A zero complex divisor raises an error.
SYMCPOW(a,integer)Integer power from -64 through 64; negative powers require a nonzero value. Exponent zero returns complex one after validation.
SYMCCONJ(a)Complex conjugate, reversing the imaginary component's sign.
SYMCREAL(a), SYMCIMAG(a)Real or imaginary component as an exact real ALGEBRAIC record.
SYMCNORM2(a)Squared magnitude real^2+imaginary^2, as a real algebraic record.
SYMCEQUAL(a,b)Exact equality: BASIC true (-1) or false (0). A work-limit failure raises an error.

SYMCEVAL(expression,a[,variable$])Exact substitution into a rational expression or guarded expression pair; variable defaults to X.
10 R=SYMALGROOT("X^2-3",1,2)
20 TURN60=SYMCOMPLEX("1/2",SYMALGDIV(R,2))
30 POINT=SYMCOMPLEX(2,1)
40 ROTATED=SYMCMUL(POINT,TURN60)
50 PRINT SYMALGCMP(SYMCNORM2(ROTATED),5)
60 PRINT SYMCEQUAL(SYMCPOW(TURN60,6),1)
70 PRINT SYMCENCLOSE(ROTATED)
80 J=SYMCOMPLEX(0,1)
90 PRINT SYMCEQUAL(SYMCEVAL("X^2+1",J),0)

These checks print 0, -1, a rectangle of rational bounds, and -1. programs/examples/symbolic_complex.bas also checks a complex signal transfer formula and shows how to extract the coordinate bounds into BASIC variables. Convert an individual bound with SYMEVAL(bound$) when a renderer or numerical simulation needs an ordinary binary64 value. Such conversion has ordinary floating-point rounding; it does not retain exact arithmetic.

SYMCEVAL accepts one variable, rational coefficients, the four arithmetic operations and constant integer powers. Use SYMCOMPLEX(0,1) for the imaginary unit; there is no I symbol in the rational formula grammar. Original denominator conditions are checked before cancellation, so (X^2+1)/(X^2+1) at i remains an error. Rational <>0 guards work with complex subjects. Ordered guards (>0, >=0, <0, <=0) require a real subject value. Equality guards (=0) are accepted when their subject evaluates to zero; non-real subjects produce a domain/condition error. Guard comparisons use a zero right-hand side, as in {"X^2",{"X<>0","X^2+1=0"}}. Elementary functions, noninteger powers, additional variables and their canceled forms are outside this evaluator's grammar. Real-only simplifications are not applied to these unsupported inputs.

Successive complex products, powers and quotients preserve a shared real algebraic generator for their components. When a new generator is needed, the engine tries theta=a+k*b for integer k from 1 through 16, solves for the old coordinates exactly, and verifies their reconstruction before selecting the root. A singular candidate is skipped. Exhausting the finite search or its work budget raises an explicit error. This avoids unnecessary degree growth when repeated operations stay in an already constructed field.

Complex arithmetic shares the real algebraic engine's degree-16 construction bound, 4096-bit normalized coefficients, work budget, and total 2048 refinement steps per call across both components. Rational formula inputs retain the existing degree-32 limit. The 8192-byte individual string and 65536-byte complete record limits apply. A composite operation may exhaust these bounds even when its final value has a simpler representation. Guaranteed minimal polynomials and algebraic coefficient support throughout every symbolic solver remain open. For roots supplied by a defining polynomial and for numerical branch evaluation, use the additional interfaces below. The independent component-arithmetic checker is tools/check-symbolic-complex.py; optional SymPy resultants cross-check the stored quotient identities and root selection.

Complex polynomial roots and branch evaluation

These calls use ordinary BASIC lists, variables and loops. Root isolation accepts univariate polynomial strings with rational coefficients, degree at most 16 before removing repeated factors. It returns every distinct root, including real roots; multiplicities are not repeated. variable$ defaults to "X". Exact bounds and tolerances use integers or rational strings, for example "1/1000". A rectangle is {realLower,realUpper,imaginaryLower,imaginaryUpper} with strictly ordered bounds. Its interior is open; a zero anywhere on the boundary raises an error, so move the bounds if needed.

FunctionResult
SYMCROOTCOUNT(polynomial$,rectangle[,variable$])Exact number of distinct roots inside the rectangle.
SYMCROOT(polynomial$,rectangle[,variable$])Exact root record; the rectangle must contain exactly one root.
SYMCROOTS(polynomial$[,tolerance[,variable$]])Complete list of distinct root records, each coordinate width at most the tolerance; default 1/1024. A nonzero constant returns an empty list; the zero polynomial raises an error.
SYMCREFINE(root[,tolerance])Same exact root with narrower rational bounds; default 1/1000000000000.
CAPPROX(value)Ordinary binary64 complex approximation of a native number, exact rational, real algebraic value, component complex record, or complex root record.

CARG(value[,k])Real argument on sheet k, default zero; undefined at zero.
