Root records have six fields:

{"COMPLEX_ROOT", polynomial$, realLower$, realUpper$, imaginaryLower$, imaginaryUpper$}

The stored polynomial is square-free, monic, and uses X. Its isolating rectangle identifies the root exactly. Records are revalidated on every public call. SYMCEQUAL compares two root records, or a root with an existing exact component value; SYMCENCLOSE also accepts root records and returns the usual pair of coordinate intervals. Other exact component operations (SYMCADD, SYMCREAL, SYMCEVAL, etc.) currently require the COMPLEX_ALGEBRAIC/real component forms. Use CAPPROX(root) with native arithmetic or CEVAL(formula$,root) for numerical calculations involving general root records. No automatic exact field conversion is claimed. Root-list order follows the isolating rectangles, not a guaranteed ordering of the complex values; select a known root using SYMCROOT.

10 ROOTS=SYMCROOTS("X^5-X+1","1/1000")
20 FOR K=1 TO LEN(ROOTS)
30 Z=CAPPROX(ROOTS(K))
40 PRINT REAL(Z);",";IMAG(Z)
50 PRINT ABS(CEVAL("X^5-X+1",ROOTS(K)))
60 NEXT K
70 PRINT CLOG(-1,0)
80 PRINT CLOG(-1,1)
90 PRINT CROOT(-1,2,1)

CEVAL accepts the complex symbolic records described below as well as strings. For raw strings, CEVAL supports + - * / ^, SIN COS TAN EXP LN SQRT SINH COSH TANH ASIN ACOS ATAN ASINH ACOSH ATANH ABS, and parentheses. Powers and functions use principal branches. I is reserved for the imaginary unit here; unknown variables and guarded lists are errors. The original expression is evaluated without real-only simplification: X/X at zero remains an error. CLOG, CARG and CPOW accept integer sheet indices from -1,000,000 through 1,000,000. Ordinary BASIC uses PI(); the string grammar uses PI.

The principal argument lies in (-PI,PI]. BASIC canonicalizes signed zero, so negative real cuts take the upper lip (imaginary=+0), while imaginary-axis cuts of inverse functions take the right lip (real=+0). A nonzero coordinate chooses its actual side. Exact input coordinates are refined before conversion; a nonzero coordinate or expression constant that underflows binary64 raises an error. Subsequent arithmetic still rounds in binary64 and can underflow. Transcendental answers are numerical approximations, with no claim of exact symbolic logarithms, automatic continuation around paths, arbitrary precision, or correct rounding on every input. Branch conventions follow the NIST logarithm/power definitions and inverse trigonometric definitions.

Exact rectangle counts use Cauchy indices of rational boundary polynomials, with verified signed remainder identities and a boundary-zero check. The method is described by Li and Paulson. Numerical guesses can accelerate isolation, but are accepted only after exact Rouche inequalities prove one root in both an inscribed and a circumscribed disk. Together these certify one root in the rectangle and none on its boundary. Pairwise disjoint certified rectangles totaling the polynomial degree establish completeness; failed proposals fall back to rational subdivision and winding counts. There is no numerical epsilon in a root count or equality decision.

The shared 4096-bit coefficient cap, 32-million coefficient-work budget, 2048 subdivision/refinement limit, 8192-byte string cap and 65536-byte record cap apply. Difficult separation or refinement can exhaust these limits even below degree 16; failure raises an error and never returns a partial root list. Complex coefficient polynomials and unrestricted symbolic branch reasoning remain outside this root-isolation interface; bounded symbolic complex calculus follows below. Run programs/examples/complex_roots_branches.bas and tools/check-complex-roots-branches.py; --sympy adds independent exact complex rectangle counts. The reference packages are test tools, not BASIC dependencies.

Symbolic complex calculus with branch conditions

Use these functions for a single complex variable. They share the CEVAL elementary grammar, including the imaginary unit I, PI, and E, but use complex identities and principal branches. The real SYMREFINE/SYMDERIV functions retain their separate real-domain contracts.

FunctionResult
SYMCSIMPLIFY(expression[,variable$])Complex-safe symbolic formula with original domain conditions retained.
SYMCBRANCH(expression,conditions[,variable$])Simplify using explicit open complex regions; retain source restrictions and the supplied assumptions.
SYMCDERIV(expression[,variable$])Symbolic holomorphic derivative with sufficient open-domain conditions. Repeated calls produce higher derivatives.
SYMCDOMAIN(expression[,variable$])Sufficient conditions for the supplied formula to have a value.
SYMCANALYTIC(expression[,variable$])Sufficient conditions for holomorphic calculus, including branch-cut exclusions.
CEVAL(formula,value[,variable$])Check the stored conditions, then numerically evaluate the complex formula.

expression is a string or an existing complex formula record. The variable defaults to X for strings and to the stored variable for records. An explicit variable on a record must match it. Other variable tokens are rejected before cancellation; there are no parameter bindings in this interface. Returned records are ordinary BASIC lists:

{"COMPLEX_FORMULA", formula$, variable$, {{predicate$,subject$},...}}

Extract the formula with F(2) and conditions with F(4). Keep the complete record when evaluating or differentiating it: extracting just the string drops its retained restrictions. Supplied records are parsed and validated, and the formula's intrinsic restrictions are collected again. A manually edited record is a new formula with user-supplied restrictions; it is not a certificate proving a relationship to some earlier expression.

The predicates on a subject z have these precise meanings:

PredicateRequired value
NONZEROz differs from zero.
OFF_NEGATIVE_REALImaginary part is nonzero, or real part is strictly positive.
OFF_REAL_OUTSIDE_UNITImaginary part is nonzero, or -1 < real(z) < 1.
OFF_IMAG_OUTSIDE_UNITReal part is nonzero, or -1 < imag(z) < 1.
OFF_REAL_TO_ONEImaginary part is nonzero, or real part is strictly greater than 1.
RIGHT_HALF, LEFT_HALFRespectively real(z)>0 and real(z)<0.
UPPER_HALF, LOWER_HALFRespectively imag(z)>0 and imag(z)<0.
LOG_STRIP-PI < imag(z) < PI.
TRIG_STRIP-PI/2 < real(z) < PI/2.
COS_STRIP0 < real(z) < PI.
HYPERBOLIC_STRIP-PI/2 < imag(z) < PI/2.
ACOSH_STRIPreal(z)>0 and -PI < imag(z) < PI.

A logarithm may have a principal value on the negative real axis, but its principal formula is not holomorphic across that cut. Thus CEVAL(SYMCSIMPLIFY("LN(X)"),-2) has a value, while CEVAL(SYMCDERIV("LN(X)"),-2) raises a branch-condition error. Constant arguments are treated as constants: SYMCDERIV("LN(-1)") is zero. Conditions are sufficient, not a minimal domain or a proof that all conditions can hold together. In particular, differentiating an unsimplified composition can retain exclusions that simplification before differentiation would avoid.

Division and canceled poles retain nonzero conditions. Inverse functions retain their singularities; analytic calculus also excludes their principal cuts. General variable or non-real exponents conservatively require a nonzero base. Constant positive rational powers allow a value at zero; noninteger powers with a varying base exclude the negative real axis and zero during analytic calculus. ABS is permitted in value expressions and for constant derivatives, but a varying complex ABS is rejected by SYMCDERIV and SYMCANALYTIC.

Safe rewrites include rational/Gaussian arithmetic, selected exact constants, EXP(LN(X))=X with X<>0, SQRT(X)^2=X, and forward functions composed with their principal inverses. LN(-1)=I*PI, LN(I)=I*PI/2, and integer/half-integer multiples of I*PI in exponentials are exact symbolic cases. Opposite compositions and branch-sensitive identities such as LN(X^2)=2*LN(X), SQRT(X^2)=X, or LN(EXP(X))=X are not applied generally. Poles are collected before any rewrite, so 0*LN(X) still excludes zero. Integer/half-integer PI trigonometric poles, including imaginary hyperbolic poles, are checked exactly where recognized.

Derivatives use complex chain, product, quotient and power rules. For example, the ACOSH(X) derivative uses 1/(SQRT(X-1)*SQRT(X+1)); merging the two square roots would select an incorrect branch in part of the complex plane. Conventions and analytic cuts follow NIST logarithms and powers, inverse trigonometric functions, and inverse hyperbolic functions.

10 D=SYMCDERIV("EXP(I*X)/(1+I*X)")
20 PRINT D(2)
30 PRINT CEVAL(D,1)
40 D2=SYMCDERIV(D)
50 PRINT CEVAL(D2,1)
60 F=SYMCSIMPLIFY("EXP(LN(X))")
70 PRINT F(2)
80 PRINT F(4)

Symbolic constants and formulas retain exact rational coefficients. CEVAL converts its input to binary64 first, including algebraic input records; it does not certify evaluation at the original exact algebraic value. For formula records, Gaussian-rational subexpressions and supported PI facts are checked exactly at that converted point, then rounded for numerical output. No epsilon is used to decide an exact zero or rational cut side. A nonzero exact computed component that underflows binary64 is an error, preventing a tiny cut distance from silently changing the branch. Remaining transcendental values and conditions use numerical evaluation; this is not interval-certified transcendental calculus or arbitrary-precision floating point. Exact symbolic rewriting may avoid intermediate rounding or overflow encountered by the original raw CEVAL string.

Limits include 8192 bytes per expression, 4096 nodes, depth 64, 128 conditions, 65536 bytes of record text, and the shared structural/coefficient work budgets. The exact Gaussian constant evaluator handles integer powers from -64 through 64; larger powers remain expressions and may use numerical evaluation. Resource failure is an error. General symbolic sheet parameters, path continuation/monodromy, multivariable complex calculus and nonholomorphic/Wirtinger calculus remain outside this implementation.

10 F=SYMCBRANCH("SQRT(X^2)",{{"LEFT_HALF","X"}})
20 PRINT F(2)
30 PRINT CEVAL(F,COMPLEX(-2,1))
40 D=SYMCDERIV(F)
50 PRINT CEVAL(D,COMPLEX(-2,1))
60 P=SYMCBRANCH("LN(EXP(I*X))",{{"LOG_STRIP","I*X"}})
70 PRINT IMAG(CEVAL(P,1.25))

Region boundaries are strictly excluded, even where a principal value might allow an identity on the boundary. There is no automatic sheet selection or case splitting outside the declared regions. Inference uses exact constants, structural subjects after unconditional folding, negation, and the inclusions ACOSH_STRIP into RIGHT_HALF/LOG_STRIP, HYPERBOLIC_STRIP into LOG_STRIP, and COS_STRIP into RIGHT_HALF. Opposite half-plane conditions on the same normalized subject, and exact false constant conditions, raise errors. Other joint contradictions may remain unresolved; this is not a satisfiability solver. Unsupported identities remain unchanged rather than being forced onto a branch.

For open-region conditions whose subjects are affine Gaussian-rational expressions in PI, comparisons use exact rational arithmetic and a certified 100-decimal-place enclosure of PI. Exact PI boundary cancellations and tiny rational displacements are preserved. A comparison unresolved by that enclosure raises an error instead of guessing. The reference checker verifies the enclosure from rational alternating-series bounds for Machin's formula. This local sign facility does not increase CEVAL's binary64 output precision or certify other transcendental computations. Other condition subjects use the existing numerical evaluation, with strict comparisons at binary64 strip boundaries.

Before differentiation or SYMCANALYTIC, stored condition subjects must also meet the sufficient holomorphic-domain checks. For example, an UPPER_HALF condition on LN(X) can hold at X=-1, but differentiation excludes that cut. A varying ABS in a condition subject is conservatively rejected by calculus. Conditions remain attached even if this sacrifices a potentially larger derivative domain. The existing expression, condition-count, storage and work limits still apply. See programs/examples/complex_branches.bas for root branches, logarithm corrections, oscillator phase and rejection outside a declared strip. Run programs/examples/complex_calculus.bas and tools/check-complex-calculus.py; --sympy adds 80-digit mpmath derivative comparisons and exact SymPy rational identities. These packages are test tools.

High-precision real numerical evaluation

HPEVAL and HPBOUNDS evaluate real expressions using bounded variable-precision integer interval arithmetic. They return decimal strings so the result's digits are not rounded back into an ordinary BASIC number.

FunctionResult
HPEVAL(expression,places[,variables,values])One decimal string rounded to places digits after the decimal point, nearest with ties to even.
HPBOUNDS(expression,places[,variables,values]){lower$,upper$} with outward-rounded decimal bounds enclosing the result. Their difference is at most 2*10^(-places).

places must be an integer from 0 through 256. It counts decimal places, not significant digits. With no bindings, the expression must contain no unbound variables. Otherwise supply both the variable-name string/list and matching scalar/list values, as with SYMEVAL. Up to eight variables are supported. Constants PI and E cannot be rebound. Integer bindings are exact; real BASIC bindings retain their existing binary64 value. Use strings such as "0.1", "1/7", or "1e-100" for exact decimal/rational inputs. String bindings must evaluate to a recognized exact rational, rather than a transcendental value.

The expression can be a string or an existing two-field real symbolic result {formula$,{condition$...}}, including derivatives and antiderivatives. Conditions and their own domains are checked before returning a result. Poles are retained through cancellation, multiplication by zero and guarded symbolic simplification. Unknown variables are rejected before cancellation. Complex formula/algebraic records are not accepted by this real interface.

The grammar includes explicit + - * / ^, parentheses, unary signs, PI, E, and all 16 elementary functions in the real symbolic grammar. LOG and SQR retain their aliases. This HP interface additionally accepts exact decimal and scientific literals inside its expression, condition and binding strings: .5, 1.25, 2.5e-30, and 1E100 are examples. No floating-point conversion is used to parse them. Ordinary symbolic APIs retain their rational-string grammar. Real branches apply: SQRT(0) is allowed, logarithms require positive arguments, inverse functions obey their real domains, and noninteger/variable powers conservatively require a strictly positive base. Integer powers permit negative bases and follow the existing 0^0=1 convention.

10 PRINT HPEVAL("PI",50)
20 PRINT HPEVAL("X+Y",30,"X,Y",{"0.1","0.2"})
30 B=HPBOUNDS("SQRT(2)",40)
40 PRINT B(1)
50 PRINT B(2)
60 D=SYMDERIV("LN(X)")
70 PRINT HPEVAL(D,40,"X","3")
80 PRINT HPEVAL("SIN(1e100)",30)

Evaluation uses outward-rounded dyadic intervals, exact rational handling for recognized rational expressions and decimal ties, integer square roots, reduced power series with explicit tail bounds, and interval range reduction. PI is computed at the working precision using Machin's formula. Exact rational logarithm inputs are normalized before conversion, allowing values such as LN(1e-1000). An unresolved sign, pole or rounding decision triggers increased working precision. HPEVAL returns only when both interval endpoints round to the same requested decimal (or exact rational rounding settles the result). It raises an error when the bounded calculation cannot settle the decision.

Returned bounds are numerical enclosures, not symbolic identity certificates. Dependency and cancellation can widen intervals; a true equality in a guard or a transcendental value exactly at a decimal rounding boundary can remain undecidable. Precision failure never silently falls back to binary64. Algorithms use the series and scaling principles described in NIST elementary computation, logarithm series, and trigonometric series.

Limits: 2048 working fractional bits, 4096 bits per stored scaled endpoint and normalized rational component, integer powers from -1024 through 1024, and exponential arguments in [-1024,1024]. Decimal-token scaling is limited to 1233 powers of ten in either direction. The existing 8192-byte expression, 4096-node/depth-64 tree, 128-condition, 65536-byte guard and shared work limits also apply; decimal expansion must fit the expression limit. Large integer parts, extreme cancellation or difficult domains can exhaust these limits even when the final mathematical answer exists.

Use the returned string directly for display or as a later exact decimal binding; that binding represents the rounded decimal, not the original irrational value. VAL converts it back to ordinary BASIC precision when a native graphics/audio/tensor API needs a number. This interface does not change ordinary numeric variables, arrays, matrices, complex arithmetic, special functions or ML kernels to high precision. Complex arbitrary-precision evaluation and high-precision nonlinear/differential solvers remain future work. The explicit rational-data matrix operations below provide high-precision linear solves. programs/examples/high_precision.bas demonstrates exact decimal data, cancellation, root bounds, symbolic slopes and large oscillator phases.

High-precision matrices and linear systems

These functions operate on real rational matrix data and return decimal strings with 0–256 digits after the decimal point. Decimal/scientific strings such as "0.1" and "1e-80" are parsed exactly; ordinary numeric inputs retain their existing integer or binary64 values. All arithmetic and pivot tests are exact rational operations until the final decimal formatting.

Rounded resultEnclosing resultOperation
HPMATMUL(A,B,places)HPMATMULBOUNDS(A,B,places)Matrix times matrix or column vector.
HPDET(A,places)HPDETBOUNDS(A,places)Determinant of a square matrix.
HPINVERSE(A,places)HPINVERSEBOUNDS(A,places)Inverse of a nonsingular square matrix.
HPLINSOLVE(A,B,places)HPLINSOLVEBOUNDS(A,B,places)Solve A*X=B with square nonsingular A and one or more right-hand sides.

A matrix is a nonempty rectangular nested list such as {{1,2},{3,4}}. Every dimension must be 1–16. For multiplication/solving, B may instead be a nonempty flat list representing a column vector. A vector B produces a vector result; a matrix B produces a matrix result, including a one-column matrix. Determinants return one string. Inverses always return a nested list of strings. Store a scalar determinant in a string variable such as D$; matrix and vector results use ordinary list variables such as X.

The BOUNDS variants return {lower,upper} in the corresponding shape: HPLINSOLVEBOUNDS(A,{1,2},p) returns two vectors; HPINVERSEBOUNDS(A,p) returns two matrices; HPDETBOUNDS returns two strings. Each lower endpoint rounds toward negative infinity and each upper endpoint toward positive infinity. Their difference is at most 10^(-places) per entry. An exactly representable decimal has equal endpoints. Rounded variants use nearest rounding with ties to even, matching HPEVAL.

10 A={{1,1},{1,"1+1e-80"}}
20 B={2,"2+1e-80"}
30 X=HPLINSOLVE(A,B,50)
40 PRINT X(1):PRINT X(2)
50 D$=HPDET(A,100):PRINT D$
60 Q=HPLINSOLVEBOUNDS({{3}},{1},30)
70 PRINT Q(1,1):PRINT Q(2,1)
80 M=HPINVERSE({{2,1},{1,3}},30)
90 R=HPMATMUL({{2,1},{1,3}},M,30)
100 PRINT R(1,1):PRINT R(2,2)

String entries use the same recognized exact-rational grammar as HPEVAL bindings. "1/7", "SQRT(4)", and "1+1e-80" are accepted. Unbound variables, complex values, algebraic/formula records, "PI", and "SQRT(2)" are rejected. All supplied cells are validated, even when multiplied by zero or when the matrix is singular. Numeric DIM arrays can be passed with A(). Exact string data can be read with READ A$ and assembled into lists. String DIM arrays retain their existing element access; whole-array A$() snapshots are not added.

Elimination uses exact nonzero row pivots and back substitution. Before rounding, solves and inverses are verified against the original equations with an exact zero residual. No floating-point singularity tolerance is used. Both inconsistent and underdetermined singular systems raise a no-unique-solution error; they do not produce a pseudoinverse or an arbitrary solution. A singular determinant is exactly zero. A nonzero determinant can also *display* as zero at too few decimal places; solving uses the exact pivots rather than this rounded display.

Bounds describe the exact result for the supplied rational data, not uncertainty in measurements or earlier rounded values. A string produced by HPEVAL or a previous matrix operation is reused as that exact rounded decimal. Rounding a solution can introduce a residual even though the internal exact solution was verified. Convert individual output strings with VAL when a native graphics, audio, or tensor API needs ordinary numeric values.

Limits are 16 rows/columns, 8192 bytes per string expression, 65536 total input string bytes per call, 4096 bits per normalized rational numerator/denominator, and the shared symbolic structural/coefficient work budgets. There is no Python, BLAS, or LAPACK dependency for these operations. Difficult coefficient growth raises an explicit resource error, even when the requested final value exists. Inversion/solving does not compute the determinant product, so a large or tiny unrepresentable determinant does not by itself prevent a bounded exact solve. High-precision irrational/complex matrix inputs, sparse systems, and nonlinear/differential solvers remain future work.

programs/examples/high_precision_linear.bas demonstrates fine pivots, exact decimal DATA, geometry transforms, inverse checks, and solution bounds.

High-precision rank, least squares and matrix factors

These operations share the rational-data matrix input rules and resource limits above. HPRANK returns an integer; the other functions return decimal strings rounded to 0–256 places, nearest with ties to even. Exact decimal input strings preserve small differences that ordinary numeric literals may already have lost.

Rounded resultEnclosing resultOperation
HPRANK(A)—Exact rank, including rectangular and zero matrices. No precision argument.
HPPINV(A,places)HPPINVBOUNDS(A,places)Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of an m by n matrix; returns an n by m matrix.
HPLSTSQ(A,B,places)HPLSTSQBOUNDS(A,B,places)Minimum-norm least-squares solution, including singular, underdetermined and inconsistent systems.
HPQR(A,places)HPQRBOUNDS(A,places)Reduced QR factors {Q,R} for m >= n and full column rank. Q is m by n; R is n by n with positive diagonal.
HPCHOLESKY(A,places)HPCHOLESKYBOUNDS(A,places)Lower triangular L with A=L*TRANSPOSE(L) for an exactly symmetric positive definite matrix.

For least squares, B must have as many rows as A. A flat vector B returns a vector X; a matrix B returns a matrix X with one solution per right-hand side. Each solution first minimizes the sum of squared residuals A*X-B, then has the smallest Euclidean norm among all minimizers. An inconsistent system can therefore succeed with a nonzero residual. Zero A returns zero X. No numerical rank threshold or truncation parameter is used. HPLINSOLVE retains its stricter requirement of a unique solution to a square system.

10 A={{1,0},{1,1},{1,2}}
20 FIT=HPLSTSQ(A,{1,2,2},30)
30 PRINT "INTERCEPT ";FIT(1):PRINT "SLOPE ";FIT(2)
40 X=HPLSTSQ({{1,1}},{2},30):PRINT X(1):PRINT X(2)
50 PRINT HPRANK({{1,1},{1,"1+1e-80"}})
60 P=HPPINV({{1,2},{2,4}},30):PRINT P(1,1)
70 QR=HPQR({{1,0},{1,1},{0,1}},30)
80 Q=QR(1):R=QR(2):PRINT R(1,1)
90 L=HPCHOLESKY({{2,1},{1,2}},30):PRINT L(2,2)

HPPINVBOUNDS and HPCHOLESKYBOUNDS return {lowerMatrix,upperMatrix}. HPLSTSQBOUNDS returns {lower,upper} with the same vector/matrix shape as X. HPQRBOUNDS returns {{Qlower,Rlower},{Qupper,Rupper}}: select B(1,1) for Q's lower matrix and B(2,2) for R's upper matrix. Each entry's interval has width at most 10^(-places) and contains the exact mathematical result for the supplied rational data.

Rank factorization and all four Moore–Penrose equations are checked exactly before pseudoinverse formatting. Least squares also verifies the normal equations and minimum-norm row-space condition. QR uses exact rational orthogonal columns before normalization; Cholesky uses exact rational LDL factors. Their reconstruction and orthogonality identities are checked before rounding. Each factor entry is a rational multiple of a square root, rounded and enclosed using integer comparisons without binary64 intermediates.

QR rejects wide or rank-deficient matrices; it does not silently remove dependent columns. Cholesky requires exact symmetry and strictly positive pivots, rejecting asymmetric, indefinite and positive semidefinite inputs. The functions validate every input cell and report resource-limit failures explicitly. Dimensions are at most 16, normalized rational components at most 4096 bits, and the shared input and work budgets still apply.

Returned factors may approximate irrational values even though inputs must be rational. Rounding can introduce reconstruction or orthogonality error; reusing output strings treats them as the rounded decimal values. Bounds enclose the exact result for the supplied data and do not represent measurement uncertainty. Irrational/complex input matrices, sparse solvers and high-precision nonlinear/differential solvers remain outside this interface. Spectral factors are described below. programs/examples/high_precision_decomposition.bas connects decimal DATA to line fitting, minimum-norm solutions, rank, pseudoinverses, QR and Cholesky bounds.

High-precision eigenvalues, singular values and inertia

These functions use the same exact rational input rules as the matrix functions above, including numeric DIM-array snapshots and decimal/rational strings.

FunctionResult
HPINERTIA(A[,shift])Integer counts {negative,zero,positive} for the eigenvalues of A-shift*I. Shift defaults to zero and accepts the same exact scalar data as matrix entries.
HPEIGVALS(A,places)Eigenvalues of an exactly symmetric square matrix, ascending, with multiplicities.
HPEIGVALSBOUNDS(A,places){lowerVector,upperVector} enclosing the corresponding ordered eigenvalues.
HPSINGVALS(A,places)Singular values of a rectangular m by n matrix, descending; exactly MIN(m,n) entries, including zero values and multiplicities.
HPSINGVALSBOUNDS(A,places){lowerVector,upperVector} enclosing the corresponding ordered singular values.

Inertia is an exact sign count, without a numerical tolerance or precision argument. For a symmetric matrix, no negative eigenvalues means positive semidefinite; no negative or zero eigenvalues means positive definite. Shifting allows BASIC programs to count modes below, at and above an exact threshold. Asymmetric and nonsquare matrices are rejected by inertia/eigenvalue functions. Singular-value functions accept any nonempty real rational rectangular matrix. These functions return values only. Use HPEIGH and HPSVD below for factors.

10 K={{2,-1},{-1,2}}
20 C=HPINERTIA(K):PRINT C(1):PRINT C(2):PRINT C(3)
30 E=HPEIGVALS(K,30):PRINT E(1):PRINT E(2)
40 C=HPINERTIA(K,1):PRINT C(2)
50 S=HPSINGVALS({{1,1},{0,1}},30):PRINT S(1):PRINT S(2)
60 B=HPEIGVALSBOUNDS({{1,1},{1,-1}},30)
70 PRINT B(1,2):PRINT B(2,2)

The value and bound functions return decimal strings at 0–256 places. Rounded values use nearest rounding with ties to even. Each interval has width at most one requested decimal unit; exactly representable values have equal endpoints. Intervals may overlap for closely spaced values, and distinct values can round to the same string. Multiplicity and exact zero detection do not use those rounded strings. HPINERTIA and HPRANK can distinguish exact degeneracy from small nonzero values.

Symmetric congruence elimination uses exact one- or two-row pivots to count signs, including zero-diagonal indefinite matrices and singular trailing blocks. Exact counts drive a decimal-grid bisection and settle midpoint ties. Singular values use the smaller of TRANSPOSE(A)*A and A*TRANSPOSE(A), formed exactly, and compare squared decimal thresholds. No binary64 Gram matrix or eigenvalue guess is used. Diagonal spectra are formatted directly, using exact square-root comparisons where needed.

Dimensions are bounded to 16, normalized rational components to 4096 bits, and the existing aggregate text, structural and coefficient work limits apply to the entire call. Dense matrices, large coefficient growth or high requested precision can exhaust those limits; the call then returns an explicit error without a partial spectrum or silently reduced precision. Bounds describe the mathematical values for the supplied rational data, not measurement uncertainty. The result is not a guarantee of high relative accuracy for values smaller than one requested decimal unit. Ordinary numeric kernels retain their precision. General real-matrix complex spectra are provided by HPCEIGVALS below. Matrices with complex entries remain outside these interfaces. programs/examples/high_precision_spectrum.bas demonstrates stability counts, unit-mass vibration frequencies, geometric stretch, dependent features and tiny exact decimal data.

High-precision eigenvectors and full singular-value factors

FunctionResult
HPEIGH(A,places){values,V} for an exactly symmetric n by n matrix. Values are ascending; columns of the n by n matrix V are the corresponding mode directions.
HPSVD(A,places){U,S,VT} for any nonempty real rational m by n matrix. U is m by m, VT is n by n, and S has MIN(m,n) descending nonnegative entries.

Inputs follow the exact rational matrix rules above; every output cell is a fixed decimal string at 0–256 places. These functions include repeated spectra, rank-deficient matrices, zero matrices and full orthogonal null-space bases. HPSVD returns full square factors (ordinary SVD returns reduced factors). Build an m by n diagonal matrix Sigma from S to reconstruct A = U*Sigma*VT. For HPEIGH, the corresponding identity is A = V*DIAG(values)*TRANSPOSE(V). Use nested list indexing, such as F(2,1,2), to access factor cells. Decimal strings work directly with HPMATMUL and HPEVAL; ordinary matrix utilities expect ordinary numeric cells, so construct a decimal transpose with list/array indexing or convert explicitly at the consumer boundary.

10 F=HPEIGH({{2,-1},{-1,2}},40):E=F(1):V=F(2)
20 PRINT E(1):PRINT V(1,1):PRINT V(2,1)
30 X=HPMATMUL(V,{"1/10",0},40):PRINT X(1):PRINT X(2)
40 F=HPSVD({{3,0},{0,-2},{0,0}},40):U=F(1):S=F(2):VT=F(3)
50 SIGMA={{S(1),0},{0,S(2)},{0,0}}
60 A=HPMATMUL(HPMATMUL(U,SIGMA,40),VT,40):PRINT A(2,2)

Accuracy contract. Let u = 10^(-places), N = MAX(rows,columns) and M = MAX(1,MAX(ABS(A(i,j)))) for the exact input entries. Every returned result passes exact integer comparisons on its final decimal strings:

  • Each entry of the factor reconstruction minus A has absolute value at most 4*N*u*M.
  • Each entry of TRANSPOSE(V)*V-I for eigenvectors, and of TRANSPOSE(U)*U-I and VT*TRANSPOSE(VT)-I for SVD, has absolute value at most 4*N*u.

These are residual guarantees for the supplied matrix and returned rounded factors. At few decimal places the stated bounds can be loose. Individual basis entries are not certified enclosures of unique exact vectors: signs are arbitrary, repeated values permit different bases, and closely spaced values can make individual directions sensitive. Small singular values can round to zero. Use HPRANK for exact rank and the separate HPEIGVALS/HPSINGVALS functions for certified nearest ties-to-even spectral values or their outward bounds. Factor values are approximations checked jointly with the basis; no componentwise correct-rounding or relative-accuracy guarantee is made.

The implementation uses bounded integer fixed-point Jacobi rotations with exact power-of-two scaling, one-sided rotations for SVD, and reorthogonalization to complete full bases. It increases working precision when the final residual checks fail, up to 2048 bits. Dimensions remain limited to 16; the shared 4096-bit rational input and structural/arithmetic work budgets apply, including retries. Difficult inputs can fail before reaching those maximum sizes. A failure returns an explicit error, never uncertified factors or silently reduced precision. General nonsymmetric/complex factors and uncertain or irrational matrix inputs remain outside this API. The BASIC example programs/examples/high_precision_factors.bas demonstrates unit-mass vibration modes, modal coordinates, a rectangular transform and covariance directions.

Exact characteristic polynomials and general complex eigenvalues

FunctionResult
SYMCHARPOLY(A[,variable$])The exact monic polynomial DET(variable*I-A) as a symbolic string, including algebraic multiplicities. The variable defaults to "X".
HPCEIGVALS(A,places)An n by 2 list of decimal strings {realPart,imaginaryPart} for all eigenvalues of an n by n real rational matrix, with algebraic multiplicities. Symmetry is not required.
HPCEIGVALSBOUNDS(A,places){lowerMatrix,upperMatrix}, each n by 2, enclosing the real and imaginary components of the corresponding eigenvalues.

All three functions accept nonempty square matrices under the exact rational matrix input rules above. Native integers retain their exact value, native reals retain their binary64 value, and decimal/rational strings retain their exact mathematical value. Complex, irrational and uncertain input cells are rejected. The characteristic polynomial variable is a case-insensitive alphanumeric identifier beginning with a letter, at most 32 characters, excluding PI and E. Its output can be passed to SYMDIFF, SYMFACTOR, SYMROOTCOUNT, SYMCROOTS and other symbolic polynomial operations. SYMCROOTS returns distinct root records; HPCEIGVALS repeats each value according to its algebraic multiplicity.

10 READ D$:A={{0,1},{-4,D$}}
20 P$=SYMCHARPOLY(A):PRINT P$
30 E=HPCEIGVALS(A,40)
40 FOR I=1 TO LEN(E):PRINT E(I,1):PRINT E(I,2):NEXT I
50 B=HPCEIGVALSBOUNDS(A,40):PRINT B(1,1,1):PRINT B(2,1,1)
60 END
70 DATA "-1/2"

This damped system has a complex conjugate pair. Real eigenvalues are returned in the same two-column shape with an exactly zero imaginary component. Repeated roots, defective matrices, nilpotent matrices and zero matrices are supported. These are eigenvalue functions; they do not return nonsymmetric eigenvectors, Jordan chains or Schur factors.

Decimal places range from 0 to 256. Each component uses nearest rounding with ties to even. Every bound interval is outward and at most one final decimal unit wide; an exactly representable component has equal endpoints. Rows are sorted by the rounded real component, then the rounded imaginary component, using numeric comparisons. Bounds use that same ordering at the requested precision. Ties are unspecified: do not treat row numbers as persistent root identities when the input or requested precision changes. Distinct roots may round to the same pair and their component intervals may overlap.

The characteristic polynomial is calculated with exact rational arithmetic. Cayley-Hamilton is checked, and independent determinant evaluations at n+1 rational points certify the polynomial identity and multiplicities. A verified square-free decomposition retains repeated roots. Linear/quadratic factors use exact rational and radical grid comparisons. Higher-degree roots use certified one-root complex rectangles; numerical Newton locations are proposals only. Exact GCD/Sturm tests on rational grid lines settle component zeros, exact grid values and halfway ties. No numerical rank or root-merging tolerance decides multiplicity or the returned digits.

Dimensions are bounded to 16, individual input strings to 8192 bytes, aggregate matrix text to 65536 bytes, normalized rational components to 4096 bits, and symbolic polynomial output to 8192 bytes. The shared structural/arithmetic work limits and 2048 root-refinement steps bound the entire call. Coefficient growth, clusters or demanding precision can exhaust the limits below the maximum size/precision; an explicit error is returned without partial spectra or silently reduced accuracy. Triangular spectra use their exact diagonal directly.

Bounds certify the supplied exact matrix, not measurement uncertainty or changes introduced by prior rounding. Nonsymmetric eigenvalues can be highly sensitive to input changes. Complex matrix inputs and nonsymmetric spectral factors remain future work. programs/examples/high_precision_general_spectrum.bas connects BASIC DATA to a damped oscillator, symbolic roots, rotation and repeated modes.

Exact real roots and interval inequality certificates

These functions accept a strict univariate polynomial string with exact rational coefficients. variable$ defaults to "X"; names are case-insensitive and PI and E are reserved. Other variable tokens, even ones that cancel, are rejected. Elementary functions, variable denominators and guarded expression lists are outside this interface. Bounds are finite exact integers or constant-expression strings such as "1/3"; floating-point and complex values are rejected. The lower bound must not exceed the upper bound.

FunctionResult
SYMSTURM(expr$[,variable$]){{chain$...},{quotient$...},{scale$...}}, an exact Sturm sequence certificate for a nonzero polynomial.
SYMSTURMCHECK(expr$,certificate[,variable$])-1 if the certificate verifies against the polynomial, otherwise 0.
SYMROOTCOUNT(expr$,lower,upper[,variable$])Number of distinct real roots in the closed interval, including both endpoints. Repeated roots count once.
SYMSIGNCERT(expr$[,variable$]){square$,remainder$,sturmCertificate} with expr = square^2 * remainder, a nonzero square-free remainder, and its Sturm certificate. Reusable across intervals.
SYMNONNEG(expr$,lower,upper[,variable$])-1 if the polynomial is nonnegative everywhere on the closed interval, otherwise 0, when the bounded exact computation succeeds.
SYMNONNEGCHECK(expr$,lower,upper,certificate[,variable$])-1 only when the supplied sign certificate verifies and establishes nonnegativity on this interval. A false claim or an incorrect certificate returns 0.

Certificates are ordinary returned BASIC lists and may be stored and reused. BASIC brace literals are numeric, so store the returned certificate rather than trying to write nested polynomial-string literals. Malformed types/shapes and resource failures raise errors. A structurally valid but incorrect certificate returns 0; this alone says nothing about whether some other certificate could prove the statement. SYMSIGNCERT itself is a decomposition, not a claim that the polynomial is nonnegative. A singleton interval tests the polynomial at its one point. The zero polynomial is nonnegative everywhere, but SYMROOTCOUNT and SYMSTURM reject it because its root set is infinite.

For a nonconstant polynomial, the sequence starts with S0=p and S1=p'. Each step certifies Si = Qi*S(i+1) - ci*S(i+2) with positive rational ci, strictly decreasing degrees, and a final exact-division identity. A nonzero constant has a one-entry chain with empty quotient and scale lists. The checker uses multiplication and coefficient comparison, without division, GCD or root search. Root counting uses exact one-sided signs at endpoints, including roots shared by the entire sequence. This avoids numeric perturbation or tolerances; see Sturm's theorem with endpoints.

Sign certificates use square-free decomposition. The checker verifies the product identity and the remainder's sequence; a constant final entry certifies square-freeness. On an interval of positive width, nonnegativity then requires a positive right-hand sign at the lower endpoint and no remainder roots strictly inside the interval. Even-multiplicity roots live in the square factor and endpoint zeros are allowed. This decides univariate rational-polynomial inequalities on a supplied interval. It does not provide quantified logic, multivariate inequalities, integer constraints or general theorem proving.

The polynomial and every certificate polynomial have degree at most 32, with bounded arbitrary-precision rational arithmetic and a shared one-million-step budget. The underlying polynomial parser also has its existing intermediate degree-64, depth, term and input limits. Each string is at most 8192 bytes; each complete certificate is at most 65536 bytes, with at most 33 chain entries, 32 quotients and 31 scales. Coefficient growth or endpoint evaluation can exceed these limits even for a low-degree problem. Such failures are errors, never approximate proof results. Long algebra operations observe BREAK.

10 P$="(X-1)^2*(X+2)"
20 C=SYMSIGNCERT(P$)
30 PRINT SYMROOTCOUNT(P$,-2,1)
40 PRINT SYMNONNEGCHECK(P$,-2,3,C)
50 PRINT SYMNONNEGCHECK(P$,-3,3,C)
60 PRINT SYMSTURMCHECK(P$,SYMSTURM(P$))
70 PRINT SYMNONNEG("X^4-2*X^2+1",-2,2)

The results are 2, -1, 0, -1, -1. The last line proves a lower bound of -1 for X^4-2*X^2 on [-2,2]. Together with exact evaluation at the feasible point X=1, where the value is -1, this establishes a global minimum for that example. These calls do not search for minimizers or return algebraic root coordinates.

Certified global polynomial optimization

These calls optimize a strict univariate rational polynomial on a finite closed rational interval. Convexity is not required. Bounds and tolerance use exact integers or constant-expression strings; floating-point and complex values are rejected. The tolerance must be positive and is an absolute objective-value gap, not an error bound on the minimizing coordinate. The selected variable defaults to X and follows the real-polynomial interface above.

FunctionResult
SYMPOLYMIN(expr$,lower,upper,tolerance[,variable$]){point$,value$,bound$,certificate} with a feasible rational point, its exact attained value, and a certified global lower bound.
SYMPOLYMAX(expr$,lower,upper,tolerance[,variable$])Same layout with a certified global upper bound.
SYMPOLYCHECK(expr$,lower,upper,tolerance,result[,direction$[,variable$]])Independently checks feasibility, the attained value, the global-bound certificate and the requested gap. Returns -1 for a verified result or 0 for a structurally valid but incorrect claim. Direction defaults to "MIN"; "MIN" and "MAX" are case-insensitive. Supply direction before a selected variable.

For minimization, bound <= true minimum <= value and value-bound <= tolerance. For maximization, value <= true maximum <= bound and bound-value <= tolerance. All these comparisons use exact rational arithmetic. The returned point need not be an exact optimizer, and no coordinate-distance, uniqueness or tie-location guarantee is made. A zero gap certifies an exact global optimum; otherwise the result certifies the stated objective gap. Irrational optimizers can therefore be approached without pretending their coordinates are rational. Constants, zero polynomials and singleton intervals are supported.

certificate is a SYMSIGNCERT result for expr-bound in minimization or bound-expr in maximization. The checker verifies that polynomial's nonnegativity on the full interval and checks value=expr(point) separately. It does not rerun the optimizer, derive stationary points, or trust the supplied value, bound or solver status. A certificate may be checked against another interval or tolerance, but acceptance depends on the full new claim. Malformed data and exhausted resource limits raise errors.

Search starts with an exact interval-Horner enclosure, then bisects the range between a global lower bound and an attained value. Each trial invokes the exact polynomial sign decision. If a better point exists, domain subdivision uses the same sign certificate to locate a negative region and a rational witness. Each successful refinement reduces the objective gap by at least half. Maximization applies this search to the negative objective. Final acceptance uses the separate certificate checker. The implementation shares the interval evaluation principle illustrated in Boost's interval-Horner example, using checked exact rational arithmetic here.

The degree limit is 32. The complete returned result has at most 65536 bytes of text, with the existing per-string and sign-certificate limits. Each objective search and each negative-region search allow at most 256 refinement iterations, within the shared one-million-step algebra budget. The 4096-bit normalized coefficient growth, endpoint evaluation or increasingly fine rational midpoints may exhaust arithmetic limits, including on low-degree polynomials. Failure returns an error without a partial solution. Smaller tolerances can be substantially more costly. BREAK remains active throughout search and verification. General multivariate constraints, transcendental objectives and algebraic coordinate output are outside this interface.

10 P$="(X^2-2)^2"
20 R=SYMPOLYMIN(P$,1,2,"1/1024")
30 PRINT "POINT: ";R(1)
40 PRINT "ATTAINED VALUE: ";R(2)
50 PRINT "GLOBAL LOWER BOUND: ";R(3)
60 PRINT "VERIFIED GAP: ";SYMPOLYCHECK(P$,1,2,"1/1024",R)
70 M=SYMPOLYMAX("X^3-3*X",-2,2,"1/128")
80 PRINT SYMPOLYCHECK("X^3-3*X",-2,2,"1/128",M,"MAX")

The first objective has its minimum at the irrational point sqrt(2). The returned rational point has an attained value within 1/1024 of the true minimum, and the two checks print -1.

Exact box-constrained quadratic optimization

FunctionResult
SYMBOXMIN(expr$,variables,lower,upper)Exact global minimum of a convex quadratic polynomial on a closed rational box. Returns {{point$...},value$,{gradient$...}}.
SYMBOXMAX(expr$,variables,lower,upper)Corresponding exact global maximum of a concave quadratic. The returned gradient belongs to the original objective.
SYMBOXCHECK(expr$,variables,lower,upper,point[,direction$])Checks a candidate independently of the search; returns -1 for a verified global optimum and 0 for an infeasible or nonoptimal point. Direction is "MIN" by default or "MAX", case-insensitively. Invalid or unsupported problems raise errors.

Use one to six distinct variable names, as a comma-separated string or a string list such as SYMVARS returns. Every variable remaining in the objective must be listed; listed variables absent from the objective are allowed. Vector order follows this explicit list. Bounds and candidate points accept comma-separated exact constant-expression strings, such as "-1,1/3", or lists containing integers or constant-expression strings. Real and complex elements are rejected; use rational strings to preserve exactness. All vectors must match the variable count. Bounds are finite, lower bounds must not exceed upper bounds, and equal bounds fix a coordinate. Variable tokens are not allowed in bounds or points.

The engine verifies positive semidefiniteness of the entire Hessian for a minimum, or of its negative for a maximum, using rational Schur complements. Indefinite quadratics and higher degrees are unsupported, including when fixed coordinates would hide the nonconvex direction. Linear, constant, and singular convex objectives are supported. Search enumerates at most 729 faces and solves the free-coordinate stationarity equations exactly. Singular faces are skipped because a flat minimum also occurs on a smaller face. It returns the first verified optimum; there is no uniqueness or tie-location promise.

The checker recomputes exact derivatives from the objective. After checking convexity and feasibility, it requires zero gradient in each interior coordinate, a nonnegative gradient at a lower bound, or a nonpositive gradient at an upper bound. For maximization it reverses those signs; fixed coordinates impose no gradient restriction. These are the box specialization of the sufficient convex KKT optimality conditions. The checker does not run the optimizer or trust a supplied value or gradient. It is a restricted optimality decision procedure, not a general theorem prover.

All symbolic coefficient, parser, output and shared work limits apply. Arithmetic uses checked rational coefficients; intermediate overflow raises an error even when an optimum exists. No tolerance, floating approximation, or best-so-far candidate is presented as an exact solution. BREAK is checked during the solve.

10 P$="(X+Y-1)^2+(Y-2)^2"
20 R=SYMBOXMIN(P$,"X,Y","0,0","3,3")
30 PRINT R(1),R(2),R(3)
40 PRINT SYMBOXCHECK(P$,"X,Y","0,0","3,3",R(1))
50 PRINT SYMBOXCHECK(P$,"X,Y","0,0","3,3","0,1")

The result has point {0,(3/2)}, value (1/2) and gradient {1,0}. The first check prints -1; the second candidate is feasible but not optimal and prints 0.

Exact quadratic optimization with linear constraints

FunctionResult
SYMQPMIN(expr$,variables,lower,upper,inequalities,equalities)Exact global minimum of a convex quadratic or linear objective with finite bounds and affine constraints. Returns a point, attained value and KKT multipliers.
SYMQPMAX(expr$,variables,lower,upper,inequalities,equalities)Exact global maximum of a concave quadratic or linear objective, with the same result layout.
SYMQPCHECK(expr$,variables,lower,upper,inequalities,equalities,result[,direction$])Independently checks a complete result. Returns -1 for a verified global optimum or 0 for a structurally valid but incorrect certificate. Direction defaults to "MIN"; "MIN" and "MAX" are case-insensitive. Malformed certificates and invalid or unsupported problems raise errors.

All six problem arguments are required. Variables and bounds use the same formats as SYMBOXMIN: one to six distinct names, finite rational bound vectors, and equal bounds to fix a coordinate. Every remaining variable in the objective or constraints must be listed. Real and complex bounds are rejected; use exact integer values or rational strings.

Each supplied inequality is an affine polynomial g(x) interpreted as g(x) <= 0; each equality is an affine polynomial h(x) interpreted as h(x) = 0. For example, "X+Y-1" in the inequality argument means X+Y <= 1. Pass semicolon-separated polynomial strings or a list of strings, such as an affine basis returned by SYMGROEBNER. Use "" or {} for no constraints. Relational syntax such as "X+Y<=1" is not accepted inside these strings. There may be at most 12 supplied inequalities and equalities combined; variable bounds do not count against this limit. Duplicates, constant constraints and dependent equalities are permitted, including constraints that make the feasible set a point or a lower-dimensional face.

The result is a nested list of exact rational strings:

{{point$...}, value$,
 {{inequalityMultiplier$...}, {equalityMultiplier$...},
  {lowerBoundMultiplier$...}, {upperBoundMultiplier$...}}}

Point and bound-multiplier order follows variables. Constraint-multiplier order follows the supplied inequalities and equalities, including redundant entries. An absent constraint group has an empty multiplier list. value$ always belongs to the original objective, including for maximization. There is no uniqueness or tie-location promise for the point or its multipliers.

For minimum problems let q = expr; for maximum problems let q = -expr. The engine requires the entire Hessian of q to be positive semidefinite, even when the constraints would hide a nonconvex direction. Linear, constant and singular convex objectives are supported. The checker verifies the original polynomial values and derivatives, feasible bounds and constraints, the reported objective value, and these exact conditions:

  • Inequality and bound multipliers are nonnegative; equality multipliers may have either sign.
  • Every inequality multiplier times its constraint value is zero. A nonzero bound multiplier requires the point to lie on that bound.
  • grad(q) + sum(lambda_i*grad(g_i)) + sum(nu_j*grad(h_j)) - lowerMu + upperMu = 0.

These convex KKT conditions certify global optimality. Checking does not rerun active-set enumeration, equality reduction or the stationarity-system solve. Independently constructed certificates are accepted in the same layout; scalar entries may be exact integers or constant-expression strings, and vectors may also be comma-separated constant-expression strings.

Search enumerates independent active constraint sets, solving rational KKT systems and checking each proposed certificate. On bounded feasible sets, flat optimal directions can be followed to smaller faces, so singular objectives can have verified solutions without choosing arbitrary free coordinates. The finite search is combinatorial: six-variable or heavily constrained problems can exhaust the shared one-million-step budget. Bounded arbitrary-precision rational arithmetic, parser and output limits apply; the combined constraint text and the complete certificate are each limited to 65,536 bytes, with at most 8,192 bytes per scalar expression. BREAK is checked during the search and verification. An infeasible problem, arithmetic overflow, exhausted work budget or failure to find a verified optimum raises an error. Such an error is not an infeasibility certificate. No approximate or partially verified optimum is returned.

10 P$="(X-2)^2+(Y-2)^2"
20 G$="X+Y-1"
30 R=SYMQPMIN(P$,"X,Y","0,0","2,2",G$,"")
40 PRINT R(1),R(2),R(3)
50 PRINT SYMQPCHECK(P$,"X,Y","0,0","2,2",G$,"",R)
60 E$="X+Y-1;2*X+2*Y-2"
70 S=SYMQPMIN("X^2+Y^2","X,Y",{0,0},{2,2},"",E$)
80 PRINT S(1),S(2),S(3)
90 PRINT SYMQPCHECK("X^2+Y^2","X,Y",{0,0},{2,2},"",E$,S)

Both points are {(1/2),(1/2)}. The first value is (9/2) with inequality multiplier 3; the second value is (1/2) with equality multipliers {-1,0}. All bound multipliers are zero. Both checks print -1.

Certified linear feasibility and infeasibility

FunctionResult
SYMLINFEAS(variables,lower,upper,inequalities,equalities)Returns either {"FEASIBLE",{point$...}} or {"INFEASIBLE",{{inequalityMultiplier$...},{equalityMultiplier$...},{lowerBoundMultiplier$...},{upperBoundMultiplier$...}}}. Every successful result includes a checked witness.
SYMLINFEASCHECK(variables,lower,upper,inequalities,equalities,result)Independently verifies the supplied point or contradiction. Returns -1 for a valid witness or 0 for a structurally valid but incorrect claim. Malformed results and unsupported inputs raise errors. Status strings are case-insensitive.

These functions use the same five constraint arguments as SYMQPMIN, with no objective. Bounds are mandatory finite rational vectors in one to six variables, and there may be at most 12 supplied affine constraints. Inequalities mean g(x) <= 0, equalities mean h(x) = 0; semicolon-separated polynomial strings and lists of polynomial strings are accepted. Empty strings or empty lists mean no supplied constraints. Lower bounds greater than upper bounds are invalid inputs; equal bounds fix a coordinate. The arithmetic and text limits of the quadratic solver apply.

A feasible witness is an exact rational point satisfying every original bound, inequality and equality. It need not be unique or optimal for any objective. The checker evaluates the original polynomials at the supplied point.

An infeasibility witness is a Farkas certificate. Its inequality and bound multipliers must be nonnegative; equality multipliers may have either sign. The checker combines the original polynomials and bounds:

sum(lambda_i*g_i) + sum(nu_j*h_j)
  + sum(lowerMu_k*(lower_k-x_k)) + sum(upperMu_k*(x_k-upper_k))

Every variable coefficient must cancel, leaving a strictly positive rational constant. At a feasible point all weighted inequalities would be nonpositive and all weighted equalities zero, so this identity proves a contradiction. Any positive rescaling is accepted; a zero or negative constant is rejected. Multiplier vectors preserve the original constraint and variable order, including redundant or zero constraints. All returned scalars are exact rational strings. Independently written certificates may also contain integer scalars or comma-separated exact vector strings.

Search first checks box corners and direct conflicts between an affine constraint and its bounds, then alternates between potential feasible vertices and potential contradiction certificates. Independent equality bases reduce each search while retaining original multiplier positions. Neither failure to find a point nor an exhausted search is treated as an infeasibility proof. Checking performs no vertex search, equality reduction or certificate-system solve. Bounded arbitrary-precision rational overflow or exhaustion of the shared one-million-step budget raises an error; such an error leaves feasibility undecided. BREAK is checked during the work.

10 G$="X+Y-1":E$="X+Y-2"
20 R=SYMLINFEAS("X,Y",{0,0},{2,2},G$,E$)
30 PRINT R
40 PRINT SYMLINFEASCHECK("X,Y",{0,0},{2,2},G$,E$,R)
50 C={"INFEASIBLE",{{2},{-2},{0,0},{0,0}}}
60 PRINT SYMLINFEASCHECK("X,Y",{0,0},{2,2},G$,E$,C)
70 F=SYMLINFEAS("X,Y",{0,0},{2,2},"","X+Y-1;X-Y")
80 PRINT F

The first result is {"INFEASIBLE",{{1},{-1},{0,0},{0,0}}}: subtracting X+Y-2 = 0 from X+Y-1 <= 0 yields the impossible inequality 1 <= 0. Both checks print -1, including the independently supplied rescaled proof. The final result is {"FEASIBLE",{"1/2","1/2"}}. PRINT displays list strings without quotation marks and may parenthesize rational fractions.

Use this function to diagnose the feasible set before calling a quadratic optimizer. It does not change the existing optimizer's result format or errors, and does not decide general nonlinear inequalities or unbounded-domain problems.

Numerical calculus

NDERIV(expression,variable,point[,step]) returns a scalar derivative. An explicit positive step retains the fixed two-point central difference using the actual representable sample spacing; an unrepresentable/nonfinite stencil is rejected. Without a step it now uses the shared adaptive Rust derivative below, returning a scalar only when its estimated tolerance is met (otherwise an error).

DERIVATIVE(fn$,point[,atol[,rtol[,initialStep[,direction[,maxeval[,maxiter]]]]]]) uses a scalar DEF FN callback and returns {value,estimatedAbsoluteError,step,evaluations,iterations,status$}:

10 DEF FNF(X)=LOG(X)
20 R=DERIVATIVE("FNF",1E-8):PRINT R
30 DEF FNEDGE(X)=LOG(1+X)
40 R=DERIVATIVE("FNEDGE",0,1E-9,1E-8,0,1):PRINT R

Defaults are atol=1E-9, rtol=1E-8, automatic initial radius (initialStep=0), central direction (0), 257 evaluations and 64 iterations. Direction 1 selects a forward derivative and -1 a backward derivative. Tolerances must be finite and nonnegative, rtol<=1, and at least one must be positive. Explicit initial radii must be positive and finite. Work limits are 5–4097 evaluations and 1–256 iterations; a complete comparison requires at least nine evaluations.

The automatic radius starts at the smaller of 0.001 and one percent of the nonzero point's magnitude, with a minimum of 64 local floating spacings; zero starts at 0.001. It is a heuristic starting scale, not knowledge of the function's natural length/time units. The engine uses five-point polynomial interpolation on actual representable coordinates, exact weighted differences and a floating roundoff estimate. It compares successive radii and, for central sampling, left/right quadratic slopes. It shrinks or enlarges the radius to balance truncation and roundoff; supply an initial radius suited to your data when the default scale is unsuitable. The reported step belongs to the best complete stencil; counts include all work and failed off-center attempts.

Only CONVERGED meets MAX(atol,rtol*ABS(value)) with a successive-radius comparison. EVALUATION_LIMIT, ITERATION_LIMIT, ROUNDOFF_LIMIT (a repeated trial radius), RESOLUTION_LIMIT (indistinguishable/nonfinite sample coordinates) and DOMAIN_LIMIT return the best complete estimate when one exists; check the status. Without a complete estimate an error is raised. Callback failure at the center always propagates. Off-center math-domain, division-by-zero and nonfinite results can cause a smaller-radius retry; other callback errors and cancellation propagate immediately. An exhausted domain-retry sequence can report DOMAIN_LIMIT. Native callback time and side effects remain caller-owned.

These are finite binary64 differences and heuristic, not certified, error estimates. No finite sampling scheme guarantees detection of every cusp, jump, high-frequency alias or callback rounding/noise problem. Bilateral checks reject ABS(X) at zero, while explicitly one-sided derivatives return its side slopes. Large input spacing can make local features unresolvable. The chosen radius, accepted estimate and reported error must be interpreted in the function's units; convergence does not prove differentiability. Higher derivatives and multivariable calculus are separate APIs and remain part of the broader calculus inventory.

FNINT(expression,variable,lower,upper[,tolerance]) uses global adaptive 7/15-point Gauss-Kronrod integration with estimated absolute tolerance (default 1E-9). Reversed bounds negate the result. The shared Rust backend refines the worst-error subinterval and tracks exact sums of panel estimates/errors. Triple products avoid prematurely underflowing weighted samples or overflowing the interval width. The defaults permit one million evaluations and 4096 retained subintervals; there is no fixed recursion-depth cutoff. FNINT still returns a scalar or raises an error. Use QUADINT for explicit diagnostics and breakpoints.

QUADINT(fn$,lower,upper[,atol[,rtol[,breakpoints[,maxeval[,maxintervals]]]]]) uses a scalar DEF FN callback and returns {value,estimatedAbsoluteError,evaluations,intervals,status$}. For example:

10 DEF FNF(X)=1/SQR(X)
20 R=QUADINT("FNF",0,1,1E-8):PRINT R
30 DEF FNJ(X)=SGN(X-.3)
40 R=QUADINT("FNJ",0,1,1E-10,0,{.3}):PRINT R

The estimated stopping tolerance is MAX(atol,rtol*ABS(value)); defaults are atol=1E-9, rtol=0. Both must be finite/nonnegative, rtol<=1, and at least one must be positive. Finite bounds may be reversed or equal. Supply up to 4095 distinct, strictly interior finite breakpoints in any order; duplicates and out-of-range points are errors. Initial panels must fit both work limits. maxeval is 15–1000000 and maxintervals is 1–65536, with defaults above. An empty interval makes no callback calls after validation and returns zero.

StatusMeaning
CONVERGEDThe sum of estimated errors meets the global tolerance.
EVALUATION_LIMITAnother complete bisection would exceed maxeval.
INTERVAL_LIMITAnother bisection would exceed the retained-panel cap.
ROUNDOFF_LIMITThe requested tolerance is below the summed roundoff estimate.
RESOLUTION_LIMITFurther refinement cannot form distinct strict-interior binary64 nodes.

Only CONVERGED claims estimated tolerance acceptance. Other statuses include the best complete partition estimate, estimated error and exact work counts; always check the status before using a result as accepted. Invalid options, an initial panel too narrow to hold the nodes, nonfinite arithmetic, callback errors and cancellation raise errors instead of publishing a partial report. The callback's parameters are scoped normally. Native callback side effects are caller-owned; the integrator does not roll them back. Callback work is bounded by count, not by time inside arbitrary native callbacks.

Error estimates use the embedded-rule difference, weighted deviation and a roundoff floor; they are not proof bounds. Finite sampling can miss narrow spikes, oscillations or discontinuities; provide known breakpoints. This is finite real quadrature, not an infinite-interval, Cauchy-principal-value or certified improper-integral solver. Integrable endpoint singularities can work, but resolution can still stop difficult inputs (for example tight integration of 1/SQR(1-X) near the representable endpoint 1). It never quietly evaluates a singular endpoint after a quadrature node rounds onto it. Result/error arithmetic outside binary64 is an explicit error. General convergence or detection of every divergent integrand is not promised. No extrapolation or automatic change of variables is currently performed.

SOLVE(expression,variable,lower,upper[,tolerance]) uses the shared Rust sign-bracketed secant/bisection search. Interpolation is followed by bisection when needed to halve the bracket during each iteration, apart from final floating spacing. FMIN and FMAX use safeguarded parabolic and golden-section searches; their value remains the location of the extremum. Defaults retain an absolute interval tolerance of 1E-9. Original extrema bounds are not sampled.

The scalar wrappers return a point after an evaluated zero, requested interval tolerance, or representable-grid exhaustion as applicable. FMIN/FMAX also retain a best sampled point on an unresolved objective plateau; use the reports below when that distinction matters. Exhausted work/iteration limits, invalid input, callback/nonfinite failures and detected non-unimodal samples raise errors.

ROOTFIND(fn$,lower,upper[,atol[,rtol[,maxeval[,maxiter]]]]) uses a scalar DEF FN callback and returns {point,value,lower,upper,lowerValue,upperValue,evaluations, iterations,status$}. value is the actual callback residual at point. MINFIND and MAXFIND use the same arguments and return the shorter {point,value,lower,upper,evaluations,iterations,status$}. In all reports, the point and its value have actually been evaluated; a limit returns the best complete state, not an unevaluated midpoint.

10 DEF FNF(X)=X^2-2
20 R=ROOTFIND("FNF",0,2,1E-12):PRINT R
30 DEF FNP(X)=(X-2)^2
40 M=MINFIND("FNP",-10,10,1E-10):PRINT M

Bounds must be finite and strictly increasing. Defaults are atol=1E-9, rtol=0, 8195 evaluations and 4096 iterations. Tolerances must be finite/nonnegative, rtol<=1, and at least one positive. Limits are 2–32771 evaluations and 1–16384 iterations. Interval acceptance requires full bracket width no greater than MAX(atol,rtol*ABS(point)); exact represented product comparisons avoid overflow in the width and premature underflow in the relative tolerance. Root endpoint values must be finite and have opposite signs unless an endpoint evaluates to zero. Extrema callbacks are evaluated strictly inside the original bounds.

StatusMeaning
ZERO_FOUNDA root callback evaluated to zero; this includes callback rounding or underflow to zero.
INTERVAL_TOLERANCEThe retained interval meets the requested width. This is not a residual test.
EVALUATION_LIMIT / ITERATION_LIMITThe declared work budget has been exhausted.
RESOLUTION_LIMITNo distinct usable interior trial point can be represented.
VALUE_RESOLUTIONEqual objective samples and a middle probe cannot resolve a strict extremum; small roundoff-sized inversions are included.
NON_UNIMODALAn equal-value pair's middle sample is materially worse, contradicting the stated unimodal assumption for those samples.

A root guarantee requires a continuous function and a genuine sign-changing bracket. A discontinuity can narrow to INTERVAL_TOLERANCE while the reported residual remains nonzero; inspect it. Roots of even multiplicity without a sign change need another method. Root interpolation uses exact weighted ratios, with bounded bisection fallback; it does not enumerate roots or prove existence for arbitrary callbacks.

Extremum searches assume a strictly unimodal objective on the interval (a monotone boundary limit can also be approached). They return approximate points inside open bounds, not proof that an endpoint optimum is attained. They reuse three objective samples and recompute golden steps from the current interval. Equal samples cause a middle probe; an inversion within 32*EPSILON times the sample scale plus eight smallest subnormals is classified as value resolution, not a material shape contradiction. This threshold is a rounding heuristic, not a bound on arbitrary callback noise. Plateaus, rounding, multimodality and narrow unsampled features can prevent reliable position accuracy. Neither these searches nor legacy FMIN/FMAX establish a global optimum for arbitrary functions.

Callbacks must remain deterministic. Errors and cancellation propagate; native callback internals are not preempted and their side effects are not rolled back. Counts include all callback attempts. Each root iteration uses at most two new samples; each extremum iteration normally uses one, or two for an equal-pair probe. Storage and exact-ratio input sizes are fixed, independent of iteration count. BASIC still applies its expression-work, recursion and BREAK controls.

Native scientific functions and 3D mathematics

Numerical qualification and platform limits are recorded in MATH_MATURITY.md. POLYFIT(x,y,degree) uses scaled Householder QR and returns coefficients in descending power order; numerically rank-deficient data raises a math-domain error. POLYADD and POLYSUB align descending-power coefficients and round each exact binary sum once; POLYMUL uses exact binary product accumulation. These operations and scaled QR fitting also share a typed Rust API through NativePolynomial. QUADRATIC scales its discriminant before solving. Signal convolution, correlation, polynomial multiplication, matrix-vector products, and matrix traces use exact binary accumulation before rounding. Native matrix-matrix multiplication retains BLAS performance and retries intermediate overflow with an exact portable kernel.

On Linux, ERF and ERFC use system libm; normal interval probabilities use complementary tails to retain small positive probabilities. BETA uses a scaled logarithmic formulation. PMT chooses discount or growth factors that avoid exponential overflow, and NPV retains cash-flow cancellation residuals. COMPOUND retains small periodic rates with logarithmic growth and combines that growth with the principal before reporting overflow. PV and FV retain zero-rate cash-flow cancellation, small remaining balances, and cancellation between opposing annuity growth terms. BSOPTION(spot,strike,rate,volatility, years,isPut[,dividendYield]) returns a CPU Black-Scholes European option price; isPut is 0 for a call and 1 for a put, and both rates are continuously compounded annual rates. It supports nonnegative volatility and time, including the expiry and zero-volatility limits. BSGREEKS accepts the same arguments and returns {price,delta,gamma,vega,theta,rho}; it requires positive time and volatility. Vega and rho are derivatives per unit change in the annualized input, and theta is annualized calendar-time decay (the negative of differentiation with respect to remaining time to expiry). BINOMIALOPTION(spot,strike,rate,volatility, years,isPut[,dividendYield[,steps]]) returns a CPU American call/put price from a Cox-Ross-Rubinstein tree. steps defaults to 256 and is bounded to 1..2048; the lattice must yield a risk-neutral probability in [0,1]. It uses constant rates, yield and volatility and allows early exercise at lattice nodes. This finite tree is an approximation, not an exact continuum price. BSVOL(price,spot,strike,rate, years,isPut[,dividendYield]) bisects for the annualized volatility matching a European option price. It requires positive time and a price in the no-arbitrage interval: the zero-volatility value is accepted as volatility zero, while prices below that value or at/above the call/put upper bound are errors. Search is bounded to volatility 1,024 and 96 bisection steps; difficult, ill-conditioned inversions near a bound may lose volatility precision. All four option functions use constant rates and volatility and exclude stochastic-volatility and portfolio-risk models. Geometry area and volume functions defer scaling until the result is formed.

List literals may contain numbers, strings and nested lists. For example, C={{"1/2","1/2"},"1/2",{{},{-1},{0,0},{0,0}}} constructs an exact symbolic optimization certificate. Unsuffixed variables store these values, and one-based indexing reads individual elements. Reconstruct a changed record with a new literal, such as D={C(1),"3/2",C(3)}. Numeric functions and numeric DIM-array assignments still require numeric elements; rational strings are consumed by the symbolic APIs. Literals are bounded to one million scalar elements, two million entries including nested containers, 32 nesting levels and 64 MiB of payload. Assignment also enforces the session's retained-storage budget.

Numerical matrices are nested real lists. A={{1,2},{3,4}} constructs a matrix; A(2,1) reads or replaces a cell, and A(1)={5,6} replaces a row. These list indices are one-based independently of OPTION BASE. Nested assignment rejects strings, invalid indices and nesting beyond 32 levels; ordinary DIM arrays keep their existing indexing rules. Functions validate rectangular shapes when used.

Dimensioned numeric arrays bridge directly to these functions through empty subscripts: A() returns an owned nested list in declared dimension order, including unwritten zeros. A()=expression replaces all elements from a list of exactly the same shape. It preserves the array's bounds and capacity, applies its declared element type, and commits only after shape, conversion, and storage checks succeed. The right-hand expression is evaluated once. Existing list values remain independently indexable; an explicit A() always selects the array, even when a scalar named A also exists.

10 OPTION BASE 1
20 DIM SAMPLES(4),RESTORED(4)
30 SAMPLES()={1,2,3,4}
40 SPECTRUM=FFT(SAMPLES())
50 RESTORED()=IFFT(SPECTRUM)
60 FOR I=1 TO 4:PRINT REAL(RESTORED(I)):NEXT I

Both OPTION BASE 0 and 1, local arrays, and BYREF array parameters use the same conversion. Snapshot list indices start at 1; original array indices retain their declared base. Destinations must already be dimensioned. Numeric arrays can carry complex FFT results; integer and real declarations enforce their usual conversions. String and whole-record arrays are not supported by this numeric bridge. Snapshots are bounded to one million numeric elements, 32 dimensions, and two million total list entries including nested containers. Assignments invalidate any cached graphics pixels associated with the array.

NORMALIZE scales before calculating magnitude, so a finite vector can be normalized even when its norm would overflow. SKEWNESS and KURTOSIS center and scale their moments to avoid overflow/underflow for very large or small finite datasets; they retain their adjusted sample conventions.

LERP(start,end,amount) preserves endpoints and supports finite interpolation between opposite extreme values without overflowing their distance. SMOOTHSTEP(edge0,edge1,value) clamps outside its edges, supports reversed edges, and scales overflowing edge distances. Equal edges report division by zero.

WRAP(value,minimum,maximum) returns a value in [minimum,maximum); equal or reversed bounds report illegal quantity. Values already inside the interval are preserved, and the upper endpoint wraps to the lower endpoint. Extreme widths avoid intermediate overflow, and operands are reduced before subtracting the origin to retain the remainder. If rounding reaches the excluded upper boundary, the result is the nearest representable value below it.

MAPRANGE(value,input0,input1,output0,output1) supports reversed ranges and extrapolation. It combines scale factors before rounding, preserving representable results even when the intermediate ratio would overflow or underflow. Input endpoints map exactly to output endpoints; symmetric ranges are mapped about zero to avoid cancellation of small values. Equal input endpoints report division by zero. A final unrepresentable result still reports real overflow.

CROSS(left,right) computes a three-dimensional cross product. Each component uses exact binary64 products and rounds only after subtraction, preserving cancellation and tiny results. Both vectors must have exactly three elements; an unrepresentable final component reports real overflow.

DOT(left,right) accumulates exact products of the converted binary64 inputs and rounds once at the end. Large cancelling products and tiny products that sum to a representable value are retained. Different lengths report a dimension mismatch; two empty vectors return zero. Final overflow remains an error.

ARANGE(start,stop,step) generates rounded start + index*step values with one fused multiply-add per element. The stop endpoint is excluded after rounding; boundary samples are checked rather than trusting only a rounded step count. Very small steps can produce repeated values. Zero steps and steps pointing away from the stop remain errors, and the list-size limit still applies.

LINSPACE(start,stop,count) includes both endpoints when count is at least two. Each intermediate value uses exact integer-weighted binary64 endpoints, then divides and rounds once, including subnormal values. A count of zero returns an empty list; a count of one returns only the starting value.

HISTOGRAM(values,bins[,minimum,maximum]) computes finite edges using exact weighted endpoints when the bounds differ. Counts use those returned rounded edges: interior boundary values go to the bin on their right, and the maximum belongs to the final bin. Repeated edges create empty bins. Values outside the bounds are ignored. Equal bounds retain the existing unit-spaced edge convention and place matching values in the final bin.

GEOMEAN requires strictly positive data. Constant data returns that value exactly; otherwise logarithms are accumulated exactly before averaging. The final result is bounded by the input minimum and maximum. Logarithm and exponential approximations still contribute floating-point error.

PERCENTILE and QUARTILE retain their linear rank interpolation. After selecting the adjacent sorted values, interpolation terms are accumulated exactly and rounded once, preserving subnormal midpoints and avoiding overflow between opposite extremes. Rank calculations themselves use binary64 arithmetic.

CUMPROD(values) keeps a scaled running product, so a prefix rounded to zero by underflow can recover when later factors bring it back into range. An actual zero factor keeps subsequent products zero. Every prefix must remain finite; a prefix overflow reports real overflow even if later factors would reduce it. Mantissa arithmetic remains binary64; these products are not exact arithmetic.

CUMSUM(values) retains an exact running sum of converted binary64 inputs, rounding each output independently. Rounding an earlier prefix does not discard residuals needed by later prefixes: CUMSUM({1E16,1,-1E16}) ends in 1. Every prefix must be representable; an overflowing prefix reports real overflow even if later cancellation would make the final total finite.

TOTAL and MEAN accumulate their converted binary64 inputs exactly before rounding the final result. MEAN divides the exact accumulated sum before that rounding; even-length MEDIAN uses the same approach for its middle pair. For example, TOTAL({1E16,1,-1E16}) returns 1 and MEAN({1E308,1E308}) returns 1E308. A genuinely unrepresentable final total still reports overflow.

In modern numeric mode, SUM(list) and SUM(expression,index,first,last[,step]) also retain cancellation residuals and round only the final sum. The indexed form still evaluates each term in binary64. List sums preserve all integer input bits; an integer-only result remains an integer and must fit signed 64 bits. A real or complex result rounds each component once. Nested list sums reduce along the outer dimension with the usual scalar broadcasting and matching-length checks. Expression work, nesting and output-size limits apply. Legacy numeric mode retains its existing intermediate range checks and summation behavior.

PRODUCT tracks scale separately so intermediate overflow or underflow does not discard a representable final product.
