Covariance, correlation and linear regression center and scale their data before forming products. Variance and standard deviation instead accumulate exact first/second moments and round the final variance or square root once. BASIC integer samples preserve all 64 bits, including mixed integer/real lists; they are not first rounded to binary64. For example, VARP({9223372036854775807,9223372036854775806}) returns 0.25. STDEVP({-1E308,1E308}) returns 1E308, although VARP for those inputs exceeds the real-number range. MODE groups positive and negative zero as the same numeric value. Statistical domain and minimum sample-size checks remain enforced.

TSAVE(path$[,handles]) writes a data-only tensor checkpoint through the normal sandboxed file store and returns its byte length. Omit handles to save every leaf in ascending handle order, or pass an ordered list of distinct leaf handles. Derived graph handles are rejected; use TDETACH for a constant snapshot when appropriate. Empty selections are valid. TLOAD(path$) validates the entire checkpoint and returns fresh leaf handles in saved order, retaining existing session tensors. TCLEAR before loading replaces a model explicitly; handles are never reused within that session. Rebuild the forward graph and call TBACKWARD before the next optimizer step.

10 W=TPARAM({.1,.2}):Y=TENSOR({1,2})
20 LOSS=TMSE(W,Y):D=TBACKWARD(LOSS):D=TADAM(.05)
30 BYTES=TSAVE("model.mbtc",{W})
40 D=TCLEAR():H=TLOAD("model.mbtc"):W=H(1)
50 Y=TENSOR({1,2}):LOSS=TMSE(W,Y):D=TBACKWARD(LOSS):D=TADAM(.05)

Checkpoints preserve finite binary64 values bit-for-bit (including signed zero), shape, trainability, and Adam first/second moments, step counts and beta values. They contain no BASIC source, executable graph, session handles or gradients. Learning rates, epsilon, data order, RNG, epoch/scheduler and other application state remain the program's responsibility. Save at optimizer boundaries for training continuation. A changed Adam beta remains an error after restore, just as before saving; learning-rate/epsilon arguments still come from the program.

The little-endian MBTC schema-1 binary format is independent of backend release versions and freely editable user source. CRC32 detects accidental corruption; it is not an authentication signature. Files are bounded to 64 MiB and the host's configured file limit, covering the engine's supported leaf/Adam state without BASIC string limits. Existing 8,192-node, one-million-elements-per-tensor and two-million-live-elements limits still apply. Unknown versions, malformed shapes, nonfinite values, invalid Adam state, CRC/truncation, capacity/handle overflow or cancellation fail before restore commits. The bounded commit appends all new leaves together and leaves existing graphs/gradients untouched. Export validation and encoding complete before atomic file replacement. File-root authorization, relative paths and symlink protections are unchanged; loading grants no host capabilities. Rust modules inside the runtime crate can use TensorEngine::save_state/restore_state with byte buffers and choose their own authorized storage.

MATHBACKEND$() reports available native BLAS/LAPACK support. MATMUL(A,B) uses LP64 CBLAS when available, with a cache-friendly Rust fallback. Inputs and output retain the one-million-element matrix limit; matrix products allow up to one billion multiply-adds and check cancellation between batches. This does not change the separate Dartmouth MAT statement budget or integer/complex semantics.

TRANSPOSE(A[,shape]), MATMUL(A,B[,leftshape[,rightshape]]), the square operations DET(A[,shape]), INVERSE(A[,shape]), and TRACE(A[,shape]), and the decomposition functions documented above accept explicit two-element {rows,columns} shapes. Every axis must be an exact nonnegative integer no greater than one million, and data must match it. Nested rows represent matrices; {} can represent any 0-by-n matrix only when its shape is supplied. {{},{}} is a 2-by-0 matrix. A fourth argument selects matrix-matrix multiplication, even for an empty right operand. With three arguments and a flat right list, the ordinary matrix-vector rule applies. The square operations reject unequal axes. For a 0-by-0 matrix, DET returns 1, INVERSE returns {}, and TRACE returns 0. These definitions support the empty identity matrix and do not infer width from an empty BASIC list. For example, a full-rank matrix's empty nullspace has the zero projector:

10 B=NULLSPACE(IDENTITY(3))
20 BT=TRANSPOSE(B,{3,0})
30 PRINT MATMUL(B,BT,{3,0},{0,3})
40 PRINT MATMUL(B,{}, {3,0})

The results are a 3-by-3 zero matrix and a three-element zero vector. Explicit shapes are checked even when the output has no entries. A product with a zero inner dimension still checks the full output allocation limit. Outputs remain ordinary nested lists; no hidden shape metadata is attached. Retain the calculated shape and supply it again when a zero-row result's width would otherwise be lost. Existing one-argument transpose and two-argument multiplication preserve their conventions. Other decompositions/tensor imports retain their own nonempty-input requirements; this is not universal empty-array support. Rust math_engine::shaped::Matrix retains both axes natively across transpose and multiplication and shares ordinary multiplication/accumulation.

KRON(A,B) (alias MATKRON) constructs a real dense Kronecker product. For A of shape m by n and B of shape p by q, the result is mp by nq; entry (i*p+r,j*q+s) equals A(i,j)*B(r,s) with zero-based mathematical indices. KRONSUM(A,B) requires square A of order m and B of order n and returns KRON(IDENTITY(n),A)+KRON(B,IDENTITY(m)), matching SciPy's argument order. These operations return ordinary nested lists that compose with MATMUL, LINSOLVE, decompositions and tensor import. For example:

10 X={{-2,1},{1,-2}}
20 L=KRONSUM(X,X)
30 PRINT MATMUL(L,{0,1,1,0})

Both operations require nonempty rectangular real matrices; empty, ragged, non-real or nonsquare sum inputs raise errors. Each input and output is limited to one million entries, with checked dimension products before output allocation. Native Rust kernels check cancellation during validation and construction. Unrepresentable results raise real overflow; ordinary binary64 product/addition rounding and underflow apply. These are dense constructors, not sparse or matrix-free operators. Large grids should use the existing sparse APIs.

KRONSMV(A,B,x) applies I_n ⊗ A + B ⊗ I_m directly to a row-major flattened vector x, where A and B are nonempty square real matrices of orders m and n. It returns a vector of length m*n without allocating the (m*n) × (m*n) operator. It is useful for grid stencils and separable systems when only the operator action is needed. Factor storage and vector length use the one-million element limit; the total nonzero-factor multiply count is capped at ten million. Products are accumulated exactly from their binary64 inputs and rounded once per output. Dimension mismatches, non-finite inputs, work-limit overruns, cancellation or unrepresentable outputs raise errors.

10 A={{2,-1},{-1,2}}
20 PRINT KRONSMV(A,A,{1,2,3,4})

KRONSCG(A,B,b[,rtol,atol,maxiter,initial]) solves (I_n ⊗ A + B ⊗ I_m)*x=b through the shared Rust conjugate-gradient kernel, without constructing the grid matrix. Both factors must be exactly symmetric; their combined operator must have a finite positive diagonal. Positive definiteness of the combined operator is a caller requirement, not a solver certificate; either factor may itself be indefinite. Jacobi equilibration is computed from the combined diagonal. Nonpositive curvature encountered during iteration returns BREAKDOWN.

The result is {x,status,iterations,residual,threshold}, matching SPCG and composable through DEF FN. Convergence uses a freshly accumulated original operator residual and threshold=MAX(atol,rtol*NORM(b)), never the recurrence residual alone. status is CONVERGED, MAXITER or BREAKDOWN. Defaults are rtol=1E-8, atol=0, maxiter=MIN(10000,MAX(20,10*m*n)), and a zero initial vector. Require 0<=rtol<1, atol>=0, at least one positive tolerance, and an integer iteration limit from 0 through 100000. A solved initial vector may return CONVERGED at iteration zero; otherwise a zero limit returns MAXITER.

The factor/vector bounds of KRONSMV apply, plus a shared per-solve budget of 100 million work units. Work exhaustion, cancellation, nonfinite input, invalid shape or unrepresentable scaling raises an error; no partial success report is returned. See the editable `matrix_free_poisson.bas` for an analytic two-mode Dirichlet Poisson problem. This API covers separable symmetric positive systems; general operator graphs and matrix-free nonsymmetric solvers remain separate capabilities.

On Linux, these functions require the standard LP64 liblapack.so.3 runtime:

FunctionResult and convention
SVD(A[,shape]){U,S,VT}, reduced factors with A=MATMUL(MATMUL(U,DIAG(S)),VT); singular values descending
QR(A[,shape]){Q,R}, reduced QR; Q has orthonormal columns
EIGH(A[,shape]){values,vectors} for real symmetric A; eigenvalues ascending, eigenvectors in columns
CHOLESKY(A[,shape])Lower factor L of a real symmetric positive-definite matrix: A=L*TRN(L)
SYMSOLVE(A,B)Solve real symmetric-indefinite A*X=B with pivoted CPU LAPACK; B may be a vector or matrix of right-hand sides
PINV(A[,rcond][,shape])SVD pseudoinverse, including rank-deficient rectangular matrices
LSTSQ(A,b[,rcond][,shape])Minimum-norm least-squares solution for a real vector b

SVD, QR, EIGH, and CHOLESKY accept an optional shape as their second argument; PINV accepts it last after rcond, and LSTSQ accepts it last after rcond. For PINV(A,{rows,columns}) and LSTSQ(A,b,{rows,columns}), a list in the optional rcond position is treated as shape metadata. The rules for dimensions and nested-list data above apply. EIGH and CHOLESKY require equal axes. For a zero-axis rectangular matrix with k=MIN(rows,columns)=0, reduced QR returns Q of shape rows-by-0 and R of shape 0-by-columns; SVD returns U of shape rows-by-0, an empty singular-value list, and VT of shape 0-by-columns. EIGH and CHOLESKY accept the 0-by-0 case. PINV returns the all-zero columns-by-rows matrix, and LSTSQ returns a zero vector of length columns. Returned values remain ordinary nested lists, so retain the declared dimensions when an output has zero rows.

SYMSOLVE(A,B) requires nonempty, square, finite, real A and checks symmetry relative to each mirrored coefficient pair. It uses LAPACK's Bunch-Kaufman diagonal pivoting, so indefinite systems with zero diagonal entries can use 2-by-2 pivots; positive definiteness is not required. A vector B returns a vector, and a matrix B returns a matrix with one solution column per right-hand side. Nonsymmetric, singular, nonfinite, dimension-mismatched and unrepresentable systems raise BASIC errors. The operation requires Linux LP64 liblapack.so.3, is bounded by the shared native-work ceiling, and checks cancellation before and after the native call. The typed Rust API is modernbasic::solve_symmetric_indefinite and accepts matrices of RHS columns.

10 A={{0,2},{2,0}}:B={4,6}:X=SYMSOLVE(A,B)
20 PRINT X(1):PRINT X(2)
30 M=SYMSOLVE(A,{{4,8},{6,10}})
40 PRINT M(1,1):PRINT M(2,2)

CLUFACT(A) factors a nonsingular square complex matrix once and returns an editable packet {packedLU,rowSwaps,originalMatrix,matrixScale}. packedLU and originalMatrix are row-major nested lists; rowSwaps contains one-based pivot rows, one per elimination step. The factorization uses scaled partial row pivoting and checks the input dimensions and finite arithmetic. CLLUSOLVE(F,b) reuses that packet for either a vector RHS or a matrix whose columns are RHS vectors. For a vector it returns {solution,residualNorm}; for a matrix it returns {solutionMatrix,residualNorms}, with each solution in the corresponding column and one fresh residual per RHS. The original matrix is retained in the packet so residuals are checked against the unscaled input. Packet fields are validated when used; malformed pivots, dimensions, scales or singular factors raise BASIC errors. Each matrix axis is limited to 128 and solve work is bounded.

CLINVERSE(A) returns the inverse of a nonsingular square complex matrix. The Rust backend factors A once with scaled partial-pivoted LU, solves all identity columns from that factor, and checks each fresh residual against the original matrix. The result is an ordinary complex nested-list matrix that composes with CLMATMUL. Each axis is limited to 128; singular, nonfinite or unrepresentable results raise errors. Native Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::inverse().

CLINSOLVE(A,b) solves a bounded square complex system with native CPU Rust partial row pivoting. A and b are nested lists containing real values or COMPLEX(real,imaginary) values. It returns {solution,residualNorm}; the residual is freshly computed from the original matrix. Systems are limited to 128 rows and singular pivots, nonfinite intermediate values and invalid shapes raise BASIC errors. Native Rust consumers can use NativeComplexMatrix::new(rows,columns,row_major_values).solve(rhs) and receive NativeComplexSolveResult with the same residual.

CLMATMUL(A,B) multiplies bounded complex matrices using exact binary product accumulation and one final rounding per real and imaginary output component. CLADJOINT(A) returns the complex conjugate transpose. Each matrix axis is limited to 128; matrix multiplication is capped at 4,194,304 real product terms and checks cancellation between output rows. Both return ordinary nested lists that compose with CLINSOLVE, CLSTSQ and other matrix consumers. Native Rust uses NativeComplexMatrix::multiply, adjoint, shape and values.

CLQR(A) computes an unpivoted reduced complex Householder factorization and returns {Q,R} with A=Q*R, orthonormal columns in Q, and upper trapezoidal R. For m-by-n A, Q is m-by-k and R is k-by-n where k=MIN(m,n). Rank-deficient matrices are accepted; columns are not pivoted and R diagonal entries are not a rank certificate. Each axis is limited to 128 and work to 16,777,216 bounded units. Cancellation and unrepresentable results raise errors. Q and R are ordinary complex nested lists, and can be recombined with CLMATMUL and CLADJOINT. Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::qr() and receive NativeComplexQrResult.

CSVDVALS(A) returns the descending singular values of any finite complex rectangular matrix. The Rust CPU backend maps it to a real block matrix, uses the Linux LP64 LAPACK singular-values-only path, then merges each duplicated complex singular value pair with one exact average. Each axis is limited to 128; work and convergence follow the shared LAPACK SVD bounds. Rank-deficient matrices return zero singular values normally. Native Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::singular_values(). The function returns values only; it does not return complex singular vectors.

CSVD(A) returns {U,S,VH} for a finite complex rectangular matrix, where A=U*D*VH, D is the diagonal matrix formed from descending nonnegative values in S, and VH contains conjugate-transposed right singular vectors. The factors are reduced: for k=MIN(rows,columns), U is rows × k, S has k values, and VH is k × columns. Each input axis is limited to 128. The Linux CPU backend calls complex LAPACK ZGESVD, scales the input before factorization, and checks factor orthogonality and the reconstruction residual before returning. Rank-deficient and zero matrices are supported. Shape, convergence, nonfinite and unrepresentable-result failures raise errors. Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::svd() and receive NativeComplexSvdResult.

CHEIGVALS(A) returns ascending real eigenvalues of a Hermitian complex matrix. The Rust CPU backend maps the Hermitian matrix to a real symmetric matrix and uses the Linux LP64 LAPACK EIGH path; eigenvalue multiplicity is preserved. A must be square and at most 128 by 128. Diagonal entries must be real; mirrored off-diagonal components are checked at a scale-relative 64-epsilon tolerance. Non-Hermitian, nonsquare, nonconvergent, or unrepresentable results raise errors. Native Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::hermitian_eigenvalues(). General complex matrices and complex eigenvectors are not handled by this function.

CHEIGEN(A) returns {eigenvalues,eigenvectors} for a bounded Hermitian complex matrix. Eigenvalues are ascending and repeated according to multiplicity; eigenvectors are normalized columns in the second matrix. The CPU Rust backend realifies the Hermitian system, recovers a complex basis from repeated real clusters, and checks each eigenpair residual before returning. Matrix axes are limited to 128. Non-Hermitian or numerically unresolved eigenpairs raise errors. Native Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::hermitian_eigen() and receive NativeComplexHermitianEigenResult.

CGEIGVALS(A) returns all general complex eigenvalues, including algebraic multiplicity. CGEIGEN(A) returns {eigenvalues,eigenvectors} for a square complex matrix that need not be Hermitian. Eigenvalues are sorted by real and then imaginary component; each matching eigenvector is a unit-norm column, but columns need not be mutually orthogonal. The Linux CPU LAPACK ZGEEV path checks each right-eigenpair residual against the original matrix before returning. Matrix axes are limited to 128 and queried complex workspace is capped at 128 MiB. Defective and repeated-root matrices are supported when the provider returns residual-checked eigenvectors; near-defective eigenvectors can be ill-conditioned, and no forward-error or eigenvector-stability guarantee is made. Native Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::eigen() and receive NativeComplexEigenResult. The editable `complex_general_eigen.bas` example checks a non-normal triangular system and a complex-conjugate pair.

For real square matrices, GEIGVALS(A) and GEIGEN(A) provide the same general nonsymmetric spectrum, returning complex eigenvalues when necessary. Typed Rust callers can use NativeRealMatrix::general_eigen(); it reuses the checked complex CPU eigensolver and returns NativeComplexEigenResult. This path has the same Linux LAPACK dependency and 128-axis bound. The editable `real_general_eigen.bas` checks the ±i modes of a real rotation matrix and their residuals.

For a real pencil, GEIGGEN(A,B) returns {alpha,beta,eigenvectors} with beta*A*x=alpha*B*x, preserving finite, infinite and indeterminate pairs. Typed Rust callers use NativeRealMatrix::generalized_eigen(&b). Both real matrices are converted to the shared complex CPU solver under the same 128-axis and Linux LAPACK limits. The editable `real_generalized_eigen.bas` checks the two-mass vibration modes against independent analytic values.

CGEIGCOND(A) returns {eigenvalues,reciprocal_conditions} in the same sorted order. Each estimate is |yᴴx|/(||y||₂||x||₂) from matched left and right eigenvectors; values near zero flag eigenvalues that may move substantially under small matrix perturbations. Both left and right residuals are checked. This is a local sensitivity estimate, not an eigenvalue error bound. NativeComplexMatrix::eigen_sensitivity() returns the same typed data in NativeComplexEigenSensitivityResult. The editable `complex_eigen_sensitivity.bas` compares a non-normal matrix with a nearly defective one. Typed real callers can use NativeRealMatrix::eigen_sensitivity() directly; it reuses the same checked CPU kernel without constructing a complex matrix.

CGEIGGEN(A,B) returns {alpha,beta,eigenvectors} for the generalized pencil A*x=(alpha/beta)*B*x. Alpha and beta are returned as jointly normalized complex values, so callers can retain the projective pair without dividing. Finite eigenvalues have nonzero beta; beta zero denotes an infinite eigenvalue; alpha and beta both zero denote an indeterminate pair. Eigenvectors are unit norm and residual-checked against beta*A*x-alpha*B*x. The Linux CPU LAPACK ZGGEV implementation supports singular B, with axes limited to 128, bounded work and a 128 MiB queried-workspace cap. Native Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::generalized_eigen() and receive NativeComplexGeneralEigenResult. The editable `complex_generalized_eigen.bas` checks finite and infinite cases.

CGEIGGENCOND(A,B) returns {alpha,beta,reciprocal_conditions} from the Linux LP64 LAPACK ZGGEVX estimator. The alpha/beta pairs and estimates keep the driver's matching order; B may be singular and infinite eigenvalues remain represented with beta zero. Estimates are nonnegative, may exceed one, and near-zero values flag sensitive eigenvalues. This is a local diagnostic rather than a forward-error bound. Typed Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::generalized_eigen_sensitivity(&b). The editable `generalized_eigen_sensitivity.bas` checks analytic modes from a two-mass vibration pencil.

CCHOLESKY(A) computes a lower-triangular complex factor L such that A=L*CLADJOINT(L) for a Hermitian positive-definite square matrix. Diagonal entries must be real; mirrored entries are checked with the same scale-relative tolerance as CHEIGVALS. The CPU Rust implementation scales the matrix before factorization and exactly accumulates the complex inner products. Indefinite, singular, non-Hermitian, nonfinite or unrepresentable inputs raise errors. Each axis is limited to 128 and factorization work to 8,388,608 bounded units. The result is an ordinary nested list and composes with CLMATMUL and CLADJOINT. Native Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::cholesky().

10 A={{4,COMPLEX(1,2)},{COMPLEX(1,-2),6}}
20 L=CCHOLESKY(A):R=CLMATMUL(L,CLADJOINT(L))
30 PRINT ABS(R(1,2)-COMPLEX(1,2))<1E-10

CLSTSQ(A,b) fits an overdetermined complex system with column-pivoted Householder QR. A must have between one and 128 rows and columns, with rows at least the column count; the matrix must have full column rank at the relative QR threshold. It returns {solution,residualNorm,normalResidualNorm}, where the normal residual is ||Aᴴ(b-Ax)||₂. Rank-deficient and underdetermined inputs raise BASIC errors. Work is bounded, scaling protects common extreme magnitudes, and the reported residuals use the original matrix. Native Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::rectangular(rows,columns,row_major_values).least_squares(rhs).

CLSTSQMIN(A,b[,rcond]) uses the reduced complex SVD to fit rectangular, rank-deficient or underdetermined systems and returns the minimum-Euclidean-norm minimizer as {solution,residualNorm,normalResidualNorm,numericalRank}. rcond must be in [0,1]; singular values at or below rcond * largestSingularValue are discarded. The default cutoff is max(rows,columns) * machineEpsilon. Numerical rank is a floating-point estimate, not an exact certificate. The matrix axes are limited to 128 and the same bounded SVD work limits apply. Native Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::least_squares_minimum_norm(rhs, rcond).

10 A={{1/SQR(2),COMPLEX(0,1/SQR(2)),0},{0,0,1}}
20 R=CLSTSQMIN(A,{COMPLEX(2,2),COMPLEX(-1,0.5)}):X=R(1)
30 PRINT X(1):PRINT X(2):PRINT X(3):PRINT R(4)
10 A={{COMPLEX(1,1),2},{COMPLEX(2,-1),COMPLEX(1,1)},{0.5,COMPLEX(-1,2)},{COMPLEX(0,2),3}}
20 B={COMPLEX(-7,4),COMPLEX(0.5,0.5),COMPLEX(2.5,-5.5),COMPLEX(-13,3.5)}
30 R=CLSTSQ(A,B):X=R(1):PRINT X(1):PRINT X(2):PRINT R(2):PRINT R(3)

CLSTSQMINM(A,B[,rcond]) fits several response columns using one reduced complex SVD and returns {solutionMatrix,fitResiduals,normalResiduals,rank, cutoff}. This shares the minimum-norm subspace and rank estimate across all responses. Axes are capped at 128 and aggregate solve work is bounded. Native Rust callers use NativeComplexMatrix::least_squares_minimum_norm_many to reuse one decomposition without constructing interpreter values.

10 A={{COMPLEX(1,1),2},{COMPLEX(0,3),COMPLEX(4,-1)}}
20 R=CLINSOLVE(A,{COMPLEX(1,5),COMPLEX(1,15)}):X=R(1)
30 PRINT X(1):PRINT X(2):PRINT R(2)

RREF(A) (alias MATRREF) computes reduced row echelon form with exact rational pivot decisions, then rounds each output once to a finite binary64 value. SYMRREF(A) preserves the exact result as canonical integer/fraction strings. RREFPIVOTS(A) returns one-based pivot-column indices, independent of OPTION BASE. RREFINFO(A) returns {exactReducedMatrix,pivotColumns,exactRank} from one reduction. Zero rows remain in their original matrix dimensions, ordered after pivot rows. All accept nonempty rectangular matrices with each dimension from 1 through 64.

Integer entries retain all integer bits. Real entries mean their exact stored binary64 values. String entries accept signed decimal/scientific literals or one quotient of two such literals, for example "0.1", "-2/7", "1e-300"; these are parsed exactly. Expressions and variable names in strings are rejected. Consequently SYMRREF({{"0.1","0.3"}}) gives {{"1","3"}}, while unquoted 0.1 and 0.3 retain their separate binary approximations. Printed strings may appear without quotation marks; the returned BASIC values remain strings.

10 A={{1,2,1},{2,4,3}}
20 PRINT RREF(A)
30 PRINT RREFPIVOTS(A)
40 PRINT RREFINFO(A)

This yields numeric rows {{1,2,0},{0,0,1}}, pivots {1,3}, and exact rank 2. The exact rank is algebraic for the supplied rational/stored-binary inputs, with no tolerance argument; it differs from numerical MATRANK. Existing HPRANK retains its documented input grammar and dimension limits and shares the exact elimination kernel. Rounded RREF can underflow small free entries or raise real overflow on unrepresentable results; use SYMRREF to preserve them.

Resource bounds include 64 KiB total string input, 8,192 bytes per literal, 1 MiB exact output text, 4,096 bits per normalized numerator/denominator, two million reduction work units and the shared 32-million-unit coefficient budget (charged by integer width). Decimal power after accounting for fractional digits is limited to [-1233,1233]. Intermediate coefficient growth can refuse a problem within the dimension limit. Rust checks cancellation while parsing, reducing and converting; failures return no partial matrix. No Python or native LAPACK service is used for exact row reduction.

COLSPACE(A[,rcond]) (alias MATCOLSPACE) returns an orthonormal basis for the numerical column space. ROWSPACE(A[,rcond]) returns an orthonormal basis for the numerical row space. NULLSPACE(A[,rcond]) (alias MATNULL) returns an orthonormal basis for the numerical right null space, including the additional right-null directions of wide matrices. All basis vectors are columns: for m by n A with numerical rank r, the output shapes are m by r, n by r and n by (n-r), respectively. Column-space vectors need not be original columns of A.

Inputs must be nonempty rectangular real matrices. The cutoff policy matches MATRANK: retain singular values whose ratio to the largest is strictly above rcond, default MAX(m,n)*2.220446049250313e-16, with rcond in [0,1]. A dropped small singular value produces an approximate null direction; increasing the cutoff can deliberately classify nonzero directions as null. This is numerical subspace estimation, not an exact algebraic certificate. SVD roundoff can affect a decision at the threshold. Entry normalization shares the condition/rank backend; extreme relative entries may underflow during scaling.

An empty basis preserves its ambient dimension using rows of empty lists: NULLSPACE(IDENTITY(2)) returns {{},{}}. A zero matrix has empty column/row bases and a full identity right-null basis. Use explicit shapes with TRANSPOSE/MATMUL when an empty basis loses its width on transposition; for an n-by-zero basis B, MATMUL(B,{}, {n,0},{0,n}) gives its zero projector. Basis signs and orientations within a repeated/degenerate subspace are not fixed; compare orthogonal projectors or residuals when comparing separate computations.

For a nonempty null basis Z, MATMUL(A,Z) is approximately zero at the selected cutoff, and MATMUL(TRANSPOSE(Z),Z) is approximately an identity. Column-space projection uses MATMUL(C,TRANSPOSE(C)) with C=COLSPACE(A):

10 A={{1,1,0,0},{0,1,1,0}}
20 Z=NULLSPACE(A)
30 V=MATMUL(Z,{2,3})
40 PRINT MATMUL(A,V)

These use checked LP64 SVD with one-million-entry input/output limits. Null-space construction also bounds full n by n right-vector workspace to one million entries and conservatively budgets 8*m*n*MIN(m,n)+8*n*n*MIN(m,n) work units against the one-billion native limit. Column/row bases use the reduced SVD budget 8*m*n*MIN(m,n). LAPACK workspace is capped at 128 MB. Native calls check cancellation before/after; Rust validation and extraction also check cancellation.

LU(A) (alias MATLU) returns {L,U,P} using partial row pivoting, with MATMUL(P,A)=MATMUL(L,U). For m by n input and k=MIN(m,n), L is m by k, U is k by n, and P is m by m. L has a unit diagonal. This convention uses the transpose of the permutation in SciPy's A=P*L*U interface.

LUFACTOR(A) returns a reusable ordinary list {packedMatrix,rowSwaps}. The packed matrix contains U on/above its diagonal and L below its diagonal, with L's ones implicit. rowSwaps has k exact integer entries: at step i, interchange row i with rowSwaps(i). The serialized indices are always one-based, independent of OPTION BASE; each pivot at step i must be in [i,m]. These are a sequence of swaps, not the final row ordering. Native Rust kernels use zero-based swaps internally. Both factor functions accept nonempty rectangular real inputs.

LUSOLVE(factors,b) requires square packed factors. It returns a vector when b is a nonempty vector, or a matrix when b supplies one or more right-hand-side columns. Reuse the same factors for multiple solves; factors and right-hand sides are not modified. For example:

10 A={{0,2},{1,3}}
20 F=LUFACTOR(A)
30 PRINT LUSOLVE(F,{2,4})
40 PRINT LUSOLVE(F,{{4,2},{8,4}})

Factor packets are editable lists; LUSOLVE checks their shape, finite entries, pivot counts/ranges and exact integral indices before native calls. This validates the packet format, not that it represents an independently supplied original A. Zero U diagonal entries are allowed for factor inspection, but solving rejects them. No fixed absolute pivot cutoff is used. Near-singular systems can still have large solution errors; use COND/RCOND and numerical residuals to assess sensitivity. This is binary64 LU, not exact rank certification or a rank-revealing replacement for SVD. Nonfinite factor/solution outputs raise real overflow.

Input, packed output, each expanded factor and RHS/result matrices retain the one-million-entry limit. LU also checks its m*m permutation limit before factorization; LUFACTOR avoids that dense permutation. Conservative work estimates are 2*m*n*MIN(m,n) for factorization and 2*n*n*rhsColumns for solving, each capped at one billion operations. These APIs use checked LP64 LAPACK DGETRF/DGETRS; cancellation is checked before/after native calls, not mid-kernel. Overflow/underflow and ill-conditioning limits still apply.

SVDVALS(A) returns the MIN(rows,columns) real singular values in descending order without allocating U/VT factors. It uses the same checked LP64 LAPACK boundary as SVD. COND(A) (alias MATCOND) estimates the real 2-norm condition number, largest/smallest singular value; RCOND(A) estimates its reciprocal. These accept nonempty rectangular real matrices, including full-row-rank wide matrices. A finite rectangular condition does not assert square invertibility. RCOND is specifically the reciprocal 2-norm condition, not LAPACK's 1-norm/infinity-norm reciprocal estimator.

MATRANK(A[,rcond]) counts singular values whose ratio to the largest is strictly above rcond, default MAX(rows,columns)*2.220446049250313e-16. The cutoff must be in [0,1]; zero retains every computed positive singular value. This is a numerical rank decision, not an exact algebraic certificate. COND and RCOND retain small computed singular values rather than discarding them at this rank cutoff. For example COND({{1,0},{0,1E-20}}) is 1E20 even though default MATRANK returns 1.

Condition/rank analysis scales entries by their largest magnitude before SVD, so changing units alone does not overflow the singular-value spectrum. All-zero matrices have rank and reciprocal condition zero. A computed zero smallest singular value makes COND raise an unbounded-condition error; a ratio exceeding binary64 range raises real overflow. BASIC real values never contain infinity or NaN. RCOND can underflow to zero. Scaling can underflow exceptionally small relative entries; near singularity, SVD roundoff may produce a tiny nonzero tail for an exactly dependent matrix. These estimates do not prove exact singularity or resolve arbitrary dynamic range. SVDVALS returns unscaled values and reports overflow if they cannot be represented, even where normalized COND succeeds. Input, work, workspace and native-call cancellation limits are those of SVD.

For PINV/LSTSQ, rcond defaults to MAX(rows,columns)*2.220446049250313e-16; values must be in [0,1]. Singular values at or below rcond times the largest are discarded. Decompositions reject empty/ragged/non-real inputs, report non-convergence/domain errors, and bound work conservatively to one billion estimated operations. LAPACK workspace is capped at 16 million doubles (128 MB). Cancellation is checked before/after each LAPACK call; a call cannot be interrupted mid-kernel. Native libraries may use threads controlled by their host settings (e.g. OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS). The appliance depends on libblas3 and liblapack3; standalone executables use the host libraries and give an error if a requested decomposition backend is absent. No Python runtime is used for these calculations.

KRONSGMRES(A,B,b[,rtol,atol,maxiter,initial,restart]) solves (I_n ⊗ A + B ⊗ I_m)*x=b using the same restarted CPU GMRES recurrence as SPGMRES, without assembling the full grid matrix. Factors are nonempty square real matrices and the field is flattened row-major, as for KRONSMV. Factors need not be symmetric or positive definite. Row equilibration is used; this interface does not assemble an ILU preconditioner. The result is {solution,status,iterations,residualNorm,threshold}. Status can be CONVERGED, MAXITER, BREAKDOWN or STAGNATED; convergence is decided using the original operator residual, with threshold MAX(rtol*NORM(b),atol).

Defaults match KRONSCG: rtol 1E-8, atol zero, maxiter CLAMP(10*dimension,20,10000) and a zero initial vector. Restart must be an integer from 1 through 128; its default is MIN(30,dimension,FLOOR(2000000/dimension)-1). The effective basis width is MIN(restart,dimension,maxiter) and (width+1)*dimension must not exceed two million entries when iteration is needed. Factor/vector caps are those of KRONSMV; solve work is limited to 100 million estimated units and iterations to 100,000. Invalid shape/options, nonfinite data and required row scaling that loses a nonzero coefficient raise recoverable errors. Singular, ill-conditioned or poorly preconditioned systems need not converge. Native Rust calls are NativeKroneckerSum::gmres and gmres_with_restart. See programs/science/matrix_free_transport.bas for a steady transport model. General fixed linear callbacks use MFGMRES, described below. Retained operator graphs remain a separate capability.

Programmable matrix-free linear systems

MFGMRES("FNOP",b[,rtol,atol,maxiter,initial,restart,preconditioner]) solves A*x=b with restarted CPU GMRES. Define a one-argument DEF FNOP(X) that returns the real list A*X; it must represent a fixed linear map throughout the solve. For example:

10 DEF FNOP(X)={4*X(1)+2*X(2),-X(1)+3*X(2)}
20 R=MFGMRES("FNOP",{2,-4})
30 PRINT R(1):REM APPROXIMATELY {1,-1}

The dimension is the length of b (1 through 1,000,000). The callback receives one list of that length and must return a finite real list of the same length. Names are case-insensitive and start with FN; ordinary parameter scoping applies, so the callback argument shadows rather than overwrites an outer variable. Other program variables and DEF FN calls can compose the operator. Statement FUNCTION/SUB procedures are not accepted by this interface.

The report is {solution,status,iterations,residualNorm,threshold}. Status is "CONVERGED", "MAXITER", "BREAKDOWN" or "STAGNATED". Every candidate is checked using a fresh b-FNOP(solution); the threshold is MAX(atol,rtol*NORM(b)). This is a global residual criterion, not a bound on solution error or every row's relative error. Callback arithmetic determines the operator's precision. The solver cannot certify linearity, repeatability, conditioning or convergence; nonlinear/time-varying/random callbacks are outside its contract. The default rtol is 1E-8, atol is zero, maxiter is MIN(10000,MAX(20,10*LEN(b))), and the initial vector is zero. Require 0<=rtol<1, atol>=0, at least one positive tolerance, and integer maxiter from 0 through 100000. Restart is an integer from 1 through 128; the default is size-aware, up to 30. Retained basis storage is capped at two million elements, so large systems may need a smaller restart.

A list-valued preconditioner supplies one positive finite divisor per row (rowScales) for left scaling. With it the solver applies FNOP(X)/rowScales internally but still checks the original callback residual. There is no automatic preconditioner; the unscaled callback output must be finite before scaling. The solver caps its own vector work at 100 million charged operations and callback applications at 10000 combined operator/preconditioner calls per solve. These limits do not account for all computation inside the callback; nested BASIC operations retain their own limits. Cancellation and callback/type/shape/domain failures propagate as recoverable errors. Failed assignment preserves its prior value, although callback side effects are not rolled back. See programs/science/matrix_free_low_rank.bas for a ridge system with two global modes, using vectors instead of a full square matrix.

The eighth argument can be a list of positive row divisors (the existing behavior) or a string naming a DEF FN, such as "FNPC". The latter must return a vector of the same length computing a fixed linear inverse action P^-1*r, where P approximates A. Supply a solve using reusable factors; do not explicitly form an inverse merely for preconditioning. The callback can be nonsymmetric. For example:

10 A={{4,2},{-1,3}}:F=LUFACTOR(A)
20 DEF FNOP(X)={DOT(A(1),X),DOT(A(2),X)}
30 DEF FNPC(X)=LUSOLVE(F,X)
40 R=MFGMRES("FNOP",{2,-4},1E-12,0,20,{0,0},1,"FNPC"):PRINT R

Both callbacks must remain fixed and linear during the solve. This is left preconditioning with ordinary restarted GMRES, not flexible GMRES; tolerance-driven inner iterative solves are generally unsuitable because they can change the map. Singular or poor preconditioners can cause breakdown/stagnation and are not certified by the solver. Every convergence decision uses a fresh original b-A*x residual, never just the preconditioned residual. Zero initial residual or maxiter=0 can return before invoking the preconditioner. All output components must be finite. Operator and preconditioner calls share the 10,000-application limit; both count toward solver vector work and cancellation checks. User callback side effects are not undone after errors; destination assignment remains atomic.

PERIODOGRAM(samples,sampleRate[,window]) returns {frequenciesHz,powerDensity} for a nonempty real sample list. sampleRate must be finite and positive. The optional real window must have the same length and nonzero energy; omission uses a rectangular window. All samples and weights must be finite. There is no implicit detrending, padding or sample selection. For N samples, bins are k*sampleRate/N, with k from 0 through FLOOR(N/2). Density is ABS(FFT(samples*window))^2/(sampleRate*SUM(window^2)); interior bins are doubled to include negative-frequency power. DC and the even-length Nyquist bin are not doubled. Units are squared sample units per Hz. Thus SUM(powerDensity)*sampleRate/N gives the window-weighted mean square. Use HANN(N), HAMMING(N) or other existing windows explicitly when desired. The Rust API is NativeSignalMath::periodogram, returning NativePeriodogram. The same input/FFT work bounds and cancellation checks apply. Normalization reduces intermediate overflow, but binary64 rounding, underflow and finite output range still apply. This estimator does not identify pitch or capture audio. Example: PRINT PERIODOGRAM({2,2,2,2},8) prints {{0,2,4},{2,0,0}}.

FFT(list) and IFFT(list) accept arbitrary positive lengths, including primes. Power-of-two transforms use radix-2 FFT; other sizes use Bluestein convolution. Forward sign is negative; inverse results are divided by the input length. Inputs are real or complex. Input length is at most one million; padded scratch length is at most 2,097,152 complex values, with a bounded transform work estimate.

The 3D functions use radians, row-major 4-by-4 matrices applied to column vectors, a right-handed world, and camera forward along negative Z. These conventions are separate from the older positive-Z point-perspective commands.

FunctionMeaning
QUATAXIS({x,y,z},angle)Unit quaternion {w,x,y,z} from a nonzero axis and radians
QUATMUL(q1,q2)Hamilton product; applies q2 then q1 for unit rotation quaternions
QUATROTATE(q,{x,y,z})Rotate using the original quaternion and its exact squared norm
QUATSLERP(q0,q1,t)Shortest-arc spherical interpolation of unit rotations; 0<=t<=1, with normalized linear interpolation near coincident rotations
ROTATE3D(q)Quaternion rotation as a 4-by-4 matrix
TRANSLATE3D(x,y,z), SCALE3D(x,y,z)Affine translation/scaling matrices
LOOKAT(eye,target,up)View matrix; rejects coincident eye/target and parallel/zero up
PERSPECTIVEMAT(fovY,aspect,near,far)Perspective projection; 0<fovY<PI, aspect>0, 0<near<far
ORTHOGRAPHIC(left,right,bottom,top,near,far)Orthographic projection with ordered extents and 0<=near<far
TRANSFORMPOINT(matrix,point)Apply homogeneous transform and divide by W; rejects W=0
TRANSFORMVECTOR(matrix,direction)Apply linear 3-by-3 part, excluding translation
TRANSFORMCOMPOSE(left,right)Compose 4-by-4 transforms, right applied first
TRANSFORMINVERSE(matrix)Invert a nonsingular 4-by-4 transform; exact-input singularity decision

Projection maps the near/far planes to normalized depth -1/+1. See programs/examples/scientific_math.bas for numerical examples.

Sparse matrices and iterative linear systems

Sparse functions store only nonzero entries and operate on real binary64 data. They accept ordinary BASIC lists and numeric DIM-array snapshots. All sparse indices are one-based, independent of OPTION BASE. Fractional indices and dimensions are rejected, rather than rounded. A matrix must have positive row and column dimensions; an all-zero matrix is allowed.

FunctionResult
SPARSE(denseMatrix)Convert a rectangular real matrix to canonical compressed sparse row (CSR) storage.
SPARSE(rows,columns,rowIndices,columnIndices,values)Assemble coordinate entries into CSR. All three lists must have equal lengths; empty lists produce a zero matrix of the requested shape.
SPSHAPE(A){rows,columns}.
SPNNZ(A)Number of retained nonzero entries.
SPDENSE(A)Convert to a nested real matrix, subject to the ordinary one-million-element dense limit.
SPMV(A,x)Sparse matrix-vector product; x is a flat real vector with one element per column.
SPQUAD(A,x)Quadratic form xᵀAx for a square CSR matrix and matching flat real vector. Uses every stored entry, without assuming symmetry or mirroring a triangle. Accumulates triple products exactly before one binary64 rounding; reports overflow if the final result is not finite.
SPISPSD(A)Exactly test positive semidefiniteness of a real symmetric CSR matrix; -1 is proved true, 0 is proved false. Shape/symmetry errors and exhausted proof budgets raise errors.
SPISNSD(A)Exactly test negative semidefiniteness, using the same rules and limits.
SPTRANSPOSE(A)Canonical sparse transpose.
SPKRON(A,B)Sparse Kronecker product A ⊗ B, returned as CSR without dense expansion.
SPKRONSUM(A,B)Sparse Kronecker sum A ⊗ I + I ⊗ B for square CSR matrices, returned as CSR.
SPCG(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,preconditioner$]]]]])Conjugate-gradient iteration for a symmetric positive-definite system; optional CPU IC(k), k=0..8, preconditioning. JACOBI remains the default. Returns {solution,status$,iterations,residualNorm,threshold}.
SPGMRES(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,restart[,preconditioner$]]]]]])Restarted GMRES for a general square real sparse system. Returns the same five-element report as SPCG.
SPBICGSTAB(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,preconditioner$]]]]])Short-recurrence BiCGSTAB for general square real sparse systems. Returns the same five-element report.
SPMINRES(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,preconditioner$]]]]])Short-recurrence MINRES for exactly symmetric real sparse systems, including indefinite matrices. Options are NONE, symmetric JACOBI scaling, or positive incomplete Cholesky IC0 through IC8. Returns the same five-element report.
SPLSQR(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,preconditioner$]]]])CPU LSQR for rectangular real sparse least-squares systems; optional "COLUMN" normalizes nonzero columns, "NONE" preserves the default. Returns {solution,status$,iterations,residualNorm,normalResidualNorm,threshold}.
SPWLSQR(A,b,w[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,preconditioner$]]]])CPU LSQR for weighted rectangular sparse least squares. Finite nonnegative row weights cannot all be zero; zero-weight rows are excluded. Optional "COLUMN" scales nonzero columns. Returns {solution,status$,iterations,normalizedResidualNorm,normalizedNormalResidualNorm,threshold,weightScale}.

Coordinate assembly sorts entries by row and column, combines duplicates using exact accumulation of the supplied binary64 values, rounds each combined value once, and removes zeros. An index must be valid even when its value is zero. SPKRON(A,B) uses row-major Kronecker ordering and admits only results within the existing 100000-axis, 250000-entry and 100-million-unit work bounds. Nonfinite coefficient products raise an error and products underflowing to zero are omitted. The resulting ordinary CSR record composes with SPMV, sparse iterative solvers and sparse direct factors. SPKRONSUM(A,B) requires square component matrices and assembles A ⊗ I + I ⊗ B directly in canonical CSR. Overlapping diagonal entries are coalesced with exact binary accumulation; dimension, entry and work limits apply before and during assembly. The result composes directly with sparse solvers, for example to build a multidimensional Laplacian without dense expansion. The public CSR record is:

{"CSR1",rows,columns,{rowPointers...},{columnIndices...},{values...}}

rowPointers has rows+1 elements. Its first element is 1, its last is SPNNZ(A)+1, and adjacent equal pointers describe an empty row. Within each row, columns must be strictly increasing and values nonzero. Every consumer validates the entire record, including metadata queries. Records are ordinary BASIC values; manual construction and copying are supported, but malformed edits raise errors. SPMV accumulates products exactly before one binary64 rounding per output row, including cases where separate products would overflow before cancellation. A final unrepresentable value raises an error.

SPCG requires a square, exactly symmetric matrix with positive diagonal entries. Symmetry compares stored binary64 values exactly, without silently changing the operator. These checks do not prove positive definiteness; that is a caller assumption. The optional final string selects "JACOBI" (default) or CPU "IC0" through "IC8". IC(k) retains entries whose symbolic level of fill is at most k; IC(0) keeps the original lower pattern. It factors the diagonally equilibrated operator and applies triangular solves in preconditioned CG. The combined lower/upper factor storage is capped at one million entries and setup and solves use the shared work budget. No pivoting is performed. Missing or nonpositive incomplete pivots return an error; retry with JACOBI or reorder the system. A successful factorization is not a proof of positive definiteness, and more fill does not guarantee fewer CG iterations. Every candidate is checked against the original system. The iteration uses diagonal equilibration and a normalized residual to reduce avoidable overflow and underflow. It solves for a correction to the initial guess, which defaults to zero. Conjugate gradients and diagonal preconditioning are described in the Netlib linear-system templates.

Defaults are rtol=1E-8, atol=0, and maxiter=MIN(10000,MAX(20,10*rows)). Require 0<=rtol<1, atol>=0, with at least one positive tolerance. maxiter is an integer from 0 through 100000. An initial guess must match b's length. Zero iterations still validates the matrix and computes the initial residual.

The stopping criterion is

NORM(b-A*x) <= MAX(rtol*NORM(b),atol).

This follows the residual convention documented for SciPy CG. The reported residual is freshly computed on the original matrix and returned solution, including b in the product accumulator before rounding. It is checked at initialization and after every iteration; an internal recurrence alone never establishes convergence. The recurrence restarts from the true residual every 64 iterations, or when its own squared residual rounds to zero. Each restart also rebases the correction on the latest solution, so cancellation against a much larger original guess does not repeatedly erase a smaller solution. Norms use scaling to avoid intermediate squared-value overflow or underflow.

StatusMeaning
"CONVERGED"The returned solution satisfies the computed residual criterion. This is not an exact-arithmetic proof, a forward-error guarantee or a certificate of positive definiteness.
"MAXITER"The iteration limit was reached; the returned vector is an approximation whose residual exceeds the threshold.
"BREAKDOWN"Nonpositive search curvature or a vanished working residual prevents continuation. The last completed approximation and its true residual are returned. This does not establish that the system is inconsistent.

iterations counts completed updates. Check the status before treating the vector as a solved system. Singular or indefinite systems may sometimes satisfy the residual criterion; there is no completeness or convergence guarantee for those inputs. Poor conditioning can make solution error large despite a small residual. A tiny relative threshold may underflow to zero, requiring a computed zero residual. Nonfinite arithmetic, unrepresentable matrix scaling, invalid inputs, BREAK and exhausted work raise BASIC errors instead of returning a success or a partial report.

Limits are 100000 rows or columns, 250000 input coordinate entries or stored nonzeros, and a shared estimated 100-million-unit work budget per call. Sparse multiplication, transpose, CG, GMRES and MINRES do not allocate rows*columns storage. Dense conversion and dense input remain capped at one million elements. Sparse records, input vectors and returned solutions also obey BASIC retained-storage limits. This is a CPU sparse foundation; higher-fill levels above IC(8), pivoted preconditioners, sparse matrix-matrix multiplication and sparse tensor autograd remain future work.

10 A=SPARSE(3,3,{1,1,2,2,2,3,3},{1,2,1,2,3,2,3},{2,-1,-1,2,-1,-1,2})
20 PRINT SPNNZ(A)
30 R=SPCG(A,{1,0,1},1E-10,0,100,{},"IC1")
40 PRINT R(2);R(3);R(4);R(5)
50 IF R(2)="CONVERGED" THEN PRINT R(1)

The matrix has seven nonzeros and the solution is approximately {1,1,1}. programs/science/sparse_poisson.bas assembles a two-dimensional five-point Poisson system, solves 1024- and 4096-unknown grids, checks second-order grid refinement, and exports the fine solution to CSV. The fine matrix would exceed the dense limit. tools/check-sparse-foundation.py independently checks CSR, products, solver residuals and solutions against Fraction arithmetic and SciPy, including a 20000-unknown diagonal system and explicit nonconvergence cases.

Nonsymmetric sparse linear systems

SPGMRES(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,restart[,preconditioner$]]]]]]) solves a square real system using restarted GMRES. Symmetry, positive diagonal and diagonal dominance are not required. A singular consistent system may converge; convergence does not prove uniqueness or a small forward error. Nonsingular systems can stagnate with a short restart, and an inconsistent system need not be diagnosed as such. The Arnoldi/GMRES method and restart limitations are described in the Netlib linear-system templates.

The first six arguments, defaults, tolerance rules, original-system stopping criterion and five-element return record match SPCG. maxiter counts total Arnoldi steps, including work across restarts, rather than restart cycles. restart is an integer from 1 through 128. Its default is MIN(30,rows,FLOOR(2000000/rows)-1). The effective cycle width is the minimum of restart, rows and maxiter. When iteration is needed, (width+1)*rows must not exceed two million basis elements; a larger request raises an error before basis allocation. An already-solved initial guess or maxiter=0 needs no basis. The existing sparse limits and shared 100-million-unit work budget still apply.

The optional final string selects "ROW" (default), "NONE", or an ILU fill level from "ILU0" through "ILU8". ROW divides each row by its largest absolute entry; an empty row has scale 1. This left preconditioner permits zero and negative diagonal entries. NONE leaves the operator unchanged. ILU0 builds a zero-fill incomplete LU using the input CSR pattern. ILU1 through ILU8 allow the corresponding maximum level of symbolic fill; all ILU factors are capped at one million entries. They apply forward/back substitutions on the left. All ILU modes require a stored diagonal and nonzero pivots; none pivots numerically. A zero pivot, nonfinite factor, factor-storage cap or exhausted work budget raises a BASIC error, so the caller can retry with ROW, NONE or a reordered matrix. All setup/application work uses the shared sparse budget. ROW scaling is prepared lazily and reused across solves of a prepared implicit stage matrix. Nonzero matrix entries that underflow under row scaling raise an error. The working residual is normalized, and Arnoldi uses two modified Gram–Schmidt passes with exact-accumulation dot products. Givens rotations and triangular substitution produce a candidate at every iteration. The reported residual is freshly computed from the original stored A, b and candidate; a small projected or preconditioned residual cannot establish success. Original residuals need not decrease monotonically under left preconditioning.

Every restart rebases the correction on the latest candidate. Near-zero Arnoldi vectors trigger a true-residual restart if further correction is possible. "CONVERGED" and "MAXITER" have the same meaning as for SPCG. "BREAKDOWN" means the working system cannot produce a usable next correction; "STAGNATED" means a completed restart cycle leaves the candidate unchanged. Both return the latest completed candidate and its original residual above the threshold. Neither proves inconsistency. A failure encountered while constructing an Arnoldi step still counts that step. If the iteration limit is reached after a candidate update, "MAXITER" takes precedence over stagnation. Arithmetic, shape, storage, work-limit and BREAK failures raise BASIC errors.

10 A=SPARSE({{4,2},{-1,3}})
20 R=SPGMRES(A,{2,-4},1E-12,0,100,{0,0},2,"ILU0")
30 PRINT R(2);R(3);R(4);R(5)
40 IF R(2)="CONVERGED" THEN PRINT R(1)

The solution is approximately {1,-1}. tools/check-gmres-foundation.py compares solutions against SciPy direct and GMRES solves, recomputes original residuals with exact rational arithmetic, checks common and independent row scales, restarts, singular systems, nonconvergence, arrays and bounded sparse storage.

Nonsymmetric short-recurrence sparse systems

SPBICGSTAB(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,preconditioner$]]]]]) solves a general square real sparse system with CPU BiCGSTAB. It does not require symmetry or a positive diagonal and uses O(rows) iteration vectors instead of a growing Krylov basis. The five-element result has the same layout and original-residual stopping rule as SPCG: {solution,status$,iterations, residualNorm,threshold}. CONVERGED requires a freshly computed residual of the original matrix and RHS; MAXITER and BREAKDOWN return the latest completed candidate and do not prove inconsistency or uniqueness. BiCGSTAB can break down on a nonsingular system when its shadow residual becomes orthogonal to a required search direction; retry with GMRES or another ordering when that occurs.

The defaults and tolerance rules match SPCG; maxiter is a total iteration limit from 0 through 100000. preconditioner$ is ROW by default, NONE, or ILU0 through ILU8. These use the shared bounded row equilibration and left incomplete-LU factors from SPGMRES; ILU setup has the same one-million-entry cap, stored-diagonal requirement and explicit zero-pivot errors. Every candidate is checked against the unscaled original system. The shared 100-million-unit work/cancellation budget applies. A finite residual is not a forward-error or conditioning guarantee, and the method currently does not pivot its ILU factors.

Symmetric-indefinite sparse systems

SPMINRES(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,preconditioner$]]]]]) solves real square systems whose stored matrix is exactly symmetric. Unlike SPCG, it accepts indefinite and singular matrices; consistent singular systems may converge, while an inconsistent system returns its best completed candidate and a residual above the threshold. BREAKDOWN does not prove inconsistency. This CPU implementation uses the short MINRES recurrence and O(rows) working vectors, with no dense conversion. preconditioner$ is NONE by default, JACOBI for symmetric diagonal scaling by the inverse square root of each absolute diagonal entry, or IC0 through IC8 for positive incomplete-Cholesky factors with bounded symbolic fill. JACOBI requires each diagonal entry to be stored and nonzero. Incomplete Cholesky requires positive stored diagonals and a positive factor at every pivot; it can fail for indefinite matrices, even though unpreconditioned MINRES accepts them. Its lower and upper factors share the one-million-entry limit. A symmetric but ill-conditioned system can still converge slowly or return MAXITER.

The tolerance, initial-guess and five-element result rules match SPCG. Convergence is decided from a freshly computed residual of the original matrix and right-hand side at every iteration. Matrix and residual scaling protect the recurrence from common extreme magnitudes; unrepresentable arithmetic or nonzero matrix coefficients lost to scaling underflow raise an error. The same 250000-entry, 100000-dimension and 100-million-unit per-call work/cancellation limits apply. tools/check-sparse-foundation.py compares indefinite tridiagonal systems through 513 unknowns with SciPy MINRES and sparse direct solves and independently recomputes residuals from exact binary64 rationals. A separately scaled indefinite system exercises JACOBI against SciPy MINRES on the explicit symmetric scaling transformation.

Rectangular sparse least squares

SPLSQR(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,preconditioner$]]]]) solves the real sparse least-squares problem minimize ||b-Ax||₂ for rectangular CSR matrices. The solver uses CPU Golub-Kahan LSQR, starts from zero and therefore targets the minimum-norm least-squares solution for underdetermined and rank-deficient systems in exact arithmetic. It does not form AᵀA or convert the operator to a dense matrix.

The six-element result is {solution,status$,iterations,residualNorm, normalResidualNorm,threshold}. residualNorm is ||b-Ax||₂ and may remain positive for an inconsistent fit. By default, normalResidualNorm is ||Aᵀ(b-Ax)||₂; with "COLUMN" scaling it is the scaled stationarity norm ||D Aᵀ(b-Ax)||₂, where D normalizes nonzero columns. CONVERGED requires this freshly recomputed quantity to be no larger than the matching max(rtol*||D Aᵀb||₂,atol) threshold (with D=I by default). MAXITER and BREAKDOWN return the best candidate and do not prove uniqueness or inconsistency. In "COLUMN" mode, each stationarity component must also meet its own relative/absolute tolerance, with a binary64 roundoff floor based on the initial gradient norm; this prevents a large column from hiding an unresolved small column. A stationary point may be non-unique when the matrix is rank deficient; zero initialization selects the minimum-norm Krylov solution subject to finite precision.

The default relative tolerance is 1E-8, the default absolute tolerance is zero, and the default iteration cap is clamp(10*max(rows,columns),20,10000). Callers may set at most 100,000 iterations. The same 100,000-axis, 250,000-entry and 100-million-unit shared work/cancellation limits as the other sparse kernels apply. Optional "COLUMN" scaling (or explicit "NONE") normalizes each nonzero column by its 2-norm and can improve convergence when column magnitudes differ. Because this is a right change of variables, it can change the selected minimum-norm solution for rank-deficient or underdetermined systems; omit it when ordinary Euclidean minimum norm is required. Zero columns remain zero, and scaling that would underflow a stored coefficient is rejected. Rust callers can use NativeCsrMatrix::lsqr(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations) for the default or lsqr_with_preconditioner(...,NativeLsqrPreconditioner::ColumnNorm) and receive a typed report with the original fit residual and mode-specific stationarity norm. Both use the original matrix; column scaling applies D only to the normal residual used as its stopping test.

SPWLSQR(A,b,w[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,preconditioner$]]]]) minimizes sum(wᵢ(bᵢ-Aᵢx)²) without densifying the CSR matrix. Weights must be finite, nonnegative and not all zero; a zero-weight row is omitted from the weighted operator. Rows use sqrt(wᵢ)/sqrt(max(w)) scaling so a common large or tiny weight factor does not overflow or cause premature ratio underflow. Its seven-element result is {solution,status$,iterations,normalizedResidualNorm, normalizedNormalResidualNorm,threshold,weightScale}. Both residual norms and the convergence threshold use normalized weights; multiply the fit norm by sqrt(weightScale) and the normal-residual norm by weightScale to recover their original weighted units. A stored coefficient that underflows during row scaling is rejected rather than silently removed. The optional COLUMN preconditioner is applied to the weighted operator and has the same minimum-norm caveat as SPLSQR(...,COLUMN).

Sparse implicit transport, diffusion and linear damping

SPBEULER(K,source,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter]]]) integrates the constant linear system u' = source - K*u using backward Euler. K is a canonical sparse matrix; source and state are flat real vectors with matching lengths. Array snapshots work. Forward time only: finish>=start and maxstep>0. All numbers and the time span must be finite. Equal endpoints return the initial row and no diagnostics, after validating all inputs.

The operator must be square and satisfy K(i,i) >= SUM(ABS(K(i,j)), j<>i) in every row. Missing diagonal entries are zero. Exact binary64 summation checks these inequalities without a tolerance. This is a sufficient dissipativity condition in the infinity norm and permits zero matrices, nonsymmetric upwind transport, diffusion and conserved modes. With symmetry it also implies positive semidefiniteness. Operators without this row dominance are rejected, even if another stability condition holds. There is no automatic boundary condition, grid assembly, mass matrix or unit conversion; assemble K and any constant boundary forcing in BASIC.

For each actual positive interval h, solve

(I+h*K)*u_next = u_previous + h*source.

The diagonal and forcing sums use exact product accumulation before binary64 rounding. The rounded shifted operator must remain strictly row diagonally dominant; loss of the identity shift at extreme scales raises an error. Nonzero off-diagonal coefficients that underflow during scaling also raise errors. The previous state is the initial linear-solver guess. Exactly symmetric shifted matrices use SPCG; others use SPGMRES with its default restart width. The prepared operator and preconditioner are reused for consecutive steps with exactly the same h. Every accepted step passes a freshly computed residual check on its rounded linear system. MAXITER, BREAKDOWN, STAGNATED, nonfinite arithmetic, invalid input, unrepresentable time increments, BREAK and exhausted limits raise BASIC errors; no partial trajectory is returned as a successful integration.

The return value is {trajectory,diagnostics}:

ElementContents
trajectoryRows {time,state1,...} including the initial row and every completed step; the final time equals finish.
diagnosticsOne row {iterations,residualNorm,threshold} per step, corresponding to trajectory row step+1. Every residual is at most its threshold.

Defaults are rtol=1E-10, atol=1E-12 and the same per-solve iteration limit as SPCG. Tolerances and maxiter have the same validity rules as SPCG and apply to the linear solve, using MAX(rtol*NORM(rhs),atol). They do not estimate time-discretization error. Steps are at most maxstep apart from floating-point roundoff, with a shortened final interval. The operator always uses the difference between the returned consecutive times. A final roundoff-sized remainder is folded into the last step. A call is limited to 100000 steps and one million numeric elements combined across trajectory and diagnostics. The sparse 100-million-unit work budget is shared across all assembly, preparation and solves, and ordinary BASIC storage limits still apply. No dense matrix is built.

Backward Euler is first order in time. For this dissipative operator class it damps stiff modes without the explicit Euler stability step restriction in exact arithmetic; finite precision and inexact solves still require validation. Refine maxstep to assess accuracy and separately refine the spatial grid. The method and heat-equation stability analysis are described in the University of Illinois time-dependent PDE notes.

10 K=SPARSE({{2,-1},{-1,2}})
20 R=SPBEULER(K,{0,0},0,{1,2},1,.125,1E-11,1E-13)
30 PATHDATA=R(1):SOLVES=R(2)
40 PRINT PATHDATA(LEN(PATHDATA)):PRINT SOLVES

programs/science/implicit_heat.bas evolves a 511-component heat model with slow and fast sine modes, checks first-order time refinement against the semidiscrete analytic solution, and exports CSV. Its coarse time step is 8192 times the usual forward Euler grid stability bound. tools/check-implicit-foundation.py compares steps against SciPy sparse direct solves, recomputes residuals with Fraction, checks conserved modes, stiff decay, forcing and failures, and runs the example. This solver does not implement nonlinear or time-dependent operators/forcing, adaptive time-error control, general non-row-dominant stiff systems, events, dense interpolation, or higher-order implicit methods.

Adaptive sparse implicit integration

SPBESOLVE(K,source,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter]]]) integrates the same constant u'=source-K*u systems and requires the same weakly row-diagonally-dominant, nonnegative-diagonal operator class as SPBEULER. It adapts time steps by comparing one full backward-Euler step with two half steps. Only the two-half-step state is accepted; there is no extrapolation. The method remains first order. All three linear systems must converge before the temporal estimate is considered. A linear failure raises an error instead of being treated as a rejected time step.

Here rtol and atol are temporal tolerances. Defaults are 1E-4 and 1E-7; require 0<=rtol<1 and atol>0. maxiter is a per-linear-solve integer from 0 through 100000, with the same default as SPCG. maxstep must be positive and finish>=start; equal endpoints validate all arguments and return the initial row with empty diagnostics and zero counters. Every state and forcing component, time, tolerance and time span must be finite. Tolerances are scalar; scale mixed physical units and widely differing component magnitudes before integration.

The return value is {trajectory,diagnostics,summary}:

ElementContents
trajectoryRows {time,state1,...} for the initial state and each accepted endpoint. The final time equals finish. Rejected trial states are discarded.
diagnosticsOne row {midpoint,errorRatio,coarseSolve,firstHalfSolve,secondHalfSolve} per accepted interval. Each solve record is {iterations,residualNorm,threshold}. errorRatio is between 0 and 1, and every residual is at most its threshold.
summary{acceptedSteps,rejectedTrials,linearSolves,totalIterations}. Counts include all completed trials, including rejected ones; linearSolves=3*(acceptedSteps+rejectedTrials).

The midpoint must be representable strictly between the interval's endpoints. The matrices use the actual intervals h=next-time, h1=midpoint-time and h2=next-midpoint. The local estimate uses weight=(h1/h2+h2/h1)/2, which is 1 for equal halves. This accounts for unequal halves caused by time-coordinate rounding. Per component, the acceptance ratio is

weight*(ABS(fine-coarse)+linearAllowance) / (atol+rtol*MAX(ABS(old),ABS(fine))).

The maximum component ratio must be at most 1. The controller multiplies the actual interval by CLAMP(.9/SQRT(errorRatio),.1,2), or by 2 when the ratio is zero, then caps it at maxstep. A rejected interval leaves time and state unchanged. Endpoint adjustments may exceed maxstep by floating-point roundoff. An unrepresentable increment or midpoint, or a rejected interval that cannot shrink at the current time resolution, raises an error. Local-error estimation and the first-order square-root controller follow the principles in NTNU's numerical ODE notes, section 3.4.

Linear residuals have a separate budget. For each rounded matrix A=I+h*K, let margin be half the smallest exact-sum row-dominance margin, rounded to binary64. It must be positive. The CG or GMRES solve uses relative tolerance zero and absolute threshold .01*minimumOldScale*MIN(margin,1), where minimumOldScale=MIN_i(atol+rtol*ABS(old_i)) uses the state at the beginning of the whole trial, for all three solves. This keeps large components from hiding inaccurate small components. Threshold underflow requires a computed zero residual. Each solve's residual allowance is residualNorm/margin. linearAllowance adds the coarse and second-half allowances plus the first-half allowance divided by the second-half margin, accounting for its propagation. This uses the inverse-norm estimate from strict diagonal dominance; all reported quantities remain floating-point estimates, not interval-arithmetic certificates.

The returned ratio is a local error estimate, not a bound on accumulated global error. It does not certify model accuracy, spatial discretization, matrix/RHS rounding or unresolved behavior between output points. Check tighter tolerances and spatial refinement against analytical or independent references. The trajectory has irregular times and provides no dense interpolation or events.

Limits are 100000 trials (accepted plus rejected), one million numeric elements combined across trajectory, nested diagnostics and counters, and the shared 100-million-unit sparse work budget across all trials and solves. At most three prepared sparse operators are cached. Ordinary BASIC retained-storage limits also apply. Resource exhaustion, invalid input, nonfinite arithmetic, BREAK and linear failures return errors with no successful partial trajectory.

10 K=SPARSE({{1,0},{0,1000}})
20 R=SPBESOLVE(K,{0,0},0,{1,1},1,.25,1E-4,1E-7)
30 PATHDATA=R(1):PRINT PATHDATA(LEN(PATHDATA)):PRINT R(3)

programs/science/adaptive_heat.bas follows slow and fast heat modes, checks tolerance refinement and exports the center-point trajectory and local ratios. tools/check-adaptive-foundation.py compares accepted steps with SciPy sparse direct solves, analytical solutions, matrix exponentials and Radau trajectories; selected trials are replayed with SPBEULER and independently checked with exact Fraction residuals. Nonlinear systems, operators without the required row dominance, variable operators or forcing, mass matrices, higher-order methods and GPU execution remain outside this solver's scope.

Second-order sparse implicit integration

SPSDIRK2(K,source,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter]]]) and SPSDIRKSOLVE(K,source,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter]]]) integrate u'=source(t)-K(t)*u using the two-stage, second-order SDIRK method that is L-stable for constant-coefficient scalar decay. They require the same weakly row-diagonally-dominant, nonnegative-diagonal K as SPBEULER; state and source are real lists or array snapshots. Either K or source may instead name a one-argument DEF FN of time, as described below. The method is described in MOOSE's LStableDirk2 documentation, which cites Alexander (1977). Constant K lets both stages share a sparse shifted operator; variable K(t) requires distinct stage matrices. Both stages use residual-checked CG for exactly symmetric shifted matrices, or GMRES otherwise. Every linear solve must converge.

With gamma=1-1/SQRT(2), beta=(1-gamma)/gamma, actual interval h, rounded stage interval s=gamma*h, A1=I+s*K(start+s) and A2=I+s*K(nextTime), the implementation solves

A1*stage = old + s*source(start+s)
A2*next  = (1-beta)*old + beta*stage + s*source(nextTime)

The initial guesses are old and stage, respectively. Eliminating the explicit K*stage product avoids forming large intermediate derivatives. Matrix diagonals and RHS products are accumulated exactly before rounding to binary64. Each rounded shifted matrix must retain strict row dominance. An underflowed stage interval or nonzero off-diagonal entry is an error.

A list source supplies the same vector at both stages. A time-dependent source is a compact function-name string, case-insensitive with surrounding whitespace ignored, for example "FNDRIVE":

10 DEF FNDRIVE(T)={COS(T)+2*SIN(T)}
20 R=SPSDIRKSOLVE(SPARSE({{2}}),"FNDRIVE",0,{0},1,.1,1E-5,1E-8)
30 P=R(1):PRINT P(LEN(P)):REM EXACT SOLUTION IS SIN(T)

Define the function before the solver call. It must take exactly one scalar time argument and return a flat list of exactly one finite real value per state component, even for a one-component system. Arrays and read-only model parameters are available in the function body; its time parameter temporarily shadows any caller variable of the same name. The source receives no trial state, so this API does not implement state-dependent nonlinear forcing.

Use a deterministic function of time and fixed model data. Sampling order includes rejected trials: two source evaluations per fixed step, and six per completed adaptive trial (coarse step, first half, second half; stage then endpoint for each). Samples are recomputed without caching. Avoid random numbers, wall-clock values and side effects in the source; otherwise retries do not represent the same ODE. The returned counters and diagnostic structure are unchanged, so total source samples equal the number of linear solves on a successful callback call.

The first-stage time is the binary64 sum start+gamma*h, using each actual full/half interval. It must lie strictly inside that interval. Its collapse onto an endpoint raises an error if either coefficient is a function; calls with constant matrix and source data do not require an absolute stage time. The second stage samples the exact step endpoint. Callback shape/type/domain errors and nonfinite values stop the call with no successful partial trajectory. Zero-duration calls validate the function name and its one-argument signature without evaluating its body.

Source samples share the sparse work budget, with an additional maximum of 600000 evaluations per call. BASIC's existing expression, recursion and storage limits also apply to the function body; sample counts do not measure arbitrary work inside that body. Choose maxstep to resolve the source and split integration at known discontinuities. Local sampling can miss narrow pulses or rapidly oscillating forcing. Smooth, resolved forcing is needed for second-order convergence; very stiff forcing problems can show order reduction, so verify time refinement rather than relying only on the nominal method order.

A time-dependent K function must return a canonical SPARSE(...) matrix with the same square dimension as the initial state. Each sampled matrix is checked for nonnegative diagonal and weak row diagonal dominance; each rounded shifted stage matrix must retain strict dominance. The sparsity pattern may change. Dense numeric lists are not implicitly converted to sparse matrices.

10 DEF FNK(T)=SPARSE({{1+T}})
20 R=SPSDIRKSOLVE("FNK",{0},0,{1},1,.1,1E-5,1E-8)
30 P=R(1):PRINT P(LEN(P)):REM EXACT SOLUTION IS EXP(-T-T^2/2)

A variable operator is sampled and its shifted linear system rebuilt at every stage, even for equal step lengths or repeated endpoint times. Only the current stage's prepared system is retained; constant operators keep their existing three-entry cache. This avoids reusing coefficients from an earlier time. Source and operator callbacks are called in that order at each stage. Each supplied callback has at most 600000 direct evaluations per call and, on successful calls, its direct sample count equals linearSolves. Extra function calls made inside a callback body are governed by the existing BASIC limits, not this direct count. Matrix parsing, dominance checks, solver selection and preparation share the sparse work budget. An invalid later stage stops the entire integration.

The operator callback receives time alone. Its signature is checked for an empty interval, but its body and matrix shape are checked only when sampled. Use nonempty finite initial state data to define its dimension. Function names, parameter scoping, deterministic-callback requirements, representable stage times and failure behavior follow the source rules above. Both callbacks may be used in one call; for example a source can use SPMV(FNK(T),knownState) to construct a problem with a known solution.

Changing coefficients need independent time refinement. Positive-semidefinite matrices at sampled times do not give this method unconditional norm decay for arbitrary time variation. For example, one fixed step of length 1 on u'=-10000*(1-t)*u, starting at 1, overshoots below -1 although the exact solution decays. Adaptive error comparison rejects that coarse trial in the qualification case. This is not a general stability certificate. Resolve coefficient variation, split at known discontinuities, and check invariants and tighter tolerances. Unsampled matrices and forcing cannot be certified by stage sampling. A nonsymmetric operator can grow in Euclidean norm even when the exact homogeneous evolution is contractive in the infinity norm. Do not apply symmetric energy-decay assumptions to transport or other nonnormal systems. The adaptive linear allowances still use strict row dominance: NORM_INFTY(A^-1) is bounded by the reciprocal minimum row margin, and the reported Euclidean residual bounds its infinity norm. Both stage margins and all existing propagation factors remain in the acceptance calculation.

programs/science/advection_diffusion.bas assembles periodic upwind transport and centered diffusion, checks second-order time refinement and tighter adaptive tolerances against semidiscrete Fourier modes, and exports a mass-checked CSV. tools/check-gmres-foundation.py also checks nonsymmetric fixed/adaptive BE, noncommuting variable SDIRK operators, stage solver switching, exact residual replays and an independent stiff Radau reference.
