They are never reused within a session.

FunctionCPU operation
TVALUE(t), TSHAPE(t)Return scalar/nested list data or a dimension list
TADD(a,b), TSUB(a,b), TMUL(a,b), TDIV(a,b)Elementwise arithmetic with right-aligned broadcasting; each aligned dimension must match or equal one
TMM(a,b)Matrix product on the last two axes; rank at least two, matching inner dimensions, and right-aligned broadcasting of leading batch dimensions
TGATHER(input,indices[,axis])Native indexed selection; one-based indices and axis (default 1). Rectangular nested indices replace the chosen axis with their shape; a scalar index removes that axis. Repeated selections accumulate gradients back to the input, enabling trainable embeddings. Indices are nondifferentiable numeric data, independent of OPTION BASE.
TCONV1D(input,weights[,stride[,padding[,dilation]]])Channel-first temporal filter: input {batch,channels,length}, weights {filters,channels,kernel}; returns {batch,filters,positions}
TCONV2D(input,weights[,stride[,padding[,dilation]]])Channel-first spatial filter: input {batch,channels,height,width}, weights {filters,channels,kernelHeight,kernelWidth}; returns {batch,filters,outHeight,outWidth}
TMAXPOOL1D(t,kernel[,stride[,padding]]), TAVGPOOL1D(t,kernel[,stride[,padding]])Native channel-first {batch,channels,length} pooling; positive kernel/stride, stride defaults to kernel and padding to zero. Padding must be smaller than kernel. Output length is INT((length+2*padding-kernel)/stride)+1.
TMAXPOOL2D(t,kernel[,stride[,padding]]), TAVGPOOL2D(t,kernel[,stride[,padding]])Native {batch,channels,height,width} pooling; scalar options apply to both axes or use {height,width} pairs. Same floor-size rule per axis. Max padding is ignored and ties choose the first valid row-major element; average pooling includes zero padding in its divisor. Both propagate gradients, including overlapping windows.
TRESHAPE(t,shape)Reshape without changing element count
TTRANSPOSE(t[,axes])Reverse axes by default, or use a complete one-based permutation such as {3,1,2}
TSUM(t[,axis]), TMEAN(t[,axis])Scalar reduction over all elements; a one-based axis reduces only that dimension and retains its size as one Exact accumulation preserves cancellation; means divide before rounding.
TRELU(t), TSIGMOID(t), TTANH(t)Differentiable activations; ReLU derivative at zero is zero
TEXP(t), TLOG(t)Elementwise exponential and natural logarithm; logarithm requires positive data
TSOFTMAX(t)Numerically stable softmax along the last axis; requires rank at least one
TMASKEDSOFTMAX(logits,mask)Last-axis softmax over included positions; mask broadcasts to the logits without expanding their shape
TMSE(prediction,target)Scalar mean squared error, equal shapes; exact squared-residual accumulation divides before final rounding
TCROSSENTROPY(logits,target)Scalar cross-entropy from logits and equal-shaped target distributions; last axis is classes, remaining axes are samples; targets must be nonnegative and each row must sum to one within 1e-10
TBACKWARD(loss)Reverse-mode gradients of a scalar tensor that depends on parameters; replaces previous gradients and returns zero
TGRAD(t)Return the most recent gradient as an ordinary BASIC scalar/list; unavailable gradients are errors
THVP(loss,parameter,direction)Exact analytic Hessian-vector product for a scalar loss, a reachable TPARAM leaf and a same-shaped direction tensor; returns an ordinary BASIC scalar/list and does not change TBACKWARD gradients
THESSIAN(loss,parameter)Materialize the exact analytic Hessian with rows/columns in the parameter's flattened row-major order; the parameter must be a reachable TPARAM leaf
TDERIV3(loss,parameter,direction)Exact analytic third directional derivative of a scalar loss through the supported CPU tensor graph
TDERIV4(loss,parameter,direction)Exact analytic fourth directional derivative of a scalar loss through the supported CPU tensor graph
TDERIV5(loss,parameter,direction)Exact analytic fifth directional derivative of a scalar loss through the supported CPU tensor graph
TDERIV6(loss,parameter,direction)Exact analytic sixth directional derivative of a scalar loss through the supported CPU tensor graph
TDERIV7(loss,parameter,direction)Exact analytic seventh directional derivative of a scalar loss through the supported CPU tensor graph
TDERIV8(loss,parameter,direction)Exact analytic eighth directional derivative of a scalar loss through the supported CPU tensor graph
TDERIV9(loss,parameter,direction)Exact analytic ninth directional derivative of a scalar loss through the supported CPU tensor graph
TSGD(rate)Apply gradient descent to reachable parameter leaves, then release the calculation graph; returns number of updated parameters
TADAM(rate[,beta1[,beta2[,epsilon]]])Adam with bias correction; defaults .9, .999, 1e-8; returns number of updated parameters
TDETACH(t)Copy data into a new constant leaf, removing its gradient connection
TSET(leaf,data)Replace a leaf with same-shaped scalar/list data; clears the graph and gradients and resets that leaf's Adam history; returns its handle
TCLEARGRAPH()Release all intermediate tensors and gradients, retaining constructor/detached leaves and Adam state; returns remaining tensor count
TCLEAR()Release all tensors, gradients and optimizer state; returns zero
TCOUNT()Count live tensor objects, useful for detecting graph accumulation

Every tensor arithmetic operation returns a new handle and records the derivative relationships. All listed arithmetic, reshape, permutation, reduction, activation and loss operations support first-order gradients, including broadcast reduction and shared inputs. THVP computes a forward-over-reverse second derivative using the existing CPU graph, without finite differences or mutation of saved gradients. For ReLU and max pooling it follows the active branch selected by the forward values; at a ReLU zero, the derivative convention is zero, and equal max-pool values follow the first winner. THESSIAN materializes a dense second-derivative matrix by applying THVP to parameter basis directions. It caps the result at one million entries and cumulative work at one billion; large Hessians should use THVP directly with an iterative solver. Both operations return ordinary BASIC data, create no tape nodes and preserve gradients saved by TBACKWARD. TDERIV3 through TDERIV9 use bounded analytic Taylor propagation, not finite differences, and return D^n loss[direction,...,direction] for the requested order. Their reachable-tape limits are four million, three million, two million, 1.5 million, one million, 750,000 and 500,000 tensor elements for orders three through nine, respectively. At ReLU zero and max-pool ties they follow the selected forward branch; these are branch-local derivatives, not classical derivatives at a kink. Orders above nine remain unsupported. TVALUE followed by ordinary BASIC arithmetic and TENSOR starts a new constant and breaks the gradient path.

10 P=TPARAM({0,0,0}):D=TENSOR({1,0,-1}):Y=TENSOR({0,1,0})
20 L=TCROSSENTROPY(P,Y):PRINT THVP(L,P,D):PRINT THESSIAN(L,P)

The direction tensor has the same shape as the selected parameter. The loss must be scalar and the parameter must be a leaf used by that loss. THESSIAN returns an n by n matrix, where n is the number of parameter elements.

TMM applies each matrix in the broadcast batch independently. For example, {2,1,3,4} multiplied by {1,5,4,6} produces shape {2,5,3,6}. The shapes here describe dimensions, not tensor values. Broadcasting reuses matrices; gradients sum contributions back into their original shapes. Vectors are not implicitly promoted to matrices: use TRESHAPE to give them explicit row or column dimensions. For batched attention, transpose just the last two axes with an explicit TTRANSPOSE permutation; the default reverses all axes.

Convolution follows the neural-network cross-correlation convention: weights are not reversed. All input channels contribute to every output filter. Stride and dilation default to one; padding defaults to zero and adds zeros symmetrically on both sides of each spatial axis. Stride/dilation must be positive integers and padding a nonnegative integer. TCONV1D takes scalar options; TCONV2D takes scalars for both axes or {height,width} pairs. There is no implicit padding or automatic output-size matching. Each output dimension is FLOOR((input + 2*padding - dilation*(kernel-1) - 1)/stride) + 1. An effective kernel larger than the padded input is an error.

Both filters differentiate inputs and weights, including shared parameters, overlapping windows, stride, padding and dilation. Add a trainable bias with TADD: use shape {1,filters,1} for 1D or {1,filters,1,1} for 2D. Groups, transposed convolution and automatic padding modes are not implemented. Convolution dots and local convolution gradients use exact binary64 product accumulation before a single rounding. Batched matrix forward operations use the existing BLAS/portable matrix backend; batched gradient contractions use exact product accumulation. Other tensor operations and accumulation across separate graph paths still use their existing binary64 arithmetic.

10 X=TENSOR({1,2,3,4},{1,1,4})
20 W=TPARAM({2,-1},{1,1,2})
30 Y=TCONV1D(X,W):PRINT TVALUE(Y)
40 LOSS=TSUM(Y):DONE=TBACKWARD(LOSS):PRINT TGRAD(W)
50 DONE=TCLEAR()

This prints {{{0,1,2}}} and weight gradient {{{6,9}}}. Numeric DIM-array snapshots work as constructor data, and TVALUE returns lists that the existing graphics commands and WAVE can consume.

TMASKEDSOFTMAX(logits,mask) supports causal and padding masks for attention. Both arguments are tensor handles. A finite nonzero mask entry includes a position, and zero excludes it, following BASIC truth semantics (-1 is true). Right-aligned singleton broadcasting is allowed, but the mask must not expand the logits' shape. Logits require rank at least one. The last dimension is the normalization axis, matching TSOFTMAX.

Excluded positions have exactly zero probability and gradient. Fully excluded rows return all zeros with zero logit gradients; such a row has zero probability mass. The maximum and normalization use only included logits, so even a large excluded logit does not distort the included probabilities. Masks are fixed discrete selection and must not require gradients; use TDETACH for a fixed snapshot of a parameter-derived mask. The operation differentiates the logits, not mask values. Forward probabilities retain the selection needed for backward; no expanded copy of the mask is retained on the tape.

10 P=TPARAM({{0,1,2},{3,4,5}})
20 M=TENSOR({{-1,0,0},{0,0,0}})
30 Y=TMASKEDSOFTMAX(P,M):PRINT TVALUE(Y)
40 L=TSUM(Y):D=TBACKWARD(L):PRINT TGRAD(P)

The probabilities are {{1,0,0},{0,0,0}} and the gradients are all zero. The shared masked/unmasked softmax pullback scales incoming adjoints before forming the weighted mean, avoiding intermediate overflow in tested extreme finite cases. Ordinary binary64 rounding/underflow still applies. Tensor live storage, work and cancellation limits apply, including atomic gradient/update failure behavior. Higher-order THVP uses the selected forward branch for piecewise operations; full Hessian materialization and further derivative orders remain separate capabilities.

TBACKWARD must precede an optimizer step. Only parameters reached by that backward pass are updated. The step releases all intermediate tensors and gradients in the session, including inference graphs, so read loss/predictions before updating. Constructor leaves survive and can be reused each epoch. Creating new TENSOR leaves inside an unbounded loop retains them until TCLEAR; reuse input handles with TSET when feeding batches. BASIC CLEAR, NEW and program replacement clear the tensor engine along with program state.

Rates and epsilon must be positive, and Adam betas must be in [0,1). Changing betas for a parameter with Adam history is rejected until TSET or TCLEAR; learning rate and epsilon may change between steps. SGD resets Adam history for updated parameters. Optimizer updates are validated before any parameter changes; a failed step preserves parameters, gradients and history. A failed backward preserves the previous complete gradient set. No implicit gradient accumulation, weight decay or clipping is performed.

10 X=TENSOR({{0},{1},{2},{3}}):Y=TENSOR({{1},{3},{5},{7}})
20 W=TPARAM({{0}}):B=TPARAM({0})
30 FOR EPOCH=1 TO 500
40 PREDICTION=TADD(TMM(X,W),B):LOSS=TMSE(PREDICTION,Y)
50 DONE=TBACKWARD(LOSS):DONE=TSGD(.05)
60 NEXT EPOCH
70 PRINT "Slope ";TVALUE(W);" intercept ";TVALUE(B)
80 DONE=TCLEAR()

Limits are explicit: rank at most eight, one million elements per tensor, 8,192 live objects and two million live data elements per session. Gradients, Adam moments and bounded temporary kernel buffers add memory beyond those data elements; this separate tensor budget is not charged to the scalar FRE budget. Each matrix product allows at most one billion multiply-adds across all batches. Convolution reserves the larger of its forward and input-gradient loop estimates against the same bound, including padded positions. Large strides can therefore still exceed the backward-work reservation. Backward checks a conservative three-times-forward work estimate for the reachable graph against one billion; THVP uses an eight-times-forward estimate and THESSIAN checks that estimate multiplied by the parameter dimension. Cancellation is checked during loops and between BLAS batches. Finite overflow, invalid shapes, expired handles and exhausted budgets are errors. TVALUE additionally incurs normal BASIC list/storage costs when assigned.

programs/ai/cpu_neural_network.bas trains a nonlinear XOR classifier and saves and reloads its weights using ordinary BASIC file commands. Its versioned text checkpoint contains model weights, not an exact-resume optimizer snapshot. programs/ai/cpu_attention.bas demonstrates a differentiable self-attention head. These are small-model building blocks, not a pretrained LLM. Batched matrix products and differentiable convolution are available as described above; Gather kernels, leaf/Adam checkpointing and analytic Hessian-vector products are available. Derivative orders above nine, sparse tensors, quantization and broader application checkpointing remain future work. The math application guide connects these functions to graphics, audio, learning and physics, with runnable examples and completion gates.

CPU collision and ray queries

These functions operate on ordinary three-element vector lists and can be used with the CPU mesh renderer or independent simulations. Boxes are axis-aligned minimum/maximum corners; inverted bounds and negative radii are errors. Touching counts as overlap. Ray direction must be nonzero, and need not be normalized.

FunctionResult
AABBHIT(minA,maxA,minB,maxB)BASIC true (-1) if the boxes touch or overlap, otherwise zero
SPHEREHIT(centerA,radiusA,centerB,radiusB)BASIC true (-1) for touching/overlapping spheres, otherwise zero
RAYAABB(origin,direction,min,max)First nonnegative ray parameter t, zero when starting inside/on the box, or -1 for no hit
RAYTRIANGLE(origin,direction,a,b,c){t,u,v} for a two-sided triangle hit, or {-1,0,0}; hit point is origin+t*direction = (1-u-v)*a+u*b+v*c

t measures physical distance only when direction has unit length. Parallel, degenerate and coplanar ray/triangle cases report no isolated crossing. Exact input-product signs classify near-parallel crossings without a tolerance. Only an unrepresentable required final parameter reports overflow; detailed hit reports below preserve finite hit points even when their parameters overflow. These queries do not automatically attach collision bodies to meshes or implement a physics solver. programs/examples/cpu_collect3d.bas supplies BASIC movement, gravity/jumping, box collision and sphere pickups around the CPU renderer. Use SELFTEST for deterministic query checks or PREVIEW for a saved frame.

Program-state commands accepted by the statement parser

The following commands alter the stored program or execution session. The interpreter accepts them through the statement parser, but they are not ordinary data-processing statements and should normally be entered at READY.:

RUN [line]
LIST [range]
NEW
LOAD path$
SAVE path$
MERGE path$
VERIFY path$

READY CONT resumes a stopped session. A stored CONT does not perform that operation and reports CAN'T CONTINUE.

Microsoft # file-channel punctuation is tokenized directly. OPEN accepts both OPEN path$ FOR mode AS #channel and the MS/GW-BASIC OPEN mode$,#channel,path$ shorthand. File access is bounded and sandboxed beneath the configured root. RANDOM files support the classic FIELD/LSET/RSET buffer workflow with GET #channel[,record] and PUT #channel[,record]; an omitted record selects the record after the last successful transfer. BINARY files support byte PUT, raw-byte destination lists with GET#, and one-based SEEK.

DIR$(directory$) starts a directory snapshot and returns its first entry; DIR$() advances it, returning "" at the end. Use DIR$(".") for the current BASIC directory. Entries retain their spelling, with / appended to directories; directories sort first, then names case-insensitively. Snapshots are limited to 4,096 entries and 256 KiB of names. They omit symbolic links, devices and other special files. This is directory enumeration, not a wildcard search. Another explicit directory argument replaces the current snapshot.

MKDIR path$ creates one directory beneath the file root; its parent must already exist. READFILE$(path$) reads a complete UTF-8 text file, subject to both the file and string byte limits. Invalid UTF-8 is an error, not a lossy conversion. WRITEFILE path$,text$ atomically replaces a complete file with the exact UTF-8 bytes, including any newlines, without adding a terminator. Failed validation leaves an existing file unchanged. These operations share the usual file-root permission and path restrictions; Linux operations retain directory descriptors to prevent a parent symlink swap from escaping the root.

A user-defined record can be transferred directly with GET|PUT #channel,[record-or-byte-position],record-variable. The position may be left empty to use the current binary position or next random record, as in PUT #1,,item. Scalar records, indexed record-array elements, and nested subrecords are supported. Direct layouts use portable little-endian signed 32-bit INTEGER, signed 64-bit LONG, IEEE binary32 SINGLE, IEEE binary64 DOUBLE, and exact UTF-8 bytes for STRING * n, in declaration order with no alignment padding. A random record may be larger than the direct layout; unused bytes are zero-filled. Dynamic STRING fields remain valid in memory but must be changed to STRING * n for direct fixed-layout transfer. Short binary and random reads leave the destination and logical file position unchanged.

Single-line DEF FN definitions accept numeric scalars/lists, canonical sparse matrices and validated sparse linear reports, and can return those value types. Canonical sparse matrix arguments and results are validated as CSR1 records using the same shape, ordering, finiteness and resource checks as other sparse functions. This supports helpers such as DEF FNK(T)=SPARSE({{1+T}}) and DEF FNAPPLY(A,X)=SPMV(A,X). Unrelated strings/mixed lists and malformed sparse records or linear reports are rejected.

REDIM [PRESERVE] name(bounds)[,...] dynamically resizes numeric or string arrays. Plain REDIM resets the resized arrays. PRESERVE retains explicitly stored values throughout the coordinate region shared by the old and new same-rank shapes, including multidimensional arrays; shrinking discards values outside that overlap. The complete comma-separated resize commits atomically and remains subject to the configured array and retained-storage limits. Omitting AS retains an explicit array declaration, including through a BYREF alias. REDIM PRESERVE cannot change the element type, and an existing record array cannot be replaced with a primitive array or vice versa. LBOUND(name[,dimension]) and UBOUND(name[,dimension]) return the stored inclusive bounds; BASIC dimension numbers are one-based regardless of the array's subscript base. They do not allocate a missing array.

CONST name=expression[,...] evaluates each initializer once and creates an immutable numeric or string scalar. Later constants in the same declaration may use earlier ones. Assignment, READ, INPUT, GET, SWAP, MID$, and other scalar destination forms cannot change a constant. CLEAR removes mutable program state while retaining declared constants.

Stored programs may declare structured procedures with SUB name[([BYVAL|BYREF] parameter,...)] through END SUB and invoke them with CALL name[(argument,...)]. Unqualified parameters and explicit BYVAL parameters are evaluated before entry and copied into each recursive call. An explicit BYREF parameter requires an exact-type assignable variable or array element and aliases that storage immediately; scalar record fields and record-array fields are valid arguments. An alias forwarded through nested or recursive SUB/FUNCTION calls continues to name the original target and does not duplicate its retained-storage charge. A whole-array formal uses explicit BYREF name() and its actual argument must use name(); BYVAL whole arrays are rejected. Whole-array aliases have an exact element kind and participate in ordinary element access, READ, MAT, REDIM [PRESERVE], ERASE, and bound queries. Record field arrays such as PEOPLE.AGE() are valid. A whole array of records uses the exact-type formal BYREF name() AS type; each field aliases the caller without copying and nested forwarding preserves the original record storage.

Parameters and undeclared scalars are otherwise local to each recursive call. DIM name AS type and DIM name(bounds) AS type inside a procedure create per-call typed scalar or array storage, including user-defined records, unless the base name is declared SHARED. STATIC name[,...] retains ordinary scalars, STATIC name AS type retains typed primitive or record scalars, and STATIC name(bounds) [AS type] retains primitive or record arrays and their first established shape between calls. Local array capacity and payload are released on return. SHARED name[,...] routes named scalars and arrays to program-global storage. Existing arrays declared outside a procedure remain global and readable there. Recursive local record arrays isolate every field; STATIC record fields and metadata persist without contaminating same-named procedures. EXIT SUB returns early. Procedure calls share the configured call-depth and retained-storage budgets with classic GOSUB and ordinary variables; failed binding/dimensioning is atomic and trappable, and declaration/control-block structure is validated before execution.

FUNCTION name[([BYVAL|BYREF] parameter,...)] through END FUNCTION declares a multi-line value-returning procedure. Assigning to the function name sets its return value; an unassigned numeric or string return slot has that type's default value. EXIT FUNCTION returns early. Functions support recursion, calls to structured SUB procedures, and the same parameter-mode, local, SHARED, STATIC, array, depth, and storage rules as SUB. Only the selected branches of IF, loop conditions, SELECT CASE, and PIECEWISE invoke functions, so stateful functions preserve language short-circuit behavior. Stored SUB and FUNCTION declarations may be called from a running program or directly at the READY. prompt. Single-line DEF FN and multi-line FUNCTION calls compose in either direction, evaluate arguments once, retain lazy PIECEWISE branches, preserve complex results, and share a bounded cross-recursion depth.

TYPE name through END TYPE declares a record layout. Each field uses field AS INTEGER|LONG|SINGLE|DOUBLE|STRING; STRING * bytes declares a fixed-width string that truncates or space-pads assignments. A field may also use field AS another_type to nest a user-defined record. Forward TYPE references are accepted, while missing types and direct or indirect recursive layouts are rejected before execution. Layout validation is bounded to 256 nested levels and 65,536 flattened primitive fields. Field names follow ordinary ModernBASIC identifier rules and therefore cannot be reserved statement words. DIM value AS type creates a scalar record and DIM values(bounds) AS type creates an array of records. Multi-level paths such as value.address.city and values(index).address.coordinates.x are accepted; listings canonicalize the latter to values.address.coordinates.x(index).

Record fields participate in normal typed assignment, expressions, DATA/READ, INPUT, LINE INPUT, file input, raw GET, storage limits, and array bounds. REDIM [PRESERVE] values(bounds) resizes every field array atomically, preserving their common coordinate region when requested, and ERASE values releases every field array and its retained payload. A stored TYPE declaration is also available to DIM commands entered at READY.. Exact-type destination = source assignment copies every field of scalar records or indexed record-array elements by value. The source is captured before any destination write, and storage-limit failure rolls the whole copy back rather than leaving a partially updated record. Nested subrecords are also assignable as whole values when their declared TYPEs match exactly. Typed whole-array formals can receive either a root record array or one of its nested subrecord arrays and can forward either alias through further SUB/FUNCTION calls.

## Statement index

This index describes the executable statement surface. Built-in expression
functions such as `ABS()`, `SIN()`, `SPRITEX()`, and `OBJECTZ()` are not
statements and are therefore not repeated here. Canonical spellings appear in
the main lists; accepted compatibility aliases are collected separately so an
alias is not mistaken for a second implementation.

Statements are case-insensitive. A colon separates statements on one source
line. `REM` and apostrophe introduce comments, and `?` tokenizes as `PRINT`.
Traditional suffixes are `$` for string, `%` for integer, `&` for long, `!`
for single precision, and `#` for double precision.
Longer variable names with keyword prefixes remain whole in scalar and indexed
assignment targets, for example `ORIGINS(I)={0,0,1}`. Exact reserved names and
compact `IF`, `FOR`, `LET` and `ON` control forms retain their existing meaning.

### Assignment, declarations, and data

```text
[LET] target = expression
MID$(string$,start[,length]) = replacement$
expression -> variable                 Unicode → is also accepted

CONST name=expression[,name=expression...]
DIM declaration[,declaration...]
REDIM [PRESERVE] declaration[,declaration...]
ERASE array[,array...]
OPTION BASE 0|1
SWAP variable,variable
CHANGE source TO destination
RANDOMIZE [seed]
CLEAR
SHARED name[,name...]
STATIC declaration[,declaration...]
COMMON name[,name...]

DATA values
READ target[,target...]
RESTORE [line]
```

`DIM` accepts ordinary arrays, typed primitive scalars and arrays, and
user-defined record scalars and arrays. `CLEAR` has the accepted `CLR` alias.

### Records and procedures

```text
TYPE name
    field AS INTEGER|LONG|SINGLE|DOUBLE|STRING [* bytes]|record-type
END TYPE

SUB name[([BYVAL|BYREF] parameter,...)]
END SUB
EXIT SUB

FUNCTION name[([BYVAL|BYREF] parameter,...)]
END FUNCTION
EXIT FUNCTION

CALL name[(arguments)]
DEF FNname(parameter[,parameter...])=expression
DEF SEG [= expression]
DEF USR[n]=service-address
DEFINT letter-range
DEFSNG letter-range
DEFDBL letter-range
DEFSTR letter-range
```

The spaced default-type forms such as `DEF INT A-Z` are accepted too. The
standalone spelling `DEFTYPE` is reserved by the tokenizer but has no
executable statement form; programs should use `DEFINT`, `DEFSNG`, `DEFDBL`,
or `DEFSTR`. Comma-separated letter ranges are validated and committed
as one declaration; a malformed range or storage failure leaves the previous
default types unchanged. Explicit type suffixes override these defaults even
for values that have not been assigned yet.

### Input and output

```text
PRINT [items]
PRINT USING format$;items
WRITE [items]
INPUT [prompt;]variable[,variable...]
LINE INPUT [prompt;]string-variable
GET variable

WIDTH columns
LOCATE row[,column[,cursor-visible]]
VIEW PRINT [top TO bottom]
HOME
HTAB column
VTAB row
TEXTCOLOR [foreground[,background]]
LPRINT [items]
LLIST [range]
NULL count
TRON
TROFF
```

`GET variable` is the console/key-input form. File-channel `GET #` is listed
with the file statements below. `LINEINPUT` is accepted as the compact spelling
of `LINE INPUT`.

Text rows are one-based 1 through 25 and columns are one-based 1 through 80;
explicit out-of-range `LOCATE`, `HTAB`, `VTAB`, or `VIEW PRINT` coordinates
raise `IllegalQuantity`. `VIEW PRINT` with no bounds restores the full screen.
`HOME` clears through the text backend and moves to column 1 at the active
region's top. `TEXTCOLOR` accepts zero through `0xFFFFFF`; one argument changes
the foreground, two change both colors, and no arguments restore defaults.
`TEXTCELL(row,column[,field])` queries the same bounded logical cells in batch,
terminal, and graphical sessions. The default field 0 returns the Unicode
codepoint, field 1 returns the foreground color, and field 2 returns the
background color. Blank cells return codepoint 32. Invalid coordinates or
field selectors raise `IllegalQuantity`.
These identifier-encoded names remain ordinary assignable variables when
immediately followed by `=`.

`PRINT` column tracking and `WIDTH` wrapping count Unicode characters rather
than UTF-8 bytes. Numeric `PRINT USING` fields accept only integer and real
values; strings, complex values, and lists report `TypeMismatch`.

`LPRINT` and `LPRINT USING` append to `modernbasic_print.spool` beneath the
configured output root (or file root when no separate output root is supplied).
The spool obeys the per-file byte ceiling and rejects symlink targets. It does
not discover a physical printer or write to a shared temporary path. An
embedding host may approve one explicit spool path through `RunOptions`.

### Control flow

```text
END
STOP
SLEEP [seconds]

GOTO line                         GO TO line is accepted
GOSUB line                        GO SUB line is accepted
RETURN

IF condition THEN statement-or-line [ELSE statement-or-line]
IF condition GOTO line
IF condition THEN
    block
[ELSE
    block]
END IF

FOR variable=start TO limit [STEP increment]
NEXT [variable]
WHILE condition
WEND
DO [WHILE|UNTIL condition]
LOOP [WHILE|UNTIL condition]
REPEAT
UNTIL condition

EXIT FOR
EXIT WHILE
EXIT DO
EXIT REPEAT
```

`SLEEP` uses seconds and accepts fractional durations. A queued keypress ends
both timed and indefinite sleep; Ctrl+Escape/BREAK remains interruptible.

`RETURN` has no destination argument. It resumes at the exact statement after
the corresponding `GOSUB`. Block-IF endings `ENDIF`, `IFEND`, and `IF END` are
accepted aliases for `END IF`.

Selection supports both the standard and BBC-family structured forms:

```text
SELECT CASE expression
CASE value[,value...]
CASE low TO high
CASE IS comparison value
CASE ELSE
END SELECT

CASE expression OF
WHEN value-or-range
OTHERWISE
ENDCASE
```

`ENDSELECT`, `ENDCASE`, `END CASE`, and `CEND` are accepted compact endings.
Errors while evaluating branch values, ranges, or comparisons use the active
`ON ERROR` handler. `ERL` identifies the enclosing selection statement;
`RESUME` retries selection and `RESUME NEXT` skips to its next statement
(normally the first branch marker, which skips the remaining selection).

### Files, memory, and host-approved services

```text
OPEN path$ FOR INPUT|OUTPUT|APPEND|RANDOM|BINARY AS #channel [LEN=record-size]
OPEN mode$,#channel,path$
OPEN #channel,path$,mode$
CLOSE [#channel[,#channel...]]

PRINT #channel,items
WRITE #channel,items
INPUT #channel,variables
LINE INPUT #channel,string-variable
GET #channel,...
PUT #channel,...
FIELD #channel,width AS string$[,width AS string$...]
LSET string$=expression$
RSET string$=expression$
SEEK #channel,position
CMD #channel[,print-list]

KILL path$
NAME old$ AS new$
MKDIR path$
WRITEFILE path$,text$
CHAIN path$[,line]
MERGE path$
LOAD path$
SAVE path$
VERIFY path$

POKE address,value
OUT port,value
WAIT milliseconds
WAIT port,mask[,xor]
SYS service-address[,arguments]
CALL service-address[,arguments]
```

`PRINT#`, `WRITE#`, `INPUT#`, `LINE INPUT#`, and `GET#` are accepted compact
file-channel spellings. `PEEK`, `INP`, and `USR` are expression functions, not
statements. Memory, ports, and callable services are bounded virtual or
host-approved resources; these forms never expose unrestricted host hardware.

`INPUT#` consumes comma- or line-separated fields until every requested
destination has a value. Fields left on the same line remain available to the
next read; `LINE INPUT#` and `GET#` continue at that same byte position. A trailing
comma contributes an empty field. Quoted fields may contain commas and newlines;
doubled quotes decode to one quote, matching `WRITE#` output. The total raw field
bytes collected by one `INPUT#` statement must fit the configured input-byte
limit. Conversion or storage failure leaves all destination values unchanged.

During execution, `MERGE` installs the combined program immediately and
continues after the executing statement's line and colon position. Saved loop,
subroutine, procedure, and error-resume positions retain their line and colon
positions when inserted lines shift the executable layout. If a replacement
line has fewer statements, a removed position continues at the end of that
line. `MERGE` rebuilds the DATA cursor without clearing variables or default
type declarations.

`CHAIN` starts the loaded program with COMMON values, arrays, and their declared
types retained. Non-COMMON declarations and prior error-handler/resume state
are cleared; the new program installs its own `ON ERROR` handler if needed.

### Networking and host web services

```text
WEB OPEN url$
WEB GET url$,response$
WEB POST url$,body$,response$[,content-type$]
WEB DOWNLOAD url$,path$

PLAY AUDIO source$
PLAY VIDEO source$
```

Network access is a host capability and is disabled by default. Start a CLI
session with `--network`, or set `RunOptions::network_enabled` through the
library API. `WEB OPEN` hands an HTTP(S) address to the operating system's
default browser; on Linux this uses `xdg-open`. The browser remains responsible
for HTML, JavaScript, logins, cookies, accessibility, downloads initiated by a
page, and licensed/DRM playback. For an owned graphical Chromium surface controlled from BASIC, use the optional
`WEB VIEW` interface described in [Browser](BROWSER.md). `WEB VIEW OPEN` also
requires the host network grant; it is separate from the external `WEB OPEN` handoff.

`WEB GET` returns one UTF-8 response in a string variable. `WEB POST` sends a
string body and returns a UTF-8 response; its default content type is
`application/json`, and an optional fourth argument selects another content
type. Use `WEB DOWNLOAD` for binary data: it performs an HTTP(S) GET and writes
the response beneath the output sandbox. The host `curl` executable performs
HTTP, redirects, and TLS through fixed arguments. URLs are limited to HTTP and
HTTPS; embedded credentials are rejected. Requests starting with HTTPS keep
every redirect on HTTPS; HTTP entry points may redirect to HTTP or HTTPS.
POST redirects use GET after 301/302/303, while 307/308 retain the method and
body. Transfers honor interruption during request writes, response reads and
process exit, have a 30-second deadline, and responses are bounded by
`--max-network-bytes` (16 MiB by default). Downloads must also fit the configured
file limit.

`PLAY AUDIO` and `PLAY VIDEO` accept either an existing sandboxed local path
or a direct HTTP(S) media URL when the capability is enabled. For a stored
program, the loader reads or fetches the complete bounded source before
`READY.`; FFmpeg later decodes those retained bytes through fixed arguments and
the existing 30-minute media-duration ceiling. A normal YouTube, Netflix, or
other web-page URL is not a direct media source; pass that page to `WEB OPEN`
so the installed browser can handle its site logic and any licensed playback.

MAT PRINT A;
MAT target=source

MAT target=left-right
MAT target=left*right

### Exact symbolic polynomial mathematics

The polynomial functions in this section accept expression strings and return exact results for
**polynomials over rational numbers**, including multiple variables. Integer
literals, variable names, parentheses, unary signs, `+`, `-`, `*`, division by a
nonzero constant, and nonnegative integer literal powers are supported.
Multiplication must be explicit. Decimals, functions such as `SIN`, and variable
denominators are rejected. Write `3/2`, not `1.5`. Variable names are ASCII
alphanumeric, start with a letter, and are case-insensitive; output names are
uppercase. Calculus selects `X` unless another variable is supplied.

| Function | Exact result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMSIMPLIFY$(expr$[,variable$])` | Expanded polynomial with reduced rational coefficients, ordered by descending total degree and then lexicographic powers with alphabetically ordered variables. |
| `SYMDIFF$(expr$[,variable$])` | Partial derivative with respect to the selected variable; all other variables are held constant. |
| `SYMINT$(expr$[,variable$])` | Polynomial antiderivative with the term independent of the selected variable set to zero. The general answer adds an arbitrary function of the other variables, or a constant in the univariate case. |
| `SYMPROVE(left$,right$[,variable$])` | `-1` if canonical coefficients prove a polynomial identity in all variables; `0` if the polynomials differ. Unsupported statements raise errors. |
| `SYMVARS(expr$)` | Alphabetically ordered list of variable-name strings remaining after simplification. A constant returns an empty list. |
| `SYMGRAD(expr$,variables)` | List of partial-derivative strings in the explicitly requested variable order. |
| `SYMHESSIAN(expr$,variables)` | Nested list of second-partial-derivative strings. Entry `(i,j)` differentiates with respect to the requested variables `i` and `j`. |
| `SYMSUBST$(expr$,variable$,replacement$)` | Exact substitution of one polynomial for the selected variable, followed by expansion. Inserted expressions are not recursively substituted again. |
| `SYMDIV(dividend$,divisor$[,variable$])` | Univariate only: two strings `{quotient$,remainder$}` satisfying the polynomial division identity. |
| `SYMGCD$(left$,right$[,variable$])` | Univariate only: monic polynomial GCD; `GCD(0,0)` returns `0`. |
| `SYMMIN(expr$,lower$,upper$[,variable$])` | Univariate only: two exact constant-expression strings `{location$,value$}` for the global minimum of a degree-at-most-two polynomial on a closed rational interval. |
| `SYMMAX(expr$,lower$,upper$[,variable$])` | Corresponding global maximum. |

For gradients and Hessians, `variables` is a comma-separated string such as
`"Y,X,Z"`, or the string list returned by `SYMVARS`. A nonempty set of distinct
names is required; duplicates are rejected case-insensitively. An absent variable
has zero derivative. BASIC brace literals remain numeric, so use a string to
specify variable order. Returned derivative strings can be indexed, printed, and
passed directly to other symbolic functions. For existing calls, the optional
identifier on `SYMSIMPLIFY$` and `SYMPROVE` remains accepted and validated; it does
not restrict the variable set or change the canonical ordering.

Division, GCD, and the univariate `SYMMIN`/`SYMMAX` optimizers require every input
expression to use only the selected variable. Optimization bounds must be
constant rational expressions. Equal bounds are allowed; reversed bounds are
rejected. Endpoints and any interior stationary point are compared exactly;
ties retain the lower endpoint. These univariate calls accept either curvature.
For convex multivariable problems with box constraints, use the separate calls
below. General linear constraints, integer and nonlinear optimization are not
supplied by these symbolic functions.

`SYMPROVE` is a decision procedure for polynomial identities, not a general
purpose theorem prover. A false result means the expressions are not identical,
not that they differ at every point. No floating-point samples are used as proof.
Division by a variable expression is rejected even when cancellation seems
possible: `X/X` must not silently become an everywhere-defined constant.
Powers are polynomial powers (`P^0` is the constant polynomial `1`).

Exact rational coefficients use dynamically allocated arbitrary-precision integers
with a 4096-bit limit on each normalized numerator and positive denominator
(about 1233 decimal digits). Small coefficients keep an inline signed-integer
fast path. Each addition, multiplication and division reduces its result before
applying the size limit; temporary cross-products can exceed it. An intermediate
*normalized* result beyond the limit fails even if a later expression would
cancel it. Zero denominators always raise an error.

Total degree is limited to 64, input and individual output expressions to 8192
bytes, variable names to 32 characters, and parser recursion to 32 levels. Sparse
multivariable operations allow at most eight distinct input/requested variable
names per call, 2048 intermediate terms, and one million charged algebra steps.
A separate per-call budget of 32 million coefficient-work units charges rational
arithmetic by squared 64-bit limb width and checks BREAK. Existing certificate,
term, recursion and output limits still apply; arbitrary precision is bounded,
not unlimited computation. Every returned expression fits its parser's input
limit and can be used in another symbolic call.

`SYMEVAL` converts exact rational constants directly to binary64 with one rounding
(ties to even), including subnormal values. It does not divide two independently
rounded floating-point coefficients. Finite binary64 variable bindings can all
be represented exactly for symbolic domain checks. Rational subexpressions and
guard signs are evaluated exactly before conversion where the coefficient limits
permit it. BASIC retains its canonical single zero representation. Ordinary BASIC numeric
variables, tensor kernels and transcendental function evaluation still use their
existing machine-number types; this does not add arbitrary-precision floats.

Polynomial degrees retain their existing limits. General constant integer-power
evaluation and some integration searches use signed 128-bit exponents. Exhaustive
integer-divisor/Kronecker factor searches use exact big integers for primitive
coefficients, divisors, sampled values and interpolated factors. Primitive
coefficients, common denominators and integer Horner intermediates have a 4096-bit
limit. Prime powers are stripped before generating complete divisor lists; large
smooth integers can therefore finish without scanning up to their square roots.
Difficult remaining integer factors can still exhaust the search budget. These
bounded searches fail explicitly rather than return unfinished factors. The big-integer implementation is vendored in `src/vendor`,
compiled into ModernBASIC, and available to standalone compiled BASIC programs
without a Python or external big-integer runtime.

```basic
10 P$="X^2*Y+Y^3"
20 PRINT SYMDIFF$(P$,"Y")
30 G=SYMGRAD(P$,"X,Y"):PRINT G(1),G(2)
40 H=SYMHESSIAN(P$,SYMVARS(P$)):PRINT H(1,2)
50 PRINT SYMSUBST$(P$,"X","Y+1")
60 PRINT SYMPROVE("(X+Y)*(X-Y)","X^2-Y^2")
```

### Elementary symbolic calculus with domain conditions

A separate expression-tree API supports real elementary functions and general
powers while retaining domain conditions through simplification and repeated
differentiation. Bounded antiderivative rules use the same guarded result format.
The polynomial APIs above retain their exact polynomial grammar.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMDERIV(expression[,variable$])` | `{formula$,{condition$...}}` for a partial derivative, with sufficient real smooth-domain conditions. Defaults to variable `X`. Accepts a source string or a complete guarded symbolic result. |
| `SYMREFINE(expression[,assumptions])` | `{formula$,{condition$...}}` simplified using bounded exact sign deductions and real identities. Accepts a string or guarded result; optional assumptions are one condition string or a list of condition strings. Assumptions remain attached to the result. |
| `SYMANTIDERIV(expression[,variable$])` | `{formula$,{condition$...}}` for one antiderivative on its stated real domain. Defaults to `X`. Accepts a string or complete guarded result. Unsupported integrands raise an explicit error. |
| `SYMPARTFRAC(expression[,variable$])` | `{formula$,{condition$...}}` for an exact univariate rational partial-fraction decomposition. Defaults to `X`; accepts a string or guarded result. Original domain restrictions survive cancellation. |
| `SYMDEFINTEGRAL(expression,start,finish[,variable$])` | Exact symbolic proper integral of a supported rational function, after proving its source domain covers the closed interval. Returns a guarded pair usable with `SYMEVAL`. |
| `SYMLIMIT(expression,point[,variable$[,side$]])` | Exact finite or infinite rational-function limit, with an algebraic witness and local domain flags. See below for the result format. |
| `SYMLIMITCHECK(expression,point,result[,variable$[,side$]])` | Checks the limit witness and domain classification using exact polynomial identities. |
| `SYMSERIES(expression,point,order[,variable$[,side$]])` | Rational Taylor/Laurent expansion, including an exact remainder and reusable guarded approximation. |
| `SYMSERIESCHECK(expression,point,order,result[,variable$[,side$]])` | Checks all series coefficients together by polynomial multiplication and validates the returned approximation, remainder and guards. |
| `SYMTAYLOR(expression,point,order[,variable$])` | Elementary-function Taylor polynomial with symbolic coefficients and retained source/center conditions. |
| `SYMFACTOR(expression[,variable$])` | `{formula$,{condition$...}}` containing a complete factorization of a univariate rational-coefficient polynomial over the rationals, when the bounded exact algorithm finishes. Defaults to `X`; accepts a string or guarded result. |
| `SYMDOMAIN(expression)` | List of conditions sufficient for evaluating a source string or guarded calculus result. These describe the supported real branches, not a solved set of intervals. |
| `SYMEVAL(expression[,variables,values])` | Finite binary64 evaluation after checking its conditions. Pass a source string or a complete guarded symbolic result. With no bindings, every variable still needed by the formula or conditions must be absent. |

Expressions accept integer literals, rational expressions such as `1/3`, names,
parentheses, unary signs, and `+ - * / ^`. Multiplication must be explicit;
decimal and exponent-format literals inside these symbolic expression strings are
unsupported. The separate `HPEVAL`/`HPBOUNDS` interface below accepts them exactly.
Powers associate to the right; `-X^2` means `-(X^2)`. Variable denominators and
variable exponents are supported. `PI` and `E` are reserved constants in this API.
Names are case-insensitive, ASCII alphanumeric, start with a letter, and have at
most 32 characters. All trigonometric arguments are radians.

Supported functions are `SIN`, `COS`, `TAN`, `EXP`, `LN`, `SQRT`, `SINH`, `COSH`,
`TANH`, `ASIN`, `ACOS`, `ATAN`, `ASINH`, `ACOSH`, `ATANH`, and `ABS`. `LOG` aliases
natural logarithm `LN`, and `SQR` aliases `SQRT`. Differentiation uses chain,
product, quotient, and general power rules. Rational coefficients stay exact;
functions remain symbolic. `SYMINT$` retains its polynomial-only contract;
`SYMANTIDERIV` supplies the separate elementary integration rules below.
The elementary rules follow the
[NIST DLMF formulas](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.7), including its
[trigonometric](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.20) and
[inverse-function derivatives](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.24).

For bindings, `variables` is a comma-separated string such as `"Y,X"` or a list
of name strings. `values` is a numeric list in that order; a scalar is accepted
for a single variable. An empty string/list with an empty value list is allowed.
Names must be distinct, and `PI`/`E` cannot be rebound. Unknown variables and
mismatched lengths are errors. Integer bindings use the runtime's checked real
conversion; real-valued bindings can contain decimal/exponent literals.

Conditions form a conjunction. They are expression strings ending in `>0`,
`>=0`, or `<>0`. Inputs also accept `<0`, `<=0`, and `=0`; these are normalized
to conditions on the subject or its negative. The right-hand side must be literal
zero: write `X-1>0` for a bound at one. The API keeps the original expression's restrictions even when
simplification removes the restricted operation: the derivative of `X/X` has
formula `0` and condition `X<>0`, and the derivative of `0*LN(X)` retains `X>0`.
Pass the **entire result** to `SYMEVAL`, `SYMDERIV`, or `SYMANTIDERIV` to preserve
these conditions. Extracting only `D(1)` discards the original conditions.

| Operation | Value-domain condition | Sufficient derivative-domain condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a/u`, negative integer powers of `u` | `u<>0` | Same |
| `LN(u)` | `u>0` | Same |
| `SQRT(u)` | `u>=0` | `u>0` |
| `TAN(u)` | `COS(u)<>0` | Same |
| `ASIN(u)`, `ACOS(u)` | `1-u^2>=0` | `1-u^2>0` |
| `ACOSH(u)` | `u-1>=0` | `u-1>0` |
| `ATANH(u)` | `1-u^2>0` | Same |
| `ABS(u)` | None beyond the argument's domain | `u<>0` |
| Noninteger or variable powers `u^v` | `u>0` | Same |

Nonnegative constant integer powers allow any real base, with `u^0=1`, including
`0^0`. The domain of the original base and exponent expressions is still kept.
Negative bases with noninteger or variable exponents are outside this real
branch convention, even when a particular rational exponent could have a real
root. All other operations retain the conditions of their arguments.

Derivative conditions are sufficient, not necessarily maximal. For example,
`SQRT(X^4)` is differentiable at zero, but the conservative rule excludes that
point; partial derivatives can also be restricted by an independent variable's
boundary. The basic calculus rules do not solve inequalities, prove all conditions
jointly satisfiable, or infer removable singularities. `SYMREFINE` adds the bounded
reasoning described below. A condition that simplifies to a
false rational constant is rejected; other conditions are checked on evaluation.

`SYMEVAL` and numerical condition checks use binary64 arithmetic, not formal
proofs of domain membership near singularities. Intermediate overflow or an
unrepresentable result raises an error; underflow may round to zero. The engine
recognizes integer/half-integer multiples of `PI` built by rational arithmetic,
including representable bound values, so known poles such as `TAN(PI/2)` and
`TAN(PI*(X+1)/2)` at `X=0` are rejected rather than evaluated at a rounded angle.
This recognition does not cover every algebraically equivalent expression.

Each source/output expression is limited to 8192 bytes, each tree to 4096 nodes
and 64 levels, parser nesting to 128 levels, and a call to eight variable names.
There are at most 128 conditions and 65536 bytes of serialized conditions.
Bounded arbitrary-precision rational coefficients and the shared one-million-step work budget
apply to construction, simplification, differentiation, integration, and evaluation. Output
is reparsed before return to ensure it remains usable within these limits.
Resource failures and BREAK interrupt the operation without a partial result.

```basic
10 D=SYMDERIV("EXP(SIN(X^2))")
20 PRINT D(1),D(2)
30 PRINT SYMEVAL(D,"X",1)
40 L=SYMDERIV("LN(X)")
50 PRINT L
60 D2=SYMDERIV(L)
70 PRINT SYMEVAL(D2,"X",2)
80 PRINT SYMDOMAIN("SQRT(X)")
```

`L` contains formula `(1/X)` and condition `X>0`. Its second derivative evaluates
to `-0.25` at `X=2`; evaluating that complete result at a negative `X` is an error.

#### Exact limits and local series

`SYMLIMIT` and `SYMSERIES` accept univariate rational functions, as strings or
guarded expression pairs. Their coefficients and conditions must reduce to
rational expressions in the selected variable. The variable defaults to `X`.
Parameters requiring additional assumptions, nonrational functions, oscillatory
limits and fractional-power series are outside these two calls.

`point` is a BASIC integer, an exact rational constant string such as `"1/3"`,
or `"+INF"`/`"-INF"` (`"INF"` also means positive infinity). BASIC real values
are rejected here to avoid silently rounding an exact center. At a finite point,
`side$` is `"LEFT"`, `"RIGHT"`, or the default `"BOTH"`. At infinity use `"BOTH"`;
the sign of infinity already selects the direction.

The limit result is:

```text
{status$, value$, {numeratorCoefficients...}, {denominatorCoefficients...},
 {leftAllowed,rightAllowed}}
```

Coefficients and finite values are exact rational strings. Coefficients are in
ascending powers of a local coordinate `T`: `T=X-point` at finite points and
`T=1/X` at infinity. The two flags are BASIC booleans (`-1` or `0`) for small
negative and positive `T`, respectively. The denominator witness is nonzero.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `FINITE` | `value$` is the exact rational limit. |
| `+INF`, `-INF` | Divergence to the stated infinity. `value$` is empty. |
| `DNE` | Both sides are allowed but their infinite limits disagree. `value$` is empty. |
| `OUTSIDE_DOMAIN` | At least one requested side has no allowed punctured neighborhood. `value$` is empty. |

`BOTH` requires both neighborhoods, even for a source restricted to one side.
Use `RIGHT` for a right boundary or `LEFT` for a left boundary. Conditions are
classified by the sign and parity of the first nonzero local rational
coefficient. An equality that holds only at the center does not supply a
neighborhood. Contradictions already reduced to false constants can raise a
domain error during input validation. Other unsupported conditions raise an
error instead of an undecided claim being labeled as a limit.

A limit can exist at an excluded point: `(X^2-1)/(X-1)` has limit `2` at `1`.
This operation does not change the original expression's domain. No numerical
samples or floating-point comparisons decide these results. `SYMLIMITCHECK`
verifies the witness by exact cross multiplication, checks the local conditions,
and replays the leading-coefficient classification. Rational rescalings of a valid
witness are accepted; a well-formed false claim returns `0`.

`SYMSERIES` returns:

```text
{approximation, firstExponent, order, {coefficients...}, exactRemainder,
 {leftAllowed,rightAllowed}}
```

`approximation` and `exactRemainder` are ordinary guarded expression pairs for
use with `SYMEVAL` and other expression APIs. The series coefficients are exact
rational strings, in ascending exponents from `firstExponent` through `order`.
Negative exponents form the Laurent principal part. At infinity this is an
expansion in `1/X`. If the first nonzero term has exponent greater than `order`,
the coefficient list is empty and the approximation is zero. The identically
zero function uses first exponent zero and zero coefficients.

On the retained source domain, **source = approximation + exactRemainder**.
The remainder has local order at least `order+1`. Rational functions have a
convergent Laurent expansion in some sufficiently small punctured neighborhood;
these calls do not calculate its convergence radius. The exact remainder can be
evaluated directly when assessing approximation error. It retains source poles
and is itself evaluated using ordinary binary64 arithmetic. A series is not a
global identity between the source and its truncated approximation.

`SYMSERIESCHECK` checks the low coefficients of `A-B*H`, without repeating the
producer's division recurrence, then verifies the canonical approximation,
remainder, order and guard fields. Edited or incorrect records return `0`;
malformed data and resource exhaustion raise errors. Series construction requires
every requested side to be allowed and raises an error otherwise.

The rational input layer retains its degree-32 intermediate bound. Series order
is an integer from 0 through 32, with at most 65 Laurent coefficients. Exact
remainder and certificate products may have degree up to 96. Records contain at
most 65536 text bytes, individual strings at most 8192 bytes, and existing
coefficient, expression-tree, guard and work budgets apply. A resource failure
never returns a partial series, guessed limit or successful certificate.

```basic
10 L=SYMLIMIT("(X^2-1)/(X-1)",1)
20 PRINT L(1),L(2)
30 PRINT SYMLIMITCHECK("(X^2-1)/(X-1)",1,L)
40 PRINT SYMLIMIT("1/X",0,"X","LEFT")
50 S=SYMSERIES("1/(X^2*(1-X))",0,3)
60 PRINT S(2),S(4)
70 PRINT SYMEVAL(S(1),"X",0.1),SYMEVAL(S(5),"X",0.1)
80 PRINT SYMSERIESCHECK("1/(X^2*(1-X))",0,3,S)
90 PRINT SYMSERIES("(X^2+1)/(X-1)","+INF",3)
```

`SYMTAYLOR` additionally handles the supported real elementary functions and
independent parameters, using exact symbolic differentiation and substitution.
Its finite center must be an integer or rational string, and order is 0 through
16. It returns `{approximation,{coefficientExpressions...},center$,order}`.
Coefficient `k+1` is `f^(k)(center)/k!`, as an expression string; constants such
as `EXP(1/3)` remain symbolic. The approximation is a guarded expression pair.
This API provides a local Taylor polynomial, without an automatic error bound or
convergence-radius claim. Use `SYMSERIES` for rational poles and exact remainders.

Taylor construction retains source restrictions, sufficient smooth-domain
conditions, and those conditions evaluated at the center. For example, the
expansion of `LN(X+Y)` at zero requires `Y>0`. Rationally false center conditions
raise domain errors. Unresolved parameter or elementary-constant conditions stay
attached and are checked by `SYMEVAL`; construction does not prove their joint
satisfiability. An isolated equality in the selected variable cannot justify a
Taylor expansion. Nonsmooth centers such as `ABS(X)` at zero are rejected by the
conservative domain rules. Refinement may establish a wider smooth domain first.
Existing expression/work limits can be reached before order 16 on complex
compositions. Total result text is bounded to 65536 bytes.

```basic
10 T=SYMTAYLOR("SIN(X)",0,7)
20 PRINT T(2)
30 PRINT SYMEVAL(T(1),"X",0.2)
40 U=SYMTAYLOR("X^Y",1,3)
50 PRINT U(2)
60 PRINT SYMEVAL(U(1),"X,Y",{1.1,2.5})
```

#### Assumptions and real-expression refinement

`SYMREFINE` combines exact sign information from constants, sums, products,
quotients, integer powers and selected elementary functions. It propagates
conditions through negation, absolute values, powers, products/quotients with a
known factor sign, and sign-preserving functions. Contradictions established by
these deductions are errors; a successful result does **not** prove that every
remaining condition can hold simultaneously. Unresolved expressions stay symbolic.

Examples:

| Input | Refined formula | Retained restriction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^2)")` | `ABS(X)` | None |
| `SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^4)")` | `X^2` | None |
| `SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^2)","X<0")` | `-X` | `X<0` |
| `SYMREFINE("ABS(X+Y)",{"X>=0","Y>=0"})` | `X+Y` | Both assumptions |
| `SYMREFINE("LN(EXP(X))")` | `X` | None |
| `SYMREFINE("EXP(LN(X))")` | `X` | `X>0` |
| `SYMREFINE("X","X=0")` | `0` | `X=0` |

The identities include exact rational square roots, square roots of even powers,
even powers of square roots/absolute values, and forward functions applied to
their real inverse (`SIN(ASIN(X))`, for example). Reverse compositions such as
`ASIN(SIN(X))` are not generally identities. Square-root products split only when
both factors are known nonnegative. Refinement retains source poles and function
domains, even after cancellation. Only conditions proved structurally true
without using the assumptions are discarded; a condition cannot prove itself away.

Calculus requires a neighborhood in the selected variable. When differentiating
or integrating a guarded result, variable-dependent `>=0` conditions become
`>0` unless structural sign reasoning already proves them everywhere
nonnegative. This conservatively excludes uncertain boundaries. An equality such
as `X=0` cannot justify replacing `X` by zero and then reporting its derivative
as zero: that calculus call is rejected. To obtain a derivative at a point,
differentiate first, then refine/evaluate. Assumptions on independent parameters
remain valid when differentiating another variable.

For example, `SYMDERIV(SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^4)"))` gives `2*X` and is evaluable at
zero. Refining an already guarded derivative preserves its stored exclusions.
`SYMDERIV(SYMREFINE("ABS(X)","X>=0"))` excludes zero; it does not claim that
`ABS(X)` is differentiable there.

This is conditional real algebra, not a general inequality/feasibility solver or
complex branch engine. Numerical evaluation still has binary64 rounding,
underflow and overflow limits; identities may avoid intermediate overflow that
the original spelling would encounter. Refinement shares the expression, guard,
variable, coefficient and work limits above, with at most 1024 internal sign
facts. It uses the shared bounded arbitrary-precision coefficient arithmetic.

```basic
10 F=SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^2)","X<0")
20 PRINT F
30 PRINT SYMEVAL(F,"X",-3)
40 D=SYMDERIV(SYMREFINE("SQRT(X^4)"))
50 PRINT SYMEVAL(D,"X",0)
60 P=SYMREFINE(SYMDERIV("X"),"X=0")
70 PRINT SYMEVAL(P,"X",0)
```

#### Bounded real antiderivatives

`SYMANTIDERIV` returns one primitive `F`, with sufficient conditions under which
its partial derivative equals the input integrand. It omits the arbitrary
integration constant; in multiple variables this constant may be any function
independent of the selected variable, separately on each connected domain
component. It accepts and returns the same guarded pairs as `SYMDERIV`, allowing
integration and differentiation to be composed without dropping restrictions.

Supported rules include:

| Pattern | Scope |
| --- | --- |
| Constants, sums, differences, polynomial expressions | Constants may be expressions in other variables. Products of polynomial sums can be expanded within limits. |
| Powers `u^n` | Constant rational or parameter exponents independent of the integration variable. Uses `u^(n+1)/(n+1)`; literal exponent `-1` uses `LN(ABS(u))`. |
| `a^u` | Base independent of the integration variable, on the existing positive-base branch, with `LN(a)<>0`. |
| Elementary functions of `u` | All 16 functions listed above, including inverse functions, logarithm and absolute value. |
| Reciprocal kernels | `1/(1+u^2)`, `1/(1-u^2)`, `1/(u^2-1)`, reciprocals of their square roots, `1/COS(u)^2`, and `1/COSH(u)^2`. Even integer powers can supply the squared inner expression. |
| Substitution | The remaining product must be an exact constant multiple of `du/dx`. Affine arguments are a special case. |
| Integration by parts | A polynomial times `EXP(a*x+b)`, `SIN(a*x+b)`, or `COS(a*x+b)`, where `a` and `b` are independent of `x` and `a<>0`. |
| Finite harmonic products | A polynomial times products of nonnegative integer powers of `SIN(a*x+b)` and `COS(c*x+d)`, optionally multiplied by affine exponentials. Arguments may have different slopes and offsets. Integer powers and reciprocals of affine exponentials are combined exactly. |

Rational combinations of `SIN(u)`, `COS(u)` and `TAN(u)` with a common
affine argument also use `T=TAN(u/2)`. Rational combinations of `EXP(u)`,
`SINH(u)`, `COSH(u)` and `TANH(u)` with a common affine argument use `T=EXP(u)`.
The transformed rational integrand includes the exact Jacobian and passes through
the same bounded partial-fraction integrator. Its coefficients must be rational,
and its denominator must have supported linear/quadratic rational factors.
Negative function powers and denominators such as `2+COS(X)` are supported.

Affine slopes and offsets may contain independent parameters. A symbolic slope
is retained as a nonzero condition; a zero-slope parameter case requires separate
simplification. Different recognized affine arguments, non-affine arguments,
mixed circular/exponential kernels and unsupported transformed factors are
rejected. Circular results retain the additional chart restriction
`COS(u/2)<>0`. The primitive is valid separately on the resulting connected
components; it is not claimed to be a single continuous global primitive across
chart boundaries. Original integrand poles remain excluded after cancellation.

Here `u` can be a composite expression. The matcher combines rational
coefficients and commutative products with integer powers. Sums and function
arguments remain structural atoms in the substitution matcher. The harmonic
product rule uses exact finite exponential identities for sine and cosine; it
does not search arbitrary trigonometric identities or decide general equivalence.
A mathematically equivalent spelling
can therefore fall outside the supported patterns. No numerical sampling is
used to choose an integration rule.

Examples include `2*X*COS(X^2)`, `COS(X)*EXP(SIN(X))`, `X/(1+X^2)`,
`X/(1+X^4)`, `(X+1)*(X+2)`, `X^2*SIN(2*X)`, `EXP(X)*SIN(X)`,
`X^2*EXP(-X)*COS(3*X)`, and `SIN(X)^4*COS(2*X)^2`. Bounded rational partial
fractions extend these rules as described below. Arbitrary elementary products,
special-function primitives, and general integration
algorithms are not implemented: `EXP(X^2)`, `SIN(X^2)`, `X^X`, and
`1/(X^3+X+1)` produce an unsupported-integral error. This error does not assert
that an antiderivative fails to exist.

Source smooth-domain conditions are collected **before** simplification, and
the primitive's smooth-domain conditions are added afterward. These conditions
are conservative, just as for `SYMDERIV`: boundary points may be excluded even
when a primitive exists there. Generated parameter denominators must be nonzero.
For example, `SIN(Y*X)` produces a primitive restricted to `Y<>0`; substitute a
literal zero into the source to integrate that exceptional branch. `X^Y` excludes
`Y=-1`, which is handled by the explicit source `X^(-1)`. Numerical evaluation
retains the binary64 accuracy and intermediate-overflow limitations above.

The harmonic rule uses exact rational coefficients, checks conjugate pairing,
and solves the polynomial coefficient equations for each real sine/cosine pair.
Zero rates and frequencies recognized by exact structural algebra use a separate
polynomial primitive. For symbolic exponential rate `a` and harmonic frequency
`b`, a nonconstant pair requires `a^2+b^2<>0`. Either rate may individually be
zero. If parameter values make both zero, substitute those values into the source
and integrate that branch separately. The result does not automatically contain
piecewise parameter cases. Rate normalization combines rational multiples of
identical products; it is not a general assumption solver.

The primitive of `1/X` uses `LN(ABS(X))`, valid on either side of zero. Integrating
the **guarded derivative** of `LN(X)` retains its original condition `X>0`.
`SYMANTIDERIV` does not check continuity over an interval; subtracting endpoint
values alone does not check for intervening poles or domain gaps. Use
`SYMDEFINTEGRAL` for supported proper rational integrals as described below.
Improper integrals remain unsupported.

The additional limits are 128 distinct multiplicative atoms, degree 64 for
polynomial expansion, and degree 16 for the integration-by-parts or harmonic
polynomial. Harmonic expansion additionally limits the total sine/cosine power
to 16 and intermediate complex harmonic terms to 128. Trigonometric reciprocals,
fractional powers and non-affine arguments are outside this additional rule;
some remain supported by the earlier substitution/reciprocal rules.
The shared expression-size, output, coefficient and work limits still apply and
can be reached before those degree limits. All-or-error behavior applies to sums
as well: no partially integrated result is returned.

The elementary primitives can be checked by differentiation; references include
the NIST DLMF sections on [logarithmic and exponential integrals](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.10),
[trigonometric integrals](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.26), and
[hyperbolic integrals](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.40).

```basic
10 F=SYMANTIDERIV("2*X*EXP(X^2)")
20 PRINT F
30 PRINT SYMEVAL(SYMDERIV(F),"X",1)
40 L=SYMANTIDERIV("1/X")
50 PRINT SYMEVAL(L,"X",-2)
60 PRINT SYMANTIDERIV("X^2*SIN(2*X)")
```

#### Rational functions and partial fractions

`SYMPARTFRAC` decomposes a rational function into a polynomial part and proper
fractions with linear or quadratic denominators, including repeated factors.
After elementary simplification, the formula must use only rational coefficients,
the selected variable, `+ - * /`, and constant integer powers. Other variables
are not treated as symbolic coefficients by this rational layer. Existing
conditions in a guarded input are retained even if they involve other variables.

For example, `(X^2+3*X+5)/(X+1)` decomposes into `X+2+3/(X+1)`.
All coefficients, GCDs, divisions and the coefficient-system solve use checked
exact rational arithmetic. The implementation recombines the result and checks
the exact numerator identity before returning it. This follows the usual
[partial-fraction method](https://openstax.org/books/calculus-volume-2/pages/3-4-partial-fractions),
with polynomial division first for improper fractions.

Denominator discovery uses square-free decomposition, written linear/quadratic
subexpressions checked by exact GCDs, bounded rational-root search, and exact
quadratic-factor discovery over the rationals. The quadratic search specializes
the [Kronecker divisibility/interpolation method](https://mate.dm.uba.ar/~krick/KrMSRI98.pdf):
it clears denominators and content, enumerates possible integer leading
coefficients and values at two integer points, interpolates candidates, and
checks divisibility by exact polynomial division. All factor multiplicities are
verified by multiplying the factors back together before partial fractions.
Quadratics with rational roots are split into linear factors; other quadratics
remain intact, including those with irrational real roots.

Thus `1/(X^4+5*X^2+4)` and `1/((X^2+1)*(X^2+4))` are both supported, as
are expanded products with nonmonic rational factors and repeated factors.
Subject to the limits below, discovery covers denominators whose irreducible
factors over the rationals all have degree one or two. Factors of higher degree
remain unsupported: for example, `1/(X^4+1)` cannot be decomposed by this layer,
even though it has quadratic factors over an algebraic extension of the
rationals. Output grouping can depend on the written factors.

`SYMANTIDERIV` automatically uses this rational layer when the earlier elementary
rules do not apply. It integrates repeated linear factors using powers and
`LN(ABS(...))`. Quadratic fractions split into a logarithmic derivative and a
reciprocal-quadratic primitive, using `ATAN` or real logarithms according to the
exact discriminant sign. Higher powers of quadratics use a finite recurrence.
Square roots of rational constants remain symbolic where needed; no approximate
root finding chooses a factor or an integration formula.

Original restrictions are collected before rational cancellation. Thus the
decomposition of `(X^2-1)/(X-1)` has formula equivalent to `X+1` but still
rejects `X=1`. Keep the complete guarded result when composing `SYMPARTFRAC`,
`SYMANTIDERIV`, `SYMDERIV`, and `SYMEVAL`. Rational identity does not imply that
two original expressions have identical domains. Numerical evaluation retains
the binary64 limitations above, particularly near poles and when large terms
cancel; the exact decomposition does not promise uniformly accurate evaluation.

This layer limits intermediate numerator/denominator degree to 32, reduced
denominator degree to 16, and the magnitude of integer powers to 32. It stores
at most 64 distinct small-factor hints and 2048 divisors per integer coefficient
or sampled value used by factor search. Integer factorization uses exact trial
division with repeated prime-power removal; primality is never assumed from a
probabilistic test. Trial division, interpolation, candidate evaluation, GCDs and
coefficient solving share the one-million-step work budget. Big-integer operations
also consume the shared 32-million-unit coefficient budget. Large coefficient
factor searches can exhaust either budget even at small degree. The existing 4096-bit
coefficient, expression-size and guard limits apply. These additional limits
belong to the rational layer; previously supported elementary rules retain
their own limits. Unsupported factors and resource exhaustion return errors;
an exhausted search is not reported as proof of irreducibility. Explicitly
writing factors can avoid expensive discovery even when the expanded spelling
exhausts the budget.

```basic
10 A=SYMPARTFRAC("(3*X+2)/(X^3-X^2-2*X)")
20 PRINT A
30 F=SYMANTIDERIV("(X+2)/(X^2+2*X+3)^3")
40 PRINT F
50 PRINT SYMEVAL(SYMDERIV(F),"X",1)
60 PRINT SYMPARTFRAC("(X^2-1)/(X-1)")
```

#### Exact polynomial factorization over the rationals

`SYMFACTOR` factors a polynomial into its rational leading coefficient and
monic irreducible factors over **Q**, with repeated factors represented by
integer powers. Factor order is unspecified. Zero and constant inputs return
their constant formula; zero is not assigned an irreducible factorization.
For example, `X^8+3*X^4+2` factors into `(X^4+1)*(X^4+2)`. Both quartics are
irreducible over Q. Likewise `X^2-2` stays quadratic: factorization over real,
complex, or algebraic-number coefficient domains is outside this call.

After elementary simplification and exact rational cancellation, the input must
be a polynomial in the selected variable with rational coefficients. Other
variables are not symbolic coefficients. The complete guarded result can be
stored in a BASIC variable and passed to `SYMEVAL`, `SYMDERIV`, `SYMANTIDERIV`,
or `SYMFACTOR` again. Original and inherited conditions survive cancellation:
factoring `(X^6-1)/(X^3-1)` still excludes `X=1`. Preserve the complete result
when composing calls; extracting just `F(1)` discards its conditions.

The algorithm uses exact square-free decomposition, small-factor discovery,
and bounded [Kronecker interpolation/divisibility search](https://mate.dm.uba.ar/~krick/KrMSRI98.pdf)
through every possible proper factor degree. A successful
[Rabin finite-field irreducibility test](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~cdm/pdf/41-ffields.pdf)
at one of the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, or 13 can prove a factor irreducible over Q
without exhaustive search or a potentially expensive square-free GCD. Reductions that lose degree are skipped; inconclusive
modular tests fall back to exact search. Every returned product, including its
multiplicities, is checked against the original monic polynomial by exact
multiplication. Euclidean GCD remainders are normalized to reduce intermediate
coefficient growth.

This API limits the polynomial degree after cancellation to **16**, intermediate
rational-polynomial degree to 32, and remaining integer power magnitudes to 32.
It shares the bounded arbitrary-precision rational arithmetic, 64 small-factor hints, 2048
divisors per sampled integer, one-million-step work budget, and expression/guard
limits described above. Search can be expensive even at modest degree; degree
16 is a ceiling, not a promise that every input up to that degree succeeds.
Coefficient overflow, work exhaustion, and other limits raise errors, without
returning a partial product or asserting that an unsearched residual is
irreducible. These limits also apply to explicitly written products.

Factoring a denominator into higher-degree irreducibles does not extend the
linear/quadratic denominator restriction of `SYMPARTFRAC` or the rational
antiderivative rules.

```basic
10 F=SYMFACTOR("X^8+3*X^4+2")
20 PRINT F
30 PRINT SYMEVAL(F,"X",2)
40 PRINT SYMEVAL(SYMDERIV(F),"X",2)
50 PRINT SYMFACTOR("(Y^3+Y+1)^3","Y")
```

### Exact multivariate division, ideals, and proof certificates

These calls work over rational-coefficient polynomials with the same fixed graded
lexicographic order as `SYMSIMPLIFY$`: total degree first, then powers of
alphabetically ordered variable names. For lexicographic elimination use the
separate `SYMELIMINATE` family below. These calls do not solve for numerical roots.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMDIVMULTI(expr$,divisors)` | `{{quotient$...},remainder$}` satisfying `expr = sum(quotient(i)*divisor(i)) + remainder`. Uses divisors in the supplied order; zero divisors are errors. |
| `SYMGROEBNER(generators)` | List of strings forming the monic reduced Gröbner basis, ordered by descending leading monomial. Zero and redundant generators are removed. |
| `SYMREDUCE$(expr$,generators)` | Canonical normal form after completing the generators to a Gröbner basis. |
| `SYMIDEALMEMBER(expr$,generators)` | `-1` when the polynomial belongs to the generated ideal, otherwise `0`, after a successful exact computation. |
| `SYMIDEALCERT(expr$,generators)` | `{{multiplier$...},remainder$}` expressing the input as a combination of the original generators plus its canonical normal form. Multipliers retain the original generator order, including zero and duplicate entries. |
| `SYMIDEALCHECK(expr$,generators,multipliers)` | `-1` exactly when `expr = sum(multiplier(i)*generator(i))`. A valid but incorrect certificate returns `0`; malformed input, mismatched counts, or exceeded limits raise errors. |

`generators`, `divisors`, and `multipliers` accept a semicolon-separated string,
such as `"X*Y-1;Y^2-1"`, or a list of polynomial strings returned by another call.
An empty string or empty list denotes an empty collection. Empty entries inside a
nonempty string are errors. BASIC brace literals also accept polynomial strings,
for example `{"X*Y-1","Y^2-1"}`, and nested certificate lists. A relation such as `X=Y` is supplied
as the polynomial `X-Y`, whose value is assumed to be zero.

Multivariate division by an arbitrary list has an order-dependent remainder.
A nonzero remainder from `SYMDIVMULTI` does not establish nonmembership. Use
`SYMREDUCE$` or `SYMIDEALMEMBER` for that decision; both complete the basis first.
The zero ideal has an empty basis and leaves every input unchanged. A basis
containing a nonzero constant reduces to `{1}` and every polynomial belongs to
that ideal. These conventions also apply to empty and all-zero generator lists.

Basis construction uses bounded Buchberger completion and reduced-basis
normalization, with polynomial witnesses propagated back to the original input.
The certificate checker is separate: it only multiplies, adds, and compares exact
coefficients. It neither constructs a Gröbner basis nor trusts the search's
membership decision. The certificate remainder must be zero to prove membership;
for a nonzero remainder, the multipliers prove membership of `expr-remainder`.
See [the algebraic basis and membership criterion](https://aszanto.math.ncsu.edu/MA722/ln-01.pdf#page=11).

This proves polynomial-combination identities, not arbitrary mathematical
statements or all consequences of equations. For example, `X` does not belong to
the ideal generated by `X^2`, even though `X^2=0` implies `X=0` over the real or
complex numbers. A negative ideal-membership result is not a counterexample to
such a logical implication. Radical ideals, inequalities, integer arithmetic,
