factorization, and general theorem proving are outside these calls. Use the
separate radical-membership functions below for polynomial consequences over
all complex solutions.

In addition to the shared symbolic limits, collections and retained intermediate
bases allow at most 32 polynomials. Input collections and retained basis/proof
collections are limited to 8192 terms; polynomial string collections are limited
to 65536 bytes, with the usual 8192-byte limit on each expression. Intermediate
bases count before redundant elements are removed. Certificate growth can reach
a limit even when the final reduced basis would be small. The one-million-step
budget includes proof construction, and every long reduction checks BREAK.
Any arithmetic, degree, storage, or work-limit failure raises an error; no partial
basis or unverified membership answer is returned.

```basic
10 G$="X*Y-1;Y^2-1"
20 B=SYMGROEBNER(G$):PRINT B
30 PRINT SYMREDUCE$("X^2-1",B)
40 C=SYMIDEALCERT("X^2-1",G$)
50 PRINT C(1),C(2)
60 PRINT SYMIDEALCHECK("X^2-1",G$,C(1))
70 PRINT SYMIDEALCHECK("X^2",G$,C(1))
```

The basis is `{Y^2-1,X-Y}`. The normal form and certificate remainder are zero.
The original certificate checks successfully (`-1`); changing the target to
`X^2` makes that same certificate fail (`0`).

### Exact polynomial elimination and completeness certificates

These functions remove selected variables from an ideal of rational polynomials.
They return a monic reduced basis for the elimination ideal: every polynomial
combination of the input equations that contains only retained variables.
`generators` accepts a semicolon-separated string or a list of polynomial strings,
as above. `eliminateVariables` accepts a comma-separated string or a list of
distinct variable names. Names are case-insensitive and follow the multivariate
polynomial identifier rules. An empty string or `{}` removes no variables.
Names absent from the generators are allowed and count toward the variable limit.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMELIMINATE(generators,eliminateVariables)` | List of polynomial strings forming the reduced elimination basis. |
| `SYMELIMCERT(generators,eliminateVariables)` | `{eliminationBasis,fullLexBasis,{proofRow...}}`. Each row contains one polynomial multiplier per original generator and proves `fullLexBasis(i) = sum(proofRow(i,j)*generator(j))`. Zero and duplicate generator slots are retained. |
| `SYMELIMCHECK(generators,eliminateVariables,certificate)` | `-1` for a verified complete certificate, `0` for a well-formed incorrect claim. Malformed shape, mismatched dimensions, arithmetic overflow and exceeded resource limits raise errors. |

The order is **pure lexicographic**, with eliminated variables first in the
supplied order, then all remaining generator variables alphabetically. Basis
entries are sorted by descending leading monomial in this order. Text within
each polynomial retains the usual graded-lex rendering, so its first printed
term need not be its lexicographic leading term. For example, eliminating `X`
from `X^2-Y;X-Z` returns `{-Z^2+Y}`; the lexicographic leading term is `Y`.
Passing no elimination variables returns the complete lexicographic basis.
The order and signatures of `SYMGROEBNER` and the existing ideal functions are
unchanged.

The checker first requires a nonzero, monic, sorted, reduced full basis. Exact
proof identities show that each basis polynomial belongs to the original ideal.
It then reduces every original generator to zero, establishing the reverse
inclusion, and verifies that every required S-polynomial reduces to zero by
Buchberger's criterion. The product criterion skips pairs with relatively prime
leading monomials. Finally, the elimination list must equal precisely the full
basis entries free of eliminated variables. This verifies completeness using
bounded division and exact arithmetic; it does not run basis completion or trust
a partial list of consequences. See the
[elimination theorem](https://aszanto.math.ncsu.edu/MA722/ln-01.pdf).
Both producing functions perform this check before returning a result.

This is elimination of polynomial ideals, not real quantifier elimination or a
decision about whether every projected point lifts to a solution. For example,
eliminating `X` from `X*Y-1` returns `{}`, although `Y=0` has no corresponding
solution. Eliminating `X` from `X^2+1` also returns `{}`, without asserting that a
real root exists. Removing an unrelated variable from `X^2` leaves `{X^2}`;
the operation does not take radicals. A unit ideal returns `{1}`, even when all
variables are removed; an empty or all-zero ideal returns `{}`.

Limits are degree 64, eight variables, 2048 terms per polynomial, 32 input and
retained intermediate basis polynomials, 8192 aggregate terms in a retained
basis/proof collection or complete certificate, 8192 bytes per polynomial, and
65536 bytes across the entire certificate. Coefficients use checked signed
bounded arbitrary-precision rational arithmetic. The one-million-step budget includes construction
and verification, with BREAK checkpoints. Lexicographic reduction can increase
total degree, so inputs below the degree ceiling can still exceed an intermediate
limit. Both producers enforce complete-certificate bounds, even when only the
elimination list is requested. An exceeded limit raises an error and never
returns a partial basis. The checker rejects nonzero polynomial variables outside
the input ring (generator variables together with the elimination variables).

```basic
10 G={"X-T^2","Y-T^3"}
20 C=SYMELIMCERT(G,"T")
30 PRINT C(1)
40 PRINT SYMELIMCHECK(G,"T",C)
50 P={{"Y-Z^2"},{"X-Z","Y-Z^2"},{{"0","1"},{"-1","X+Z"}}}
60 PRINT SYMELIMCHECK("X^2-Y;X-Z","X",P)
```

The curve basis is `{X^3-Y^2}`. Both the generated certificate and the separately
written certificate verify as `-1`.

### Exact radical membership and algebraic consequences

`SYMRADICALMEMBER(expr$,generators)` decides whether some positive integer power
of the query polynomial belongs to the ideal generated by the supplied
polynomials. For rational coefficients, this is equivalent to the query vanishing
at every common **complex** zero of the generators. Each generator is interpreted
as an equation with value zero. Collections use the same semicolon-string or
polynomial-string-list format as the ideal APIs above.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMRADICALMEMBER(expr$,generators)` | `-1` for radical membership and `0` for nonmembership after a completed, verified computation. |
| `SYMRADICALCERT(expr$,generators)` | `{status$,auxiliary$,fullLexBasis,{proofRow...}}`, where status is `"MEMBER"` or `"NONMEMBER"`. |
| `SYMRADICALCHECK(expr$,generators,certificate)` | `-1` if the supplied certificate correctly proves its stated status, including `"NONMEMBER"`; `0` for a well-formed incorrect claim. Malformed input and exceeded limits raise errors. |

For example, `SYMIDEALMEMBER("X","X^2")` returns `0`, whereas
`SYMRADICALMEMBER("X","X^2")` returns `-1`: `X^2=0` forces `X=0` over the
complex numbers. The zero polynomial always belongs to the radical, the zero
ideal contains no nonzero query, and inconsistent equations whose ideal contains
`1` imply every query polynomial vanishes on their empty solution set.

This is the ordinary algebraic radical, not the real radical. For example,
`SYMRADICALMEMBER("X","X^2+Y^2")` returns `0`, although the real equation
`X^2+Y^2=0` forces `X=Y=0`. Also, `SYMRADICALMEMBER("1","X^2+1")` returns `0`:
there are complex solutions even though there are no real ones. A negative result
does not assert a real counterexample, provide counterexample coordinates, or
decide inequalities. These functions decide membership of a query; they do not
return generators for the radical ideal or prove arbitrary logical statements.

Certificates use the
[Rabinowitsch criterion](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-972-algebraic-techniques-and-semidefinite-optimization-spring-2006/4d8f08c592cb68218a3791479bf7cc4e_lecture_14.pdf#page=3).
For a fresh auxiliary variable `T`, extend the original generators `F` by the
single polynomial `1-T*expr`. The query belongs to the radical exactly when this
augmented ideal has the reduced basis `{1}`. Every proof row supplies multipliers
for the original generators in their original order, including zero/duplicate
slots, followed by one multiplier for `1-T*expr`. The row must reproduce its full
basis polynomial exactly. Thus a positive certificate directly proves an identity
`1 = sum(multiplier(j)*F(j)) + lastMultiplier*(1-T*expr)`.

The complete basis uses pure lexicographic order with the auxiliary variable
first, followed by original/query variables alphabetically. Polynomial text
retains the usual graded-lex rendering. Generated auxiliary names are `MBRAD`,
`MBRAD1`, etc., choosing the first unused name. A supplied certificate may use any
valid fresh variable name; names are case-insensitive. Even names canceled out of
the original expressions count as used. Proof polynomials cannot introduce
additional nonzero variables outside this fixed ring.

The checker verifies monic sorted reduced form, exact proof identities, reverse
ideal inclusion and Buchberger's criterion, without running completion. It then
requires `{1}` for `"MEMBER"` and a nonunit complete basis for `"NONMEMBER"`.
An incomplete set of valid consequences cannot certify nonmembership. Both
producing APIs verify the complete certificate before returning a decision.

There are at most **seven distinct input variables** and **31 original
generators**, reserving one variable and one generator for the criterion. These
reservations apply even for constant queries and unit ideals. Nonzero query
degree is at most 63 so `1-T*expr` fits degree 64; original generators and all
intermediates have degree at most 64. Proof growth can exceed this limit even for
small inputs. The remaining limits are bounded arbitrary-precision rationals, 2048
terms per polynomial, 32 retained basis polynomials, 8192 aggregate terms in a
retained basis/proof collection, 8192 bytes per polynomial, 65536 bytes across the
complete certificate (including status/name), and one million work steps shared
by construction and verification, with BREAK checkpoints. No output is returned
when a limit is exceeded, and a failed search is never interpreted as
nonmembership. The boolean API enforces the same certificate limits.

```basic
10 PRINT SYMRADICALMEMBER("X","X^2")
20 C=SYMRADICALCERT("X+Y","X^2;Y^3")
30 PRINT C(1)
40 PRINT SYMRADICALCHECK("X+Y","X^2;Y^3",C)
50 P={"MEMBER","T",{"1"},{{"T^2","1+T*X"}}}
60 PRINT SYMRADICALCHECK("X","X^2",P)
70 N={"NONMEMBER","T",{"T*Y-1","X^2"},{{"0","-1"},{"1","0"}}}
80 PRINT SYMRADICALCHECK("Y","X^2",N)
```

The membership decision is `-1`, the generated status is `MEMBER`, and all three
certificate checks return `-1`. The separately written positive certificate uses
`1 = T^2*X^2 + (1+T*X)*(1-T*X)`.

### Polynomial implications with nonzero assumptions

These calls decide whether a rational polynomial query must vanish whenever a
list of polynomial equations holds and every supplied nonzero condition holds.
The domain is **complex numbers**, as with radical membership. `equations` and
`nonzero` each accept a semicolon-separated string or a list of polynomial
strings. Equations mean `F(i)=0`; conditions mean `H(i)<>0`. Empty strings or
lists impose no conditions of that type. Supply the query `X-Y` to ask whether
`X=Y` follows; comparison operators are not part of the polynomial grammar.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMIMPLIES(expr$,equations,nonzero)` | `-1` when the query is zero at every complex point satisfying the assumptions; `0` otherwise, after a completed verified computation. |
| `SYMIMPLYCERT(expr$,equations,nonzero)` | `{status$,auxiliary$,fullLexBasis,{proofRow...}}`, with status `"IMPLIED"` or `"NOTIMPLIED"`. |
| `SYMIMPLYCHECK(expr$,equations,nonzero,certificate)` | `-1` if the supplied certificate correctly proves its status, including `"NOTIMPLIED"`; `0` for a well-formed incorrect claim. Malformed input or exceeded limits raise errors. |

For example, `SYMIMPLIES("X","X*Y","Y")` returns `-1`: if `X*Y=0` and
`Y<>0`, then `X=0`. Removing the nonzero assumption returns `0`, because the
equation also permits `Y=0` with nonzero `X`. Conditions are conjoined, so
`"Y;Z"` requires both `Y<>0` and `Z<>0`. Repeated factors, constant conditions,
zero/duplicate equations, and rational coefficients are supported. With an
empty nonzero list the decision agrees with `SYMRADICALMEMBER` within the
documented resource limits.

An implication is true when its assumptions have no solutions. In particular,
a zero polynomial in `nonzero` makes **every query vacuously implied**. So do
contradictions such as `X=0` together with `X<>0`. An `IMPLIED` certificate does
not assert that the assumptions are consistent. To test inconsistency over the
complex numbers, use the query `"1"`: a successful `-1` means the assumptions
have no complex solution; `0` means at least one complex solution exists. The API
does not return solution coordinates. It does not decide implications restricted
to real numbers: `SYMIMPLIES("X","X^2+Y^2","Y")` returns `0`, even though
those assumptions have no real solution. Strict signs, ordered inequalities,
disjunctions, integer domains and arbitrary quantified logic are unsupported.

The implementation forms `P = expr * product(nonzero)`, where the empty product
is `1`, then applies the radical criterion above to `P`. This is valid because
over a field a product is nonzero exactly when each factor is nonzero. The
certificate proves completeness of the augmented ideal
`<equations, 1-T*P>`, using a fresh auxiliary variable `T`. A proof row contains
one multiplier for each **original equation**, including zero and duplicate
slots, followed by one multiplier for `1-T*P`. Nonzero assumptions are incorporated
into `P`; they do not have individual multiplier slots. Every row must reproduce
its corresponding full-basis polynomial exactly.

The independent checker verifies both ideal inclusions, monic sorted reduced
form and Buchberger's criterion without completing a basis. It requires the unit
basis `{1}` for `IMPLIED` and a complete nonunit basis for `NOTIMPLIED`. A partial
set of valid consequences cannot certify a negative result. Both producing APIs
perform the same check before returning. A negative decision establishes a
complex counterexample exists, without asserting a real counterexample exists.

The auxiliary name is generated as `MBIMPL`, `MBIMPL1`, etc., avoiding all names
in the query, equations and conditions, including canceled names. Supplied
certificates may choose any valid fresh name. The lexicographic variable order
places that name first and all remaining names alphabetically. Polynomial text
retains graded-lex rendering. Certificates can be reused for condition permutations
when the product is unchanged; equivalent assumptions do not necessarily produce
identical certificates.

Limits are seven distinct input variables, 31 equations and 32 nonzero conditions.
The parsed query/equation/condition collection has at most 8192 terms in total.
Each input and intermediate polynomial is limited to degree 64 and 2048 terms;
the nonzero combined polynomial `P` must have degree at most 63 to leave room for
`T`. Thus individually small factors may still exceed the product limit. Every
input is parsed and counted before handling a zero query or zero condition; such
a zero avoids unnecessary multiplication of the other factors. One auxiliary
variable and one equation slot remain reserved even in these cases. The existing
32-polynomial basis limit, bounded arbitrary-precision rationals, 8192 retained certificate
terms, 8192 bytes per polynomial, 65536 total certificate text bytes and shared
one-million-step budget apply. Product construction and verification both consume
the budget and check BREAK. Failures raise errors and never return `NOTIMPLIED`
or a partial proof. The boolean API enforces complete-certificate output limits.

```basic
10 PRINT SYMIMPLIES("X","X*Y","Y")
20 PRINT SYMIMPLIES("X","X*Y",{})
30 C=SYMIMPLYCERT("X-Y","(X-Y)^2*Z","Z")
40 PRINT C(1)
50 PRINT SYMIMPLYCHECK("X-Y","(X-Y)^2*Z","Z",C)
60 P={"IMPLIED","T",{"1"},{{"T","1"}}}
70 PRINT SYMIMPLYCHECK("X","X*Y","Y",P)
80 PRINT SYMIMPLIES("1","X*Y","X;Y")
```

The decisions on lines 10 and 20 are `-1` and `0`. Both certificates verify as
`-1`. The final decision is `-1` because its assumptions are inconsistent.

### Exact sums of squares and real polynomial certificates

These functions use exact rational polynomial strings in up to eight real
variables. They provide global nonnegativity witnesses and check polynomial
inequalities under real assumptions. Comparison operators, elementary functions,
variable denominators and complex coefficients are outside the grammar.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMSOS(expr$)` | Constructs a weighted sum-of-squares certificate for a globally nonnegative polynomial of total degree at most two, subject to resource limits. Raises an error for a quadratic that takes negative values, higher degree, or exhausted limits. |
| `SYMSOSCHECK(expr$,certificate)` | `-1` if the supplied weighted squares reproduce the target exactly and every weight is nonnegative; `0` for a well-formed invalid proof. Supports higher-degree supplied proofs. |
| `SYMREALCHECK(expr$,inequalities,equations,certificate)` | `-1` if the supplied certificate proves `expr>=0` whenever every inequality `G(i)>=0` and equation `F(j)=0` holds. Returns `0` for a well-formed invalid proof. |

An SOS certificate is a list of pairs `{{weight$,polynomial$},...}` representing
`sum(weight(i)*polynomial(i)^2)`. Both entries are **strings**; weights must be
exact rational constant expressions with no variable tokens, even canceled ones.
Nonnegative rational weights avoid introducing irrational square roots. Zero
weights are accepted, but their polynomial entries are still parsed and counted.
The empty certificate `{}` represents zero. Supplied proofs can use repeated
squares and need not match the constructor's choice of decomposition. A negative
weight invalidates a proof even when its polynomial is zero or another row would
cancel it.

`SYMSOS` builds the augmented Gram matrix on `1` and the variables, then completes
squares with exact rational Schur complements. Zero pivots require a zero
remaining row, so singular nonnegative forms are supported. The constant and
linear terms participate in the test: a positive-semidefinite Hessian by itself
does not establish global nonnegativity. The returned proof is expanded and
checked before return; the separate checker only expands supplied identities
and does not rerun construction. No floating-point tolerance or sampling is used.
Construction is limited to quadratics, even for obvious higher-degree squares.

For `SYMREALCHECK`, each assumption collection is a semicolon-separated string
or list of polynomial strings; an empty string or list means no assumptions of
that type. Inequalities are always interpreted as **greater than or equal to
zero**. Preserve zero, duplicate and original-order constraint slots. The
certificate has three elements:

`{freeSOS,{inequalitySOS1,...},{equationMultiplier1$,...}}`

The checker verifies the exact identity

`expr = freeSOS + sum(inequalitySOS(i)*G(i)) + sum(equationMultiplier(j)*F(j))`.

Here each SOS denotes its expanded weighted squares. There must be one SOS
certificate per original inequality and one arbitrary polynomial multiplier
string per original equation. Equation multipliers may have either sign.
No assumptions are silently added or removed. This is a sufficient proof format;
the checker does not search for a certificate or decide whether every true
inequality has a certificate in this form. The underlying SOS/Gram and real
algebraic certificate constructions are described in
[Parrilo's Sum of Squares Programs and Polynomial Inequalities](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-972-algebraic-techniques-and-semidefinite-optimization-spring-2006/63d6e45650205ceef6701971a9b4621c_lecture_22.pdf).

Use the target `objective-bound` to certify a lower bound, or `bound-objective`
for an upper bound. This proves a bound only; it does not produce a feasible
optimizer or prove attainment. An accepted target `-1` proves the assumptions
have **no real solution**. Other accepted targets may hold vacuously on an empty
feasible set. A rejected certificate says nothing about whether the target is
actually nonnegative. Nonnegative multivariate polynomials need not be sums of
squares; there is no general SDP search, real quantifier elimination, strict-sign
reasoning, integer-domain reasoning or completeness claim here.

Limits apply to the whole request: eight distinct variable tokens (including
canceled variables), 32 inequalities, 32 equations, 128 square rows across all
SOS groups, 8192 parsed terms across target/assumptions/certificate and 65536
combined input text bytes. Each polynomial string is limited to 8192 bytes and
each polynomial/intermediate to 2048 terms and total degree 64. Square bases
have degree at most 32, including bases with zero weight. Products with nonlinear
constraints can exceed the degree or intermediate limits even when each input
fits. Bounded arbitrary-precision rational arithmetic and one shared million-step
work budget apply to parsing, construction, expansion and checking, with BREAK
checkpoints. Malformed shapes, wrong slot counts, unsupported input, coefficient
overflow or exceeded limits raise errors. A false checker result is never used
to report an exhausted computation. All supplied entries are parsed and counted
before rejecting negative weights; invalid weights need not be expanded.

```basic
10 P$="(X-Y+1)^2+Y^2/3"
20 S=SYMSOS(P$)
30 PRINT SYMSOSCHECK(P$,S)
40 H={{"1/3","X^2-Y^2"},{"2","X*Y-1"}}
50 PRINT SYMSOSCHECK("(X^2-Y^2)^2/3+2*(X*Y-1)^2",H)
60 C={SYMSOS("Y^2"),{SYMSOS("1")},{}}
70 PRINT SYMREALCHECK("1-X^2","1-X^2-Y^2",{},C)
80 D={SYMSOS("X^2"),{},{"-1"}}
90 PRINT SYMREALCHECK("-1",{},"X^2+1",D)
```

All four checks return `-1`. Line 70 proves `X^2<=1` on the unit disk;
line 90 proves `X^2+1=0` has no real solution.

### Proper definite integrals of rational functions

`SYMDEFINTEGRAL(expression,start,finish[,variable$])` returns the guarded pair
`{valueExpression$,conditions}`. The integrand is a univariate rational expression
or an existing guarded pair; coefficients are exact rationals. Endpoints are
BASIC integers or exact rational-expression strings, such as `"1/3"`.
The variable defaults to `"X"`. Other free parameters, binary64 endpoint values,
algebraic endpoints and infinite endpoints are unsupported.

Before constructing the result, the engine proves that every original domain
condition holds on the **entire closed interval** between the endpoints. This
includes denominator conditions collected before cancellation and any supplied
rational inequalities/equalities. Exact Sturm root counts handle endpoint,
interior, repeated and irrational roots. Square-free sign certificates establish
nonnegative conditions, including conditions that touch zero. Each internal
certificate is checked by polynomial identities. No sampling or floating-point
root estimates establish the domain.

Only then does the bounded rational integrator produce a real primitive and
subtract its endpoint values. Its denominator factors must be supported rational
linear/quadratic factors; logarithms use absolute values, and quadratic terms
use real arctangents or logarithms. The rational primitive's variable singularities
are roots already excluded by the domain check. Circular half-angle substitution
primitives are not used here because their extra chart boundaries need separate
handling. Constant radical/logarithm conditions from the final expression remain
in its guarded pair. `SYMEVAL` produces the ordinary binary64 approximation.

```basic
10 A=SYMDEFINTEGRAL("X^2",0,1)
20 PRINT A(1)
30 B=SYMDEFINTEGRAL("1/(X^2+1)",-1,1)
40 PRINT SYMEVAL(B)
50 C=SYMDEFINTEGRAL("1/X",1,2)
60 PRINT C(1)
```

The first result is exact `1/3`, the second evaluates to `PI/2`, and the third is
an exact logarithmic expression. Reversing endpoints negates the integral.
Equal endpoints return zero only after validating the source domain at that
point; no factor search is required in this case.

`SYMDEFINTEGRAL("1/X",-1,1)` is an error, even though subtracting the finite
endpoint values of `LN(ABS(X))` would produce zero. Likewise, `1/(X^2-2)` on
`[1,2]` is rejected because of the irrational pole, and `(X^2-1)/(X-1)` on
`[0,2]` is rejected because its original source excludes `X=1`. The latter has
an integrable continuous extension, but choosing that extension is a separate
explicit operation. This API does not compute improper integrals, principal
values, removable-hole extensions, elementary nonrational integrals or
piecewise/parameter case splits. Domain failure, unsupported input and resource
exhaustion are errors; none returns a partial integral.

The existing degree-32 rational input, degree-16 factorized denominator,
4096-bit normalized coefficient, expression, guard, output and shared work
limits apply. Exact symbolic output does not remove binary64 cancellation or
conditioning limitations when evaluating it. See
`programs/examples/symbolic_definite_integrals.bas` and
`tools/check-symbolic-definite.py` for executable checks.

### Exact real algebraic numbers

These calls retain a real polynomial root exactly and calculate rational
functions of that root. They do not round the root to a BASIC real before doing
arithmetic. This is useful for exact geometry, polynomial equilibria, irrational
ratios and checking identities that would otherwise have numerical residuals.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMALGROOT(poly$,lower,upper[,variable$])` | Exact selected root, requiring precisely one distinct root in the closed rational interval. |
| `SYMALGROOTS(poly$,lower,upper[,tolerance[,variable$]])` | Sorted list of all distinct real roots in the closed interval. Each isolating interval has width at most the positive rational tolerance, default `1/1000000000000`. Repeated roots appear once. |
| `SYMALGADD(a,b)`, `SYMALGSUB(a,b)`, `SYMALGMUL(a,b)`, `SYMALGDIV(a,b)` | Exact arithmetic with real algebraic records or rational scalars, including independently selected roots within the degree/work limits below. Division by an exactly zero value is an error. |
| `SYMALGPOW(a,integer)` | Exact integer power, from -64 through 64. Negative powers require a nonzero value; exponent zero returns one after input validation. |
| `SYMALGSIGN(a)` | Exact sign: `-1`, `0`, or `1`. These are sign codes, not BASIC Boolean values. |
| `SYMALGCMP(a,b)` | Exact sign of `a-b`, including independently selected roots within the same degree/work limits as arithmetic. |
| `SYMALGEVAL(expression,a[,variable$])` | Substitutes the exact algebraic value into a univariate rational expression or guarded pair, checking its original rational domain conditions exactly. |
| `SYMALGENCLOSE(a[,tolerance])` | Two exact rational-expression strings `{lower$,upper$}` enclosing the value, with width at most the positive tolerance. The default is `1/1000000000000`. |

Endpoints, tolerances and rational scalar operands are BASIC integers or exact
rational-expression strings. Binary64 inputs are rejected; use `"1/10"` instead
of `0.1`. The selected input variable defaults to `"X"`; internal record
polynomials always use `X`. Polynomial coefficients are rational, with no other
free variables. The inherited polynomial parser and exponent limits apply to
constant expressions too; large decimal integer literals avoid its exponent
limit.

An algebraic result is an ordinary serializable six-field BASIC list:

```text
{"ALGEBRAIC", polynomial$, lower$, upper$, numerator$, denominator$}
```

It means `numerator(alpha)/denominator(alpha)`, where `alpha` is the unique root
of `polynomial` in `[lower,upper]`. The polynomial is normalized to monic,
square-free form. Equal endpoints select an exact rational root. If an input
interval selects a root at one endpoint, the constructor tightens it to that
point. Numerator and denominator are reduced modulo the defining polynomial;
the denominator must be nonzero **at the selected root**, even for reducible
defining polynomials. Each public operation validates the record anew. A
malformed or ambiguous record, or a removable denominator hole in a supplied
record, produces an error. Rational-only arithmetic also returns this record
format; `SYMALGENCLOSE` can expose its exact singleton rational value.

```basic
10 A=SYMALGROOT("X^2-2",1,2)
20 PRINT SYMALGCMP(SYMALGMUL(A,A),2)
30 B=SYMALGEVAL("(X+1)/(X-1)",A)
40 PRINT SYMALGCMP(B,SYMALGADD(3,SYMALGMUL(2,A)))
50 PRINT SYMALGENCLOSE(A,"1/100000000000000000000")
60 Q=SYMALGROOT("X^5-X-1",1,2)
70 PRINT SYMALGSIGN(SYMALGEVAL("X^5-X-1",Q))
```

The comparison/sign results in this example are exact zeros. The enclosure is
a pair of rational bounds, not an arbitrary-precision floating-point value.
`SYMEVAL(bound$)` converts an individual bound to ordinary binary64 when needed
for rendering or simulation. Further floating-point calculations retain their
usual rounding and conditioning limits.

Arithmetic accepts independently constructed real roots. The same BASIC calls
work for `sqrt(2)+sqrt(3)`, opposite roots, and dependent values such as
`sqrt(8)-2*sqrt(2)`. A common selected root still uses the smaller polynomial
arithmetic path. Otherwise, exact multiplication matrices construct a polynomial
for the result; rational interval arithmetic and Sturm counts select its real
root. No numerical equality threshold is used.

```basic
10 W=SYMALGROOT("X^2-2",1,2)
20 H=SYMALGROOT("X^2-3",1,2)
30 AREA=SYMALGMUL(W,H)
40 PRINT SYMALGCMP(SYMALGPOW(AREA,2),6)
50 PERIMETER=SYMALGMUL(2,SYMALGADD(W,H))
60 PRINT SYMALGENCLOSE(PERIMETER,"1/1000000000000")
```

The first result is exactly zero. All values remain BASIC lists, and programs
can save, pass and reuse the resulting records with the existing `SYMALG` calls.
See `programs/examples/symbolic_combinations.bas` for the complete geometry demo.

The independent-root path first expresses each operand as a selected root of
its own square-free annihilating polynomial. Denominator factors at other roots
are removed before modular inversion; division by zero at the selected value
remains an error. A multiplication-matrix characteristic polynomial removes
repeated conjugate values, so `(root(X^16-2))^8` can use a quadratic polynomial.
The product of the resulting operand dimensions must be at most **16** before
constructing the combined matrix. This is a construction bound, even if a later
cancellation could give a lower-degree answer. The polynomials need not be
minimal; irrelevant factors and successive combinations can exhaust the bound.

The engine checks modular inverses, quotient identities, the characteristic
recurrence's zero-matrix identity and each rebased polynomial's annihilation
identity. Characteristic-polynomial trace identities are described in
[Haber's notes](https://scipp-legacy.pbsci.ucsc.edu/~haber/webpage/charpoly.pdf).
The test oracle separately uses exact biquadratic arithmetic and optional
SymPy Sylvester resultants. Neither reference package is needed by BASIC.

Guaranteed minimal-polynomial construction and algebraic coefficients for all
existing symbolic solvers remain unsupported. Exact complex values assembled
from real algebraic components use the separate `SYMC` functions below.
Expressions such as `SIN(alpha)` and `SQRT(alpha)` are outside `SYMALGEVAL`;
it accepts rational functions and rational guards.

Sturm sequences establish root counts and are checked by polynomial identities.
A GCD detects exact zero at the selected root before any inconclusive interval
refinement. Nonzero signs and value bounds use exact rational interval Horner
arithmetic and bisection. Thus failure to separate a difficult case within the
resource budget raises an error rather than returning an approximate equality
or incomplete root list. This polynomial-plus-isolating-interval representation
is also described in the [CGAL algebraic kernel manual](https://doc.cgal.org/6.1/Algebraic_kernel_d/index.html);
ModernBASIC uses its existing Sturm machinery and has no CGAL runtime dependency.

Defining polynomials have degree 1 through 16 before square-free reduction;
rational expressions and record numerator/denominator inputs retain the
existing degree-32 bound. Each call permits at most 2048 interval-refinement or
isolation-subdivision steps in total, plus the shared coefficient/work budgets.
The 4096-bit normalized coefficient cap, 8192-byte individual string cap and
65536-byte output-record cap also apply. These limits may be reached before a
requested tolerance or nominal degree; there is no guarantee that every input
within the size limits will finish. See `programs/examples/symbolic_algebraic.bas`,
`programs/examples/symbolic_combinations.bas`, `tools/check-symbolic-algebraic.py`
and `tools/check-symbolic-combinations.py` for executable checks.

### Exact complex algebraic values

`SYMCOMPLEX(real,imaginary)` constructs an exact value `real + i*imaginary`
from rational scalars or `SYMALG` records. Each component may use independently
selected real roots. Values remain ordinary BASIC lists:

```text
{"COMPLEX_ALGEBRAIC", realRecord, imaginaryRecord}
```

The component records use the six-field `ALGEBRAIC` format above. A manually
constructed complex record may also contain exact integer or rational-string
components. Every public operation validates both components, including when
projecting one part or taking the zeroth power. Complex components cannot be
nested inside one another. Floating-point and native numeric complex values
are rejected; `"1/10"` supplies an exact tenth. Arithmetic accepts an exact real
scalar or `SYMALG` record wherever a complex operand is expected, promoting it
to a zero imaginary part.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMCOMPLEX(real,imaginary)` | Complex algebraic record with two exact real components. |
| `SYMCADD(a,b)`, `SYMCSUB(a,b)` | Exact complex sum or difference. |
| `SYMCMUL(a,b)`, `SYMCDIV(a,b)` | Exact product or quotient. A zero complex divisor raises an error. |
| `SYMCPOW(a,integer)` | Integer power from -64 through 64; negative powers require a nonzero value. Exponent zero returns complex one after validation. |
| `SYMCCONJ(a)` | Complex conjugate, reversing the imaginary component's sign. |
| `SYMCREAL(a)`, `SYMCIMAG(a)` | Real or imaginary component as an exact real `ALGEBRAIC` record. |
| `SYMCNORM2(a)` | Squared magnitude `real^2+imaginary^2`, as a real algebraic record. |
| `SYMCEQUAL(a,b)` | Exact equality: BASIC true (`-1`) or false (`0`). A work-limit failure raises an error. |
| `SYMCENCLOSE(a[,tolerance])` | `{{realLower$,realUpper$},{imaginaryLower$,imaginaryUpper$}}`; each rational interval has width at most the positive tolerance, default `1/1000000000000`. |
| `SYMCEVAL(expression,a[,variable$])` | Exact substitution into a rational expression or guarded expression pair; variable defaults to `X`. |

```basic
10 R=SYMALGROOT("X^2-3",1,2)
20 TURN60=SYMCOMPLEX("1/2",SYMALGDIV(R,2))
30 POINT=SYMCOMPLEX(2,1)
40 ROTATED=SYMCMUL(POINT,TURN60)
50 PRINT SYMALGCMP(SYMCNORM2(ROTATED),5)
60 PRINT SYMCEQUAL(SYMCPOW(TURN60,6),1)
70 PRINT SYMCENCLOSE(ROTATED)
80 J=SYMCOMPLEX(0,1)
90 PRINT SYMCEQUAL(SYMCEVAL("X^2+1",J),0)
```

These checks print `0`, `-1`, a rectangle of rational bounds, and `-1`.
`programs/examples/symbolic_complex.bas` also checks a complex signal transfer
formula and shows how to extract the coordinate bounds into BASIC variables.
Convert an individual bound with `SYMEVAL(bound$)` when a renderer or numerical
simulation needs an ordinary binary64 value. Such conversion has ordinary
floating-point rounding; it does not retain exact arithmetic.

`SYMCEVAL` accepts one variable, rational coefficients, the four arithmetic
operations and constant integer powers. Use `SYMCOMPLEX(0,1)` for the imaginary
unit; there is no `I` symbol in the rational formula grammar. Original denominator
conditions are checked before cancellation, so `(X^2+1)/(X^2+1)` at `i` remains
an error. Rational `<>0` guards work with complex subjects. Ordered guards
(`>0`, `>=0`, `<0`, `<=0`) require a real subject value. Equality guards (`=0`)
are accepted when their subject evaluates to zero; non-real subjects produce a
domain/condition error. Guard comparisons use a zero right-hand side, as in
`{"X^2",{"X<>0","X^2+1=0"}}`. Elementary functions, noninteger powers,
additional variables and their canceled forms are outside this evaluator's
grammar. Real-only simplifications are not applied to these unsupported inputs.

Successive complex products, powers and quotients preserve a shared real
algebraic generator for their components. When a new generator is needed, the
engine tries `theta=a+k*b` for integer `k` from 1 through 16, solves for the old
coordinates exactly, and verifies their reconstruction before selecting the
root. A singular candidate is skipped. Exhausting the finite search or its
work budget raises an explicit error. This avoids unnecessary degree growth
when repeated operations stay in an already constructed field.

Complex arithmetic shares the real algebraic engine's degree-16 construction
bound, 4096-bit normalized coefficients, work budget, and total 2048 refinement
steps per call across both components. Rational formula inputs retain the
existing degree-32 limit. The 8192-byte individual string and 65536-byte complete
record limits apply. A composite operation may exhaust these bounds even when
its final value has a simpler representation. Guaranteed minimal polynomials
and algebraic coefficient support throughout every symbolic solver remain open.
For roots supplied by a defining polynomial and for numerical branch evaluation,
use the additional interfaces below. The independent component-arithmetic checker is
`tools/check-symbolic-complex.py`; optional SymPy resultants cross-check the
stored quotient identities and root selection.

### Complex polynomial roots and branch evaluation

These calls use ordinary BASIC lists, variables and loops. Root isolation accepts
univariate polynomial strings with **rational coefficients**, degree at most 16
before removing repeated factors. It returns every distinct root, including real
roots; multiplicities are not repeated. `variable$` defaults to `"X"`. Exact
bounds and tolerances use integers or rational strings, for example `"1/1000"`.
A rectangle is `{realLower,realUpper,imaginaryLower,imaginaryUpper}` with strictly
ordered bounds. Its interior is open; a zero anywhere on the boundary raises an
error, so move the bounds if needed.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMCROOTCOUNT(polynomial$,rectangle[,variable$])` | Exact number of distinct roots inside the rectangle. |
| `SYMCROOT(polynomial$,rectangle[,variable$])` | Exact root record; the rectangle must contain exactly one root. |
| `SYMCROOTS(polynomial$[,tolerance[,variable$]])` | Complete list of distinct root records, each coordinate width at most the tolerance; default `1/1024`. A nonzero constant returns an empty list; the zero polynomial raises an error. |
| `SYMCREFINE(root[,tolerance])` | Same exact root with narrower rational bounds; default `1/1000000000000`. |
| `CAPPROX(value)` | Ordinary binary64 complex approximation of a native number, exact rational, real algebraic value, component complex record, or complex root record. |
| `CLOG(value[,k])` | `ln(abs(value)) + i*(arg(value)+2*PI*k)`, default sheet `k=0`; zero is an error. |
| `CARG(value[,k])` | Real argument on sheet `k`, default zero; undefined at zero. |
| `CROOT(value,n[,k])` | Selected numerical nth root, `1<=n<=1024`; integer `k` is reduced modulo `n`, default zero. All roots of zero are zero. |
| `CPOW(value,exponent[,k])` | Numerical power using logarithm sheet `k`; integer powers are independent of `k`. `0^0=1`, positive real powers of zero are zero; other zero powers raise an error. |
| `CEVAL(expression$,value[,variable$])` | Numerical complex formula evaluation, including `I`, `PI`, `E` and elementary functions; default variable `X`. |

Root records have six fields:

```text
{"COMPLEX_ROOT", polynomial$, realLower$, realUpper$, imaginaryLower$, imaginaryUpper$}
```

The stored polynomial is square-free, monic, and uses `X`. Its isolating rectangle
identifies the root exactly. Records are revalidated on every public call.
`SYMCEQUAL` compares two root records, or a root with an existing exact component
value; `SYMCENCLOSE` also accepts root records and returns the usual pair of
coordinate intervals. Other exact component operations (`SYMCADD`, `SYMCREAL`,
`SYMCEVAL`, etc.) currently require the `COMPLEX_ALGEBRAIC`/real component forms.
Use `CAPPROX(root)` with native arithmetic or `CEVAL(formula$,root)` for numerical
calculations involving general root records. No automatic exact field conversion
is claimed. Root-list order follows the isolating rectangles, not a guaranteed
ordering of the complex values; select a known root using `SYMCROOT`.

```basic
10 ROOTS=SYMCROOTS("X^5-X+1","1/1000")
20 FOR K=1 TO LEN(ROOTS)
30 Z=CAPPROX(ROOTS(K))
40 PRINT REAL(Z);",";IMAG(Z)
50 PRINT ABS(CEVAL("X^5-X+1",ROOTS(K)))
60 NEXT K
70 PRINT CLOG(-1,0)
80 PRINT CLOG(-1,1)
90 PRINT CROOT(-1,2,1)
```

`CEVAL` accepts the complex symbolic records described below as well as strings.
For raw strings, `CEVAL` supports `+ - * / ^`, `SIN COS TAN EXP LN SQRT SINH COSH TANH ASIN ACOS
ATAN ASINH ACOSH ATANH ABS`, and parentheses. Powers and functions use principal
branches. `I` is reserved for the imaginary unit here; unknown variables and
guarded lists are errors. The original expression is evaluated without real-only
simplification: `X/X` at zero remains an error. `CLOG`, `CARG` and `CPOW` accept
integer sheet indices from -1,000,000 through 1,000,000. Ordinary BASIC uses
`PI()`; the string grammar uses `PI`.

The principal argument lies in `(-PI,PI]`. BASIC canonicalizes signed zero, so
negative real cuts take the upper lip (`imaginary=+0`), while imaginary-axis cuts
of inverse functions take the right lip (`real=+0`). A nonzero coordinate chooses
its actual side. Exact input coordinates are refined before conversion; a
nonzero coordinate or expression constant that underflows binary64 raises an
error. Subsequent arithmetic still rounds in binary64 and can underflow.
Transcendental answers are numerical approximations, with no claim of exact
symbolic logarithms, automatic continuation around paths, arbitrary precision,
or correct rounding on every input. Branch conventions follow the
[NIST logarithm/power definitions](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.2) and
[inverse trigonometric definitions](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.23).

Exact rectangle counts use Cauchy indices of rational boundary polynomials,
with verified signed remainder identities and a boundary-zero check. The method
is described by [Li and Paulson](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.03922).
Numerical guesses can accelerate isolation, but are accepted only after exact
Rouche inequalities prove one root in both an inscribed and a circumscribed disk.
Together these certify one root in the rectangle and none on its boundary.
Pairwise disjoint certified rectangles totaling the polynomial degree establish
completeness; failed proposals fall back to rational subdivision and winding
counts. There is no numerical epsilon in a root count or equality decision.

The shared 4096-bit coefficient cap, 32-million coefficient-work budget, 2048
subdivision/refinement limit, 8192-byte string cap and 65536-byte record cap apply.
Difficult separation or refinement can exhaust these limits even below degree
16; failure raises an error and never returns a partial root list. Complex
coefficient polynomials and unrestricted symbolic branch reasoning remain outside
this root-isolation interface; bounded symbolic complex calculus follows below. Run `programs/examples/complex_roots_branches.bas` and
`tools/check-complex-roots-branches.py`; `--sympy` adds independent exact complex
rectangle counts. The reference packages are test tools, not BASIC dependencies.

### Symbolic complex calculus with branch conditions

Use these functions for a single complex variable. They share the `CEVAL`
elementary grammar, including the imaginary unit `I`, `PI`, and `E`, but use
complex identities and principal branches. The real `SYMREFINE`/`SYMDERIV`
functions retain their separate real-domain contracts.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMCSIMPLIFY(expression[,variable$])` | Complex-safe symbolic formula with original domain conditions retained. |
| `SYMCBRANCH(expression,conditions[,variable$])` | Simplify using explicit open complex regions; retain source restrictions and the supplied assumptions. |
| `SYMCDERIV(expression[,variable$])` | Symbolic holomorphic derivative with sufficient open-domain conditions. Repeated calls produce higher derivatives. |
| `SYMCDOMAIN(expression[,variable$])` | Sufficient conditions for the supplied formula to have a value. |
| `SYMCANALYTIC(expression[,variable$])` | Sufficient conditions for holomorphic calculus, including branch-cut exclusions. |
| `CEVAL(formula,value[,variable$])` | Check the stored conditions, then numerically evaluate the complex formula. |

`expression` is a string or an existing complex formula record. The variable
defaults to `X` for strings and to the stored variable for records. An explicit
variable on a record must match it. Other variable tokens are rejected before
cancellation; there are no parameter bindings in this interface. Returned records
are ordinary BASIC lists:

```text
{"COMPLEX_FORMULA", formula$, variable$, {{predicate$,subject$},...}}
```

Extract the formula with `F(2)` and conditions with `F(4)`. Keep the complete
record when evaluating or differentiating it: extracting just the string drops
its retained restrictions. Supplied records are parsed and validated, and the
formula's intrinsic restrictions are collected again. A manually edited record
is a new formula with user-supplied restrictions; it is not a certificate proving
a relationship to some earlier expression.

The predicates on a subject `z` have these precise meanings:

| Predicate | Required value |
| --- | --- |
| `NONZERO` | `z` differs from zero. |
| `OFF_NEGATIVE_REAL` | Imaginary part is nonzero, or real part is strictly positive. |
| `OFF_REAL_OUTSIDE_UNIT` | Imaginary part is nonzero, or `-1 < real(z) < 1`. |
| `OFF_IMAG_OUTSIDE_UNIT` | Real part is nonzero, or `-1 < imag(z) < 1`. |
| `OFF_REAL_TO_ONE` | Imaginary part is nonzero, or real part is strictly greater than 1. |
| `RIGHT_HALF`, `LEFT_HALF` | Respectively `real(z)>0` and `real(z)<0`. |
| `UPPER_HALF`, `LOWER_HALF` | Respectively `imag(z)>0` and `imag(z)<0`. |
| `LOG_STRIP` | `-PI < imag(z) < PI`. |
| `TRIG_STRIP` | `-PI/2 < real(z) < PI/2`. |
| `COS_STRIP` | `0 < real(z) < PI`. |
| `HYPERBOLIC_STRIP` | `-PI/2 < imag(z) < PI/2`. |
| `ACOSH_STRIP` | `real(z)>0` and `-PI < imag(z) < PI`. |

A logarithm may have a principal value on the negative real axis, but its
principal formula is not holomorphic across that cut. Thus
`CEVAL(SYMCSIMPLIFY("LN(X)"),-2)` has a value, while
`CEVAL(SYMCDERIV("LN(X)"),-2)` raises a branch-condition error. Constant arguments
are treated as constants: `SYMCDERIV("LN(-1)")` is zero. Conditions are sufficient,
not a minimal domain or a proof that all conditions can hold together. In
particular, differentiating an unsimplified composition can retain exclusions
that simplification before differentiation would avoid.

Division and canceled poles retain nonzero conditions. Inverse functions retain
their singularities; analytic calculus also excludes their principal cuts.
General variable or non-real exponents conservatively require a nonzero base.
Constant positive rational powers allow a value at zero; noninteger powers with
a varying base exclude the negative real axis and zero during analytic calculus.
`ABS` is permitted in value expressions and for constant derivatives, but a
varying complex `ABS` is rejected by `SYMCDERIV` and `SYMCANALYTIC`.

Safe rewrites include rational/Gaussian arithmetic, selected exact constants,
`EXP(LN(X))=X` with `X<>0`, `SQRT(X)^2=X`, and forward functions composed with their
principal inverses. `LN(-1)=I*PI`, `LN(I)=I*PI/2`, and integer/half-integer multiples
of `I*PI` in exponentials are exact symbolic cases. Opposite compositions and
branch-sensitive identities such as `LN(X^2)=2*LN(X)`, `SQRT(X^2)=X`, or
`LN(EXP(X))=X` are not applied generally. Poles are collected before any rewrite,
so `0*LN(X)` still excludes zero. Integer/half-integer PI trigonometric poles,
including imaginary hyperbolic poles, are checked exactly where recognized.

Derivatives use complex chain, product, quotient and power rules. For example,
the `ACOSH(X)` derivative uses `1/(SQRT(X-1)*SQRT(X+1))`; merging the two square
roots would select an incorrect branch in part of the complex plane. Conventions
and analytic cuts follow [NIST logarithms and powers](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.2),
[inverse trigonometric functions](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.23), and
[inverse hyperbolic functions](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.37).

```basic
10 D=SYMCDERIV("EXP(I*X)/(1+I*X)")
20 PRINT D(2)
30 PRINT CEVAL(D,1)
40 D2=SYMCDERIV(D)
50 PRINT CEVAL(D2,1)
60 F=SYMCSIMPLIFY("EXP(LN(X))")
70 PRINT F(2)
80 PRINT F(4)
```

Symbolic constants and formulas retain exact rational coefficients. `CEVAL`
converts its input to binary64 first, including algebraic input records; it does
not certify evaluation at the original exact algebraic value. For formula
records, Gaussian-rational subexpressions and supported PI facts are checked
exactly at that converted point, then rounded for numerical output. No epsilon
is used to decide an exact zero or rational cut side. A nonzero exact computed
component that underflows binary64 is an error, preventing a tiny cut distance
from silently changing the branch. Remaining transcendental values and conditions
use numerical evaluation; this is not interval-certified transcendental calculus
or arbitrary-precision floating point. Exact symbolic rewriting may avoid
intermediate rounding or overflow encountered by the original raw `CEVAL` string.

Limits include 8192 bytes per expression, 4096 nodes, depth 64, 128 conditions,
65536 bytes of record text, and the shared structural/coefficient work budgets.
The exact Gaussian constant evaluator handles integer powers from -64 through
64; larger powers remain expressions and may use numerical evaluation. Resource
failure is an error. General symbolic sheet
parameters, path continuation/monodromy, multivariable complex calculus and
nonholomorphic/Wirtinger calculus remain outside this implementation.

#### Conditional complex branch simplification

`SYMCBRANCH` takes a list of `{predicate$,subject$}` pairs, using the predicates
above. An empty list uses only known constant facts. It accepts the same strings
and `COMPLEX_FORMULA` records as `SYMCSIMPLIFY`; the optional variable follows the
same rules. The result remains an ordinary four-field complex formula record.
Assumptions stay attached through simplification, evaluation and repeated
differentiation, even when the resulting formula is constant. Their subjects
also retain intrinsic poles, so an assumption about `X/X` cannot admit zero.

| Original expression | Sufficient region assumptions | Rewritten formula |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SQRT(U^2)` or `(U^2)^(1/2)` | `RIGHT_HALF` on `U` | `U` |
| `SQRT(U^2)` or `(U^2)^(1/2)` | `LEFT_HALF` on `U` | `-U` |
| `LN(EXP(U))` | `LOG_STRIP` on `U` | `U` |
| `ASIN(SIN(U))`, `ATAN(TAN(U))` | `TRIG_STRIP` on `U` | `U` |
| `ACOS(COS(U))` | `COS_STRIP` on `U` | `U` |
| `ASINH(SINH(U))`, `ATANH(TANH(U))` | `HYPERBOLIC_STRIP` on `U` | `U` |
| `ACOSH(COSH(U))` | `ACOSH_STRIP` on `U` | `U` |
| `LN(U*V)`, `LN(U/V)` | `RIGHT_HALF` on both operands | `LN(U)+LN(V)`, `LN(U)-LN(V)` |
| `SQRT(U*V)`, `SQRT(U/V)` | `RIGHT_HALF` on both operands | `SQRT(U)*SQRT(V)`, `SQRT(U)/SQRT(V)` |
| `LN(U^2)` | `RIGHT_HALF` on `U` | `2*LN(U)` |
| `LN(-U)` | `UPPER_HALF` or `LOWER_HALF` on `U` | Respectively `LN(U)-I*PI` or `LN(U)+I*PI` |
| `LN(U^2)` | `LEFT_HALF` and `UPPER_HALF` on `U` | `2*LN(U)-2*I*PI` |
| `LN(U^2)` | `LEFT_HALF` and `LOWER_HALF` on `U` | `2*LN(U)+2*I*PI` |

Here `U` and `V` denote expressions in the single selected variable, not extra
parameter bindings. Logarithmic product/quotient expansion also accepts an
explicit `LOG_STRIP` condition on `LN(U)+LN(V)` or `LN(U)-LN(V)`.
`LN(U^V)` becomes `V*LN(U)` when that latter expression is explicitly in
`LOG_STRIP`; the condition itself excludes any pole in `LN(U)`.
Original restrictions remain in every case.

```basic
10 F=SYMCBRANCH("SQRT(X^2)",{{"LEFT_HALF","X"}})
20 PRINT F(2)
30 PRINT CEVAL(F,COMPLEX(-2,1))
40 D=SYMCDERIV(F)
50 PRINT CEVAL(D,COMPLEX(-2,1))
60 P=SYMCBRANCH("LN(EXP(I*X))",{{"LOG_STRIP","I*X"}})
70 PRINT IMAG(CEVAL(P,1.25))
```

Region boundaries are strictly excluded, even where a principal value might
allow an identity on the boundary. There is no automatic sheet selection or
case splitting outside the declared regions. Inference uses exact constants,
structural subjects after unconditional folding, negation, and the inclusions
`ACOSH_STRIP` into `RIGHT_HALF`/`LOG_STRIP`, `HYPERBOLIC_STRIP` into `LOG_STRIP`,
and `COS_STRIP` into `RIGHT_HALF`. Opposite half-plane conditions on the same
normalized subject, and exact false constant conditions, raise errors. Other
joint contradictions may remain unresolved; this is not a satisfiability solver.
Unsupported identities remain unchanged rather than being forced onto a branch.

For open-region conditions whose subjects are affine Gaussian-rational
expressions in `PI`, comparisons use exact rational arithmetic and a certified
100-decimal-place enclosure of `PI`. Exact PI boundary cancellations and tiny
rational displacements are preserved. A comparison unresolved by that enclosure
raises an error instead of guessing. The reference checker verifies the enclosure
from rational alternating-series bounds for Machin's formula. This local sign
facility does not increase `CEVAL`'s binary64 output precision or certify other
transcendental computations. Other condition subjects use the existing numerical
evaluation, with strict comparisons at binary64 strip boundaries.

Before differentiation or `SYMCANALYTIC`, stored condition subjects must also meet
the sufficient holomorphic-domain checks. For example, an `UPPER_HALF` condition
on `LN(X)` can hold at `X=-1`, but differentiation excludes that cut. A varying
`ABS` in a condition subject is conservatively rejected by calculus. Conditions
remain attached even if this sacrifices a potentially larger derivative domain.
The existing expression, condition-count, storage and work limits still apply.
See `programs/examples/complex_branches.bas` for root branches, logarithm
corrections, oscillator phase and rejection outside a declared strip.
Run `programs/examples/complex_calculus.bas` and
`tools/check-complex-calculus.py`; `--sympy` adds 80-digit mpmath derivative
comparisons and exact SymPy rational identities. These packages are test tools.

### High-precision real numerical evaluation

`HPEVAL` and `HPBOUNDS` evaluate real expressions using bounded variable-precision
integer interval arithmetic. They return decimal strings so the result's digits
are not rounded back into an ordinary BASIC number.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `HPEVAL(expression,places[,variables,values])` | One decimal string rounded to `places` digits after the decimal point, nearest with ties to even. |
| `HPBOUNDS(expression,places[,variables,values])` | `{lower$,upper$}` with outward-rounded decimal bounds enclosing the result. Their difference is at most `2*10^(-places)`. |

`places` must be an integer from 0 through 256. It counts decimal places, not
significant digits. With no bindings, the expression must contain no unbound
variables. Otherwise supply both the variable-name string/list and matching
scalar/list values, as with `SYMEVAL`. Up to eight variables are supported.
Constants `PI` and `E` cannot be rebound. Integer bindings are exact; real BASIC
bindings retain their existing binary64 value. Use strings such as `"0.1"`,
`"1/7"`, or `"1e-100"` for exact decimal/rational inputs. String bindings must
evaluate to a recognized exact rational, rather than a transcendental value.

The expression can be a string or an existing two-field real symbolic result
`{formula$,{condition$...}}`, including derivatives and antiderivatives. Conditions
and their own domains are checked before returning a result. Poles are retained
through cancellation, multiplication by zero and guarded symbolic simplification.
Unknown variables are rejected before cancellation. Complex formula/algebraic
records are not accepted by this real interface.

The grammar includes explicit `+ - * / ^`, parentheses, unary signs, `PI`, `E`,
and all 16 elementary functions in the real symbolic grammar. `LOG` and `SQR`
retain their aliases. This HP interface additionally accepts exact decimal and
scientific literals inside its expression, condition and binding strings:
`.5`, `1.25`, `2.5e-30`, and `1E100` are examples. No floating-point conversion
is used to parse them. Ordinary symbolic APIs retain their rational-string grammar.
Real branches apply: `SQRT(0)` is allowed, logarithms require positive arguments,
inverse functions obey their real domains, and noninteger/variable powers
conservatively require a strictly positive base. Integer powers permit negative
bases and follow the existing `0^0=1` convention.

```basic
10 PRINT HPEVAL("PI",50)
20 PRINT HPEVAL("X+Y",30,"X,Y",{"0.1","0.2"})
30 B=HPBOUNDS("SQRT(2)",40)
40 PRINT B(1)
50 PRINT B(2)
60 D=SYMDERIV("LN(X)")
70 PRINT HPEVAL(D,40,"X","3")
80 PRINT HPEVAL("SIN(1e100)",30)
```

Evaluation uses outward-rounded dyadic intervals, exact rational handling for
recognized rational expressions and decimal ties, integer square roots, reduced
power series with explicit tail bounds, and interval range reduction. PI is
computed at the working precision using Machin's formula. Exact rational
logarithm inputs are normalized before conversion, allowing values such as
`LN(1e-1000)`. An unresolved sign, pole or rounding decision triggers increased
working precision. `HPEVAL` returns only when both interval endpoints round to the
same requested decimal (or exact rational rounding settles the result). It
raises an error when the bounded calculation cannot settle the decision.

Returned bounds are numerical enclosures, not symbolic identity certificates.
Dependency and cancellation can widen intervals; a true equality in a guard or
a transcendental value exactly at a decimal rounding boundary can remain
undecidable. Precision failure never silently falls back to binary64. Algorithms
use the series and scaling principles described in
[NIST elementary computation](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.45),
[logarithm series](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.6), and
[trigonometric series](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.19).

Limits: 2048 working fractional bits, 4096 bits per stored scaled endpoint and
normalized rational component, integer powers from -1024 through 1024, and
exponential arguments in `[-1024,1024]`. Decimal-token scaling is limited to
1233 powers of ten in either direction. The existing 8192-byte expression,
4096-node/depth-64 tree, 128-condition, 65536-byte guard and shared work limits
also apply; decimal expansion must fit the expression limit. Large integer
parts, extreme cancellation or difficult domains can exhaust these limits even
when the final mathematical answer exists.

Use the returned string directly for display or as a later exact decimal
binding; that binding represents the rounded decimal, not the original
irrational value. `VAL` converts it back to ordinary BASIC precision when a
native graphics/audio/tensor API needs a number. This interface does not change
ordinary numeric variables, arrays, matrices, complex arithmetic, special
functions or ML kernels to high precision. Complex arbitrary-precision
evaluation and high-precision nonlinear/differential solvers remain future work.
The explicit rational-data matrix operations below provide high-precision linear solves.
`programs/examples/high_precision.bas` demonstrates exact decimal data,
cancellation, root bounds, symbolic slopes and large oscillator phases.

### High-precision matrices and linear systems

These functions operate on real rational matrix data and return decimal strings
with 0–256 digits after the decimal point. Decimal/scientific strings such as
`"0.1"` and `"1e-80"` are parsed exactly; ordinary numeric inputs retain their
existing integer or binary64 values. All arithmetic and pivot tests are exact
rational operations until the final decimal formatting.

| Rounded result | Enclosing result | Operation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HPMATMUL(A,B,places)` | `HPMATMULBOUNDS(A,B,places)` | Matrix times matrix or column vector. |
| `HPDET(A,places)` | `HPDETBOUNDS(A,places)` | Determinant of a square matrix. |
| `HPINVERSE(A,places)` | `HPINVERSEBOUNDS(A,places)` | Inverse of a nonsingular square matrix. |
| `HPLINSOLVE(A,B,places)` | `HPLINSOLVEBOUNDS(A,B,places)` | Solve `A*X=B` with square nonsingular A and one or more right-hand sides. |

A matrix is a nonempty rectangular nested list such as `{{1,2},{3,4}}`.
Every dimension must be 1–16. For multiplication/solving, B may instead be a
nonempty flat list representing a column vector. A vector B produces a vector
result; a matrix B produces a matrix result, including a one-column matrix.
Determinants return one string. Inverses always return a nested list of strings.
Store a scalar determinant in a string variable such as `D$`; matrix and vector
results use ordinary list variables such as `X`.

The `BOUNDS` variants return `{lower,upper}` in the corresponding shape:
`HPLINSOLVEBOUNDS(A,{1,2},p)` returns two vectors;
`HPINVERSEBOUNDS(A,p)` returns two matrices; `HPDETBOUNDS` returns two strings.
Each lower endpoint rounds toward negative infinity and each upper endpoint
toward positive infinity. Their difference is at most `10^(-places)` per entry.
An exactly representable decimal has equal endpoints. Rounded variants use
nearest rounding with ties to even, matching `HPEVAL`.

```basic
10 A={{1,1},{1,"1+1e-80"}}
20 B={2,"2+1e-80"}
30 X=HPLINSOLVE(A,B,50)
40 PRINT X(1):PRINT X(2)
50 D$=HPDET(A,100):PRINT D$
60 Q=HPLINSOLVEBOUNDS({{3}},{1},30)
70 PRINT Q(1,1):PRINT Q(2,1)
80 M=HPINVERSE({{2,1},{1,3}},30)
90 R=HPMATMUL({{2,1},{1,3}},M,30)
100 PRINT R(1,1):PRINT R(2,2)
```

String entries use the same recognized exact-rational grammar as `HPEVAL`
bindings. `"1/7"`, `"SQRT(4)"`, and `"1+1e-80"` are accepted. Unbound variables,
complex values, algebraic/formula records, `"PI"`, and `"SQRT(2)"` are rejected.
All supplied cells are validated, even when multiplied by zero or when the
matrix is singular. Numeric DIM arrays can be passed with `A()`. Exact string
data can be read with `READ A$` and assembled into lists. String DIM arrays
retain their existing element access; whole-array `A$()` snapshots are not added.

Elimination uses exact nonzero row pivots and back substitution. Before rounding,
solves and inverses are verified against the original equations with an exact
zero residual. No floating-point singularity tolerance is used. Both inconsistent
and underdetermined singular systems raise a no-unique-solution error; they do
not produce a pseudoinverse or an arbitrary solution. A singular determinant is
exactly zero. A nonzero determinant can also *display* as zero at too few decimal
places; solving uses the exact pivots rather than this rounded display.

Bounds describe the exact result for the supplied rational data, not uncertainty
in measurements or earlier rounded values. A string produced by `HPEVAL` or a
previous matrix operation is reused as that exact rounded decimal. Rounding a
solution can introduce a residual even though the internal exact solution was
verified. Convert individual output strings with `VAL` when a native graphics,
audio, or tensor API needs ordinary numeric values.

Limits are 16 rows/columns, 8192 bytes per string expression, 65536 total input
string bytes per call, 4096 bits per normalized rational numerator/denominator,
and the shared symbolic structural/coefficient work budgets. There is no Python,
BLAS, or LAPACK dependency for these operations. Difficult coefficient growth
raises an explicit resource error, even when the requested final value exists.
Inversion/solving does not compute the determinant product, so a large or tiny
unrepresentable determinant does not by itself prevent a bounded exact solve.
High-precision irrational/complex matrix inputs,
sparse systems, and nonlinear/differential solvers remain future work.

`programs/examples/high_precision_linear.bas` demonstrates fine pivots, exact
decimal DATA, geometry transforms, inverse checks, and solution bounds.

### High-precision rank, least squares and matrix factors

These operations share the rational-data matrix input rules and resource limits
above. `HPRANK` returns an integer; the other functions return decimal strings
rounded to 0–256 places, nearest with ties to even. Exact decimal input strings
preserve small differences that ordinary numeric literals may already have lost.

| Rounded result | Enclosing result | Operation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HPRANK(A)` | — | Exact rank, including rectangular and zero matrices. No precision argument. |
| `HPPINV(A,places)` | `HPPINVBOUNDS(A,places)` | Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of an m by n matrix; returns an n by m matrix. |
| `HPLSTSQ(A,B,places)` | `HPLSTSQBOUNDS(A,B,places)` | Minimum-norm least-squares solution, including singular, underdetermined and inconsistent systems. |
| `HPQR(A,places)` | `HPQRBOUNDS(A,places)` | Reduced QR factors `{Q,R}` for m >= n and full column rank. Q is m by n; R is n by n with positive diagonal. |
| `HPCHOLESKY(A,places)` | `HPCHOLESKYBOUNDS(A,places)` | Lower triangular L with `A=L*TRANSPOSE(L)` for an exactly symmetric positive definite matrix. |

For least squares, B must have as many rows as A. A flat vector B returns a
vector X; a matrix B returns a matrix X with one solution per right-hand side.
Each solution first minimizes the sum of squared residuals `A*X-B`, then has
the smallest Euclidean norm among all minimizers. An inconsistent system can
therefore succeed with a nonzero residual. Zero A returns zero X. No numerical
rank threshold or truncation parameter is used. `HPLINSOLVE` retains its stricter
requirement of a unique solution to a square system.

```basic
10 A={{1,0},{1,1},{1,2}}
20 FIT=HPLSTSQ(A,{1,2,2},30)
30 PRINT "INTERCEPT ";FIT(1):PRINT "SLOPE ";FIT(2)
40 X=HPLSTSQ({{1,1}},{2},30):PRINT X(1):PRINT X(2)
50 PRINT HPRANK({{1,1},{1,"1+1e-80"}})
60 P=HPPINV({{1,2},{2,4}},30):PRINT P(1,1)
70 QR=HPQR({{1,0},{1,1},{0,1}},30)
80 Q=QR(1):R=QR(2):PRINT R(1,1)
90 L=HPCHOLESKY({{2,1},{1,2}},30):PRINT L(2,2)
```

`HPPINVBOUNDS` and `HPCHOLESKYBOUNDS` return `{lowerMatrix,upperMatrix}`.
`HPLSTSQBOUNDS` returns `{lower,upper}` with the same vector/matrix shape as X.
`HPQRBOUNDS` returns `{{Qlower,Rlower},{Qupper,Rupper}}`: select `B(1,1)` for
Q's lower matrix and `B(2,2)` for R's upper matrix. Each entry's interval has
width at most `10^(-places)` and contains the exact mathematical result for the
supplied rational data.

Rank factorization and all four Moore–Penrose equations are checked exactly
before pseudoinverse formatting. Least squares also verifies the normal
equations and minimum-norm row-space condition. QR uses exact rational
orthogonal columns before normalization; Cholesky uses exact rational LDL
factors. Their reconstruction and orthogonality identities are checked before
rounding. Each factor entry is a rational multiple of a square root, rounded
and enclosed using integer comparisons without binary64 intermediates.

QR rejects wide or rank-deficient matrices; it does not silently remove
dependent columns. Cholesky requires exact symmetry and strictly positive
pivots, rejecting asymmetric, indefinite and positive semidefinite inputs.
The functions validate every input cell and report resource-limit failures
explicitly. Dimensions are at most 16, normalized rational components at most
4096 bits, and the shared input and work budgets still apply.

Returned factors may approximate irrational values even though inputs must be
rational. Rounding can introduce reconstruction or orthogonality error; reusing
output strings treats them as the rounded decimal values. Bounds enclose the
exact result for the supplied data and do not represent measurement uncertainty.
Irrational/complex input matrices, sparse solvers and high-precision
nonlinear/differential solvers remain outside this interface. Spectral factors
are described below.
`programs/examples/high_precision_decomposition.bas` connects decimal DATA to
line fitting, minimum-norm solutions, rank, pseudoinverses, QR and Cholesky bounds.

### High-precision eigenvalues, singular values and inertia

These functions use the same exact rational input rules as the matrix functions
above, including numeric DIM-array snapshots and decimal/rational strings.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `HPINERTIA(A[,shift])` | Integer counts `{negative,zero,positive}` for the eigenvalues of `A-shift*I`. Shift defaults to zero and accepts the same exact scalar data as matrix entries. |
| `HPEIGVALS(A,places)` | Eigenvalues of an exactly symmetric square matrix, ascending, with multiplicities. |
| `HPEIGVALSBOUNDS(A,places)` | `{lowerVector,upperVector}` enclosing the corresponding ordered eigenvalues. |
| `HPSINGVALS(A,places)` | Singular values of a rectangular m by n matrix, descending; exactly `MIN(m,n)` entries, including zero values and multiplicities. |
| `HPSINGVALSBOUNDS(A,places)` | `{lowerVector,upperVector}` enclosing the corresponding ordered singular values. |

Inertia is an exact sign count, without a numerical tolerance or precision
argument. For a symmetric matrix, no negative eigenvalues means positive
semidefinite; no negative or zero eigenvalues means positive definite. Shifting
allows BASIC programs to count modes below, at and above an exact threshold.
Asymmetric and nonsquare matrices are rejected by inertia/eigenvalue functions.
Singular-value functions accept any nonempty real rational rectangular matrix.
These functions return values only. Use `HPEIGH` and `HPSVD` below for factors.

```basic
10 K={{2,-1},{-1,2}}
20 C=HPINERTIA(K):PRINT C(1):PRINT C(2):PRINT C(3)
30 E=HPEIGVALS(K,30):PRINT E(1):PRINT E(2)
40 C=HPINERTIA(K,1):PRINT C(2)
50 S=HPSINGVALS({{1,1},{0,1}},30):PRINT S(1):PRINT S(2)
60 B=HPEIGVALSBOUNDS({{1,1},{1,-1}},30)
70 PRINT B(1,2):PRINT B(2,2)
```

The value and bound functions return decimal strings at 0–256 places. Rounded
values use nearest rounding with ties to even. Each interval has width at most
one requested decimal unit; exactly representable values have equal endpoints.
Intervals may overlap for closely spaced values, and distinct values can round
to the same string. Multiplicity and exact zero detection do not use those
rounded strings. `HPINERTIA` and `HPRANK` can distinguish exact degeneracy from
small nonzero values.

Symmetric congruence elimination uses exact one- or two-row pivots to count
signs, including zero-diagonal indefinite matrices and singular trailing blocks.
Exact counts drive a decimal-grid bisection and settle midpoint ties.
Singular values use the smaller of `TRANSPOSE(A)*A` and `A*TRANSPOSE(A)`, formed
exactly, and compare squared decimal thresholds. No binary64 Gram matrix or
eigenvalue guess is used. Diagonal spectra are formatted directly, using exact
square-root comparisons where needed.

Dimensions are bounded to 16, normalized rational components to 4096 bits, and
the existing aggregate text, structural and coefficient work limits apply to
the entire call. Dense matrices, large coefficient growth or high requested
precision can exhaust those limits; the call then returns an explicit error
without a partial spectrum or silently reduced precision. Bounds describe the
mathematical values for the supplied rational data, not measurement uncertainty.
The result is not a guarantee of high relative accuracy for values smaller than
one requested decimal unit. Ordinary numeric kernels retain their precision.
General real-matrix complex spectra are provided by `HPCEIGVALS` below.
Matrices with complex entries remain outside these interfaces. `programs/examples/high_precision_spectrum.bas`
demonstrates stability counts, unit-mass vibration frequencies, geometric
stretch, dependent features and tiny exact decimal data.

### High-precision eigenvectors and full singular-value factors

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `HPEIGH(A,places)` | `{values,V}` for an exactly symmetric n by n matrix. Values are ascending; columns of the n by n matrix V are the corresponding mode directions. |
| `HPSVD(A,places)` | `{U,S,VT}` for any nonempty real rational m by n matrix. U is m by m, VT is n by n, and S has `MIN(m,n)` descending nonnegative entries. |

Inputs follow the exact rational matrix rules above; every output cell is a
fixed decimal string at 0–256 places. These functions include repeated spectra,
rank-deficient matrices, zero matrices and full orthogonal null-space bases.
`HPSVD` returns full square factors (ordinary `SVD` returns reduced factors).
Build an m by n diagonal matrix Sigma from S to reconstruct `A = U*Sigma*VT`.
For `HPEIGH`, the corresponding identity is `A = V*DIAG(values)*TRANSPOSE(V)`.
Use nested list indexing, such as `F(2,1,2)`, to access factor cells. Decimal
strings work directly with `HPMATMUL` and `HPEVAL`; ordinary matrix utilities
expect ordinary numeric cells, so construct a decimal transpose with list/array
indexing or convert explicitly at the consumer boundary.

```basic
10 F=HPEIGH({{2,-1},{-1,2}},40):E=F(1):V=F(2)
20 PRINT E(1):PRINT V(1,1):PRINT V(2,1)
30 X=HPMATMUL(V,{"1/10",0},40):PRINT X(1):PRINT X(2)
40 F=HPSVD({{3,0},{0,-2},{0,0}},40):U=F(1):S=F(2):VT=F(3)
50 SIGMA={{S(1),0},{0,S(2)},{0,0}}
60 A=HPMATMUL(HPMATMUL(U,SIGMA,40),VT,40):PRINT A(2,2)
```

**Accuracy contract.** Let `u = 10^(-places)`, `N = MAX(rows,columns)` and
`M = MAX(1,MAX(ABS(A(i,j))))` for the exact input entries. Every returned result
passes exact integer comparisons on its final decimal strings:

- Each entry of the factor reconstruction minus A has absolute value at most
  `4*N*u*M`.
- Each entry of `TRANSPOSE(V)*V-I` for eigenvectors, and of
  `TRANSPOSE(U)*U-I` and `VT*TRANSPOSE(VT)-I` for SVD, has absolute value at most
  `4*N*u`.

These are residual guarantees for the supplied matrix and returned rounded
factors. At few decimal places the stated bounds can be loose. Individual basis
entries are not certified enclosures of unique exact vectors: signs are
arbitrary, repeated values permit different bases, and closely spaced values
can make individual directions sensitive. Small singular values can round to
zero. Use `HPRANK` for exact rank and the separate `HPEIGVALS`/`HPSINGVALS`
functions for certified nearest ties-to-even spectral values or their outward
bounds. Factor values are approximations checked jointly with the basis; no
componentwise correct-rounding or relative-accuracy guarantee is made.

The implementation uses bounded integer fixed-point Jacobi rotations with exact
power-of-two scaling, one-sided rotations for SVD, and reorthogonalization to
complete full bases. It increases working precision when the final residual
checks fail, up to 2048 bits. Dimensions remain limited to 16; the shared 4096-bit
rational input and structural/arithmetic work budgets apply, including retries.
Difficult inputs can fail before reaching those maximum sizes. A failure returns
an explicit error, never uncertified factors or silently reduced precision.
General nonsymmetric/complex factors and uncertain or irrational matrix inputs
remain outside this API. The BASIC example
`programs/examples/high_precision_factors.bas` demonstrates unit-mass vibration
modes, modal coordinates, a rectangular transform and covariance directions.

### Exact characteristic polynomials and general complex eigenvalues

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SYMCHARPOLY(A[,variable$])` | The exact monic polynomial `DET(variable*I-A)` as a symbolic string, including algebraic multiplicities. The variable defaults to `"X"`. |
| `HPCEIGVALS(A,places)` | An n by 2 list of decimal strings `{realPart,imaginaryPart}` for all eigenvalues of an n by n real rational matrix, with algebraic multiplicities. Symmetry is not required. |
| `HPCEIGVALSBOUNDS(A,places)` | `{lowerMatrix,upperMatrix}`, each n by 2, enclosing the real and imaginary components of the corresponding eigenvalues. |

All three functions accept nonempty square matrices under the exact rational
matrix input rules above. Native integers retain their exact value, native reals
retain their binary64 value, and decimal/rational strings retain their exact
mathematical value. Complex, irrational and uncertain input cells are rejected.
The characteristic polynomial variable is a case-insensitive alphanumeric
identifier beginning with a letter, at most 32 characters, excluding PI and E.
Its output can be passed to `SYMDIFF`, `SYMFACTOR`, `SYMROOTCOUNT`, `SYMCROOTS`
and other symbolic polynomial operations. `SYMCROOTS` returns distinct root
records; `HPCEIGVALS` repeats each value according to its algebraic multiplicity.

```basic
10 READ D$:A={{0,1},{-4,D$}}
20 P$=SYMCHARPOLY(A):PRINT P$
30 E=HPCEIGVALS(A,40)
40 FOR I=1 TO LEN(E):PRINT E(I,1):PRINT E(I,2):NEXT I
50 B=HPCEIGVALSBOUNDS(A,40):PRINT B(1,1,1):PRINT B(2,1,1)
60 END
70 DATA "-1/2"
```

This damped system has a complex conjugate pair. Real eigenvalues are returned
in the same two-column shape with an exactly zero imaginary component. Repeated
roots, defective matrices, nilpotent matrices and zero matrices are supported.
These are eigenvalue functions; they do not return nonsymmetric eigenvectors,
Jordan chains or Schur factors.

Decimal places range from 0 to 256. Each component uses nearest rounding with
ties to even. Every bound interval is outward and at most one final decimal unit
wide; an exactly representable component has equal endpoints. Rows are sorted
by the rounded real component, then the rounded imaginary component, using
numeric comparisons. Bounds use that same ordering at the requested precision.
Ties are unspecified: do not treat row numbers as persistent root identities
when the input or requested precision changes. Distinct roots may round to the
same pair and their component intervals may overlap.

The characteristic polynomial is calculated with exact rational arithmetic.
Cayley-Hamilton is checked, and independent determinant evaluations at n+1
rational points certify the polynomial identity and multiplicities. A verified
square-free decomposition retains repeated roots. Linear/quadratic factors use
exact rational and radical grid comparisons. Higher-degree roots use certified
one-root complex rectangles; numerical Newton locations are proposals only.
Exact GCD/Sturm tests on rational grid lines settle component zeros, exact grid
values and halfway ties. No numerical rank or root-merging tolerance decides
multiplicity or the returned digits.

Dimensions are bounded to 16, individual input strings to 8192 bytes, aggregate
matrix text to 65536 bytes, normalized rational components to 4096 bits, and
symbolic polynomial output to 8192 bytes. The shared structural/arithmetic work
