`(I_n ⊗ A + B ⊗ I_m)*x=b` using the same restarted CPU GMRES recurrence
as `SPGMRES`, without assembling the full grid matrix. Factors are nonempty
square real matrices and the field is flattened row-major, as for `KRONSMV`.
Factors need not be symmetric or positive definite. Row equilibration is used;
this interface does not assemble an ILU preconditioner. The result is
`{solution,status,iterations,residualNorm,threshold}`. Status can be `CONVERGED`,
`MAXITER`, `BREAKDOWN` or `STAGNATED`; convergence is decided using the original
operator residual, with threshold `MAX(rtol*NORM(b),atol)`.

Defaults match `KRONSCG`: rtol `1E-8`, atol zero, maxiter
`CLAMP(10*dimension,20,10000)` and a zero initial vector. Restart must be an
integer from 1 through 128; its default is
`MIN(30,dimension,FLOOR(2000000/dimension)-1)`. The effective basis width is
`MIN(restart,dimension,maxiter)` and `(width+1)*dimension` must not exceed two
million entries when iteration is needed. Factor/vector caps are those of
`KRONSMV`; solve work is limited to 100 million estimated units and iterations
to 100,000. Invalid shape/options, nonfinite data and required row scaling that
loses a nonzero coefficient raise recoverable errors. Singular, ill-conditioned
or poorly preconditioned systems need not converge. Native Rust calls are
`NativeKroneckerSum::gmres` and `gmres_with_restart`.
See `programs/science/matrix_free_transport.bas` for a steady transport model.
General fixed linear callbacks use `MFGMRES`, described below. Retained operator
graphs remain a separate capability.

### Programmable matrix-free linear systems

`MFGMRES("FNOP",b[,rtol,atol,maxiter,initial,restart,preconditioner])` solves `A*x=b`
with restarted CPU GMRES. Define a one-argument `DEF FNOP(X)` that returns the
real list `A*X`; it must represent a fixed linear map throughout the solve.
For example:

```basic
10 DEF FNOP(X)={4*X(1)+2*X(2),-X(1)+3*X(2)}
20 R=MFGMRES("FNOP",{2,-4})
30 PRINT R(1):REM APPROXIMATELY {1,-1}
```

The dimension is the length of `b` (1 through 1,000,000). The callback receives
one list of that length and must return a finite real list of the same length.
Names are case-insensitive and start with `FN`; ordinary parameter scoping
applies, so the callback argument shadows rather than overwrites an outer
variable. Other program variables and `DEF FN` calls can compose the operator.
Statement `FUNCTION`/`SUB` procedures are not accepted by this interface.

The report is `{solution,status,iterations,residualNorm,threshold}`. Status is
`"CONVERGED"`, `"MAXITER"`, `"BREAKDOWN"` or `"STAGNATED"`. Every candidate is
checked using a fresh `b-FNOP(solution)`; the threshold is
`MAX(atol,rtol*NORM(b))`. This is a global residual criterion, not a bound on
solution error or every row's relative error. Callback arithmetic determines the
operator's precision. The solver cannot certify linearity, repeatability,
conditioning or convergence; nonlinear/time-varying/random callbacks are outside
its contract. The default `rtol` is 1E-8, `atol` is zero, `maxiter` is
`MIN(10000,MAX(20,10*LEN(b)))`, and the initial vector is zero.
Require `0<=rtol<1`, `atol>=0`, at least one positive tolerance, and integer
`maxiter` from 0 through 100000. Restart is an integer from 1 through 128;
the default is size-aware, up to 30. Retained basis storage is capped at two
million elements, so large systems may need a smaller restart.

A list-valued `preconditioner` supplies one positive finite divisor per row
(`rowScales`) for left scaling. With it the solver applies `FNOP(X)/rowScales` internally but still
checks the original callback residual. There is no automatic preconditioner;
the unscaled callback output must be finite before scaling. The solver caps
its own vector work at 100 million charged operations and callback applications
at 10000 combined operator/preconditioner calls per solve. These limits do not account for all computation inside the
callback; nested BASIC operations retain their own limits. Cancellation and
callback/type/shape/domain failures propagate as recoverable errors. Failed
assignment preserves its prior value, although callback side effects are not
rolled back. See `programs/science/matrix_free_low_rank.bas` for a ridge system
with two global modes, using vectors instead of a full square matrix.


The eighth argument can be a list of positive row divisors (the existing behavior)
or a string naming a `DEF FN`, such as `"FNPC"`. The latter must return a vector
of the same length computing a **fixed linear inverse action** `P^-1*r`, where
P approximates A. Supply a solve using reusable factors; do not explicitly form
an inverse merely for preconditioning. The callback can be nonsymmetric.
For example:

```basic
10 A={{4,2},{-1,3}}:F=LUFACTOR(A)
20 DEF FNOP(X)={DOT(A(1),X),DOT(A(2),X)}
30 DEF FNPC(X)=LUSOLVE(F,X)
40 R=MFGMRES("FNOP",{2,-4},1E-12,0,20,{0,0},1,"FNPC"):PRINT R
```

Both callbacks must remain fixed and linear during the solve. This is left
preconditioning with ordinary restarted GMRES, not flexible GMRES; tolerance-driven
inner iterative solves are generally unsuitable because they can change the map.
Singular or poor preconditioners can cause breakdown/stagnation and are not
certified by the solver. Every convergence decision uses a fresh **original**
`b-A*x` residual, never just the preconditioned residual. Zero initial residual
or `maxiter=0` can return before invoking the preconditioner. All output components
must be finite. Operator and preconditioner calls share the 10,000-application
limit; both count toward solver vector work and cancellation checks. User callback
side effects are not undone after errors; destination assignment remains atomic.

`PERIODOGRAM(samples,sampleRate[,window])` returns
`{frequenciesHz,powerDensity}` for a nonempty real sample list. `sampleRate`
must be finite and positive. The optional real window must have the same length
and nonzero energy; omission uses a rectangular window. All samples and weights
must be finite. There is no implicit detrending, padding or sample selection.
For N samples, bins are `k*sampleRate/N`, with k from 0 through FLOOR(N/2).
Density is `ABS(FFT(samples*window))^2/(sampleRate*SUM(window^2))`;
interior bins are doubled to include negative-frequency power. DC and the
even-length Nyquist bin are not doubled. Units are squared sample units per Hz.
Thus `SUM(powerDensity)*sampleRate/N` gives the window-weighted mean square.
Use `HANN(N)`, `HAMMING(N)` or other existing windows explicitly when desired.
The Rust API is `NativeSignalMath::periodogram`, returning `NativePeriodogram`.
The same input/FFT work bounds and cancellation checks apply. Normalization
reduces intermediate overflow, but binary64 rounding, underflow and finite
output range still apply. This estimator does not identify pitch or capture audio.
Example: `PRINT PERIODOGRAM({2,2,2,2},8)` prints `{{0,2,4},{2,0,0}}`.

`FFT(list)` and `IFFT(list)` accept arbitrary positive lengths, including primes.
Power-of-two transforms use radix-2 FFT; other sizes use Bluestein convolution.
Forward sign is negative; inverse results are divided by the input length.
Inputs are real or complex. Input length is at most one million; padded scratch
length is at most 2,097,152 complex values, with a bounded transform work estimate.

The 3D functions use radians, row-major 4-by-4 matrices applied to column vectors,
a right-handed world, and camera forward along negative Z. These conventions
are separate from the older positive-Z point-perspective commands.

| Function | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `QUATAXIS({x,y,z},angle)` | Unit quaternion `{w,x,y,z}` from a nonzero axis and radians |
| `QUATMUL(q1,q2)` | Hamilton product; applies q2 then q1 for unit rotation quaternions |
| `QUATROTATE(q,{x,y,z})` | Rotate using the original quaternion and its exact squared norm |
| `QUATSLERP(q0,q1,t)` | Shortest-arc spherical interpolation of unit rotations; `0<=t<=1`, with normalized linear interpolation near coincident rotations |
| `ROTATE3D(q)` | Quaternion rotation as a 4-by-4 matrix |
| `TRANSLATE3D(x,y,z)`, `SCALE3D(x,y,z)` | Affine translation/scaling matrices |
| `LOOKAT(eye,target,up)` | View matrix; rejects coincident eye/target and parallel/zero up |
| `PERSPECTIVEMAT(fovY,aspect,near,far)` | Perspective projection; 0<fovY<PI, aspect>0, 0<near<far |
| `ORTHOGRAPHIC(left,right,bottom,top,near,far)` | Orthographic projection with ordered extents and 0<=near<far |
| `TRANSFORMPOINT(matrix,point)` | Apply homogeneous transform and divide by W; rejects W=0 |
| `TRANSFORMVECTOR(matrix,direction)` | Apply linear 3-by-3 part, excluding translation |
| `TRANSFORMCOMPOSE(left,right)` | Compose 4-by-4 transforms, right applied first |
| `TRANSFORMINVERSE(matrix)` | Invert a nonsingular 4-by-4 transform; exact-input singularity decision |

Projection maps the near/far planes to normalized depth -1/+1. See
`programs/examples/scientific_math.bas` for numerical examples.


### Sparse matrices and iterative linear systems

Sparse functions store only nonzero entries and operate on real binary64 data.
They accept ordinary BASIC lists and numeric DIM-array snapshots. All sparse
indices are **one-based**, independent of `OPTION BASE`. Fractional indices and
dimensions are rejected, rather than rounded. A matrix must have positive row
and column dimensions; an all-zero matrix is allowed.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `SPARSE(denseMatrix)` | Convert a rectangular real matrix to canonical compressed sparse row (CSR) storage. |
| `SPARSE(rows,columns,rowIndices,columnIndices,values)` | Assemble coordinate entries into CSR. All three lists must have equal lengths; empty lists produce a zero matrix of the requested shape. |
| `SPSHAPE(A)` | `{rows,columns}`. |
| `SPNNZ(A)` | Number of retained nonzero entries. |
| `SPDENSE(A)` | Convert to a nested real matrix, subject to the ordinary one-million-element dense limit. |
| `SPMV(A,x)` | Sparse matrix-vector product; `x` is a flat real vector with one element per column. |
| `SPQUAD(A,x)` | Quadratic form `xᵀAx` for a square CSR matrix and matching flat real vector. Uses every stored entry, without assuming symmetry or mirroring a triangle. Accumulates triple products exactly before one binary64 rounding; reports overflow if the final result is not finite. |
| `SPISPSD(A)` | Exactly test positive semidefiniteness of a real symmetric CSR matrix; -1 is proved true, 0 is proved false. Shape/symmetry errors and exhausted proof budgets raise errors. |
| `SPISNSD(A)` | Exactly test negative semidefiniteness, using the same rules and limits. |
| `SPTRANSPOSE(A)` | Canonical sparse transpose. |
| `SPKRON(A,B)` | Sparse Kronecker product `A ⊗ B`, returned as CSR without dense expansion. |
| `SPKRONSUM(A,B)` | Sparse Kronecker sum `A ⊗ I + I ⊗ B` for square CSR matrices, returned as CSR. |
| `SPCG(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,preconditioner$]]]]])` | Conjugate-gradient iteration for a symmetric positive-definite system; optional CPU IC(k), `k=0..8`, preconditioning. JACOBI remains the default. Returns `{solution,status$,iterations,residualNorm,threshold}`. |
| `SPGMRES(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,restart[,preconditioner$]]]]]])` | Restarted GMRES for a general square real sparse system. Returns the same five-element report as `SPCG`. |
| `SPBICGSTAB(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,preconditioner$]]]]])` | Short-recurrence BiCGSTAB for general square real sparse systems. Returns the same five-element report. |
| `SPMINRES(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,preconditioner$]]]]])` | Short-recurrence MINRES for exactly symmetric real sparse systems, including indefinite matrices. Options are NONE, symmetric JACOBI scaling, or positive incomplete Cholesky IC0 through IC8. Returns the same five-element report. |
| `SPLSQR(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,preconditioner$]]]])` | CPU LSQR for rectangular real sparse least-squares systems; optional `"COLUMN"` normalizes nonzero columns, `"NONE"` preserves the default. Returns `{solution,status$,iterations,residualNorm,normalResidualNorm,threshold}`. |
| `SPWLSQR(A,b,w[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,preconditioner$]]]])` | CPU LSQR for weighted rectangular sparse least squares. Finite nonnegative row weights cannot all be zero; zero-weight rows are excluded. Optional `"COLUMN"` scales nonzero columns. Returns `{solution,status$,iterations,normalizedResidualNorm,normalizedNormalResidualNorm,threshold,weightScale}`. |

Coordinate assembly sorts entries by row and column, combines duplicates using
exact accumulation of the supplied binary64 values, rounds each combined value
once, and removes zeros. An index must be valid even when its value is zero.
`SPKRON(A,B)` uses row-major Kronecker ordering and admits only results within
the existing 100000-axis, 250000-entry and 100-million-unit work bounds.
Nonfinite coefficient products raise an error and products underflowing to zero
are omitted. The resulting ordinary CSR record composes with `SPMV`, sparse
iterative solvers and sparse direct factors.
`SPKRONSUM(A,B)` requires square component matrices and assembles
`A ⊗ I + I ⊗ B` directly in canonical CSR. Overlapping diagonal entries are
coalesced with exact binary accumulation; dimension, entry and work limits apply
before and during assembly. The result composes directly with sparse solvers,
for example to build a multidimensional Laplacian without dense expansion.
The public CSR record is:

`{"CSR1",rows,columns,{rowPointers...},{columnIndices...},{values...}}`

`rowPointers` has `rows+1` elements. Its first element is 1, its last is
`SPNNZ(A)+1`, and adjacent equal pointers describe an empty row. Within each row,
columns must be strictly increasing and values nonzero. Every consumer validates
the entire record, including metadata queries. Records are ordinary BASIC values;
manual construction and copying are supported, but malformed edits raise errors.
`SPMV` accumulates products exactly before one binary64 rounding per output row,
including cases where separate products would overflow before cancellation.
A final unrepresentable value raises an error.

`SPCG` requires a square, exactly symmetric matrix with positive diagonal entries.
Symmetry compares stored binary64 values exactly, without silently changing the
operator. These checks do **not** prove positive definiteness; that is a caller
assumption. The optional final string selects `"JACOBI"` (default) or CPU
`"IC0"` through `"IC8"`. IC(k) retains entries whose symbolic level of fill is
at most k; IC(0) keeps the original lower pattern. It factors the diagonally
equilibrated operator and applies triangular solves in preconditioned CG. The
combined lower/upper factor storage is capped at one million entries and setup
and solves use the shared work budget. No pivoting is performed. Missing or
nonpositive incomplete pivots return an error; retry with `JACOBI` or reorder
the system. A successful factorization is not a proof of positive definiteness,
and more fill does not guarantee fewer CG iterations. Every candidate is
checked against the original system.
The iteration uses diagonal equilibration and a normalized residual
to reduce avoidable overflow and underflow. It solves for a correction to the
initial guess, which defaults to zero. Conjugate gradients and diagonal
preconditioning are described in the
[Netlib linear-system templates](https://www.netlib.org/linalg/old_html_templates/subsection2.6.3.1.html).

Defaults are `rtol=1E-8`, `atol=0`, and
`maxiter=MIN(10000,MAX(20,10*rows))`. Require `0<=rtol<1`, `atol>=0`, with at
least one positive tolerance. `maxiter` is an integer from 0 through 100000.
An initial guess must match `b`'s length. Zero iterations still validates the
matrix and computes the initial residual.

The stopping criterion is

`NORM(b-A*x) <= MAX(rtol*NORM(b),atol)`.

This follows the residual convention documented for
[SciPy CG](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.sparse.linalg.cg.html).
The reported residual is freshly computed on the original matrix and returned
solution, including `b` in the product accumulator before rounding. It is checked
at initialization and after every iteration; an internal recurrence alone never
establishes convergence. The recurrence restarts from the true residual every
64 iterations, or when its own squared residual rounds to zero. Each restart also
rebases the correction on the latest solution, so cancellation against a much
larger original guess does not repeatedly erase a smaller solution. Norms use scaling
to avoid intermediate squared-value overflow or underflow.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `"CONVERGED"` | The returned solution satisfies the computed residual criterion. This is not an exact-arithmetic proof, a forward-error guarantee or a certificate of positive definiteness. |
| `"MAXITER"` | The iteration limit was reached; the returned vector is an approximation whose residual exceeds the threshold. |
| `"BREAKDOWN"` | Nonpositive search curvature or a vanished working residual prevents continuation. The last completed approximation and its true residual are returned. This does not establish that the system is inconsistent. |

`iterations` counts completed updates. Check the status before treating the
vector as a solved system. Singular or indefinite systems may sometimes satisfy
the residual criterion; there is no completeness or convergence guarantee for
those inputs. Poor conditioning can make solution error large despite a small
residual. A tiny relative threshold may underflow to zero, requiring a computed
zero residual. Nonfinite arithmetic, unrepresentable matrix scaling, invalid
inputs, BREAK and exhausted work raise BASIC errors instead of returning a
success or a partial report.

Limits are 100000 rows or columns, 250000 input coordinate entries or stored
nonzeros, and a shared estimated 100-million-unit work budget per call. Sparse
multiplication, transpose, CG, GMRES and MINRES do not allocate `rows*columns` storage. Dense
conversion and dense input remain capped at one million elements. Sparse records,
input vectors and returned solutions also obey BASIC retained-storage limits.
This is a CPU sparse foundation; higher-fill levels above IC(8), pivoted
preconditioners, sparse matrix-matrix multiplication and sparse tensor autograd
remain future work.

```basic
10 A=SPARSE(3,3,{1,1,2,2,2,3,3},{1,2,1,2,3,2,3},{2,-1,-1,2,-1,-1,2})
20 PRINT SPNNZ(A)
30 R=SPCG(A,{1,0,1},1E-10,0,100,{},"IC1")
40 PRINT R(2);R(3);R(4);R(5)
50 IF R(2)="CONVERGED" THEN PRINT R(1)
```

The matrix has seven nonzeros and the solution is approximately `{1,1,1}`.
`programs/science/sparse_poisson.bas` assembles a two-dimensional five-point
Poisson system, solves 1024- and 4096-unknown grids, checks second-order grid
refinement, and exports the fine solution to CSV. The fine matrix would exceed
the dense limit. `tools/check-sparse-foundation.py` independently checks CSR,
products, solver residuals and solutions against Fraction arithmetic and SciPy,
including a 20000-unknown diagonal system and explicit nonconvergence cases.

### Nonsymmetric sparse linear systems

`SPGMRES(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,restart[,preconditioner$]]]]]])` solves a square real
system using restarted GMRES. Symmetry, positive diagonal and diagonal dominance
are not required. A singular consistent system may converge; convergence does
not prove uniqueness or a small forward error. Nonsingular systems can stagnate
with a short restart, and an inconsistent system need not be diagnosed as such.
The Arnoldi/GMRES method and restart limitations are described in the
[Netlib linear-system templates](https://netlib.org/templates/templates.html).

The first six arguments, defaults, tolerance rules, original-system stopping
criterion and five-element return record match `SPCG`. `maxiter` counts **total
Arnoldi steps**, including work across restarts, rather than restart cycles.
`restart` is an integer from 1 through 128. Its default is
`MIN(30,rows,FLOOR(2000000/rows)-1)`. The effective cycle width is the minimum of
`restart`, `rows` and `maxiter`. When iteration is needed, `(width+1)*rows` must
not exceed two million basis elements; a larger request raises an error before
basis allocation. An already-solved initial guess or `maxiter=0` needs no basis.
The existing sparse limits and shared 100-million-unit work budget still apply.

The optional final string selects `"ROW"` (default), `"NONE"`, or an ILU fill
level from `"ILU0"` through `"ILU8"`.
`ROW` divides each row by its largest absolute entry; an empty row has scale 1.
This left preconditioner permits zero and negative diagonal entries. `NONE`
leaves the operator unchanged. `ILU0` builds a zero-fill incomplete LU using the
input CSR pattern. `ILU1` through `ILU8` allow the corresponding maximum level
of symbolic fill; all ILU factors are capped at one million entries. They apply
forward/back substitutions on the left. All ILU modes require a stored diagonal
and nonzero pivots; none pivots numerically. A zero pivot, nonfinite factor,
factor-storage cap or exhausted work budget raises a BASIC error, so the caller
can retry with `ROW`, `NONE` or a reordered matrix. All setup/application work
uses the shared sparse budget. `ROW` scaling is
prepared lazily and reused across solves of a prepared implicit stage matrix.
Nonzero matrix entries that underflow under row scaling raise an error. The
working residual is normalized, and Arnoldi uses two modified Gram–Schmidt
passes with exact-accumulation dot products. Givens rotations and triangular
substitution produce a candidate at every iteration. The reported residual is
freshly computed from the **original** stored `A`, `b` and candidate; a small
projected or preconditioned residual cannot establish success. Original residuals
need not decrease monotonically under left preconditioning.

Every restart rebases the correction on the latest candidate. Near-zero Arnoldi
vectors trigger a true-residual restart if further correction is possible.
`"CONVERGED"` and `"MAXITER"` have the same meaning as for `SPCG`.
`"BREAKDOWN"` means the working system cannot produce a usable next correction;
`"STAGNATED"` means a completed restart cycle leaves the candidate unchanged.
Both return the latest completed candidate and its original residual above the
threshold. Neither proves inconsistency. A failure encountered while constructing
an Arnoldi step still counts that step. If the iteration limit is reached after
a candidate update, `"MAXITER"` takes precedence over stagnation. Arithmetic,
shape, storage, work-limit and BREAK failures raise BASIC errors.

```basic
10 A=SPARSE({{4,2},{-1,3}})
20 R=SPGMRES(A,{2,-4},1E-12,0,100,{0,0},2,"ILU0")
30 PRINT R(2);R(3);R(4);R(5)
40 IF R(2)="CONVERGED" THEN PRINT R(1)
```

The solution is approximately `{1,-1}`. `tools/check-gmres-foundation.py` compares
solutions against SciPy direct and GMRES solves, recomputes original residuals
with exact rational arithmetic, checks common and independent row scales,
restarts, singular systems, nonconvergence, arrays and bounded sparse storage.

### Nonsymmetric short-recurrence sparse systems

`SPBICGSTAB(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,preconditioner$]]]]])` solves a
general square real sparse system with CPU BiCGSTAB. It does not require
symmetry or a positive diagonal and uses O(rows) iteration vectors instead of
a growing Krylov basis. The five-element result has the same layout and
original-residual stopping rule as `SPCG`: `{solution,status$,iterations,
residualNorm,threshold}`. `CONVERGED` requires a freshly computed residual of
the original matrix and RHS; `MAXITER` and `BREAKDOWN` return the latest
completed candidate and do not prove inconsistency or uniqueness. BiCGSTAB can
break down on a nonsingular system when its shadow residual becomes orthogonal
to a required search direction; retry with GMRES or another ordering when that
occurs.

The defaults and tolerance rules match `SPCG`; `maxiter` is a total iteration
limit from 0 through 100000. `preconditioner$` is `ROW` by default, `NONE`, or
`ILU0` through `ILU8`. These use the shared bounded row equilibration and left
incomplete-LU factors from `SPGMRES`; ILU setup has the same one-million-entry
cap, stored-diagonal requirement and explicit zero-pivot errors. Every candidate
is checked against the unscaled original system. The shared 100-million-unit
work/cancellation budget applies. A finite residual is not a forward-error or
conditioning guarantee, and the method currently does not pivot its ILU
factors.

### Symmetric-indefinite sparse systems

`SPMINRES(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,initial[,preconditioner$]]]]])` solves real square systems
whose stored matrix is exactly symmetric. Unlike `SPCG`, it accepts indefinite
and singular matrices; consistent singular systems may converge, while an
inconsistent system returns its best completed candidate and a residual above
the threshold. `BREAKDOWN` does not prove inconsistency. This CPU implementation
uses the short MINRES recurrence and O(rows) working vectors, with no dense
conversion. `preconditioner$` is `NONE` by default, `JACOBI` for symmetric
diagonal scaling by the inverse square root of each absolute diagonal entry, or
`IC0` through `IC8` for positive incomplete-Cholesky factors with bounded
symbolic fill. JACOBI requires each diagonal entry to be stored and nonzero.
Incomplete Cholesky requires positive stored diagonals and a positive factor at
every pivot; it can fail for indefinite matrices, even though unpreconditioned
MINRES accepts them. Its lower and upper factors share the one-million-entry
limit. A symmetric but ill-conditioned system can still converge slowly or
return `MAXITER`.

The tolerance, initial-guess and five-element result rules match `SPCG`.
Convergence is decided from a freshly computed residual of the original matrix
and right-hand side at every iteration. Matrix and residual scaling protect the
recurrence from common extreme magnitudes; unrepresentable arithmetic or
nonzero matrix coefficients lost to scaling underflow raise an error. The same
250000-entry, 100000-dimension and 100-million-unit per-call work/cancellation
limits apply. `tools/check-sparse-foundation.py` compares indefinite tridiagonal
systems through 513 unknowns with SciPy MINRES and sparse direct solves and
independently recomputes residuals from exact binary64 rationals. A separately
scaled indefinite system exercises JACOBI against SciPy MINRES on the explicit
symmetric scaling transformation.

### Rectangular sparse least squares

`SPLSQR(A,b[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,preconditioner$]]]])` solves the real sparse least-squares
problem `minimize ||b-Ax||₂` for rectangular CSR matrices. The solver uses CPU
Golub-Kahan LSQR, starts from zero and therefore targets the minimum-norm
least-squares solution for underdetermined and rank-deficient systems in exact
arithmetic. It does not form `AᵀA` or convert the operator to a dense matrix.

The six-element result is `{solution,status$,iterations,residualNorm,
normalResidualNorm,threshold}`. `residualNorm` is `||b-Ax||₂` and may remain
positive for an inconsistent fit. By default, `normalResidualNorm` is
`||Aᵀ(b-Ax)||₂`; with `"COLUMN"` scaling it is the scaled stationarity norm
`||D Aᵀ(b-Ax)||₂`, where `D` normalizes nonzero columns. `CONVERGED` requires
this freshly recomputed quantity to be no larger than the matching
`max(rtol*||D Aᵀb||₂,atol)` threshold (with `D=I` by default). `MAXITER` and
`BREAKDOWN` return the best candidate and do not prove uniqueness or
inconsistency. In `"COLUMN"` mode, each stationarity component must also meet
its own relative/absolute tolerance, with a binary64 roundoff floor based on
the initial gradient norm; this prevents a large column from hiding an
unresolved small column. A stationary point may
be non-unique when the matrix is rank deficient; zero initialization selects
the minimum-norm Krylov solution subject to finite precision.

The default relative tolerance is `1E-8`, the default absolute tolerance is
zero, and the default iteration cap is `clamp(10*max(rows,columns),20,10000)`.
Callers may set at most 100,000 iterations. The same 100,000-axis, 250,000-entry
and 100-million-unit shared work/cancellation limits as the other sparse
kernels apply. Optional `"COLUMN"` scaling (or explicit `"NONE"`) normalizes each nonzero column by
its 2-norm and can improve convergence when column magnitudes differ. Because
this is a right change of variables, it can change the selected minimum-norm
solution for rank-deficient or underdetermined systems; omit it when ordinary
Euclidean minimum norm is required. Zero columns remain zero, and scaling that
would underflow a stored coefficient is rejected. Rust callers can use
`NativeCsrMatrix::lsqr(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations)` for the default or
`lsqr_with_preconditioner(...,NativeLsqrPreconditioner::ColumnNorm)` and receive
a typed report with the original fit residual and mode-specific stationarity
norm. Both use the original matrix; column scaling applies `D` only to the
normal residual used as its stopping test.

SPWLSQR(A,b,w[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter[,preconditioner$]]]]) minimizes
sum(wᵢ(bᵢ-Aᵢx)²) without densifying the CSR matrix. Weights must be finite,
nonnegative and not all zero; a zero-weight row is omitted from the weighted
operator. Rows use sqrt(wᵢ)/sqrt(max(w)) scaling so a common large or tiny
weight factor does not overflow or cause premature ratio underflow. Its
seven-element result is {solution,status$,iterations,normalizedResidualNorm,
normalizedNormalResidualNorm,threshold,weightScale}. Both residual norms and
the convergence threshold use normalized weights; multiply the fit norm by
sqrt(weightScale) and the normal-residual norm by weightScale to recover their
original weighted units. A stored coefficient that underflows during row
scaling is rejected rather than silently removed. The optional COLUMN
preconditioner is applied to the weighted operator and has the same
minimum-norm caveat as SPLSQR(...,COLUMN).

### Sparse implicit transport, diffusion and linear damping

`SPBEULER(K,source,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter]]])`
integrates the constant linear system `u' = source - K*u` using backward Euler.
`K` is a canonical sparse matrix; `source` and `state` are flat real vectors with
matching lengths. Array snapshots work. Forward time only: `finish>=start` and
`maxstep>0`. All numbers and the time span must be finite. Equal endpoints return
the initial row and no diagnostics, after validating all inputs.

The operator must be square and satisfy
`K(i,i) >= SUM(ABS(K(i,j)), j<>i)` in every row. Missing diagonal entries are zero.
Exact binary64 summation checks these inequalities without a tolerance. This is
a sufficient dissipativity condition in the infinity norm and permits zero
matrices, nonsymmetric upwind transport, diffusion and conserved modes. With
symmetry it also implies positive semidefiniteness. Operators without this row
dominance are rejected, even if another stability condition holds. There
is no automatic boundary condition, grid assembly, mass matrix or unit conversion;
assemble `K` and any constant boundary forcing in BASIC.

For each actual positive interval `h`, solve

`(I+h*K)*u_next = u_previous + h*source`.

The diagonal and forcing sums use exact product accumulation before binary64
rounding. The rounded shifted operator must remain **strictly** row diagonally
dominant; loss of the identity shift at extreme scales raises an error. Nonzero
off-diagonal coefficients that underflow during scaling also raise errors.
The previous state is the initial linear-solver guess. Exactly symmetric shifted
matrices use `SPCG`; others use `SPGMRES` with its default restart width. The
prepared operator and preconditioner are reused for consecutive steps with exactly the same `h`.
Every accepted step passes a freshly computed residual check on its rounded
linear system. `MAXITER`, `BREAKDOWN`, `STAGNATED`, nonfinite arithmetic, invalid input,
unrepresentable time increments, BREAK and exhausted limits raise BASIC errors;
no partial trajectory is returned as a successful integration.

The return value is `{trajectory,diagnostics}`:

| Element | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `trajectory` | Rows `{time,state1,...}` including the initial row and every completed step; the final time equals `finish`. |
| `diagnostics` | One row `{iterations,residualNorm,threshold}` per step, corresponding to trajectory row `step+1`. Every residual is at most its threshold. |

Defaults are `rtol=1E-10`, `atol=1E-12` and the same per-solve iteration limit as
`SPCG`. Tolerances and `maxiter` have the same validity rules as `SPCG` and apply
to the **linear solve**, using `MAX(rtol*NORM(rhs),atol)`. They do not estimate
time-discretization error. Steps are at most `maxstep` apart from floating-point
roundoff, with a shortened final interval. The operator always uses the difference
between the returned consecutive times. A final roundoff-sized remainder is
folded into the last step. A call is limited to 100000 steps and one million
numeric elements **combined** across trajectory and diagnostics. The sparse
100-million-unit work budget is shared across all assembly, preparation and
solves, and ordinary BASIC storage limits still apply. No dense matrix is built.

Backward Euler is first order in time. For this dissipative operator class it
damps stiff modes without the explicit Euler stability step restriction in exact
arithmetic; finite precision and inexact solves still require validation.
Refine `maxstep` to assess accuracy and separately refine the spatial grid.
The method and heat-equation stability analysis are described in the
[University of Illinois time-dependent PDE notes](https://fischerp.cs.illinois.edu/cs598/docs/notes_time1b.pdf).

```basic
10 K=SPARSE({{2,-1},{-1,2}})
20 R=SPBEULER(K,{0,0},0,{1,2},1,.125,1E-11,1E-13)
30 PATHDATA=R(1):SOLVES=R(2)
40 PRINT PATHDATA(LEN(PATHDATA)):PRINT SOLVES
```

`programs/science/implicit_heat.bas` evolves a 511-component heat model with slow
and fast sine modes, checks first-order time refinement against the semidiscrete
analytic solution, and exports CSV. Its coarse time step is 8192 times the usual
forward Euler grid stability bound. `tools/check-implicit-foundation.py` compares
steps against SciPy sparse direct solves, recomputes residuals with Fraction,
checks conserved modes, stiff decay, forcing and failures, and runs the example.
This solver does not implement nonlinear or time-dependent operators/forcing,
adaptive time-error control, general non-row-dominant stiff systems, events, dense
interpolation, or higher-order implicit methods.

### Adaptive sparse implicit integration

`SPBESOLVE(K,source,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter]]])`
integrates the same constant `u'=source-K*u` systems and requires the same
weakly row-diagonally-dominant, nonnegative-diagonal operator class as `SPBEULER`.
It adapts time steps by comparing one full backward-Euler step with two half
steps. Only the two-half-step state is accepted; there is no extrapolation.
The method remains first order. All three linear systems must converge before
the temporal estimate is considered. A linear failure raises an error instead
of being treated as a rejected time step.

Here `rtol` and `atol` are **temporal** tolerances. Defaults are `1E-4` and `1E-7`;
require `0<=rtol<1` and `atol>0`. `maxiter` is a per-linear-solve integer from 0
through 100000, with the same default as `SPCG`. `maxstep` must be positive and
`finish>=start`; equal endpoints validate all arguments and return the initial
row with empty diagnostics and zero counters. Every state and forcing component,
time, tolerance and time span must be finite. Tolerances are scalar; scale mixed
physical units and widely differing component magnitudes before integration.

The return value is `{trajectory,diagnostics,summary}`:

| Element | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `trajectory` | Rows `{time,state1,...}` for the initial state and each accepted endpoint. The final time equals `finish`. Rejected trial states are discarded. |
| `diagnostics` | One row `{midpoint,errorRatio,coarseSolve,firstHalfSolve,secondHalfSolve}` per accepted interval. Each solve record is `{iterations,residualNorm,threshold}`. `errorRatio` is between 0 and 1, and every residual is at most its threshold. |
| `summary` | `{acceptedSteps,rejectedTrials,linearSolves,totalIterations}`. Counts include all completed trials, including rejected ones; `linearSolves=3*(acceptedSteps+rejectedTrials)`. |

The midpoint must be representable strictly between the interval's endpoints.
The matrices use the actual intervals `h=next-time`, `h1=midpoint-time` and
`h2=next-midpoint`. The local estimate uses
`weight=(h1/h2+h2/h1)/2`, which is 1 for equal halves. This accounts for unequal
halves caused by time-coordinate rounding. Per component, the acceptance ratio is

`weight*(ABS(fine-coarse)+linearAllowance) / (atol+rtol*MAX(ABS(old),ABS(fine)))`.

The maximum component ratio must be at most 1. The controller multiplies the
actual interval by `CLAMP(.9/SQRT(errorRatio),.1,2)`, or by 2 when the ratio is
zero, then caps it at `maxstep`. A rejected interval leaves time and state
unchanged. Endpoint adjustments may exceed `maxstep` by floating-point roundoff.
An unrepresentable increment or midpoint, or a rejected interval that cannot
shrink at the current time resolution, raises an error. Local-error estimation
and the first-order square-root controller follow the principles in
[NTNU's numerical ODE notes, section 3.4](https://www.math.ntnu.no/emner/TMA4320/2024v/notater/NumODE1.pdf).

Linear residuals have a separate budget. For each rounded matrix `A=I+h*K`, let
`margin` be half the smallest exact-sum row-dominance margin, rounded to binary64.
It must be positive. The CG or GMRES solve uses relative tolerance zero and absolute
threshold `.01*minimumOldScale*MIN(margin,1)`, where
`minimumOldScale=MIN_i(atol+rtol*ABS(old_i))` uses the state at the beginning of
the **whole trial**, for all three solves. This keeps large components from
hiding inaccurate small components. Threshold underflow requires a computed
zero residual. Each solve's residual allowance is `residualNorm/margin`.
`linearAllowance` adds the coarse and second-half allowances plus the first-half
allowance divided by the second-half margin, accounting for its propagation.
This uses the inverse-norm estimate from strict diagonal dominance; all reported
quantities remain floating-point estimates, not interval-arithmetic certificates.

The returned ratio is a **local error estimate**, not a bound on accumulated
global error. It does not certify model accuracy, spatial discretization,
matrix/RHS rounding or unresolved behavior between output points. Check tighter
tolerances and spatial refinement against analytical or independent references.
The trajectory has irregular times and provides no dense interpolation or events.

Limits are 100000 trials (accepted plus rejected), one million numeric elements
combined across trajectory, nested diagnostics and counters, and the shared
100-million-unit sparse work budget across all trials and solves. At most three
prepared sparse operators are cached. Ordinary BASIC retained-storage limits
also apply. Resource exhaustion, invalid input, nonfinite arithmetic, BREAK and
linear failures return errors with no successful partial trajectory.

```basic
10 K=SPARSE({{1,0},{0,1000}})
20 R=SPBESOLVE(K,{0,0},0,{1,1},1,.25,1E-4,1E-7)
30 PATHDATA=R(1):PRINT PATHDATA(LEN(PATHDATA)):PRINT R(3)
```

`programs/science/adaptive_heat.bas` follows slow and fast heat modes, checks
tolerance refinement and exports the center-point trajectory and local ratios.
`tools/check-adaptive-foundation.py` compares accepted steps with SciPy sparse
direct solves, analytical solutions, matrix exponentials and Radau trajectories;
selected trials are replayed with `SPBEULER` and independently checked with exact
Fraction residuals. Nonlinear systems, operators without the required row
dominance, variable operators or forcing, mass matrices, higher-order methods
and GPU execution remain outside
this solver's scope.

### Second-order sparse implicit integration

`SPSDIRK2(K,source,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter]]])`
and `SPSDIRKSOLVE(K,source,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol[,maxiter]]])`
integrate `u'=source(t)-K(t)*u` using the two-stage, second-order SDIRK method
that is L-stable for constant-coefficient scalar decay. They require the same
weakly row-diagonally-dominant, nonnegative-diagonal `K` as `SPBEULER`; state and source are real lists or array
snapshots. Either `K` or `source` may instead name a one-argument `DEF FN`
of time, as described below. The method is described in [MOOSE's LStableDirk2 documentation](https://mooseframework.inl.gov/source/timeintegrators/LStableDirk2.html),
which cites Alexander (1977). Constant `K` lets both stages share a sparse
shifted operator; variable `K(t)` requires distinct stage matrices. Both stages
use residual-checked CG for exactly symmetric shifted matrices, or GMRES otherwise.
Every linear solve must converge.

With `gamma=1-1/SQRT(2)`, `beta=(1-gamma)/gamma`, actual interval `h`,
rounded stage interval `s=gamma*h`, `A1=I+s*K(start+s)` and
`A2=I+s*K(nextTime)`, the implementation solves

```text
A1*stage = old + s*source(start+s)
A2*next  = (1-beta)*old + beta*stage + s*source(nextTime)
```

The initial guesses are `old` and `stage`, respectively. Eliminating the explicit
`K*stage` product avoids forming large intermediate derivatives. Matrix diagonals
and RHS products are accumulated exactly before rounding to binary64. Each
rounded shifted matrix must retain strict row dominance. An underflowed stage
interval or nonzero off-diagonal entry is an error.

A list source supplies the same vector at both stages. A time-dependent source
is a compact function-name string, case-insensitive with surrounding whitespace
ignored, for example `"FNDRIVE"`:

```basic
10 DEF FNDRIVE(T)={COS(T)+2*SIN(T)}
20 R=SPSDIRKSOLVE(SPARSE({{2}}),"FNDRIVE",0,{0},1,.1,1E-5,1E-8)
30 P=R(1):PRINT P(LEN(P)):REM EXACT SOLUTION IS SIN(T)
```

Define the function before the solver call. It must take exactly one scalar time
argument and return a flat list of exactly one finite real value per state
component, even for a one-component system. Arrays and read-only model parameters
are available in the function body; its time parameter temporarily shadows any
caller variable of the same name. The source receives no trial state, so this
API does not implement state-dependent nonlinear forcing.

Use a deterministic function of time and fixed model data. Sampling order includes
rejected trials: two source evaluations per fixed step, and six per completed
adaptive trial (coarse step, first half, second half; stage then endpoint for each).
Samples are recomputed without caching. Avoid random numbers, wall-clock values
and side effects in the source; otherwise retries do not represent the same
ODE. The returned counters and diagnostic structure are unchanged, so total
source samples equal the number of linear solves on a successful callback call.

The first-stage time is the binary64 sum `start+gamma*h`, using each actual
full/half interval. It must lie strictly inside that interval. Its collapse onto
an endpoint raises an error if either coefficient is a function; calls with
constant matrix and source data do not require an absolute stage time. The second stage samples the exact step endpoint.
Callback shape/type/domain errors and nonfinite values stop the call with no
successful partial trajectory. Zero-duration calls validate the function name
and its one-argument signature without evaluating its body.

Source samples share the sparse work budget, with an additional maximum of
600000 evaluations per call. BASIC's existing expression, recursion and storage
limits also apply to the function body; sample counts do not measure arbitrary
work inside that body. Choose `maxstep` to resolve the source and split integration
at known discontinuities. Local sampling can miss narrow pulses or rapidly
oscillating forcing. Smooth, resolved forcing is needed for second-order
convergence; very stiff forcing problems can show order reduction, so verify
time refinement rather than relying only on the nominal method order.

A time-dependent `K` function must return a canonical `SPARSE(...)` matrix with
the same square dimension as the initial state. Each sampled matrix is checked
for nonnegative diagonal and weak row diagonal dominance; each
rounded shifted stage matrix must retain strict dominance. The sparsity pattern
may change. Dense numeric lists are not implicitly converted to sparse matrices.

```basic
10 DEF FNK(T)=SPARSE({{1+T}})
20 R=SPSDIRKSOLVE("FNK",{0},0,{1},1,.1,1E-5,1E-8)
30 P=R(1):PRINT P(LEN(P)):REM EXACT SOLUTION IS EXP(-T-T^2/2)
```

A variable operator is sampled and its shifted linear system rebuilt at **every
stage**, even for equal step lengths or repeated endpoint times. Only the current
stage's prepared system is retained; constant operators keep their existing
three-entry cache. This avoids reusing coefficients from an earlier time. Source
and operator callbacks are called in that order at each stage. Each supplied
callback has at most 600000 direct evaluations per call and, on successful calls,
its direct sample count equals `linearSolves`. Extra function calls made inside a
callback body are governed by the existing BASIC limits, not this direct count.
Matrix parsing, dominance checks, solver selection and preparation share the sparse work
budget. An invalid later stage stops the entire integration.

The operator callback receives time alone. Its signature is checked for an empty
interval, but its body and matrix shape are checked only when sampled. Use
nonempty finite initial state data to define its dimension. Function names,
parameter scoping, deterministic-callback requirements, representable stage times
and failure behavior follow the source rules above. Both callbacks may be used
in one call; for example a source can use `SPMV(FNK(T),knownState)` to construct a
problem with a known solution.

Changing coefficients need independent time refinement. Positive-semidefinite
matrices at sampled times do **not** give this method unconditional norm decay
for arbitrary time variation. For example, one fixed step of length 1 on
`u'=-10000*(1-t)*u`, starting at 1, overshoots below -1 although the exact solution
decays. Adaptive error comparison rejects that coarse trial in the qualification
case. This is not a general stability certificate. Resolve coefficient variation,
split at known discontinuities, and check invariants and tighter tolerances.
Unsampled matrices and forcing cannot be certified by stage sampling.
A nonsymmetric operator can grow in Euclidean norm even when the exact
homogeneous evolution is contractive in the infinity norm. Do not apply symmetric
energy-decay assumptions to transport or other nonnormal systems. The adaptive
linear allowances still use strict row dominance: `NORM_INFTY(A^-1)` is bounded
by the reciprocal minimum row margin, and the reported Euclidean residual bounds
its infinity norm. Both stage margins and all existing propagation factors remain
in the acceptance calculation.

`programs/science/advection_diffusion.bas` assembles periodic upwind transport
and centered diffusion, checks second-order time refinement and tighter adaptive
tolerances against semidiscrete Fourier modes, and exports a mass-checked CSV.
`tools/check-gmres-foundation.py` also checks nonsymmetric fixed/adaptive BE,
noncommuting variable SDIRK operators, stage solver switching, exact residual
replays and an independent stiff Radau reference. General non-row-dominant stiff
systems, nonlinear state dependence and stronger preconditioners remain future work.

For scalar decay `u'=-lambda*u`, the exact-arithmetic amplification is
`(1+(2*gamma-1)*x)/(1+gamma*x)^2`, where `x=h*lambda`. Its magnitude tends to zero
as `x` grows, damping unresolved stiff modes. **Positivity is not guaranteed**:
large steps can give negative values from positive initial values. Use temporal
refinement and check physical constraints. Second order describes the convergence
rate on resolved smooth solutions; it does not make a large step accurate.

**Fixed steps.** `SPSDIRK2` caps each step at `maxstep` and shortens the final
interval to reach `finish` exactly. `rtol` and `atol` are **linear residual**
tolerances, defaulting to `1E-10` and `1E-12`, with the same validation and
per-solve `maxiter` as `SPCG`. They do not control temporal error.
The result is `{trajectory,diagnostics}`. Trajectory rows are `{time,state1,...}`.
Each diagnostic row is `{stage1Solve,stage2Solve}`, and each solve record is
`{iterations,residualNorm,threshold}`. Halving `maxstep` should reduce the time
error by approximately four once the solution is resolved and linear/rounding
errors are small.

**Adaptive steps.** `SPSDIRKSOLVE` compares one full SDIRK2 step with two half
steps, requiring **six linear solves per trial**. It accepts the two-half-step
state without extrapolation. `rtol` and `atol` are **temporal** tolerances,
defaulting to `1E-5` and `1E-8`; require `0<=rtol<1` and `atol>0`.
The result is `{trajectory,diagnostics,summary}`:

| Element | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `trajectory` | Initial row and accepted endpoint rows `{time,state1,...}`. |
| `diagnostics` | Accepted interval records `{midpoint,errorRatio,coarseStep,firstHalfStep,secondHalfStep}`. Each step contains `{stage1Solve,stage2Solve}`; each solve is `{iterations,residualNorm,threshold}`. |
| `summary` | `{acceptedSteps,rejectedTrials,linearSolves,totalIterations}`, including rejected work. `linearSolves=6*(acceptedSteps+rejectedTrials)`. |

As with `SPBESOLVE`, the recorded midpoint must lie strictly between the endpoints.
For actual half intervals `h1` and `h2`, the second-order estimator weight is
`(h1/h2+h2/h1-1)/3`, equal to `1/3` for equal halves. The acceptance ratio is

`MAX_i(weight*(ABS(fine_i-coarse_i)+linearAllowance)/(atol+rtol*MAX(ABS(old_i),ABS(fine_i))))`.

Accept only a ratio at most 1. The next interval uses the factor
`CLAMP(.9/errorRatio^(1/3),.1,2)`, or 2 for a zero ratio, capped at `maxstep`.
Rejected trials preserve time and state. A rejected interval that cannot shrink
at the current time resolution raises an error.

Let `m1,m2` be half the smallest exact-sum row-dominance margins of rounded
`A1,A2`, rounded to binary64. Each stage uses its own margin `m`, linear-solver relative
tolerance zero and absolute threshold `.001*minimumOldScale*MIN(m,1)`, where
`minimumOldScale=MIN_i(atol+rtol*ABS(old_i))` uses the state at the start of the
**whole trial**, for all six solves. For stage residual norms `r1,r2`, one method
step has residual allowance `r2/m2 + beta*(r1/m1)/m2`. Its propagation estimate is
`(ABS(1-beta)+beta/m1)/m2`. Constant matrices have `m1=m2`. The trial's `linearAllowance` sums the coarse and
second-half allowances plus the first-half allowance times the second-half
propagation estimate. This accounts for first-stage errors entering the second
stage and first-half errors entering the second half. These are floating-point
estimates, not interval certificates; matrix/RHS rounding is excluded.

Both functions require finite inputs, positive `maxstep` and `finish>=start`.
Equal endpoints still validate inputs and return the initial row, empty
diagnostics and, for the adaptive method, zero counters. Limits are 100000 state
components, 250000 public matrix nonzeros, 100000 fixed steps or adaptive trials,
one million numbers across the entire result, and a shared 100-million-unit
sparse work budget. At most three systems are cached for constant `K`, or one
current-stage system for variable `K(t)`. BASIC storage limits also apply. Linear failures, invalid inputs, nonfinite arithmetic,
unrepresentable stages/times, BREAK and resource exhaustion raise errors with
no successful partial trajectory.

```basic
10 K=SPARSE({{1,0},{0,1000}})
20 R=SPSDIRKSOLVE(K,{0,0},0,{1,1},1,.25,1E-5,1E-8)
30 PATHDATA=R(1):PRINT PATHDATA(LEN(PATHDATA)):PRINT R(3)
```

`programs/science/sdirk_heat.bas` checks fixed-step and tolerance refinement for
a heat equation with slow and fast modes, and exports `sdirk-heat.csv`.
`tools/check-sdirk-foundation.py` checks independent SciPy stage solves,
exact-rational residual replays of both stages, analytical amplification,
second-order refinement, Radau and matrix-exponential references, conservation,
large sparse states, and failure behavior.

Local-error estimates do not bound accumulated global error, spatial/model error,
rounding or unresolved behavior between samples. Nonlinear or non-row-dominant stiff
systems, state-dependent operators, mass matrices, events, dense output,
methods above order two and GPU execution remain unfinished.

`programs/science/forced_heat.bas` uses a `DEF FN` source to drive a heat equation
with a slow oscillation and fast transient. It checks time/tolerance refinement
and writes `forced-heat.csv`. `tools/check-time-source-foundation.py` compares
manufactured coupled solutions, independently assembled SciPy stages, both-stage
Fraction residual replays and stiff Radau trajectories. It also checks exact
constant-source compatibility, rejected-trial timing, large sparse states and
malformed callbacks.

`programs/science/variable_heat.bas` uses a sparse operator callback for a heat
equation whose diffusion coefficient is `1+t`, checks time/tolerance refinement,
and writes `variable-heat.csv`. `tools/check-time-operator-foundation.py` checks
noncommuting coupled matrix paths, both-stage residual replays, variable stiff
Radau references, changing sparsity, conservation, invalid later stages and exact
constant-callback compatibility.

### CPU physics and differential equations

Physics models are programmable BASIC equations, not a fixed list of simulated
objects. `DEF FN` now accepts and returns numeric lists (including nested lists)
as well as scalars; parameters shadow caller variables without changing them.
The physics callbacks below use a **flat, nonempty real state vector** and a
compact function name string. Define the function before calling the solver:

```basic
10 DEF FN MOTION(TT,YY)={YY(2),-YY(1)-.1*YY(2)}
20 PATHDATA=ODESOLVE("FNMOTION",0,{1,0},10,.05,1E-8,1E-10)
30 LASTROW=LEN(PATHDATA):PRINT PATHDATA(LASTROW)
```

| Function | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `DAEINIT(fn,differentialCount,time,guess[,rtol[,atol]])` | Explicit index-one consistent-state initialization. Holds the supplied differential values fixed and solves for algebraic states at the supplied time. Returns one state vector; defaults `rtol=1E-10`, `atol=1E-12`. |
| `DAESTEP(fn,differentialCount,time,state,step[,rtol[,atol]])` | Semi-explicit index-one backward Euler. Callback returns differential RHS values first, then algebraic constraint residuals. Requires consistent initial constraints. Defaults `rtol=1E-10`, `atol=1E-12`; returns one state vector. |
| `DAESOLVE(fn,differentialCount,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol]])` | Adaptive first-order DAE trajectory with step doubling, returning `{time,state1,...}` rows. Defaults `rtol=1E-5`, `atol=1E-8`. Positive maximum step; reverse/equal endpoints supported. |
| `ODEEVENT(fn$,event$,start,state,finish,maxstep[,direction[,rtol[,atol[,timetol[,tangenttol[,eventscan[,eventdepth]]]]]]])` | Adaptive RK4 with a terminal scalar event returned by a second `DEF FN(time,state)` as a **one-element list**. Returns `{trajectory,found}`; `found=-1` means stopped at an event, `0` means reached finish. A positive `tangenttol` opts into bounded tangency search for direction 0. `eventscan` samples each accepted step at 1–256 equal intervals (default 1); `eventdepth` bisects each scan interval 0–8 additional levels (default 0), stopping at the first detected crossing. |
| `IMPLICITEVENT(fn$,event$,start,state,finish,maxstep[,direction[,rtol[,atol[,timetol[,tangenttol[,eventscan[,eventdepth]]]]]]])` | Same event contract using adaptive nonlinear backward Euler, at most 64 dense/numerical states or 4,096 with CSR1. Defaults and local accuracy limitations follow `IMPLICITSOLVE`; optional tangency search operates on the linear dense interpolant. `eventscan` and `eventdepth` have the same bounded sampling behavior. |
| `ODEEVENTS(fn$,events$,start,state,finish,maxstep[,directions[,rtol[,atol[,timetol[,tangenttol[,eventscan[,eventdepth]]]]]]])` | Adaptive RK4 with 1–64 simultaneous event functions returned as one real list. Nonterminal crossings and opt-in tangencies are recorded while integration continues. Returns `{trajectory,eventRecords}`, each record `{time,eventIndex,state...}`. `eventscan` and `eventdepth` refine each accepted step to reveal multiple crossings inside it. |
| `IMPLICITEVENTS(fn$,events$,start,state,finish,maxstep[,directions[,rtol[,atol[,timetol[,tangenttol[,eventscan[,eventdepth]]]]]]])` | Same nonterminal vector-event contract using adaptive nonlinear backward Euler. Supports at most 64 dense/numerical states or 4,096 with CSR1 and uses the solver's linear dense interpolant. `eventscan` and `eventdepth` have the same bounded sampling behavior. |
| `ODEHYBRID(fn$,event$,reset$,start,state,finish,maxstep[,direction[,rtol[,atol[,timetol[,tangenttol[,eventscan[,maxevents[,eventdepth]]]]]]]])` | CPU adaptive RK4 with one scalar guard callback and a BASIC reset callback. Stops each segment at a localized event, applies the reset to the state, then continues to `finish`. Returns `{trajectory,eventRecords}`; each event record is `{time,preState...,postState...}`, and the trajectory contains both phase states at the event time. Defaults `maxevents` to 1000 (maximum 10000). |
| `IMPLICITHYBRID(fn$,event$,reset$,start,state,finish,maxstep[,direction[,rtol[,atol[,timetol[,tangenttol[,eventscan[,maxevents[,eventdepth]]]]]]]])` | Same bounded hybrid contract using adaptive nonlinear backward Euler, including optional analytic dense/CSR1 Jacobians and linear dense-output localization. |
| `IMPLICITSOLVE(fn$,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol]])` | Adaptive nonlinear backward Euler using one full and two half steps. Returns `{time,state1,...}` rows at the initial, final and accepted intermediate times, with the two-half-step state. Up to 64 dense/numerical components or 4,096 with CSR1; positive `maxstep`; reverse/equal endpoints supported. Defaults `rtol=1E-5`, `atol=1E-8`. Local error estimates do not bound global trajectory error. |
| `IMPLICITSTEP(fn$,time,state,step[,rtol[,atol]])` | Nonlinear backward Euler: solves `z=state+step*F(time+step,z)`, returning one state vector. Signed nonzero step; at most 64 dense/numerical components or 4,096 with CSR1. Newton with shared adaptive numerical, dense analytic or sparse analytic Jacobians and backtracking; defaults `rtol=1E-10`, `atol=1E-12` bound the equation residual, **not time-integration error**. First order; no adaptive steps or event detection. Nonconvergence/singular Jacobians are errors; reduce the step or rescale. |
| `RK4STEP(fn$,time,state,step)` | Classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta; returns the state after one signed, nonzero step. Callback `FN...(time,state)` returns `dstate/dtime`. No error estimate or stability guarantee. |
| `ODESOLVE(fn$,start,state,finish,maxstep[,rtol[,atol]])` | Adaptive RK4 step doubling. Returns rows `{time,state1,...}` including the initial and final states and each accepted intermediate step. `maxstep` is positive; reverse integration is selected by `finish<start`. Equal endpoints return the initial row. |
| `VERLETSTEP(fn$,time,position,velocity,step)` | Velocity Verlet; returns `{newPosition,newVelocity}`. Callback takes `(time,position)` and returns **acceleration**, independent of velocity. Position and velocity must have the same length. Use RK4/ODESOLVE for velocity-dependent forces such as drag. |
| `LAPLACE1D(field,spacing[,periodic])` | Centered second spatial derivative on a uniform 1D grid. At least three points; positive spacing. |
| `LAPLACIAN(field,shape,spacing[,periodic])` | Sum of centered second derivatives on a flat 1D/2D/3D rectangular grid. `shape` and `spacing` are matching lists; every dimension has at least three points. Last index varies fastest. Example: a `ny` by `nx` field has shape `{ny,nx}` and spacing `{dy,dx}`. |

`ODESOLVE` defaults to `rtol=1E-7`, `atol=1E-9`; relative tolerance must be
nonnegative and absolute tolerance positive. A trial compares one full RK4
step with two half steps. It accepts the two-half-step state when **every**
component's estimated local error `ABS(fine-coarse)/15` is at most
`atol+rtol*MAX(ABS(old),ABS(fine))`. The controller uses a safety factor of .9,
fifth-root error scaling and growth/shrink factors bounded to [.1,2]. These
are local estimates, not guaranteed global errors. Tolerances are scalar;
nondimensionalize or scale variables with different magnitudes/units.
Accepted times are irregular; there is no dense interpolation or event location.
Final steps may exceed `maxstep` by floating-point roundoff to land exactly on
`finish`. Unrepresentable time increments, nonfinite calculations, invalid
callback shapes and work/output exhaustion raise errors; no partial trajectory
is returned. Overflow during a trial is an error, not an automatic retry.

For both spatial operators, `periodic=0` (default) sets the result at every
boundary point to zero. In a method-of-lines evolution this holds the initial
boundary values fixed; it does **not** impose zero field values or Neumann
conditions automatically. `periodic=1` wraps each axis (omit duplicated endpoint
samples). No other boundary mode is implicit. Operators are second-order in
space. Explicit time integration of discretized PDEs must resolve the grid's
fastest modes; tolerances alone do not establish stability or physical accuracy.

`DAESTEP` and `DAESOLVE` support semi-explicit index-one systems
`x'=f(t,x,z)`, `0=g(t,x,z)`. Order the state as `{x...,z...}` and supply the
exact integer number of differential components, strictly between zero and state
length. The callback returns `{f...,g...}`. Its optional dense/CSR1 Jacobian is
`d{f,g}/d{x,z}`, using the same single name or `{rhs$,jacobian$}` convention.
The algebraic block `dg/dz` must be nonsingular along the chosen solution branch;
there is no automatic index classification, reduction or branch-uniqueness proof.

Differential residual rows are `xnew-xold-step*f(tnew,xnew,znew)`; algebraic
rows remain `g(tnew,xnew,znew)` **without multiplication by the time step**.
The dense or sparse Newton matrix follows these row semantics. All residuals
use `atol+rtol*max(abs(old),abs(new))` component scales. Normalize constraint
equations and states to compatible units; a single scalar absolute tolerance
cannot express arbitrary physical unit scales. A nonlinear residual tolerance
is not a trajectory error bound. Adaptive error estimates include both parts of
the state, with the existing tighter inner Newton tolerances and budgets.

`DAEINIT` explicitly solves `g(time,x,z)=0` from an algebraic guess while
preserving differential values exactly in binary64. It reuses the same mixed
callback and optional dense/CSR1 Jacobian as DAE stepping. Its analytic/sparse differential
Newton rows are identity rows; algebraic rows remain `dg/dy`. The numerical
path differentiates and solves only the algebraic block. Each trial restores
the supplied differential prefix exactly, including native signed-zero bits.
Constraint convergence uses `atol+rtol*abs(currentState)` so a huge old guess
cannot relax the final constraint tolerance. No time step or time advancement is
performed. Native consumers use `nonlinear::initialize` on a configured equation.

Initialization is local: different guesses may select different regular branches.
It neither proves the DAE index nor finds all roots. Callbacks, including their
unused differential outputs, must be finite over the guess and trial domain.
Nonexistent roots, singular Jacobians, budget exhaustion, invalid data or
cancellation return errors without mutating the supplied guess or assigning a
partial result. Already-consistent guesses can return without a Jacobian call.
The 24-Newton/12-backtracking, state, callback/component and sparse work limits
are shared with stepping. Match initialization tolerances to the subsequent
solver's initial-consistency requirements.

```basic
10 DEF FN MODEL(TT,YY)={YY(2),YY(1)+YY(2)-1}
20 Y=DAEINIT("FNMODEL",1,0,{0,0})
30 P=DAESOLVE("FNMODEL",1,0,Y,2,.2)
```

Before stepping, the original `g(start,state)` must satisfy the requested
component tolerance using the initial state scale. Inconsistent input is an
error; ordinary stepping does not silently project or repair initial data.
Call `DAEINIT` explicitly when consistent algebraic states are not yet known. Equal endpoints
still evaluate and check the mixed callback. For index-one systems the initial
differential derivative is given by `f`; algebraic derivative consistency follows
from the smooth constraint branch. No initial derivative vector is requested.
Native consumers configure the same kernel with `Equation::set_dae`.
Explicit RK4 rejects a native equation configured as a DAE.

```basic
10 DEF FN MODEL(TT,YY)={YY(2),YY(1)+YY(2)-1}
20 DEF FN JAC(TT,YY)={{0,1},{1,1}}
30 PRINT DAESTEP({"FNMODEL","FNJAC"},1,0,{0,1},.1)
40 P=DAESOLVE({"FNMODEL","FNJAC"},1,0,{0,1},2,.2)
```

This model evolves `x'=z` while enforcing `x+z=1`. DAE state, sparse work,
trajectory, cancellation and failure limits follow the implicit ODE solvers.
The supported class does not include unrestricted residual DAEs depending on
arbitrary `y'`, higher-index constraints, silent/automatic consistent initialization,
DAE event interpolation or variable-order BDF. Use the ODE event APIs only for
ODE models; their interpolants do not enforce nonlinear DAE constraints.

`ODEEVENT` and `IMPLICITEVENT` test the initial state and accepted step endpoints.
`direction=0` (default) permits either sign crossing, `1` permits negative-to-positive,
and `-1` permits positive-to-negative **in integration order**, including reverse
integration. An exact initial zero stops immediately regardless of direction, before
any RHS evaluation. Equal endpoints still evaluate the event once. An absent event
returns the ordinary final trajectory with `found=0`. The final row is the localized
event state; no later rows are returned. All earlier rows are accepted steps.

Events must be continuous and side-effect free. By default, endpoint detection
can miss two or more crossings within a step and tangent roots with no sign
change unless the optional `tangenttol` search is enabled. The optional final
`eventscan` samples each accepted step at 1–256 equal intervals (default 1).
Optional `eventdepth` bisects every scan interval zero to eight additional times
(default 0), for at most 4096 intervals per accepted step across the two options.
Terminal solvers stop at the first detected sign crossing. Refinement can reveal
closely packed crossings and multiple extrema that a coarse scan misses, but
roots can remain hidden within the finest interval; increase scan resolution or
reduce `maxstep` for rapidly varying events. When `tangenttol` is supplied,
terminal tangency search also examines each refined interval and stops at the
first qualifying contact. It assumes at most one relevant smooth minimum per
refined interval. The scan cannot certify that every root or extremum was found.
Choose `maxstep`, scan count and refinement depth to resolve event geometry;
event time tolerance does not control trajectory error.
Localization bisects the interpolated accepted-step curve at most 80 times:
`ODEEVENT` uses cubic Hermite state interpolation with endpoint RHS derivatives;
`IMPLICITEVENT` uses linear interpolation, consistent with its first-order method.
No extra flow integration is performed during localization. `timetol` is positive,
default `1E-9`, with an 8-ulp-scale time floor. A narrow bracket bounds time on the
interpolant, not the exact physical solution. A discontinuous event can violate
root assumptions. For nonsmooth forcing split the integration interval yourself.

For terminal events, a positive `tangenttol` opts into a bounded search when
`direction=0`; it uses the event callback's units and assumes one relevant
minimum per refined interval. With `eventscan=1` and `eventdepth=0`, that interval
is the whole accepted step. The default omits tangency searches.

RHS calls, event calls and localization share the 200,000 evaluation and
50-million component-work budgets. Event errors and interrupts propagate without
partial trajectories or assigned results. Solver tolerances default to `1E-7,1E-9`
for `ODEEVENT` and `1E-5,1E-8` for `IMPLICITEVENT`. Ordinary solver APIs retain
their existing contracts.

`ODEEVENTS` accepts one vector-valued event callback returning 1–64 finite real
values. Its optional `directions` list has one `-1`, `0` or `1` entry per event;
omitting it enables either crossing for every event. It records exact initial
zeros and later sign crossings without stopping the trajectory. The result is
`{trajectory,eventRecords}`; each event record is `{time,eventIndex,state...}`
with a one-based event index. Records follow integration order, and roots found
at the same accepted step are ordered by event index. The trajectory always
continues to `finish` unless a callback, solver, cancellation or resource limit
fails. Event records are bounded to 10,000 and the ordinary result-element cap.
The callback must keep the same vector length and be side-effect free. By
default, detection samples accepted endpoints, so tangencies and multiple
crossings hidden inside one step can be missed. The optional final `eventscan`
sets 1–256 equal intervals per accepted step (default 1); `eventdepth` bisects
each interval zero to eight additional levels (default 0), with a combined cap
of 4096 intervals per accepted step. The solver checks event values at each
subdivision and localizes sign changes independently on the original dense
curve, so it can report multiple roots within one accepted
step. This bounded scan can still miss an even number of roots within its finest
subdivision and does not prove that all roots were found; increase scan count or
refinement depth, or reduce `maxstep` for rapidly oscillating events. Scan callback work shares the
ordinary solver budgets. Supplying a positive `tangenttol` enables a bounded
golden-section search for an interior same-sign minimum on each refined
interval; with `eventscan=1` and `eventdepth=0`, this is the accepted dense
segment. A candidate is recorded when its absolute event value is at most
`tangenttol`. This value is in the event function's units, and
`direction`/`directions` must be 0 for tangencies to count. The tangent search
assumes at most one relevant smooth minimum per refined interval, so multiple
extrema packed inside the finest interval can remain hidden. Choose `maxstep`,
scan count and refinement depth to resolve event geometry. `ODEEVENTS` uses the
same cubic Hermite dense state curve and time-tolerance limits as `ODEEVENT`.
The runnable BASIC example `programs/science/tangent_events.bas` covers terminal
and nonterminal contacts plus rejection of a nearby nonzero minimum.

`IMPLICITEVENTS` uses the same 1–64 event-vector, direction, record-limit,
initial-zero, `tangenttol`, `eventscan` and `eventdepth` rules, but follows adaptive nonlinear backward
Euler. It localizes on the linear interpolation between the accepted implicit
states and retains `IMPLICITSOLVE` tolerances and state/Jacobian limits. Its
event callback shares the nonlinear solver's evaluation and component-work
budgets. Use `{rhs$,jacobian$}` for the optional analytic dense or CSR1 Jacobian.
The runnable example `programs/science/implicit_events.bas` demonstrates
direction-filtered crossings and a nonterminal tangent contact.

`ODEHYBRID` and `IMPLICITHYBRID` use one scalar guard callback and one reset
callback `(time,state)`. On each localized event, the reset must return a finite
real list with the same state width; the solver records the pre-reset and
post-reset states at the same timestamp and resumes integration from the
post-reset state. A guard that is exactly zero at the initial state triggers one
immediate reset. After a reset on the guard surface, the solver resumes without
re-triggering that same zero; the guard must leave zero and later cross again to
produce another event. The optional `maxevents` defaults to 1000 and is bounded
to 1–10000. Reaching the event cap, callback failure or a work limit fails the
whole call without returning a partial result. Event localization uses the same
interpolants, bounded `eventscan`, optional `tangenttol`, direction rules and
per-trajectory work budgets described above. For rapidly changing guards,
select `maxstep` and scan count carefully; the finite scan cannot guarantee that
all roots were found.

Nonlinear implicit step, trajectory and event APIs accept either the existing
RHS function name or the two-name
list `{rhs$,jacobian$}` as their first argument. The named Jacobian function
takes `(time,state)` and must return an ordinary **n-by-n nested real matrix**, with entry `(i,j)` equal to
`d RHS_i / d state_j` at the supplied time/state. Return the RHS Jacobian,
not `I-step*J` and not a time derivative. For example:

```basic
10 DEF FN RHS(TT,YY)={-100*YY(1)-YY(1)^3}
20 DEF FN JAC(TT,YY)={{-100-3*YY(1)^2}}
30 PRINT IMPLICITSTEP({"FNRHS","FNJAC"},0,{1},.1)
40 P=IMPLICITSOLVE({"FNRHS","FNJAC"},0,{1},1,.2)
```

The Rust Newton solver forms `I-step*J` and applies its usual residual scaling,
backtracking and linear solve. It requests a fresh Jacobian only when a Newton
correction is needed. One dense-matrix callback counts as one evaluation and n-squared
component work in the shared budgets; RHS/event evaluations retain their usual
charges. Invalid shape, nonfinite data, domain/callback errors and cancellation
are fatal, with no fallback to numerical differentiation or partial assignment.
A wrong finite Jacobian may slow or prevent convergence; supplying derivatives
does not prove their correctness. Accepted solutions still satisfy the nonlinear
residual criterion. Smoothness, root uniqueness and time-accuracy limitations
remain unchanged. Explicit RK4/Verlet APIs continue to accept a single RHS name.

The Jacobian function may instead return a validated `CSR1` record produced by
`SPARSE`. Sparse Jacobians enable up to 4,096 state components in nonlinear
steps, adaptive trajectories and terminal-event solves. Numerical/dense Jacobians
retain their 64-state limit; a nonstationary larger model must supply CSR1.
The Rust solver assembles `(I-step*J)/rowScale` in sparse form, inserting missing
identity diagonal entries, and reuses residual-checked, row-equilibrated restarted
GMRES without dense conversion or a diagonal-dominance requirement. For example:

```basic
10 DEF FN RHS(TT,YY)={-YY(1)^3,-2*YY(2)^3}
20 DEF FN JAC(TT,YY)=SPARSE(2,2,{1,2},{1,2},{-3*YY(1)^2,-6*YY(2)^2})
30 PRINT IMPLICITSTEP({"FNRHS","FNJAC"},0,{1,1},.1)
```

A sparse callback charges the state length plus stored entries to component
work after its bounded result is validated. Canonical CSR rules and 250,000-entry
limits apply, including the shifted residual matrix. Sparse assembly and Krylov
work share a cumulative 100-million work budget across all Newton attempts and
steps. GMRES restart is at most 30, with at most `min(1000,max(40,2*n))`
iterations per correction; the existing two-million-element basis cap applies.
Linear correction tolerances are `rtol=1E-10`, `atol=1E-12` on the scaled
residual system. Every candidate is checked against its true stored residual.
Iteration/breakdown results request a smaller adaptive step; malformed data,
callback/domain, work-limit and cancellation errors are fatal. Fixed steps report
nonconvergence. No sparse direct factorization or general DAE solver is implied.
Native modules may use `SparseJacobian::new` with canonical zero-based CSR and
`Equation::with_derivative` with `Derivative::Sparse`, without BASIC records.

Analytic derivatives can avoid central-difference probes outside a model's valid
state domain and reduce RHS work. They do not constrain Newton/backtracking trial
states; those can still leave the domain. Native backend modules may use
`physics::Equation::new` with Rust RHS/Jacobian closures and
`physics::nonlinear::step` (or the native RK4 method) without BASIC value-list
callbacks. Each fresh equation owns cumulative callback/component budgets.

`IMPLICITSOLVE` compares the full step with the two-half-step result using
`max(abs(fine-coarse)/(atol+rtol*max(abs(old),abs(fine))))<=1`.
The first-order method adapts with a square-root controller; accepted values are
not extrapolated. Newton residual tolerances are `min(.01*rtol,1E-10)` and
`min(.01*atol,1E-12)`; unrepresentable positive inner tolerance is refused.
Newton nonconvergence or a singular Newton matrix reduces the step. Callback
errors, cancellation, nonfinite arithmetic and shared work limits propagate
immediately. There are at most 10,000 attempted steps per call, sharing the
200,000 callback and 50-million component-evaluation limits across all trials.
There is no event detection, dense output, positivity preservation or DAE support.
Smooth trial-state equations and step/tolerance refinement remain necessary;
local sampling can miss unresolved forcing. Failures return no partial trajectory.

`IMPLICITSTEP` allows at most 24 Newton iterations, each with a fresh dense Jacobian
and at most 12 backtracking trials. Its residual criterion is
`max(abs(z-y-h*F)/(atol+rtol*max(abs(y),abs(z))))<=1`. Relative tolerance must
be nonnegative and absolute tolerance positive. Callbacks should be smooth and
side-effect free; trial states may leave a physical domain. Callback errors propagate
immediately. Backward Euler damps stable linear modes, but nonlinear root existence,
uniqueness, positivity and global convergence are not guaranteed. Refine the step
to assess physical accuracy. No trajectory or partial state is returned on failure.

The callback-based physics solvers use binary64 CPU arithmetic, up to 4,096 state components
(64 for dense/numerical implicit solvers, 4,096 for sparse-Jacobian paths),
200,000 equation evaluations and 50 million derivative-component evaluations
per call. A returned trajectory contains at most one million numeric elements
including times. Spatial operators accept up to one million field elements.
Existing BASIC retained-storage, expression work/depth and cancellation limits
also apply. Integrate in shorter intervals or stream fixed steps to CSV for long
runs. Callbacks are `DEF FN` expressions and can compose other `DEF FN` functions
and native math kernels; structured multiline `FUNCTION`/`SUB` callbacks are not
supported by these solver calls. Custom time steppers, boundary conditions and
model algorithms can also be implemented using ordinary BASIC procedures/loops.
Keep solver callbacks deterministic; random draws or state-changing functions
will be repeated on rejected steps.

`programs/science/orbit_verlet.bas` checks energy and angular momentum over ten
orbits; `heat_diffusion.bas` checks spatial convergence against an analytical
heat solution; `wave_3d.bas` checks a 3D wave against its semidiscrete eigenmode.
All export CSV using BASIC file commands and run as source or packaged ELF apps.
`tools/check-physics-foundation.py` adds SciPy reference, convergence, boundary,
invalid-input and backward-time checks. Python/SciPy are test dependencies only.

This is a reusable initial-value/PDE foundation. It does not implement a complete
