TEXT COLOR = white
COLORS

COLORS lists the 32 supported names. Names are case-insensitive; use the single-word spellings below:

black       white       red         green
blue        yellow      cyan        magenta
orange      purple      pink        brown
gray        darkgray    lightgray   navy
teal        olive       maroon      gold
beige       ivory       coral       salmon
violet      indigo      turquoise   lightblue
lightgreen  darkgreen   darkblue    skyblue

Hexadecimal #rrggbb values also work. Changes apply immediately to the hub and program-window defaults and save automatically to modernbasic.cfg in the configured file root. Previously printed text keeps its original colors. The startup options --screen-color and --text-color and entries in that configuration file accept the same names. These are hub preferences; BASIC programs use TEXTCOLOR for their own text colors.

In the graphical system hub and at a graphical READY. prompt, HELP, MANUAL, or F1 opens the complete offline user manual. Use Up/Down, Page Up/Page Down, Home/End, or the mouse wheel to navigate; / starts a case-insensitive search, F3 finds the next match, and Escape or F1 closes the viewer. A function key remains available to a running BASIC program: F1 opens the manual only while that program window is at READY.. In a terminal REPL, HELP prints the quick command list and MANUAL or HELP MANUAL prints the complete embedded manual.

AUTO displays the next line number before each entry. An asterisk marks an existing line (100* ), so you can see when entering a body will replace it. An empty entry leaves AUTO mode. Reaching the highest supported line number saves that final line and returns to normal command entry automatically.

RENUM updates standalone numeric branch destinations, including ON branch lists and IF/THEN/ELSE line targets. It preserves ordinary numeric data, array subscripts, computed destination expressions, ON ERROR GOTO 0, and RESUME 0. Computed destinations may need manual adjustment after renumbering.

At an application READY prompt, EXIT, QUIT, or BYE closes that application's window and releases its resources. To power off the Debian appliance, use SHUTDOWN in the system hub and confirm with Y. This shuts down the guest OS and stops its VM, or powers off the physical machine. RESTART restarts BASIC.

System-hub BASH opens or focuses a separate Bash administration window. In the Debian appliance it runs as root for the trusted local console operator; BASIC remains unprivileged. F12 switches focus between the hub and Bash, and Bash exit or its window close button ends the administration session. System-hub SETTINGS opens the OS settings center. Sound settings list real outputs (including HDMI/TV names), choose the default for new playback, select connectors, set volume from 0 to 100%, mute/unmute, and play a two-second left/right test. A test never changes the default output, volume, or mute state. Existing playback may need to be restarted after changing the default output.

DISPLAY, RESOLUTION, or SETTINGS DISPLAY opens Display Settings directly. It lists actual monitor modes with Apply, Keep and Revert controls. Unconfirmed mode changes revert automatically after 15 seconds or on closing the page. Closing Display Settings opened from the center returns to the center.

The Wi-Fi page finds networks, opens a masked-password connection dialog, supports hidden networks, and manages saved networks, disconnection and the wireless radio. Choose Remember for automatic reconnection or Connect once for a temporary profile. Cancel during connection restores the previous connection on that adapter. A connection failure also attempts restoration; if the settings process disappears, NetworkManager attempts restoration within three minutes. Joining Wi-Fi does not prove Internet access: some networks require a captive-portal login.

Bluetooth provides adapter selection, a bounded nearby-device scan, pairing-code confirmation and masked PIN entry, connect/disconnect, explicit trust, and device removal. Pairing does not select an audio output; use Sound after connecting a speaker. Trust allows future connections/services without another prompt. Pairing keys persist on installed systems; radio power follows BlueZ boot policy. See docs/BLUETOOTH_SETUP.md for setup and cancellation details.

Keyboard layout and time zone offers a layout/variant picker with a 20-second typing test and automatic revert unless Keep is chosen. The saved graphical keyboard map is restored when BASIC starts. Time-zone changes require confirmation and persist through Debian’s time service. See docs/REGIONAL_SETUP.md.

Removable drives lists device identities and volume mount locations. Mount and unmount require confirmation. Remove drive unmounts all eligible volumes before power-off/eject; busy-device errors stop removal without forcing it. Cancel before confirmation makes no change. Stop during an operation waits for its reply and skips remaining steps. Mounts are not automatically restored at reboot. See docs/REMOVABLE_DRIVES.md for file access, permissions and recovery.

Power and update pages show status and instructions for the F12 administration tools. Settings never open an administrator shell automatically. Most settings run as the BASIC user. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, regional settings and storage each use a separate confined helper account; these features add no direct backend permission to BASIC programs. See docs/WIFI_SETUP.md for Wi-Fi credential storage and recovery.

SETUP reopens the first-run setup checklist. The appliance opens this checklist on startup until Finish is selected; canceling or opening the manual postpones completion. Finish saves $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/modernbasic/setup-v1.complete (or ~/.config/modernbasic/setup-v1.complete). Audio preferences are managed by the Linux audio session; confirmed display preferences are saved by the appliance. The live medium has no persistent overlay: these settings and setup completion last only until power-off. Installed systems retain their settings. Ordinary host development launches do not open setup automatically. Settings require the Python 3, Zenity, PulseAudio utilities and NetworkManager/libnma bindings supplied in the distribution.

Accepted READY aliases are RENUMBER for RENUM, SCRATCH for NEW, CHDIR for CD, FILES/CAT/CATALOG/LS for DIR, REN/RENAME for NAME, and EXIT/BYE for QUIT. AUTO, DELETE, EDIT, and RENUM deliberately reject execution from inside a running program. KILL and NAME also have sandboxed executable statement forms.

Plain DIR, or DIR with a directory path, groups entries as DIRECTORY FOLDERS, BASIC PROGRAMS, and OTHER FILES. This keeps .bas programs prominent while leaving their data and support files available at the bottom. A pattern such as DIR *.dat narrows the listing under MATCHING FILES. DIR /S and TREE remain explicit recursive views of every file and subfolder.

The READY file browser reports only BASIC-visible paths. Its root is programs, so child directories appear as programs/examples or programs/music; the long canonical host path remains internal. Listings do not repeat the root name; they begin with the DIRECTORY FOLDERS, BASIC PROGRAMS, and OTHER FILES section headings. File sizes, entry counts, and byte totals are reported. Existing components and wildcards are case-insensitive. / and \ are BASIC-root aliases, both slash styles work as separators, parent navigation clamps at the root, and recursive TREE browsing is bounded and does not follow symbolic links.

Execution preparation and first-use assets

Creating an execution session and LOAD/LOADB validate the resident execution plan before READY.. This includes split statements, line indexes, structured control definitions, and DATA items. It does not open declared images, media, or SoundFont banks. A statement that is never reached does not load its assets.

Asset paths and SoundFont voice ranges may be evaluated expressions. When an operation executes, the runtime resolves and loads its input, validates it, and retains successful inputs for reuse. Missing or invalid assets report an error at that operation; they do not reject an otherwise valid LOAD. Repeated RUN uses already retained inputs. Relative asset paths are anchored to the loaded program's directory; CD changes the ordinary file directory, not this anchor. The soundfont/ prefix selects the configured read-only bank directory.

Generated image and WAV outputs are retained when produced for subsequent use. Replacing the program or closing its window releases the old capability state and assets. A syntax/control-validation failure during LOAD retains the old program. Immediate statements follow the same first-use asset rules.

integer literals, not expressions. Inspection never allocates arrays or evaluates
functions; missing scalars retain BASIC default-value rules. Strings are quoted
with escaped controls. Use INSPECT during STOP/STEP and CONT to resume. These are
READY commands, not new stored-program statements.

The graphical system hub additionally accepts `EDIT SPRITE` and `EDIT FONT`.
They launch independent graphical asset-editor windows, leaving running BASIC
programs and their graphics/audio state undisturbed. The commands are hub
operations rather than statements stored in a BASIC program.

At the system hub, use color names to customize the default screen and text:

```text
SCREEN COLOR = navy
TEXT COLOR = white
COLORS
```

`COLORS` lists the 32 supported names. Names are case-insensitive; use the
single-word spellings below:

```text
black       white       red         green
blue        yellow      cyan        magenta
orange      purple      pink        brown
gray        darkgray    lightgray   navy
teal        olive       maroon      gold
beige       ivory       coral       salmon
violet      indigo      turquoise   lightblue
lightgreen  darkgreen   darkblue    skyblue
```

Hexadecimal `#rrggbb` values also work. Changes apply immediately to the hub
and program-window defaults and save automatically to `modernbasic.cfg` in
the configured file root. Previously printed text keeps its original colors.
The startup options `--screen-color` and `--text-color` and entries in that
configuration file accept the same names. These are hub
preferences; BASIC programs use `TEXTCOLOR` for their own text colors.

In the graphical system hub and at a graphical `READY.` prompt, `HELP`,
`MANUAL`, or **F1** opens the complete offline user manual. Use Up/Down,
Page Up/Page Down, Home/End, or the mouse wheel to navigate; `/` starts a
case-insensitive search, **F3** finds the next match, and **Escape** or **F1**
closes the viewer. A function key remains available to a running BASIC program:
F1 opens the manual only while that program window is at `READY.`. In a terminal
REPL, `HELP` prints the quick command list and `MANUAL` or `HELP MANUAL` prints
the complete embedded manual.

`AUTO` displays the next line number before each entry. An asterisk marks an
existing line (`100* `), so you can see when entering a body will replace it.
An empty entry leaves AUTO mode. Reaching the highest supported line number
saves that final line and returns to normal command entry automatically.

`RENUM` updates standalone numeric branch destinations, including ON branch
lists and IF/THEN/ELSE line targets. It preserves ordinary numeric data, array
subscripts, computed destination expressions, `ON ERROR GOTO 0`, and `RESUME 0`.
Computed destinations may need manual adjustment after renumbering.

At an application READY prompt, `EXIT`, `QUIT`, or `BYE` closes that application's
window and releases its resources. To power off the Debian appliance, use
`SHUTDOWN` in the system hub and confirm with `Y`. This shuts down the guest OS
and stops its VM, or powers off the physical machine. `RESTART` restarts BASIC.

System-hub `BASH` opens or focuses a separate Bash administration window.
In the Debian appliance it runs as root for the trusted local console operator;
BASIC remains unprivileged. F12 switches focus between the hub and Bash, and
Bash `exit` or its window close button ends the administration session.
System-hub `SETTINGS` opens the OS settings center. Sound settings list real
outputs (including HDMI/TV names), choose the default for new playback, select
connectors, set volume from 0 to 100%, mute/unmute, and play a two-second left/right
test. A test never changes the default output, volume, or mute state. Existing
playback may need to be restarted after changing the default output.

`DISPLAY`, `RESOLUTION`, or `SETTINGS DISPLAY` opens Display Settings directly.
It lists actual monitor modes with Apply, Keep and Revert controls. Unconfirmed
mode changes revert automatically after 15 seconds or on closing the page.
Closing Display Settings opened from the center returns to the center.

The Wi-Fi page finds networks, opens a masked-password connection dialog, supports
hidden networks, and manages saved networks, disconnection and the wireless radio.
Choose Remember for automatic reconnection or Connect once for a temporary profile.
Cancel during connection restores the previous connection on that adapter. A
connection failure also attempts restoration; if the settings process disappears,
NetworkManager attempts restoration within three minutes. Joining Wi-Fi does not
prove Internet access: some networks require a captive-portal login.

Bluetooth provides adapter selection, a bounded nearby-device scan, pairing-code
confirmation and masked PIN entry, connect/disconnect, explicit trust, and device
removal. Pairing does not select an audio output; use Sound after connecting a
speaker. Trust allows future connections/services without another prompt. Pairing
keys persist on installed systems; radio power follows BlueZ boot policy. See
`docs/BLUETOOTH_SETUP.md` for setup and cancellation details.

Keyboard layout and time zone offers a layout/variant picker with a 20-second
typing test and automatic revert unless Keep is chosen. The saved graphical
keyboard map is restored when BASIC starts. Time-zone changes require confirmation
and persist through Debian’s time service. See `docs/REGIONAL_SETUP.md`.

Removable drives lists device identities and volume mount locations. Mount and
unmount require confirmation. Remove drive unmounts all eligible volumes before
power-off/eject; busy-device errors stop removal without forcing it. Cancel before
confirmation makes no change. Stop during an operation waits for its reply and
skips remaining steps. Mounts are not automatically restored at reboot. See
`docs/REMOVABLE_DRIVES.md` for file access, permissions and recovery.

Power and update pages show status and instructions for the F12
administration tools. Settings never open an administrator shell automatically.
Most settings run as the BASIC user. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, regional settings and storage each use a separate
confined helper account; these features add no direct backend permission to BASIC
programs. See `docs/WIFI_SETUP.md` for Wi-Fi credential storage and recovery.

`SETUP` reopens the first-run setup checklist. The appliance opens this checklist
on startup until Finish is selected; canceling or opening the manual postpones
completion. Finish saves `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/modernbasic/setup-v1.complete` (or
`~/.config/modernbasic/setup-v1.complete`). Audio preferences are managed by the
Linux audio session; confirmed display preferences are saved by the appliance.
The live medium has no persistent overlay: these settings and setup completion
last only until power-off. Installed systems retain their settings. Ordinary
host development launches do not open setup automatically. Settings require the
Python 3, Zenity, PulseAudio utilities and NetworkManager/libnma bindings supplied
in the distribution.

Accepted READY aliases are `RENUMBER` for `RENUM`, `SCRATCH` for `NEW`,
`CHDIR` for `CD`, `FILES`/`CAT`/`CATALOG`/`LS` for `DIR`,
`REN`/`RENAME` for `NAME`, and `EXIT`/`BYE` for `QUIT`. `AUTO`, `DELETE`,
`EDIT`, and `RENUM` deliberately reject execution from inside a running
program. `KILL` and `NAME` also have sandboxed executable statement forms.

Plain `DIR`, or `DIR` with a directory path, groups entries as `DIRECTORY
FOLDERS`, `BASIC PROGRAMS`, and `OTHER FILES`. This keeps `.bas` programs
prominent while leaving their data and support files available at the bottom.
A pattern such as `DIR *.dat` narrows the listing under `MATCHING FILES`.
`DIR /S` and `TREE` remain explicit recursive views of every file and subfolder.

The READY file browser reports only BASIC-visible paths. Its root is `programs`,
so child directories appear as `programs/examples` or `programs/music`; the
long canonical host path remains internal. Listings do not repeat the root
name; they begin with the `DIRECTORY FOLDERS`, `BASIC PROGRAMS`, and `OTHER
FILES` section headings. File sizes, entry counts, and byte totals are reported.
Existing components and wildcards are case-insensitive. `/` and `\` are
BASIC-root aliases, both slash styles work as
separators, parent navigation clamps at the root, and recursive `TREE` browsing
is bounded and does not follow symbolic links.

### Execution preparation and first-use assets

Creating an execution session and `LOAD`/`LOADB` validate the resident execution
plan before `READY.`. This includes split statements, line indexes, structured
control definitions, and DATA items. It does not open declared images, media,
or SoundFont banks. A statement that is never reached does not load its assets.

Asset paths and SoundFont voice ranges may be evaluated expressions. When an
operation executes, the runtime resolves and loads its input, validates it, and
retains successful inputs for reuse. Missing or invalid assets report an error
at that operation; they do not reject an otherwise valid `LOAD`. Repeated `RUN`
uses already retained inputs. Relative asset paths are anchored to the loaded
program's directory; `CD` changes the ordinary file directory, not this anchor.
The `soundfont/` prefix selects the configured read-only bank directory.

Generated image and WAV outputs are retained when produced for subsequent use.
Replacing the program or closing its window releases the old capability state
and assets. A syntax/control-validation failure during LOAD retains the old
program. Immediate statements follow the same first-use asset rules.

documents.title: Graphics
documents.html:
The canonical graphics statement families are:

SCREEN       CLS          COLOR          PALETTE
PSET         PRESET       LINE           BRUSH
RECTANGLE    CIRCLE       ELLIPSE        PAINT
MOVE         DRAWTO       DRAW           POLYGON
GRADIENT     RADIALGRADIENT
ARC          BEZIER       ROUNDEDRECT
OPACITY      BLEND
TRANSLATE    ROTATE       SCALE
NGON         STAR         PATH           BITMAP
PERSPECTIVE  OBJECT       LIGHT
DEPTHGRID    DEPTHPERCEPTION
GRIDON       GRIDOFF      GRIDPOINT
LAYER        ENDLAYER     GROUP          ENDGROUP
TEXT         FONT
SPRITE       MOVESPRITE   SPRITEMOTION   ADVANCESPRITES
BUFFER       FRAME        FLIP
SCREENSHOT   SAVEIMAGE    DISPLAY
FLIPBOOK     VIDEO

The principal family subcommands and operating modes are:

SCREEN TEXT|GRAPHICS|GRAPHICS2D|GRAPHICS3D|SPLIT
SCREEN STANDARD|HD|HDPLUS|FULLHD|QHD|ULTRAWIDE|UHD
SCREEN classic-mode
SCREEN width,height[,background]

PAINT (x,y)[,fill[,border]]
PAINT TEXTURE path$,seed,scale,octaves,color1,color2[,opacity[,blend$]]
PAINT FILTER "BLUR",radius
PAINT FILTER "SHARPEN",amount
PAINT FILTER "COLOR",brightness,contrast,saturation

BITMAP path$,x,y,width,height
BITMAP WARP path$,anchor-x,anchor-y,width,height,angle,bend,turn[,light]

OBJECT SHAPE id,x,y,z,width,height,fill[,stroke]
OBJECT MOVE id,x,y,z
FONT path$,cell-width,cell-height[,first-codepoint]
FONT BUILTIN
FONT SYSTEM "sans"
FONT SYSTEM "monospace"
FONT SYSTEM "ui"
FONT SYSTEM "ui-monospace"
SPRITE IMAGE id,path$,x,y,width,height[,transparent-color]
SPRITE IMAGE id,path$,(x,y,z),width,height[,transparent-color]
SPRITE ORIENT id,HORIZON|SCREEN

OBJECT SCALE id,width,height
OBJECT CAMERA x,y,z
OBJECT LIGHT id,x,y,z,intensity,range,color
OBJECT REMOVE id
OBJECT CLEAR

FLIPBOOK CREATE id,template$,first,last,fps
FLIPBOOK REMOVE id
FLIPBOOK CLEAR

VIDEO START path$,fps[,soundtrack$]
VIDEO FRAME
VIDEO STOP
VIDEO EXPORT flipbook-id,path$[,soundtrack$]

Accepted graphics aliases are RECT for RECTANGLE, OVAL for ELLIPSE, BEGINLAYER for LAYER, BEGINGROUP for GROUP, BLIT for SPRITE, and RENDER for SAVEIMAGE. Each pair reaches one implementation rather than duplicating the feature.

The organized calculator-style graph family is:

GRAPH CLEAR
GRAPH DISPLAY [path$]
GRAPH WINDOW xmin,xmax,xscale,ymin,ymax,yscale
GRAPH FUNCTION expression[,color]        GRAPH PLOT is an alias
GRAPH INVERSE expression[,color]
GRAPH LINE ...                           GRAPH CIRCLE ...
GRAPH TEXT ...
GRAPH HORIZONTAL ...                     GRAPH VERTICAL ...
GRAPH TANGENT ...                        GRAPH SHADE ...
GRAPH GRID ON|OFF
GRAPH AXES ON|OFF
GRAPH LABELS ON|OFF
GRAPH COORDS ON|OFF
GRAPH ZOOM STANDARD|TRIG|DECIMAL|SQUARE

The direct TI-style graph spellings are:

CLRDRAW       DISPGRAPH
ZSTANDARD     ZTRIG         ZDECIMAL      ZSQUARE
AXESON        AXESOFF
LABELON       LABELOFF
COORDON       COORDOFF
GLINE         HORIZONTAL    VERTICAL      GCIRCLE
DRAWF         DRAWINV       TANGENT       SHADE
FNON          FNOFF         GRAPHSTYLE
PXL-ON        PXL-OFF       PXL-CHANGE
PT-ON         PT-OFF        PT-CHANGE
GTEXT

Direct GRIDON and GRIDOFF belong to the retained depth-grid graphics family because that dispatcher has priority. Use GRAPH GRID ON and GRAPH GRID OFF for the calculator graph grid. Scatter, histogram, parametric, and polar renderers are command-line library facilities, not BASIC statements.

The Artist-derived renderer is built into the Rust library; no external graphics compatibility renderer is selected at runtime.

RECT and RECTANGLE accept either x,y,width,height[,stroke[,fill[,stroke_width]]] or the endpoint form (x1,y1)-(x2,y2)[,stroke[,fill[,stroke_width]]]. Graphics colors may be palette indexes, hexadecimal strings, or case-insensitive names such as "RED", "SKYBLUE", and "GOLD"; #RRGGBBAA adds an alpha channel. Lines, circles, ellipses, rounded rectangles, and their filled/stroked edges use subpixel coverage in the integrated raster and video renderer. BRUSH (x1,y1)-(x2,y2),size,color[,hardness[,opacity[,flow]]] paints an antialiased soft or hard stroke. size is 0.1 through 2048 logical pixels; hardness, opacity, and flow are independently normalized from 0 through 1. The retained command is rendered identically for the live screen, still-image output, and video frames.

MOVE x,y changes the current drawing point. DRAWTO x,y[,color[,width]] draws from that point and makes the destination the new current point. Additional DRAWTO fields are not part of the language syntax.

BITMAP path$,x,y,width,height accepts bounded P6 PPM plus PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, and TIFF stills. Compressed images are decoded locally through fixed FFmpeg arguments; URLs and decoder options are not accepted. Alpha from formats that carry it is retained, and premultiplied bilinear filtering prevents dark fringes at transparent edges.

BITMAP WARP path$,anchor-x,anchor-y,width,height,angle,bend,turn[,light] is the deformable form in the same statement family. The source bottom center is anchored at (anchor-x,anchor-y); angle is clockwise degrees, bend and turn are normalized from -1 through 1, and optional light is 0 through 2 with a default of 1. A bounded texture mesh curves the centerline, foreshortens and shades the turned surface, and preserves source alpha. This suits leaves, flags, cloth, and other photographed or painted flexible objects without introducing a second bitmap command. PNG export follows the complete raster path, so imported photographic pixels, alpha compositing, warping, and vector painting all survive into the exported still instead of being dropped by a vector-only conversion.

PAINT (x,y)[,fill[,border]] flood-fills from the seed pixel. Without a border argument, it replaces the connected region matching the seed's rendered color. With a border argument, it crosses intervening rendered colors and stops at pixels matching that border, preserving the classic Microsoft behavior. DRAW's Pfill,border macro command uses the same renderer and palette colors. Custom screens are limited to 16,777,216 pixels so framebuffer and flood-fill allocations remain bounded.

Modern raster painting stays in that classic statement family:

PAINT TEXTURE path$,seed,scale,octaves,color1,color2[,opacity[,blend$]]
PAINT FILTER "BLUR",radius
PAINT FILTER "SHARPEN",amount
PAINT FILTER "COLOR",brightness,contrast,saturation

PAINT TEXTURE synthesizes deterministic smooth fractal detail and clips it to each closed subpath. seed selects the repeatable pattern, scale is 0.25 through 4096 logical pixels, octaves is 1 through 8, opacity is 0 through 1, and the optional blend uses the existing BLEND mode names. Layer two or more scales to build macro color variation and fine surface grain without a source bitmap. PAINT FILTER finishes the complete raster accumulated so far: blur radius is 0 through 32 pixels, sharpen amount is 0 through 4, and the three color multipliers are each 0 through 4. These are retained, deterministic, memory-bounded raster operations used by screen presentation, PPM/PNG capture, FLIPBOOK, and VIDEO output. Like imported bitmap pixels, procedural textures and finished pixels are raster effects and are not emitted as editable SVG objects.

SCREEN width,height[,background] defines the logical graphics device, not a request to change the physical monitor mode. All drawing, sprite, collision, mouse, screenshot, and video coordinates use that logical pixel grid. Resizing the host window never changes the BASIC screen or its aspect ratio. The native game presets are:

PresetLogical size
HD1280x720
HDPLUS1600x900
FULLHD / FHD1920x1080
QHD2560x1440
ULTRAWIDE / UWQHD3440x1440
UHD / 4K3840x2160

STANDARD remains 1024x768. Quoted "720P", "900P", "1080P", "1440P", and "2160P" aliases are also accepted. The native shell defaults to --graphics-scale fit, centering the complete device with black letterbox or pillarbox bars. Program window frames are kept within the desktop when created or resized by SCREEN; the full logical canvas scales to fit that window. Smaller programs retain their own independent window sizes. --graphics-scale stretch explicitly fills the host graphics region and may distort the image. Initial window profiles are --display-profile compact (800x600), desktop (1100x760), hd (1280x720), and fullhd (1920x1080); --width and --height override either dimension, and the shell clamps the initial size to the available physical display. These host options do not alter BASIC language behavior or exported image/video resolution. SCREEN TEXT, SCREEN GRAPHICS, SCREEN GRAPHICS2D, SCREEN GRAPHICS3D, and SCREEN SPLIT select the visible operating mode without changing the host display. A numeric or SCREEN width,height[,background] configuration resets the logical graphics device to 2D and clears retained perspective state.

Point-perspective graphics reuse classic pixel and sprite statements and keep one organized OBJECT family:

10 SCREEN FULLHD
20 PERSPECTIVE 960,500,900,1,10000,.25
30 PSET (-30,0,180),"WHITE"
40 OBJECT SHAPE TOWER,0,0,100,20,80,"GOLD","BROWN"
50 SPRITE IMAGE SHIP,"assets/sprite1.ppm",(25,0,70),12,8,"BLACK"
60 OBJECT LIGHT SUN,-40,80,30,1.2,500,"WHITE"
70 MOVESPRITE SHIP,30,5,60
80 SPRITEMOTION SHIP,2,0,-4,0,0,1

PERSPECTIVE horizon-x,horizon-y,focal-length[,near,far,ambient] configures the vanishing point, depth clipping, and base light. It also selects 3D mode. Every retained world pixel, object, and 3D sprite stores X, Y, and Z in memory; positive Y is up, the camera looks toward positive Z, and Z supplies depth. The world is one bounded native map containing up to 65,536 combined objects, sprites, and XYZ pixels plus 256 point lights. Updating a camera or entity changes this retained state rather than rebuilding a separate scene graph.

Image assets are decoded once during program preparation and owned by shared memory. An XYZ image sprite stores only its texture mapping and transform; the renderer reuses a bounded 64 MiB per-thread pixel cache. Frame rendering does not reopen the source file, and many sprites may share one texture allocation.

Classic PSET (x,y)[,color] remains an immediate 2D canvas pixel. RGB(red,green,blue) and RGBA(red,green,blue,alpha) construct true-color values from integer channels in the inclusive range 0 through 255. They return canonical #rrggbb and #rrggbbaa color strings, keeping true colors distinct from numeric palette indices. Consecutive identity-coordinate PSET operations on one scanline are retained as one raster run; SCREENLOCK and SCREENUNLOCK suppress intermediate presentations during large pixel loops. PSET (x,y,z)[,color] stores a one-world-unit pixel at that XYZ coordinate; its projected square grows nearer the camera and shrinks farther away. PRESET (x,y,z) removes the retained pixel at that exact coordinate.

Classic SPRITE id,x,y,width,height[,fill[,stroke]] remains a 2D screen sprite. SPRITE id,(x,y,z),width,height[,fill[,stroke]] stores an XYZ sprite whose coordinate is its bottom-center anchor. SPRITE IMAGE id,path$,(x,y,z),width,height[,transparent-color] maps one prepared image onto the same retained 3D billboard. PPM, PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, and TIFF are accepted; the optional color is an exact RGB transparency key, while "NONE" preserves source alpha. The mapped pixels receive ambient and point-light tint without producing a per-sprite copy.

MOVESPRITE id,x,y[,z] moves either form; omitting Z preserves an XYZ sprite depth. SPRITEMOTION keeps its 2D id,vx,vy[,ax,ay] form and adds id,vx,vy,vz[,ax,ay,az]. ADVANCESPRITES seconds integrates all axes. SPRITE ORIENT id,HORIZON yaws a mapped XYZ sprite toward the configured perspective horizon. Its nose shifts toward the vanishing point and its width foreshortens, while horizontal image rows remain horizontal so the craft does not roll onto its side. The transform is recomputed after every world or camera move. SPRITE ORIENT id,SCREEN restores the usual camera-facing, axis-aligned billboard. The command rejects 2D and untextured sprites. SPRITEX, SPRITEY, SPRITEZ, SPRITESCALE, SPRITEVX, SPRITEVY, SPRITEVZ, SPRITEAX, SPRITEAY, and SPRITEAZ query retained state. A 2D sprite reports Z zero and scale one. Collision tests use the current projected bounds of XYZ sprites. Sprite and object statement/query identifiers may be bare names or string expressions such as ID$="DRONE1":PRINT SPRITEZ(ID$); this supports compact loops over pooled world entities.

OBJECT SHAPE id,x,y,z,width,height,fill[,stroke] stores a billboard object with the same bottom-center convention. OBJECT MOVE, OBJECT SCALE, OBJECT CAMERA, OBJECT LIGHT, OBJECT REMOVE, and OBJECT CLEAR are the mutating members for these legacy billboards; polygonal meshes use the additions below. OBJECTX, OBJECTY, OBJECTZ, OBJECTSCALE, OBJECTWIDTH, and OBJECTHEIGHT query retained object state.

Projection uses screen-scale=focal-length/(entity-z-camera-z). Entities outside the near/far interval are clipped. Every visible pixel, object, and sprite is sorted together from far to near, so depth controls both scaling and layering. Each OBJECT LIGHT id,x,y,z,intensity,range,color applies the same bounded distance-attenuated shading to every retained entity type, including the per-channel tint of mapped sprite pixels. This creates the 3D illusion on the 2D canvas without pretending to be a polygonal mesh renderer.

The additional polygonal mesh pipeline uses these OBJECT commands:

OBJECT MESH id,vertices,triangles,color
OBJECT NORMALS id,cornerNormals
OBJECT TRANSFORM id,modelMatrix
OBJECT VIEW viewMatrix,projectionMatrix
OBJECT SUN x,y,z,ambient
OBJECT TEXTURE id,path$
OBJECT IMAGE id,imageName$[,filter$]
OBJECT RENDER

Vertices are a nested list of {x,y,z} or {x,y,z,u,v} rows; triangles are one-based index triples. Defining a mesh replaces that mesh's geometry, model transform and texture. Mesh names are case-insensitive, 1..128 bytes. Models and views must be affine 4-by-4 matrices; projection matrices use the conventions above. OBJECT SUN gives the world-space direction toward the light and ambient brightness in [0,1]. Faces default to flat Lambert lighting; winding determines the normal, with no backface culling. Materials must be opaque. Textures use the existing confined image loader and shared prepared-image storage, nearest-neighbor sampling and clamped UV coordinates; V=0 is the image bottom. Texture alpha below 128 discards a fragment; other fragments are opaque. Blended transparency is not implemented.

OBJECT IMAGE id,imageName$[,filter$] instead binds a snapshot of a named linear RGBA IMAGE buffer, with LINEAR (default) or NEAREST filtering. UVs describe image edges: (0,0) is the top left, V increases downward, and pixel centers are ((x+.5)/width,(y+.5)/height), matching IMAGE HEIGHTMESH. Coordinates clamp at edges. This path decodes the material color to linear RGB, uses shared Rust perspective interpolation, alpha-correct sampling, face normals and cosine lighting, then clips and encodes the result to display sRGB. Alpha below .5 discards a fragment without writing depth; survivors are opaque. This explicit path preserves OBJECT TEXTURE's legacy byte-lighting and UV rules.

Binding shares the image and its existing memory reservation without copying pixels. Replacing/freeing the named buffer leaves the bound snapshot unchanged; its memory stays charged until the last owner releases it. IMAGE CLEAR, BASIC CLEAR and RUN release names but do not remove an existing mesh's snapshot. OBJECT REMOVE/CLEAR, redefining the mesh, replacing its texture, numeric SCREEN and full program replacement release the binding. A failed binding preserves the old texture. See programs/examples/image_surface.bas for an editable scene.

OBJECT NORMALS id,cornerNormals opts into smooth per-pixel lighting. Supply one row per triangle, each containing three nonzero finite {nx,ny,nz} normals in triangle-corner order. MESHCORNERNORMALS3D generates these from indexed geometry; authored normals are also accepted. Inputs are normalized and replaced atomically. {} restores flat shading. Redefining/removing the mesh or resetting the graphics world releases the normals. These bounded values add 72 bytes per triangle, within the existing 100,000-triangle scene cap.

Normals are in model coordinates. The renderer applies the model's cofactor map, preserving indexed winding through reflections; it clips and interpolates the transformed normals perspective-correctly, then normalizes for per-pixel lighting. A zero transformed/interpolated normal is an error and leaves the draw buffer unchanged. Supplied normals need not agree with face normals; the caller owns that choice. A geometrically collapsed face remains skipped as before.

Smooth lighting uses linear color for plain materials and either texture source. For OBJECT TEXTURE with normals enabled, its bottom-origin endpoint UVs and nearest sampling remain, but sampled sRGB bytes are decoded before lighting. OBJECT IMAGE keeps its top-left image-edge UVs and alpha-aware filtering. The default flat OBJECT TEXTURE path retains byte lighting. Opaque/cutout coverage still applies; smooth lighting does not add antialiasing, blended transparency, geometric subdivision, shadows or physical light transport. See programs/examples/smooth_surface.bas for flat/smooth image comparisons.

OBJECT RENDER rasterizes all meshes together onto the current draw buffer, using six-plane homogeneous clipping, per-pixel depth testing and perspective- correct texture coordinates. Call it after updating transforms and clearing the frame; FLIP presents the buffer as usual. Existing 2D drawing can be used for annotations. OBJECT REMOVE id removes a mesh or a legacy billboard, and OBJECT CLEAR clears both worlds. Numeric SCREEN resets both. Meshes and legacy billboards have separate depth systems; billboards are not occluded by mesh depth.

This is a CPU renderer. Each scene allows 1,024 meshes, 200,000 vertices and 100,000 triangles in total. Each render allows at most 8,388,608 pixels and 100 million bounding-box samples, with cancellation checks between faces and scanline batches. Rendering failure leaves the draw buffer unchanged. GPU rendering, shadows, skeletal animation, scene-format interchange, hierarchy, physics and picking remain future work. Source-controlled procedural meshes and animation are demonstrated in programs/examples/mesh_science.bas.

SCREEN GRAPHICS2D hides the projected world without deleting it; SCREEN GRAPHICS3D shows it again. CLS clears ordinary drawing state, while OBJECT CLEAR releases the XYZ entity mappings and lights. Prepared image assets deliberately remain available for later sprites until another program is loaded or the session closes. A numeric or named-resolution SCREEN configuration resets the world. Live display, PPM/PNG export, screenshots, and video all use the same projection; raster-mapped images are not emitted as editable SVG image objects.

The bundled programs/games/neon_depth_runner.bas is a playable end-to-end example. It creates keyed textures with native drawing commands, retains them in memory, shares the drone/orb pixels across instances, and combines XYZ motion, camera/light updates, depth sorting, projected collision, and scalable HUD drawing. Its title screen selects HD, Full HD, QHD, ultrawide, or UHD.

GRADIENT id,x1,y1,x2,y2,color1,color2 and RADIALGRADIENT id,cx,cy,radius,color1,color2 define smooth paints. Pass "url(#id)" as a shape's fill to use one in live raster, SVG, screenshot, and video output. For example:

10 GRADIENT SKY,0,0,0,720,"#050817","#4A285D"
20 RECTANGLE 0,0,1280,720,"none","url(#SKY)",1

OPACITY value and BLEND mode$ modify the most recently drawn shape. Available raster/SVG modes are normal, multiply, screen, overlay, darken, lighten, difference, xor, add, exclusion, color-dodge, color-burn, hard-light, soft-light, erase, hue, saturation, color, and luminosity. Raster compositing uses bounded shape-local work buffers rather than allocating two full screens for every effect.

SCREENCONTROL flag,value controls the program window: flag 0 sets its title with a string; flags 1, 2 and 3 enable/disable fullscreen, resizing and pointer visibility with a numeric Boolean. Flag 4 opts into application-owned Close requests: SCREENCONTROL 4,1 makes INKEY$ return "CLOSE" when the window manager asks to close a running program. The program must handle that event and use END when ready, for example after confirming unsaved work. The default and SCREENCONTROL 4,0 close normally. Ctrl+Escape remains available to interrupt. Flag 5 publishes a string to the system clipboard: SCREENCONTROL 5,text$. The window serves UTF-8 text while it remains open; PRIMARY selection ownership is unchanged. As with other window controls, this has no effect without a connected graphical window. An external clipboard manager is needed to retain the text after the window closes.

Running graphical programs receive CTRL+A, CTRL+C and CTRL+X through INKEY$, in addition to CTRL+N/O/S/F/Z/Y (each returned separately). Arrow, Home/End and Page Up/Down events include held modifiers, such as SHIFT+LEFT, CTRL+HOME or CTRL+SHIFT+END. Unmodified names are unchanged. Ctrl+V and Shift+Insert continue to deliver clipboard contents as queued text.

Graphical BASIC applications can launch and manage independent BASIC windows:

TASK BROWSER ID
TASK APP "writer",ID
TASK APP "editor","notes.txt",ID
TASK RUN "program.bas",ID
TASK SOURCE SOURCE$,"draft.bas",ID
TASK LIST TASKS$
TASK FOCUS ID
TASK STOP ID
TASK CLOSE ID
TASK ERROR MESSAGE$

TASK BROWSER ID launches the bundled BASIC browser application in an independent program window, inheriting the caller's workspace and network permission. Its interface is BASIC; website rendering uses the optional native browser backend.

TASK APP name$,ID launches a bundled BASIC application: editor, files, office, writer, sheet or slides. Office starts in Writer mode with the Office window title and access to the other modes. TASK APP "editor",path$,ID opens a workspace text file in a new editor window. Each launch has separate document and interpreter state. Applications inherit the caller's capabilities and file/output roots. The bundled desktop, browser and Office native executables default to ~/ModernBASIC when no host --file-root is supplied; default setup creates Programs and rejects linked workspace/Programs directories. A missing home requires an explicit root, never a fallback to the process working directory. This bundled-application policy does not change ordinary COMPILE programs, which retain their working-directory default. Explicit host capability options remain separate from BASIC arguments after --.

TASK LINUXAPPS list$ lists visible registered Linux desktop applications as newline-separated desktop ID<TAB>display name<TAB>description rows. TASK LINUXLAUNCH desktopId$ requests a launch of an ID from that list. Both need host --linux-apps; network/native-compilation permissions do not imply it. The host uses system Python/PyGObject/GIO to apply desktop-entry rules. These commands do not expose host filesystem browsing or accept arbitrary commands. Launched Linux applications retain their own filesystem access and native UI.

TASK RUN reads a bounded source snapshot inside the current file workspace; .m64b selects the tokenized program format. TASK SOURCE runs supplied source text using a workspace-relative document path for its title and static assets, without writing that path. Both return the new numeric task ID in a scalar variable and leave the caller running. Children inherit the caller's capabilities, file/output roots and execution limits, with separate interpreter state. Static assets resolve relative to the selected source path. Task startup errors use normal ON ERROR handling; TASK ERROR retrieves and clears the last task error message. Runtime failures are displayed in the child's own window.

TASK LIST returns the caller's open descendant windows, sorted by ID, as newline- terminated rows of ID, state and filename separated by tabs. States are RUNNING, READY, STOPPED and ERROR. Focus, Stop and Close accept only IDs launched by that caller or its descendants. Sibling and unrelated applications are excluded. Closing an intermediate app reparents its children to its caller; children continue running. Stop interrupts execution while preserving its window; Close destroys the window and discards its session, so application code should confirm when needed. Requests are bounded, and at most 32 program windows can exist in one graphical session. Task operations require a graphical program window; headless use reports an error. TASK ERROR works without a window.

TASK EDIT path$ opens the system text editor; pass "" for a blank document. The default is Microsoft Edit, requiring --linux-apps, system Python with GTK 3 and VTE 2.91, and msedit (or MODERNBASIC_EDIT_BINARY). The supplied path is resolved inside the BASIC workspace, rejecting absolute paths, traversal and symlinks. Microsoft Edit's own file dialogs subsequently use normal Linux user permissions. Startup errors use normal ON ERROR / TASK ERROR handling. The editor runs independently and appears in the native-window taskbar. TASK PREFSAVE "text_editor","basic" selects the optional built-in BASIC editor; "microsoft" restores the default. TASK APP "editor" always selects the built-in BASIC editor and retains its task-ID interface.

TASK WINDOWS WINDOWS$ returns up to 256 taskbar windows as newline-terminated X11 window ID<TAB>state<TAB>title rows. States are OPEN, ACTIVE, and MINIMIZED. These window IDs are separate from BASIC task IDs. Without --linux-apps, only caller-owned BASIC descendants are included. With that capability, eligible native X11 windows are also included; ownership restrictions still apply to other BASIC windows in the same runtime. Docks and skip-taskbar windows are omitted; titles are sanitized and limited to 200 characters.

TASK WINDOW windowID,action$ accepts restore, minimize, maximize (toggle), and close. Restore activates the window and switches to its workspace when needed. Close asks the window manager for a normal close, allowing the application to prompt for unsaved work. Missing or no-longer-eligible IDs are a no-op, so a stale taskbar click cannot terminate the desktop. These commands require a graphical window and an EWMH-compatible X11 window manager for native controls; they do not provide native Wayland window management.

TEXT x,y,size,text$[,color] draws text at a pixel size with an alphabetic baseline at y. On Linux, FONT SYSTEM "sans" selects modern sans-serif controls and FONT SYSTEM "monospace" selects a code/editor face. These use Pango/Cairo for antialiasing, Unicode shaping and installed-font fallback. The desktop, Office and browser use FONT SYSTEM "ui" (Noto Sans), with "ui-monospace" (Noto Sans Mono) in the editor. Install libpangocairo-1.0-0, fonts-noto-core and fonts-noto-mono on Debian; installed-font fallback remains available. Pango 1.44 or newer is required. Missing native libraries produce an error when a system face is selected.

TEXTWIDTH(text$,size,family$) returns the rendered advance in pixels for "sans" (also "sans-serif"), "monospace", "ui" or "ui-monospace", using the same font service. Fractional advances keep caret placement consistent when windows resize. Vector interfaces using system fonts render directly at the fitted window resolution, instead of shrinking an already rasterized font. Exported graphics retain their logical resolution, and bitmap/pixel art keeps its original sampling. System sizes must be greater than zero and at most 512 pixels. Each text run is limited to 65,536 UTF-8 bytes, a byte-count times size of 1,000,000, and a 4 MiB coverage mask; the shared per-thread text cache is bounded to 8 MiB and 512 entries. These limits prevent unbounded native raster allocations.

FONT BUILTIN restores the portable ASCII drawing face, which needs no host font service. FONT path$,cell-width,cell-height[,first-codepoint] selects a preloaded bitmap sheet for later TEXT statements. Glyph cells are read left-to-right and top-to-bottom. Their alpha and brightness form a mask that is tinted by the TEXT color, so a portable black-and-white PPM sheet works as well as an alpha PNG. Image dimensions must be exact multiples of the positive cell dimensions. The default first codepoint is printable ASCII 32. Reduced bitmap glyphs use bilinear coverage filtering clamped to their own atlas cell; native-size and enlarged pixel fonts retain their original pixels.

The system-hub command EDIT FONT opens the built-in graphical 8x8 editor in an independent window. It covers ASCII 32 through 127 and exports the complete 16-by-6 sheet as assets/custom_font.ppm, ready for FONT "assets/custom_font.ppm",8,8,32. S saves, L loads, and U undoes/redoes the last edit or mouse stroke. The filename dialog accepts another relative path; its parent directory must already exist. Loading accepts 128x48 binary PPM (P6, max value 255) with strictly black or white pixels, including header comments and CRLF line endings. Larger Office font atlases and TrueType fonts are outside this pixel editor's format. Invalid files leave the current font unchanged. Both editors confirm saves and unsaved quit/window-close requests; staged saves preserve the old destination if writing fails. Explicit hub task termination still stops the editor immediately.

CLS [color] deterministically clears the selected drawing buffer, its sprite state, and its current drawing point. A front-buffer clear is presented immediately; a back-buffer clear becomes visible only at FLIP, preserving tear-free double-buffer rules. CLS in text mode clears text, while an argument-free CLS in SCREEN SPLIT clears both the text region and selected graphics buffer. Retained raster acceleration is required to produce the exact same pixels as a cold render after a clear.

SPRITE id,x,y,width,height[,fill[,stroke]] creates or replaces a visible axis-aligned sprite, and MOVESPRITE id,x,y moves it. SPRITE IMAGE id,path$,x,y,width,height[,transparent-color] creates the same named motion/collision object from a preloaded PPM, PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, or TIFF image. The optional color makes exactly matching RGB pixels transparent; omit it or pass "NONE" to preserve the image's native alpha. Image sprites work with MOVESPRITE, SPRITEMOTION, ADVANCESPRITES, buffer swapping, and collision traps without a parallel visual object to keep synchronized. Using (x,y,z) in place of the two screen coordinates maps that image into the retained 3D world; its prepared pixels are shared, projected, depth-sorted, and lit as described above.

The system-hub command EDIT SPRITE opens the built-in graphical sprite editor in an independent window. It provides eight 24x21 slots, four paint colors, keyboard and mouse drawing, copy, auto-cursor, X/Y expansion previews, and live preview. Each slot exports directly to assets/sprite1.ppm through assets/sprite8.ppm; use black as the optional transparent color. S saves and L loads the current slot, with an editable relative filename. Imports must be 24x21 P6 images (max value 255) using the editor's black, white, green, orange, and pink palette. Other colors are rejected instead of being silently changed. U undoes/redoes the last edit or stroke; copy asks before replacing the next slot. Quit checks unsaved changes across all eight slots. Left drag paints, right drag erases, and clicking a palette swatch selects its ink.

For any sprite form, PCOLLISION(a,b) tests one pair; PCOLLISION(a) tests that sprite against all others. A true query is -1, false is 0, and edge-only contact is not overlap. ON COLLISION GOSUB line registers an edge-triggered handler; COLLISION ON, OFF, and STOP enable, discard, or suspend delivery. The matching RETURN re-arms the trap.

SPRITEMOTION id,vx,vy[,ax,ay] gives a classic 2D sprite velocity and optional acceleration in logical pixels per second. The retained XYZ form and its depth queries are defined in the point-perspective section above. ADVANCESPRITES seconds advances every sprite with deterministic constant-acceleration motion; one step is limited to 60 seconds. SPRITEX, SPRITEY, SPRITEVX, SPRITEVY, SPRITEAX, and SPRITEAY query either sprite form, for example SPRITEX(SHIP). Explicit stepping makes animation repeatable during testing and video export instead of coupling physics to host rendering speed.

FLIPBOOK CREATE id,template$,first,last,fps creates an ordered movie asset from frames already decoded and retained in RAM at program load. The template contains exactly one contiguous number field, for example "page####.ppm"; frame 7 then maps to page0007.ppm. Every numbered still must already exist in the sandbox, FPS is 1 through 120, and the sequence is bounded to 30 minutes. FLIPBOOK REMOVE id removes one retained sequence and FLIPBOOK CLEAR removes all of them.

PLAY FLIPBOOK id[,loops[,soundtrack$]] projects complete frames sequentially at the retained rate, which is the electronic equivalent of flipping a paper book. It checks Ctrl+Escape between frames and preserves the logical screen's aspect ratio by bilinear scaling and letterboxing. VIDEO EXPORT id,path$[,soundtrack$] sends the same retained still sequence directly to an MP4, WebM, or animated GIF. It is the declarative counterpart to procedural VIDEO START/FRAME/STOP; there is one frame stream and one encoder, not a duplicate movie implementation.

Classic named-note forms such as PLAY "C4/4 E4/4" are unchanged. The explicit modern forms PLAY AUDIO source$ and PLAY VIDEO source$ decode sandboxed local media or, with the network capability enabled, direct HTTP(S) media streams. PLAY FLIPBOOK plays a retained still sequence. Local audio supports WAV, MP3, FLAC, Ogg, Opus, M4A, and AAC; local video supports MP4, WebM, Matroska, MOV, AVI, and M4V. Direct podcast/audio or video stream URLs may be played. Web pages such as YouTube and Netflix are opened with WEB OPEN so the host browser—not the media decoder—handles site code, accounts, and licensed playback.

VIDEO START path$,fps[,soundtrack$] begins a bounded program-generated recording; VIDEO FRAME appends the currently displayed graphics screen, and VIDEO STOP finishes it. Paths must end in .mp4, .webm, or .gif, the frame rate is 1 through 120, all frames retain the first frame's dimensions, and a recording is limited to 30 minutes. An optional soundtrack must be an existing sandboxed .wav output (normally created by WAVEFILE) and is supported for MP4 and WebM; GIF remains silent. Short audio is padded with silence and long audio is clipped so the submitted video frames define the recording duration. Encoding uses the host FFmpeg executable through a fixed argument interface—BASIC cannot supply filters, shell text, camera input, or editor commands. END and BASIC STOP safely finish an active nonempty recording. Generated VIDEO, WAVEFILE, SCREENSHOT, SAVEIMAGE, RENDER, and explicit graph-display files use the separately sandboxed output root when one is configured; packaged CLI and shell sessions gather them in the project root's output/ directory. Ordinary BASIC data files remain under the file root. MP4 output uses a high-quality H.264 CRF 17 encode, a bounded real-time encoder configuration, and the compatible 4:2:0 pixel format. See programs/demos/modernbasic_capabilities_presentation.bas for a live, wall-clock-synchronized program-generated soundtrack and animation (with an explicit RECORDING=1 export mode), and programs/demos/programmed_animation_video.bas for a complete six-second, 1920x1080, 60 fps graphics-only programmed scene. It uses BUFFER and FLIP so live display presents complete frames instead of partial redraws.

Graphical-shell programs can poll MOUSEX(), MOUSEY(), MOUSEINSIDE(), and MOUSEBUTTON(1..3). Coordinates are mapped through the fitted viewport to the logical BASIC screen even when the native window is resized; letterbox and pillarbox bars are outside the device and make MOUSEINSIDE() false. INKEY$() removes the oldest queued key without waiting; printable keys are returned as characters and navigation keys as names such as LEFT, RIGHT, UP, DOWN, ENTER, or ESC. The queue is bounded to 64 entries. Headless runs return zero/false mouse state and an empty key string.
