## Graphics

The canonical graphics statement families are:

```text
SCREEN       CLS          COLOR          PALETTE
PSET         PRESET       LINE           BRUSH
RECTANGLE    CIRCLE       ELLIPSE        PAINT
MOVE         DRAWTO       DRAW           POLYGON
GRADIENT     RADIALGRADIENT
ARC          BEZIER       ROUNDEDRECT
OPACITY      BLEND
TRANSLATE    ROTATE       SCALE
NGON         STAR         PATH           BITMAP
PERSPECTIVE  OBJECT       LIGHT
DEPTHGRID    DEPTHPERCEPTION
GRIDON       GRIDOFF      GRIDPOINT
LAYER        ENDLAYER     GROUP          ENDGROUP
TEXT         FONT
SPRITE       MOVESPRITE   SPRITEMOTION   ADVANCESPRITES
BUFFER       FRAME        FLIP
SCREENSHOT   SAVEIMAGE    DISPLAY
FLIPBOOK     VIDEO
```

The principal family subcommands and operating modes are:

```text
SCREEN TEXT|GRAPHICS|GRAPHICS2D|GRAPHICS3D|SPLIT
SCREEN STANDARD|HD|HDPLUS|FULLHD|QHD|ULTRAWIDE|UHD
SCREEN classic-mode
SCREEN width,height[,background]

PAINT (x,y)[,fill[,border]]
PAINT TEXTURE path$,seed,scale,octaves,color1,color2[,opacity[,blend$]]
PAINT FILTER "BLUR",radius
PAINT FILTER "SHARPEN",amount
PAINT FILTER "COLOR",brightness,contrast,saturation

BITMAP path$,x,y,width,height
BITMAP WARP path$,anchor-x,anchor-y,width,height,angle,bend,turn[,light]

OBJECT SHAPE id,x,y,z,width,height,fill[,stroke]
OBJECT MOVE id,x,y,z
FONT path$,cell-width,cell-height[,first-codepoint]
FONT BUILTIN
FONT SYSTEM "sans"
FONT SYSTEM "monospace"
FONT SYSTEM "ui"
FONT SYSTEM "ui-monospace"
SPRITE IMAGE id,path$,x,y,width,height[,transparent-color]
SPRITE IMAGE id,path$,(x,y,z),width,height[,transparent-color]
SPRITE ORIENT id,HORIZON|SCREEN

OBJECT SCALE id,width,height
OBJECT CAMERA x,y,z
OBJECT LIGHT id,x,y,z,intensity,range,color
OBJECT REMOVE id
OBJECT CLEAR

FLIPBOOK CREATE id,template$,first,last,fps
FLIPBOOK REMOVE id
FLIPBOOK CLEAR

VIDEO START path$,fps[,soundtrack$]
VIDEO FRAME
VIDEO STOP
VIDEO EXPORT flipbook-id,path$[,soundtrack$]
```

Accepted graphics aliases are `RECT` for `RECTANGLE`, `OVAL` for `ELLIPSE`,
`BEGINLAYER` for `LAYER`, `BEGINGROUP` for `GROUP`, `BLIT` for `SPRITE`, and
`RENDER` for `SAVEIMAGE`. Each pair reaches one implementation rather than
duplicating the feature.

The organized calculator-style graph family is:

```text
GRAPH CLEAR
GRAPH DISPLAY [path$]
GRAPH WINDOW xmin,xmax,xscale,ymin,ymax,yscale
GRAPH FUNCTION expression[,color]        GRAPH PLOT is an alias
GRAPH INVERSE expression[,color]
GRAPH LINE ...                           GRAPH CIRCLE ...
GRAPH TEXT ...
GRAPH HORIZONTAL ...                     GRAPH VERTICAL ...
GRAPH TANGENT ...                        GRAPH SHADE ...
GRAPH GRID ON|OFF
GRAPH AXES ON|OFF
GRAPH LABELS ON|OFF
GRAPH COORDS ON|OFF
GRAPH ZOOM STANDARD|TRIG|DECIMAL|SQUARE
```

The direct TI-style graph spellings are:

```text
CLRDRAW       DISPGRAPH
ZSTANDARD     ZTRIG         ZDECIMAL      ZSQUARE
AXESON        AXESOFF
LABELON       LABELOFF
COORDON       COORDOFF
GLINE         HORIZONTAL    VERTICAL      GCIRCLE
DRAWF         DRAWINV       TANGENT       SHADE
FNON          FNOFF         GRAPHSTYLE
PXL-ON        PXL-OFF       PXL-CHANGE
PT-ON         PT-OFF        PT-CHANGE
GTEXT
```

Direct `GRIDON` and `GRIDOFF` belong to the retained depth-grid graphics
family because that dispatcher has priority. Use `GRAPH GRID ON` and
`GRAPH GRID OFF` for the calculator graph grid. Scatter, histogram,
parametric, and polar renderers are command-line library facilities, not BASIC
statements.

The Artist-derived renderer is built into the Rust library; no external
graphics compatibility renderer is selected at runtime.

`RECT` and `RECTANGLE` accept either
`x,y,width,height[,stroke[,fill[,stroke_width]]]` or the endpoint form
`(x1,y1)-(x2,y2)[,stroke[,fill[,stroke_width]]]`. Graphics colors may be
palette indexes, hexadecimal strings, or case-insensitive names such as
`"RED"`, `"SKYBLUE"`, and `"GOLD"`; `#RRGGBBAA` adds an alpha channel.
Lines, circles, ellipses, rounded rectangles, and their filled/stroked edges
use subpixel coverage in the integrated raster and video renderer.
`BRUSH (x1,y1)-(x2,y2),size,color[,hardness[,opacity[,flow]]]` paints an
antialiased soft or hard stroke. `size` is 0.1 through 2048 logical pixels;
hardness, opacity, and flow are independently normalized from 0 through 1.
The retained command is rendered identically for the live screen, still-image
output, and video frames.

`MOVE x,y` changes the current drawing point. `DRAWTO
x,y[,color[,width]]` draws from that point and makes the destination the new
current point. Additional `DRAWTO` fields are not part of the language syntax.

`BITMAP path$,x,y,width,height` accepts bounded P6 PPM plus PNG, JPEG, WebP,
BMP, and TIFF stills. Compressed images are decoded locally through fixed
FFmpeg arguments; URLs and decoder options are not accepted. Alpha from formats
that carry it is retained, and premultiplied bilinear filtering prevents dark
fringes at transparent edges.

`BITMAP WARP path$,anchor-x,anchor-y,width,height,angle,bend,turn[,light]` is
the deformable form in the same statement family. The source bottom center is
anchored at `(anchor-x,anchor-y)`; angle is clockwise degrees, bend and turn are
normalized from -1 through 1, and optional light is 0 through 2 with a default
of 1. A bounded texture mesh curves the centerline, foreshortens and shades the
turned surface, and preserves source alpha. This suits leaves, flags, cloth, and
other photographed or painted flexible objects without introducing a second
bitmap command. PNG export follows the complete raster path, so imported
photographic pixels, alpha compositing, warping, and vector painting all survive
into the exported still instead of being dropped by a vector-only conversion.

`PAINT (x,y)[,fill[,border]]` flood-fills from the seed pixel. Without a
border argument, it replaces the connected region matching the seed's rendered
color. With a border argument, it crosses intervening rendered colors and stops
at pixels matching that border, preserving the classic Microsoft behavior.
`DRAW`'s `Pfill,border` macro command uses the same renderer and palette
colors.
Custom screens are limited to 16,777,216 pixels so framebuffer and flood-fill
allocations remain bounded.

Modern raster painting stays in that classic statement family:

```basic
PAINT TEXTURE path$,seed,scale,octaves,color1,color2[,opacity[,blend$]]
PAINT FILTER "BLUR",radius
PAINT FILTER "SHARPEN",amount
PAINT FILTER "COLOR",brightness,contrast,saturation
```

`PAINT TEXTURE` synthesizes deterministic smooth fractal detail and clips it to
each closed subpath. `seed` selects the repeatable pattern, `scale` is 0.25
through 4096 logical pixels, `octaves` is 1 through 8, opacity is 0 through 1,
and the optional blend uses the existing `BLEND` mode names. Layer two or more
scales to build macro color variation and fine surface grain without a source
bitmap. `PAINT FILTER` finishes the complete raster accumulated so far: blur
radius is 0 through 32 pixels, sharpen amount is 0 through 4, and the three
color multipliers are each 0 through 4. These are retained, deterministic,
memory-bounded raster operations used by screen presentation, PPM/PNG capture,
FLIPBOOK, and VIDEO output. Like imported bitmap pixels, procedural textures and
finished pixels are raster effects and are not emitted as editable SVG objects.

`SCREEN width,height[,background]` defines the logical graphics device, not a
request to change the physical monitor mode. All drawing, sprite, collision,
mouse, screenshot, and video coordinates use that logical pixel grid. Resizing
the host window never changes the BASIC screen or its aspect ratio. The native
game presets are:

| Preset | Logical size |
|---|---:|
| `HD` | 1280x720 |
| `HDPLUS` | 1600x900 |
| `FULLHD` / `FHD` | 1920x1080 |
| `QHD` | 2560x1440 |
| `ULTRAWIDE` / `UWQHD` | 3440x1440 |
| `UHD` / `4K` | 3840x2160 |

`STANDARD` remains 1024x768. Quoted `"720P"`, `"900P"`, `"1080P"`,
`"1440P"`, and `"2160P"` aliases are also accepted. The native shell
defaults to `--graphics-scale fit`, centering the complete device with
black letterbox or pillarbox bars. Program window frames are kept within the
desktop when created or resized by `SCREEN`; the full logical canvas scales to
fit that window. Smaller programs retain their own independent window sizes.
`--graphics-scale stretch` explicitly fills
the host graphics region and may distort the image. Initial window profiles are
`--display-profile compact` (800x600), `desktop` (1100x760), `hd` (1280x720),
and `fullhd` (1920x1080); `--width` and `--height` override either dimension,
and the shell clamps the initial size to the available physical display. These
host options do not alter BASIC language behavior or exported image/video
resolution. `SCREEN TEXT`, `SCREEN GRAPHICS`, `SCREEN GRAPHICS2D`,
`SCREEN GRAPHICS3D`, and `SCREEN SPLIT` select the visible operating mode
without changing the host display. A numeric or
`SCREEN width,height[,background]` configuration resets the logical graphics
device to 2D and clears retained perspective state.

Point-perspective graphics reuse classic pixel and sprite statements and keep
one organized `OBJECT` family:

```basic
10 SCREEN FULLHD
20 PERSPECTIVE 960,500,900,1,10000,.25
30 PSET (-30,0,180),"WHITE"
40 OBJECT SHAPE TOWER,0,0,100,20,80,"GOLD","BROWN"
50 SPRITE IMAGE SHIP,"assets/sprite1.ppm",(25,0,70),12,8,"BLACK"
60 OBJECT LIGHT SUN,-40,80,30,1.2,500,"WHITE"
70 MOVESPRITE SHIP,30,5,60
80 SPRITEMOTION SHIP,2,0,-4,0,0,1
```

`PERSPECTIVE horizon-x,horizon-y,focal-length[,near,far,ambient]` configures
the vanishing point, depth clipping, and base light. It also selects 3D mode.
Every retained world pixel, object, and 3D sprite stores X, Y, and Z in memory;
positive Y is up, the camera looks toward positive Z, and Z supplies depth.
The world is one bounded native map containing up to 65,536 combined objects,
sprites, and XYZ pixels plus 256 point lights. Updating a camera or entity
changes this retained state rather than rebuilding a separate scene graph.

Image assets are decoded once during program preparation and owned by shared
memory. An XYZ image sprite stores only its texture mapping and transform; the
renderer reuses a bounded 64 MiB per-thread pixel cache. Frame rendering does
not reopen the source file, and many sprites may share one texture allocation.

Classic `PSET (x,y)[,color]` remains an immediate 2D canvas pixel.
`RGB(red,green,blue)` and `RGBA(red,green,blue,alpha)` construct true-color
values from integer channels in the inclusive range 0 through 255. They return
canonical `#rrggbb` and `#rrggbbaa` color strings, keeping true colors distinct
from numeric palette indices. Consecutive identity-coordinate PSET operations
on one scanline are retained as one raster run; `SCREENLOCK` and
`SCREENUNLOCK` suppress intermediate presentations during large pixel loops.
`PSET (x,y,z)[,color]` stores a one-world-unit pixel at that XYZ coordinate;
its projected square grows nearer the camera and shrinks farther away.
`PRESET (x,y,z)` removes the retained pixel at that exact coordinate.

Classic `SPRITE id,x,y,width,height[,fill[,stroke]]` remains a 2D screen
sprite. `SPRITE id,(x,y,z),width,height[,fill[,stroke]]` stores an XYZ sprite
whose coordinate is its bottom-center anchor. `SPRITE IMAGE
id,path$,(x,y,z),width,height[,transparent-color]` maps one prepared image onto
the same retained 3D billboard. PPM, PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, and TIFF are
accepted; the optional color is an exact RGB transparency key, while `"NONE"`
preserves source alpha. The mapped pixels receive ambient and point-light tint
without producing a per-sprite copy.

`MOVESPRITE id,x,y[,z]` moves either form; omitting Z preserves an XYZ sprite
depth. `SPRITEMOTION` keeps its 2D `id,vx,vy[,ax,ay]` form and adds
`id,vx,vy,vz[,ax,ay,az]`. `ADVANCESPRITES seconds` integrates all axes.
`SPRITE ORIENT id,HORIZON` yaws a mapped XYZ sprite toward the configured
perspective horizon. Its nose shifts toward the vanishing point and its width
foreshortens, while horizontal image rows remain horizontal so the craft does
not roll onto its side. The transform is recomputed after every world or camera
move. `SPRITE ORIENT id,SCREEN` restores the usual camera-facing, axis-aligned
billboard. The command rejects 2D and untextured sprites.
`SPRITEX`, `SPRITEY`, `SPRITEZ`, `SPRITESCALE`, `SPRITEVX`, `SPRITEVY`,
`SPRITEVZ`, `SPRITEAX`, `SPRITEAY`, and `SPRITEAZ` query retained state. A 2D
sprite reports Z zero and scale one. Collision tests use the current projected
bounds of XYZ sprites. Sprite and object statement/query identifiers may be
bare names or string expressions such as `ID$="DRONE1":PRINT SPRITEZ(ID$)`;
this supports compact loops over pooled world entities.

`OBJECT SHAPE id,x,y,z,width,height,fill[,stroke]` stores a billboard object
with the same bottom-center convention. `OBJECT MOVE`, `OBJECT SCALE`,
`OBJECT CAMERA`, `OBJECT LIGHT`, `OBJECT REMOVE`, and `OBJECT CLEAR` are the
mutating members for these legacy billboards; polygonal meshes use the additions below.
`OBJECTX`, `OBJECTY`, `OBJECTZ`, `OBJECTSCALE`, `OBJECTWIDTH`, and
`OBJECTHEIGHT` query retained object state.

Projection uses `screen-scale=focal-length/(entity-z-camera-z)`. Entities
outside the near/far interval are clipped. Every visible pixel, object, and
sprite is sorted together from far to near, so depth controls both scaling and
layering. Each `OBJECT LIGHT id,x,y,z,intensity,range,color` applies the same
bounded distance-attenuated shading to every retained entity type, including
the per-channel tint of mapped sprite pixels. This creates the 3D illusion on
the 2D canvas without pretending to be a polygonal mesh renderer.

The additional polygonal mesh pipeline uses these `OBJECT` commands:

```text
OBJECT MESH id,vertices,triangles,color
OBJECT NORMALS id,cornerNormals
OBJECT TRANSFORM id,modelMatrix
OBJECT VIEW viewMatrix,projectionMatrix
OBJECT SUN x,y,z,ambient
OBJECT TEXTURE id,path$
OBJECT IMAGE id,imageName$[,filter$]
OBJECT RENDER
```

Vertices are a nested list of `{x,y,z}` or `{x,y,z,u,v}` rows; triangles are
one-based index triples. Defining a mesh replaces that mesh's geometry, model
transform and texture. Mesh names are case-insensitive, 1..128 bytes. Models
and views must be affine 4-by-4 matrices; projection matrices use the conventions
above. `OBJECT SUN` gives the world-space direction toward the light and ambient
brightness in [0,1]. Faces default to flat Lambert lighting; winding determines the
normal, with no backface culling. Materials must be opaque. Textures use the
existing confined image loader and shared prepared-image storage, nearest-neighbor
sampling and clamped UV coordinates; V=0 is the image bottom. Texture alpha below
128 discards a fragment; other fragments are opaque. Blended transparency is not
implemented.

`OBJECT IMAGE id,imageName$[,filter$]` instead binds a snapshot of a named
linear RGBA `IMAGE` buffer, with `LINEAR` (default) or `NEAREST` filtering.
UVs describe image edges: (0,0) is the top left, V increases downward, and
pixel centers are `((x+.5)/width,(y+.5)/height)`, matching `IMAGE HEIGHTMESH`.
Coordinates clamp at edges. This path decodes the material color to linear RGB,
uses shared Rust perspective interpolation, alpha-correct sampling, face normals
and cosine lighting, then clips and encodes the result to display sRGB.
Alpha below .5 discards a fragment without writing depth; survivors are opaque.
This explicit path preserves `OBJECT TEXTURE`'s legacy byte-lighting and UV rules.

Binding shares the image and its existing memory reservation without copying
pixels. Replacing/freeing the named buffer leaves the bound snapshot unchanged;
its memory stays charged until the last owner releases it. `IMAGE CLEAR`, BASIC
`CLEAR` and `RUN` release names but do not remove an existing mesh's snapshot.
`OBJECT REMOVE/CLEAR`, redefining the mesh, replacing its texture, numeric `SCREEN`
and full program replacement release the binding. A failed binding preserves
the old texture. See `programs/examples/image_surface.bas` for an editable scene.

`OBJECT NORMALS id,cornerNormals` opts into smooth per-pixel lighting. Supply
one row per triangle, each containing three nonzero finite `{nx,ny,nz}` normals
in triangle-corner order. `MESHCORNERNORMALS3D` generates these from indexed
geometry; authored normals are also accepted. Inputs are normalized and replaced
atomically. `{}` restores flat shading. Redefining/removing the mesh or resetting
the graphics world releases the normals. These bounded values add 72 bytes per
triangle, within the existing 100,000-triangle scene cap.

Normals are in model coordinates. The renderer applies the model's cofactor map,
preserving indexed winding through reflections; it clips and interpolates the
transformed normals perspective-correctly, then normalizes for per-pixel lighting.
A zero transformed/interpolated normal is an error and leaves the draw buffer
unchanged. Supplied normals need not agree with face normals; the caller owns
that choice. A geometrically collapsed face remains skipped as before.

Smooth lighting uses linear color for plain materials and either texture source.
For `OBJECT TEXTURE` with normals enabled, its bottom-origin endpoint UVs and
nearest sampling remain, but sampled sRGB bytes are decoded before lighting.
`OBJECT IMAGE` keeps its top-left image-edge UVs and alpha-aware filtering.
The default flat `OBJECT TEXTURE` path retains byte lighting. Opaque/cutout
coverage still applies; smooth lighting does not add antialiasing, blended
transparency, geometric subdivision, shadows or physical light transport.
See `programs/examples/smooth_surface.bas` for flat/smooth image comparisons.

`OBJECT RENDER` rasterizes all meshes together onto the current draw buffer,
using six-plane homogeneous clipping, per-pixel depth testing and perspective-
correct texture coordinates. Call it after updating transforms and clearing the
frame; FLIP presents the buffer as usual. Existing 2D drawing can be used for
annotations. `OBJECT REMOVE id` removes a mesh or a legacy billboard, and
`OBJECT CLEAR` clears both worlds. Numeric SCREEN resets both. Meshes and legacy
billboards have separate depth systems; billboards are not occluded by mesh depth.

This is a CPU renderer. Each scene allows 1,024 meshes, 200,000 vertices and
100,000 triangles in total. Each render allows at most 8,388,608 pixels and
100 million bounding-box samples, with cancellation checks between faces and
scanline batches. Rendering failure leaves the draw buffer unchanged. GPU
rendering, shadows, skeletal animation, scene-format interchange, hierarchy,
physics and picking remain future work. Source-controlled procedural meshes and
animation are demonstrated in `programs/examples/mesh_science.bas`.

`SCREEN GRAPHICS2D` hides the projected world without deleting it;
`SCREEN GRAPHICS3D` shows it again. `CLS` clears ordinary drawing state, while
`OBJECT CLEAR` releases the XYZ entity mappings and lights. Prepared image
assets deliberately remain available for later sprites until another program
is loaded or the session closes. A numeric or named-resolution `SCREEN`
configuration resets the world. Live display, PPM/PNG export, screenshots, and
video all use the same projection; raster-mapped images are not emitted as
editable SVG image objects.

The bundled `programs/games/neon_depth_runner.bas` is a playable end-to-end
example. It creates keyed textures with native drawing commands, retains them
in memory, shares the drone/orb pixels across instances, and combines XYZ
motion, camera/light updates, depth sorting, projected collision, and scalable
HUD drawing. Its title screen selects HD, Full HD, QHD, ultrawide, or UHD.

`GRADIENT id,x1,y1,x2,y2,color1,color2` and
`RADIALGRADIENT id,cx,cy,radius,color1,color2` define smooth paints. Pass
`"url(#id)"` as a shape's fill to use one in live raster, SVG, screenshot, and
video output. For example:

```basic
10 GRADIENT SKY,0,0,0,720,"#050817","#4A285D"
20 RECTANGLE 0,0,1280,720,"none","url(#SKY)",1
```

`OPACITY value` and `BLEND mode$` modify the most recently drawn shape.
Available raster/SVG modes are `normal`, `multiply`, `screen`, `overlay`,
`darken`, `lighten`, `difference`, `xor`, `add`, `exclusion`, `color-dodge`,
`color-burn`, `hard-light`, `soft-light`, `erase`, `hue`, `saturation`,
`color`, and `luminosity`. Raster compositing uses bounded shape-local work
buffers rather than allocating two full screens for every effect.

`SCREENCONTROL flag,value` controls the program window: flag 0 sets its title
with a string; flags 1, 2 and 3 enable/disable fullscreen, resizing and pointer
visibility with a numeric Boolean. Flag 4 opts into application-owned Close
requests: `SCREENCONTROL 4,1` makes `INKEY$` return `"CLOSE"` when the window
manager asks to close a running program. The program must handle that event and
use `END` when ready, for example after confirming unsaved work. The default
and `SCREENCONTROL 4,0` close normally. Ctrl+Escape remains available to interrupt.
Flag 5 publishes a string to the system clipboard: `SCREENCONTROL 5,text$`.
The window serves UTF-8 text while it remains open; PRIMARY selection ownership
is unchanged. As with other window controls, this has no effect without a
connected graphical window. An external clipboard manager is needed to retain
the text after the window closes.

Running graphical programs receive `CTRL+A`, `CTRL+C` and `CTRL+X` through
`INKEY$`, in addition to `CTRL+N/O/S/F/Z/Y` (each returned separately).
Arrow, Home/End and Page Up/Down events include held modifiers, such as
`SHIFT+LEFT`, `CTRL+HOME` or `CTRL+SHIFT+END`. Unmodified names are unchanged.
Ctrl+V and Shift+Insert continue to deliver clipboard contents as queued text.

Graphical BASIC applications can launch and manage independent BASIC windows:

```basic
TASK BROWSER ID
TASK APP "writer",ID
TASK APP "editor","notes.txt",ID
TASK RUN "program.bas",ID
TASK SOURCE SOURCE$,"draft.bas",ID
TASK LIST TASKS$
TASK FOCUS ID
TASK STOP ID
TASK CLOSE ID
TASK ERROR MESSAGE$
```

`TASK BROWSER ID` launches the bundled BASIC browser application in an independent
program window, inheriting the caller's workspace and network permission. Its
interface is BASIC; website rendering uses the optional native browser backend.

`TASK APP name$,ID` launches a bundled BASIC application: `editor`, `files`,
`office`, `writer`, `sheet` or `slides`. Office starts in Writer mode with the
Office window title and access to the other modes. `TASK APP "editor",path$,ID` opens a workspace
text file in a new editor window. Each launch has separate document and interpreter
state. Applications inherit the caller's capabilities and file/output roots.
The bundled desktop, browser and Office native executables default to
`~/ModernBASIC` when no host `--file-root` is supplied; default setup creates
`Programs` and rejects linked workspace/Programs directories. A missing home
requires an explicit root, never a fallback to the process working directory.
This bundled-application policy does not change ordinary `COMPILE` programs,
which retain their working-directory default. Explicit host capability options
remain separate from BASIC arguments after `--`.

`TASK LINUXAPPS list$` lists visible registered Linux desktop applications as
newline-separated `desktop ID<TAB>display name<TAB>description` rows.
`TASK LINUXLAUNCH desktopId$` requests a launch of an ID from that list. Both need
host `--linux-apps`; network/native-compilation permissions do not imply it.
The host uses system Python/PyGObject/GIO to apply desktop-entry rules. These
commands do not expose host filesystem browsing or accept arbitrary commands.
Launched Linux applications retain their own filesystem access and native UI.

`TASK RUN` reads a bounded source snapshot inside the current file workspace;
`.m64b` selects the tokenized program format. `TASK SOURCE` runs supplied source
text using a workspace-relative document path for its title and static assets,
without writing that path. Both return the new numeric task ID in a scalar
variable and leave the caller running. Children inherit the caller's capabilities,
file/output roots and execution limits, with separate interpreter state. Static
assets resolve relative to the selected source path. Task startup errors use
normal `ON ERROR` handling; `TASK ERROR` retrieves and clears the last task error
message. Runtime failures are displayed in the child's own window.

`TASK LIST` returns the caller's open descendant windows, sorted by ID, as newline-
terminated rows of `ID`, state and filename separated by tabs. States are
`RUNNING`, `READY`, `STOPPED` and `ERROR`. Focus, Stop and Close accept only IDs
launched by that caller or its descendants. Sibling and unrelated applications
are excluded. Closing an intermediate app reparents its children to its caller;
children continue running. Stop interrupts execution while preserving its window;
Close destroys the window and discards its session, so application code should
confirm when needed. Requests are bounded, and at most 32 program windows can
exist in one graphical session. Task operations require a graphical program
window; headless use reports an error. `TASK ERROR` works without a window.

`TASK EDIT path$` opens the system text editor; pass `""` for a blank document.
The default is Microsoft Edit, requiring `--linux-apps`, system Python with GTK 3
and VTE 2.91, and `msedit` (or `MODERNBASIC_EDIT_BINARY`). The supplied path is
resolved inside the BASIC workspace, rejecting absolute paths, traversal and
symlinks. Microsoft Edit's own file dialogs subsequently use normal Linux user
permissions. Startup errors use normal `ON ERROR` / `TASK ERROR` handling.
The editor runs independently and appears in the native-window taskbar.
`TASK PREFSAVE "text_editor","basic"` selects the optional built-in BASIC editor;
`"microsoft"` restores the default. `TASK APP "editor"` always selects the built-in
BASIC editor and retains its task-ID interface.

`TASK WINDOWS WINDOWS$` returns up to 256 taskbar windows as newline-terminated
`X11 window ID<TAB>state<TAB>title` rows. States are `OPEN`, `ACTIVE`, and
`MINIMIZED`. These window IDs are separate from BASIC task IDs. Without
`--linux-apps`, only caller-owned BASIC descendants are included. With that
capability, eligible native X11 windows are also included; ownership restrictions
still apply to other BASIC windows in the same runtime. Docks and skip-taskbar
windows are omitted; titles are sanitized and limited to 200 characters.

`TASK WINDOW windowID,action$` accepts `restore`, `minimize`, `maximize` (toggle),
and `close`. Restore activates the window and switches to its workspace when
needed. Close asks the window manager for a normal close, allowing the
application to prompt for unsaved work. Missing or no-longer-eligible IDs are a
no-op, so a stale taskbar click cannot terminate the desktop. These commands
require a graphical window and an EWMH-compatible X11 window manager for native
controls; they do not provide native Wayland window management.

`TEXT x,y,size,text$[,color]` draws text at a pixel size with an alphabetic
baseline at `y`. On Linux, `FONT SYSTEM "sans"` selects modern sans-serif
controls and `FONT SYSTEM "monospace"` selects a code/editor face. These use
Pango/Cairo for antialiasing, Unicode shaping and installed-font fallback.
The desktop, Office and browser use `FONT SYSTEM "ui"` (Noto Sans), with
`"ui-monospace"` (Noto Sans Mono) in the editor. Install `libpangocairo-1.0-0`,
`fonts-noto-core` and `fonts-noto-mono` on Debian; installed-font fallback
remains available. Pango 1.44 or newer is required. Missing native libraries
produce an error when a system face is selected.

`TEXTWIDTH(text$,size,family$)` returns the rendered advance in pixels for
`"sans"` (also `"sans-serif"`), `"monospace"`, `"ui"` or `"ui-monospace"`,
using the same font service. Fractional advances keep caret placement consistent
when windows resize. Vector interfaces using system fonts render directly at
the fitted window resolution, instead of shrinking an already rasterized font.
Exported graphics retain their logical resolution, and bitmap/pixel art keeps
its original sampling.
System sizes must be greater than zero and at most 512 pixels. Each text run
is limited to 65,536 UTF-8 bytes, a byte-count times size of 1,000,000, and a
4 MiB coverage mask; the shared per-thread text cache is bounded to 8 MiB and
512 entries. These limits prevent unbounded native raster allocations.

`FONT BUILTIN` restores the portable ASCII drawing face, which needs no host
font service. `FONT path$,cell-width,cell-height[,first-codepoint]` selects a
preloaded bitmap sheet for later `TEXT` statements. Glyph cells are read
left-to-right and top-to-bottom. Their alpha and brightness form a mask that is
tinted by the `TEXT` color, so a portable black-and-white PPM sheet works as
well as an alpha PNG. Image dimensions must be exact multiples of the positive
cell dimensions. The default first codepoint is printable ASCII 32. Reduced
bitmap glyphs use bilinear coverage filtering clamped to their own atlas cell;
native-size and enlarged pixel fonts retain their original pixels.

The system-hub command `EDIT FONT` opens the built-in graphical 8x8 editor in
an independent window. It covers ASCII 32 through 127 and exports the complete
16-by-6 sheet as `assets/custom_font.ppm`, ready for `FONT
"assets/custom_font.ppm",8,8,32`. `S` saves, `L` loads, and `U` undoes/redoes the
last edit or mouse stroke. The filename dialog accepts another relative path;
its parent directory must already exist. Loading accepts 128x48 binary PPM
(P6, max value 255) with strictly black or white pixels, including header
comments and CRLF line endings. Larger Office font atlases and TrueType fonts
are outside this pixel editor's format. Invalid files leave the current font
unchanged. Both editors confirm saves and unsaved quit/window-close requests;
staged saves preserve the old destination if writing fails. Explicit hub task
termination still stops the editor immediately.

`CLS [color]` deterministically clears the selected drawing buffer, its sprite
state, and its current drawing point. A front-buffer clear is presented
immediately; a back-buffer clear becomes visible only at `FLIP`, preserving
tear-free double-buffer rules. `CLS` in text mode clears text, while an
argument-free `CLS` in `SCREEN SPLIT` clears both the text region and selected
graphics buffer. Retained raster acceleration is required to produce the exact
same pixels as a cold render after a clear.

`SPRITE id,x,y,width,height[,fill[,stroke]]` creates or replaces a visible
axis-aligned sprite, and `MOVESPRITE id,x,y` moves it. `SPRITE IMAGE
id,path$,x,y,width,height[,transparent-color]` creates the same named
motion/collision object from a preloaded PPM, PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, or TIFF
image. The optional color makes exactly matching RGB pixels transparent; omit
it or pass `"NONE"` to preserve the image's native alpha. Image sprites work
with `MOVESPRITE`, `SPRITEMOTION`, `ADVANCESPRITES`, buffer swapping, and
collision traps without a parallel visual object to keep synchronized.
Using `(x,y,z)` in place of the two screen coordinates maps that image into the
retained 3D world; its prepared pixels are shared, projected, depth-sorted, and
lit as described above.

The system-hub command `EDIT SPRITE` opens the built-in graphical sprite editor
in an independent window. It provides eight 24x21 slots, four paint colors,
keyboard and mouse drawing, copy, auto-cursor, X/Y expansion previews, and live
preview. Each slot exports directly to `assets/sprite1.ppm` through
`assets/sprite8.ppm`; use black as the optional transparent color. `S` saves
and `L` loads the current slot, with an editable relative filename. Imports
must be 24x21 P6 images (max value 255) using the editor's black, white, green,
orange, and pink palette. Other colors are rejected instead of being silently
changed. `U` undoes/redoes the last edit or stroke; copy asks before replacing
the next slot. Quit checks unsaved changes across all eight slots. Left drag
paints, right drag erases, and clicking a palette swatch selects its ink.

For any sprite form, `PCOLLISION(a,b)` tests one pair; `PCOLLISION(a)`
tests that sprite against all others. A true query is
`-1`, false is `0`, and edge-only contact is not overlap. `ON COLLISION GOSUB
line` registers an edge-triggered handler; `COLLISION ON`, `OFF`, and `STOP`
enable, discard, or suspend delivery. The matching `RETURN` re-arms the trap.

`SPRITEMOTION id,vx,vy[,ax,ay]` gives a classic 2D sprite velocity and
optional acceleration in logical pixels per second. The retained XYZ form and
its depth queries are defined in the point-perspective section above.
`ADVANCESPRITES seconds` advances every sprite with deterministic
constant-acceleration motion; one step is limited to 60 seconds. `SPRITEX`,
`SPRITEY`, `SPRITEVX`, `SPRITEVY`, `SPRITEAX`, and `SPRITEAY` query either
sprite form, for example `SPRITEX(SHIP)`. Explicit stepping makes animation
repeatable during testing and video export instead of coupling physics to host
rendering speed.

`FLIPBOOK CREATE id,template$,first,last,fps` creates an ordered movie asset
from frames already decoded and retained in RAM at program load. The template contains exactly
one contiguous number field, for example `"page####.ppm"`; frame 7 then maps
to `page0007.ppm`. Every numbered still must already exist in the sandbox, FPS
is 1 through 120, and the sequence is bounded to 30 minutes. `FLIPBOOK REMOVE
id` removes one retained sequence and `FLIPBOOK CLEAR` removes all of them.

`PLAY FLIPBOOK id[,loops[,soundtrack$]]` projects complete frames sequentially
at the retained rate, which is the electronic equivalent of flipping a paper
book. It checks Ctrl+Escape between frames and preserves the logical screen's
aspect ratio by bilinear scaling and letterboxing. `VIDEO EXPORT
id,path$[,soundtrack$]` sends the same retained still sequence directly to an
MP4, WebM, or animated GIF. It is the declarative counterpart to procedural
`VIDEO START`/`FRAME`/`STOP`; there is one frame stream and one encoder, not a
duplicate movie implementation.

Classic named-note forms such as `PLAY "C4/4 E4/4"` are unchanged. The explicit
modern forms `PLAY AUDIO source$` and `PLAY VIDEO source$` decode sandboxed
local media or, with the network capability enabled, direct HTTP(S) media
streams. `PLAY FLIPBOOK` plays a retained still sequence. Local audio supports
WAV, MP3, FLAC, Ogg, Opus, M4A, and AAC; local video supports MP4, WebM,
Matroska, MOV, AVI, and M4V. Direct podcast/audio or video stream URLs may be
played. Web pages such as YouTube and Netflix are opened with `WEB OPEN` so the
host browser—not the media decoder—handles site code, accounts, and licensed
playback.

`VIDEO START path$,fps[,soundtrack$]` begins a bounded program-generated
recording;
`VIDEO FRAME` appends the currently displayed graphics screen, and `VIDEO STOP`
finishes it. Paths must end in `.mp4`, `.webm`, or `.gif`, the frame rate is 1
through 120, all frames retain the first frame's dimensions, and a recording is
limited to 30 minutes. An optional soundtrack must be an existing sandboxed
`.wav` output (normally created by `WAVEFILE`) and is supported for MP4 and
WebM; GIF remains silent. Short audio is padded with silence and long audio is
clipped so the submitted video frames define the recording duration. Encoding
uses the host FFmpeg executable through a fixed
argument interface—BASIC cannot supply filters, shell text, camera input, or
editor commands. `END` and BASIC `STOP` safely finish an active nonempty
recording. Generated `VIDEO`, `WAVEFILE`, `SCREENSHOT`, `SAVEIMAGE`, `RENDER`,
and explicit graph-display files use the separately sandboxed output root when
one is configured; packaged CLI and shell sessions gather them in the project
root's `output/` directory. Ordinary BASIC data files remain under the file
root. MP4 output uses a high-quality H.264 CRF 17 encode, a bounded real-time
encoder configuration, and the compatible 4:2:0 pixel format. See
`programs/demos/modernbasic_capabilities_presentation.bas` for a live,
wall-clock-synchronized program-generated soundtrack and animation (with an
explicit `RECORDING=1` export mode), and
`programs/demos/programmed_animation_video.bas` for a complete six-second,
1920x1080, 60 fps graphics-only programmed scene. It uses
`BUFFER` and `FLIP` so live display presents complete frames instead of partial
redraws.

Graphical-shell programs can poll `MOUSEX()`, `MOUSEY()`, `MOUSEINSIDE()`, and
`MOUSEBUTTON(1..3)`. Coordinates are mapped through the fitted viewport to the
logical BASIC screen even when the native window is resized; letterbox and
pillarbox bars are outside the device and make `MOUSEINSIDE()` false.
`INKEY$()` removes the oldest queued key
without waiting; printable keys are returned as characters and navigation keys
as names such as `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `UP`, `DOWN`, `ENTER`, or `ESC`. The queue is
bounded to 64 entries. Headless runs return zero/false mouse state and an empty
key string.

documents.title: Audio
documents.html:
See AUDIO_REFERENCE.md for parameter ranges and note notation. The complete canonical audio statement family is:

SYNTHPROFILE  VOICES       OSCILLATORS   TEMPO
VOICE         WAVE         OSCILLATOR    ADSR
PULSEWIDTH    VOL          STEREO        PAN
MIXER         FILTER       FILTERADSR    LFO
GLIDE         DRIVE        DSP
EXPRESSION    MODULATION   SUSTAIN       PITCHBEND
REVERB        CHORUS
PLAY          SOUND        BEEP
SOUNDFONT     INSTRUMENT
WAVEFILE      SAY          SING

The media and playback subforms are:

PLAY sequence$[,default-beats]
PLAY voice,sequence$[,default-beats]
PLAY AUDIO source$
PLAY VIDEO source$
PLAY FLIPBOOK id[,loops[,soundtrack$]]

SOUND frequency,voice,duration-ms[,level][,end-frequency][,steps]
SOUND ON|OFF|WAIT|RESUME

WAVEFORM is an accepted alias for WAVE and ENVELOPE is an accepted alias for ADSR; there is no dialect selector or duplicate audio engine. Global CLEAR resets audio state along with the rest of mutable program state.

The canonical arbitrary-frequency oscillator statement is SOUND frequency,voice,duration-ms[,level][,end-frequency][,steps]. Its first three arguments are required. It generates a tone, which can represent a musical note when the supplied frequency is that note's frequency. It does not interpret note notation: PLAY is the separate named-note and sequencing statement. The complete native voice patch configures SOUND: a profile-selected bank of 1 through 8 OSCILLATOR slots, WAVE for slot 1, PULSEWIDTH, ADSR, per-voice FILTER, FILTERADSR, targeted LFO, GLIDE, DRIVE, VOL, and STEREO. MIXER voice,synth-level,midi-level independently routes PLAY to the computer synthesizer, the MIDI/SoundFont instrument, or both.

documents.title: Safety and resource limits
documents.html:
Default batch runs limit executed statements, string size, retained storage, array elements, DATA items, matrix work, files, stacks, audio duration, and render dimensions. The interactive shell may run without a finite statement budget because it provides a user BREAK path; the other bounds remain active. The graphical shell permits at most 32 simultaneous program tasks. Each task owns interpreter and renderer workers plus independent screen, audio, and runtime state; close an existing task before opening another at that limit. Expression syntax is limited to 32 nested delimiter, unary, call, list, or right-associative power levels; exceeding that budget returns a structured runtime error rather than exhausting the host stack.

WAIT milliseconds is an interruptible native delay. Classic WAIT port,mask[,xor] observes the bounded virtual port bank; it never executes privileged host I/O. SYS and CALL can reach only services registered through the host library API. PEEK and POKE never address arbitrary host memory. ENVIRON$ and COMMAND$ expose only the bounded values explicitly supplied in RunOptions; unrelated host variables and invocation details remain private. Network statements are disabled unless the host grants the network capability. HTTP response and file limits remain active after permission is granted; the browser and media decoder receive only validated HTTP(S) addresses through fixed host command arguments. ON TIMER(seconds) GOSUB line accepts a positive interval up to one day; TIMER ON, OFF, and STOP control statement-boundary delivery. Timer and collision handlers use the bounded GOSUB stack, do not re-enter themselves, and are deferred while a structured procedure frame is active.

## Safety and resource limits

Default batch runs limit executed statements, string size, retained storage,
array elements, `DATA` items, matrix work, files, stacks, audio duration, and
render dimensions. The interactive shell may run without a finite statement
budget because it provides a user BREAK path; the other bounds remain active.
The graphical shell permits at most 32 simultaneous program tasks. Each task
owns interpreter and renderer workers plus independent screen, audio, and
runtime state; close an existing task before opening another at that limit.
Expression syntax is limited to 32 nested delimiter, unary, call, list, or
right-associative power levels; exceeding that budget returns a structured
runtime error rather than exhausting the host stack.

`WAIT milliseconds` is an interruptible native delay. Classic
`WAIT port,mask[,xor]` observes the bounded virtual port bank; it never executes
privileged host I/O. `SYS` and `CALL` can reach only services registered through
the host library API. `PEEK` and `POKE` never address arbitrary host memory.
`ENVIRON$` and `COMMAND$` expose only the bounded values explicitly supplied in
`RunOptions`; unrelated host variables and invocation details remain private.
Network statements are disabled unless the host grants the network capability.
HTTP response and file limits remain active after permission is granted; the
browser and media decoder receive only validated HTTP(S) addresses through
fixed host command arguments.
`ON TIMER(seconds) GOSUB line` accepts a positive interval up to one day;
`TIMER ON`, `OFF`, and `STOP` control statement-boundary delivery. Timer and
collision handlers use the bounded GOSUB stack, do not re-enter themselves,
and are deferred while a structured procedure frame is active.

10 X=7
20 PRINT EVAL("X*3+1")

10 LIBRARY "math.bas"
20 PRINT DOUBLEIT(21)
30 END

math.bas:

10 FUNCTION DOUBLEIT(N)
20 DOUBLEIT=N*2
30 END FUNCTION

Persistent debugger stops

READY commands:

BREAK
BREAK AT line [AFTER count]
BREAK ON scalar [AFTER count]
BREAK ON scalar CHANGE [AFTER count]
BREAK ON scalar comparison literal [AFTER count]
UNBREAK id
UNBREAK ALL

BREAK lists numbered entries. UNBREAK without an argument also clears all entries. Up to 256 entries are retained in a session. AFTER n stops on every nth matching occurrence; counters reset on a fresh RUN. A line breakpoint stops before the first statement of that line, including loop/branch revisits. CONT skips that specific stop once, then executes the pending statement. STEP executes one statement and resumes normal breakpoint behavior afterward.

CHANGE compares the scalar's value immediately before/after a statement in the active procedure scope. Indexed files

10 OPEN "customers.idx" FOR INDEXED AS #1
20 WRITE #1,"ALICE",42,"active"
30 WRITE #1,"BOB",17,"pending"
40 READ #1,"ALICE",AGE,STATE$
50 READNEXT #1,KEY$,AGE,STATE$
60 DELETEKEY #1,"ALICE"
70 CLOSE #1

The first value of indexed WRITE# is a nonempty string key. Remaining values use the normal WRITE# field encoding. Writing an existing key replaces its logical record. READ# retrieves by key; READNEXT# reads the next strictly greater key, assigning both its key and fields. The first READNEXT after OPEN returns the lowest key. EOF reports whether a greater key exists; LOC counts live keys through the cursor; LOF reports physical file bytes. CLOSE and CLOSE-all include indexed channels. An indexed channel retains its opened descriptor across CHDIR.

Break events and phoneme speech

10 ON BREAK GOSUB 100
20 BREAK ON
30 PRINT "WORKING"
40 END
100 PRINT "BREAK REQUESTED"
110 RETURN

Stored-program BREAK ON/OFF controls interception by ON BREAK GOSUB. ON BREAK GOSUB 0 removes the handler. With interception disabled, an interrupt stops normally. A second interrupt while the handler is active always stops. RETURN resumes at the interrupted statement boundary. 10 PHONEMES$=TRANSLATE$("Hello","en-us")
20 SAY PHONEMES$,150,110,0.8,"en-us"

GET/PUT raster captures and imported bitmap pixels remain true-color snapshots, so they do not acquire indexed-bitplane behavior.

Shared output windows and native menus

10 WINDOW OPEN 1,"Plot",640,480
20 SCREEN 640,456,"BLACK"
30 MENU 1,0,1,"Actions"
40 MENU 1,1,2,"Checked item"
50 MENU 1,2,0,"Disabled item"
60 ON MENU GOSUB 200:MENU ON
70 WINDOW OPEN 2,"Results",640,480
80 VALUE=42:PRINT VALUE
90 WINDOW OUTPUT 1
100 M=MENU(0):IF M<>0 THEN PRINT M;MENU(1)
110 K$=INKEY$:IF K$="CLOSE" THEN WINDOW CLOSE 1:END
120 WAIT 20:GOTO 100
200 M=MENU(0):ITEM=MENU(1):RETURN

Coordinate WINDOW (x1,y1)-(x2,y2) is unchanged.

All targets share variables, arrays, files, functions and procedures. They retain separate graphics buffers, palette/drawing state, text cells/cursor/print region, flipbooks, menus, menu traps and keyboard/pointer queues. INPUT and LINPUT use the selected window. A window-manager close normally queues "CLOSE" in that child's INKEY$ queue; explicit WINDOW CLOSE releases it. Windows persist at STOP/READY, close when their session is discarded or source resources are replaced, and close before a fresh RUN. Selecting outputs while SCREENLOCK or video capture is active is rejected. TASK windows remain separate interpreters. Hardware-specific Amiga window flags and absolute placement operands are not aliases for these statements.

MENU menu,item,state[,title$] creates or updates host-managed pull-down menus for the selected output. Menu IDs are 1..10; item 0 defines the title and items 1..19 define choices. MENU RESET removes the custom menus and their trap. Labels wrap onto additional menu-bar rows when needed; the menu bar reserves space above the BASIC display.

A stopped trap observes a selection when re-enabled; OFF discards pending trap notification, while explicit MENU polling remains available. A burst can coalesce into one trap; drain MENU(0) in the handler. No handler runs in the middle of a blocking input statement. Pattern masks, sprite collisions and autonomous motion

10 SCREEN 320,200,"BLACK"
20 DIM PAT%(1):PAT%(0)=&HAAAA:PAT%(1)=&H5555
30 PATTERN &HF0F0,PAT%
40 LINE (10,10)-(90,70),"WHITE",BF
50 PATTERN
60 SPRITE SHIP,100,80,16,16,"RED"
70 SPRITEHIT SHIP,2,5
80 SPRITEMOTION SHIP,20,0
90 ANIMATION ON,30
100 WAIT 1000
110 ANIMATION OFF

PATTERN [line-mask][,area-array] affects subsequent retained lines, filled shapes, text and flood fills. The mask accepts -32768..65535 as 16 bits. The one-dimensional area array contains 1,2,4,...,256 rows; each row supplies 16 bits, most significant bit at the left. Array values are copied when PATTERN executes. Omitted operands retain their previous setting; bare PATTERN restores solid drawing. SCREEN resets patterns; CLS preserves them. Zero bits leave existing pixels untouched. This portable raster convention does not reproduce chipset-specific line phase/antialiasing. Patterned SVG exports use exact pixel runs and reject output beyond 64 MiB.

SPRITEHIT id,category,hit-mask assigns unsigned 16-bit collision filters. Two objects qualify when either object's category intersects the other's hit mask. Hit-mask bit 0 enables border contact. Existing programs retain the default category/mask 65534, so border traps are opt-in. PBORDER(id) reports left=1, top=2, right=4 and bottom=8, combined when necessary; touching an edge counts.

SPRITEMASK id,array copies a two-dimensional numeric array indexed (row,column). Nonzero cells are solid. Each dimension is at most 256 and mask storage is limited to 1,048,576 cells per graphics buffer. The mask scales with the sprite's bounds; overlapping logical screen-pixel centers must be solid in both shapes. Without masks, rectangle/projected-rectangle overlap remains the default. Masks are explicitly supplied and do not automatically infer bitmap alpha. PCOLLISION and ON COLLISION use these filters, shapes and enabled borders. The event trap reports the start of any contact; inspect pairs/PBORDER in the handler, and separate objects before expecting another edge notification.

ANIMATION ON[,fps] starts autonomous 2D sprite motion at 1..60 fps (default 30), for up to 4096 sprites. The native window keeps rendering elapsed-time positions even during INPUT, LINPUT or WAIT. BASIC synchronizes positions at statement boundaries; handlers also run at those boundaries. ANIMATION OFF synchronizes and freezes the current positions. Each output window owns its animation state. Native timing is not deterministic replay or a chipset timer, and a host may render fewer frames under load. Use ADVANCESPRITES for deterministic simulation and 3D motion. SCREENLOCK and VIDEO START require ANIMATION OFF; use explicit stepping for batched or recorded frames. An untrapped user Break stops all session animations. Repeated motion-only frames coalesce retained movement commands rather than adding an unbounded command history. Close the window or use ANIMATION OFF to stop a retained animation before leaving an interactive program.

Bounded editable input fields

10 NAME$="JASON     "
20 LINPUT "Name: ",USING NAME$,NAME$
30 LINPUT USING "!",ANSWER$
40 PRINT NAME$;ANSWER$;INPUTEND()

LINPUT [prompt$,] USING mask$,destination$ edits one ASCII field, including spaces, quotes and commas. A mask expression beginning with a string literal starts empty and uses that literal expression's length as its width. A mask starting with ! also commits automatically when filled. Other expressions prefill the field with their value. Width is 1..80, bounded further by session input/string limits; in the native window it must fit the remaining logical row.

Typing overwrites. Left/Right move without deleting; Home/End reposition; Backspace replaces the previous character with a space; Delete removes the current character; Tab inserts a space and drops overflow. Ctrl-H/Ctrl-F, Ctrl-D and Ctrl-I supply the corresponding classic controls. Enter commits; Escape commits with terminator 27. INPUTEND() reports the last terminator (13 for Enter or automatic completion). Native X11 input displays edits as they happen. Reader-driven runs accept equivalent ASCII control bytes; ordinary terminal canonical mode may require Enter to deliver them. Unused trailing positions of a new field are not stored; spaces in a prefilled value are kept. An interrupted/failed read leaves the destination unchanged. Use SCREEN TEXT or SPLIT to make the field visible in graphical programs.

executes. Omitted operands retain their previous setting; bare PATTERN restores
solid drawing. SCREEN resets patterns; CLS preserves them. Zero bits leave
existing pixels untouched. Area masks repeat in logical screen coordinates
after transformations; strokes repeat their mask along the path. This portable
raster convention does not reproduce chipset-specific line phase/antialiasing.
Patterned SVG exports use exact pixel runs and reject output beyond 64 MiB.

`SPRITEHIT id,category,hit-mask` assigns unsigned 16-bit collision filters. Two
objects qualify when either object's category intersects the other's hit mask.
Hit-mask bit 0 enables border contact. Existing programs retain the default
category/mask 65534, so border traps are opt-in. `PBORDER(id)` reports left=1,
top=2, right=4 and bottom=8, combined when necessary; touching an edge counts.

`SPRITEMASK id,array` copies a two-dimensional numeric array indexed `(row,column)`.
Nonzero cells are solid. Each dimension is at most 256 and mask storage is
limited to 1,048,576 cells per graphics buffer. The mask scales with the sprite's
bounds; overlapping logical screen-pixel centers must be solid in both shapes.
Without masks, rectangle/projected-rectangle overlap remains the default.
Masks are explicitly supplied and do not automatically infer bitmap alpha.
PCOLLISION and ON COLLISION use these filters, shapes and enabled borders.
The event trap reports the start of any contact; inspect pairs/PBORDER in the
handler, and separate objects before expecting another edge notification.

`ANIMATION ON[,fps]` starts autonomous 2D sprite motion at 1..60 fps (default 30),
for up to 4096 sprites. The native window keeps rendering elapsed-time positions
even during INPUT, LINPUT or WAIT. BASIC synchronizes positions at statement
boundaries; handlers also run at those boundaries. `ANIMATION OFF` synchronizes
and freezes the current positions. Each output window owns its animation state.
Native timing is not deterministic replay or a chipset timer, and a host may
render fewer frames under load. Use ADVANCESPRITES for deterministic simulation
and 3D motion. SCREENLOCK and VIDEO START require ANIMATION OFF; use explicit stepping for
batched or recorded frames. An untrapped user Break stops all session animations.
Repeated motion-only frames coalesce retained movement commands rather than
adding an unbounded command history. Close the window or use ANIMATION OFF to
stop a retained animation before leaving an interactive program.

### Bounded editable input fields

```basic
10 NAME$="JASON     "
20 LINPUT "Name: ",USING NAME$,NAME$
30 LINPUT USING "!",ANSWER$
40 PRINT NAME$;ANSWER$;INPUTEND()
```

`LINPUT [prompt$,] USING mask$,destination$` edits one ASCII field, including
spaces, quotes and commas. A mask expression beginning with a string literal
starts empty and uses that literal expression's length as its width. A mask
starting with `!` also commits automatically when filled. Other expressions
prefill the field with their value. Width is 1..80, bounded further by session
input/string limits; in the native window it must fit the remaining logical row.

Typing overwrites. Left/Right move without deleting; Home/End reposition;
Backspace replaces the previous character with a space; Delete removes the
current character; Tab inserts a space and drops overflow. Ctrl-H/Ctrl-F,
Ctrl-D and Ctrl-I supply the corresponding classic controls. Enter commits;
Escape commits with terminator 27. `INPUTEND()` reports the last terminator
(13 for Enter or automatic completion). Native X11 input displays edits as they
happen. Reader-driven runs accept equivalent ASCII control bytes; ordinary
terminal canonical mode may require Enter to deliver them. Unused trailing
positions of a new field are not stored; spaces in a prefilled value are kept.
An interrupted/failed read leaves the destination unchanged. Use SCREEN TEXT
or SPLIT to make the field visible in graphical programs.

documents.html:
LPSOLVE(cost,A,columnBounds,rowBounds[,sense$[,options[,offset]]]) solves a continuous linear model. MIPSOLVE(cost,A,columnBounds,rowBounds,kinds[,sense$[,options[,offset]]]) uses the same model with a flat kinds list: 0 is continuous and 1 is integer. Integer variables bounded by 0 and 1 are binary. sense$ is "MIN" (default) or "MAX". The objective is cost·x + offset; offset defaults to zero.

A is a canonical SPARSE/CSR1 matrix. An empty list {} means zero constraint rows, with the column count taken from cost; it does not change the ordinary positive-dimension CSR1 contract. Each bounds entry is {lower,upper}. Use an empty list {} for an absent endpoint, for example {{0,4},{1,{}}}. Row bounds apply to A*x. Lists remain ordinary editable BASIC data and compose through DEF FN.

The optional options list supplies a prefix of {seconds,iterationLimit,nodeLimit,tolerance,presolve}. Defaults are {10,100000,100000,1E-7,-1}. Seconds must be 0 through 60; iteration limit 0 through 200000; node limit 0 through 100000; absolute feasibility tolerance 1E-10 through 1E-4. Presolve is off for 0 and on for a nonzero integer. Iteration and node limits are per native phase; the worker also enforces process resource and wall limits.

10 C={1,1}:A=SPARSE({{0,1},{1,2},{3,2}})
20 B={{0,4},{1,{}}}:D={{{},7},{5,15},{6,{}}}
30 R=LPSOLVE(C,A,B,D)
40 PRINT R(2):X=R(3):PRINT X:PRINT R(4)
50 R=MIPSOLVE(C,A,B,D,{1,1})
60 PRINT R(2):PRINT R(4)

Both calls return the nine-element HIGHS1 record:

FieldMeaning
1"HIGHS1", identifying the data schema.
2Native termination string, such as "OPTIMAL", "INFEASIBLE", "UNBOUNDED", "UNBOUNDED_OR_INFEASIBLE", "TIMELIMIT", "ITERATIONLIMIT", or "INTERRUPTED".
3Candidate point, or {} when a native feasible primal solution is unavailable.
4Objective recomputed by Rust, or {} without a primal point.
5Activities recomputed from the original CSR matrix, or {} without a primal point.
6{withinTolerance,boundViolation,rowViolation,integralityViolation}, or {} without a primal point. withinTolerance is -1 or 0 and checks the explicit absolute tolerance.
7Native {columnMarginals,rowMarginals} for a continuous model with an available dual solution; otherwise {}. No MIP dual certificate is returned.
8Raw native {modelStatus,loadStatus,runStatus,primalStatus,dualStatus}.
9Native objective, or {} without a primal point; compare with field 4 when assessing numerical quality.

Termination and dual fields report native claims. Rust independently recomputes primal quality; passing its tolerance check does not certify exact feasibility, duality or global optimality. Limits can return a candidate without an optimality claim. An absent solution is never replaced by a zero vector or objective. Canonical report records may pass through DEF FN; schema validation is data transport, not a mathematical certificate.

This backend requires the pinned HiGHS 1.10.0 provider and Linux worker dispatch. HIGHSBACKEND() runs a real worker probe before returning its backend identity. Missing providers, worker failure or resource refusal raise BASIC errors and support normal ON ERROR recovery. Each solve uses a fresh worker. Cancellation and supervisor death stop its native work. Worker containment does not provide a filesystem/network sandbox.

The current provider admits at most 100000 variables/rows and 250000 nonzeros. Raw stored matrix values must satisfy 1E-12 < ABS(A) < 1E15; finite bounds and cost coefficients must have magnitude below 1E20. These admission checks prevent HiGHS from silently dropping coefficients or interpreting finite data as infinity. QPSOLVE additionally applies the exact row equilibration described below, but it does not expand these raw input limits. Unsupported models are rejected rather than clipped or silently changed. Finite objective offsets are separate from the cost-coefficient limit. BASIC QPSOLVE handles admitted continuous convex quadratic models through the isolated Rust worker. Broader randomized/reference qualification, image/provider deployment and architecture/hardware acceptance remain open.

Exact rational LP optimization through QSopt_ex

EXACTLPSOLVE(sense$,cost,A,rowBounds,columnBounds[,seconds]) sends a continuous linear program to the optional QSopt_ex esolver provider through a bounded Rust worker. sense$ is "MIN" or "MAX". cost is a nonempty vector of up to 64 exact values, A is a dense list of up to 64 rows and 64 columns, and the two bounds lists use {lower,upper} pairs in the same order as A's rows and the variables. Use {} for an absent endpoint; rows need at least one finite bound. Variables with both endpoints absent are free. The time limit defaults to 10 seconds and must be in 0.05 through 60 seconds.

Supply coefficients and bounds as strings when they must retain exact decimal or fraction meaning: "0.1" means exactly one tenth, and "1/3" means exactly one third. BASIC numeric values are converted from their shortest decimal display; for example, the numeric expression 1/3 has already rounded to binary64, so use the string "1/3" to request the exact fraction. Ratios are reduced and returned as integer or numerator/denominator strings.

10 C={"1/3"}:A={{"3"}}:B={{"1",{}}}:D={{"0",{}}
20 R=EXACTLPSOLVE("MIN",C,A,B,D)
30 PRINT R(2):PRINT R(3):X=R(4):PRINT X(1)

EXACTLPSOLVE returns a six-element QSEX1 record: tag, status string, exact objective string (empty when no candidate exists), exact primal vector (empty when unavailable), status code (1 optimal, 2 infeasible, 3 unbounded), and a receiver-side status-verification flag (1 or 0). For OPTIMAL, Rust recomputes each row, bound and objective using arbitrary-precision integer ratios, then checks exact reduced-cost stationarity, row-dual signs and complementary slackness. For INFEASIBLE, Rust verifies normalized nonnegative Farkas multipliers that cancel all variables and produce a strict contradiction. For UNBOUNDED, Rust verifies an exact feasible base point plus a recession direction satisfying every row and variable bound direction and strictly improving the objective. The flag is 1 only when that proof passes. Do not interpret an empty candidate as a zero vector. The editable example is programs/examples/exact_rational_lp.bas.

The optional provider defaults to /usr/bin/esolver; set MODERNBASIC_QSOPT_EX_EXECUTABLE to another absolute executable path. The worker admits QSopt_ex 2.5.10, uses private temporary files, CPU/address-space/file-size limits and process-group cleanup, and rejects malformed or inconsistent results. The provider is not bundled or installed by ModernBASIC. Debian's CLI package is GPL-3-or-later, so provider distribution and notices need a separate release review. Independent dual certificates, broader rational/reference families, cross-target provider tests, image packaging and hardware acceptance remain open.

Native convex quadratic optimization

QPSOLVE(cost,Q,A,columnBounds,rowBounds[,sense$[,options[,offset]]]) solves a continuous convex quadratic model with objective 0.5*xᵀ*Q*x + cost·x + offset. Q is the full symmetric CSR1 Hessian; it must be positive semidefinite for MIN and negative semidefinite for MAX. A and bounds use the same CSR1 and {lower,upper} forms as LPSOLVE; {} for A means zero constraint rows. Variables are continuous. Mixed-integer and nonconvex quadratic models are rejected before starting the worker.

The optional sense$, options prefix and offset follow the LP/MIP rules above. The Rust backend applies lossless power-of-two objective and variable scaling, then independently scales each constraint row so its largest transformed coefficient is near one. It applies the same exact row transform to finite row bounds and maps row duals back before checking the original model. The lower- triangular Hessian is passed to HiGHS and checked for retention; Rust then recomputes the original objective and checks the primal against every original bound and row. Scaling is exact and binary; a transform that would round, underflow or overflow a coefficient or finite bound is rejected instead of silently changing the model.

10 Q=SPARSE({{2}}) 20 R=QPSOLVE({-2},Q,{},{{0,4}},{}) 30 X=R(3):K=R(10) 40 PRINT R(2):PRINT X(1):PRINT R(4):PRINT K(6)

QPSOLVE returns a ten-element HIGHSQP1 record:

FieldMeaning
1HIGHSQP1, identifying the quadratic result schema.
2Native model termination string.
3Candidate point, or {} when unavailable.
4Original quadratic objective recomputed by Rust, or {} without a point.
5Row activities recomputed from the original A, or {} without a point.
6{withinTolerance,boundViolation,rowViolation,integralityViolation}; the last value is zero for continuous QP.
7Native {columnMarginals,rowMarginals}, or {} when unavailable.
8{loadStatus,runStatus,modelStatus,primalStatus,dualStatus}.
9Native objective in the solver's exactly scaled units, or {}.
10{primalFeasibility,stationarity,dualFeasibility,complementarity,tolerance,passes}, or {} when primal or dual data is unavailable.

The receiver recomputes the four relative KKT residuals from the original constraints, scaled objective and dual vectors. passes is -1 or 0. It is a numerical check, not an exact certificate; native termination remains a solver claim when KKT data is absent or fails. Candidate reports and KKT fields compose through DEF FN as validated ordinary BASIC data.

Exact integer factorization with PARI/GP

PARIFACTORS(integer$[,seconds]) returns the exact factorization of a nonzero integer as rows {prime$,multiplicity}. The input may be a BASIC integer, an exact integral real no larger than 2^53 in magnitude, or a signed decimal string up to 256 digits. Prime values are returned as decimal strings so no digits are lost. A negative input starts with the row {"-1",1}; 1 returns {} and -1 returns only its sign row. Zero is an error. The optional time limit defaults to 10 seconds and is bounded to 0.05–60 seconds.

10 F=PARIFACTORS("-1000000016000000063") 20 PRINT F(1,1) 30 PRINT F(2,1);" ^ ";F(2,2) 40 PRINT F(3,1);" ^ ";F(3,2)

The Rust receiver launches the configured PARI/GP executable in a separate, supervised process group, admits only the PARI/GP 2.15.4 version string tested in the current host prototype, starts it with a fixed 64 MiB PARI stack inside the worker's 512 MiB address-space cap, and caps execution time and output. Set MODERNBASIC_PARI_GP to select the executable; the default is /usr/bin/gp. Rust checks the response format and reconstructs the input exactly from all returned factors before BASIC receives it. The worker requests rigorous primality proofs from PARI/GP and checks each returned prime with isprime. The receiver caps aggregate multiplicity by the input's bit length and stops product reconstruction as soon as it exceeds the submitted integer, bounding verification work even for a malformed provider response. This receiver check validates product and schema; it does not independently re-prove PARI's primality certificates. The 64 MiB initial stack avoids the provider's small default stack on larger proof workloads; the worker's memory and time limits still apply. Runtime package hashes/build IDs, cross-target and packaged-image tests, and redistribution/license review remain open. Debian stable's 2.17.2 build has not yet been admitted. PARI/GP is optional and is not bundled.

The Rust API factor_integer_with_pari returns signedness separately from the distinct positive factors and their multiplicities. Embedding applications must call dispatch_native_math_worker at startup or use the explicit-worker variant. The BASIC API uses the same Rust validation and worker boundary.

Exact integer systems with 4ti2

ZSOLVE(A,rhs[,relations[,signs[,seconds]]]) solves an integer linear system through the optional 4ti2 provider. A is a dense list of integer rows; rhs has one integer per row. Relations are strings <, =, or > (also <=, ==, >=); the default is equality for every row. Sign entries are 0 for a free variable or 1 for a nonnegative variable; the default is nonnegative. The optional time limit defaults to 10 seconds and is capped at 60 seconds.

10 R=ZSOLVE({{1,1}},{2}) 20 X=R(2) 30 FOR I=1 TO LEN(X) 40 P=X(I):PRINT P(1);",";P(2) 50 NEXT I

ZSOLVE returns a four-element 4TI2Z1 record: the tag, minimal inhomogeneous solutions, homogeneous generators, and free generators. Each matrix stores one integer vector per row. programs/examples/integer_lattice.bas is an editable working example. Values enter as BASIC integers or decimal strings; real inputs must be exact integers no larger than 2^53 in magnitude. Results fitting signed 64-bit integers are BASIC integers, while larger values are returned as decimal strings so their digits remain exact.

The Rust receiver rechecks every returned vector against the original rows, relations and signs. This verifies candidate vectors, not completeness of the provider's generated sets. Models are capped at 128 rows/columns, 16,384 matrix cells and 256 decimal digits per integer. Frames/results are capped at 4 MiB; the isolated worker has a 512 MiB address-space limit, a CPU/wall-time deadline and an 8 MiB per-file cap. The optional 4ti2 C API provider is loaded from the system runtime (libzsolve.so.0 and lib4ti2common.so.0 by default); it is not bundled. On the qualified amd64 build, Rust checks the ELF GNU build IDs of these files and the direct GMP/GMPXX libraries before loading them. The Markov path also checks the 4ti2gmp executable and direct 4ti2/GMP libraries. A mismatched build is rejected and follows BASIC error handling. These fingerprints identify tested files but do not authenticate package signatures or every transitively loaded system library. Cross-target, package-image and GPL notice/release qualification remain open. Evidence: output/4ti2-evaluation-2026-10-23/runtime-identity-v2.json.

HBASIS(A[,seconds]) computes a Hilbert basis for the nonnegative integer kernel of A; GRAVER(A[,seconds]) computes a Graver basis of its integer kernel. MARKOV(A[,seconds]) computes a Markov basis for nonnegative fibers. Each returns a two-element record: 4TI2H1, 4TI2G1 or 4TI2M1, followed by a matrix whose rows are exact integer vectors. For example, the Hilbert and Graver bases of {{1,-1}} each contain {1,1}, while the Markov basis for {{1,1}} contains {1,-1}. All workers share the same time, memory, frame, file and integer-size limits as ZSOLVE. Rust checks every vector is in the kernel, checks Hilbert vectors are nonnegative, and removes duplicate rows. Provider project files live in an owner-only mode-0700 temporary directory that is removed when the worker finishes. These checks do not prove a returned basis is complete. The Markov operation runs the 4ti2 4ti2gmp executable inside the isolated worker; set MODERNBASIC_4TI2_MARKOV_EXECUTABLE when it is not on PATH. Independent completeness references, cross-target tests, packaged-image qualification and GPL notice/release review remain open. Before Markov calculation, the isolated worker requires 4ti2gmp --version to identify 4ti2 1.6.10 with arbitrary- precision integers; unsupported releases and non-GMP builds are rejected. The probe has a five-second deadline, retains at most 4096 bytes, stays in the worker's process group, and is bounded by the worker's 8 MiB file-size limit while writing private output files. The qualified amd64 worker checks GNU build IDs for the loaded libzsolve/lib4ti2common C API, its direct GMP/GMPXX libraries, and the Markov executable and direct 4ti2/GMP libraries before use. Other architectures and complete package-image/transitive-library attestation remain open; see output/4ti2-evaluation-2026-10-23/runtime-identity-v2.json.

Exact sparse curvature proofs

SPISPSD and SPISNSD use the stored binary64 coefficients as exact rationals; there is no floating eigenvalue tolerance or rounding of row sums. A singular semidefinite matrix can be proved true, and a tiny negative direction is not rounded into zero. Canonical CSR arguments compose through DEF FN.

Symmetric diagonal dominance supplies an exact sparse certificate, supporting large diagonal/Laplacian-type matrices without dense expansion. Otherwise the shared symbolic/native engine uses exact Schur-complement elimination, bounded by one million dense cells, 128 million retained numerator/denominator bits, 4096 bits per normalized integer and arithmetic/work budgets. These are logical proof bounds, not process-wide memory isolation. An inconclusive large or resource-limited proof raises an error; it never returns an approximate answer. Nonsquare or nonsymmetric inputs also raise errors.

10 A=SPARSE({{1,2},{2,4}})
20 PRINT SPISPSD(A):PRINT SPISNSD(A)
30 B=SPARSE({{1,1},{1,0.9999999999999999}})
40 PRINT SPISPSD(B)

The results are -1, 0 and 0. These predicates qualify curvature; they are not QP solvers. Native QP scaling, independent optimality checks and solver integration remain separate tasks.
