constraints, scaled objective and dual vectors. passes is -1 or 0. It is a
numerical check, not an exact certificate; native termination remains a solver
claim when KKT data is absent or fails. Candidate reports and KKT fields compose
through DEF FN as validated ordinary BASIC data.

### Exact integer factorization with PARI/GP

`PARIFACTORS(integer$[,seconds])` returns the exact factorization of a nonzero
integer as rows `{prime$,multiplicity}`. The input may be a BASIC integer, an
exact integral real no larger than 2^53 in magnitude, or a signed decimal string
up to 256 digits. Prime values are returned as decimal strings so no digits are
lost. A negative input starts with the row `{"-1",1}`; `1` returns `{}` and
`-1` returns only its sign row. Zero is an error. The optional time limit
defaults to 10 seconds and is bounded to 0.05–60 seconds.

    10 F=PARIFACTORS("-1000000016000000063")
    20 PRINT F(1,1)
    30 PRINT F(2,1);" ^ ";F(2,2)
    40 PRINT F(3,1);" ^ ";F(3,2)

The Rust receiver launches the configured PARI/GP executable in a separate,
supervised process group, admits only the PARI/GP 2.15.4 version string tested
in the current host prototype, starts it with a fixed 64 MiB PARI stack inside
the worker's 512 MiB address-space cap, and caps execution time and output. Set
`MODERNBASIC_PARI_GP` to select the executable; the default is `/usr/bin/gp`.
Rust checks the response format and reconstructs the input exactly from all
returned factors before BASIC receives it. The worker requests rigorous
primality proofs from PARI/GP and checks each returned prime with `isprime`.
The receiver caps aggregate multiplicity by the input's bit length and stops
product reconstruction as soon as it exceeds the submitted integer, bounding
verification work even for a malformed provider response.
This receiver check validates product and schema; it does not independently
re-prove PARI's primality certificates. The 64 MiB initial stack avoids the
provider's small default stack on larger proof workloads; the worker's memory
and time limits still apply. Runtime package hashes/build IDs,
cross-target and packaged-image tests, and redistribution/license review remain
open. Debian stable's 2.17.2 build has not yet been admitted. PARI/GP is optional
and is not bundled.

The Rust API `factor_integer_with_pari` returns signedness separately from the
distinct positive factors and their multiplicities. Embedding applications
must call `dispatch_native_math_worker` at startup or use the explicit-worker
variant. The BASIC API uses the same Rust validation and worker boundary.

### Exact integer systems with 4ti2

`ZSOLVE(A,rhs[,relations[,signs[,seconds]]])` solves an integer linear system
through the optional 4ti2 provider. `A` is a dense list of integer rows; `rhs`
has one integer per row. Relations are strings `<`, `=`, or `>` (also `<=`,
`==`, `>=`); the default is equality for every row. Sign entries are `0` for a
free variable or `1` for a nonnegative variable; the default is nonnegative.
The optional time limit defaults to 10 seconds and is capped at 60 seconds.

    10 R=ZSOLVE({{1,1}},{2})
    20 X=R(2)
    30 FOR I=1 TO LEN(X)
    40 P=X(I):PRINT P(1);",";P(2)
    50 NEXT I

`ZSOLVE` returns a four-element `4TI2Z1` record: the tag, minimal inhomogeneous
solutions, homogeneous generators, and free generators. Each matrix stores one
integer vector per row. `programs/examples/integer_lattice.bas` is an editable
working example. Values enter as BASIC integers or decimal strings; real inputs
must be exact integers no larger than 2^53 in magnitude. Results fitting signed
64-bit integers are BASIC integers, while larger values are returned as decimal
strings so their digits remain exact.

The Rust receiver rechecks every returned vector against the original rows,
relations and signs. This verifies candidate vectors, not completeness of the
provider's generated sets. Models are capped at 128 rows/columns, 16,384 matrix
cells and 256 decimal digits per integer. Frames/results are capped at 4 MiB;
the isolated worker has a 512 MiB address-space limit, a CPU/wall-time deadline
and an 8 MiB per-file cap. The optional 4ti2 C API provider is loaded from
the system runtime
(`libzsolve.so.0` and `lib4ti2common.so.0` by default); it is not bundled. On the
qualified amd64 build, Rust checks the ELF GNU build IDs of these files and the
direct GMP/GMPXX libraries before loading them. The Markov path also checks the
`4ti2gmp` executable and direct 4ti2/GMP libraries. A mismatched build is
rejected and follows BASIC error handling. These fingerprints identify tested
files but do not authenticate package signatures or every transitively loaded
system library. Cross-target, package-image and GPL notice/release qualification
remain open. Evidence: `output/4ti2-evaluation-2026-10-23/runtime-identity-v2.json`.

`HBASIS(A[,seconds])` computes a Hilbert basis for the nonnegative integer
kernel of `A`; `GRAVER(A[,seconds])` computes a Graver basis of its integer
kernel. `MARKOV(A[,seconds])` computes a Markov basis for nonnegative fibers.
Each returns a two-element record: `4TI2H1`, `4TI2G1` or `4TI2M1`, followed by
a matrix whose rows are exact integer vectors. For example, the Hilbert and
Graver bases of `{{1,-1}}` each contain `{1,1}`, while the Markov basis for
`{{1,1}}` contains `{1,-1}`. All workers share the same time, memory, frame,
file and integer-size limits as `ZSOLVE`. Rust checks every vector is in the
kernel, checks Hilbert vectors are nonnegative, and removes duplicate rows.
Provider project files live in an owner-only mode-0700 temporary directory that
is removed when the worker finishes.
These checks do not prove a returned basis is complete. The Markov operation
runs the 4ti2 `4ti2gmp` executable inside the isolated worker; set
`MODERNBASIC_4TI2_MARKOV_EXECUTABLE` when it is not on `PATH`. Independent
completeness references, cross-target tests, packaged-image qualification and
GPL notice/release review remain open. Before Markov calculation, the isolated
worker requires `4ti2gmp --version` to identify 4ti2 1.6.10 with arbitrary-
precision integers; unsupported releases and non-GMP builds are rejected. The
probe has a five-second deadline, retains at most 4096 bytes, stays in the
worker's process group, and is bounded by the worker's 8 MiB file-size limit
while writing private output files. The qualified amd64 worker checks GNU
build IDs for the loaded `libzsolve`/`lib4ti2common` C API, its direct GMP/GMPXX
libraries, and the Markov executable and direct 4ti2/GMP libraries before use.
Other architectures and complete package-image/transitive-library attestation
remain open; see `output/4ti2-evaluation-2026-10-23/runtime-identity-v2.json`.

### Exact sparse curvature proofs

`SPISPSD` and `SPISNSD` use the stored binary64 coefficients as exact rationals;
there is no floating eigenvalue tolerance or rounding of row sums. A singular
semidefinite matrix can be proved true, and a tiny negative direction is not
rounded into zero. Canonical CSR arguments compose through `DEF FN`.

Symmetric diagonal dominance supplies an exact sparse certificate, supporting
large diagonal/Laplacian-type matrices without dense expansion. Otherwise the
shared symbolic/native engine uses exact Schur-complement elimination, bounded
by one million dense cells, 128 million retained numerator/denominator bits,
4096 bits per normalized integer and arithmetic/work budgets. These are logical
proof bounds, not process-wide memory isolation. An inconclusive large or
resource-limited proof raises an error; it never returns an approximate answer.
Nonsquare or nonsymmetric inputs also raise errors.

```basic
10 A=SPARSE({{1,2},{2,4}})
20 PRINT SPISPSD(A):PRINT SPISNSD(A)
30 B=SPARSE({{1,1},{1,0.9999999999999999}})
40 PRINT SPISPSD(B)
```

The results are -1, 0 and 0. These predicates qualify curvature; they are not QP
solvers. Native QP scaling, independent optimality checks and solver integration
remain separate tasks.

documents.title: Multivariable descriptive statistics
documents.html:
Gamma and chi-square distributions

GAMMAPDF(x,shape,scale) returns the gamma probability density; GAMMACDF(x,shape,scale) returns the lower-tail probability, and GAMMASF(x,shape,scale) returns the upper-tail probability directly. Shape and scale must be finite and positive; scale is the scale parameter, not its reciprocal rate. The mean is shape*scale and variance is shape*scale^2 when those expressions are representable. CHISQPDF(x,df), CHISQCDF(x,df) and CHISQSF(x,df) use the same Rust backend with shape df/2 and scale 2. Degrees of freedom must be finite and positive; fractional values are accepted.

Use the survival function for a small upper-tail p-value. For example, CHISQSF(100,2) is approximately 1.92874984796392E-22, while subtracting CHISQCDF(100,2) from one loses that value to floating-point rounding.

10 PRINT GAMMAPDF(2,3,1):PRINT GAMMACDF(2,3,1)
20 PRINT GAMMASF(50,1,1):PRINT CHISQSF(100,2)

Samples must be finite. Negative samples have density and lower-tail probability zero, and upper-tail probability one. At zero, the gamma density is zero for shape greater than one, 1/scale for shape one, and singular for shape below one (an overflow error). Probability calculations use bounded series/continued fractions with cancellation checks and a 10,000-iteration limit. Large shapes use an asymptotic expansion. These are binary64 numerical estimates; convergence failure raises an error and does not return a partial result. Tiny probabilities can underflow, and densities beyond finite range raise overflow. Lower and upper inverse probabilities are available through GAMMAINV, GAMMAINVSF, CHISQINV and CHISQINVSF; see the inverse-function section below.

Student's t distribution

TPDF(t,df) returns the density, TCDF(t,df) the lower-tail probability, and TSF(t,df) the directly evaluated upper-tail probability. Degrees of freedom df must be finite and positive; there is no one-million-degree restriction. TINV(p,df) and TINVSF(p,df) return lower- and upper-tail critical values for 0 < p < 1. Infinite endpoint quantiles are rejected.

These functions share the bounded CPU Rust backend. Inversion uses one range check and at most 63 coordinate bisections, with cancellation checks and explicit overflow for a quantile beyond finite binary64. Results are numerical estimates, not certified bounds or correctly rounded guarantees for every input.

All five functions accept scalar arguments or flat numeric lists. Scalars broadcast over lists; multiple lists must have equal lengths. The result cap is one million elements. An invalid element aborts the whole assignment without changing the destination. Long batches remain cancellable.

10 DF=9:T=2.262157163
20 P=2*TSF(ABS(T),DF)
30 C=TINVSF(.025,DF)
40 PRINT "TWO-SIDED P: ";P
50 PRINT "95% CRITICAL T: ";C
60 PRINT "DENSITY: ";TPDF(T,DF)

TINV(.975,10) and TINVSF(.025,10) are approximately 2.22813885198627. Use the direct tail instead of subtracting a CDF close to one. TSF(1E200,1) is approximately 3.1830988618379E-201 and TINVSF(1E-200,1) approximately 3.1830988618379E199. Central mass and logarithmic tails are retained separately so squaring a large t statistic does not erase a representable probability. The reference example is programs/science/student_t_distribution.bas.

TTEST1(sample,mu[,confidence]) performs a two-sided one-sample t test of the sample mean against mu. It returns {t,df,p,lower,upper}: signed t statistic, degrees of freedom, two-sided p-value, and the central confidence interval (95% by default). The sample must contain at least two finite, nonconstant values, and confidence must be strictly between zero and one. The interval and p-value use the same bounded Student's t kernels as TCDF and TINV.

10 X={4.8,5.1,4.9,5.0,5.2}:R=TTEST1(X,4.8,.95)
20 PRINT "T STATISTIC: ";R(1):PRINT "DEGREES OF FREEDOM: ";R(2)
30 PRINT "TWO-SIDED P VALUE: ";R(3)
40 PRINT "95% CONFIDENCE INTERVAL: ";R(4);" TO ";R(5)

The result is an ordinary BASIC list, so its fields can be saved or combined with other BASIC calculations. For independent samples with unequal variances, use TTEST2; for naturally matched observations, pass their explicit paired differences to TTEST1. Pooled-variance tests and a full multiple-testing workflow are not provided.

TTEST2(first,second[,confidence]) performs Welch's two-sided independent- samples test, which does not assume equal population variances. It returns the same five fields as TTEST1, with the estimate defined as mean(first)-mean(second). The degrees of freedom use the Welch-Satterthwaite formula. Each sample must contain at least two finite observations, both groups cannot be constant, their combined size is limited to one million values, and confidence defaults to 95%. This is not a pooled-variance or paired test; use explicit paired differences with TTEST1 when observations are naturally matched.

10 A={2.1,2.3,2.0,2.4,2.2}:B={1.6,1.8,1.7,1.9,1.5}
20 R=TTEST2(A,B):PRINT "WELCH T: ";R(1):PRINT "DF: ";R(2)
30 PRINT "TWO-SIDED P VALUE: ";R(3)
40 PRINT "95% CI FOR MEAN DIFFERENCE: ";R(4);" TO ";R(5)

COVMATRIX(matrix [, sampleFlag]) returns a covariance matrix with matrix rows as observations and columns as variables. The optional flag defaults to 1 (sample covariance, divisor n-1); use 0 for population covariance, divisor n. CORRMATRIX(matrix) returns the Pearson correlation matrix. Both functions require rectangular finite data and are bounded by matrix-size and work limits; correlation additionally requires at least two observations and nonconstant columns.

MULTIREG(predictors, responses [, interceptFlag]) returns {coefficients,intercept,rank,residualNorm,normalResidualNorm} from the shared CPU SVD least-squares solver. Rows are observations; columns are predictors. The default flag 1 fits an intercept; 0 omits it. Rank-deficient designs return a minimum-norm solution and numerical rank.

HUBERREG(predictors,responses,delta[,interceptFlag[,maxIterations[,tolerance]]]) fits a multivariable linear model with CPU iteratively reweighted SVD least squares. delta is the positive Huber threshold in response units; no residual scale is estimated. The optional intercept flag defaults to 1, the iteration limit to 50 (range 1..100), and coefficient relative tolerance to 1E-8. The result is {coefficients,intercept,rank,iterations,converged,normalizedMeanLoss,lossScale,normalizedStationarity}. The stationarity field is the maximum column-scaled mean Huber gradient magnitude; it supports diagnostics but is not a formal certificate. The reported mean Huber loss is normalized by lossScale; multiply it by lossScale^2 to recover response-squared units when representable. A false convergence flag means the iteration or descent limit was reached. The design is limited to 256 columns and a conservative cumulative 100-million work estimate; rank-deficient fits report the SVD numerical rank. The caller must choose delta for the response units; a threshold that underflows when normalized to the data scale is rejected. See the editable `huber_regression.bas` example.

LOGITREG(predictors,responses[,interceptFlag[,lambda[,maxIterations[,tolerance]]]]) fits a binary logistic model using damped Newton steps and the shared CPU SVD solver. Responses must contain both exact labels 0 and 1. Predictors are scaled by each column's actual maximum absolute value, including maxima below one (all-zero columns use scale one); reported slopes are converted back to the original units. lambda defaults to 1 and applies L2 regularization to the scaled slopes, not the intercept. The intercept flag defaults to 1; iteration limit defaults to 50 and accepts 1..100; the regularized gradient-infinity tolerance defaults to 1E-8. The result is {coefficients,intercept,rank,iterations,converged,meanNegativeLogLikelihood,gradientNorm}. A false convergence flag is a bounded solver outcome, not a valid optimum certificate. Fits are limited to 128 predictor columns and a conservative 50-million operation estimate, with cancellation checks. This is binary classification only; it does not provide categorical encoding, confidence intervals, or a multi-class solver. See the editable `logistic_regression.bas` example.

THEILSEN(x,y) returns {slope,intercept,medianAbsoluteResidual,pairCount} for the CPU Theil-Sen simple linear trend estimator. It takes the median of all pairwise slopes with distinct predictor values, then the median of y-slope*x for the intercept. This resists a minority of response outliers without fitting an ordinary least-squares model first. Inputs must have equal lengths from 2 to 1414, with finite values; at most one million predictor pairs are processed. Repeated predictor values are skipped, and an input with no distinct pair is an error. This is a robust trend estimate, not a confidence interval, full multivariable regression, or a claim about the data-generating process. See the editable `theil_sen.bas` example.

LSTSQM(A,B[,rcond]) solves the real least-squares system A X ≈ B for multiple RHS columns using one SVD of A. It returns {solutionMatrix,fitResidualNorms,normalResidualNorms,numericalRank}; each output and residual entry follows the corresponding column of B. The default relative cutoff is MAX(rows,columns)*EPSILON. Rank-deficient and underdetermined systems return the minimum-norm solution within that threshold.

WLSTSQ(A,b,weights[,rcond]) and WLSTSQM(A,B,weights[,rcond]) perform weighted real least squares. The weight vector has one finite, nonnegative value per observation and must contain at least one positive value; zero excludes that row. WLSTSQ returns {coefficients,fitResidual,normalResidual,rank,weightScale} and WLSTSQM returns {solutionMatrix,fitResiduals,normalResiduals,rank,weightScale}. Rows are normalized by the maximum input weight before SVD. Residual norms are reported on this normalized scale; multiply the fit residual by SQR(weightScale) and the normal residual by weightScale to recover original scaling when representable.

Flexible matrix-free linear systems

MFFGMRES("FNOP",b,"FNPC"[,rtol,atol,maxiter,initial,restart]) solves the fixed linear system FNOP(x)=b with restarted flexible right preconditioning. FNPC(v) returns an approximate inverse action, a finite real list matching v. It may be nonlinear or change between calls, including a tolerance-driven inner Krylov solve. FNOP itself must remain a fixed linear map. Each returned inverse direction is stored and used when updating x; the solver never reapplies FNPC to a combination of directions. Thus this interface supports inner iterative solves that are unsuitable for the fixed-left-preconditioner MFGMRES contract.

10 DEF FNOP(X)={4*X(1)+2*X(2),-X(1)+3*X(2)}
20 DEF FNPOINT(R)=R(1)
30 DEF FNPC(X)=FNPOINT(MFGMRES("FNOP",X,.2,0,2))
40 R=MFFGMRES("FNOP",{2,-4},"FNPC"):PRINT R

The output, tolerance convention, iteration bounds and scoped one-list DEF FN calling rules match MFGMRES. The preconditioner name is the third required argument. The default restart is up to 30, reduced to fit both the Arnoldi basis V and stored inverse directions Z. For effective restart k, (2*k+1)*LEN(b) must not exceed 2,000,000 retained elements; a nontrivial solve therefore cannot fit more than 666,666 unknowns even at restart 1. The input dimension limit remains 1,000,000, allowing an already-converged initial guess to return without a basis. Every candidate uses a fresh original b-FNOP(x) residual; an inner convergence claim or small Hessenberg residual cannot certify the outer solution.

The 100-million solver-work and 10,000 combined callback-application limits, finite/shape checks, cancellation and recoverable assignment behavior still apply. A converged initial guess or zero maximum iterations does not call FNPC. There is no guarantee that arbitrary inverse actions span useful directions; zero/singular/poor maps may return BREAKDOWN, STAGNATED or MAXITER. Callback internals have their own budgets and side effects are not rolled back. See programs/science/flexible_inner_outer.bas: a 1,024-state nonlocal transport system uses capped, loose-tolerance SPGMRES inner solves. An inner MAXITER vector is deliberately only an approximate direction; the outer solve must independently meet its requested residual tolerance.

Robust geometry and simple polygons

ORIENT2D(a,b,c) takes three {x,y} points and returns 1 for counterclockwise, -1 for clockwise or 0 for exact collinearity. ORIENT3D(a,b,c,d) takes four {x,y,z} points and returns the sign of det(b-a,c-a,d-a); the origin and the positive unit X/Y/Z points give 1. The signs refer to the exact binary64 input coordinates, including cases whose determinant would underflow or overflow. They do not snap nearby points together. Numeric literals/previous calculations have already been rounded before the predicate receives them.

SEGMENTREL2D(a,b,c,d) classifies the two closed 2D segments a–b and c–d: 0 disjoint, 1 touching at one point (including an endpoint/interior contact), 2 crossing at both segment interiors, 3 collinear overlap of positive length. Zero-length segments are accepted as points. This reports topology, not rounded intersection coordinates.

POLYAREA2D(vertices), POLYSIGNEDAREA2D(vertices) and POLYPERIMETER2D(vertices) measure a simple polygon given as {{x1,y1},{x2,y2},...}. Area is positive; signed area is positive for counterclockwise ordering and negative for clockwise ordering. The perimeter includes the last-to-first edge. An optional repeated closing vertex is removed.

POINTINPOLY2D(vertices,point) returns 0 outside, 1 inside or 2 on the boundary. Boundary decisions use exact-input orientation and coordinate bounds; containment uses a division-free winding count and works for concave polygons in either winding order.

Polygons require 3–4096 finite vertices after removing the optional closing point. Repeated edge vertices, backtracking adjacent edges, nonadjacent touching, crossings, overlaps and zero exact area are errors. Straight intermediate edge vertices are accepted. Holes/multiple rings are not supported by these calls. Validation checks all nonadjacent edge pairs, up to 8,382,464, with cancellation checkpoints. BASIC validates each polygon argument on each call; native Rust can retain the validated polygon for repeated O(n) queries without allocation.

The exact product accumulator sums the shoelace area before one final rounding. A nonzero area below binary64 range and overflowing measurements return errors; classification remains usable at those scales. Perimeter uses rounded hypot edge lengths and an exact sum, not an exact algebraic length. Solid booleans, holes and CAD model export remain separate work. Centroid and triangulation APIs follow below. See programs/science/planar_profile.bas for a dimensioned concave profile.

Polygon centroids and mesh triangles

POLYCENTROID2D(vertices) returns the uniform-area center {x,y} of a validated simple polygon. This is an area-weighted centroid, not a vertex average; it can lie outside a concave polygon. Exact binary64-input moments and area are divided before one ties-to-even rounding. The result remains usable when separately reporting area would overflow or underflow. A tiny coordinate may round to zero. The same exact-ratio rounding kernel serves symbolic coefficients.

POLYTRIANGLES2D(vertices) returns n-2 rows of three one-based indices into the supplied polygon, after removing its optional repeated closing point. Every triangle has nonzero exact area and the polygon's winding. Original collinear boundary vertices are retained; no new vertices are inserted. Triangle choice is deterministic, but callers should depend on the partition/index contracts rather than a specific diagonal sequence. Pass these faces directly to OBJECT MESH with matching {x,y,z} vertices, as in programs/science/profile_mesh.bas.

Both calls use the existing 3–4096 vertex simple-polygon validation. Triangulation uses exact orientation signs, O(n) temporary/output storage and O(n squared) work: fewer than 4*n*n point visits after validation, with cancellation checkpoints. Centroids use O(n) accumulation and bounded temporary integers. Errors/cancellation do not replace a BASIC assignment's previous value. Neither call supports holes, self-intersections or multiple rings. Triangulation is not a Delaunay/quality mesher, and a planar triangle partition alone is not a closed printable solid.

Indexed 3D meshes and polygon extrusion

All mesh calls take vertices={{x,y,z},...} and faces={{i,j,k},...} with one-based integer indices, matching OBJECT MESH. Inputs require 3–200,000 finite vertices and 1–100,000 nondegenerate triangles. Every vertex must be used. Invalid/fractional indices, repeated indices in a face, duplicate faces ignoring winding, and exactly collinear triangles are errors. Distinct indices at the same coordinates remain distinct; no tolerance-based welding or automatic repair occurs.

  • MESHTOPOLOGY3D(vertices,faces) returns `{vertexCount,edgeCount,faceCount, componentCount,boundaryEdges,nonmanifoldEdges,windingConflicts, nonmanifoldVertices,eulerCharacteristic,closedOrientedManifold}`. Components connect through indexed edges. Boundary edges have one face; non-manifold edges have more than two. Winding conflicts count two-face edges traversed in the same direction. Vertex checks detect disconnected fans and links that are neither a cycle nor a single boundary path. Euler is V-E+F. The final BASIC boolean is -1 only when all four defect counts are zero.
  • MESHBOUNDS3D(vertices,faces) returns {{xmin,ymin,zmin},{xmax,ymax,zmax}}.
  • MESHAREA3D(vertices,faces) returns total triangle surface area. Cross products use exact input products, separate exponents preserve tiny/huge components, norms are rounded binary64, and normalized areas are exactly accumulated before final scaling. This is an approximate radical sum, not guaranteed correctly rounded exact area; faces can overlap and their areas are still added.
  • MESHSIGNEDVOLUME3D(vertices,faces) requires closed, consistently oriented manifold index topology. It returns the exact original-coordinate determinant sum divided by six, rounded once. Outward faces give positive contributions; reversed shells give negative contributions. Multiple shells add algebraically. A magnitude below binary64 can round to zero; overflow is an error. Area uses the same zero-underflow/overflow policy. Input coordinate units determine squared area and cubed volume units; there is no implicit millimeter conversion.
  • POLYEXTRUDE3D(polygon,height) returns {vertices,faces} for a positive finite height along +Z. It reuses validated simple-polygon triangulation, preserves every boundary vertex, and produces outward faces for either polygon winding. The first vertex layer is at zero, the second at height. Holes remain unsupported. For n profile vertices there are 2n vertices and 4n-4 triangular faces.

Example: M=POLYEXTRUDE3D(P,5):V=M(1):F=M(2) followed by the measurement calls or OBJECT MESH "part",V,F,"#65d6b1". The freely editable workload is programs/science/extruded_profile.bas; pass PREVIEW to render its part.

Topology and measurement are shared Rust kernels. Mesh admission/topology use O(V+F log F) work and O(V+F) storage; measurements are O(F), with bounded exact accumulators and cancellation checkpoints. Area retains O(F) scaled values. Sorting is bounded by the stated limits and checks cancellation before/after; most traversal loops check every 256 items. Failed calls preserve previous BASIC assignments. Native consumers can retain the immutable mesh and reuse validation.

Closed index topology is not solid/printing certification. These calls do not detect intersecting triangles, intersecting shells, inward nested components, coincident geometry or minimum wall thickness. Signed volume is algebraic for such inputs, not a physical union volume. Self-intersection/solid containment, CAD booleans, model import/export, slicer and physical-printer acceptance remain separate requirements. Do not treat the final topology boolean as those checks.

Exact triangle contacts and mesh self-intersections

TRIANGLEHIT3D(a,b) accepts two triangles, each {{x,y,z},{x,y,z},{x,y,z}}, and returns -1 if their closed sets intersect or 0 if disjoint. Point/edge contacts, transverse crossings, coplanar overlap and containment are included. Nonfinite or exactly degenerate triangles are errors. Decisions use exact signs for the input binary64 coordinates; no snapping tolerance or rounded intersection point is introduced. Coordinate-aligned planes use exact comparisons/projections; other cases reuse the shared fixed-limb 3D determinant sign kernel.

MESHSELFHIT3D(vertices,faces[,maxWork]) returns -1 at the first proven improper face intersection, or 0 only after completing the scan. MESHINTERSECTIONS3D( vertices,faces[,maxPairs[,maxWork]]) returns every improper face pair as sorted {{i,j},...} rows, with one-based face indices, i<j, in lexicographic order. An empty list means the completed scan found no improper contacts.

A mesh intersection is improper when it extends beyond an edge or vertex indexed by both faces. Adjacent folded or oppositely sided coplanar faces may share their edge. Coplanar faces overlapping on the same side of a shared edge are reported. Faces sharing one vertex are still checked for overlap/crossing elsewhere. Geometric contacts between distinct, unwelded indices are reported even when coordinates coincide. These are spatial checks; they do not repair or weld data.

The same mesh admission rules and limits apply: up to 200,000 used finite vertices and 100,000 nondegenerate, nonduplicate index triangles. Each BASIC call constructs a bounded balanced bounding-box hierarchy. Native Rust callers can retain the immutable index. Construction costs O(F log F) work and O(F) storage; scans prune nonoverlapping boxes but worst-case candidate work is quadratic.

maxPairs defaults to 10,000 and accepts integers 1–100,000. maxWork defaults to 4,000,000 and accepts integers 1–100,000,000. Work counts both hierarchy node-pair visits and leaf face-pair visits, including bounds rejection. A pair limit or work limit failure is an error with no partial-success result. The existence query may stop early after a proven hit; it never returns false from an incomplete scan. A valid crowded/fan-shaped mesh can exhaust the budget and require a larger limit. Cancellation leaves the source mesh and previous BASIC assignment intact. These limits bound operation counts; they are not a cross-hardware latency guarantee.

Use these calls alongside MESHTOPOLOGY3D, rather than interpreting its topology flag as a spatial test. A closed, consistently oriented surface may still cross itself; conversely, nonintersecting nested shells still require containment and orientation-by-nesting checks before interpreting a physical solid domain. These predicates alone do not implement solid booleans, minimum-wall analysis, model interchange, slicing or printer acceptance. The topology/measurement constructors do not run this optional spatial scan automatically.

programs/science/mesh_intersections.bas constructs two parts and checks their clean, separated and crossing configurations using these shared Rust functions.

Closed solid domains, cavities and point containment

These CPU Rust-backed operations require a finite indexed triangle mesh with closed manifold topology and consistent winding within every connected shell. They perform the exact mesh-intersection scan and reject surface crossings, coincident unwelded contacts and touching shells. A work limit or interruption is an error, never evidence that validation completed.

  • MESHSHELLS3D(vertices, faces [, maxWork]) returns rows {firstFace, faceCount, nestingDepth, inputOrientation} in ascending first-face order. Faces are one-based. Input orientation is the exact signed-volume sign 1 (outward) or -1 (inward), even if a rounded volume underflows/overflows. Depth counts containing shells: even depth bounds material, odd depth a cavity.
  • POINTINMESH3D(vertices, faces, point [, maxWork]) returns 0 outside material, 1 inside material, or 2 on a face, edge or vertex. point has three finite coordinates. A cavity is outside; an island inside that cavity is inside.
  • POINTSINMESH3D(vertices, faces, points [, maxWork]) classifies up to 100,000 three-coordinate rows and returns corresponding 0/1/2 values. It validates and indexes the mesh once, sharing one query-work budget across the entire batch. Empty input returns {} after successful mesh validation. Errors return no partial list. Prefer this to rebuilding a large mesh for each point.
  • MESHVOLUME3D(vertices, faces [, maxWork]) returns the material volume under even/odd shell fill, subtracting cavities and adding nested islands. Input shell reversals do not change this result. It sums exact original-coordinate determinants with parity-correct signs, divides by six and rounds once to binary64. Final overflow is an error; a positive volume below the binary64 range can round to zero. Coordinates carry caller-chosen length units and volume has the cube of those units.
  • MESHORIENT3D(vertices, faces [, maxWork]) returns a new one-based face list with outward material boundaries and inward cavity boundaries. It preserves the vertex list, indices and face order, reversing only whole shells. It does not modify either input or repair inconsistent winding within a shell.

All five functions retain the mesh admission limits of 200,000 vertices and 100,000 nondegenerate faces. maxWork is an integer in 1..100000000, default 4,000,000. It independently caps the intersection phase, the combined shell- nesting phase, and (when applicable) the single point or complete point-batch phase. Work counts visited BVH nodes/pairs and candidate face visits as documented for each phase. Initial mesh/index construction and exact volume accumulation have their own bounded linear or O(F log F) loops and cancellation checks; maxWork is not a wall-clock timeout or an allocation-byte budget.

Containment uses exact binary64-input predicates with a symbolic projected-ray perturbation to assign shared edges/vertices consistently. No represented numeric "epsilon" or coordinate nudging is used. Boundary points are checked exactly. Shell nesting uses representative vertices against other disjoint shells, not bounding-box containment. Native Rust retains an immutable reusable index; individual BASIC calls build their own index. Worst-case overlapping bounds can still require quadratic intersection work or shell-count times face-count nesting work; budgets fail explicitly. Batch query work is also bounded.

MESHSIGNEDVOLUME3D retains its original algebraic signed-volume contract and index-topology precondition. These new domain operations add embedding/nesting validation and parity fill. Neither API proves a chosen manufacturing tolerance, minimum wall thickness, support suitability, slicer interoperability or physical printability. Arbitrary mesh repair, solid booleans, curved CAD surfaces and model-format interchange remain separate work. See programs/science/hollow_part.bas for an editable cavity/orientation workload.

## Multivariable descriptive statistics

### Gamma and chi-square distributions

`GAMMAPDF(x,shape,scale)` returns the gamma probability density;
`GAMMACDF(x,shape,scale)` returns the lower-tail probability, and
`GAMMASF(x,shape,scale)` returns the upper-tail probability directly. Shape and
scale must be finite and positive; scale is the scale parameter, not its
reciprocal rate. The mean is `shape*scale` and variance is `shape*scale^2` when
those expressions are representable. `CHISQPDF(x,df)`, `CHISQCDF(x,df)` and
`CHISQSF(x,df)` use the same Rust backend with shape `df/2` and scale `2`.
Degrees of freedom must be finite and positive; fractional values are accepted.

Use the survival function for a small upper-tail p-value. For example,
`CHISQSF(100,2)` is approximately `1.92874984796392E-22`, while subtracting
`CHISQCDF(100,2)` from one loses that value to floating-point rounding.

```basic
10 PRINT GAMMAPDF(2,3,1):PRINT GAMMACDF(2,3,1)
20 PRINT GAMMASF(50,1,1):PRINT CHISQSF(100,2)
```

Samples must be finite. Negative samples have density and lower-tail probability
zero, and upper-tail probability one. At zero, the gamma density is zero for
shape greater than one, `1/scale` for shape one, and singular for shape below
one (an overflow error). Probability calculations use bounded series/continued
fractions with cancellation checks and a 10,000-iteration limit. Large shapes
use an asymptotic expansion. These are binary64 numerical estimates; convergence
failure raises an error and does not return a partial result. Tiny probabilities
can underflow, and densities beyond finite range raise overflow. Lower and upper
inverse probabilities are available through `GAMMAINV`, `GAMMAINVSF`, `CHISQINV`
and `CHISQINVSF`; see the inverse-function section below.

### Student's t distribution

`TPDF(t,df)` returns the density, `TCDF(t,df)` the lower-tail probability,
and `TSF(t,df)` the directly evaluated upper-tail probability. Degrees of freedom
`df` must be finite and positive; there is no one-million-degree restriction.
`TINV(p,df)` and `TINVSF(p,df)` return lower- and upper-tail critical values for
`0 < p < 1`. Infinite endpoint quantiles are rejected.

These functions share the bounded CPU Rust backend. Inversion uses one range
check and at most 63 coordinate bisections, with cancellation checks and explicit
overflow for a quantile beyond finite binary64. Results are numerical estimates,
not certified bounds or correctly rounded guarantees for every input.

All five functions accept scalar arguments or flat numeric lists. Scalars
broadcast over lists; multiple lists must have equal lengths. The result cap is
one million elements. An invalid element aborts the whole assignment without
changing the destination. Long batches remain cancellable.

```basic
10 DF=9:T=2.262157163
20 P=2*TSF(ABS(T),DF)
30 C=TINVSF(.025,DF)
40 PRINT "TWO-SIDED P: ";P
50 PRINT "95% CRITICAL T: ";C
60 PRINT "DENSITY: ";TPDF(T,DF)
```

`TINV(.975,10)` and `TINVSF(.025,10)` are approximately `2.22813885198627`.
Use the direct tail instead of subtracting a CDF close to one.
`TSF(1E200,1)` is approximately `3.1830988618379E-201` and
`TINVSF(1E-200,1)` approximately `3.1830988618379E199`. Central mass and
logarithmic tails are retained separately so squaring a large t statistic does
not erase a representable probability. The reference example is
`programs/science/student_t_distribution.bas`.

`TTEST1(sample,mu[,confidence])` performs a two-sided one-sample t test of the
sample mean against `mu`. It returns `{t,df,p,lower,upper}`: signed t statistic,
degrees of freedom, two-sided p-value, and the central confidence interval
(95% by default). The sample must contain at least two finite, nonconstant
values, and `confidence` must be strictly between zero and one. The interval
and p-value use the same bounded Student's t kernels as `TCDF` and `TINV`.

```basic
10 X={4.8,5.1,4.9,5.0,5.2}:R=TTEST1(X,4.8,.95)
20 PRINT "T STATISTIC: ";R(1):PRINT "DEGREES OF FREEDOM: ";R(2)
30 PRINT "TWO-SIDED P VALUE: ";R(3)
40 PRINT "95% CONFIDENCE INTERVAL: ";R(4);" TO ";R(5)
```

The result is an ordinary BASIC list, so its fields can be saved or combined
with other BASIC calculations. For independent samples with unequal variances,
use `TTEST2`; for naturally matched observations, pass their explicit paired
differences to `TTEST1`. Pooled-variance tests and a full multiple-testing
workflow are not provided.

`TTEST2(first,second[,confidence])` performs Welch's two-sided independent-
samples test, which does not assume equal population variances. It returns the
same five fields as `TTEST1`, with the estimate defined as
`mean(first)-mean(second)`. The degrees of freedom use the Welch-Satterthwaite
formula. Each sample must contain at least two finite observations, both groups
cannot be constant, their combined size is limited to one million values, and
confidence defaults to 95%. This is not a pooled-variance or paired test; use
explicit paired differences with `TTEST1` when observations are naturally
matched.

```basic
10 A={2.1,2.3,2.0,2.4,2.2}:B={1.6,1.8,1.7,1.9,1.5}
20 R=TTEST2(A,B):PRINT "WELCH T: ";R(1):PRINT "DF: ";R(2)
30 PRINT "TWO-SIDED P VALUE: ";R(3)
40 PRINT "95% CI FOR MEAN DIFFERENCE: ";R(4);" TO ";R(5)
```

`COVMATRIX(matrix [, sampleFlag])` returns a covariance matrix with matrix rows
as observations and columns as variables. The optional flag defaults to `1`
(sample covariance, divisor `n-1`); use `0` for population covariance, divisor
`n`. `CORRMATRIX(matrix)` returns the Pearson correlation matrix. Both functions
require rectangular finite data and are bounded by matrix-size and work limits;
correlation additionally requires at least two observations and nonconstant
columns.

`MULTIREG(predictors, responses [, interceptFlag])` returns
`{coefficients,intercept,rank,residualNorm,normalResidualNorm}` from the shared
CPU SVD least-squares solver. Rows are observations; columns are predictors.
The default flag `1` fits an intercept; `0` omits it. Rank-deficient designs
return a minimum-norm solution and numerical rank.

`HUBERREG(predictors,responses,delta[,interceptFlag[,maxIterations[,tolerance]]])`
fits a multivariable linear model with CPU iteratively reweighted SVD least
squares. `delta` is the positive Huber threshold in response units; no residual
scale is estimated. The optional intercept flag defaults to `1`, the iteration
limit to `50` (range `1..100`), and coefficient relative tolerance to `1E-8`.
The result is `{coefficients,intercept,rank,iterations,converged,normalizedMeanLoss,lossScale,normalizedStationarity}`.
The stationarity field is the maximum column-scaled mean Huber gradient
magnitude; it supports diagnostics but is not a formal certificate. The reported
mean Huber loss is normalized by `lossScale`; multiply it by `lossScale^2` to recover response-squared units when representable. A false
convergence flag means the iteration or descent limit was reached. The design is
limited to 256 columns and a conservative cumulative 100-million work estimate;
rank-deficient fits report the SVD numerical rank. The caller must choose `delta`
for the response units; a threshold that underflows when normalized to the data
scale is rejected. See the editable
[`huber_regression.bas`](../programs/science/huber_regression.bas) example.

`LOGITREG(predictors,responses[,interceptFlag[,lambda[,maxIterations[,tolerance]]]])`
fits a binary logistic model using damped Newton steps and the shared CPU SVD
solver. Responses must contain both exact labels `0` and `1`. Predictors are
scaled by each column's actual maximum absolute value, including maxima below
one (all-zero columns use scale one); reported slopes
are converted back to the original units. `lambda` defaults to `1` and applies
L2 regularization to the scaled slopes, not the intercept. The intercept flag
defaults to `1`; iteration limit defaults to `50` and accepts `1..100`; the
regularized gradient-infinity tolerance defaults to `1E-8`. The result is
`{coefficients,intercept,rank,iterations,converged,meanNegativeLogLikelihood,gradientNorm}`.
A false convergence flag is a bounded solver outcome, not a valid optimum
certificate. Fits are limited to 128 predictor columns and a conservative
50-million operation estimate, with cancellation checks. This is binary
classification only; it does not provide categorical encoding, confidence
intervals, or a multi-class solver. See the editable
[`logistic_regression.bas`](../programs/science/logistic_regression.bas) example.

`THEILSEN(x,y)` returns `{slope,intercept,medianAbsoluteResidual,pairCount}`
for the CPU Theil-Sen simple linear trend estimator. It takes the median of all
pairwise slopes with distinct predictor values, then the median of `y-slope*x`
for the intercept. This resists a minority of response outliers without fitting
an ordinary least-squares model first. Inputs must have equal lengths from 2 to
1414, with finite values; at most one million predictor pairs are processed.
Repeated predictor values are skipped, and an input with no distinct pair is an
error. This is a robust trend estimate, not a confidence interval, full
multivariable regression, or a claim about the data-generating process. See the
editable [`theil_sen.bas`](../programs/science/theil_sen.bas) example.

`LSTSQM(A,B[,rcond])` solves the real least-squares system `A X ≈ B` for
multiple RHS columns using one SVD of `A`. It returns
`{solutionMatrix,fitResidualNorms,normalResidualNorms,numericalRank}`; each
output and residual entry follows the corresponding column of `B`. The default
relative cutoff is `MAX(rows,columns)*EPSILON`. Rank-deficient and
underdetermined systems return the minimum-norm solution within that threshold.

`WLSTSQ(A,b,weights[,rcond])` and `WLSTSQM(A,B,weights[,rcond])` perform
weighted real least squares. The weight vector has one finite, nonnegative value
per observation and must contain at least one positive value; zero excludes that
row. `WLSTSQ` returns `{coefficients,fitResidual,normalResidual,rank,weightScale}`
and `WLSTSQM` returns `{solutionMatrix,fitResiduals,normalResiduals,rank,weightScale}`.
Rows are normalized by the maximum input weight before SVD. Residual norms are
reported on this normalized scale; multiply the fit residual by `SQR(weightScale)`
and the normal residual by `weightScale` to recover original scaling when
representable.


### Flexible matrix-free linear systems

`MFFGMRES("FNOP",b,"FNPC"[,rtol,atol,maxiter,initial,restart])` solves the fixed
linear system `FNOP(x)=b` with restarted flexible **right** preconditioning.
`FNPC(v)` returns an approximate inverse action, a finite real list matching v.
It may be nonlinear or change between calls, including a tolerance-driven inner
Krylov solve. FNOP itself must remain a fixed linear map. Each returned inverse
direction is stored and used when updating x; the solver never reapplies FNPC to
a combination of directions. Thus this interface supports inner iterative solves
that are unsuitable for the fixed-left-preconditioner `MFGMRES` contract.

```basic
10 DEF FNOP(X)={4*X(1)+2*X(2),-X(1)+3*X(2)}
20 DEF FNPOINT(R)=R(1)
30 DEF FNPC(X)=FNPOINT(MFGMRES("FNOP",X,.2,0,2))
40 R=MFFGMRES("FNOP",{2,-4},"FNPC"):PRINT R
```

The output, tolerance convention, iteration bounds and scoped one-list `DEF FN`
calling rules match `MFGMRES`. The preconditioner name is the third required
argument. The default restart is up to 30, reduced to fit both the Arnoldi basis V
and stored inverse directions Z. For effective restart k, `(2*k+1)*LEN(b)` must
not exceed 2,000,000 retained elements; a nontrivial solve therefore cannot fit
more than 666,666 unknowns even at restart 1. The input dimension limit remains
1,000,000, allowing an already-converged initial guess to return without a basis.
Every candidate uses a fresh original `b-FNOP(x)` residual; an inner convergence
claim or small Hessenberg residual cannot certify the outer solution.

The 100-million solver-work and 10,000 combined callback-application limits,
finite/shape checks, cancellation and recoverable assignment behavior still
apply. A converged initial guess or zero maximum iterations does not call FNPC.
There is no guarantee that arbitrary inverse actions span useful directions;
zero/singular/poor maps may return BREAKDOWN, STAGNATED or MAXITER. Callback
internals have their own budgets and side effects are not rolled back.
See `programs/science/flexible_inner_outer.bas`: a 1,024-state nonlocal transport
system uses capped, loose-tolerance SPGMRES inner solves. An inner MAXITER vector
is deliberately only an approximate direction; the outer solve must independently
meet its requested residual tolerance.


### Robust geometry and simple polygons

`ORIENT2D(a,b,c)` takes three `{x,y}` points and returns `1` for counterclockwise,
`-1` for clockwise or `0` for exact collinearity. `ORIENT3D(a,b,c,d)` takes four
`{x,y,z}` points and returns the sign of `det(b-a,c-a,d-a)`; the origin and the
positive unit X/Y/Z points give `1`. The signs refer to the exact binary64 input
coordinates, including cases whose determinant would underflow or overflow.
They do not snap nearby points together. Numeric literals/previous calculations
have already been rounded before the predicate receives them.

`SEGMENTREL2D(a,b,c,d)` classifies the two closed 2D segments `a–b` and `c–d`:
`0` disjoint, `1` touching at one point (including an endpoint/interior contact),
`2` crossing at both segment interiors, `3` collinear overlap of positive length.
Zero-length segments are accepted as points. This reports topology, not rounded
intersection coordinates.

`POLYAREA2D(vertices)`, `POLYSIGNEDAREA2D(vertices)` and
`POLYPERIMETER2D(vertices)` measure a simple polygon given as
`{{x1,y1},{x2,y2},...}`. Area is positive; signed area is positive for
counterclockwise ordering and negative for clockwise ordering. The perimeter
includes the last-to-first edge. An optional repeated closing vertex is removed.

`POINTINPOLY2D(vertices,point)` returns `0` outside, `1` inside or `2` on the
boundary. Boundary decisions use exact-input orientation and coordinate bounds;
containment uses a division-free winding count and works for concave polygons
in either winding order.

Polygons require 3–4096 finite vertices after removing the optional closing
point. Repeated edge vertices, backtracking adjacent edges, nonadjacent touching,
crossings, overlaps and zero exact area are errors. Straight intermediate edge
vertices are accepted. Holes/multiple rings are not supported by these calls.
Validation checks all nonadjacent edge pairs, up to 8,382,464, with cancellation
checkpoints. BASIC validates each polygon argument on each call; native Rust
can retain the validated polygon for repeated O(n) queries without allocation.

The exact product accumulator sums the shoelace area before one final rounding.
A nonzero area below binary64 range and overflowing measurements return errors;
classification remains usable at those scales. Perimeter uses rounded hypot
edge lengths and an exact sum, not an exact algebraic length. Solid booleans, holes and CAD model export remain separate work.
Centroid and triangulation APIs follow below.
See `programs/science/planar_profile.bas` for a dimensioned concave profile.


### Polygon centroids and mesh triangles

`POLYCENTROID2D(vertices)` returns the uniform-area center `{x,y}` of a validated
simple polygon. This is an area-weighted centroid, not a vertex average; it can
lie outside a concave polygon. Exact binary64-input moments and area are divided
before one ties-to-even rounding. The result remains usable when separately
reporting area would overflow or underflow. A tiny coordinate may round to zero.
The same exact-ratio rounding kernel serves symbolic coefficients.

`POLYTRIANGLES2D(vertices)` returns `n-2` rows of three **one-based** indices into
the supplied polygon, after removing its optional repeated closing point. Every
triangle has nonzero exact area and the polygon's winding. Original collinear
boundary vertices are retained; no new vertices are inserted. Triangle choice
is deterministic, but callers should depend on the partition/index contracts
rather than a specific diagonal sequence. Pass these faces directly to
`OBJECT MESH` with matching `{x,y,z}` vertices, as in
`programs/science/profile_mesh.bas`.

Both calls use the existing 3–4096 vertex simple-polygon validation. Triangulation
uses exact orientation signs, O(n) temporary/output storage and O(n squared) work:
fewer than `4*n*n` point visits after validation, with cancellation checkpoints.
Centroids use O(n) accumulation and bounded temporary integers. Errors/cancellation
do not replace a BASIC assignment's previous value. Neither call supports holes,
self-intersections or multiple rings. Triangulation is not a Delaunay/quality
mesher, and a planar triangle partition alone is not a closed printable solid.


### Indexed 3D meshes and polygon extrusion

All mesh calls take `vertices={{x,y,z},...}` and `faces={{i,j,k},...}` with
**one-based integer** indices, matching `OBJECT MESH`. Inputs require 3–200,000
finite vertices and 1–100,000 nondegenerate triangles. Every vertex must be used.
Invalid/fractional indices, repeated indices in a face, duplicate faces ignoring
winding, and exactly collinear triangles are errors. Distinct indices at the same
coordinates remain distinct; no tolerance-based welding or automatic repair occurs.

- `MESHTOPOLOGY3D(vertices,faces)` returns `{vertexCount,edgeCount,faceCount,
  componentCount,boundaryEdges,nonmanifoldEdges,windingConflicts,
  nonmanifoldVertices,eulerCharacteristic,closedOrientedManifold}`.
  Components connect through indexed edges. Boundary edges have one face;
  non-manifold edges have more than two. Winding conflicts count two-face edges
  traversed in the same direction. Vertex checks detect disconnected fans and
  links that are neither a cycle nor a single boundary path. Euler is V-E+F.
  The final BASIC boolean is `-1` only when all four defect counts are zero.
- `MESHBOUNDS3D(vertices,faces)` returns `{{xmin,ymin,zmin},{xmax,ymax,zmax}}`.
- `MESHAREA3D(vertices,faces)` returns total triangle surface area. Cross products
  use exact input products, separate exponents preserve tiny/huge components,
  norms are rounded binary64, and normalized areas are exactly accumulated before
  final scaling. This is an approximate radical sum, not guaranteed correctly
  rounded exact area; faces can overlap and their areas are still added.
- `MESHSIGNEDVOLUME3D(vertices,faces)` requires closed, consistently oriented
  manifold index topology. It returns the exact original-coordinate determinant
  sum divided by six, rounded once. Outward faces give positive contributions;
  reversed shells give negative contributions. Multiple shells add algebraically.
  A magnitude below binary64 can round to zero; overflow is an error. Area uses
  the same zero-underflow/overflow policy. Input coordinate units determine
  squared area and cubed volume units; there is no implicit millimeter conversion.
- `POLYEXTRUDE3D(polygon,height)` returns `{vertices,faces}` for a positive finite
  height along +Z. It reuses validated simple-polygon triangulation, preserves
  every boundary vertex, and produces outward faces for either polygon winding.
  The first vertex layer is at zero, the second at height. Holes remain unsupported.
  For n profile vertices there are 2n vertices and 4n-4 triangular faces.

Example: `M=POLYEXTRUDE3D(P,5):V=M(1):F=M(2)` followed by the measurement calls
or `OBJECT MESH "part",V,F,"#65d6b1"`. The freely editable workload is
`programs/science/extruded_profile.bas`; pass `PREVIEW` to render its part.

Topology and measurement are shared Rust kernels. Mesh admission/topology use
O(V+F log F) work and O(V+F) storage; measurements are O(F), with bounded exact
accumulators and cancellation checkpoints. Area retains O(F) scaled values.
Sorting is bounded by the stated limits and checks cancellation before/after;
most traversal loops check every 256 items. Failed calls preserve previous BASIC
assignments. Native consumers can retain the immutable mesh and reuse validation.

**Closed index topology is not solid/printing certification.** These calls do not
detect intersecting triangles, intersecting shells, inward nested components,
coincident geometry or minimum wall thickness. Signed volume is algebraic for
such inputs, not a physical union volume. Self-intersection/solid containment,
CAD booleans, model import/export, slicer and physical-printer acceptance remain
separate requirements. Do not treat the final topology boolean as those checks.


### Exact triangle contacts and mesh self-intersections

`TRIANGLEHIT3D(a,b)` accepts two triangles, each `{{x,y,z},{x,y,z},{x,y,z}}`,
and returns `-1` if their closed sets intersect or `0` if disjoint. Point/edge
contacts, transverse crossings, coplanar overlap and containment are included.
Nonfinite or exactly degenerate triangles are errors. Decisions use exact signs
for the input binary64 coordinates; no snapping tolerance or rounded intersection
point is introduced. Coordinate-aligned planes use exact comparisons/projections;
other cases reuse the shared fixed-limb 3D determinant sign kernel.

`MESHSELFHIT3D(vertices,faces[,maxWork])` returns `-1` at the first proven improper
face intersection, or `0` only after completing the scan. `MESHINTERSECTIONS3D(
vertices,faces[,maxPairs[,maxWork]])` returns every improper face pair as sorted
`{{i,j},...}` rows, with **one-based face indices**, `i<j`, in lexicographic order.
An empty list means the completed scan found no improper contacts.

A mesh intersection is improper when it extends beyond an edge or vertex indexed
by both faces. Adjacent folded or oppositely sided coplanar faces may share their
edge. Coplanar faces overlapping on the same side of a shared edge are reported.
Faces sharing one vertex are still checked for overlap/crossing elsewhere.
Geometric contacts between distinct, unwelded indices are reported even when
coordinates coincide. These are spatial checks; they do not repair or weld data.

The same mesh admission rules and limits apply: up to 200,000 used finite vertices
and 100,000 nondegenerate, nonduplicate index triangles. Each BASIC call constructs
a bounded balanced bounding-box hierarchy. Native Rust callers can retain the
immutable index. Construction costs O(F log F) work and O(F) storage; scans prune
nonoverlapping boxes but worst-case candidate work is quadratic.

`maxPairs` defaults to 10,000 and accepts integers 1–100,000. `maxWork` defaults
to 4,000,000 and accepts integers 1–100,000,000. Work counts both hierarchy node-pair
visits and leaf face-pair visits, including bounds rejection. A pair limit or work
limit failure is an error with no partial-success result. The existence query may
stop early after a proven hit; it never returns false from an incomplete scan.
A valid crowded/fan-shaped mesh can exhaust the budget and require a larger limit.
Cancellation leaves the source mesh and previous BASIC assignment intact. These
limits bound operation counts; they are not a cross-hardware latency guarantee.

Use these calls alongside `MESHTOPOLOGY3D`, rather than interpreting its topology
flag as a spatial test. A closed, consistently oriented surface may still cross
itself; conversely, nonintersecting nested shells still require containment and
orientation-by-nesting checks before interpreting a physical solid domain.
These predicates alone do not implement solid booleans, minimum-wall analysis,
model interchange, slicing or printer acceptance. The topology/measurement
constructors do not run this optional spatial scan automatically.

`programs/science/mesh_intersections.bas` constructs two parts and checks their
clean, separated and crossing configurations using these shared Rust functions.

### Closed solid domains, cavities and point containment

These CPU Rust-backed operations require a finite indexed triangle mesh with
closed manifold topology and consistent winding within every connected shell.
They perform the exact mesh-intersection scan and reject surface crossings,
coincident unwelded contacts and touching shells. A work limit or interruption is
an error, never evidence that validation completed.

- `MESHSHELLS3D(vertices, faces [, maxWork])` returns rows
  `{firstFace, faceCount, nestingDepth, inputOrientation}` in ascending first-face
  order. Faces are one-based. Input orientation is the exact signed-volume sign
  `1` (outward) or `-1` (inward), even if a rounded volume underflows/overflows.
  Depth counts containing shells: even depth bounds material, odd depth a cavity.
- `POINTINMESH3D(vertices, faces, point [, maxWork])` returns `0` outside material,
  `1` inside material, or `2` on a face, edge or vertex. `point` has three finite
  coordinates. A cavity is outside; an island inside that cavity is inside.
- `POINTSINMESH3D(vertices, faces, points [, maxWork])` classifies up to 100,000
  three-coordinate rows and returns corresponding `0/1/2` values. It validates
  and indexes the mesh once, sharing one query-work budget across the entire
  batch. Empty input returns `{}` after successful mesh validation. Errors return
  no partial list. Prefer this to rebuilding a large mesh for each point.
- `MESHVOLUME3D(vertices, faces [, maxWork])` returns the material volume under
  even/odd shell fill, subtracting cavities and adding nested islands. Input
  shell reversals do not change this result. It sums exact original-coordinate
  determinants with parity-correct signs, divides by six and rounds once to
  binary64. Final overflow is an error; a positive volume below the binary64
  range can round to zero. Coordinates carry caller-chosen length units and
  volume has the cube of those units.
- `MESHORIENT3D(vertices, faces [, maxWork])` returns a new one-based **face list**
  with outward material boundaries and inward cavity boundaries. It preserves
  the vertex list, indices and face order, reversing only whole shells. It does
  not modify either input or repair inconsistent winding within a shell.

All five functions retain the mesh admission limits of 200,000 vertices and
100,000 nondegenerate faces. `maxWork` is an integer in `1..100000000`, default
4,000,000. It independently caps the intersection phase, the combined shell-
nesting phase, and (when applicable) the single point or complete point-batch
phase. Work counts visited BVH nodes/pairs and candidate face visits as documented
for each phase. Initial mesh/index construction and exact volume accumulation
have their own bounded linear or `O(F log F)` loops and cancellation checks;
`maxWork` is not a wall-clock timeout or an allocation-byte budget.

Containment uses exact binary64-input predicates with a symbolic projected-ray
perturbation to assign shared edges/vertices consistently. No represented numeric
"epsilon" or coordinate nudging is used. Boundary points are checked exactly.
Shell nesting uses representative vertices against other disjoint shells, not
bounding-box containment. Native Rust retains an immutable reusable index;
individual BASIC calls build their own index. Worst-case overlapping bounds can
still require quadratic intersection work or shell-count times face-count
nesting work; budgets fail explicitly. Batch query work is also bounded.

`MESHSIGNEDVOLUME3D` retains its original algebraic signed-volume contract and
index-topology precondition. These new domain operations add embedding/nesting
validation and parity fill. Neither API proves a chosen manufacturing tolerance,
minimum wall thickness, support suitability, slicer interoperability or physical
printability. Arbitrary mesh repair, solid booleans, curved CAD surfaces and
model-format interchange remain separate work. See
`programs/science/hollow_part.bas` for an editable cavity/orientation workload.

documents.title: STL triangle-model files
documents.html:
MESH READ path$, destination [, format$] imports geometry into {vertices,faces,{format$,nonzeroAttributeCount,solidBlockCount}}; face indices are one-based. The default format "STL" detects ASCII or binary STL. "STL-ASCII" and "STL-BINARY" explicitly select a parser. Facet order and winding are preserved; exact equal coordinates are welded to shared indices, with signed zero normalized. There is no tolerance-based welding or repair.

MESH WRITE path$, vertices, faces [, format$ [, maxError]] exports a validated triangle surface. Default "STL-ASCII" preserves finite binary64 coordinates through scientific decimal text. Binary STL stores float32 coordinates: select "STL-BINARY" and supply a finite nonnegative absolute coordinate-error allowance in the model's units. Default zero permits only exactly representable coordinates. Overflow, excessive rounding, collapsed triangles and merging of distinct indexed vertices are errors. ASCII export also rejects coincident distinct indexed vertices because importing STL would merge them. "STL" is read-only detection.

Both statements use the ordinary BASIC file workspace (--file-root), the same path confinement and atomic replacement policy as ordinary file operations. They do not require graphics initialization. An invalid import preserves its destination; validation/encoding errors and cancellation before file commit preserve an existing file. Replacement is atomic. If the final directory sync fails after replacement, an I/O error can be reported with the new file already visible; this follows ordinary FileStore durability semantics. Input and output each have a 64 MiB codec cap, reduced by a smaller configured file limit. The mesh limits are 100,000 triangles and 200,000 unique vertices. Cancellation is checked while converting records and before assignment/file commit.

ASCII reading accepts blank lines, CRLF, case-insensitive keywords, an optional UTF-8 BOM, named/multiple solid blocks and omitted facet normals. Records are limited to 4,096 bytes; mismatched provided end names and malformed/truncated sequences are errors. Binary input must have exactly the declared record length; a valid binary length takes precedence over a header starting with solid. Nonfinite fields, degenerate or duplicate indexed triangles are rejected. Finite supplied normals are advisory: winding defines geometry, and export calculates unit normal hints. Binary attribute/color fields are ignored, counted when nonzero, and exported as zero. Solid names are not preserved.

STL carries no standardized units or scene/appearance description. Set units by agreement with the receiving tool. Open or nonmanifold surfaces can be imported for diagnosis; import/export alone does not establish a valid printable solid. Use MESHTOPOLOGY3D, MESHSELFHIT3D, MESHSHELLS3D and MESHVOLUME3D as appropriate. After binary rounding, re-import and validate the actual exported geometry: rounding may create spatial intersections even without collapsed faces. General solid repair, booleans, other formats, slicers and physical-printer verification remain separate requirements. See programs/science/stl_part.bas for a millimetre hollow part and both encodings.
