## Explicit color-space and alpha mathematics

These numerical functions use shared CPU Rust kernels. Color triples are
`{red,green,blue}` and RGBA rows are `{red,green,blue,alpha}`. Alpha is finite
coverage in `[0,1]`; finite RGB channels may be negative or exceed one for
extended-gamut/HDR computations. These functions do not clip, tone-map, adapt
white points or change existing graphics commands. `RGB`/`RGBA` still construct
byte-channel graphics strings; divide stored bytes by 255 before sRGB decoding.

| Function | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `SRGBLINEAR(rgb)` | Decode normalized extended sRGB to linear-light sRGB. |
| `LINEARSRGB(rgb)` | Encode linear-light sRGB using the extended sRGB transfer. |
| `RGBXYZ(linearRgb)` | Linear sRGB primaries to CIE XYZ with D65 white, relative Y=1. |
| `XYZRGB(xyz)` | Inverse D65 transform; negative/out-of-gamut channels remain numerical values. |
| `RGBLUMINANCE(linearRgb)` | Relative Y component of the same D65 transform. Decode sRGB first. |
| `RGBPREMULT(rgba)` | Multiply RGB by alpha; return premultiplied RGBA. |
| `RGBUNPREMULT(rgba)` | Divide premultiplied RGB by alpha; zero alpha requires zero RGB and returns transparent black. |
| `RGBCOMPOSITE(source,destination[,operator$])` | Composite straight linear RGBA; return straight linear RGBA. Default `"SOURCE-OVER"`. |
| `RGBMIX(first,second,t)` | Interpolate in premultiplied linear RGBA for `0<=t<=1`; return straight RGBA. Transparent hidden colors do not create fringes. |
| `RGBTRANSFORMBATCH(rows,transform$)` | Apply `"SRGB-LINEAR"`, `"LINEAR-SRGB"`, `"RGB-XYZ"` or `"XYZ-RGB"` to rows of three channels. |
| `RGBCOMPOSITEBATCH(sourceRows,destinationRows[,operator$])` | Composite equal-sized lists of RGBA rows with one native call; same operator/default as the scalar function. |

Compositing names are case-insensitive: `CLEAR`, `COPY`, `DESTINATION`,
`SOURCE-OVER`, `DESTINATION-OVER`, `SOURCE-IN`, `DESTINATION-IN`, `SOURCE-OUT`,
`DESTINATION-OUT`, `SOURCE-ATOP`, `DESTINATION-ATOP`, `XOR`. These twelve coverage
operators are distinct from artistic blend modes. Additive/lighter behavior is
not defined by this bounded-alpha API. Interpret both inputs in the same linear
RGB space; the kernel does not infer or automatically convert color spaces.

Transfer functions use the standard breakpoints .04045 and .0031308, with
sign-reflected power branches for negative channels. The rounded standard
breakpoints introduce a small discontinuity, so exact inversion at the join is
not promised. Powers use approximate binary64 math; final overflow errors.
XYZ products use binary64 matrix coefficients and an exact product accumulator
before one rounding. No general color-management/profile claim is implied.

Compositing and mixing form binary64 coverage factors (including `1-alpha` and
`1-t`), then retain their exact products and exact weighted color ratios until
rounding the returned channels. The RGB ratio uses the unrounded coverage sum.
Alpha rounds separately; if it underflows to zero the result is transparent
black. Premultiplication itself can lose tiny values through underflow, so its
inverse cannot restore lost information. Nonfinite inputs, invalid alpha,
shapes/operators and unrepresentable division results are errors.

Batches contain at most 250,000 rows; empty equal-shaped batches are valid.
Existing BASIC retained-value limits can impose a smaller practical limit.
Use strips/blocks for larger images. Inputs stay unchanged and failures or
cancellation return no partial result. Native batches avoid per-pixel BASIC
calls; exact fractional-alpha ratios may use bounded integer scratch storage.
These are numerical operations, not a promise of real-time full-frame throughput.

`programs/science/color_compositing.bas` uses batch transforms/compositing and an
optional `PREVIEW` argument to paint a comparison through BASIC. It saves
`color-compositing.png` in the configured screenshot output workspace. This
example supplements the kernels; tracing, color profiles, image buffers, advanced
shading and full production-image/video workflows remain separate open work.

### Shared image buffers (`IMAGE`)

`IMAGE` operates on named Rust buffers without opening a display. Names are
case-sensitive strings (1–255 bytes, no controls), separate from BASIC variables.
Pixels are straight **linear-light RGBA**: finite signed/HDR RGB, alpha 0–1.
Coordinates use top-left origin, x right, y down. Pixel `(0,0)` has center
`(.5,.5)` and covers `[0,1) × [0,1)`.

| Statement | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `IMAGE CREATE name$,w,h[,rgba]` | Fill with a linear RGBA list; default transparent black. |
| `IMAGE FROM name$,w,h,rows[,encoding$]` | Import row-major `{ {r,g,b,a}, ... }`; encoding `LINEAR` (default) or `SRGB` (RGB transfer only). |
| `IMAGE LOAD name$,path$` | Read the current image file through the asset root; decode RGB as sRGB and preserve alpha. |
| `IMAGE RESIZE source$,result$,w,h[,filter$[,maxSamples]]` | Resize using `AUTO` (default), `NEAREST`, `LINEAR`, or `AREA`. |
| `IMAGE MIRROR source$,result$,horizontal,vertical` | Exact pixel reflection; each flag is 0 or 1. |
| `IMAGE COMPOSITE source$,destination$,result$[,operator$]` | Equal-size images; same twelve operators as `RGBCOMPOSITE`, default `SOURCE-OVER`. |
| `IMAGE SAMPLE name$,x,y,result[,filter$[,border$]]` | Return one RGBA list; `LINEAR`/`NEAREST`, `CLAMP`/`TRANSPARENT`, defaults `LINEAR`,`CLAMP`. |
| `IMAGE UV name$,u,v,result[,filter$[,border$]]` | Normalized image-edge coordinates; top-left origin, V downward. Same filters/borders/defaults as `IMAGE SAMPLE`. Pixel centers are `((x+.5)/w,(y+.5)/h)`. |
| `IMAGE INFO name$,result` | Return `{width,height}`. |
| `IMAGE PIXELS name$,x,y,w,h,result` | Return a row-major RGBA list for a zero-based integer rectangle. |
| `IMAGE SAVE name$,path$[,backgroundRgb]` | Write opaque P6 `.ppm` in the output root; flatten over a linear RGB background (default black), clip display gamut, then encode sRGB bytes. |
| `IMAGE FREE name$` / `IMAGE CLEAR` | Release one/all named image buffers. `IMAGE CLEAR` preserves BASIC variables. |

`AUTO` uses pixel-cell area averaging on each shrinking axis and linear
interpolation on each enlarging/unchanged axis. `AREA` always averages cell
intersection; `LINEAR` samples at centers and is not an anti-alias filter for
large reductions. All resize borders clamp. Filtering averages premultiplied
color/coverage and returns straight RGBA; rounded-zero coverage becomes
transparent black, avoiding hidden-color fringes. Nearest, mirroring and
same-size copies preserve hidden RGB. Geometry/weights use binary64; exact
product sums/ratios avoid intermediate overflow/underflow for those weights.

Dimensions are positive integers, at most 16,777,216 pixels per image. There are
at most 64 named buffers; each consumes 32 bytes/pixel from the existing per-run
and shared asset budgets (1 GiB each). Replacements require room for old and new
images simultaneously and occur only on success. Loading also charges decoder
scratch; saving charges encoded bytes. BASIC list import/extraction is capped at
250,000 pixels and also obeys ordinary retained-value limits. `CLEAR`, `RUN` and
program replacement release buffers; `END` retains them in the interactive
session. `maxSamples` defaults to 100,000,000, accepts 1–1,000,000,000 and bounds
planned source taps, including duplicate/zero boundary taps; exact accumulation
may make multiple bounded passes. Extreme anisotropic operations may exceed
this budget and can be split into separate axis resizes.

Load uses existing PPM/native and optional external compressed-image decoders;
this API does not add a codec or color-profile management. `SAVE` is explicitly
opaque PPM, not alpha-preserving PNG. With asset/output roots pointing to the
same permitted directory, saved images can be displayed by `BITMAP`. Existing
byte-oriented renderer filtering remains unchanged. See
`programs/science/image_resampling.bas` for an editable consumer and `PREVIEW`.

### Image filtering, gradients and projective warps

| Statement | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `IMAGE CONVOLVE source$,result$,kernel[,border$[,maxSamples]]` | Centered convolution with an odd rectangular nested kernel (each axis 1–63). Nonnegative weights with positive total are normalized; RGB/alpha are filtered in premultiplied linear light. Default border `CLAMP`; `TRANSPARENT` includes zero outside pixels in the fixed weight total. |
| `IMAGE CHANNELFILTER source$,channel$,kernel,result[,border$[,maxSamples]]` | Unnormalized signed convolution of straight `RED`, `GREEN`, `BLUE`, `ALPHA` or linear D65 `LUMINANCE`. Returns `{width,height,{row-major scalar values}}`. Hidden straight RGB remains data; choose alpha/coverage convolution when filtering visible color. |
| `IMAGE GRADIENT source$,channel$,spacing,result[,border$[,maxSamples]]` | Normalized 3×3 Sobel derivatives. Positive finite `{dx,dy}` gives physical pixel spacing; result is `{width,height,{{gx,gy},...}}`, with positive axes right/down. Default `CLAMP`; `TRANSPARENT` uses zero extension. |
| `IMAGE WARP source$,result$,w,h,matrix[,filter$[,border$[,samplesPerAxis[,maxSamples]]]]` | Finite nonsingular 3×3 **destination-to-source** homogeneous matrix. Pixel centers are `(.5,.5)`. Defaults `LINEAR`, `TRANSPARENT`, one sample per axis; `NEAREST` and `CLAMP` are available. A regular 1–16 subpixel grid per axis averages premultiplied color/coverage. |

Convolution reverses the kernel: `out(x,y)=sum(kernel(j,i)*in(x+cx-i,y+cy-j))`.
For example, `{{1,0,-1}}` measures the right-minus-left difference. Zero signed
kernels are valid; signed output may be negative/HDR. Sobel divides its weighted
difference by `8*spacing` with exact accumulation/division, avoiding intermediate
overflow. Output fields remain composable BASIC lists with at most 250,000 pixels.
They share the ordinary retained-value limits and scoped asset admission.

Warp divides the first two mapped coordinates by the third. A denominator that
vanishes or changes sign anywhere in the full output rectangle is rejected;
there is no guessed value at a projective horizon. Exact determinant signs and
homogeneous ratios preserve very small/large common matrix scales. The matrix is
already the inverse map: no silent inversion or coordinate convention change.
Subpixel integration reduces aliasing but is a bounded regular grid, not an
adaptive or exact anisotropic reconstruction filter. For axis-aligned heavy
minification, `IMAGE RESIZE ...,"AREA"` remains available.

All operations preserve their source and replace destinations only on success,
including in-place names. Work limits count planned kernel taps (including zero
coefficients), 18 taps/pixel for gradients, or `grid²*(1 or 4)` per warp pixel.
They retain the image-wide 16,777,216-pixel cap, shared memory limits, cancellation
and explicit finite-result errors. Coverage convolution canonicalizes zero alpha
to zero RGB; nearest warp with one sample preserves the original hidden RGB.
See `programs/science/image_processing.bas` for an editable image consumer.

### Image regions and height surfaces

`IMAGE TRACE name$,channel$,threshold,result[,maxEdges]` traces selected **pixel
cells** from a named image. Channels are `RED`, `GREEN`, `BLUE`, `ALPHA`, and
`LUMINANCE` (linear D65). Selection is inclusive: channel value >= threshold.
RGB/luminance selection uses straight channels, including hidden RGB; select
`ALPHA` when coverage is intended. Thresholds must be finite.

The result is `{rings,signedAreas,selectedPixels,boundaryEdges}`. Each ring is
`{{x,y},...}`, implicitly closed without repeating its first point. Coordinates
are integer image edges, with top-left origin and y down. Collinear runs reduce
to corners. Positive signed areas surround selected regions and negative areas
surround holes; their sum equals the selected pixel count. Foreground uses four
edge neighbors and background uses eight neighbors; diagonal foreground cells
remain separate. Boundaries can touch or revisit vertices at diagonal background
contacts. Such rings are not automatically valid simple polygons. Hole grouping,
smoothing, antialiased subpixel tracing and general polygon-with-holes
triangulation are separate operations. `maxEdges` bounds **unit boundary edges**,
not the reduced corner count; default 100,000, range 1–1,000,000. Empty selections
return empty rings/areas and zero counts.

`IMAGE HEIGHTMESH name$,channel$,origin,spacing,heightScale,result` constructs an
explicitly sampled height surface. `origin={x0,y0,z0}` places the first sample
center; `spacing={dx,dy}` contains positive finite physical grid steps.
`z=z0+heightScale*channelValue`, with signed finite scale. No threshold, alpha
masking, clipping or depth inference is implicit. Dimensions must be at least
2×2. Result is `{vertices,faces,uv}`: vertices and faces use the existing mesh
layout (BASIC face indices start at 1); normalized UVs are pixel centers
`{(x+.5)/width,(y+.5)/height}`. Each grid cell has two triangles along its
upper-left/lower-right diagonal, with +Z orientation in XY. Use the first two
result fields with existing mesh analysis, `OBJECT MESH` or `MESH WRITE`.

The shared mesh caps are 200,000 vertices and 100,000 triangles. Rounded XY
coordinates must remain strictly increasing; overflow or collapsed spacing is
an error. This is an **open sampled surface**, not a watertight printable solid.
Both statements preserve the destination on failure and support cancellation.
Temporary contour/geometry/value conversion is conservatively charged to the
shared asset budget, and returned lists obey the normal BASIC storage limits.
See `programs/science/image_geometry.bas`: its default mode checks results,
`PREVIEW` draws contours and a height surface, and `EXPORT` writes an ASCII STL
surface into the file root.


### Linear lumped circuits — `CIRCUIT`

Rust owns the model and assembles modified nodal equations `E*x' + G*x = B*u`.
Use SI units: volts, amperes, ohms, farads, henries, siemens and hertz. Node 0 is
ground; `nodeCount` declares nodes 1 through N. Current is positive from the first
terminal `p` to the second `n`; voltage is `V(p)-V(n)`. Terminals must differ.
Component rows are ordinary editable BASIC lists:

| Row | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `{"R",p,n,ohms}` | Positive resistance |
| `{"C",p,n,farads}` | Positive capacitance |
| `{"L",p,n,henries}` | Positive inductance; current becomes a state unknown |
| `{"I",p,n}` | Independent current source |
| `{"V",p,n}` | Independent voltage source; current becomes a state unknown |
| `{"VCCS",p,n,cp,cn,siemens}` | Output current = gain times control voltage |
| `{"VCVS",p,n,cp,cn,gain}` | Output voltage = gain times control voltage |
| `{"CCCS",p,n,controlElement,gain}` | Output current = gain times control current |
| `{"CCVS",p,n,controlElement,ohms}` | Output voltage = gain times control current |

Control voltages use `V(cp)-V(cn)`. Current controls reference a **one-based
component row**, including forward references, which must be L, V, VCVS or CCVS.
Controlled gains may be signed or zero. All values must be finite. Source values
are supplied separately in independent I/V component order, allowing one model
to serve different DC values, AC phasors and time-dependent forcing.

```basic
10 CIRCUIT CREATE "rc",2,{{"V",1,0},{"R",1,2,1000},{"C",2,0,1E-6}}
20 CIRCUIT DC "rc",{1},D
30 CIRCUIT AC "rc",159.15494309189535,{1},A
40 X=A(1)
50 PRINT X(2)
60 CIRCUIT FREE "rc"
```

- `CIRCUIT CREATE name$,nodeCount,components`: validated, atomic replacement.
- `CIRCUIT DC name$,sources,result[,solver$]`: capacitors are open and inductors
  short at DC. A singular DC topology returns an error.
- `CIRCUIT AC name$,frequencyHz,sources,result[,solver$]`: finite nonnegative Hz,
  complex or real source phasors, using `exp(+j*omega*t)` and `G+j*omega*E`.
- Both solves return `{state,residual,backwardError,solver$}`. `state` contains
  N node voltages followed by currents of L/V/VCVS/CCVS components in row order.
  `residual` contains physical KCL/constraint defects, with mixed A/V units.
  `backwardError` is maximum `abs(A*x-b)/(abs(A)*abs(x)+abs(b))`, evaluated
  componentwise; AC uses the equivalent real block equations. Results exceeding
  `1E-10` are rejected. A small backward error is not a forward-error or
  conditioning guarantee.
- `CIRCUIT INFO name$,result`: `{nodes,elements,sources,unknowns,branchMap,sourceRows}`.
  Branch map gives each component's one-based state position, or zero if absent.
- `CIRCUIT SYSTEM name$,result`: `{G,E,B}`, canonical `CSR1` matrices. With no
  independent sources, B is `{}` (native Rust uses an N-by-zero CSR matrix).
- `CIRCUIT RESIDUAL name$,state,derivative,sources,result`: `E*x'+G*x-B*u`.
- `CIRCUIT JACOBIAN name$,coefficient,result`: canonical CSR `G+coefficient*E`.
  Cancellation can change its nonzero pattern; do not assume a fixed KLU pattern.
- `CIRCUIT FREE name$` and `CIRCUIT CLEAR`: release retained models. BASIC
  `CLEAR`, `RUN` and program replacement also release models.

`solver$` is `"AUTO"` (default), `"DENSE"` or `"SPARSE"`. Dense is the shared
pure Rust solver through 128 DC unknowns or 64 AC unknowns. AUTO selects sparse
above these limits. Sparse requires the qualified CPU UMFPACK 6.3.5 provider;
provider absence is an error. Models admit at most 2,048 state unknowns, 10,000
components and 64 named models. Assembly, retained models and solve working sets
are admitted against the shared asset budget; sparse solves reserve 384 MiB
conservatively against native fill/work ceilings. No persistent factor cache is
created. Row scaling rejects lost nonzero coefficients; coefficient overflow or
underflow is an error. Failed construction/solves preserve prior models/results.

The linear component forms remain ideal and lumped. Semiconductor extensions,
operating points, bias-dependent AC and bounded index-one transients are documented
below. Higher-index reduction, broader device physics, noise, netlist import and
SPICE compatibility remain open. Direct residual/DAE composition still requires
caller-provided variable IDs and initial conditions; CIRCUIT TRANSIENT derives
its own capacitor-incidence coordinates for its supported topology.

Circuit solves may apply at most two iterative correction solves against exact
physical-equation residuals, retaining only improvements. This controls loss of
accuracy from row scaling in mixed-unit AC networks. A final componentwise
backward error above `1E-10` still fails; the tolerance is never loosened.


### Semiconductor circuits, operating points and small-signal response

Additional component rows use the same Rust circuit model and SI units:

| Row | Device law |
| --- | --- |
| `{"D",anode,cathode,Is,N,kelvin}` | Shockley junction with positive saturation current, emission coefficient and absolute temperature |
| `{"DQ",anode,cathode,Is,N,kelvin,C0,Vj,M,Fc,TT}` | Shockley junction with depletion and diffusion charge storage; see below |
| `{"NPN",collector,base,emitter,Is,betaF,betaR,kelvin}` | Reciprocal static Ebers–Moll NPN model |
| `{"PNP",collector,base,emitter,Is,betaF,betaR,kelvin}` | Mirrored-polarity reciprocal static Ebers–Moll PNP model |

`Is` is the saturation current (D) or transport current (NPN/PNP) **at the supplied
actual temperature**. No nominal-temperature scaling of Is or material bandgap
is inferred. D/NPN/PNP parameters must be finite and positive. DQ charge
parameters have the separate ranges below. Bipolar gains are
common-emitter forward/reverse gains. Bipolar terminals may share nodes, including
diode-connected collector/base wiring; at least two distinct nodes are required.
Device currents enter the device. Native bipolar current/Jacobian ordering is
collector, base, emitter. Reverse breakdown, high injection, Early effect,
thermal feedback and noise are not included. D/NPN/PNP have no internal charge
or transit time; DQ adds the explicitly specified junction charge model.
Use explicit R/C/L components for external parasitics; those do not turn this
static model into a validated high-frequency device model.

DQ uses `C0` in farads, `Vj` in volts, dimensionless `M` and `Fc`, and `TT` in
seconds. Require finite `Vj>0`, `C0>=0`, `M>=0`, `0<=Fc<1`, `TT>=0`, with at least
one of C0/TT positive. All parameters describe the actual temperature. Diffusion-
only and hyperabrupt (M>1) junctions are supported. Values beyond binary64 range,
or capacitance below its representable positive range, produce explicit errors.

Below `Fc*Vj`, depletion capacitance is `C0*(1-v/Vj)^(-M)`; its integrated charge
uses Q(0)=0, including the logarithmic M=1 limit. Above that boundary, capacitance
continues along its tangent and charge continues quadratically. Diffusion adds
`TT*I(v)` to charge, `TT*dI/dv` to capacitance. This is a quasistatic model; it
adds no separate carrier-transport state. Model references:
[ngspice manual](https://ngspice.sourceforge.io/docs/ngspice-manual.pdf) and
[device equations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ngspice/ngspice/master/src/spicelib/devices/dio/dioload.c).

`CIRCUIT DEVICE name$,elementIndex,volts,result` evaluates a D or DQ device at the
supplied junction voltage and returns `{current,conductance,charge,capacitance,
capacitanceSlope}` in A, S, C, F and F/V. Element indices are one-based; D returns
zero for the three storage fields. It does not solve the surrounding circuit.
Failed evaluations preserve the previous destination.

DQ participates in AC, LINEARIZE, TRANSIENT, SWITCH, and both checkpoint APIs.
LINEARIZE's E is the complete capacitance/inductance matrix at the given bias;
MATRICES, STORAGE's massCSR and CONSTRAINTS' D contain only constant linear
storage. Their differential IDs and prescribed-storage maps include DQ, and the
Rust solver adds state-dependent charge and prescribed-source-rate terms.
Consequently the earlier linear coordinate equation needs these extra DQ terms.
The full transient Jacobian includes `C'(v)*vprime` as well as `coefficient*C(v)`.
Ramping-source corners use right-hand displacement currents, including at the
final sample. A prescribed voltage jump across DQ requires an ideal impulse and
is rejected. Finite resistance switches preserve DQ voltage/charge. Saved state
uses retained voltage coordinates and exact model parameters; no extra user
state variables are introduced. See `programs/science/junction_charge.bas`.

Dynamic bipolar models are described below. This does not add MOS models, breakdown, high injection, sidewall
or series-resistance parameters, thermal feedback, noise or non-quasistatic
transport. Compose explicit external R/C/L components as appropriate. Numerical
qualification is separate from physical-device and installed-OS acceptance.

`NPNQ` and `PNPQ` extend the reciprocal Ebers–Moll transistor with two
quasistatic charge branches. Their component rows are
`{kind$,collector,base,emitter,Is,betaF,betaR,kelvin,Cbe,Vbe,Mbe,Fcbe,TF,Cbc,Vbc,Mbc,Fcbc,TR}`.
Each branch uses the DQ depletion/continuation law above. Diffusion charge uses
the transport current `Is*EXPM1(v/VT)` multiplied by TF or TR, without dividing
by beta. A branch with both C0 and transit time zero has no storage; its Vj/M/Fc
must still satisfy their parameter ranges. Both branches may be disabled for
the static limit. Tied terminals introduce no spurious differential coordinate.

For NPN, the charge vector in collector/base/emitter order is
`{-Qbc,Qbe+Qbc,-Qbe}`. For PNP, reverse the junction voltages and the terminal
charge signs. The full terminal capacitance matrix is the derivative of that
vector, and its Hessian supplies the state-dependent transient Jacobian.
The shared engine accounts for both branches in AC, source-rate loads, storage
constraints, dense/KLU transients, switching and ordinary/switched restart.
Independent voltage jumps across either active branch require unsupported impulses.

`CIRCUIT DEVICE name$,elementIndex,{Vc,Vb,Ve},result` accepts NPN/PNP/NPNQ/PNPQ
and returns `{currents,jacobian,charges,capacitance,chargeHessian}`. All terminal
axes use collector/base/emitter order. The first and third entries contain three
numbers; the second/fourth are 3-by-3 lists; the fifth is a 3-by-3-by-3 list.
`capacitance(r,c)=dQ(r)/dV(c)` in farads and
`chargeHessian(r,c,k)=d2Q(r)/dV(c)/dV(k)` in F/V. Static devices return zero
storage fields. A scalar remains the diode DEVICE input; malformed inputs leave
the result unchanged. See `programs/science/transistor_charge.bas`.

The physical reference is the quasistatic depletion/ideal-transit-time part of
the [ngspice BJT model](https://ngspice.sourceforge.io/docs/ngspice-manual.pdf)
and its [charge equations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ngspice/ngspice/master/src/spicelib/devices/bjt/bjtload.c).
This implementation does not include bias-dependent transit times, base-width
modulation, high injection, excess phase, substrate charge, intrinsic series
resistance, self-heating, breakdown or noise. It does not claim full Gummel–Poon
or physical-device parity. These advanced bipolar extensions remain open; the long-channel MOS model is described next.

`CIRCUIT OP name$,sources,result[,guess[,options]]` solves the full nonlinear DC
equations. Sources keep independent I/V row order; `{}` or an omitted guess starts
from zero. `options` is
`{relative,currentAbs,voltageAbs,maxIterations,maxSourceSteps,solver$}`; defaults
are `{1E-9,1E-12,1E-9,200,64,"AUTO"}`. Relative tolerance is in `[0,1)`, both
absolute tolerances positive, total iterations 1..1000 and source attempts 0..128.
A zero source-attempt limit disables continuation. Each stage permits up to 64
Newton solves, within the total budget; each solve permits 24 line-search trials.
There is also a 26,000 evaluation ceiling. Scoped interruption remains active.

The result is
`{state,residual,scaledResidual,scaledStep,iterations,evaluations,sourceAttempts,backtracks,solver$,sourceFractions}`.
State ordering is unchanged. Both scaled convergence measures must be at most 1:
KCL uses current tolerances and voltage constraints use voltage tolerances; state
steps use voltage tolerances for nodes and current tolerances for branches.
Residual scales include the absolute tolerance plus relative tolerance times the
sum of absolute physical equation contributions. Step scales include the absolute
tolerance plus relative tolerance times the larger old/proposed state magnitude.
A small residual alone does not establish convergence; even zero residuals require
a nonsingular Jacobian solve. These checks do not establish uniqueness or a
condition-number/forward-error certificate for arbitrary nonlinear networks.

Newton uses analytic device derivatives, current-column/row scaling and damped
steps with forward-junction limiting. If the direct solve fails, source continuation
may start at zero independent-source amplitudes and increase them adaptively.
Only full-amplitude convergence is returned: `sourceFractions` ends at 1; direct
success gives `{1}`, while successful continuation starts with 0. No artificial
node-to-ground conductance or modified device law is silently added. Failure gives
an error with work counts and preserves the destination variable and named model.

- `CIRCUIT AC name$,Hz,sources,result,solver$,bias` computes the incremental
  response about the supplied state. Obtain the bias from `CIRCUIT OP`; this
  command cannot independently validate a bias without the DC source values.
- `CIRCUIT LINEARIZE name$,bias,result` returns `{J,E,B}` for the incremental
  equation `E*deltaX'+J*deltaX=B*deltaU`. It is a tangent model, not an affine
  substitute for the complete nonlinear circuit.
- `CIRCUIT JACOBIAN name$,coefficient,result[,state[,derivative]]` returns
  `dF/dx+coefficient*dF/dxprime`. Nonlinear models require state; omitted
  derivative means zero. Supply the actual derivative for DQ transient Newton
  steps, including its capacitance-slope term. Canonical sparse slots may change.
  `CIRCUIT RESIDUAL` includes conduction and nonlinear charge currents.
- Existing `CIRCUIT DC`, bias-free `AC`, `SYSTEM` and stateless `JACOBIAN` reject
  nonlinear models instead of ignoring their devices. Existing linear programs
  retain their interfaces.

```basic
10 CIRCUIT CREATE "amp",3,{{"V",1,0},{"V",2,0},{"R",1,3,1000},{"NPN",3,2,0,1E-15,100,1,300}}
20 CIRCUIT OP "amp",{5,.65},P
30 CIRCUIT AC "amp",1000,{0,1},A,"AUTO",P(1)
40 X=P(1):GAIN=A(1)
50 PRINT X(3);REAL(GAIN(3))
```

Model-count/state/component limits and optional sparse-provider requirements from
the linear circuit foundation still apply. Nonlinear solve admission additionally
reserves model-sized scratch space. Models store no mutable operating point or
factor cache. Higher-index transient reduction, advanced process-calibrated devices,
advanced transistor models, state-triggered events/recovery, noise and production workflows remain
open; this interface does not claim SPICE compatibility.


### Long-channel MOS terminal charge

`NMOSQ` and `PMOSQ` use the native constant-depletion-slope charge-sheet model:

```basic
{"NMOSQ",drain,gate,source,bulk,threshold,beta,n,kelvin,CoxWL,bodyIs,bodyN,Cj0,Vj,M,Fc,TT}
```

All four terminal nodes can be distinct or tied; at least two distinct nodes
are required. `threshold` is the charge-reference voltage in the equation below
(volts), `beta=mu*Cox*W/L` is in A/V^2, `n>=1` is the constant depletion slope,
and `CoxWL>0` is total channel oxide capacitance in farads. Beta and temperature
must be positive. Both bulk-to-drain/source junctions use the supplied DQ law;
`bodyIs`, `bodyN`, `Cj0>0`, `Vj`, `M`, `Fc`, `TT` have the DQ meanings. All
parameters describe the supplied actual temperature; there is no temperature
extrapolation or manufacturer-model parameter conversion. PMOS uses the same
positive normalized threshold as an otherwise mirrored NMOS.

For NMOS, let `UT=k*T/q`,
`a_s=(Vgs-threshold+(n-1)*Vbs)/(n*UT)`, `a_d=a_s-Vds/UT`.
The native solver finds positive endpoint charges from `2*q+ln(q)=a`, and uses
`Id=2*n*beta*UT^2*(qs*(qs+1)-qd*(qd+1))`. A separate difference calculation
preserves small represented Vds even when rounded endpoint charges coincide.
Ward–Dutton integration assigns channel charge to drain/source. With total
inversion charge QI, the linearized depletion law is
`Qbulk=-CoxWL*(n-1)/n*(Vgb-threshold)-(n-1)/n*QI`; gate charge makes the
terminal sum zero. Explicit bulk junction currents/charges are then added.
PMOS mirrors voltages and currents/charges, with derivatives transformed
consistently. This is a specified constant-slope long-channel approximation,
not a complete EKV/BSIM model or a process-calibrated SPICE model.

`CIRCUIT DEVICE name$,elementIndex,{Vd,Vg,Vs,Vb},result` returns
`{currents,jacobian,charges,capacitance,chargeHessian}` in drain/gate/source/bulk
order: lengths 4, 4x4, 4, 4x4, 4x4x4. Derivatives are signed `dI/dV`, `dQ/dV`,
and `d2Q/dV2`; off-diagonal entries do not use SPICE's negated convention.
The capacitance matrix need not be symmetric. Native terminal equations share
DC bias, incremental AC, transient residuals and the complete rate Jacobian.
Changing terminal bias changes capacitance; it is not a collection of fixed
pairwise capacitors. Storage topology retains three independent terminal
voltage differences (fewer for tied terminals), including during source
corners, switching and checkpoint/resume. Ideal source jumps that force an
instantaneous stored-charge change require impulses and are rejected.

The implementation rejects nonfinite inputs, unrepresentable results and gate
capacitance below binary64 resolution. It does not invent capacitance floors.
It covers weak/moderate/strong inversion within the stated model. It does not
include nonlinear process-dependent body depletion/accumulation, mobility
reduction, short-channel effects, velocity saturation, channel-length
modulation, DIBL, intrinsic overlap/series elements, breakdown, noise, thermal
feedback or non-quasistatic transport. External R/C elements remain composable.
Numerical references verify these equations, not physical transistor accuracy.
See `programs/science/mos_inverter.bas` for a freely editable CMOS consumer.

### Circuit storage coordinates and time-domain simulation

`CIRCUIT STORAGE name$,result` returns `{differentialIDs,parents,massCSR}`.
IDs contain one entry per physical unknown: 1 denotes a stored coordinate, 0 an
algebraic coordinate. `parents` has one entry per non-ground node and uses the
same physical node numbers as the component list. A node pointing to itself is
an algebraic root; any other node coordinate is `V(node)-V(parent)` (ground is 0).
For ordinary index-one models, inductor currents are stored coordinates and
voltage-source currents are algebraic; the capacitor-only forest is unchanged.
For independent-voltage capacitor loops, a voltage-first forest separates known
voltage differences from free capacitor state. Inductor/current cutsets use signed
cycle-current coordinates; some branch coordinates become prescribed sums of
source currents. `massCSR` contains only free derivative columns of `E*T`.
IDs refer to these coordinates, not directly to physical node voltages/currents.
Controlled-voltage capacitor loops additionally use exact linear constraints
from source laws and linear capacitor-component KCL. This can combine several
voltage/current coordinates. For those models `parents` describes the initial
forest only: use CONSTRAINTS' T and inverseT for the final coordinate meaning.

`CIRCUIT CONSTRAINTS name$,result` exposes the reduction as
`{T,inverseT,S,D,H,prescribedIDs}`. Matrices use `CSR1`; zero-axis matrices are `{}`.
Physical state is `x=T*y`, while `inverseT` maps physical guesses to coordinates.
`prescribedIDs` marks coordinates fixed by `(S*u)(k)`; the other rows of S are
zero. The reduced residual is `F(T*y,0,u) + massCSR*yprime + D*uprime = 0`.
H maps source values to their prescribed contributions to stored capacitor
voltage differences and inductor currents, in element order excluding other
parts. H detects source jumps requiring ideal current/voltage impulses. These
maps are immutable Rust outputs; CONSTRAINTS performs no time integration.

`CIRCUIT SWITCH name$,times,sources,switches,result[,initial[,options]]` runs
state-triggered resistance changes using the shared CPU Rust/IDA engine. Each
switch is `{resistorElement,controlP,controlN,low,high,onOhms,offOhms,initialMode}`.
The element index is one-based and must identify a unique existing resistor;
control voltage is V(controlP)-V(controlN), with node zero as ground. Both
resistances must be finite and positive, and `low < high`. An off switch turns
on at `high`; an on switch turns off at `low`. Initial mode is 0 or 1. The named
circuit remains immutable; changed resistances apply only to this run.

Options are `{relative,voltageAbs,currentAbs,maxSteps,maxStep,maxEvents}`,
defaulting to `{1E-8,1E-10,1E-12,20000,0,1000}`. Time/source/initial-state units
match TRANSIENT. The result is `{transientResult,events,finalModes,eventEvaluations,
finalCoordinates}`. `transientResult` has the ordinary TRANSIENT layout. Each event
is `{time,switchIndex,newMode,physicalStateBefore,physicalStateAfter}`; switches
are one-based, modes are 0/1. Output samples at switching times and source jumps
use the consistent right-hand state. Initial conditions outside a switch's
active threshold trigger a transition at the first time. Simultaneous roots and
zero-time algebraic cascades are processed in switch-index order. Hysteresis and
a finite event limit prevent unbounded toggling; incompatible cascades fail.

Capacitor voltage differences and inductor currents stay fixed during switching;
algebraic voltages/currents and derivatives are recomputed. No-free-storage
circuits use an internal clock for continuous root localization; that clock is
omitted from public states. Dense solves cover up to 256 internal variables and
structural KLU up to 1024 (a pure algebraic circuit needs one extra clock).
There are at most 64 switches, 10,000 transitions and one million retained event
state components; reduce maxEvents for large circuits. Aggregate callback work,
steps and memory are bounded. A failed/cancelled run preserves the destination.

Choose maxStep to resolve fast controls and hysteresis larger than meaningful
numerical noise. Finite root sampling cannot guarantee detection of tangencies
or arbitrarily packed crossings. This API models finite resistance changes,
not ideal zero/infinite-resistance topology changes or impulsive redistribution.
`finalCoordinates` exposes retained storage values for analysis. For portable
continuation, use `CIRCUIT SWITCHADVANCE` with the same arguments as SWITCH;
its destination is `{switchedResult,checkpoint$}`. Continue with
`CIRCUIT SWITCHRESUME name$,checkpoint$,times,result`, which returns the same
pair. Recreate the identical ordered base circuit when resuming in another
process, then supply the saved string and an increasing time list starting
exactly at the saved absolute time. The original switches, current modes,
source schedules and numerical options come from the record.

`MBCSW1:` text contains a versioned binary record encoded as uppercase hex.
It retains physical state and exact reduced storage coordinates, so small
capacitor differences survive even when large common-mode voltages round both
node readings to the same value. Saved states are after source jumps and switch
cascades; resuming does not repeat those boundary events. Native solver history
is rebuilt, so resumed trajectories agree within solver tolerances rather than
necessarily bit for bit. Step/event budgets apply separately to each call.

The binary record is limited to 1 MiB; BASIC string and shared asset limits also
apply. Decoding validates size, checksum, model identity, finite values, source
schedules, state/coordinate consistency and switch modes. The checksum detects
corruption; it does not authenticate a record. Errors and cancellation leave
the destination unchanged. Ordinary ADVANCE/RESUME retain their MBCIR1 format
and cannot consume switched records. See `programs/science/switched_circuit_restart.bas`.

`CIRCUIT TRANSIENT name$,times,sources,result[,initial[,options]]` uses the shared
CPU SUNDIALS IDA backend and analytic Rust residual/Jacobian assembly. `times` is
an increasing list of at least two finite times in seconds. Sources follow the
independent-source order from `CIRCUIT INFO`; values are volts for V sources and
amperes for I sources. Source forms are:

- A number or `{"DC",value}`: constant amplitude.
- `{"SIN",offset,amplitude,hz,phaseRadians}`: sinusoid with nonnegative frequency.
- `{"STEP",time,before,after}`: one explicitly timed jump.
- `{"PWL",{{time,value},...}}`: continuous piecewise-linear samples.
- `{"TABLE",{{time,leftValue,rightValue},...}}`: ramps between knots with explicit
  jumps at knots. Before the first knot use its left value; after the last use
  its right value. Times must strictly increase; each knot has one time.

An omitted or empty initial list starts at the DC operating point for the first
right-hand source values. An explicit list uses physical node/branch order and
fixes initial capacitor voltage differences and inductor currents. IDA corrects
algebraic guesses and consistent derivatives without changing those stored values.
For a zero-charge/zero-current start pass a zero vector of the full physical size.
An unsupported topology, failed operating point or initialization is an error.

Options are `{relative,voltageAbs,currentAbs,maxSteps,maxStep}`; defaults are
`{1E-8,1E-10,1E-12,20000,0}`. Relative tolerance is strictly between 0 and 1;
absolute tolerances must be finite and positive. They apply to voltage-difference/
root-voltage coordinates and branch-current coordinates, respectively. `maxSteps`
is a total across all source intervals (1..100000); zero `maxStep` lets IDA choose.
Physical node-voltage error also depends on accumulation along the capacitor tree;
tolerances do not constitute a global error certificate.

The result is `{rows,steps,residualCalls,jacobianCalls,errorTestFailures,segments,
differentialIDs,parents,algebraicIterations}`. Each row is `{time,physicalState...}` in the original
node/branch order. Only requested times are returned. A sample exactly at a source
jump contains the consistent right-hand algebraic values and continuous stored
coordinates, including jumps at the final output time. Every table knot splits
integration into smooth source intervals. IDA may interpolate inside an interval;
it never sees the next source jump through an unnoticed internal step. Failed
solves, cancellation and work-limit errors preserve the previous BASIC target.

Circuits with no stored coordinates use an operating-point solve at each requested
time. `steps`, `jacobianCalls` and `errorTestFailures` are zero for this algebraic
sweep; `algebraicIterations` reports total Newton solves and is zero for IDA.
`maxSteps` bounds that total Newton count for algebraic sweeps (at most 1000 per
sample). The relative/current/voltage tolerances apply to OP acceptance, and
`maxStep` has no effect. Sources are evaluated at their right limits and previous
solutions seed later guesses. These are algebraic balances, including DQ
currents forced by prescribed voltage derivatives; no free stored state is
advanced. They do not establish uniqueness, stability or physical hysteresis. The existing OP AUTO policy
uses optional UMFPACK above 128 unknowns. No differential state is fabricated.

This path admits 1024 physical unknowns, 10000 output times and at most 1000000
output cells including time, 1024 knots per source, 10000 source knots in total
and 1024 smooth intervals. Through 256 unknowns it uses IDA's dense analytic
solve; from 257 through 1024 it selects the qualified CPU KLU sparse solver.
The sparse path derives a fixed pattern from topology, permits exactly zero
coefficients in structural slots and corrects initial and jump-time constraints
with the same analytic Jacobian. At most 250000 structural slots are admitted;
KLU factor allocations are capped at 64 MiB. Missing KLU is an explicit error.
Matrix-free/Krylov circuit transients remain open. Transient admission also includes the conservative AUTO operating-point working
set (384 MiB of logical reservation above 128 unknowns), because initial bias or
a zero-storage sweep may need the sparse provider. STORAGE reserves only layout/
CSR work and retains the full model state limit; TRANSIENT has a 1024-state
limit. A reservation is an admission ceiling, not an upfront resident allocation.
The source/state work shares the asset budget; callbacks
have aggregate 200000-call and 50000000 work-unit limits. Independent-voltage
capacitor loops and independent-current inductor cutsets are reduced by incidence
trees, without numerical rank thresholds or artificial shunts. Pure voltage-source
loops and floating/current-only components still produce explicit diagnostics.
Controlled-voltage capacitor loops now use the shared Rust exact linear reduction
where linear constraints can be isolated. It supports stored-voltage/current
controls, linear algebraic controls, feedback and nonlinear charge loads; it does
not perform general nonlinear constraint differentiation. Rank uses exact
represented coefficients, with no numerical cutoff. Nonfinite or nonzero
underflowing coordinate-map entries, dependent input-waveform requirements and
resource exhaustion fail explicitly. Other singular/higher-index systems can
fail numerical initialization; topology is not a general well-posedness proof.
The fallback admits 128 MiB of extra working storage, at most 8192 entries per
exact sparse matrix, 2000000 elimination/map operations and 4096 bits per exact
integer. Actual resident usage depends on the model. Absolute tolerances apply
to transformed coordinates; ill-conditioned reconstruction can amplify errors.
SWITCH rejects resistance changes that alter the constrained coordinate/source
maps until explicit projection to a new basis is implemented. Unchanged maps
retain continuous charge/flux behavior and the existing checkpoint APIs.
General nonlinear/higher-index reduction, impulse redistribution and production
SPICE parity remain open. Sine phase uses exact reduction of represented finite
binary64 time/frequency products; input and sampling precision still apply.

`programs/science/circuit_transients.bas` demonstrates an editable BASIC request
for a stepped RC response. `programs/science/controlled_filter.bas` demonstrates
Miller feedback and portable continuation. The numerical implementation is in Rust.


For reduced circuits, constant/sine/table derivatives are evaluated analytically
on the selected smooth interval. At source corners, including a final-time knot,
algebraic output uses the right-hand derivative. A model with no free stored
coordinates uses the shared damped Newton solver with D*uprime forcing; its
`algebraicIterations` counts those solves. Source continuation scales values and
derivative loads together. All physical node voltages and branch currents remain
in the original order in TRANSIENT results.

Explicit initial values must satisfy prescribed capacitor-voltage and
inductor-current constraints within the requested tolerances. This is checked
before entering native solvers; algebraic guesses remain correctable. An interior
or final source jump with nonzero H*(uRight-uLeft) is rejected as requiring an
ideal impulse, including jumps between requested samples. Simultaneous common-mode
jumps with zero stored-state change are allowed. This API does not model impulse
currents/voltages or impulsive energy redistribution. At the starting time the
right-hand source state defines the initial problem; no prior history is assumed.

Each coordinate/source matrix admits at most 250000 entries; matrix transforms,
current-cut construction and aggregate jump checks have explicit ten-million
contribution/work bounds. Storage admission also covers source-coordinate,
derivative and stored-source maps. Default initial bias still requires a unique
operating point; otherwise supply physically consistent stored initial values.
`programs/science/circuit_constraints.bas` demonstrates both reductions.


### Circuit simulation checkpoints

`CIRCUIT ADVANCE name$,times,sources,result[,initial[,options]]` accepts the
same inputs as `CIRCUIT TRANSIENT`, returning `{transientResult,checkpoint$}`.
The first field is the unchanged nine-field TRANSIENT result. The second is a
versioned text record of the final **right-hand** physical state, absolute time,
complete source schedules, numerical options and exact ordered circuit definition.
Use ordinary `WRITEFILE path$,result(2)` and `READFILE$(path$)` for persistence.

`CIRCUIT RESUME name$,checkpoint$,times,result` returns the same two-field pair
and a new checkpoint. Recreate the identical circuit model first; its name may
differ, but nodes, ordered components, terminals, parameters and control references
must match exactly. Times are absolute, strictly increasing, with at least two
entries; the first must equal the saved time. Saved schedules retain their original
time/phase, including knots and right-hand derivative changes. The saved tolerances
and per-call work limits are reused. Changes to model, sources or tolerances require
an explicit new TRANSIENT/ADVANCE run with appropriate initial conditions.

A checkpoint contains exact binary64 values encoded as text, not executable code
or live solver handles. Its bounded format rejects unknown versions, corruption,
nonfinite or invalid fields, malformed schedules and incompatible model identity.
Its corruption checksum is not authentication. Native binary records are limited
to 1 MiB; text is at most twice that plus its prefix and also obeys the session's
string limit (1 MiB by default). ADVANCE checks the exact output size and memory
admission before solving. Failed/cancelled ADVANCE or RESUME leaves the destination
and circuit unchanged; both trajectory and checkpoint are assigned together.

Restart reconstructs the numerical solver and consistent algebraic state. It
preserves saved physical stored state and source time, but does not serialize the
adaptive solver's internal history or promise identical step counts/bitwise
trajectories. Accuracy is checked against the stated tolerances and independent
references. Repeated calls receive fresh per-call work budgets. State-triggered
switches, impulse redistribution and changing circuit topology at a restart need
additional APIs/qualification. See `programs/science/circuit_restart.bas`.

Checkpoint records also retain the **reduced storage coordinates** and resume
from those values directly. Rounded physical node voltages can hide a small
capacitor difference under a large common-mode voltage; re-deriving stored state
from those voltages would lose charge. Native `storage_coordinates()` exposes the
saved coordinates. Resume checks physical/coordinate agreement within accumulated
roundoff and prescribed-source compatibility before entering a provider. The
qualification includes a one-volt capacitor state hidden under a 1e16-volt common
mode, saved in one process and recovered after that common mode is removed.


### Shared surface functions

- `PERSPECTIVEWEIGHTS(barycentric,clipW)` returns three perspective-correct
  weights proportional to `barycentric(i)/clipW(i)`.
- `PERSPECTIVEINTERPOLATE(barycentric,clipW,attributes)` returns 1–16 channels
  from three equal-width vertex rows. Barycentric values must be finite,
  nonnegative with positive total; clip W values must be finite and positive.
  Exact product sums and ratios round each final attribute once, preserving
  representable results even when a reciprocal or a rounded weight would fail.
- `LAMBERTLIGHT(normal,light,ambient)` returns ambient plus the remaining gain
  times the positive normalized cosine. Directions must be finite and nonzero;
  ambient is 0–1. Light points toward the source. This is an artistic flat
  diffuse gain, not a radiometric BRDF or a complete lighting simulation.
- `RGBSHADE(albedoRGBA,texelRGBA,gain)` multiplies straight **linear** RGB and
  nonnegative gain, with exact triple products and one final rounding. RGB may
  be signed/HDR; alpha inputs are 0–1 and multiply separately. Final overflow
  is an error. Decode encoded colors with `SRGBLINEAR` before shading.

These functions share the Rust kernels used by `OBJECT IMAGE`. The renderer
defaults to flat faces; `OBJECT NORMALS` enables the smooth path documented below.
Opaque/cutout coverage and existing raster bounds still apply; blended
transparency, antialiasing and shadows remain open.


### Crease-separated mesh normals

`MESHCORNERNORMALS3D(vertices,faces[,creaseRadians])` returns one set of three
unit corner normals per triangle: `{{{nx,ny,nz},{...},{...}},...}`. Vertices and
one-based faces use the shared validated triangle-mesh contract. The default
crease is pi; the permitted interval is 0–pi. Zero explicitly returns flat face
normals. Other values join adjacent corners only across indexed edges shared by
two consistently wound faces whose rounded face-normal angle is at most the
crease. Boundary, nonmanifold and conflicting-winding edges stay hard. Vertex-only
contacts, separate indices and coincident positions are not welded. Smooth fans
are the connected components across permitted edges; the crease is a local edge
rule, not a limit on the total angle across a large fan.

Each fan sums **oriented face area vectors**, then normalizes. Exact coordinate
product sums preserve large cancellation and extreme scales; this is area
weighting, not angle weighting. A zero sum is undefined and fails explicitly.
Topology, cancellation and existing 200,000-vertex/100,000-face limits apply.
The crease comparison and final normalization are floating operations, not exact
angular predicates. Smooth normals change shading, not the mesh silhouette.

`NORMALTRANSFORM3D(normal,matrix)` returns `normalize(cofactor(matrix)*normal)`
for a finite 3×3 linear map. This is an **oriented** normal: reflections follow
indexed winding. For invertible maps the cofactor is determinant times inverse
transpose; it is not the ordinary vector transform. No inverse is formed.
Rank-two maps are accepted when the mapped area vector remains nonzero; a zero
input or mapped normal fails. Exact triple-product sums avoid intermediate
range loss. This same Rust operation serves `OBJECT NORMALS` transforms.

### Explicit phase units and vector angles

`SINPI(x)`, `COSPI(x)`, `TANPI(x)` interpret real x as a multiple of PI.
`SINCOSPHASE(time,frequency[,phaseRadians])` returns `{sine,cosine}` for
`2*PI*time*frequency + phaseRadians` (offset defaults to zero). Time and frequency
may be signed finite real values. Rust reduces their exact represented product
before rounding, retaining fractional cycles even when multiplication would lose
them or overflow. Quarter-cycle axes with zero offset are exact. The radian
offset uses the platform math library's original-argument reduction. This same
kernel drives CIRCUIT SIN source values and derivatives; circuit frequency must
still be nonnegative. Values remain binary64 approximations, with absolute rather
than relative accuracy near cancellation between the cycle and radian phases.
This does not recover precision already lost when computing the input time, or
make widely spaced output samples resolve high-frequency motion.

`SIND(x)`, `COSD(x)`, `TAND(x)` accept real degrees. `SINCOSPI(x)` and
`SINCOSD(x)` return `{sine,cosine}`. Reduction precedes multiplication by PI,
so represented integer/half-integer or 90-degree axes are exact. Exact tangent
poles raise division-by-zero errors. `SINCPI(x)` is normalized sinc, with value
one at zero and exact zeros at nonzero integers. Ordinary SIN/COS/TAN retain
radian semantics; there is no global angle mode. These functions are real-only.

`VANGLE3D(a,b)` takes two nonzero length-3 vectors and returns [0,PI] radians.
`ANGLE2D(a,b)` takes length-2 vectors and returns their signed counterclockwise
angle in [-PI,PI], with exactly opposite vectors at +PI. Shared Rust dot/cross
accumulators avoid premature overflow and cancellation. Zero vectors are errors.
`SECH` and `CSCH` preserve representable tiny tails without forming an overflowing
COSH/SINH intermediate; CSCH(0) remains an error. Native/BASIC zeros are canonical.
See [Trigonometry](TRIGONOMETRY.md) for the complete units, domain and precision
inventory, including existing real/complex functions and remaining gates.

Real `ACOSH` and native `NativeTrigonometry::acosh` use a cancellation-free
`log1p` expression near one, shared with `BasicReal::acosh`. This preserves
accuracy for inputs immediately above the real domain endpoint.

Real `ATANH`, `BasicReal::atanh` and `NativeTrigonometry::atanh` share an odd-
symmetric `log1p` path, preserving tiny inputs and accuracy near both +/-1
boundaries. Inputs on or beyond those real boundaries remain errors.

Switch control voltages and restored-mode validation use one exact accumulation
of both coordinate rows before rounding. This retains small stored control
differences under large common-mode voltages and prevents false transitions
caused by subtracting separately rounded node readings.

documents.title: Point projections and clearances
documents.html:
PROJECTLINE2D(p,origin,direction), PROJECTRAY2D(p,origin,direction) and PROJECTSEGMENT2D(p,a,b) have corresponding 3D forms. Points/directions are ordinary two- or three-element lists. PROJECTPLANE3D(p,origin,normal) uses the plane through origin with the supplied normal. Direction/normal need not have unit length. A line permits any real parameter; a ray starts at origin and extends in the positive direction; a segment includes both endpoints.

Each returns {closestPoint,offset,distance}. offset is input point minus the mathematical closest point, and distance is its unsigned Euclidean length in the same units as the coordinates. Offset is computed independently of the rounded closest point. Use the returned distance for clearance tests: subtracting the returned point can lose a small separation at large coordinates. Components are binary64, so a rounded point is not guaranteed to lie exactly on the primitive. There is no hidden positional tolerance or coordinate snapping.

10 R=PROJECTSEGMENT3D({3,4,0},{0,0,0},{2,0,0})
20 PRINT R(1): REM {2,0,0}, closest point
30 PRINT R(2): REM {1,4,0}, offset
40 PRINT R(3): REM SQR(17), distance

A segment whose endpoints coincide is a point. Zero line/ray direction and zero plane normal are errors. Inputs must be finite with the required dimension; nonfinite final coordinates, offsets or distance produce an overflow error and leave an assignment target unchanged. A huge line parameter alone is not an error: it is never needed to form the result. Distance rounds the square root of an exact squared-residual ratio using integer comparisons, so even individually underflowed offset components do not erase a representable distance. Point/offset components are rounded once from exact rational expressions in the represented inputs; distance is also correctly rounded for the represented inputs. Results are binary64 values, not exact symbolic distances or certified interval bounds.

The Rust NativeGeometry methods project_line, project_ray, project_segment accept [f64;N] for N=2 or 3 and return NativePointProjection<N> with public point, offset, distance fields. project_plane accepts 3D inputs. Native distance(a,b) shares the implementation used by BASIC DIST and DIST3D. All queries honor native cancellation and have constant bounded work and storage; small fixed-size accumulators/temporary vectors do not grow with scene size. These are individual point/primitive queries, not an acceleration index or a continuous collision solver. No external numerical provider is required.

## Point projections and clearances

`PROJECTLINE2D(p,origin,direction)`, `PROJECTRAY2D(p,origin,direction)` and
`PROJECTSEGMENT2D(p,a,b)` have corresponding `3D` forms. Points/directions are
ordinary two- or three-element lists. `PROJECTPLANE3D(p,origin,normal)` uses the
plane through origin with the supplied normal. Direction/normal need not have
unit length. A line permits any real parameter; a ray starts at origin and extends
in the positive direction; a segment includes both endpoints.

Each returns `{closestPoint,offset,distance}`. `offset` is input point minus the
mathematical closest point, and distance is its unsigned Euclidean length in the
same units as the coordinates. Offset is computed independently of the rounded
closest point. Use the returned distance for clearance tests: subtracting the
returned point can lose a small separation at large coordinates. Components are
binary64, so a rounded point is not guaranteed to lie exactly on the primitive.
There is no hidden positional tolerance or coordinate snapping.

```basic
10 R=PROJECTSEGMENT3D({3,4,0},{0,0,0},{2,0,0})
20 PRINT R(1): REM {2,0,0}, closest point
30 PRINT R(2): REM {1,4,0}, offset
40 PRINT R(3): REM SQR(17), distance
```

A segment whose endpoints coincide is a point. Zero line/ray direction and zero
plane normal are errors. Inputs must be finite with the required dimension;
nonfinite final coordinates, offsets or distance produce an overflow error and
leave an assignment target unchanged. A huge line parameter alone is not an
error: it is never needed to form the result. Distance rounds the square root of an exact squared-residual ratio
using integer comparisons, so even individually underflowed
offset components do not erase a representable distance. Point/offset components
are rounded once from exact rational expressions in the represented inputs;
distance is also correctly rounded for the represented inputs. Results are
binary64 values, not exact symbolic distances or certified interval bounds.

The Rust `NativeGeometry` methods `project_line`, `project_ray`, `project_segment`
accept `[f64;N]` for N=2 or 3 and return `NativePointProjection<N>` with public
`point`, `offset`, `distance` fields. `project_plane` accepts 3D inputs. Native
`distance(a,b)` shares the implementation used by BASIC `DIST` and `DIST3D`.
All queries honor native cancellation and have constant bounded work and storage;
small fixed-size accumulators/temporary vectors do not grow with scene size.
These are individual point/primitive queries, not an acceleration index or a
continuous collision solver. No external numerical provider is required.

documents.title: Exact-input spatial hit reports
documents.html:
Rust and BASIC share exact represented-input classification for closed box overlap, closed-ball overlap, forward ray/box intervals and isolated ray/triangle crossings. AABBHIT, SPHEREHIT, RAYAABB and RAYTRIANGLE retain their existing signatures and miss conventions. Touching counts as overlap. Zero-radius balls are points; zero-width box axes are allowed. Bounds must be ordered, radii nonnegative and directions nonzero. All coordinates and dimensions must be finite 3D values.

RAYBOXHIT3D(origin,direction,min,max) returns an empty list for a miss, otherwise {entryPoint,exitPoint,entryParameter,exitParameter}. Each point is a three-element list. Each parameter field is {t} if the parameter rounds to a finite binary64 value, or {} if it overflows. The interval is clipped to t>=0, so starting inside the box produces the original point and {0} at entry. The exit point remains available even when its parameter overflows. RAYAABB only needs the entry parameter; an unrepresentable exit no longer causes a spurious overflow error.

RAYTRIANGLEHIT3D(origin,direction,a,b,c) returns an empty list when there is no isolated forward-ray crossing within the closed triangle. A hit returns {point,barycentric,parameter}, with three weights for a,b,c and a parameter field using the same {t} / {} convention. The triangle is two-sided. Parallel, coplanar and degenerate triangles have no isolated crossing in this API and return an empty list; constructing coplanar overlap segments remains separate work. There is no near-parallel tolerance. A representable nonzero determinant is not required: exact product signs decide the hit before any coordinate is rounded.

10 H=RAYTRIANGLEHIT3D({.25,.25,1},{0,0,-1},{0,0,0},{1,0,0},{0,1,0})
20 IF LEN(H)=0 THEN END
30 PRINT H(1): REM {.25,.25,0}, hit point
40 PRINT H(2): REM {.5,.25,.25}, weights for a,b,c
50 T=H(3): IF LEN(T)>0 THEN PRINT T(1)

A ray uses origin+t*direction; t is physical distance only for a unit direction. Very small positive parameters may round to zero. Use the returned point instead of reconstructing it from a rounded parameter. Point, parameter and barycentric components are independently rounded once from exact rational expressions in the represented inputs. Rounded weights may not sum to exactly one, and a rounded hit point need not lie exactly on the mathematical surface. Classification uses the unrounded inputs, with no implicit snapping or positional tolerance.

The legacy RAYAABB and RAYTRIANGLE calls still report overflow when the required hit parameter does not fit; the detailed reports preserve the finite point in that case. Other invalid inputs produce errors before assignment, preserving targets. These constant-sized queries honor native cancellation and use bounded exact product/ratio kernels already shared by the math engine. They need no numerical provider and do not attach physics bodies or create a spatial acceleration index.

Native crate-root NativeGeometry exposes:

  • aabbs_intersect_3d(min_a,max_a,min_b,max_b) -> Result<bool,Error>.
  • spheres_intersect_3d(a,ra,b,rb) -> Result<bool,Error> for closed balls.
  • ray_box_3d(origin,direction,min,max) -> Result<Option<NativeRayBoxHit3>,Error>. The report has entry and exit, both NativeRayPoint3 {point,parameter}.
  • ray_triangle_3d(origin,direction,a,b,c) -> Result<Option<NativeRayTriangleHit3>,Error>. The report has point, barycentric, and parameter.

Points and weights are [f64;3]. Report parameters are Option<f64>: None means parameter overflow, while the outer None means no reported hit. General geometry, mesh-wide constructions, other primitive pairs, broader curve/path families and installed CAD/physics qualification remain open. Triangle point coordinates and linear closest pairs are described in their dedicated sections below.

Evidence: output/spatial-queries-2026-10-26/validation.json when accepted. The independent reference uses exact rational squared-distance and slab equations, plus an exact Gaussian-elimination solve of the ray/triangle affine system. programs/science/ray_picking.bas is an editable consumer, including the three reproduced defects and optional-parameter examples.

coplanar and degenerate triangles have no isolated crossing in this API and return
an empty list; constructing coplanar overlap segments remains separate work.
There is no near-parallel tolerance. A representable nonzero determinant is not
required: exact product signs decide the hit before any coordinate is rounded.

```basic
10 H=RAYTRIANGLEHIT3D({.25,.25,1},{0,0,-1},{0,0,0},{1,0,0},{0,1,0})
20 IF LEN(H)=0 THEN END
30 PRINT H(1): REM {.25,.25,0}, hit point
40 PRINT H(2): REM {.5,.25,.25}, weights for a,b,c
50 T=H(3): IF LEN(T)>0 THEN PRINT T(1)
```

A ray uses `origin+t*direction`; t is physical distance only for a unit direction.
Very small positive parameters may round to zero. Use the returned point instead
of reconstructing it from a rounded parameter. Point, parameter and barycentric
components are independently rounded once from exact rational expressions in the
represented inputs. Rounded weights may not sum to exactly one, and a rounded hit
point need not lie exactly on the mathematical surface. Classification uses the
unrounded inputs, with no implicit snapping or positional tolerance.

The legacy `RAYAABB` and `RAYTRIANGLE` calls still report overflow when the required
hit parameter does not fit; the detailed reports preserve the finite point in that
case. Other invalid inputs produce errors before assignment, preserving targets.
These constant-sized queries honor native cancellation and use bounded exact
product/ratio kernels already shared by the math engine. They need no numerical
provider and do not attach physics bodies or create a spatial acceleration index.

Native crate-root `NativeGeometry` exposes:

- `aabbs_intersect_3d(min_a,max_a,min_b,max_b) -> Result<bool,Error>`.
- `spheres_intersect_3d(a,ra,b,rb) -> Result<bool,Error>` for closed balls.
- `ray_box_3d(origin,direction,min,max) -> Result<Option<NativeRayBoxHit3>,Error>`.
  The report has `entry` and `exit`, both `NativeRayPoint3 {point,parameter}`.
- `ray_triangle_3d(origin,direction,a,b,c) -> Result<Option<NativeRayTriangleHit3>,Error>`.
  The report has `point`, `barycentric`, and `parameter`.

Points and weights are `[f64;3]`. Report parameters are `Option<f64>`: `None` means
parameter overflow, while the outer `None` means no reported hit. General geometry,
mesh-wide constructions, other primitive pairs, broader curve/path families and
installed CAD/physics qualification remain open. Triangle point coordinates and
linear closest pairs are described in their dedicated sections below.

Evidence: `output/spatial-queries-2026-10-26/validation.json` when accepted.
The independent reference uses exact rational squared-distance and slab equations,
plus an exact Gaussian-elimination solve of the ray/triangle affine system.
`programs/science/ray_picking.bas` is an editable consumer, including the three
reproduced defects and optional-parameter examples.

documents.title: Shared polynomial curves
documents.html:
BASIC accepts two, three or four control points, each consistently 2D or 3D, defining linear, quadratic or cubic Bezier curves on parameter 0 through 1. Coincident controls, closed curves, cusps and collinear reversals are valid. Nonfinite coordinates, inconsistent dimensions and parameters outside this interval are errors.

  • BEZIERPOINT(controls,t) returns the point.
  • BEZIERDERIV(controls,t[,order]) returns a parameter derivative. Order defaults to 1 and may be 0 through 3; orders above the degree return zero.
  • BEZIERSPLIT(controls,t) returns {leftControls,rightControls}. Each new curve uses parameter 0 through 1, so derivative magnitudes change with its span.
  • BEZIERSAMPLE(controls,tolerance[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]]) returns {parameters,points,{maximumDeviation},status}. An empty deviation list means the estimate exceeds binary64 range. The ordered polyline covers the whole curve, even when a limit prevents convergence. Status is CONVERGED, SEGMENT_LIMIT or RESOLUTION_LIMIT; only CONVERGED meets the tolerance. Defaults are 4096 segments and depth 40; hard limits are 65536 segments and depth 52. Tolerance is positive, finite and expressed in coordinate units.
  • BEZIERLENGTH(controls[,absTol[,relTol[,maxEvaluations[,maxIntervals]]]]) returns {length,estimatedAbsoluteError,evaluations,intervals,status}. Defaults/limits match shared quadrature: absolute tolerance 1E-9, zero relative tolerance, one million evaluations and 4096 intervals. Only CONVERGED meets the estimated tolerance. The error estimate is heuristic.

Crate-root NativeBezier<N>::new(&[[f64;N]]) exposes the same kernels for N=2/3: degree, control_points, point, derivative, split, sample_uniform, sample(NativeCurveSamplingOptions) and length(NativeQuadratureOptions). NativeCurveSamples<N> contains parameters, points, optional maximum_deviation and NativeCurveSamplingStatus. Uniform sampling takes 1..65536 segments. Native calls observe shared cancellation and allocate bounded storage. BASIC returns ordinary lists; user programs remain freely editable.

Curve components and derivatives accumulate exact products of original binary64 inputs and round once. Split controls independently round from their exact de Casteljau expressions; evaluating a rounded subcurve need not reproduce the unsplit curve bit for bit. Final derivative overflow is an error. Length normalizes speed by a power of two derived from exact control differences and rescales its report. This retains subnormal lengths and avoids unrepresentable intermediate speeds when the final length is finite. Numerical quadrature is not a certified length enclosure; cusp/resolution/work limits remain explicit.

Adaptive sampling splits the worst remaining interval. Its conservative displacement estimate uses h^2/8 times a componentwise bound on the original second derivative, plus endpoint rounding margins. It handles collinear reversals and coincident endpoints. Points are evaluated from the original curve, avoiding repeated subdivision drift. Coordinate tolerance does not imply screen-space accuracy after an arbitrary transform.

The preexisting BASIC BEZIER drawing statement and renderer C/Q paths now use this backend with adaptive sampling in local coordinates (0.25 units, at most 256 segments, depth 24), replacing private fixed-16-segment formulas. Rendering uses the complete approximation at these limits; its existing API does not report mathematical tolerance status. SVG output retains analytic paths. Screen-space transform-aware quality and sustained installed rendering remain separate qualification tasks.

Definitions follow the primary MIT evaluation/subdivision reference and Michigan Tech derivative notes. The chord estimate uses the linear interpolation remainder. No external curve code or dependency is incorporated.

Rational surfaces, broader curve families, composite continuity and arc-length parameterization and CAD/physics application qualification remain open. General triangle queries are now covered in the triangle section below. Evidence: output/bezier-curves-2026-10-26/validation.json once verified.

documents.title: Shared 3D transforms and camera math
documents.html:
Crate-root NativeTransform3 stores a finite row-major 4-by-4 matrix applied to column vectors. new(matrix) accepts singular matrices; identity() and matrix() construct/read the value. translation([x,y,z]), scaling([x,y,z]) and rotation(NativeQuaternion) build affine transforms. Zero scales are allowed. compose(right) applies right first, then self. inverse() returns the inverse of any nonsingular finite 4-by-4 input when its rounded coefficients fit binary64. It uses exact-input cofactors/determinants; exact singularity is an error, with no arbitrary small-pivot rejection threshold. This specialized inverse does not change general dense BASIC INVERSE.

BASIC adds TRANSFORMCOMPOSE(left,right) and TRANSFORMINVERSE(matrix). Existing TRANSLATE3D, SCALE3D, ROTATE3D, TRANSFORMPOINT, TRANSFORMVECTOR, LOOKAT, ORTHOGRAPHIC and PERSPECTIVEMAT use this same Rust implementation. Native point([x,y,z]) divides exact homogeneous row sums before rounding; exact W=0 is an error. Native vector([x,y,z]) uses only the upper-left 3-by-3 block, ignoring translation and the last row. It is not a projective tangent or surface-normal transform; normals have the separate NativeSurfaceMath::oriented_normal / NORMALTRANSFORM3D API.

NativeQuaternion::rotate_vector evaluates the original-input Hamilton sandwich divided by the exact squared norm. Tiny vector components are not scaled away. Rotation matrix entries and raw Hamilton product components also round once from original-input expressions. Zero quaternions cannot define rotations. A returned matrix rounds each coefficient before later application: direct quaternion rotation can therefore retain small effects that its rounded matrix cannot represent. Likewise an inverse matrix is rounded; ill-conditioned transforms can amplify rounding and an inverse round trip need not be exact.

look_at(eye,target,up) uses exact differences/cross products to detect degeneracy, then approximate normalization to build a right-handed view whose forward direction is -Z. Coincident eye/target and zero/parallel up are errors. Translation uses exact dot products with the final rounded basis. orthographic(left,right,bottom,top,near,far) accepts ordered x/y extents and 0<=near<far. perspective(fovY,aspect,near,far) accepts radians 0<fovY<PI, aspect>0 and 0<near<far. Both map near/far to normalized depth -1/+1. Projection depth/orthographic coefficients retain exact endpoint differences; perspective field-of-view coefficients use approximate trigonometry. Axis-angle construction, quaternion normalization and SLERP also remain floating approximations; these are not symbolic or interval-valued rotations.

Inputs and required outputs must be finite. Invalid shape, degeneracy, exact singularity, cancellation or final overflow raises an error before assignment. Underflow rounds to the nearest representable value, possibly zero. Exact arithmetic prevents avoidable intermediate overflow, not true output overflow. Work/storage are bounded per 4-by-4 operation, and native queries honor the shared cancellation token. No external math provider or GPU is required.

programs/science/camera_transforms.bas composes a camera, animates quaternion poses and checks model/inverse consistency. Independent qualification uses Fraction homogeneous arithmetic, a separate Gauss-Jordan inverse, exact Hamilton products and a 120-digit camera reference. Evidence is recorded in output/geometry-transforms-2026-10-26/validation.json when accepted. Mesh-wide constructions, other primitive closest pairs, broader curve/path families and sustained installed graphics/CAD/physics workloads remain open; this checkpoint does not complete general geometry.

## Standalone program launch mode

`COMPILE` distinguishes graphics statements from ordinary identifiers using the
interpreter's statement and IF/ELSE boundaries. Names such as `VIEW`, `SCREEN` or
`TASK` in scalar assignments, expressions, DATA and comments do not select the
window wrapper. Actual graphics statements retain window mode; graphical exports
also accept `--headless`. Console input/file forms stay in console mode. Selection
is static and does not predict reachability or dynamically loaded code. See
[Create a native executable](PROGRAMMING_GUIDE.md#create-a-native-executable).

documents.title: Triangle coordinates and closest points
documents.html:
TRIANGLECOORDS2D(p,a,b,c) returns signed barycentric coordinates of p in the triangle's affine frame. Its 3D form first projects p orthogonally to the triangle plane. These coordinates may lie outside the triangle. PROJECTTRIANGLE2D(p,a,b,c) and PROJECTTRIANGLE3D instead find the closest point on the closed triangle, including its interior.

All four take ordinary 2D/3D point lists and return {point,offset,distance,weights,feature$,degenerate}. Offset is p minus the unrounded point; distance is its unsigned Euclidean length. Weights are ordered A, B, C. The feature string is "FACE", "AB", "BC", "CA", "A", "B", "C", or (coordinates only) "OUTSIDE". In 3D the feature classifies the projected point, not whether p lies in the plane.

10 R=PROJECTTRIANGLE3D({2,2,3},{0,0,0},{2,0,0},{0,2,0})
20 PRINT R(1): REM {1,1,0}
30 PRINT R(4): REM {0,0.5,0.5}
40 PRINT R(5): REM BC
50 PRINT R(3): REM SQR(11), actual clearance

A collinear or coincident triangle has no unique plane coordinates: TRIANGLECOORDS reports an illegal-quantity error. PROJECTTRIANGLE treats it as its segment/point convex hull and returns degenerate=-1 (otherwise 0). Degenerate weights still reconstruct the exact closest point before rounding, but are not unique. Ties select AB, BC, CA in that order, and a zero-length edge selects its first vertex. Relabelling degenerate vertices may change weights and feature without changing the point or distance.

Point/offset components and weights round once from exact rational expressions; distance uses a correctly rounded square root of the exact squared residual. Classification and candidate-distance comparisons occur before rounding, with no geometric tolerance. A weight that rounds to zero can still denote an exact positive contribution. Rounded weights need not sum to exactly one; subtracting the returned point need not reproduce the returned offset. Use distance directly for clearances. If an unbounded coordinate weight cannot fit binary64, weights is an empty list; finite point/offset/distance remain available. Closest-triangle weights always fit. Required nonfinite outputs produce overflow errors, and failed assignments leave their old value intact. All inputs must be finite and have the requested dimension. Native cancellation is honored.

Rust exports NativeTriangleProjection<N>, NativeTriangleFeature and NativeGeometry::triangle_coordinates/project_triangle for N=2 or 3. The report has point, offset, distance, barycentric: Option<[f64;3]>, feature, and degenerate fields. Feature has as_str(). These kernels use existing bounded integer arithmetic and shared final rounding, with no new dependency. There are only four input points, at most three edge candidates, and fixed binary64 exponent bounds; work/storage do not grow with a mesh. This exact path costs more than unchecked floating-point formulas; it is not a mesh acceleration structure or continuous collision engine.

Full geometry inventory, reference sources and qualification: GEOMETRY.md.
