## Rational Bezier curves and conics

`RBEZIER(coordinates,weights[,mode])` creates an editable
`{"RBEZIER1",coordinates,weights,mode}` packet. The shared Rust type is
`NativeRationalBezier<2>` or `NativeRationalBezier<3>`, with two to four
controls (degree one through three). Modes are case-insensitive:

- `"WEIGHTED"` (default): coordinates are Euclidean control points. The numerator
  controls are the exact products of those coordinates and their weights.
  Native construction is `NativeRationalBezier::new(points,weights)`.
- `"HOMOGENEOUS"`: coordinates already are numerator controls; they are not
  multiplied by weights. A nonzero numerator with zero weight represents a
  control direction at infinity. Native construction is
  `NativeRationalBezier::from_homogeneous(numerators,weights)`.

All coordinate/weight inputs must be finite, with one weight per control and at
least one nonzero weight. Zero and negative weights are supported. These two
representations are intentionally distinct: a zero weight removes a weighted
Euclidean control's contribution, while a homogeneous zero-weight numerator
can contribute a direction at infinity.

| BASIC operation | Shared native operation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RBEZIERPOINT(curve,t)` | `point(t)` | Two-/three-component point |
| `RBEZIERDERIV(curve,t[,order])` | `derivative(t,order)` | Original-parameter derivative; default order 1, supported 0–3 |
| `RBEZIERBATCH(curve,parameters[,order])` | `evaluate_many(parameters,order)` | Input-order rows; default order 0 |
| `RBEZIERSAMPLE(curve,segments)` | `sample_uniform(segments)` | `segments+1` point rows with uniform parameter spacing |
| `RBEZIERSPLIT(curve,t)` | `split(t)` | Two child curves with parameters mapping to `[0,t]` and `[t,1]` |

Native getters are `coordinates()`, `weights()`, `is_homogeneous()` and
`degree()`. Parameters must be finite and inside `[0,1]`. There is no implicit
extrapolation. Derivatives of a rational curve need not vanish above its
numerator degree. The common curve fraction core evaluates the represented
numerator and denominator exactly, forms quotient derivatives, and rounds only
the returned components. This avoids premature weight-product overflow and
rounded cancellation. Weighted endpoint points retain the original coordinates
verbatim when their denominator is nonzero.

The exact represented denominator must be nonzero at every queried parameter.
A zero denominator is an error, even for a removable `0/0`; no epsilon cutoff or
automatic limiting value is substituted. Signed weights can create poles and
unbounded portions. Successful point or batch queries do not certify that the
whole interval is pole-free. Uniform sampling is neither arc-length spacing nor
a geometric error bound, and joining samples across an unqueried pole is unsafe.
Positive weights provide the usual control-hull property in weighted mode.

Subdivision evaluates the homogeneous de Casteljau controls in exact arithmetic.
Each returned weight and coordinate is rounded once. A child uses weighted
coordinates where finite dehomogenization is possible, otherwise homogeneous
coordinates retain its infinite controls. Splitting returns an error if a
nonzero weight rounds to zero, all child weights vanish, or the chosen output
representation cannot be finite. No common rescaling rescue is attempted.
Subsequent queries use the rounded child data; repeated splitting can accumulate
error and perturb denominator roots. Child derivatives use their new local
parameters, so compare them with the parent's derivatives multiplied by the
appropriate parameter-scale power.

Batches accept at most 65,536 parameters. Uniform sampling accepts 1–65,536
segments. The shared 65,536-bit reduced numerator/denominator bound limits exact
arithmetic; intermediate temporaries can be larger. Traversals check
cancellation, and batch/subdivision errors return no partial result. Final
unrepresentable components raise `RealOverflow`. Editable BASIC packets require
no registration or backend version changes.

For example, `RBEZIER({{1,0},{0,1},{-1,0}},{1,0,1},"HOMOGENEOUS")` represents
the upper half of a unit circle without irrational input weights. The
`programs/science/rational_conic.bas` consumer scales this construction into a
3D CAD ellipse and checks its tangents and subdivision. Definitions follow the
[Michigan Tech rational curve notes](https://pages.mtu.edu/~shene/COURSES/cs3621/NOTES/curves/rational.html)
and the [homogeneous circular-arc construction](https://www.cs.sjsu.edu/faculty/pollett/216.1.10s/Lec09022010.html).
No external implementation or new dependency is incorporated.

Qualification: exact Bernstein-polynomial and independent symbolic derivative
references, conic identities, subdivision data, native/BASIC/export parity and
resource/cancellation checks in
`output/rational-bezier-2026-10-26/validation.json` when accepted.
NURBS/rational surfaces, composite/arc-length workflows and broader CAD,
math/application/OS/hardware acceptance remain open.

### Exact rational-curve interval checks

`RBEZIERDOMAIN(curve[,from,to[,maxRefinements]])` calls the shared Rust
`NativeRationalBezier::domain(from,to,NativeRationalDomainOptions)`.
The default closed interval is `[0,1]`; explicit bounds must be finite,
ordered and inside that interval. Subdivision budget defaults to 256 and
accepts 0–4096. Zero requests exact counts with any unresolved intervals retained.
BASIC applies its usual integer conversion to the budget (for example, 1.5
becomes 2); the native Rust option is an integer.

The result is freely readable BASIC data:

```text
{"RDOMAIN1",{from,to},status$,refinements,counts,{intervals...}}
counts = {distinct,denominatorMultiplicity,removable,poles,poleMultiplicity}
interval = {lower,upper,"EXACT"|"OPEN",counts}
```

All counts refer to exact polynomials formed from the represented input
coordinates and weights, including unrounded weighted products.
`distinct` counts denominator zeros; `denominatorMultiplicity` includes
repetition. A common polynomial GCD across **every** numerator and the denominator
identifies cancellations. `removable` counts zeros fully removed by cancellation;
`poles` counts the remaining distinct poles; `poleMultiplicity` sums their orders
after cancellation (the largest remaining order across coordinates).
A partially cancelled root remains a pole. Raw `0/0` is still undefined for
point/derivative queries, so only zero **denominator** roots establishes a usable
whole interval.

`EXACT` is a singleton exactly representable root. `OPEN` means roots lie
strictly between the bounds; roots at either bound are reported separately.
Reports cover the whole requested closed interval without duplicate endpoint
counts. The status is:

- `REGULAR`: no denominator zeros in the entire closed interval.
- `ISOLATED`: every root is an exact singleton or is alone between adjacent
  binary64 bounds. These are enclosures, not rounded root estimates.
- `RESOLUTION_LIMIT`: distinct roots share an adjacent-binary64 gap; exact
  counts and multiplicities are retained without claiming separate locations.
- `REFINEMENT_LIMIT`: the budget ended with at least one wider interval.
  Counts remain exact; some other intervals may also contain unresolved clusters.

Root counting reuses the algebra engine's exact Sturm kernel with one-sided
endpoint signs; multiplicities use repeated polynomial GCDs. The algebra
certificate checker retains independent multiplication-identity verification.
Curve coefficients retain the 65,536-bit reduced fraction bound; symbolic
coefficients retain their existing 4,096-bit and charged-work policies.
Domain checks additionally cap polynomial work at 2,000,000 charged steps.
Cancellation or arithmetic/work exhaustion raises an error with no partial report.
Binary64 bit-range subdivision bounds refinement even near subnormal parameters.

`REGULAR` certifies denominator absence only: it does not certify finite
rounded coordinates, safe derivative magnitudes, geometric accuracy, or
regular nonzero tangents. Edited or rounded subdivided curves must be checked
again. NURBS, surfaces and composite
arc-length workflows remain open.

`programs/science/rational_domain.bas` demonstrates a pole missed by uniform
sampling and a checked conic. Qualification uses independent exact SymPy
polynomials, GCDs and interval counts
([SymPy polynomial reference](https://docs.sympy.org/latest/modules/polys/reference.html)),
native/BASIC/export parity and resource/recovery checks. Evidence:
`output/rational-domain-2026-10-27/validation.json` when accepted.

### Adaptive rational-curve polylines

`RBEZIERADAPT(curve,tolerance[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]])` calls
`NativeRationalBezier::sample(NativeCurveSamplingOptions)` and returns:

```text
{parameters,points,{maximumDeviation},status$}
```

The default limits are 4096 segments and depth 40. Rational sampling accepts
1–65,536 segments and depth 1–1074; the existing polynomial sampler retains its
own depth limit of 52. BASIC uses its usual integer conversion for the limits.
Tolerance must be positive and finite. Parameters cover `[0,1]` in increasing
order, with one more point than segments. Each point is the same correctly
rounded original-curve query returned by `RBEZIERPOINT`.

The finite deviation bounds the Euclidean distance from **every exact curve
point in each parameter interval to its corresponding rounded output segment**.
It is a geometric, one-sided bound. It does not bound same-parameter linear
interpolation, tangent error, arc-length spacing, or the reverse distance from
the segment to the curve. Nonlinear rational parameterizations of straight
segments may therefore have a zero geometric bound.

The Rust implementation first performs an exact whole-interval denominator
check. Any denominator zero, including removable `0/0` and endpoint zeros,
raises an error before a polyline is returned. It then computes exact homogeneous
Bernstein controls restricted from the original curve to each candidate
interval. These are scratch values, not rounded child packets. If their
nonzero weights have one sign, the curve is a convex combination of their
dehomogenized controls. A zero weight with all-zero numerators contributes
nothing; a zero weight with a nonzero numerator has no finite hull bound yet.

For each finite exact control, Rust projects onto the actual rounded output
segment and computes an exact L1 residual. The largest residual conservatively
bounds Euclidean distance over the whole convex hull, including endpoint
rounding. The reported value rounds upward once. This also handles coincident
endpoints and collinear backtracking without mistaking an infinite line for a
finite segment. Mixed-sign controls or directions at infinity trigger
refinement until a finite bound is established or a limit is reached.
The [nonnegative-weight convex-hull property](https://pages.mtu.edu/~shene/COURSES/cs3621/NOTES/spline/NURBS/NURBS-property.html)
supplies the geometric basis; common negative weight scales are equivalent.

`CONVERGED` means every segment's bound is at most the requested tolerance.
`SEGMENT_LIMIT` and `RESOLUTION_LIMIT` retain a complete ordered polyline;
the latter covers the requested depth or an unavailable distinct binary64
midpoint. Inspect the status before treating the tolerance as achieved.
`{maximumDeviation}` is empty if no finite bound was established, including
unresolved control weights or bound overflow. Limits return an estimate to
inspect, not permission to claim accuracy.

The heap stores finite panel metadata and points, not a growing tree of exact
controls. At most `2*maxSegments-1` panels are evaluated; exact scratch arithmetic
retains the shared 65,536-bit reduced fraction limit. Cancellation is checked
during refinement and homogeneous restriction. Arithmetic/work failure or an
unrepresentable sampled coordinate raises an error with no partial result.
A finite geometric certificate does not promise finite derivatives or regular
tangents. Subnormal geometry and bounds may hit the final point-rounding floor.

Qualification includes independent exact change-of-variable Bernstein
certificates, dense exact point-to-segment comparisons, compressed-parameter
curves, homogeneous underflow, native resources/cancellation and interpreted/
exported BASIC parity. Consumer: `programs/science/adaptive_conic.bas`.
Evidence: `output/rational-sampling-2026-10-27/validation.json` when accepted.
NURBS/surfaces, composite continuity and arc-length
parameterization, and broader application/OS/hardware acceptance remain open.


### Certified rational-curve length

`RBEZIERLENGTH(curve[,absTol[,relTol[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]]]])` calls
`NativeRationalBezier<N>::length(NativeCurveLengthOptions)` for the complete
2D/3D linear, quadratic or cubic curve on [0,1]. It returns:

`{value,{absoluteError},lowerBound,{upperBound},segments,status$}`

Native fields have the corresponding snake_case names in
`NativeCurveLengthReport`. Optional numbers are empty lists/`None` when no
finite upper certificate has been established; then `value=lowerBound` and
there is no accuracy claim. `NativeCurveLengthStatus` is `CONVERGED`,
`SEGMENT_LIMIT` or `RESOLUTION_LIMIT`. Both bounds cover the **whole path**,
including repeated traversal, even on a limit. The estimate is the rounded
midpoint of a finite enclosure; `absoluteError` bounds its distance to either
end. Only `CONVERGED` meets
`absoluteError <= max(absTol,relTol*abs(value))`, compared without floating
overflow/underflow.

Defaults are absolute and relative tolerances `1e-6`, 4096 segments and depth
1074. Tolerances must be finite/nonnegative with at least one positive;
segments are 1..65536 and depth is 1..1074. BASIC integer options use the
language's usual integer conversion. A supplied absolute tolerance alone
leaves the default relative tolerance enabled; pass zero explicitly to
disable it. Depth exhaustion or no interior binary64 midpoint reports
`RESOLUTION_LIMIT`. Limits do not report success or silently omit intervals.

The engine first rejects every exact raw denominator zero on [0,1], including
removable and endpoint zeros. Each panel restricts the **original exact
homogeneous data**, with the same bounded Rust arithmetic used by sampling.
For a finite same-sign control polygon, endpoint distance is a lower bound
and control-polygon length is an upper bound. Mixed signs or a nonzero
direction at infinity require refinement before providing that upper bound.
Zero homogeneous controls contribute nothing.

Why the upper bound is valid: for normalized positive rational Bernstein
weights `lambda_i`, put `S_k=sum(i>k,lambda_i)`. Then
`S'_k=sum(j<=k<i,(i-j)*lambda_i*lambda_j)/(t*(1-t)) >= 0`.
Writing the curve as `P_0+sum((P_(k+1)-P_k)*S_k)` and integrating the triangle
inequality bounds its length by the control polygon. The same argument
applies after dropping zero controls and flipping a common negative sign.
Exactly collinear controls in endpoint order give the endpoint distance
directly. Collinear backtracking is **not** discarded. The normalized basis
and its positivity are described in
[Piller's rational-curve notes](https://web.uni-miskolc.hu/~matip/geometric_en/pages/05_Racional.html);
the length enclosure follows from the argument above.

Squared distances, homogeneous quotients and accumulated bounds remain exact
until directed binary64 rounding. Correctly rounded shared rational square
roots avoid premature overflow or loss of tiny distances. Earlier bounds are
retained when later rounding is less tight. A loose polygon that overflows
does not reject a finite curve: its upper bound stays absent until refinement.
An exact chord or accumulated lower bound beyond binary64 range is an error.
Cancellation/arithmetic errors return no partial report. The shared exact
fraction cap is 65536 bits after reduction; at most `2*maxSegments-1` panels
are evaluated and only compact panel metadata is retained.

These are conservative geometric length certificates, not a speed-quadrature
error estimate. They cover even a regular cubic whose length is exactly 2
but whose motion is compressed around t=0.5 beyond neighboring binary64
parameters. Very tight tolerances can require many subdivisions or return a
limit; no claim of arbitrary precision or arc-length parameterization is made.

`output/rational-length-2026-10-27/validation.json`.

### B-spline and NURBS curve foundations

The shared CPU Rust `NativeBSplineBasis` and `NativeNurbs<N>` types support
degree 0..16 curves with up to 65536 controls in 2D or 3D. This is a knot-vector
representation, distinct from interpolation through data points.

- `BSPLINE(degree,knots,points)` constructs a polynomial curve with unit weights.
- `NURBS(degree,knots,points,weights[,mode$])` constructs a rational curve.
  Mode is `"WEIGHTED"` (Euclidean control points, default) or `"HOMOGENEOUS"`
  (numerator controls, allowing directions at infinity).
- Both return freely editable `{"NURBS1",degree,knots,coordinates,weights,mode$}`.
- `NURBSPOINT(curve,t[,side$])` evaluates a point.
- `NURBSDERIV(curve,t[,order[,side$]])` uses order 1 by default; orders 0..3
  refer to the **original knot coordinate**, not a normalized span.
- `NURBSBATCH(curve,parameters[,order[,side$]])` returns complete input-order
  values (default order 0), with at most 65536 queries.
- `BSPLINEBASIS(curve,t[,order[,side$]])` returns `{firstControl,values}`:
  at most degree+1 local **polynomial** basis values or derivatives, before
  rational weighting. The BASIC index is one based; native
  `NativeSplineBasisValues.first_control` is zero based.

With `n` controls and degree `p`, exactly `n+p+1` knots are required, all
finite and nondecreasing. Each multiplicity is at most `p+1` and `n>=p+1`.
The active interval is closed `[knots[p],knots[n]]` in zero-based notation,
and must have positive width. Unclamped and nonuniform vectors are supported.
No extrapolation, parameter wrapping or automatic knot snapping occurs.
An unclamped endpoint generally does not equal the first/last control point.
Degree zero represents piecewise constants.

Side is `"AUTO"` by default: right-hand span at interior knots, left-hand span
at the final endpoint. `"LEFT"` and `"RIGHT"` explicitly choose the limit at
a join, including derivatives. Requesting an exterior side at the first/last
active endpoint is an error. Repeated knots can reduce continuity or create
a discontinuity at multiplicity `p+1`; evaluating both sides makes this visible.
This API does not silently smooth or join disconnected pieces.

Native construction is `NativeBSplineBasis::new(degree,&knots)` and
`NativeNurbs::new(degree,&knots,&points,&weights)`, with `polynomial` and
`from_homogeneous` alternatives. Basis accessors expose `degree`, `knots`,
`control_count` and `interval`. `basis.evaluate(t,order,NativeKnotSide)`
returns the compact local basis report. Curve `point` and `derivative` use
automatic sides; `point_on` and `derivative_on` take `NativeKnotSide` explicitly.
`evaluate_many(&parameters,order,side)` is complete or returns an error.

Evaluation computes exact local Cox-de Boor derivative jets, retaining the
original binary64 knot/control/weight data. It reuses the rational Bezier
engine's exact quotient recurrence, then rounds each final component once.
Extreme knot spans, weighted products and derivative cancellations do not
overflow prematurely. Signed-zero coordinates are preserved when the basis
is exactly one-hot in weighted mode. Rational derivatives may be nonzero
above the polynomial degree. Shared exact fractions are capped at 65536 bits
after reduction; exhaustion is an error, with no approximate fallback.
See [Shene's basis derivation](https://pages.mtu.edu/~shene/COURSES/cs3621/NOTES/spline/bspline-basis.html)
for the polynomial recurrence and local-support construction.

Signed and zero weights are admitted except all-zero vectors. Admission is
**not** whole-curve regularity certification: each query rejects its raw zero
denominator, including removable 0/0 and zero-weight spans. A zero denominator
elsewhere is not searched for by point/batch queries. A finite local polynomial
basis can be queried even if the rational curve has a pole at that parameter.
Nonfinite inputs, inconsistent dimensions, invalid orders/sides and
unrepresentable final components return errors.

Native construction stores O(n) data; a query uses O(log n) span search,
O(p^2*(order+1)) exact basis work and O(p*(order+1)) temporary storage.
It does not scan unrelated controls. BASIC packets are revalidated on each
call; use `NURBSBATCH` to amortize that cost. Cancellation is checked during
admission, basis construction and output computation; no partial batch escapes.

`programs/science/nurbs_path.bas` demonstrates a closed 3D multi-span conic and
checks the one-sided tangent join. Evidence when accepted:
`output/nurbs-curves-2026-10-27/validation.json`. Knot insertion/refinement,
global domain certification, NURBS adaptive sampling/length, surfaces, broader
continuity workflows and inverse arc-length traversal remain open, along with
general math/application/OS/hardware acceptance.


### Exact NURBS whole-span domains

`NURBSDOMAIN(curve[,maxRefinements])` calls
`NativeNurbs<N>::domain(NativeNurbsDomainOptions)`. It examines **every nonempty
knot span over its closed interval**, using original knots and homogeneous
data. At an internal join both incident polynomial spans are included, even
when `NURBSPOINT` with `"AUTO"` selects only the right one. This is a traversal
regularity check, not just a collection of point queries.

The BASIC report is:
`{"NDOMAIN1",{from,to},status$,refinements,finiteCounts,zeroSpanCount,spans}`.
Each span row is:
`{knotSpanIndex,{a,b},status$,refinements,{counts},roots}`.

Indices refer to the original knot vector, one based in BASIC and zero based
in `NativeNurbsSpanDomain.span_index`. Zero-width knot spans are skipped.
Native `NativeNurbsDomainReport` fields are `interval`, `status`,
`refinements`, `finite_counts`, `zero_denominator_spans` and `spans`.
A native span has `interval` and `domain: Option<NativeRationalDomainReport>`.

For a nonidentically-zero denominator, `counts` and `finiteCounts` have the
five entries `{distinct,denominatorMultiplicity,removable,poles,poleMultiplicity}`.
They count **span-root incidences**, not unique global parameter values.
A zero at a shared knot is counted once for each incident closed polynomial
span; its multiplicity or removable/pole classification can differ by side.
Each root row is `{lo,hi,"EXACT"|"OPEN",counts}` in the **original knot
coordinate**. `EXACT` is a singleton represented root. `OPEN` excludes both
bounds and contains exactly the stated root counts. Common factors are
cancelled for pole classification only when shared by every numerator
coordinate; raw denominator zeros remain invalid point queries.

A denominator identically zero over a span has `"ZERO_DENOMINATOR"` status,
empty `counts`/`roots` and native `domain=None`. Its infinitely many undefined
parameters are represented by the span, **not** a finite root count.
`zeroSpanCount` counts these spans; `finiteCounts` sums only the other spans.
This applies whether or not their numerator polynomials also vanish.

Top-level status is `"REGULAR"` only when all closed-span denominators are
proved nonzero. Other statuses are `"ISOLATED"`, `"RESOLUTION_LIMIT"`,
`"REFINEMENT_LIMIT"` and `"UNDEFINED_SPANS"`. Undefined spans take precedence,
then a refinement limit, then a resolution limit. Individual span reports
retain the other details. `ISOLATED` means each finite root is exact or lies
alone between adjacent binary64 values. Multiple roots sharing one adjacent
gap give `RESOLUTION_LIMIT`. Every finite count and interval remains complete
when refinement or coordinate resolution prevents further isolation.

The default global refinement budget is 256, with an allowed range 0..4096
and BASIC's usual integer conversion. Earlier spans consume the shared budget;
later spans are still classified exactly and retain their enclosing intervals.
Zero budget requests exact counts without interior refinement. Signed binary64
lattice bisection handles negative knots, subnormals and intervals crossing zero;
both signed zeros have one canonical representation in reports. Affine mapping
to each normalized span is performed exactly, never by rounded child packets.

The Rust backend uses exact homogeneous de Boor span polynomials and the same
generic polynomial/Sturm classifier as rational Bezier domains. Strictly
same-sign, nonzero local weights provide an immediate regularity proof from
the nonnegative partition of unity. All-zero local weights identify an
undefined span directly. Other cases retain exact coefficients through gcd,
multiplicity and root counting.

Degree and control-count admission remain 0..16 and at most 65536 controls.
One call has a 2,000,000-step polynomial/work budget and at most 65536 root
interval records; exact fractions remain capped at 65536 bits after reduction.
These resource limits, arithmetic failures and cancellation return errors,
never a partial clean report. Work limits do not silently skip later spans.
Native report storage is bounded by the number of nonempty spans and root
records. The result establishes denominator regularity only: it does not
certify continuity across joins, finite binary64 point/derivative outputs,
self-intersection freedom or machining clearance.

`output/nurbs-domain-2026-10-27/validation.json`.
NURBS knot refinement, adaptive sampling/length, surfaces, continuity and
inverse arc-length workflows, and broader math/application/OS/hardware

### NURBS knot refinement

`NURBSREFINE(curve,insertedKnots[,mode$])` inserts an unordered multiset of
finite knots within the closed active interval. It returns:
`{"NREFINE1",refinedCurve,status$,insertedCount,roundedControls,{errorBound}}`.
Use the second entry as an ordinary freely editable `NURBS1` curve.
Mode defaults to the input mode; explicit `"WEIGHTED"` or `"HOMOGENEOUS"`
also permits representation conversion with an empty insertion list.

The Rust API is `NativeNurbs<N>::refine(&[f64])` or
`refine_as(&[f64],homogeneous:bool)`, returning
`NativeNurbsRefinementReport<N>` with `curve`, `inserted`, `rounded_controls`,
`homogeneous_error_bound` and `status:NativeNurbsRefinementStatus`.

Exact homogeneous Boehm insertion preserves the original curve over the same
closed active domain, including both sides of internal joins and nonclamped
endpoints. Sorting makes insertion order deterministic. Each final multiplicity
must be at most degree+1; this includes existing occurrences. Degree zero and
full multiplicity are supported. Exterior knots and overfull multiplicities
are rejected. No extrapolation, periodic wrapping or automatic knot removal occurs.

Working numerator/weight coefficients remain exact throughout the entire
batch. A streaming buffer retains at most degree+2 controls, so repeated
insertions do not repeatedly copy the full curve. Output coefficients are
converted only after their last use. Unmodified controls keep their original
bits when retaining the mode; an empty same-mode request is a bit-preserving copy.

`"EXACT"` means every represented output homogeneous coefficient equals its
ideal exact refinement coefficient. For weighted output the represented
numerator is the exact product of its binary64 point and weight. `"ROUNDED"`
means at least one coefficient differs; `roundedControls` counts affected
controls. The optional error bound is an upward-rounded maximum absolute error
over all numerator and weight coefficients. Nonnegative partition-of-unity
basis functions also bound each homogeneous VALUE error by this maximum on
each active closed span. An empty bound means this maximum exceeds binary64
range. It is **not** a geometric distance, derivative bound or validity
certificate: division near zero weight can amplify errors arbitrarily.
Recheck the returned curve with `NURBSDOMAIN` before domain-sensitive use.

Weighted output cannot represent a zero-weight control with a nonzero
homogeneous numerator (a direction at infinity); request homogeneous output.
A zero numerator and zero weight is representable with zero Euclidean
coordinates. Nonzero weights that round to zero and overflowing returned
components are errors. Homogeneous output can overflow even when a weighted
representation fits; select the representation explicitly when needed.
No partial curve escapes on admission, arithmetic, work or cancellation errors.

Limits remain degree 0..16 and 65536 final controls. The call uses an
8,000,000-step work cap and the shared 65536-bit reduced-fraction cap.
Sorting is O(m log m), span lookup O(m log n), knot merging/output O(n+m),
and local coefficient work
O(m*degree*dimension), excluding bounded big-integer arithmetic; working exact
control storage is O(degree*dimension), with O(n+m) output storage.
`programs/science/nurbs_refinement.bas` refines a closed exact circular path
and checks its output through the same native-backed BASIC APIs.
Evidence when accepted: `output/nurbs-refinement-2026-10-27/validation.json`.
Adaptive NURBS sampling/length, surfaces, continuity/arc-length workflows and
general math/application/OS/hardware qualification remain open.


### Certified adaptive NURBS pieces

`NURBSADAPT(curve[,tolerance[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]]])` samples every nonempty
closed active knot span. Defaults are `1e-3`, `4096` and `40`. It returns
`{"NSAMPLE1",status$,segments,{maximumDeviation},pieces}`. Each piece is
`{knotSpanIndex,{from,to},parameters,points,{maximumDeviation},status$}`.
Draw each piece separately. Even a continuous join retains two incident endpoints;
a discontinuous join never adds a fabricated connecting segment. Original knot
indices are one based in BASIC and zero based in Rust.

Native `NativeNurbs<N>::sample(NativeCurveSamplingOptions)` returns
`NativeNurbsSamples<N>` with `pieces`, `segments`, `maximum_deviation` and `status`.
Each `NativeNurbsSamplePiece<N>` has `span_index`, `interval` and
`samples:NativeCurveSamples<N>`. Piece parameters increase strictly and include
both closed-span endpoints. Sampling uses exact original homogeneous span
polynomials and exact Bernstein restrictions, never rounded refinement packets.

The deviation certificate bounds Euclidean distance from every point of the
original exact curve to its corresponding rounded output chord. Positive/common-
sign rational control hulls and exact projection give upward-rounded L1 bounds,
shared with rational Bezier sampling. Zero-weight/zero-numerator controls may be
omitted; mixed signs or a zero-weight direction may require subdivision before
a finite hull certificate exists. An empty bound means no finite certificate.
This is geometric distance, not same-parameter, tangent, length or inverse-
distance error. Repeated traversal can lie on a chord without increasing this
error; use a length operation for travel distance.

Only `CONVERGED` meets tolerance. `SEGMENT_LIMIT` and `RESOLUTION_LIMIT` retain
complete ordered output for every span, with honest per-piece/global bounds.
Blocked panels remain in the result while other refinable panels continue.
The global status prioritizes an unmet segment budget over blocked depth/float
resolution, and otherwise converges only when every piece meets tolerance.
Limits are global: `maxSegments` must be 1..65536 and at least the number of
nonempty spans. An insufficient initial budget is an error, not a partial path.
The output has at most segments+pieces points (131072 overall).

Finite tolerance must be positive. Depth is 1..2100; the larger cap covers the
full signed finite knot range down to subnormal spacings. Midpoints are formed
exactly before one final binary64 rounding, avoiding subtraction overflow.
Adjacent parameter values and depth limits cannot imply convergence by themselves.

Whole-span exact domain validation precedes output: raw zeros (even removable),
hidden one-sided poles and entirely undefined spans are errors. Domain analysis
keeps its 2,000,000-step cap. Sampling then has a separate 16,000,000-step budget,
the shared 65536-bit reduced-fraction cap, and at most one cached exact span.
Heap/output storage is O(maxSegments+spans), not an exact-coefficient cache for
every panel. Work/arithmetic/cancellation errors return no partial report.
A regular denominator does not guarantee finite point outputs; output overflow
also returns an error. Curve degree remains 0..16 and controls at most 65536.

`programs/science/nurbs_sampling.bas` checks a circular path and a disconnected
piecewise path through the BASIC interface. Evidence when accepted:
`output/nurbs-sampling-2026-10-27/validation.json`.
Rational surfaces, continuity/arc-length workflows and broad
math/application/OS/hardware qualification remain open.

### Certified NURBS path length

`NURBSLENGTH(curve[,absoluteTolerance[,relativeTolerance[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]]]])`
returns `{value,{absoluteError},lowerBound,{upperBound},segments,status$}`.
Defaults are `1e-6,1e-6,4096,1074`. Native Rust uses
`NativeNurbs::<2/3>::length(NativeCurveLengthOptions)` and the shared
`NativeCurveLengthReport` / `NativeCurveLengthStatus` types.

The result sums traversal length over **every nonempty closed knot span**.
Repeated travel counts; jumps between disconnected pieces do not. Degree-zero
pieces contribute zero. Each span uses its own endpoint continuations, including
both sides of repeated knots. This is curve length, not the length of sampled
chords, and does not depend on a rounded knot-refinement packet.

Exact original homogeneous span polynomials are restricted in Bernstein form.
Outward-rounded endpoint norms give lower bounds; positive-weight rational
control polygons give upper bounds. For arbitrary degree, the rational Bernstein
basis has monotone cumulative weights, so total variation is bounded by that
polygon. Ordered collinear controls reduce to endpoint distance; reversing
controls do not. Exact aggregate sums and intersections of earlier valid bounds
avoid losing certificates to floating-point addition or refinement roundoff.
Signed/zero weights are supported: mixed-sign restricted hulls may initially have
no finite upper certificate and refine until one becomes available.

`CONVERGED` means `absoluteError <= MAX(absoluteTolerance,relativeTolerance*value)`,
compared exactly. Both tolerances must be finite/nonnegative, at least one
positive. `SEGMENT_LIMIT` and `RESOLUTION_LIMIT` retain complete path bounds,
including unresolved spans. `{}` for upper bound/error means no finite upper
certificate has been established; the reported value then equals the lower
bound and is not a converged estimate. A blocked span does not prevent other
spans from refining. Parameter means are exact before rounding, including
intervals from `-MAX` to `+MAX`. Lack of a representable interior parameter can
yield `RESOLUTION_LIMIT` even though an exact real curve has interior motion.

Global segment cap: `1..65536`, at least one per nonempty span; an insufficient
budget is an error rather than partial coverage. Depth cap: `1..2100` per original
span. All existing degree/control limits apply. Exact domain preflight rejects
every raw denominator zero (including removable 0/0 and endpoints) and undefined
span. The separate domain work limit remains in force. Length adds a
16,000,000-step work cap and uses the existing 65,536-bit fraction limit,
cancellation checks, a bounded panel heap and one cached exact span. Work/bit
exhaustion, cancellation or certified lower-bound overflow returns an error
without a partial report. A loose polygon upper bound that overflows is unknown,
not evidence that the actual length overflows. Absolute point coordinates may
be unrepresentable while a finite length remains certifiable.

`programs/science/nurbs_length.bas` checks a closed circular path and disconnected
cutting segments with a feed-time calculation. Independent exact Cox span
polynomials and high-precision integrals qualify the bounds, including limits,
backtracking and extreme scales; native and exported consumers are also required.
Evidence when accepted: `output/nurbs-length-2026-10-27/validation.json`.
Inverse arc-length traversal, rational surfaces, composite continuity workflows
and broad math/application/OS/hardware acceptance remain open.

### Tensor-product B-spline and NURBS surfaces

The Rust `NativeNurbsSurface<N>` engine supports 2D/3D coordinates, independent
U/V degrees `0..16`, nonuniform/repeated/nonclamped knots and at most **65536 total
controls**. Degree zero and discontinuous patches are valid. BASIC constructors:

- `BSPLINESURFACE({uDegree,vDegree},uKnots,vKnots,points)` uses unit weights.
- `NURBSSURFACE({uDegree,vDegree},uKnots,vKnots,points,weights[,mode$])` accepts
  `"WEIGHTED"` Euclidean points (default) or `"HOMOGENEOUS"` numerator controls.
- Points are a rectangular U-row/V-column grid of coordinate lists; weights
  have the same U/V shape. Native arrays are flattened U-major/V-fast:
  `index=u*vCount+v`. Each knot vector determines its axis control count.
- The freely editable packet is
  `{"NSURFACE1",{uDegree,vDegree},uKnots,vKnots,points,weights,mode$}`.

`NURBSSURFACEPOINT(S,u,v[,uSide$[,vSide$]])` returns a coordinate list.
`NURBSSURFACEDERIV(S,u,v,uOrder,vOrder[,uSide$[,vSide$]])` returns a mixed
partial, with orders independently `0..3` (including `(3,3)`).
`NURBSSURFACEBATCH(S,{{u,v},...}[,uOrder[,vOrder[,uSide$[,vSide$]]]])`
returns complete input-order results; both derivative orders default to zero.
Each side defaults to `"AUTO"`: the right continuation at interior knots,
the left continuation at the final active endpoint. `"LEFT"`/`"RIGHT"`
apply independently to U and V. A side pointing outside an active domain is
an error; no extrapolation or snapping occurs. Endpoint continuations are
computed from the selected nonempty knot spans.

Native constructors are `new([p,q],[&uKnots,&vKnots],&points,&weights)`,
`from_homogeneous(...)` and `polynomial([p,q],[&uKnots,&vKnots],&points)`.
Accessors expose `bases()`, `shape()`, `coordinates()`, `weights()` and
`is_homogeneous()`. Queries are `point([u,v])`,
`point_on([u,v],[uSide,vSide])`, `derivative([u,v],[du,dv])`,
`derivative_on([u,v],[du,dv],[uSide,vSide])` and
`evaluate_many(&parameters,[du,dv],[uSide,vSide])`. Sides use `NativeKnotSide`.

The backend reuses exact local Cox-de Boor basis jets. Numerator/denominator
products, mixed quotient differentiation and original-knot scaling stay exact
until each final component rounds once to binary64. Rational derivatives can
remain nonzero above the polynomial degree. Zero/signed weights are admitted
except an all-zero weight array; every query rejects a raw zero denominator,
including removable 0/0. Homogeneous input permits directions at infinity in
the control net. Weighted one-hot queries preserve the original control's
signed zeros after the denominator check.

Inputs, outputs and knots must be finite. Shape, degree, total control, query
and derivative limits are checked. Batches contain at most 65536 parameter
pairs and preflight all parameter domains before computing results. A shared
16,000,000 charged-step budget covers a complete query/batch, including local
basis and mixed-jet work; each query does not receive a fresh batch budget.
The existing reduced-fraction 65536-bit cap and cancellation checks also apply.
Exhaustion, cancellation, a zero denominator or final overflow returns an error
without partial output. A BASIC query revalidates the entire editable packet;
batching amortizes that cost. Native queries use only the local
`(uDegree+1)*(vDegree+1)` control neighborhood after construction.

This is a **pointwise surface foundation**, with exact original-data derivative
evaluation. It does not certify a whole patch free of denominator zeros or
provide tessellation error bounds, trimming/intersections, area integration or
a complete CAD system. Those and inverse arc-length traversal remain open.
`programs/science/nurbs_surface.bas` exercises a rational cylinder and its
tangents. Required qualification includes exact independent polynomial/series
references, SciPy comparisons where supported, analytic sphere/cylinder models,
large grids, cancellation, BASIC recovery and standalone export.
Evidence when accepted: `output/nurbs-surface-2026-10-27/validation.json`.
Broader math/application/OS/image/architecture/hardware gates remain open.

### Whole-patch NURBS surface denominator certificates

`NURBSSURFACEDOMAIN(surface[,maxCells[,maxDepth]])` examines **every nonempty
closed U/V knot rectangle**, with separate one-sided continuations at joins.
It returns
`{"NSDOMAIN1",{{uFrom,uTo},{vFrom,vTo}},status$,patches,refinements,zeroCells,unresolvedCells,cells}`.
Each cell is
`{{uSpan,vSpan},{{u0,u1},{v0,v1}},status$,{lowerW,upperW},witnesses}`.
Span indices are one-based in BASIC and zero-based in Rust. Cells are ordered
by original patch and rectangle coordinates. They cover every patch completely;
shared edges are included on both sides.

Native Rust uses `NativeNurbsSurface::domain(NativeNurbsSurfaceDomainOptions)`
and typed `NativeNurbsSurfaceDomainReport` / `NativeNurbsSurfaceDomainCell`
records. Report/cell status types are `NativeNurbsSurfaceDomainStatus` and
`NativeNurbsSurfaceDomainCellStatus`. Defaults are 4096 total cells and depth
40 per axis. Limits: cells `1..65536` and depth `1..2100`. At least one cell per
original knot rectangle is required; insufficient initial coverage is an error.

Cell meanings:

- `POSITIVE` / `NEGATIVE` certify a strictly nonzero denominator throughout
  the closed cell, including real parameter pairs between binary64 values.
- `IDENTICALLY_ZERO` certifies the denominator is zero everywhere in the cell.
- `ZERO_WITNESS` provides one parameter pair with an exact raw denominator zero.
- `SIGN_CHANGE` provides two parameter pairs with exact opposite denominator
  signs; continuity within that patch proves at least one zero between them.
- `CELL_LIMIT` / `RESOLUTION_LIMIT` mean unresolved. They never mean regular.
  Resolution covers per-axis depth or a lack of an interior binary64 midpoint.
  Parameter-independent directions are not pointlessly subdivided.

Witnesses belong to the cell's **selected patch continuation**, which can differ
from an automatic point query at a discontinuous join. Identically-zero and
regular/limited cells have no witness list. A cell containing proved zeros is
not subdivided further just to locate every zero. `zeroCells` counts cell
incidences, not distinct zeros, poles or connected zero-set components. Raw
removable zeros are included. `unresolvedCells` is reported even when zeros
have also been proved elsewhere.

Overall status is `REGULAR` only if every cell is Positive/Negative;
`ZERO_DENOMINATOR` if any cell proves a zero; otherwise `CELL_LIMIT` takes
precedence over `RESOLUTION_LIMIT`. A finite sampled grid alone never admits
a patch as regular. Different signs in disconnected patch continuations do not
imply a zero between those patches.

The shared Rust exact de Boor channel kernel produces original-data tensor
power coefficients, converted exactly to Bernstein controls. All restrictions
use that original net; no rounded child surface is used. Convex control bounds
are rounded outwards for `lowerW/upperW`. Strict same-sign original weights
provide an inexpensive valid certificate. For a nonnegative Bernstein net
whose corners are positive, the closed-cell lower bound also uses
`minCorner * 2^(-max(uDegree-1,0)-max(vDegree-1,0))`. This follows from the
minimum of the endpoint Bernstein basis sums; degree-zero axes contribute
one. Negative nets use the same argument after a sign flip. Thus interior
zero controls do not prevent a valid strict certificate. A strict lower
bound can round to zero at extreme scales; the Positive/Negative status
comes from the exact proof, not the rounded bound alone.

Subdivision has one global cell budget, breadth-first fairness, separate
per-axis depths, overflow-safe exact midpoints and one cached exact patch.
The domain operation has a 16,000,000 charged-step limit and the existing
65536-bit reduced-fraction cap. Work/bit exhaustion or cancellation is an
error without a partial report. Cell/depth/parameter limits instead retain
complete coverage and explicitly unresolved cells.

This certifies denominator regularity only. It does not establish finite
coordinate outputs, geometric continuity, injectivity, tessellation accuracy,
surface area, or complete algebraic classification of a bivariate zero set.
Tangent zeros at nonrepresentable parameters can remain unresolved. Those
limits, trimming/intersections, area, inverse arc-length traversal and broader
math/application/OS/image/hardware gates remain explicit follow-on work.
`programs/science/nurbs_surface_domain.bas` admits a regular cylinder and
rejects a hidden tangent-zero patch before tessellation.
Evidence when accepted: `output/nurbs-surface-domain-2026-10-27/validation.json`.

### NURBSSURFACEMESH

`NURBSSURFACEMESH(S,tolerance[,maxTriangles[,maxDepth]])` converts an editable
`NSURFACE1` surface into a certified positional triangle mesh.

```basic
10 M=NURBSSURFACEMESH(S,.01,8192,40)
20 PRINT M(2),M(3),M(4)
30 REM Only CONVERGED guarantees the requested positional tolerance
```

Returns `{"NSMESH1",status$,triangleCount,{maximumDeviation},pieces}`.
Each piece is
`{{uSpan,vSpan},{{u0,u1},{v0,v1}},{uParameters,vParameters},vertices,triangles,cellDeviation,{pieceMaximumDeviation}}`.
Spans and triangle indices are one-based; vertices and cell bounds use U-major,
V-fast ordering. A finite optional bound is {bound}; {} means no finite bound.
Each grid cell produces two triangles along the (u0,v0)-(u1,v1) diagonal.

CONVERGED certifies same-parameter Euclidean positional error at most tolerance
against the actual rounded triangle vertices. TRIANGLE_LIMIT or
RESOLUTION_LIMIT retains complete original-patch coverage without claiming
the tolerance was met. Global axis cuts prevent parameter T-junctions.
Original patch seams retain separate vertices/continuations; there is no
implicit welding or closed-solid/printability guarantee. Degenerate geometric
triangles remain in the parameter cover.

tolerance must be finite and positive. Defaults: maxTriangles=8192,
maxDepth=40. Limits: 2..131072 triangles (only complete pairs) and per-axis
depth 1..2100 from each original knot interval. Every original knot rectangle
requires at least two triangles; insufficient initial capacity is an error.
Raw denominator zeros, inconclusive domain admission, nonfinite output
vertices, cancellation or hard work/arithmetic limits produce an error with
no partial result. Admission and construction share 16,000,000 charged steps
and the existing exact fraction cap. See GEOMETRY.md for certificate details
and the complete native/packet contract.

### NURBSSURFACEINDEX

`NURBSSURFACEINDEX(S,tolerance[,maxTriangles[,maxDepth[,seams$[,wrap$]]]])`
turns an editable 3D NSURFACE1 surface into a shared indexed triangle mesh.

```basic
10 M=NURBSSURFACEINDEX(S,.01,8192,40,"CONTINUOUS","NONE")
20 V=M(8,1):F=M(8,2)
30 PRINT MESHTOPOLOGY3D(V,F)
40 REM After solid/format validation, MESH WRITE can export V,F
```

Returns
`{"NINDEX1",maximumDeviation,patchCount,sourceVertexCount,joinedSeams,unjoinedSeams,{wrapU,wrapV},{vertices,faces},patchVertexMaps}`.
Faces and patch vertex maps are one-based. Wrap flags are 0/1. Patch maps follow
the original knot patches in U-major/V-fast order, and each patch's vertices
use the same order as NURBSSURFACEMESH. The error bound applies to the original
surface and the actual returned rounded triangles.

seams$ is CONTINUOUS (default) or SEPARATE. CONTINUOUS joins adjacent patch
boundaries only when their original rational functions are proven identical;
matching samples alone are insufficient. Nonidentical internal seams remain
separate. wrap$ is NONE (default), U, V or UV: explicitly identify high/low
boundaries with matching transverse parameters. Requested closure must pass
the same exact equality proof or the call fails. Wrap operates independently
of the internal seam policy. Strings are case-insensitive.

tolerance must be finite and positive. Defaults: maxTriangles=8192,
maxDepth=40; ranges 2..100000 and 1..2100. At most 200000 source/indexed
vertices are admitted. Original control/degree/exact-arithmetic limits apply.
The tessellation must converge; triangle/depth/representation limits become
errors. Degenerate/duplicate mesh faces are rejected, including when periodic
sampling is too coarse. No triangles are discarded. Raw-domain, work/bit,
coordinate, cancellation and invalid-input errors return no partial result.
Admission, tessellation, seam proof and assembly share 16000000 charged steps;
shared mesh validation additionally has its own fixed caps and cancellation.

Joined/unjoined counts refer to original patch-edge pairs; ordinary outer
boundaries do not count as unjoined. There is no global coordinate welding.
Indexed topology does not imply a closed embedded solid: use topology,
intersection/solid and STL consumers for their respective validation.
Editing output lists is allowed but invalidates the associated positional
certificate. Subsequent mesh functions validate the actual lists. See
GEOMETRY.md for the complete contract and limits.


### Distance-based curve traversal

`BEZIERTRAVEL(points,distance,tolerance[,mode$[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]]])`,
`RBEZIERTRAVEL(curve,distance,tolerance[,mode$[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]]])` and
`NURBSTRAVEL(curve,distance,tolerance[,mode$[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]]])` share
the native Rust inverse arc-length engine. `mode$` is `"DISTANCE"` (default,
nonnegative curve units) or `"FRACTION"` (0..1 of total traveled length).
Tolerance is finite and strictly positive, in distance units for both modes.
Limits default to 4096 segments and depth 1074; allowed ranges are 1..65536
and 1..2100. NURBS needs at least one segment per nonempty original knot span.

The result is
`{"CTRAVEL1",status$,parameter,span,point,{distanceError},
{prefixLower,{prefixUpper}},{totalLower,{totalUpper}},segments,inRange,pointRoundingError}`.
Optional upper/error values use an empty list when no finite bound is known.
`span` is the one-based original knot-span index; a Bezier of degree p uses
the single clamped span p+1. `inRange` is 1 only when the target is certified
inside the total traversal range. `CONVERGED` proves this AND a distance error
at most the requested tolerance. `SEGMENT_LIMIT` or `RESOLUTION_LIMIT` supplies
a candidate with its current bounds, without claiming the tolerance was met.
An absolute distance proven beyond the total length is an error; an undecided
range can instead return a limit status with `inRange=0`.

The error bounds apply to travel from the beginning to the exact original
curve point at the returned parameter and span. Position components round once;
`pointRoundingError` separately bounds Euclidean position error via an outward
L1 bound. Fractional targets use the same original total length as the prefix.
In particular, fraction 1 selects the final endpoint with zero distance residual
even when the total-length upper bound is unresolved.

Traversal counts backtracking and excludes jump distances at disconnected
knot joins. An internal join result identifies the left span and its one-sided
point; use the returned point/span rather than reevaluating that parameter with
an automatic knot-side choice. Zero distance/fraction selects the beginning;
fraction 1 selects the final endpoint. Stationary spans and zero-length paths
are supported; no uniqueness or general earliest-solution claim is made.

All original closed spans must have nonzero raw denominators, including endpoint
limits; even a removable 0/0 is rejected. The domain admission has its existing
2-million charged-work budget; traversal then has a separate 16-million budget.
Both are cancellable. Exact arithmetic is capped at 65536 bits, output nodes at
twice the segment count minus one, and coordinate/length range overflow is an
error. No partial success packet escapes cancellation or an arithmetic/work error.

Example (quadratic speed, straight geometry):
```basic
10 P={{0,0},{0,0},{4,0}}
20 R=BEZIERTRAVEL(P,0.25,1E-9,"FRACTION")
30 PRINT R(3),R(5)
```
The parameter is 0.5 and the position is {1,0}: one quarter of the distance
does not generally mean one quarter of the parameter.

TABLECREATE(schema,rows) constructs an editable {"TABLE1",schema,rows} packet. Schema entries are {"field","INTEGER"}, {"field","REAL"}, {"field","BOOLEAN"} or {"field","TEXT"}. Field names are case-sensitive, unique, 1..255 UTF-8 bytes without NUL. Use {} for a missing cell, distinct from zero, false and empty text. Booleans use integer 0/1. REAL accepts finite reals and exactly representable integers; INTEGER preserves all 64 bits. Every consumed packet is validated, including at DEF FN boundaries.

  • TABLESELECT(table,{"field",...}) selects/reorders distinct fields.
  • TABLEFILTER(table,{1,0,{},...}) keeps only true rows, in input order. The mask must contain exactly one entry per input row.
  • TABLEGROUP(table,{"key",...},{{"SUM","value","total"},...}) creates groups in first-appearance order. Single-column reductions use {operation,inputField,outputField}; operations are COUNT, SUM, MEAN, MIN, MAX, VARP, VARS, STDEVP and STDEVS. Null keys group together; signed real zero has one identity. Integer keys never convert to floats. Output names must be unique across keys and reductions. COUNT counts present cells of any type. Other reductions require numeric input, ignore nulls and return null for an all-null group. Integer SUM detects overflow. SUM/MEAN accumulate exactly before final binary64 rounding. MEAN returns REAL; SUM/MIN/MAX retain the input numeric type. Variance and deviation return REAL, preserve exact integer samples and round once from exact moments. VARP/STDEVP use the population denominator; VARS/STDEVS use the sample denominator and return null with fewer than two present observations.
  • TABLEWINDOW(table,keys,aggregates,preceding,following[,minPeriods]) appends reduction fields to the original table, preserving original row order. This accepts single-column triples and paired specifications (see below). An empty key list {} means one global partition; otherwise distinct key fields define partitions, with the same exact equality/null rules as grouping. Frames use row positions within each partition's input order, including null rows. Each frame includes the current row; preceding/following are integer row counts, 0 means current row only on that side, and -1 means unbounded. No sorting or timestamp-distance inference occurs. minPeriods defaults to 1 and counts present observations, not frame rows. Non-COUNT reductions need at least max(1,minPeriods) present observations; sample variance/deviation also need two. COUNT always returns the present count, including zero. Bounds/minPeriods are at most 1,000,000; minPeriods cannot be negative. New field names must be distinct from all original names. Exact reversible sums/moments avoid drift as values enter/leave a frame; moving min/max use ordered candidate queues. Each row's result must fit: any overflow or cancellation rejects the whole returned table.
  • TABLESORT(table,order) performs a stable multi-field sort. Order entries are {"field"[,direction$[,nulls$]]} with ASC/DESC (default ASC) and FIRST/LAST (default LAST). Null placement is independent of direction; equal keys retain their original order. Integer comparisons retain all bits, real signed zero is equal, false precedes true, and text uses UTF-8 byte order without locale collation or Unicode normalization. Order fields must be nonempty and distinct.
  • TABLERANK(table,keys,order,mode$,output$) appends ranks within exact-key partitions, retaining the original row order. Empty keys mean a global partition. Order has the TABLESORT form. ROW_NUMBER assigns consecutive 1-based positions, breaking ties by input order. RANK assigns the first position of each peer group (1,1,3); DENSE_RANK counts peer groups (1,1,2). PERCENT_RANK returns (rank-1)/(partitionSize-1), or 0 for a singleton. CUME_DIST returns the fraction of rows preceding or equal to the peer group, including null peers at their declared position. The first three return INTEGER; the last two REAL. All order fields together define peers.
  • TABLESHIFT(table,keys,field$,offset,output$) appends a previous or next observation within each partition's input order. Positive offset means lag, negative means lead, and zero copies the current field. Missing source values and out-of-range positions return null. Missing observations still occupy positions; there is no implicit null skipping or default fill value. Offsets are integers with absolute value at most 1,000,000. The appended field retains the exact source type. Sort explicitly first when needed.
  • TABLERANGE(table,keys,orderField$,aggregates,preceding,following[,minPeriods]) appends numeric-distance window reductions. Within every partition, the INTEGER or REAL order field must be present and nondecreasing; otherwise the operation fails. Both frame endpoints are inclusive, so all equal-order peers receive the same frame. A distance of zero includes all current peers. {} means unbounded on that side. Bounds are nonnegative and expressed in the order field's units; INTEGER order requires integer bounds, while REAL order accepts finite reals or exactly representable integers. Distances are compared exactly without rounding integer keys, subtracting reals approximately or overflowing endpoints. Aggregates, minimum observation counts, sample-size rules and output types match TABLEWINDOW. INTEGER ticks or REAL numeric coordinates can represent time, but units, dates, time zones, calendars and conversion remain the program's responsibility. The result retains original row order. New output names for rank, shift and range operations must be unique across the entire result schema.
  • TABLEJOIN(left,right,leftKeys,rightKeys[,kind$[,nulls$[,rightPrefix$]]]) performs an equijoin. Each key list contains distinct field names and must be nonempty; paired keys must have the same declared type. There are no implicit numeric casts. Keys compare exactly, including 64-bit integers and UTF-8 text; real signed zero has one identity. kind$ is INNER (default), LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, SEMI or ANTI. INNER emits every matching pair; LEFT/RIGHT also retain unmatched rows from that side; FULL retains unmatched rows from both sides. Missing opposite cells become {}. SEMI keeps each matching left row once; ANTI keeps each nonmatching left row. Duplicate left rows remain distinct. nulls$ is NEVER (default: any missing key component prevents a match) or EQUAL (missing components compare equal, while every other key component must also match). INNER/LEFT/FULL/SEMI/ANTI follow left input order, with matching right rows in right input order. RIGHT follows right input order, then matching left order. FULL appends unmatched right rows in right input order. Results contain all left fields followed by all right fields, including both sets of key fields. Every right name receives rightPrefix$ (default "right."). There is no automatic key coalescing or collision renaming. Final names must remain unique and within the usual field-name limits. An empty prefix is permitted when names are already disjoint. Prefixes have at most 255 UTF-8 bytes without NUL. SEMI/ANTI return left fields only; their prefix is validated but unused. Output row/cell counts and repeated text bytes are checked before allocating result row-index arrays or gathering output columns.
  • TABLEROWS(table), TABLESCHEMA(table), TABLESIZE(table) return row data, schema and {rowCount,columnCount}.

Tables support 1..256 fields, at most 1,000,000 rows and total cells, and 64 MiB of cell text. Empty row sets preserve their schema. Group output is checked before its row matrix is allocated. Group work is limited to 10 million row/key/reduction visits; window work counts keys plus two visits per reduction per input row under the same 10-million limit. Output columns count toward the table's total-cell cap. Interpreter storage limits also apply. Operations are immutable and check cancellation around backend phases and during Rust loops. Backend grouping/filter phases are not internally interruptible; this is not a hard real-time API. The core uses one worker and synchronous group cleanup. BASIC packets are revalidated/copied; native clones and projections share column buffers. Joins build a bounded Rust hash index, check cancellation while planning/materializing indices, and use the existing column backend to gather the result. Each column gather is checked before/after and is not internally interruptible. No partial result is returned on rejection or cancellation. Window partitioning and output-column construction have checkpoints before/after each backend phase. Sort/rank use interruptible stable merge sorting with at most 50 million field comparisons and 256 MiB of compared text prefixes per call. Numeric range planning uses monotone frame endpoints; reductions share the row-window engine. Shift text amplification is checked before gathering the appended column. Date/time/calendar types, typed file interchange, bounded streaming and other join predicates remain separate work. See programs/science/typed_analytics.bas, programs/science/table_joins.bas, programs/science/table_windows.bas and programs/science/ordered_analytics.bas for editable examples.

Typed CSV interchange and batch input

TABLEFROMCSV(schema,text$[,delimiter$[,header]]) parses CSV into a typed table; TABLECSV$(table[,delimiter$[,header]]) returns CSV text. Schema uses the same {{"name","INTEGER"},...} format as TABLECREATE. There is no type inference.

TABLE READCSV #channel,schema,maxRows,destination[,delimiter$[,header]] reads complete records from an ordinary file opened FOR INPUT. It returns at most maxRows rows and a schema-preserving empty table at EOF. Header defaults to 1 on each statement: use 1 for the first batch and 0 for later batches. The file channel retains its cursor; EOF(channel) works with that same cursor. Keep CSV reads at record boundaries when mixing with other channel operations.

TABLE WRITECSV path$,table[,delimiter$[,header]] streams encoded rows through the file sandbox's atomic replacement operation. Existing output survives validation, cancellation or write failure before replacement.

Delimiter defaults to comma; comma, semicolon, tab (CHR$(9)) and pipe are accepted. Header is exactly integer 0 or 1 and defaults to 1. A present header must match the declared names and order. Output uses CRLF records and quotes every nonmissing field and header; embedded quotes are doubled. Input also accepts LF and CR records. Quoted line endings and UTF-8 text are preserved. Spaces are data, not trimmed. Blank records are one missing cell, not skipped. Malformed quoting, ragged rows, invalid UTF-8 and type mismatches fail.

An unquoted empty field is missing ({}); "" is present empty TEXT. Quoted empty numeric/Boolean fields fail. INTEGER preserves all signed 64-bit values. REAL accepts signed decimal/fraction/exponent notation, rounds to finite binary64 and may underflow to zero. Integer-valued REAL input still follows REAL rounding. Boolean accepts true/false, TRUE/FALSE or 1/0. Text such as =1+1 remains literal text. CSV itself carries no schema: retain the schema separately, and ensure other tools preserve the quoted-empty distinction.

A batch admits at most one million total cells/rows, 256 fields and 64 MiB decoded TEXT; one record's decoded field bytes are also capped at 64 MiB. Each field obeys the BASIC session string limit. Text conversion additionally obeys that limit for the entire CSV string. A file read batch or complete export is capped at 256 MiB encoded bytes and the configured file budget; channel bytes accumulate across batches against that file budget. Many batches can process more than one million rows without storing the complete dataset.

A failed CSV read returns no partial table and leaves the destination unchanged; input may have advanced. After a parsing, I/O or cancellation failure, CLOSE and reopen the channel before another CSV read. Assignment errors after successful decoding can also advance the cursor. Batch size/schema/options are validated before consumption. These APIs do not provide streaming joins or global window state. See programs/science/csv_analytics.bas for a complete batch example.

Statistics across batches

TABLE ACCUMCREATE name$,schema,keys,aggregates[,maxGroups[,maxStateBytes[,maxRows]]] creates a named Rust accumulator. Schema and aggregate specifications follow TABLECREATE and TABLEGROUP conventions. Empty keys {} select one whole-dataset group. Otherwise keys must be distinct existing fields, and output names must be unique. An existing name is replaced only after successful creation.

TABLE ACCUMADD name$,table appends a batch with exactly the declared schema. TABLE ACCUMMERGE destination$,source$ combines states with identical schemas, key order and aggregate specifications. It retains destination limits and group order, then appends new source groups. The source is unchanged; self-merge deliberately doubles the observations. TABLE ACCUMRESULT name$,destination returns a typed result table. TABLE ACCUMINFO name$,destination returns {rowsSeen,groupCount,accountedStateBytes}. TABLE ACCUMRESET name$ discards observations but retains plan/limits. TABLE ACCUMFREE name$ releases state and its reservation. CLEAR and runtime resets also release all accumulators.

Single-column reductions are COUNT, SUM, MEAN, MIN, MAX, VARP, VARS, STDEVP and STDEVS. Paired reductions are described in the next section. COUNT counts present cells of any type; other reductions require INTEGER/REAL. Null values are skipped. All-null numeric groups return missing cells; sample variance/deviation require two present values. Empty whole-dataset input returns one row with COUNT zero and other results missing. Empty grouped input has no groups. Null keys group together; empty text remains distinct. Integer keys are exact, text uses UTF-8 byte equality and both signs of real zero share one key. Groups follow first appearance.

Exact internal sums and moments survive queries, updates and merges; merging does not combine rounded summaries. INTEGER sum overflow or an unrepresentable REAL result fails the query while preserving state. Later input can bring a sum back into range.

Defaults: 4,096 groups, 8 MiB accounted state, one billion rows. Hard caps: 65,536 groups, 64 MiB state, one billion rows; zero rows permits only empty input. State accounting conservatively includes metadata, container capacity, duplicated keys and reducer storage; the byte cap can be reached before the group cap. An update/merge permits ten million row-or-group × (keys + single-column reducers + twice paired reducers) steps. Input batches and result tables retain their ordinary bounds.

Updates/merges stage a bounded copy and commit only on success. Wrong schemas, cancellation and admission failures preserve previous results. BASIC permits 32 named accumulators and reserves twice each state-byte cap from the shared asset budget for retained state and transactional work. Reservations are accounting, not eager allocation. Input/output tables have their separate bounds. Bounded cloning/hash phases are not hard real-time operations.

See programs/science/streaming_analytics.bas for CSV batches, exact group keys, global statistics, merging and export. These retain summaries, not all input rows. Streaming joins, rolling-window history and persisted restart state remain separate work.

values. REAL accepts signed decimal/fraction/exponent notation, rounds to finite

rounding. Boolean accepts `true`/`false`, `TRUE`/`FALSE` or `1`/`0`. Text such as
`=1+1` remains literal text. CSV itself carries no schema: retain the schema
separately, and ensure other tools preserve the quoted-empty distinction.

A batch admits at most one million total cells/rows, 256 fields and 64 MiB
decoded TEXT; one record's decoded field bytes are also capped at 64 MiB.
Each field obeys the BASIC session string limit. Text conversion additionally
obeys that limit for the entire CSV string. A file read batch or complete export
is capped at 256 MiB encoded bytes and the configured file budget; channel bytes
accumulate across batches against that file budget. Many batches can process
more than one million rows without storing the complete dataset.

A failed CSV read returns no partial table and leaves the destination unchanged;
input may have advanced. After a parsing, I/O or cancellation failure, CLOSE and
reopen the channel before another CSV read. Assignment errors after successful
decoding can also advance the cursor. Batch size/schema/options are validated
before consumption. These APIs do not provide streaming joins or global window
state. See `programs/science/csv_analytics.bas` for a complete batch example.

### Statistics across batches

`TABLE ACCUMCREATE name$,schema,keys,aggregates[,maxGroups[,maxStateBytes[,maxRows]]]`
creates a named Rust accumulator. Schema and aggregate specifications follow TABLECREATE
and TABLEGROUP conventions. Empty keys `{}` select one whole-dataset group.
Otherwise keys must be distinct existing fields, and output names must be unique.
An existing name is replaced only after successful creation.

`TABLE ACCUMADD name$,table` appends a batch with exactly the declared schema.
`TABLE ACCUMMERGE destination$,source$` combines states with identical schemas,
key order and aggregate specifications. It retains destination limits and group order,
then appends new source groups. The source is unchanged; self-merge deliberately
doubles the observations.
`TABLE ACCUMRESULT name$,destination` returns a typed result table.
`TABLE ACCUMINFO name$,destination` returns
`{rowsSeen,groupCount,accountedStateBytes}`.
`TABLE ACCUMRESET name$` discards observations but retains plan/limits.
`TABLE ACCUMFREE name$` releases state and its reservation. CLEAR and runtime
resets also release all accumulators.

Single-column reductions are COUNT, SUM, MEAN, MIN, MAX, VARP, VARS, STDEVP and STDEVS.
Paired reductions are described in the next section.
COUNT counts present cells of any type; other reductions require INTEGER/REAL.
Null values are skipped. All-null numeric groups return missing cells; sample
variance/deviation require two present values. Empty whole-dataset input returns
one row with COUNT zero and other results missing. Empty grouped input has no
groups. Null keys group together; empty text remains distinct. Integer keys are
exact, text uses UTF-8 byte equality and both signs of real zero share one key.
Groups follow first appearance.

Exact internal sums and moments survive queries, updates and merges; merging
does not combine rounded summaries. INTEGER sum overflow or an unrepresentable
REAL result fails the query while preserving state. Later input can bring a sum
back into range.

Defaults: 4,096 groups, 8 MiB accounted state, one billion rows.
Hard caps: 65,536 groups, 64 MiB state, one billion rows; zero rows permits only
empty input. State accounting conservatively includes metadata, container
capacity, duplicated keys and reducer storage; the byte cap can be reached before
the group cap. An update/merge permits ten million row-or-group × (keys +
single-column reducers + twice paired reducers) steps. Input batches and result
tables retain their ordinary bounds.

Updates/merges stage a bounded copy and commit only on success. Wrong schemas,
cancellation and admission failures preserve previous results. BASIC permits
32 named accumulators and reserves twice each state-byte cap from the shared
asset budget for retained state and transactional work. Reservations are
accounting, not eager allocation. Input/output tables have their separate bounds.
Bounded cloning/hash phases are not hard real-time operations.

See `programs/science/streaming_analytics.bas` for CSV batches, exact group keys,
global statistics, merging and export. These retain summaries, not all input rows.
Streaming joins, rolling-window history and persisted
restart state remain separate work.

documents.title: Exact paired statistics in groups and streams
documents.html:
TABLEGROUP and TABLE ACCUMCREATE accept mixed aggregation lists. Existing three-field entries remain unchanged. Paired entries contain four fields: {"operation","xColumn","yColumn","outputName"}. Supported operations are PAIRCOUNT, COVARP, COVARS, CORREL, SLOPE, INTERCEPT and RSQUARED. Requested output order is preserved, following grouping keys.

A pair contributes only when both cells are non-null. Both columns must be INTEGER or REAL; mixed column types are accepted without discarding integer bits. PAIRCOUNT counts complete pairs and returns zero for an empty group. COVARP divides centered products by n; COVARS uses n-1. Empty covariance and sample covariance with fewer than two pairs return null. CORREL and RSQUARED return null when either variable has zero variance. SLOPE and INTERCEPT fit y = slope*x + intercept and return null for fewer than two pairs or constant x; constant y has slope zero and its constant intercept.

Rust retains exact sums, squares and cross-products, including across batch merges. Covariance, slope, intercept and R-squared are rounded once from exact ratios; correlation rounds its exact square root directly. No rounded slope is used to calculate the intercept, and R-squared is not a square of rounded correlation. A nonrepresentable requested result raises a real-overflow error without discarding a stream's state. Ordinary input/table/stream caps apply; a pair charges two input operations and its fixed exact moment storage.

BASIC COVARP/COVARIANCE/CORREL/LINREG use the same exact paired kernels and now preserve INTEGER list values. Their existing invalid-sample errors remain: LINREG requires nonconstant x and y because its report includes correlation. COVMATRIX/CORRMATRIX share the exact real-input kernel; matrix inputs retain their existing REAL conversion rules. Weighted or multiple-predictor streaming fits and persisted recovery are separate work. See programs/science/paired_analytics.bas. Qualification when accepted: output/table-pair-2026-10-27.

documents.title: Paired row and numeric-range windows
documents.html:
TABLEWINDOW and TABLERANGE accept mixed single-column triples and paired four-field specifications from the paired-statistics section. Output fields follow the specified order and are appended to original rows. Row-frame positions include missing observations; numeric-range frames include both endpoints and every equal-axis peer, using the existing exact distance checks.

For a paired output, minPeriods counts rows where both numeric values are present. PAIRCOUNT always returns that complete-pair count, regardless of minPeriods. Other pair outputs require at least max(1,minPeriods) pairs; sample covariance also requires two, and correlation/fit outputs retain their existing constant-variable rules. Single-column minimum/count rules are unchanged.

Rust adds and removes exact sums, squares and cross-products as frame boundaries move. Each source observation enters and leaves a state at most once per partition/reduction; windows do not rescan every frame. Result conversion rounds once from the exact active-frame state. Repeated queries and removal of extreme values do not discard small residuals. Identical consecutive frames reuse their computed result. Overflow, admission failure or cancellation yields no partial output table and leaves the input unchanged.

The existing one-million-cell/row, 256-field and text/output caps remain. Work admission charges two updates per input per reducer; paired reducers read two inputs. Result arithmetic is bounded by the finite-number exponent range. These APIs operate on one admitted table. Cross-batch rolling history, time-zone and calendar frames, joins across streams and persisted state remain open. See programs/science/rolling_pair_analytics.bas. Evidence when accepted: output/table-pair-window-2026-10-27.

documents.title: Rolling statistics across input batches
documents.html:
TABLE ROLLCREATE name$,schema,keys,aggregates,preceding[,minPeriods[,maxGroups[,maxStateBytes[,maxRows]]]] creates a named trailing row-window state. A nonnegative INTEGER preceding value includes that many earlier rows of the same group and the current row. An empty list {} means the whole group prefix. Empty keys select one global group. Rows retain input order; interleaved groups retain independent history.

Aggregation entries are {"MEAN","x","average"} or paired entries such as {"SLOPE","x","y","gain"}, with the same operations, exact INTEGER handling, null rules and minPeriods behavior as TABLEWINDOW. minPeriods defaults to 1; COUNT and PAIRCOUNT always report their respective present counts.

TABLE ROLLADD name$,table,destination processes a batch and returns its original columns plus the requested aggregate columns. Later batches continue from the last successful update. The declared schema must match exactly. A failed update, output conversion, destination assignment or cancellation preserves the state. Each emitted row must have representable results; an overflow rejects the whole batch, even if a later row would have brought a sum back into range.

TABLE ROLLINFO name$,destination returns {rowsSeen,groupCount,accountedStateBytes,retainedRows}. TABLE ROLLRESET name$ discards observations and history, retaining the plan and limits. TABLE ROLLFREE name$ releases the state. CLEAR and runtime reset release all rolling states. There are at most 32 named rolling states, sharing the existing asset budget with other assets and table accumulators.

Limits default to 4,096 groups, 8 MiB accounted state and one billion lifetime rows. Hard limits are 65,536 groups, 64 MiB state and one billion rows. BASIC reserves twice maxStateBytes to cover retained state and one staged copy. These are conservative admission charges, not a measurement of process memory. Finite preceding and minPeriods bounds are at most one million; output tables still obey the one-million-cell and 256-field limits. Each update admits at most ten million key/reducer work units. Cancellation is cooperative.

Finite frames retain at most preceding+1 reducer observations per group, with memory charged before admission; unrelated input text/columns are not retained. Prefix windows use fixed-size reducers per group and retain no row history. Groups remain until RESET/FREE and still consume their group/key budget.

The native Rust interface is NativeTableRollingWindow::new for single-column plans or new_with_aggregations for mixed plans, using NativeTableWindowOptions with following=Some(0) and NativeTableAccumulatorLimits. update(&table) atomically returns a new table; updated(&table) returns a staged state and output without changing the original, allowing callers to validate output before committing. It also exposes rows_seen, group_count, state_bytes, retained_rows, limits, options and reset.

This is a causal row-window API. Lookahead, cross-batch numeric/calendar range frames, streaming joins and persisted state recovery remain open. Source/native qualification does not establish installed-OS or other-architecture availability. Example: programs/science/streaming_rolling.bas.
