documents.title: Civil dates, business calendars and dated cash flows
documents.html:
Civil dates are INTEGER days relative to 1970-01-01. The supported proleptic Gregorian range is 0001-01-01 through 9999-12-31 (-719162 through 2932896). There are no timezones, daylight-saving transitions, locale guesses or fictitious 1900-02-29. Existing clock-oriented DATE$ behavior is unchanged.

FunctionContract
CIVILDATE(year,month,day)Construct a valid date; reject invalid fields.
CIVILPARSE(text$)Parse exactly ten ASCII characters in YYYY-MM-DD form.
CIVILFORMAT$(date)Format exactly YYYY-MM-DD.
CIVILPARTS(date)Return {year,month,day,weekday}, Monday=1 through Sunday=7.
CIVILADD(date,amount[,unit$[,preserveMonthEnd]])Signed INTEGER increment; units DAYS (default), MONTHS or YEARS. Missing target days clamp to month end. The optional 0/1 flag additionally preserves an original month end for MONTHS/YEARS.
DAYCOUNT(start,end[,basis$])Signed day count under the named convention.
YEARFRAC(start,end[,basis$])Fraction of a year, rounded once from an exact integer ratio.
YEARFRACRATIO(start,end[,basis$])Return {numerator,denominator}; denominator is positive, and the ratio need not be reduced.
BUSCAL(holidays[,weekendMask])Construct an editable {"BUSCAL1",mask,holidays} record. Holidays are date integers.
BUSISDAY(calendar,date)Return 1 for an open date, otherwise 0.
BUSCOUNT(calendar,start,end)Count open dates in [start,end); reverse endpoints negate the count.
BUSADD(calendar,date,amount)Advance by signed business days, excluding the start. Zero returns the start unchanged.
BUSADJUST(calendar,date,convention$)Apply the explicit adjustment convention below.
DATEDNPV(rate,amounts,dates,valuationDate[,basis$])Value dated cash flows using an annual effective rate and explicit valuation date.

Day-count basis defaults to ACT365F. Supported spellings are:

  • ACT365F: actual elapsed days divided by 365.
  • ACT360: actual elapsed days divided by 360.
  • ACTACTISDA: actual days in each calendar year divided by that year's 365/366 days. Whole intervening years contribute one each; integer arithmetic combines the two partial years before the single final division.
  • 30E360: European/Eurobond 30E/360; replace each day 31 by 30 and use 360*(endYear-startYear)+30*(endMonth-startMonth)+endDay-startDay. February keeps its actual day number. This is a separate convention from 30E/360 ISDA, US/NASD and coupon-schedule-dependent Actual/Actual methods.

All four day-count/year-fraction operations are signed and antisymmetric. Intervals with identical endpoints have zero length. ACTACTISDA day counts are actual elapsed days; its year-fraction denominator depends on the endpoint years.

Weekend mask bits 0..6 mean Monday..Sunday. The default 96 closes Saturday and Sunday. Masks 0..126 are accepted; all seven weekdays cannot be closed. BUSCAL admits at most 65,536 supplied holidays, removes duplicates and omits holidays already closed by the weekend mask. No national holidays, observed-day rules or exchange schedules are implicit. Every BASIC operation validates the calendar record; native callers can reuse its prepared Rust representation.

Business adjustment names are UNADJUSTED, FOLLOWING, PRECEDING, MODFOLLOWING and MODPRECEDING. Modified conventions switch direction if the first adjustment would cross a month boundary. At the supported calendar boundary they try the opposite direction. Open dates remain unchanged. If no valid date can be returned within the supported range, the operation reports an error. Counting uses whole weeks and sorted holiday ranges; advancing uses a bounded binary search rather than walking through every intervening day.

DATEDNPV uses: SUM(amount[i] * (1 + rate)^(-YEARFRAC(valuationDate, dates[i], basis))). The rate must be finite and greater than -1. Amount/date list lengths must match and are capped at one million. Empty lists return zero. Dates can be unsorted, repeated or before valuation; valuation-day flows are included without discount, and earlier flows compound forward. Monetary amounts/results use binary64, including conversion of BASIC INTEGER amounts; they are not fixed-decimal money.

Discount weights use log1p/exp. Finite weights and amounts are multiplied and summed with the existing exact product accumulator before final rounding, which preserves cancellation even when an individual product would overflow. A weight outside binary64 uses the existing scaled-principal fallback; an unrepresentable fallback term or final result raises overflow. Transcendental approximation and ill-conditioned cancellation remain relevant; this is not certified valuation or a correctly rounded transcendental sum. Cancellation is checked while preparing inputs and after the bounded exact accumulation phase. Native inputs are immutable; errors return no partial result.

Native exports: NativeCivilDate, NativeDayCount, NativeBusinessCalendar, NativeBusinessConvention and NativeDatedCashflow. NativeFinancialMath exposes dated_net_present_value(rate,flows,valuation,basis). Native date construction, parsing, formatting and arithmetic use checked values. Calendar operations share the same rules as BASIC. Example: programs/finance/dated_cashflows.bas.

This checkpoint adds no new registry package: Chrono 0.4.45 was already vendored and pinned through the table dependencies. Its direct dependency enables only the standard-library date support, with clock/timezone defaults disabled. Existing upstream license files and archive/file checksums remain intact. Chrono supplies checked Gregorian dates; ModernBASIC supplies the public bounds, business-calendar contract, exact day-count ratios and financial integration.

References inspected for date APIs and convention comparison: Chrono NaiveDate, QuantLib Actual/Actual implementations, QuantLib 30/360 implementations. QuantLib is a comparison reference, not a new runtime dependency or copied engine.

Remaining financial work includes schedule generation/stubs, additional day-count families, country/exchange calendar datasets, instrument-specific calibration and additional return models, currency/decimal rounding, portfolio risk and wider model qualification. Timezone timestamps, persisted calendar identities, typed DATE table columns, installed OS and other CPU architectures retain separate acceptance gates.

documents.html:
DATESCHEDULE builds contractual dates from an original anchor, with short/long front/back stubs, optional month-end preservation and explicit stub boundaries. Native exports: NativeDateSchedule, NativeScheduleOptions, NativeScheduleInterval, NativeScheduleStub, NativeAccrualOptions and NativeAccrualPeriod. The immutable schedule exposes generate, from_dates, dates and accrual_periods.

See DATE_SCHEDULES.md for complete signatures, defaults, indexing, limits, cancellation, stub/adjustment rules and remaining scope.

documents.title: Shared adaptive numerical Jacobians in physics
documents.html:
Backward-Euler and index-one DAE numerical Newton paths reuse the Rust adaptive Jacobian kernel with scaled coordinates, cached samples and cumulative budget checks. Numerical DAE initialization holds the differential prefix fixed during all probes. See Physics Jacobians for domain recovery, analytic/CSR behavior, limits and the previously failing boundary examples.

Complex elementary ranges and canonical branch cuts

Complex exponential/trigonometric scaling preserves small representable components near overflow/underflow. Native BasicComplex and BASIC use the same kernels. See trigonometry contracts for canonical cut sides, domain errors, independent references and remaining limits.

Shared angular coordinates and graphics phase

ROTATE2D, TOPOLAR, TORECT, ATAN2, RAD and DEG share checked Rust coordinate operations. Degree drawing paths reuse the same phase kernels. See angular coordinate contracts for native APIs, signed radius/zero conventions, numerical bounds and evidence.

Checked reciprocal trigonometry and source inventory

SEC, CSC, COT and COTH share NativeTrigonometry::sec, csc, cot and coth, completing typed native access to the six existing real reciprocal functions. See reciprocal contracts and the complete angle-operation inventory for radians, represented poles, overflow, complex-input restrictions, independent references and the separate installed/architecture/certification gates.

Shared Rust error functions

ERF and ERFC now share the checked native Rust error-function kernel. ERFC retains small upper tails that subtraction from ERF loses. See implementation, provenance and numerical limits.

Shared normal-distribution math

NORMALPDF, interval-valued NORMALCDF, and INVNORM share native Rust distribution kernels. NORMALSF evaluates the upper tail directly and INVNORMSF inverts a supplied upper-tail probability. Each accepts optional mean and standard deviation after its sample/probability arguments. See contracts, methods and numerical limits.

Shared discrete count distributions

BINOMSF(n,p[,k]), GEOMETSF(p,k) and POISSONSF(mean,k) return P(X>k) directly. Existing PDF/CDF calls share the same checked Rust backend. Binomial scalar calls avoid full-table allocation; geometric calls preserve tiny probabilities; Poisson calls use the shared gamma kernels. See the native/BASIC contracts and resource limits.

Shared continuous probability laws

Exponential, uniform and Weibull PDF/CDF functions now share checked native Rust kernels. Direct upper tails and lower/upper inverse functions are available: EXPSF/EXPINV/EXPINVSF, UNIFORMSF/UNIFORMINV/UNIFORMINVSF and WEIBULLSF/WEIBULLINV/WEIBULLINVSF. See argument order, probability domains and numerical limits.

Shared exponential scaling

SCALEEXP(value,power) computes the real product value*exp(power) while retaining representable results even when the exponential alone underflows or overflows. Both inputs must be finite. Genuine final overflow raises an error; underflow may return zero. See Rust API, shared consumers and numerical limits.

Beta probability distribution

BETAPDF(x,alpha,beta), BETACDF(x,alpha,beta) and BETASF(x,alpha,beta) evaluate the density, lower probability and direct upper tail of a beta distribution on [0,1]. Both shapes are finite and positive. BETAINV(p,alpha,beta) and BETAINVSF(p,alpha,beta) invert lower and directly supplied upper probabilities; p includes 0 and 1.

For example, PRINT BETACDF(.5,2,5) prints 0.890625. Use BETASF for a tiny upper tail rather than subtracting a rounded CDF from one. All five functions share the Rust backend; see the native contract for endpoints, overflow, bounded work and precision limits, and programs/science/beta_distribution.bas for an editable example.

Gamma and chi-square inverse probabilities

GAMMAINV(p,shape,scale) and GAMMAINVSF(p,shape,scale) return lower and directly supplied upper quantiles. CHISQINV(p,df) and CHISQINVSF(p,df) use the same Rust gamma kernel with shape df/2 and scale 2. Shapes, scales and degrees of freedom are positive and finite.

Lower probabilities satisfy 0 <= p < 1; upper probabilities satisfy 0 < p <= 1. The finite endpoint returns zero. Invalid probabilities raise illegal quantity; an interior quantile outside the finite numeric range raises real overflow. Use a directly supplied small upper probability instead of subtracting it from one. These four inverse functions accept scalar arguments or flat numeric lists. Scalars broadcast over a list; multiple lists must have equal lengths. Results are limited to one million elements, and evaluation checks for cancellation between elements. A failing element aborts the whole assignment without changing its destination.

Example: PRINT CHISQINVSF(.05,2) prints approximately 5.991464547107982. The native contract describes work limits, cancellation, logarithmic tails and coordinate precision. programs/science/gamma_quantiles.bas demonstrates reliability thresholds and a variance interval under its stated normal-observation assumptions.

FRAME2DSOLVE and FRAME2DSTIFFNESS

FRAME2DSOLVE(nodes,members,loads,supports) calls the shared Rust static planar frame solver. Nodes are {{x,y},...}. Member rows are {start,end,E,A,I} or {start,end,E,A,I,qx,qy}. All BASIC node and DOF indices are one based; DOFs 1/2/3 mean global x/y translation and counterclockwise rotation. E, A and I are positive Young's modulus, section area and second area moment. Optional uniform loads qx/qy are local axial/transverse force per member length. Local x runs from start to end and local y is 90 degrees counterclockwise.

Loads contain one {Fx,Fy,Mz} row per node. Supports contain {node,dof,prescribed_displacement} rows; omitted DOFs remain free. Repeated constraints are errors. Nonzero support settlements are allowed. Use consistent physical units; the engine does not perform dimensional unit checking.

The result is {displacements,reactions,member_end_forces,nodal_energy,backward_error}. Displacement and reaction matrices have three columns. Member forces have six local components {Fx1,Fy1,M1,Fx2,Fy2,M2} acting on each member. Free-DOF reactions are zero. Energy refers to the nodal interpolation; it excludes within-element deformation energy from distributed loads. FRAME2DSTIFFNESS(nodes,members) returns the unconstrained 3*nodes square matrix for other math operations.

Limits: 2–64 nodes and 1–1,024 members, finite representable binary64 data/results, stable supports on every connected component. Linear elastic, small-displacement, rigid-joint Euler–Bernoulli axial/bending response only; no shear deformation, hinges, nonlinear/dynamic/buckling response or structural design-code checks. Invalid or cancelled calculations leave an assignment destination unchanged.

10 N={{0,0},{2,0}}
20 E={{1,2,200E9,.01,8E-6}}
30 L={{0,0,0},{0,-1000,0}}
40 C={{1,1,0},{1,2,0},{1,3,0}}
50 R=FRAME2DSOLVE(N,E,L,C):D=R(1):F=R(2)
60 PRINT D(2,2):PRINT F(1,2):PRINT F(1,3)

This two-metre cantilever gives tip deflection -0.0016666666667 m, vertical reaction 1,000 N and support moment 2,000 N m. See the native API's planar-frame section for numerical diagnostics and full model limits.

FRAME2DFIELD and FRAME2DENERGY

FRAME2DFIELD(nodes,members,displacements,queries) evaluates the shared Rust continuous beam fields. Nodes and members use the FRAME2DSOLVE format. Displacements contain one global {ux,uy,theta} row per node, normally the first item returned by FRAME2DSOLVE. Each query is {member,fraction}, where member indices are one based and fraction is between 0 (start) and 1 (end). Up to 65,536 queries are accepted; order and repetition are preserved.

Each returned row is: {x,y,ux,uy,u,v,theta,N,V,M,epsilon,kappa}.

Here x/y are undeformed global coordinates; ux/uy are global displacements; u/v are local axial/transverse displacements; theta is counterclockwise slope; N is tensile axial force; V is shear; M is bending moment; epsilon is axial strain; kappa is curvature. The conventions are N=EA*u', V=-EI*v''', M=EI*v'', so N'=-qx, V'=-qy and M'=-V. Uniform-load deformation inside a member is included, even when its nodal displacements are all zero.

FRAME2DENERGY(nodes,members,displacements) returns {nodal_energy,member_load_energy,total_energy}. This supplements the existing FRAME2DSOLVE nodal-energy value with deformation energy between nodes. Both functions evaluate the supplied kinematics and member loads; they do not check that these displacements solve a particular global load/support problem. Invalid input or cancellation leaves the assignment destination unchanged.

10 N={{0,0},{4,0}}
20 E={{1,2,200E9,.01,8E-6,0,-600}}
30 D={{0,0,0},{0,0,0}}
40 F=FRAME2DFIELD(N,E,D,{{1,0},{1,.5},{1,1}})
50 U=FRAME2DENERGY(N,E,D)
60 PRINT F(2,6):PRINT F(2,10):PRINT U(3)

This uniformly loaded four-metre beam has both ends fixed. Its midpoint deflects -0.00025 m, the midpoint bending moment is 400 N m, and the total strain energy is 0.16 J. The nodal-energy term is zero. The same consistent-unit and linear Euler–Bernoulli model limits as FRAME2DSOLVE apply.

documents.title: Units and checked measurements
documents.html:
Use UNITCONVERT(value,from$,to$) for scalar/list/matrix measurements, for example UNITCONVERT({100,250},"mm","m"). Unit strings are case-sensitive and use explicit multiplication, division, integer powers and parentheses.

QTY(value,unit$) creates a dimension-checked measurement. Combine quantities with QADD, QSUB, QMUL, QDIV, QPOW (integer -32..32) or QSQRT; extract a numeric result with QVALUE(quantity,unit$). Example: QVALUE(QMUL(QTY(2,"kg"),QTY(9.81,"m/s^2")),"N") gives 19.62. Adding incompatible dimensions raises an error. Ordinary list arithmetic does not provide these checks.

QPOINT(20,"degC") is a temperature reading; QTY(5,"deltaC") is a difference. Point minus point gives a difference; point plus/minus difference gives a point. Point plus point and multiplicative operations on points fail. QVALUE(point,"K") explicitly supplies a Kelvin scalar to a physical model. UNITCONVERT converts temperature readings directly; use deltaC/deltaF/K for intervals. Offset units degC/degF cannot appear in products or powers.

UNITINFO(unit$) returns {scale,offset,{length,mass,time,current,temperature, amount,luminous_intensity},affine_flag}, where the seven dimension entries are exponents. Quantity packets are {SI_value,{7 dimension exponents},point_flag}; the flag is 0 for a linear quantity and 1 for a temperature point. Packets remain editable BASIC lists; every Q operation revalidates them.

Supported units, prefixes, numerical precision and resource limits are in docs/NATIVE_MATH_API.md, section "Physical units and dimension-checked quantities". Units use SI dimensions; semantic distinctions such as torque versus energy and radians versus dimensionless values need application-level checks. Existing solvers consume numeric arrays; explicitly convert their inputs and outputs. See programs/science/unit_checked_engineering.bas.

## Units and checked measurements

Use `UNITCONVERT(value,from$,to$)` for scalar/list/matrix measurements, for example
`UNITCONVERT({100,250},"mm","m")`. Unit strings are case-sensitive and use
explicit multiplication, division, integer powers and parentheses.

`QTY(value,unit$)` creates a dimension-checked measurement. Combine quantities
with `QADD`, `QSUB`, `QMUL`, `QDIV`, `QPOW` (integer -32..32) or `QSQRT`;
extract a numeric result with `QVALUE(quantity,unit$)`. Example:
`QVALUE(QMUL(QTY(2,"kg"),QTY(9.81,"m/s^2")),"N")` gives 19.62.
Adding incompatible dimensions raises an error. Ordinary list arithmetic
does not provide these checks.

`QPOINT(20,"degC")` is a temperature reading; `QTY(5,"deltaC")` is a difference.
Point minus point gives a difference; point plus/minus difference gives a point.
Point plus point and multiplicative operations on points fail.
`QVALUE(point,"K")` explicitly supplies a Kelvin scalar to a physical model.
`UNITCONVERT` converts temperature readings directly; use `deltaC/deltaF/K`
for intervals. Offset units `degC/degF` cannot appear in products or powers.

`UNITINFO(unit$)` returns `{scale,offset,{length,mass,time,current,temperature,
amount,luminous_intensity},affine_flag}`, where the seven dimension entries
are exponents. Quantity packets are `{SI_value,{7 dimension exponents},point_flag}`;
the flag is 0 for a linear quantity and 1 for a temperature point.
Packets remain editable BASIC lists; every Q operation revalidates them.

Supported units, prefixes, numerical precision and resource limits are in
`docs/NATIVE_MATH_API.md`, section "Physical units and dimension-checked quantities".
Units use SI dimensions; semantic distinctions such as torque versus energy
and radians versus dimensionless values need application-level checks.

documents.title: Propagating measurement uncertainty
documents.html:
UNCERTPROP(J,C) takes an output-by-input Jacobian and an input covariance matrix. It returns {output_covariance,standard_uncertainties} using J*C*TRANSPOSE(J), including correlations. UNCERTSTD(J,C) returns only standard uncertainties and supports finite results even when their squares would overflow or underflow.

QUNCERTPROP(J,C,input_units$,output_units$) and QUNCERTSTD use matrices of quantity packets plus lists of unit strings. Covariance entries require the product of their input dimensions; derivative entries require output/input dimensions. Extract results with QVALUE. Temperature uncertainties are intervals (K/deltaC/deltaF); points and offset units are rejected.

Covariance must be exactly symmetric and positive semidefinite for its stored values; failed or resource-limited proofs raise errors. No automatic tolerance or diagonal adjustment alters it. A reusable Rust model avoids repeated proof. The supplied Jacobian linearizes the model at its nominal values; these are first-order estimates, not nonlinear error bounds or confidence intervals. Check derivative reports before using estimated Jacobians.

## Propagating measurement uncertainty

`UNCERTPROP(J,C)` takes an output-by-input Jacobian and an input covariance
matrix. It returns `{output_covariance,standard_uncertainties}` using
`J*C*TRANSPOSE(J)`, including correlations. `UNCERTSTD(J,C)` returns only
standard uncertainties and supports finite results even when their squares
would overflow or underflow.

`QUNCERTPROP(J,C,input_units$,output_units$)` and `QUNCERTSTD` use matrices of
quantity packets plus lists of unit strings. Covariance entries require the
product of their input dimensions; derivative entries require output/input
dimensions. Extract results with `QVALUE`. Temperature uncertainties are
intervals (`K/deltaC/deltaF`); points and offset units are rejected.

Covariance must be exactly symmetric and positive semidefinite for its stored
values; failed or resource-limited proofs raise errors. No automatic tolerance
or diagonal adjustment alters it. A reusable Rust model avoids repeated proof.
The supplied Jacobian linearizes the model at its nominal values; these are
first-order estimates, not nonlinear error bounds or confidence intervals.
Check derivative reports before using estimated Jacobians.

See `docs/NATIVE_MATH_API.md`, "First-order multivariate measurement uncertainty",
for precision, empty-shape and work contracts. The example
`programs/science/measurement_uncertainty.bas` combines voltage/current
correlation with unit-checked resistance uncertainty.

documents.title: Exact decimal arithmetic
documents.html:
Use decimal strings or exact BASIC INTEGER values with these functions. REAL inputs are rejected so a previously rounded binary fraction cannot silently be treated as exact decimal input. Every $ function returns a decimal string.

FunctionResult
DECIMAL$(value, places [, mode$])Round/pad a decimal to the specified places.
DECADD$(a,b,places[,mode$])Exact sum followed by one rounding.
DECSUB$(a,b,places[,mode$])Exact difference followed by one rounding.
DECMUL$(a,b,places[,mode$])Exact product followed by one rounding.
DECDIV$(a,b,places[,mode$])Exact quotient followed by one rounding; zero divisor fails.
DECFMA$(a,b,c,places[,mode$])Exact a*b+c followed by one rounding.
DECSUM$(values,places[,mode$])Sum a flat list, then round once; empty list gives zero.
DECPOW$(value,exponent,places[,mode$])Integer power, then round once; exponent -1024..1024.
DECCMP(a,b)-1, 0 or 1 for less than, equal or greater than.
DECVAL(value)Explicit approximate REAL conversion.

places is an integer from -1024 through 1024. Positive values specify fractional decimal places; negative values round to tens/hundreds/etc. The default mode$ is "HALF_EVEN". Alternatives are "HALF_UP" and "HALF_DOWN" (nearest with ties away from/toward zero), "UP" and "DOWN" (always away from/toward zero), "CEILING", "FLOOR", and "UNNECESSARY" (error if rounding would discard a nonzero part). Names are case-sensitive.

For example, PRINT DECADD$("0.1","0.2",2) prints 0.30. PRINT DECSUM$({"0.005","0.005"},2) prints 0.01: totals and line items can require different rounding policies, so the program chooses where to round. Positive scale preserves trailing zeros; negative zero becomes positive zero. DECPOW$(0,0,places) gives one, while zero to a negative power fails. DECVAL can lose decimal digits, underflow to zero or reject overflow; DECCMP retains exact decimal comparison.

Inputs are at most 4096 ASCII bytes, with parsed decimal scale -1024..1024. The shared rational backend bounds normalized integers to 4096 bits and arithmetic work to 32 million units per operation. DECSUM$ admits at most one million entries, subject to interpreter storage and arithmetic limits. All calls support cancellation and ordinary failed-assignment recovery. These functions provide arithmetic; currency identity and application-specific financial rules are the program's responsibility. Example: programs/finance/decimal_ledger.bas.

documents.title: Mean tests for independent and paired observations
documents.html:
TTEST1(sample,null_mean[,confidence]) performs a one-sample mean test; TTEST2(first,second[,confidence]) performs Welch's independent unequal-variance test. Their report is {t,df,two_sided_p,lower,upper}. Exact single/pair moments now retain INTEGER inputs and small differences around large common offsets.

TTESTPAIRED(first,second[,confidence[,null_difference]]) uses observations paired by position and exact first-second differences. The null difference defaults to zero. TTESTPOOLED(first,second[,confidence]) is the independent equal-variance procedure; choose it only when that population-variance assumption is appropriate. All confidence levels default to 0.95 and must lie strictly between zero and one. Intervals describe the mean (one sample) or mean difference (other tests), independent of the hypothesized value.

Each sample needs at least two finite INTEGER/REAL values. Lists must be flat, paired lengths must match, and at most one million observations total are accepted (500,000 pairs). Missing values are not silently removed. A zero relevant variance or unrepresentable final report fails atomically; intermediate variance, difference or standard-deviation overflow does not by itself fail. Small confidence levels retain their central coverage instead of rounding it away in subtraction from one. Distribution accuracy and the study's sampling/ normality/independence assumptions still matter; these are numerical procedures, not automatic validation of a study. Example: programs/science/paired_measurements.bas.

documents.title: Updating numeric list items
documents.html:
A scalar list uses one-based item indices: A(2)=7 replaces one item and A(1,2)=9 follows nested lists. A numeric list can replace a selected numeric item or subtree. Existing symbolic siblings remain intact; string replacements through this numeric update interface still fail. Copy assignment (B=A) and BYVAL parameters retain independent values. Scalar lists and DIM arrays remain separate namespaces; DIM-array indexing keeps its existing bounds.

The runtime checks the complete index path, numeric type/depth and retained storage charge before modifying an item. Failure leaves both the list and its storage charge unchanged. During mutation, only the replaced subtree is traversed for payload accounting; unrelated items are not copied. Local, SHARED, STATIC and scalar BYREF destinations follow their existing variable scope. A later default-type declaration still applies to an existing list destination. Expression evaluation borrows visible scalar values; ordinary copy assignment, BYVAL arguments and materialized expression results continue to own their values. Example: programs/science/indexed_measurements.bas.

documents.title: Expression scope and mathematical callback bindings
documents.html:
Local, SHARED, STATIC and scalar BYREF values remain visible under the same scope precedence. The evaluator borrows their retained payloads while reading an expression, including list indexing and dynamic EVAL strings. Mathematical iteration variables and DEF FN parameters use temporary bindings that shadow outer names without copying unrelated variables. Outer values and retained storage charges remain unchanged after a callback returns or fails.

DIM-array element aliases retain scalar snapshots because expression evaluation can mutate the array store by creating implicit arrays. Copies required for normal value assignment, BYVAL parameters and returned results remain part of BASIC value semantics. Scope-map construction depends on visible binding count; nested callback lookup depends on nesting depth, within existing execution limits. This is not a claim that all expressions have constant execution cost.

SADD materializes only explicitly requested strings, one at a time, with the same virtual segment, stable address, NUL-termination and left-to-right error behavior. It does not copy unrelated variables. The public Rust evaluator entry points still accept the existing Variables map. Example: programs/science/scoped_measurements.bas.

Fisher F probabilities and critical values

BASIC functionResult
FPDF(x,df1,df2)Density of the central F law
FCDF(x,df1,df2)Lower cumulative probability
FSF(x,df1,df2)Direct upper-tail probability
FINV(p,df1,df2)Lower critical value
FINVSF(p,df1,df2)Upper critical value from a directly supplied probability

Here df1 is the numerator's degrees of freedom and df2 is the denominator's. Use positive finite degrees with exactly representable positive halves; unrepresentable subnormal halves are rejected. Each argument can be a scalar or a numeric list; supplied lists must have equal length. Scalars broadcast across lists. Empty compatible lists return an empty list. A bad member or cancellation leaves an assignment's previous value intact.

For example, FCDF(1,2,2) is 0.5, FPDF(1,2,2) is 0.25 and FINVSF(.05,2,2) is approximately 19. Use FSF directly for small upper probabilities: subtracting a rounded FCDF result from one can lose them. Negative x is outside support and returns zero density/CDF and unit survival. At x=0 the density overflows when df1<2. FINV(0,df1,df2) and FINVSF(1,df1,df2) return zero; the opposite probability endpoints overflow. An interior critical value beyond the finite numeric range also overflows.

The Rust backend bounds numerical work, supports interruption and reports numerical failure. It estimates probabilities using binary64 arithmetic; it does not certify intervals or implement noncentral F/ANOVA models. See programs/science/variance_comparison.bas for an editable consumer that compares two normal-population sample variances and prints critical values.

Variance and one-way group comparisons

FTEST2(first, second [, confidence [, null_ratio]]) uses independent numeric sample lists. Defaults: confidence=0.95, null_ratio=1. It returns {F, numerator_df, denominator_df, two_sided_p, ratio_lower, ratio_upper}. F is sample-variance(first)/sample-variance(second)/null_ratio; the interval estimates the population variance ratio without dividing by the null ratio. Samples each need at least two values and positive variance; null_ratio must be positive, and 1e-6 <= confidence < 1.

ANOVA1({group1, group2, ...}) returns {F, between_df, within_df, p, eta_squared} for ordinary equal-variance one-way ANOVA. Groups may have unequal lengths; at least two nonempty groups and more observations than groups are required. Singleton or constant individual groups are accepted if combined within-group variation is positive. All-constant groups are rejected. Eta squared is between-group variation divided by total variation.

Both calls accept at most one million observations in total and preserve INTEGER precision before forming the floating-point report. Exact Rust moments prevent spurious overflow/underflow in intermediate variances and sums of squares. Positive F/interval endpoints that cannot be represented above zero fail explicitly; overflowing results fail explicitly. P-values use the rounded F. Invalid calls leave an assigned destination unchanged. Cancellation is supported.

Variance F tests assume independent normal samples; ordinary ANOVA additionally assumes a common within-group variance. These calls do not validate assumptions or provide Welch, repeated-measures, factorial or post-hoc analysis. See programs/science/group_comparisons.bas.

Welch one-way ANOVA

ANOVAWELCH({group1, group2, ...}) returns {F, numerator_df, denominator_df, p} for comparing independent normal populations whose variances may differ. Group sizes may differ, but every group needs at least two numeric observations and positive sample variance. At least two groups are required; combined observations are limited to one million.

Rust supplies the same kernel used by native applications. Exact sample moments retain INTEGER precision and large offsets; bounded high-precision weights keep extreme variance scales usable. Invalid inputs leave the destination unchanged, and cancellation is supported. Unrepresentable positive F values fail explicitly. The p-value uses Welch's approximate F law and rounded F/degrees.

This does not check normality or independence and does not provide post-hoc, repeated-measures or factorial analysis. The equal-variance procedure remains ANOVA1. Editable example: programs/science/unequal_variance_groups.bas.

Adjusting multiple p-values

PADJUST(probabilities [, method [, family_size]]) returns a list of adjusted p-values in the same order. The default method is "HOLM". Accepted names are "NONE", "BONFERRONI", "HOLM", "HOCHBERG", "HOMMEL", "BH" (alias "FDR"), and "BY", ignoring ASCII case and surrounding whitespace. Every probability must be finite and in [0,1]. Empty lists are allowed.

The family size defaults to the list length; an explicit value must be an integer between that length and 1,000,000. Larger sizes conservatively account for omitted tests. The input/output limit is one million probabilities. Hommel additionally limits 2*m*(m-1) to 20 million estimated work units; at most 3,162 supplied probabilities are accepted for this method.

Holm/Bonferroni address family-wise error; BH/BY address false discovery rate. Holm, Bonferroni and BY allow arbitrary dependence between valid tests. Hochberg/Hommel and BH require additional dependence assumptions; see the native API reference. The backend does not infer a suitable family or validate the original tests. The returned values can be compared with the user's chosen significance level. Errors/cancellation leave assigned destinations unchanged. Example combining shared Welch tests with Holm: programs/science/multiple_comparisons.bas.

Range and cancellation in harmonic means

HARMEAN accepts finite signed nonzero observations. Reciprocal integer bounds retain small terms even when enormous positive and negative terms cancel; the result is rounded only after division. Zero observations remain a division error, and a zero reciprocal sum or unrepresentable result raises real overflow. An exceptional ambiguous rounding case uses exact rational arithmetic capped at 16,384 intermediate denominator bits and 50 million estimated bit-work units; exceeding that bound raises illegal quantity. Computation is cancellable.

documents.title: Overview
documents.html:
ModernBASIC uses shared CPU Rust kernels. BASIC source remains an editable consumer. This inventory covers the elementary angle API and identifies what its checkpoint proves; it does not close all general-purpose mathematics or installed-OS/hardware acceptance.

FamilyBASIC / direct RustContract and boundaries
Radian directSIN, COS, TAN; BasicReal and BasicComplex methodsReal arguments are finite binary64 radians. Large-argument reduction is supplied by the target math library. SIN(PI()) operates on the rounded stored PI and is not an exact mathematical axis. Complex arguments use analytic functions; overflowing final components are errors.
Radian inverseASIN, ACOS, ATN; matching real/complex methodsReal asin/acos require [-1,1]; atan accepts finite reals. Results are radians. Explicit complex inputs select principal branches. Real out-of-domain inputs do not silently become complex.
HyperbolicSINH, COSH, TANH, ASINH, ACOSH, ATANH; real/complex methodsReal acosh requires x>=1; real atanh requires -1<x<1. Final overflow is an error. Inverse complex functions use principal branches; zeros are canonicalized, so signed-zero sides of branch cuts are not independently representable.
ReciprocalSEC, CSC, COT, SECH, CSCH, COTH; matching NativeTrigonometry methodsReal only. A computed zero denominator is a division-by-zero error. Radian reciprocal trig retains the rounded-input semantics above. SECH/CSCH use scaled decaying exponentials, preserving representable subnormal tails after sinh/cosh would overflow; final underflow may round to zero. CSCH(0) is a pole.
Explicit phaseSINPI, COSPI, TANPI, SINCOSPI; NativeTrigonometry::{sin_pi,cos_pi,tan_pi,sin_cos_pi}Real x represents PI*x. Reduce the stored x modulo two before multiplying by PI. Exact represented integer/half-integer axes return exact 0 or +/-1; TANPI at half-integers is an error. Pairs are {sine,cosine}.
Explicit degreesSIND, COSD, TAND, SINCOSD; native *_degrees methodsReal degrees, reduced modulo 360 before conversion. Exact represented multiples of 90 retain exact axes even for very large inputs. TAND at odd multiples of 90 is an error. These operations do not change the units of ordinary SIN/COS/TAN.
Normalized sincSINCPI; native sinc_pisin(PI*x)/(PI*x), continuously extended to 1 at zero. Integer nonzero x gives exactly zero. Both batch and streaming windowed-sinc resamplers use the same kernel. The streaming allocation, group-delay, endpoint and rate contracts remain unchanged.
Angular geometryVANGLE3D(a,b), ANGLE2D(a,b); native angle_between3, signed_angle2Nonzero finite length-3 or length-2 vectors. The first returns [0,PI]; the second returns the counterclockwise signed angle in [-PI,PI], with exact opposite vectors at +PI. Exact original-coordinate dot/cross products precede scaled norm/atan2 evaluation. Zero vectors are errors.
Coordinates/conversionsATAN2(y,x), TOPOLAR(x,y), TORECT(r,angle), ROTATE2D(x,y,angle), RAD, DEGRadians for angular coordinates, ordinary componentwise unit conversion for RAD/DEG. Shared NativeTrigonometry and NativeGeometry methods expose native coordinate operations. TOPOLAR/ATAN2 at the canonical zero pair return zero, an API convention rather than a geometrically defined direction.

New explicit phase, reciprocal hyperbolic and vector-angle methods are available at crate root as NativeTrigonometry; they do not require interpreter values. All new BASIC functions require real arguments, including rejection of a complex value whose imaginary part happens to be zero. Exact integer promotion follows the normal BASIC rule: an integer that binary64 cannot preserve is rejected. No phase operation can recover fractions already lost when storing its input. Native zero results follow BASIC's canonical positive-zero convention.

Scalar phase/hyperbolic functions perform fixed work with no allocation. Vector angles use bounded exact-product accumulators for two or three components, then binary64 normalization and atan2; they are not arbitrary-precision angle results. Neither the elementary functions nor these compositions promise correct rounding on every platform. Axis cases are exact; remaining outputs have floating-point error, especially near poles. A tangent sufficiently close to a pole may overflow. The scalar kernels finish in bounded work without an interrupt loop; callers processing long collections remain responsible for cancellation boundaries.

Qualification for the source checkpoint is recorded in output/trigonometry-2026-10-26/validation.json once passing. The independent tools/check-trigonometry.py compares real and off-cut complex elementary functions, subnormal hyperbolic tails, explicit units and nearly parallel/extreme vectors against 400-digit mpmath and exact rational vector products. Rust tests cover poles, nonfinite inputs, exact axes, error recovery and same-rate streaming identity across chunk boundaries. Signal regression and independent spectral checks cover the migrated sinc consumers. The editable programs/science/trigonometry.bas composes an exactly closed profile and periodic sample table; compare its interpreter and standalone output and direct native use.

The complex branch-boundary and angular-coordinate source checkpoints below extend this original evidence. Remaining gates include certified/correctly rounded transcendental bounds where required, broader geometry workflows, other targets and refreshed installed images. Wider algebra/calculus/geometry, engineering and media requirements remain open.

Real ACOSH and native NativeTrigonometry::acosh use a cancellation-free log1p expression near one, shared with BasicReal::acosh. This preserves accuracy for inputs immediately above the real domain endpoint.

## Overview

ModernBASIC uses shared CPU Rust kernels. BASIC source remains an editable
consumer. This inventory covers the elementary angle API and identifies what
its checkpoint proves; it does not close all general-purpose mathematics or
installed-OS/hardware acceptance.

| Family | BASIC / direct Rust | Contract and boundaries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Radian direct | `SIN`, `COS`, `TAN`; `BasicReal` and `BasicComplex` methods | Real arguments are finite binary64 radians. Large-argument reduction is supplied by the target math library. `SIN(PI())` operates on the rounded stored PI and is not an exact mathematical axis. Complex arguments use analytic functions; overflowing final components are errors. |
| Radian inverse | `ASIN`, `ACOS`, `ATN`; matching real/complex methods | Real asin/acos require [-1,1]; atan accepts finite reals. Results are radians. Explicit complex inputs select principal branches. Real out-of-domain inputs do not silently become complex. |
| Hyperbolic | `SINH`, `COSH`, `TANH`, `ASINH`, `ACOSH`, `ATANH`; real/complex methods | Real acosh requires x>=1; real atanh requires -1<x<1. Final overflow is an error. Inverse complex functions use principal branches; zeros are canonicalized, so signed-zero sides of branch cuts are not independently representable. |
| Reciprocal | `SEC`, `CSC`, `COT`, `SECH`, `CSCH`, `COTH`; matching `NativeTrigonometry` methods | Real only. A computed zero denominator is a division-by-zero error. Radian reciprocal trig retains the rounded-input semantics above. SECH/CSCH use scaled decaying exponentials, preserving representable subnormal tails after sinh/cosh would overflow; final underflow may round to zero. CSCH(0) is a pole. |
| Explicit phase | `SINPI`, `COSPI`, `TANPI`, `SINCOSPI`; `NativeTrigonometry::{sin_pi,cos_pi,tan_pi,sin_cos_pi}` | Real x represents PI*x. Reduce the stored x modulo two before multiplying by PI. Exact represented integer/half-integer axes return exact 0 or +/-1; TANPI at half-integers is an error. Pairs are {sine,cosine}. |
| Explicit degrees | `SIND`, `COSD`, `TAND`, `SINCOSD`; native `*_degrees` methods | Real degrees, reduced modulo 360 before conversion. Exact represented multiples of 90 retain exact axes even for very large inputs. TAND at odd multiples of 90 is an error. These operations do not change the units of ordinary SIN/COS/TAN. |
| Normalized sinc | `SINCPI`; native `sinc_pi` | sin(PI*x)/(PI*x), continuously extended to 1 at zero. Integer nonzero x gives exactly zero. Both batch and streaming windowed-sinc resamplers use the same kernel. The streaming allocation, group-delay, endpoint and rate contracts remain unchanged. |
| Angular geometry | `VANGLE3D(a,b)`, `ANGLE2D(a,b)`; native `angle_between3`, `signed_angle2` | Nonzero finite length-3 or length-2 vectors. The first returns [0,PI]; the second returns the counterclockwise signed angle in [-PI,PI], with exact opposite vectors at +PI. Exact original-coordinate dot/cross products precede scaled norm/atan2 evaluation. Zero vectors are errors. |
| Coordinates/conversions | `ATAN2(y,x)`, `TOPOLAR(x,y)`, `TORECT(r,angle)`, `ROTATE2D(x,y,angle)`, `RAD`, `DEG` | Radians for angular coordinates, ordinary componentwise unit conversion for RAD/DEG. Shared NativeTrigonometry and NativeGeometry methods expose native coordinate operations. TOPOLAR/ATAN2 at the canonical zero pair return zero, an API convention rather than a geometrically defined direction. |

New explicit phase, reciprocal hyperbolic and vector-angle methods are available
at crate root as `NativeTrigonometry`; they do not require interpreter values.
All new BASIC functions require real arguments, including rejection of a complex
value whose imaginary part happens to be zero. Exact integer promotion follows
the normal BASIC rule: an integer that binary64 cannot preserve is rejected.
No phase operation can recover fractions already lost when storing its input.
Native zero results follow BASIC's canonical positive-zero convention.

Scalar phase/hyperbolic functions perform fixed work with no allocation. Vector
angles use bounded exact-product accumulators for two or three components, then
binary64 normalization and atan2; they are not arbitrary-precision angle results.
Neither the elementary functions nor these compositions promise correct rounding
on every platform. Axis cases are exact; remaining outputs have floating-point
error, especially near poles. A tangent sufficiently close to a pole may overflow.
The scalar kernels finish in bounded work without an interrupt loop; callers
processing long collections remain responsible for cancellation boundaries.

Qualification for the source checkpoint is recorded in
`output/trigonometry-2026-10-26/validation.json` once passing. The independent
`tools/check-trigonometry.py` compares real and off-cut complex elementary
functions, subnormal hyperbolic tails, explicit units and nearly parallel/extreme
vectors against 400-digit mpmath and exact rational vector products. Rust tests
cover poles, nonfinite inputs, exact axes, error recovery and same-rate streaming
identity across chunk boundaries. Signal regression and independent spectral
checks cover the migrated sinc consumers. The editable
`programs/science/trigonometry.bas` composes an exactly closed profile and periodic
sample table; compare its interpreter and standalone output and direct native use.

The complex branch-boundary and angular-coordinate source checkpoints below
extend this original evidence. Remaining gates include certified/correctly rounded
transcendental bounds where required, broader geometry workflows, other targets
and refreshed installed images. Wider algebra/calculus/geometry, engineering
and media requirements remain open.

Real `ACOSH` and native `NativeTrigonometry::acosh` use a cancellation-free
`log1p` expression near one, shared with `BasicReal::acosh`. This preserves
accuracy for inputs immediately above the real domain endpoint.

Real `ATANH`, `BasicReal::atanh` and `NativeTrigonometry::atanh` share an odd-
symmetric `log1p` path, preserving tiny inputs and accuracy near both +/-1
boundaries. Inputs on or beyond those real boundaries remain errors.

documents.title: Complex elementary scaling and branch boundaries
documents.html:
The shared BasicComplex methods supply SIN/COS/TAN, SINH/COSH/TANH, their six inverses, EXP, LOG and SQR to BASIC and native Rust callers. Results contain finite binary64 components; a representable small component is not intentionally discarded merely because the other component is large.

Large exponential products split the exponent by exact factors of two or four and multiply the trigonometric factor before final expansion. When the unscaled hyperbolic value fits, its ordinary direct value is used, avoiding amplification of subnormal rounding by premature splitting. Overflowing hyperbolic products apply their factor of one half after expansion. This avoids the loss from subtracting rounded LOG(2) from a large argument or adding LOG of a tiny factor to it. TAN/TANH delay multiplication of the two decaying exponential factors to retain representable subnormal tails. Near the real axis, complex ATN uses its first-order imaginary expression for extremely small inputs to avoid double rounding a nonzero component to zero. These are binary64 accuracy improvements, not correctly-rounded or certified transcendental functions.

BASIC canonicalizes both signs of zero. Consequently exact cuts select these documented sides; supply a nonzero displacement to select the other side:

FunctionCut and canonical approachExample
ASIN, ACOSReal axis outside [-1,1], from positive imaginary valuesASIN(COMPLEX(2,0)) has positive imaginary part; ACOS(COMPLEX(2,0)) has negative imaginary part.
ATANHReal axis outside [-1,1], from positive imaginary valuesATANH(COMPLEX(2,0)) has imaginary part PI/2. The endpoints +/-1 are errors.
ACOSHReal axis below 1, from positive imaginary valuesACOSH(COMPLEX(-2,0)) has imaginary part PI.
ATNImaginary axis beyond +/-I, from positive real valuesATN(COMPLEX(0,2)) has real part PI/2. The endpoints +/-I are errors.
ASINHImaginary axis beyond +/-I, from positive real valuesASINH(COMPLEX(0,2)) has positive real part and imaginary part PI/2.
LOG, SQRNegative real axis, from positive imaginary valuesLOG(COMPLEX(-1,0)) = I*PI; SQR(COMPLEX(-1,0)) = I. LOG(0) is an error.

Principal inverse identities apply only within their branches. Conjugation or odd symmetry at an exact cut must account for canonical zero: replacing a positive-zero approach with its mathematical negative-zero counterpart is not representable in this BASIC value type. Real arguments continue to use real domains; an out-of-domain real input does not automatically become complex.

The scalar methods use fixed work and no heap allocation. Callers running long native loops remain responsible for cancellation boundaries. BASIC retains its normal execution limits and error recovery. True result overflow is an error; underflow may round to zero. Target libm still supplies elementary real exponentials, logarithms and trigonometric reduction.

The expanded independent checker is tools/check-complex-elementary.py. Its 800-digit references cover both cut sides, branch endpoints, extreme/disparate components, subnormal values, true poles and overflow. The checkpoint in output/complex-elementary-2026-10-27 includes reproduced failures, native/BASIC regressions, resource measurements and interpreter/export parity. This qualification does not close certified-transcendental, other-target, installed image or broader mathematics/workflow requirements.

documents.title: Angular coordinates and graphics phase
documents.html:
BASIC ROTATE2D(x,y,radians), TOPOLAR(x,y), TORECT(radius,radians), ATAN2(y,x), RAD(degrees) and DEG(radians) share checked Rust native operations:

  • NativeGeometry::rotate_2d([x,y],radians) and rotate_2d_degrees([x,y],degrees) return counterclockwise rotated coordinates.
  • NativeGeometry::to_polar([x,y]) returns [radius,angle], with a nonnegative radius and principal radian angle in [-PI,PI]. The origin is [0,0].
  • NativeGeometry::to_rectangular(radius,radians) preserves the existing BASIC signed-radius convention: a negative radius reverses both coordinates.
  • NativeTrigonometry::sin_cos_radians, atan2, to_radians and to_degrees expose the corresponding scalar kernels. Argument order for atan2 is (y,x).

Native and BASIC zeros are canonical: the negative x axis selects +PI, including a native negative-zero y input. Non-finite native points/radii are rejected; non-finite angles and result overflow are errors. Genuine underflow may round to zero. RAD/DEG convert the angle magnitude without wrapping. For large degree phases and exact represented 90-degree axes, use SINCOSD/SIND/COSD or the native degree rotation directly; converting to radians first can discard phase.

ROTATE2D combines the original-coordinate products in a bounded exact accumulator, then rounds each component once. The coefficients remain target-libm binary64 sine/cosine values; their uncertainty can dominate a nearly cancelled result. This is not a guarantee of correctly rounded transcendental rotation, nor can a polar round trip recover coordinate information already lost to binary64 rounding.

The artist renderer's degree ROTATE, ARC endpoints, bitmap warp rotations and SVG elliptical-arc axis rotations reuse the same degree phase reduction. BASIC DRAW uses the checked degree rotation with its existing clockwise-screen convention and existing angle limits. Large represented phases therefore agree with their degree remainders, and quarter-turn cursor moves retain exact axes. Other affine/path/raster calculations retain their existing approximation limits.

These scalar kernels have bounded stack/work use and no per-call heap allocation. Native callers arrange cancellation boundaries in long loops; normal BASIC execution retains its interpreter cancellation boundaries. There is no new thread pool, GPU dependency or optional provider requirement.

Independent reference checks are registered as angular-coordinates in tools/qualify-math.py. Evidence: output/angular-coordinates-2026-10-27. The wider geometry/trigonometry inventory and installed OS/hardware workflows remain separate acceptance requirements.

documents.title: Reciprocal functions and consolidated source audit
documents.html:
SEC, CSC, COT and COTH now call NativeTrigonometry::sec, csc, cot and coth, respectively. Together with the existing sech and csch methods, all six real reciprocal functions have shared typed Rust/BASIC entry points. Arguments are finite reals; the first three use radians. COTH uses 1/TANH(x), avoiding large SINH/COSH intermediates. Poles with a computed zero denominator report division by zero; an overflowing final reciprocal reports a range error. Signed zero is canonical, and complex arguments remain outside these real-only function contracts. Native non-finite inputs are rejected before evaluation.

The represented floating value PI/2 is not exact mathematical pi/2. Therefore SEC(PI()/2) is a large finite value rather than an exact-phase pole. TANPI(.5) and TAND(90) do represent exact phase poles and report division by zero. This distinction is preserved consistently between BASIC and direct native calls. Close to a pole, the input's uncertainty can dominate the answer; reciprocal evaluation cannot restore lost phase information.

The source audit covers all 36 named BASIC angle operations below. Independent suites exercise numerical behavior, while the contract tests exercise the same public native/BASIC paths. BasicReal/BasicComplex are checked native value types; no interpreter instance is needed by Rust consumers.

FamilyBASIC operationsCurrent reference and integration evidence
Real/complex direct and inverseSIN, COS, TAN, ASIN, ACOS, ATNtrigonometry and complex-elementary reference suites; reciprocal_trig_tests checks every native/BASIC entry; complex_elementary_tests checks branch boundaries and recovery
Real/complex hyperbolic and inverseSINH, COSH, TANH, ASINH, ACOSH, ATANHtrigonometry and complex-elementary suites; near-one, both-domain-boundary, subnormal and branch-cut tests
Real reciprocalsSEC, CSC, COT, SECH, CSCH, COTHreciprocal-trig at 800 digits, including adjacent represented pole/range values; reciprocal_trig_tests
PI and degree phaseSINPI, COSPI, TANPI, SINCOSPI, SIND, COSD, TAND, SINCOSDtrigonometry suite; exact axes, neighboring poles, native/BASIC parity
Normalized sinc and product phaseSINCPI, SINCOSPHASEtrigonometry and phase-waveforms suites; streaming sinc chunk tests and circuit-source phase tests
Vector anglesANGLE2D, VANGLE3Dexact rational dot/cross plus high-precision angular reference; near-parallel, extreme-scale and zero-vector tests
Coordinates and unitsATAN2, TOPOLAR, TORECT, ROTATE2D, RAD, DEGangular-coordinates suite; native/BASIC parity, exact rotation products, polar conventions, renderer pixels and DRAW cursor tests

Scalar calls use fixed work and no per-call heap allocation or thread pool. Native loops provide their own cancellation boundaries; BASIC retains normal statement-level cancellation and failed-assignment preservation. The editable programs/science/reciprocal_trig.bas composes ray geometry, reciprocal identities, explicit degrees and complex trigonometry. Qualification includes independent references, direct native CPU use, recovery, and identical interpreted/exported output without a per-program runtime build cache.

Current source audit evidence requires a passing receipt at output/reciprocal-trig-2026-10-27/validation.json and its inventory.json. The source inventory is not installed-system acceptance. Certified transcendental bounds, other CPU/architecture math libraries, refreshed OS images and device/ application acceptance remain open under TASKS.md. Binary64/libm limits and unsupported complex reciprocal conveniences remain explicit; all wider algebra, calculus, geometry, physics, engineering, media and analytics requirements persist.

The matrix shares storage, validation and numerical kernels with the sparse/physics backend. This document covers direct Rust matrix APIs and their shared numerical kernels. ## Overview

Use `modernbasic::NativeCsrMatrix` through the integrated ModernBASIC Rust crate
and its current Linux build dependencies. The matrix shares storage, validation
and numerical kernels with the sparse/physics backend. This document covers direct Rust matrix APIs and their shared numerical kernels.
BASIC users also have the separate optimization frontends `LPSOLVE`, `MIPSOLVE`
and the currently admitted continuous convex-QP candidate API `QPSOLVE`; see
[Native LP/MIP and shared Rust application APIs](#native-lpmip-and-shared-rust-application-apis).

documents.title: Shared CPU quaternion rotations
documents.html: The crate root exports NativeQuaternion for Rust graphics, animation and physics consumers. from_components([w,x,y,z]) validates finite values; from_axis_angle(axis, angle) constructs a unit rotation from a nonzero axis and radians. multiply is the raw Hamilton product, with composition order matching BASIC QUATMUL. rotate_vector and rotation_matrix divide original-input expressions by the exact squared norm, rounding each result once. slerp(rhs, amount) performs shortest-arc spherical interpolation for amount in [0,1]; antipodal inputs are sign-aligned and nearly parallel inputs use normalized linear interpolation. These methods are the same kernels used by BASIC QUATAXIS, QUATMUL, QUATROTATE, ROTATE3D and QUATSLERP, so Rust backends can reuse the rotation behavior without constructing interpreter values.
documents.text:
## Shared CPU quaternion rotations

The crate root exports `NativeQuaternion` for Rust graphics, animation and
physics consumers. `from_components([w,x,y,z])` validates finite values;
`from_axis_angle(axis, angle)` constructs a unit rotation from a nonzero axis
and radians. `multiply` is the raw Hamilton product, with composition order
matching BASIC `QUATMUL`. `rotate_vector` and `rotation_matrix` divide original-input expressions by the
exact squared norm, rounding each result once. `slerp(rhs, amount)` performs
shortest-arc spherical interpolation for `amount` in `[0,1]`; antipodal inputs
are sign-aligned and nearly parallel inputs use normalized linear
interpolation. These methods are the same kernels used by BASIC `QUATAXIS`,
`QUATMUL`, `QUATROTATE`, `ROTATE3D` and `QUATSLERP`, so Rust backends can reuse
the rotation behavior without constructing interpreter values.

documents.title: Reproducible CPU random streams
documents.html: modernbasic::random::BasicRng is the deterministic generator used by BASIC RND, RAND, RANDINT, RANDNORM, and RANDBIN. Rust consumers can call snapshot_text() and restore_text() to save and resume an exact stream position, including the cached value used by RND(0). The MBRNG1 snapshot is fixed-format, checksummed and data-only; restore validates the complete record before changing state. BASIC exposes the same operation as RNGSTATE$() and RNGRESTORE(checkpoint$). This is reproducibility state, not an entropy source or a cryptographic random generator, and it does not checkpoint application or scheduler state.
documents.text:
## Reproducible CPU random streams

`modernbasic::random::BasicRng` is the deterministic generator used by BASIC
`RND`, `RAND`, `RANDINT`, `RANDNORM`, and `RANDBIN`. Rust consumers can call
`snapshot_text()` and `restore_text()` to save and resume an exact stream
position, including the cached value used by `RND(0)`. The `MBRNG1` snapshot is
fixed-format, checksummed and data-only; restore validates the complete record
before changing state. BASIC exposes the same operation as `RNGSTATE$()` and
`RNGRESTORE(checkpoint$)`. This is reproducibility state, not an entropy source
or a cryptographic random generator, and it does not checkpoint application or
scheduler state.

documents.title: CPU residual differential-algebraic systems
documents.html:
NativeIda::integrate exposes the same serial CPU SUNDIALS IDA kernel as BASIC IDASOLVE to Rust consumers. Supply strictly monotone output times, consistent initial state and derivative vectors, and one NativeIdaVariableKind for each state component. The residual closure evaluates F(t,y,y') = 0 and returns one finite residual per component. NativeIdaOptions carries relative and component-wise absolute tolerances, maximum steps, maximum step size, and either a dense solver (up to 256 states), SPGMR (up to 4,096 states, Krylov dimension up to 256), or provider-dependent KLU (up to 1,024 states). The typed result contains requested time/state samples and solver work diagnostics. Errors, cancellation, and work-limit failures return no partial trajectory. NativeIda::consistent_initial_conditions calls IDA's index-one initialization to correct algebraic state and differential derivative components from nearby guesses; a second time establishes the integration direction. Results report residual, preconditioner, and operator callback counts. The direct Rust API is also qualified on stiff Robertson chemistry in both dense analytic-Jacobian and SPGMR/J-times modes, checking the algebraic mass constraint and the final state against the independent SciPy Radau/BDF reference recorded for the same DAE workload. NativeIda::integrate_hybrid supports up to 64 scalar root guards with per-guard Any/Rising/Falling filters, one-based reset callbacks, bounded event counts, and state projection back onto index-one constraints. Its typed event records preserve root times and states before and after reset; the trajectory contains both root states. Direct Rust forward sensitivity integration is available through NativeIda::integrate_variational and NativeIda::integrate_variational_hybrid; the latter combines IDASens trajectory sensitivities with event-time and reset saltation derivatives. NativeIda::integrate_hybrid_with_jacobian composes those event/reset semantics with a dense analytic Newton matrix, including consistency restoration after each reset. NativeIda::integrate_hybrid_with_jacobian_times_and_preconditioner provides the corresponding SPGMR path for larger systems, keeping analytic matrix-free products and inverse-diagonal setup active across resets. NativeIda::integrate_hybrid_with_sparse_jacobian combines hybrid resets with fixed-pattern CSR/KLU matrices, including the post-reset consistency solve. NativeIda::integrate_with_jacobian_times_and_preconditioner combines the analytic SPGMR operator with a checked inverse-diagonal setup callback. NativeIda::integrate_with_sparse_jacobian accepts a fixed-pattern canonical CSR matrix from NativeCsrMatrix and uses the CPU KLU direct solver when that provider is available. For dense solves, NativeIda::integrate_with_jacobian accepts a Rust callback returning the combined Newton matrix dF/dy + c_j dF/dy'; it validates finite square matrices and shares the same bounded IDA kernel. For larger matrix-free systems, NativeIda::integrate_with_jacobian_times supplies that Newton operator to SPGMR as a direct product callback without materializing a matrix.

Native IDA parameter sensitivity estimates

NativeIda::integrate_parametric accepts an F(t,y,y',p) residual closure and returns the base trajectory plus parameter sensitivities. It computes symmetric finite differences at relative steps h and h/2, then applies Richardson extrapolation. Up to eight parameters are accepted; one base solve and four perturbed solves per parameter are performed. The result includes total steps, residual evaluations and per-sample Richardson difference estimates. Those estimates cover finite-difference truncation only, not the IDA trajectory error.

NativeIdaSensitivityOptions supports optional initial-state and initial- derivative sensitivities, which are included when each perturbed initial-value problem is formed. Its default relative perturbation is 1e-3; the supported range is (0,0.1]. The residual callback must be deterministic, and symmetric perturbations must remain inside its valid parameter domain. Dense and SPGMR solves are supported. This finite-difference API works with the default IDA provider and does not claim a variational IDASens solve or support the IDA KLU path. Sensitivity values are estimates, not certified error bounds. Independent analytic qualification is recorded in the validation record.

NativeIda::integrate_variational uses SUNDIALS IDASens to evolve forward sensitivity equations while sharing one DAE solve. It accepts up to eight parameters, optional initial state and derivative sensitivities, and separate sensitivity tolerances. Dense and SPGMR use integrate_variational; fixed-pattern CSR/KLU uses integrate_variational_with_sparse_jacobian. Build the optional CPU provider with tools/prepare-sundials.py --with-idas (combine with --with-klu to retain sparse capability); the default provider remains unchanged and returns a clear availability error for this API. Variational hybrid/event- time propagation uses integrate_variational_hybrid; it computes the smooth trajectory with IDASens and estimates event/reset map derivatives with bounded centered differences and Richardson refinement. Variational Dense and SPGMR hybrid cases pass closed-form one- and three-parameter checks. SPGMR's initial step is seeded from the requested interval and sensitivity tolerances, including after reset restarts. For hybrid reset projection up to 256 states, a bounded dense direct solve is used only to restore algebraic consistency; the configured SPGMR solver is restored for the subsequent trajectory. Larger SPGMR reset projections, KLU hybrid sensitivities, other-target packaging and broader scientific DAE qualification remain open. One- and two-parameter analytic exponential systems, including the KLU path, pass against the IDAS provider in tests/native_ida_sensitivity_tests.rs.

NativeIda::integrate_hybrid_parametric accepts a NativeIdaHybridSensitivityRequest containing the output grid, fixed initial conditions, parameters, hybrid solver limits and relative perturbation. It estimates sensitivities of localized IDA event times and pre-reset/post-reset states. It uses one base integration and four perturbed integrations per parameter, with centered differences at h and h/2 and Richardson extrapolation. The result reports event sensitivities, finite-difference error estimates and aggregate solver work. It accepts at most eight parameters and is bounded by the native IDA per-solve limits plus shared work and output-size caps. Initial state and derivative are held fixed while parameters vary. Every perturbed solve must preserve the base event count and ordered event indices; changes in event topology fail rather than return a local derivative across a discontinuity. The estimates exclude trajectory error from IDA tolerances and do not propagate sensitivity through the post-event trajectory. Dense and SPGMR solvers are supported; sparse KLU hybrid solves are not. This is a finite-difference estimator, not variational IDASens saltation analysis. tests/native_ida_api_tests.rs checks event-time and reset-state sensitivities against a closed-form parameterized threshold-and-reset DAE.

Editable BASIC code can call the finite-difference estimator with IDAHYBRIDSENS. IDAHYBRIDVAR exposes the variational hybrid API: the BASIC residual/event/reset callbacks pass parameters explicitly, IDASens evolves smooth-trajectory derivatives, and bounded centered differences with Richardson refinement linearize the event and reset maps. Its result contains trajectory sensitivities and event-time/pre/post-reset sensitivities with error estimates. Dense and unpreconditioned SPGMR are available; KLU and user Jacobian callbacks remain unavailable through these hybrid sensitivity statements. The language reference and tests/ida_tests.rs document and verify the callback and result shapes against the closed-form rate/threshold/reset DAE.

The typed Rust KLU path has been qualified at its current 1,024-state amd64 provider limit on a periodic heat DAE with a fixed three-entry-per-row matrix. The trajectory is compared at four times with the exact discrete Fourier-mode decay reference. This workload validates the current provider cap; it does not establish KLU support on other targets or for larger systems. See the reproducible qualification record.

documents.title: CPU dense real matrices
documents.html:
The crate root exports NativeRealMatrix, NativeRealSolveResult, NativeRealMultiSolveResult, NativeRealLuFactor, NativeRealLeastSquaresResult, NativeRealEigenResult, NativeRealMatrixDiagnostics, NativeRealQrResult and NativeRealSvdResult for direct Rust consumers. Construct a finite row-major matrix with NativeRealMatrix::new(rows,columns,values). Storage is capped at one million values; explicit zero-axis shapes are retained. transpose() and multiply() return new typed matrices, and multiplication uses the checked Rust kernel shared with BASIC MATMUL (BLAS when available, bounded Rust fallback otherwise).

NativeRealStatistics provides typed percentile and median with the same linear-interpolation convention as BASIC PERCENTILE/MEDIAN, plus mean, sample/population variance, sample/population standard_deviation, root_mean_square, sample/population covariance, correlation, and simple linear_regression over finite slices. Quantile calls accept nonempty slices of at most one million finite binary64 samples and a percentile in [0,100]; they reject invalid inputs and nonfinite interpolated results. skewness and kurtosis expose the same bias-corrected sample standardized moments as BASIC SKEWNESS and KURTOSIS; they require at least three and four samples respectively. linear_regression returns NativeRealLinearRegression with slope, intercept, correlation and R-squared. These share kernels with BASIC list statistics, check sample-size and finite-result limits, and do not construct interpreter values. Variance/deviation use exact first/second moments with one final rounding, also shared with typed grouped/window statistics. The native slice interface takes f64; BASIC and typed INTEGER tables retain all integer bits. Higher moments retain their scale-normalized kernels; paired moments now use exact accumulation. A variance may overflow even when its standard deviation remains representable; callers can request the latter directly. NativeRealStatistics::covariance_matrix(&observations, sample) and correlation_matrix(&observations) accept a row-major NativeRealMatrix with observations in rows and variables in columns, returning square matrices in variable order. They use the same exact paired-moment kernels as BASIC COVMATRIX and CORRMATRIX, accumulate each symmetric pair once, and reject empty/ragged input, non-finite values, too few observations and constant variables for correlation. Covariance supports sample (sample=true) or population denominators. The BASIC COVMATRIX(matrix [, sampleFlag]) defaults to sample covariance; flag 1 selects sample and 0 population covariance. CORRMATRIX(matrix) returns Pearson correlations and requires at least two observations with nonzero variance in every variable. Matrix output is bounded by the shared one-million-element matrix cap, and the operation has a 50-million observation-variable-pair work limit with cancellation checkpoints.

NativeRealStatistics::multiple_regression and BASIC MULTIREG(predictors, responses [, interceptFlag]) fit several predictors with the same bounded CPU SVD least-squares kernel as NativeRealMatrix::least_squares/LSTSQ. The default flag 1 adds an intercept; 0 omits it. The BASIC result is {coefficients,intercept,rank,residualNorm,normalResidualNorm}. Coefficients follow predictor-column order. Rank uses the shared relative singular-value cutoff, and deficient or underdetermined designs return a minimum-norm fit; rank is a numerical diagnostic, not an exact independence certificate. Residual norms are recomputed against the fitted design and response. This is least squares, not a statistical inference package: standard errors, hypothesis tests and automatic categorical encoding are not provided.

NativeRealStatistics::logistic_regression and BASIC LOGITREG share the same bounded damped-Newton binary classifier. Rust callers pass row-observation predictors, finite exact 0/1 responses, an intercept flag, nonnegative L2 penalty, iteration limit and positive tolerance. Each predictor is scaled by its actual maximum absolute value (including values below one; an all-zero column uses scale one), slopes are converted back on return, and the penalty is applied to scaled slopes only. NativeRealLogisticRegression reports numerical rank, accepted iterations, convergence status, unregularized mean negative log-likelihood and regularized gradient infinity norm. Rank and convergence are numerical diagnostics rather than statistical certificates. Work is estimated before fitting and capped at 50 million operations; at most 128 predictor columns and 100 iterations are accepted. The solver requires both response classes and checks cancellation while building and evaluating the model.

documents.title: Gamma and chi-square probabilities
documents.html:
The crate-root NativeGammaDistribution is an immutable CPU distribution with validated positive, finite parameters. Construct it with new(shape, scale) or chi_square(degrees_of_freedom); the latter preserves the logarithmic shape even when halving a subnormal degree of freedom would round to zero. Call pdf(x), cdf(x), survival(x), or probabilities(x) for [lower_tail, upper_tail] from one evaluation. BASIC GAMMAPDF, GAMMACDF, GAMMASF, CHISQPDF, CHISQCDF and CHISQSF call this same kernel. quantile(p) and inverse_survival(p) add lower and directly supplied upper inverses, exposed through BASIC GAMMAINV(p,shape,scale), GAMMAINVSF(p,shape,scale), CHISQINV(p,df) and CHISQINVSF(p,df). Successful scalar evaluations allocate no heap storage and reuse the native cancellation checkpoint mechanism.

Samples must be finite. Nonpositive samples follow the support and zero-density rules in the language reference. The singular density at zero for shape below one, or an unrepresentable finite density, returns Error::RealOverflow. Series and continued fractions stop after at most 10,000 iterations with an error if they do not converge. Large-shape tails use a two-term uniform asymptotic expansion. Scaled logarithms and direct survival evaluation preserve representable tails and densities that would be lost by naive division, subtraction, or subtracting large log-gamma values. Results are binary64 estimates, with no promise of correctly rounded or exhaustive-domain accuracy.

tools/check-gamma-accuracy.py compares the BASIC API with SciPy, analytic identities, Decimal density references and independent integration of the gamma density. The native/BASIC parity and cancellation tests are in tests/probability_tests.rs. Inverse checks are in tests/gamma_quantile_tests.rs and tools/check-gamma-quantiles.py. Lower inverses accept 0 <= p < 1, and upper inverses accept 0 < p <= 1; the finite support endpoint returns zero. Other probability values raise illegal quantity; nonfinite inputs raise real overflow. An interior quantile beyond the finite binary64 coordinate range also raises real overflow.

Inversion compares logarithmic tails, including directly supplied upper probabilities, and searches positive binary64 coordinate order. It uses at most 63 bisections plus one range check, each with the existing 10,000-iteration forward bound. Entry points, search steps and iterative kernels check interrupts. A successful search returns a representable endpoint of the adjacent coordinate bracket; the shape-one case shares the existing exponential/Weibull inverse. Coordinate rounding can dominate probability round-trip error for concentrated laws, extremely small scales and underflowed quantiles. These numerical brackets are not certified interval bounds.

Gamma inverse host qualification passed; evidence is in output/gamma-quantiles-2026-10-27. Random sampling, fitting and installed-system/ other-target application acceptance remain separate work.

documents.title: Student's t probabilities
documents.html:
NativeStudentT::pdf(t,df), cdf(t,df), survival(t,df), quantile(p,df) and inverse_survival(p,df) expose the shared CPU Student's t distribution. BASIC TPDF, TCDF, TSF, TINV and TINVSF call these kernels. Degrees of freedom accept every finite positive binary64 value. Quantiles require 0 < p < 1; nonfinite probabilities retain the existing illegal-quantity error. Finite t values are required, and invalid degrees/nonfinite samples raise errors.

The shared kernel evaluates central mass directly near zero and retains extreme tails in logarithmic form. Large degrees reuse the bounded CDFLIB-derived beta kernel with both reduced coordinates retained; very large degrees near the center use the normal limit within binary64 precision. Density normalization uses stable beta/log-gamma formulas and a bounded Stirling expansion. These are numerical estimates, without a correct-rounding or interval guarantee.

Inverse searches compare central mass near the median and logarithmic tails elsewhere. One range check plus at most 63 positive-coordinate bisections covers the full finite binary64 range. Each forward evaluation has an iteration/work limit and cancellation checks. Unrepresentable quantiles raise real overflow. Upper inverses consume the supplied upper probability directly. Use 2*survival(abs(t),df) for a two-sided p-value.

All five scalar BASIC APIs also accept flat numeric lists with scalar broadcasting and matching list lengths, capped at one million results. Evaluation checks for cancellation between elements and preserves the destination on any error. Sample-based t-test APIs still consume entire lists.

Host qualification passed; evidence is in output/student-t-complete-2026-10-27. tools/check-student-t-accuracy.py preserves the earlier center/extreme-tail coverage; tools/check-student-t-distribution.py adds high-precision density, direct-tail and independently bracketed inverse checks across the expanded range. Sampling/fitting, broader inference and installed/other-target acceptance remain separate requirements.

NativeStudentT::one_sample_test(values, hypothesized_mean, confidence_level) reuses the shared exact sample-moment kernel and returns NativeOneSampleTTest { t_statistic, degrees_of_freedom, two_sided_p_value, confidence_interval }. It requires at least two finite, nonconstant samples and a confidence level strictly between zero and one. BASIC TTEST1(sample,mu [,confidence]) returns those fields as {t,df,p,lower,upper}, defaulting to 95% confidence. The two-sided probability is computed directly from the smaller tail.
