Rectangular matrices also support reduced qr() and svd() factors. QR accepts rank deficiency but is unpivoted, so its diagonal is not a rank certificate. SVD uses Linux LP64 LAPACK, returns descending singular values and thin U/Vᵀ factors, and represents numerical rank deficiency with zero or near-zero values rather than an exact rank claim.

Square matrices support determinant(), inverse() and solve(rhs). Work and cancellation limits are inherited from those kernels. Inputs and results are finite binary64; these solve methods do not provide a forward-error guarantee. Sparse matrices remain separate APIs.

For repeated solves, NativeRealMatrix::factor_lu() returns an owned NativeRealLuFactor. Its solve(rhs) method handles vectors and solve_many accepts a NativeRealMatrix whose columns are right-hand sides. Both return fresh residual norms against the retained original matrix; factors expose their packed row-major coefficients and zero-based row swaps for inspection. Singular factorizations and malformed RHS shapes return errors. The multiple-RHS kernel uses one CPU LAPACK factorization/solve path and is also available from standalone Rust consumers without constructing interpreter values.

It supports rectangular, rank-deficient and underdetermined matrices, returning the minimum-norm solution, numerical rank, fit residual and normal-residual norm. Both residuals are recomputed against the original input. The reported rank is an SVD threshold estimate, not an exact certificate.

For a matrix B containing several RHS columns, call NativeRealMatrix::least_squares_many(&B, rcond). Input and output matrices respect the one-million-element cap; the added projections/residual calculations respect the native one-billion-operation bound and cancellation checkpoints. A zero-column RHS matrix is rejected. weighted_least_squares_many(&B, weights, rcond) accepts one finite nonnegative weight per observation and requires at least one positive weight. It scales each row by sqrt(weight/maxWeight) through separate square roots to avoid premature ratio underflow, so multiplying all weights by a common positive factor leaves the fit unchanged. Reported residuals use normalized weights; weight_scale is the maximum input weight, so the original weighted residual norm is fit_norm * sqrt(weight_scale) when representable; normal-residual norms use normal_norm * weight_scale. BASIC exposes vector and matrix-response forms as WLSTSQ(A,b,weights[,rcond]) and WLSTSQM(A,B,weights[,rcond]); zero weights exclude observations.

cholesky() returns a lower factor L for symmetric positive-definite A=L Lᵀ. symmetric_eigen() returns ascending eigenvalues and an eigenvector matrix whose columns correspond to those values. Both methods share the checked Linux CPU LAPACK kernels behind BASIC CHOLESKY and EIGH, preserve explicit empty square shapes, and reject nonsquare or invalid symmetry/definiteness domains. Repeated eigenvalues can yield different valid orthonormal bases.

solve_symmetric_indefinite(rhs) solves a square symmetric matrix against a shape-aware NativeRealMatrix of RHS columns and returns NativeRealMultiSolveResult. It uses the same LAPACK Bunch–Kaufman 1-by-1/2-by-2 pivoting as BASIC SYMSOLVE, then recomputes one residual norm per column from the original matrix and RHS. The existing crate-root solve_symmetric_indefinite(&[Vec<f64>], &[Vec<f64>]) remains available when plain nested vectors are preferable.

diagnostics(relative_cutoff) returns NativeRealMatrixDiagnostics using the same scale-normalized SVD behind BASIC MATRANK, RCOND and COND. It exposes the thresholded numerical rank and reciprocal 2-norm condition; call condition_number() for the condition estimate, which errors on a computed zero singular value or binary64 overflow. None uses max(m,n)*EPSILON for the rank cutoff; the matrix must have nonempty axes. Very small singular directions can underflow during normalization, so these remain floating-point estimates rather than exact rank certificates.

## Student's t probabilities

`NativeStudentT::pdf(t,df)`, `cdf(t,df)`, `survival(t,df)`,

Degrees of freedom accept every finite positive binary64 value. Quantiles require
`0 < p < 1`; nonfinite probabilities retain the existing illegal-quantity error.
Finite t values are required, and invalid degrees/nonfinite samples raise errors.

The shared kernel evaluates central mass directly near zero and retains extreme
tails in logarithmic form. Large degrees reuse the bounded CDFLIB-derived beta
kernel with both reduced coordinates retained; very large degrees near the
center use the normal limit within binary64 precision. Density normalization
uses stable beta/log-gamma formulas and a bounded Stirling expansion.

elsewhere. One range check plus at most 63 positive-coordinate bisections covers
the full finite binary64 range. Each forward evaluation has an iteration/work
limit and cancellation checks. Unrepresentable quantiles raise real overflow.

All five scalar BASIC APIs also accept flat numeric lists with scalar broadcasting
and matching list lengths, capped at one million results. Evaluation checks for
cancellation between elements and preserves the destination on any error.

documents.html:
The crate root exports BasicComplex, NativeComplexMatrix and NativeComplexSolveResult. Build a square row-major matrix from finite complex values, then call solve(rhs) for a CPU partial-row-pivoted solution and a fresh ||b-Ax||₂ residual. The kernel accepts dimensions through 128 and checks finite intermediate results; singular pivots and dimension errors are reported as Rust errors. BASIC CLINSOLVE(A,b) uses this same kernel and returns {solution,residualNorm}. It does not require LAPACK or interpreter values for native reuse.

NativeComplexMatrix::factor_lu() returns a reusable NativeComplexLuFactor for a nonsingular square matrix. Its solve(rhs) method returns NativeComplexSolveResult; solve_many(rhs_columns) returns NativeComplexMultiSolveResult with one solution and freshly evaluated original system residual per RHS. Factors use scaled partial row pivoting, preserve the original matrix for residual checks, and accept dimensions through 128. BASIC CLUFACT(A) and CLLUSOLVE(F,b) expose the same kernels through an editable packet; vector RHS values produce {solution,residualNorm} and matrix RHS values produce {solutionMatrix,residualNorms}. Native factor objects retain their owned data and do not depend on interpreter values.

NativeComplexMatrix::rectangular(rows,columns,row_major_values) also admits bounded rectangular matrices for least_squares(rhs). This method uses column-pivoted Householder QR for full-column-rank overdetermined systems and returns NativeComplexLeastSquaresResult with the coefficients in original column order, the original fit residual, and ||Aᴴ(b-Ax)||₂. Rank-deficient and underdetermined inputs return errors. BASIC CLSTSQ(A,b) shares this Rust kernel; its 128-by-128 shape and 4,194,304-work bounds apply.

NativeComplexMatrix::least_squares_minimum_norm_many(rhs, rcond) shares the same checked SVD across multiple RHS columns. It returns NativeComplexMultiMinNormLeastSquaresResult with a minimum-norm solution matrix, per-column fit and normal residuals, shared estimated rank and cutoff. BASIC CLSTSQMINM(A,B[,rcond]) exposes the same result as a five-item list. Aggregate work is capped at 4,194,304 units; both matrix axes and RHS count are capped at

  1. The method reuses the factorization directly in Rust without creating

interpreter values.

NativeComplexMatrix::least_squares_minimum_norm(rhs, rcond) instead uses the reduced complex SVD to handle overdetermined, underdetermined and numerically rank-deficient systems. rcond=None selects max(rows,columns)*EPSILON; an explicit finite cutoff must be in [0,1]. Singular values strictly greater than rcond * largestSingularValue are retained. The returned NativeComplexMinNormLeastSquaresResult contains the minimum-Euclidean-norm solution, freshly evaluated original fit and normal residual norms, estimated rank and the cutoff used. Rank is a floating-point estimate. BASIC CLSTSQMIN(A,b[,rcond]) returns the same fields in a four-item list. It uses the bounded CPU complex SVD path with axes capped at 128.

NativeComplexMatrix::qr() returns NativeComplexQrResult with reduced Q and R matrices. The CPU implementation uses complex Householder reflectors, scales the input before factorization, accepts rank deficiency, and returns the reconstruction A=Q*R without column pivoting. Q has m × min(m,n) shape and R has min(m,n) × n shape; axes are capped at 128 and work at 16,777,216 units. BASIC CLQR(A) uses the same factorization and returns {Q,R}.

NativeComplexMatrix::inverse() returns a square complex inverse computed from one reusable scaled LU factorization. It solves every identity column and checks original-system residuals before returning the row-major matrix. BASIC CLINVERSE(A) uses the same method; singular and unrepresentable systems return errors rather than partial results.

NativeComplexMatrix::hermitian_eigen() returns NativeComplexHermitianEigenResult: ascending real eigenvalues and a row-major complex matrix whose columns are normalized eigenvectors in matching order. The kernel uses the bounded Linux CPU symmetric LAPACK path through realification, recovers complex bases for repeated eigenvalues, and checks residuals before returning. BASIC CHEIGEN(A) shares this implementation and returns {eigenvalues,eigenvectors}.

NativeComplexMatrix::eigen() solves general square complex systems using the Linux LP64 LAPACK ZGEEV routine and returns NativeComplexEigenResult with sorted complex eigenvalues and unit-norm right-eigenvector columns. It checks every eigenpair against the original matrix with scale-normalized residuals. General non-normal eigenvectors are not required to be mutually orthogonal; near-defective systems can have sensitive eigenvectors even when residuals are small. Dimensions are capped at 128, work at one billion bounded multiply-adds, and queried complex workspace at 128 MiB. BASIC CGEIGVALS(A) returns only the eigenvalues; CGEIGEN(A) returns {eigenvalues,eigenvectors}. Non-Linux builds return the backend's explicit unavailable error.

NativeComplexMatrix::eigen_sensitivity() returns sorted eigenvalues with NativeComplexEigenSensitivityResult::reciprocal_conditions, estimated as |yᴴx|/(||y||₂||x||₂) using matched left and right eigenvectors from the same ZGEEV decomposition. Values in [0,1] near zero indicate greater local sensitivity. Left and right eigenpair residuals are checked against the scaled input. This estimate is not a forward-error bound. BASIC CGEIGCOND(A) returns {eigenvalues,reciprocal_conditions} and uses the same bounded CPU path.

NativeRealMatrix::general_eigen() accepts a real square matrix, converts its finite coefficients to the shared complex representation, and returns NativeComplexEigenResult so nonsymmetric matrices can have complex-conjugate modes. BASIC GEIGVALS(A) returns only the spectrum and GEIGEN(A) returns {eigenvalues,eigenvectors}. The path shares the 128-axis and Linux ZGEEV limits; symmetric real matrices may use EIGH for ascending real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors.

NativeRealMatrix::eigen_sensitivity() returns the sorted eigenvalues and reciprocal left/right eigenvector-overlap estimates from the same checked CPU ZGEEV path used by typed complex callers. Normal modes approach one; values near zero indicate local eigenvalue sensitivity, not a forward-error guarantee. BASIC CGEIGCOND(A) already accepts real-valued matrices and returns the same diagnostic.

NativeRealMatrix::generalized_eigen(&b) solves a real matrix pencil through the same complex ZGGEV backend, preserving projective alpha/beta pairs and complex modes. BASIC GEIGGEN(A,B) returns {alpha,beta,eigenvectors}. Both matrices must be square and have equal dimensions; the shared backend caps axes at 128 and checks the homogeneous residual.

NativeComplexMatrix::generalized_eigen(&b) solves A*x=(alpha/beta)*B*x with Linux LP64 LAPACK ZGGEV. NativeComplexGeneralEigenResult keeps each jointly normalized projective (alpha,beta) pair intact: beta zero represents an infinite eigenvalue, and alpha=beta=0 represents an indeterminate pair. Unit-norm right eigenvectors are checked against the homogeneous residual beta*A*x-alpha*B*x; singular B is supported. BASIC CGEIGGEN(A,B) returns {alpha,beta,eigenvectors}. Dimensions are capped at 128, work at one billion bounded multiply-adds and queried complex workspace at 128 MiB. Non-Linux builds return the backend's explicit unavailable error.

NativeComplexMatrix::generalized_eigen_sensitivity(&b) uses Linux LP64 LAPACK ZGGEVX with balancing disabled and returns NativeComplexGeneralEigenSensitivityResult: the projective alpha/beta pairs and LAPACK reciprocal eigenvalue-condition estimates in matching driver order. Estimates are nonnegative and may exceed one; values near zero indicate a sensitive eigenvalue. This is a local conditioning diagnostic, not a forward-error guarantee. Axes remain capped at 128. BASIC CGEIGGENCOND(A,B) returns {alpha,beta,reciprocal_conditions}.

NativeComplexMatrix::cholesky() returns a lower-triangular matrix L for Hermitian positive-definite input, with A=L*Lᴴ. The bounded CPU Rust kernel checks Hermitian structure, scales the input, and exactly accumulates each complex inner product. Nonpositive pivots return a domain error. BASIC CCHOLESKY(A) uses the same method and returns ordinary nested-list values that compose with CLMATMUL and CLADJOINT.

NativeComplexMatrix::singular_values() returns descending singular values for any bounded rectangular complex matrix. The implementation embeds A as the real matrix [[Re(A),-Im(A)],[Im(A),Re(A)]], reuses Linux LP64 LAPACK's singular-values-only routine, and exactly averages duplicated values. BASIC CSVDVALS(A) shares the same implementation. Each original axis is limited to 128; rank deficiency is supported and represented by zero singular values.

NativeComplexMatrix::svd() returns NativeComplexSvdResult containing thin left singular vectors u, descending nonnegative singular_values, and the conjugate-transposed right singular vectors vh, with A=u*D*vh. The Linux CPU implementation calls LAPACK ZGESVD, scales the input, and verifies both factor orthogonality and the original reconstruction residual. It supports tall, square, wide, rank-deficient and zero matrices with axes through 128. BASIC CSVD(A) returns the same factors as {U,S,VH} for composition with CLMATMUL and CLADJOINT.

NativeComplexMatrix::hermitian_eigenvalues() returns ascending real eigenvalues for Hermitian matrices using the Linux LP64 LAPACK path. It checks real diagonal entries and checks mirrored off-diagonal components at a scale-relative 64-epsilon tolerance. It caps dimensions at 128, preserves multiplicity, and returns no eigenvectors. BASIC CHEIGVALS(A) uses the same typed kernel.

NativeComplexMatrix also exposes shape() and a read-only row-major values() view, adjoint() for the conjugate transpose, and multiply(&rhs) for complex matrix products. Product components use the shared exact binary product accumulator, retaining cancellation without overflowing intermediate products and rounding once to binary64. Dimensions are limited to 128 and products to 4,194,304 real product terms. BASIC CLMATMUL(A,B) and CLADJOINT(A) return nested lists from the same Rust kernels.

`{alpha,beta,eigenvectors}`. Dimensions are capped at 128, work at one billion

builds return the backend's explicit unavailable error.

`NativeComplexMatrix::generalized_eigen_sensitivity(&b)` uses Linux LP64 LAPACK
`ZGGEVX` with balancing disabled and returns
`NativeComplexGeneralEigenSensitivityResult`: the projective alpha/beta pairs
and LAPACK reciprocal eigenvalue-condition estimates in matching driver order.
Estimates are nonnegative and may exceed one; values near zero indicate a
sensitive eigenvalue. This is a local conditioning diagnostic, not a
forward-error guarantee. Axes remain capped at 128. BASIC `CGEIGGENCOND(A,B)`
returns `{alpha,beta,reciprocal_conditions}`.

`NativeComplexMatrix::cholesky()` returns a lower-triangular matrix `L` for
Hermitian positive-definite input, with `A=L*Lᴴ`. The bounded CPU Rust kernel
checks Hermitian structure, scales the input, and exactly accumulates each
complex inner product. Nonpositive pivots return a domain error. BASIC
`CCHOLESKY(A)` uses the same method and returns ordinary nested-list values that
compose with `CLMATMUL` and `CLADJOINT`.

`NativeComplexMatrix::singular_values()` returns descending singular values
for any bounded rectangular complex matrix. The implementation embeds A as the
real matrix `[[Re(A),-Im(A)],[Im(A),Re(A)]]`, reuses Linux LP64 LAPACK's
singular-values-only routine, and exactly averages duplicated values. BASIC
`CSVDVALS(A)` shares the same implementation. Each original axis is limited to
128; rank deficiency is supported and represented by zero singular values.

`NativeComplexMatrix::svd()` returns `NativeComplexSvdResult` containing thin
left singular vectors `u`, descending nonnegative `singular_values`, and the
conjugate-transposed right singular vectors `vh`, with `A=u*D*vh`. The Linux
CPU implementation calls LAPACK `ZGESVD`, scales the input, and verifies both
factor orthogonality and the original reconstruction residual. It supports
tall, square, wide, rank-deficient and zero matrices with axes through 128.
BASIC `CSVD(A)` returns the same factors as `{U,S,VH}` for composition with
`CLMATMUL` and `CLADJOINT`.

`NativeComplexMatrix::hermitian_eigenvalues()` returns ascending real
eigenvalues for Hermitian matrices using the Linux LP64 LAPACK path. It checks
real diagonal entries and checks mirrored off-diagonal components at a
scale-relative 64-epsilon tolerance. It caps dimensions at 128, preserves
multiplicity, and returns no eigenvectors. BASIC `CHEIGVALS(A)`
uses the same typed kernel.

`NativeComplexMatrix` also exposes `shape()` and a read-only row-major
`values()` view, `adjoint()` for the conjugate transpose, and `multiply(&rhs)`
for complex matrix products. Product components use the shared exact binary
product accumulator, retaining cancellation without overflowing intermediate
products and rounding once to binary64. Dimensions are limited to 128 and
products to 4,194,304 real product terms. BASIC `CLMATMUL(A,B)` and
`CLADJOINT(A)` return nested lists from the same Rust kernels.

documents.title: CPU polynomial analysis
documents.html:
The crate root exports NativePolynomial, which stores finite real coefficients in highest-degree-first order and shares the kernels used by BASIC POLYEVAL, POLYADD, POLYSUB, POLYMUL, POLYDERIV, POLYINT and POLYFIT. It provides checked evaluation, arithmetic, calculus and scaled Householder-QR fitting without constructing interpreter values. Polynomial addition and subtraction use exact binary accumulation for each coefficient; multiplication uses exact binary product accumulation. Lists are limited by the runtime's existing maximum-list size, fitting is bounded by its shared work budget, and numerical rank deficiency or an unrepresentable result is an error. Monomial fits remain sensitive to conditioning; scaling and QR avoid normal-equation squaring but do not make every dataset well-conditioned.

use modernbasic::{error::Error, NativePolynomial};

fn fit() -> Result<NativePolynomial, Error> {
    let x = [-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0];
    let y = x.map(|v| 2.0 * v * v - 3.0 * v + 1.0);
    let p = NativePolynomial::fit(&x, &y, 2)?;
    assert!((p.evaluate(3.0)? - 10.0).abs() < 1e-12);
    Ok(p)
}

documents.title: Shared CPU cash-flow analysis
documents.html:
The crate root exports NativeFinancialMath for direct Rust cash-flow analysis. net_present_value(rate, cashflows) uses the same overflow-safe discounted accumulation as BASIC NPV; as in BASIC, element zero is discounted by one period, while later entries follow by period index. The rate must be finite and greater than -1, cash flows must be finite, and the list is capped at one million entries. The kernel checks cancellation while building the discounted sum and returns RealOverflow if the final result is not representable. internal_rate_of_return(cashflows, initial_guess) exposes the same bounded Newton/bracketing/bisection search as BASIC IRR; it returns one root and does not enumerate multiple roots. It requires positive and negative cash flows, checks cancellation while normalizing and evaluating, and caps total work at ten million cash-flow evaluations (IllegalQuantity if exceeded). A missing bracket or failed convergence returns the IRR math-domain error.

present_value, future_value, and payment share the BASIC PV, FV, and PMT kernels and cash-flow sign convention. Their payment_due flag selects beginning-of-period payments. Rates must exceed -1, periods must be nonnegative for present/future value and positive for payment, and all numeric inputs must be finite. compound(principal, annual_rate, periods, frequency) shares BASIC COMPOUND, including small-rate handling and the zero-period, zero-rate and full-loss boundaries. Frequency must be positive, periods must be nonnegative, and the periodic rate cannot be below -1. Their outputs are binary64. These methods price fixed, deterministic cash flows; they do not model taxes, inflation, uncertainty or portfolio risk.

## Shared CPU cash-flow analysis

The crate root exports `NativeFinancialMath` for direct Rust cash-flow analysis.
`net_present_value(rate, cashflows)` uses the same overflow-safe discounted
accumulation as BASIC `NPV`; as in BASIC, element zero is discounted by one
period, while later entries follow by period index. The rate must be finite and
greater than `-1`, cash flows must be finite, and the list is capped at one
million entries. The kernel checks cancellation while building the discounted
sum and returns `RealOverflow` if the final result is not representable.
`internal_rate_of_return(cashflows, initial_guess)` exposes the same bounded
Newton/bracketing/bisection search as BASIC `IRR`; it returns one root and does
not enumerate multiple roots. It requires positive and negative cash flows,
checks cancellation while normalizing and evaluating, and caps total work at
ten million cash-flow evaluations (`IllegalQuantity` if exceeded). A missing
bracket or failed convergence returns the `IRR` math-domain error.

`present_value`, `future_value`, and `payment` share the BASIC `PV`, `FV`, and
`PMT` kernels and cash-flow sign convention. Their `payment_due` flag selects
beginning-of-period payments. Rates must exceed `-1`, periods must be
nonnegative for present/future value and positive for payment, and all numeric
inputs must be finite. `compound(principal, annual_rate, periods, frequency)`
shares BASIC `COMPOUND`, including small-rate handling and the zero-period,
zero-rate and full-loss boundaries. Frequency must be positive, periods must
be nonnegative, and the periodic rate cannot be below `-1`. Their outputs are
binary64. These methods price fixed, deterministic cash flows; they do not
model taxes, inflation, uncertainty or portfolio risk.

documents.title: CPU European option pricing
documents.html: The crate root exports black_scholes_european_price, black_scholes_european_greeks and black_scholes_european_implied_volatility, along with their typed input/result structs. Native Rust callers share the same CPU kernels as BSOPTION, BSGREEKS and BSVOL; they do not need to construct interpreter values. Implied volatility validates the observed price against discounted no-arbitrage bounds, uses bounded bisection, accepts zero volatility at the exact intrinsic value, and limits the search to 1,024 annualized volatility and 96 bisections. As with any price inversion, estimates near a bound can be ill-conditioned.

documents.title: Bounded CPU physics equations
documents.html:
The crate root exports NativePhysicsEquation, NativePhysicsJacobian, NativePhysicsSample and NativePhysicsTrajectory for Rust callers that want the same callback validation and bounded CPU solvers as BASIC without creating interpreter Values:

use modernbasic::{error::Error, NativePhysicsEquation};

fn step() -> Result<Vec<f64>, Error> {
    let mut equation = NativePhysicsEquation::new(
        |_, state: &[f64]| Ok(vec![-state[0]]),
        None,
    );
    equation.implicit_backward_euler_step(0.0, &[1.0], 0.1, 1e-10, 1e-12)
}

rk4 and implicit_backward_euler_step advance one step. integrate_adaptive_rk4(start_time,initial_state,end_time,maximum_step,rtol,atol) uses the same adaptive RK4 step-doubling kernel as BASIC ODESOLVE and returns typed {time,state} samples, with no interpreter value conversion in the trajectory. It supports reverse integration and a zero-length interval. The optional dense analytic Jacobian uses NativePhysicsJacobian; omitting it selects the same bounded finite-difference Newton path as BASIC. Dense nonlinear operations limit state vectors to 64 components, with at most 24 Newton iterations and 12 backtracking trials. Equation callback evaluations and component work are cumulatively limited to 200,000 and 50 million; trajectory storage is bounded by the same result-size limit as BASIC. Errors, cancellation and nonfinite outputs return without a partial trajectory.

configure_index_one_dae(differential_count,state_dimension) selects the semi-explicit index-one form. initialize_consistent_state adjusts algebraic components while preserving the supplied differential components; implicit_backward_euler_step then advances the DAE and checks its initial algebraic residual. These calls do not detect a general DAE index or prove branch uniqueness. The explicit adaptive API does not integrate algebraic constraints; those remain in the implicit DAE and IDA APIs.

## Bounded CPU physics equations

The crate root exports `NativePhysicsEquation`, `NativePhysicsJacobian`,
`NativePhysicsSample` and `NativePhysicsTrajectory` for Rust callers that want
the same callback validation and bounded CPU solvers as BASIC without creating
interpreter `Value`s:

```rust
use modernbasic::{error::Error, NativePhysicsEquation};

fn step() -> Result<Vec<f64>, Error> {
    let mut equation = NativePhysicsEquation::new(
        |_, state: &[f64]| Ok(vec![-state[0]]),
        None,
    );
    equation.implicit_backward_euler_step(0.0, &[1.0], 0.1, 1e-10, 1e-12)
}
```

`rk4` and `implicit_backward_euler_step` advance one step.
`integrate_adaptive_rk4(start_time,initial_state,end_time,maximum_step,rtol,atol)`
uses the same adaptive RK4 step-doubling kernel as BASIC `ODESOLVE` and returns
typed `{time,state}` samples, with no interpreter value conversion in the
trajectory. It supports reverse integration and a zero-length interval. The
optional dense analytic Jacobian uses `NativePhysicsJacobian`; omitting it
selects the same bounded finite-difference Newton path as BASIC. Dense nonlinear
operations limit state vectors to 64 components, with at most 24 Newton
iterations and 12 backtracking trials. Equation callback evaluations and
component work are cumulatively limited to 200,000 and 50 million; trajectory
storage is bounded by the same result-size limit as BASIC. Errors, cancellation
and nonfinite outputs return without a partial trajectory.

`configure_index_one_dae(differential_count,state_dimension)` selects the

components while preserving the supplied differential components;
`implicit_backward_euler_step` then advances the DAE and checks its initial
algebraic residual. These calls do not detect a general DAE index or prove

constraints; those remain in the implicit DAE and IDA APIs.

documents.title: Native stiff and nonstiff ODE integration
documents.html:
NativeCvode::integrate exposes the shared serial CPU SUNDIALS solver to Rust applications. Select NativeCvodeMethod::Bdf for stiff systems or NativeCvodeMethod::Adams for nonstiff systems, then pass strictly monotone output times, a finite initial state, NativeCvodeOptions and an RHS closure. The typed result includes the requested trajectory and accepted-step, callback-evaluation, error-test-failure and final-order counts. The trajectory uses NativePhysicsSample and NativePhysicsTrajectory, with no BASIC Value conversion. integrate_with_jacobian adds a direct Rust dense analytic Jacobian for BDF.

Dense solves are limited to 256 states. BDF with matrix-free SPGMR supports up to 4,096 states, with Krylov dimension from 1 through min(state_count,256). The solver accepts 1 through 10,000 output times, up to 100,000 internal steps, and the shared bounded trajectory storage. Relative tolerance must be in (0,1); absolute tolerances are positive and component-wise. A maximum step of zero leaves step selection to SUNDIALS. Cancellation, provider availability and callback errors follow the same checks as BASIC CVODESOLVE.

NativeCancellationToken lets a host cancel a native math operation from another thread. Clone the token to the requesting thread and run the solver inside token.run(|| ...) on its worker thread. CVODE checks cancellation before each ordinary RHS callback, and IDA polls the token from its residual callbacks; other kernels that use the shared math checkpoints observe the same token. Cancellation returns Error::Break, remains requested until reset() is called after the operation stops, and the scoped token is removed when run returns or unwinds. This does not promise interruption inside an individual native-library call that does not poll a math checkpoint. See the focused cancellation qualification. integrate_until_root stops at the first detected scalar sign crossing and returns root_event_found; a tangency without a sign change is not guaranteed to be found. integrate_parametric returns forward sensitivity trajectories indexed by parameter, requested time and state, for up to 16 parameters. The integrate_until_root_parametric estimates terminal-event time and total event-state derivatives for up to 16 parameters. It performs a base solve and four perturbed solves per parameter, using centered differences at relative steps h = relative_perturbation * max(abs(parameter), 1) and h/2 with Richardson extrapolation. Optional initial-state sensitivities are included. The result carries the base trajectory, event time and state, derivatives, finite-difference error estimates, and aggregate integration/step/callback counts. The first transversal crossing must remain the same under every perturbation. Error estimates cover finite-difference refinement only; they do not include solver trajectory error, and branch changes or tangencies invalidate the estimate. That estimator does not offer adjoint sensitivities. The crate-root integrate_until_root_variational instead integrates analytic total sensitivity equations with CVODES and combines the fixed-time sensitivities with a supplied event gradient using the first-order event-time and total event-state derivative formulas. It reports the transversality denominator and rejects zero or cancellation-dominated roots. This API relies on the caller supplying correct sensitivity equations and event partials; CVODE tolerances control integration error but are not rigorous global error bounds, and the API does not estimate modeling error. BASIC programs can call the same bounded operation as CVODEEVENTSENS; its argument and result layout are specified in the language reference. Editable BASIC programs can use CVODEEVENTVAR to supply those callbacks; see the language reference.

callback-evaluation, error-test-failure and final-order counts. The trajectory
uses `NativePhysicsSample` and `NativePhysicsTrajectory`, with no BASIC `Value`
conversion. `integrate_with_jacobian` adds a direct Rust dense analytic Jacobian
for BDF.

to 4,096 states, with Krylov dimension from 1 through `min(state_count,256)`.
The solver accepts 1 through 10,000 output times, up to 100,000 internal steps,
and the shared bounded trajectory storage. Relative tolerance must be in
`(0,1)`; absolute tolerances are positive and component-wise. A maximum step of
zero leaves step selection to SUNDIALS. Cancellation, provider availability and
callback errors follow the same checks as BASIC `CVODESOLVE`.

other kernels that use the shared math checkpoints observe the same token. Cancellation returns `Error::Break`, remains requested until
`reset()` is called after the operation stops, and the scoped token is removed
when `run` returns or unwinds. This does not promise interruption inside an
individual native-library call that does not poll a math checkpoint. See the
[focused cancellation qualification](../output/native-math-cancellation-token-2026-10-25/validation.json).

returns `root_event_found`; a tangency without a sign change is not guaranteed
to be found. `integrate_parametric` returns forward sensitivity trajectories
indexed by parameter, requested time and state, for up to 16 parameters. The
`integrate_until_root_parametric` estimates terminal-event time and total
event-state derivatives for up to 16 parameters. It performs a base solve and
four perturbed solves per parameter, using centered differences at relative
steps `h = relative_perturbation * max(abs(parameter), 1)` and `h/2` with
Richardson extrapolation. Optional initial-state
sensitivities are included. The result carries the base trajectory, event time
and state, derivatives, finite-difference error estimates, and aggregate
integration/step/callback counts. The first transversal crossing must remain
the same under every perturbation. Error estimates cover finite-difference
refinement only; they do not include solver trajectory error, and branch
changes or tangencies invalidate the estimate. That estimator does not offer
adjoint sensitivities. The crate-root `integrate_until_root_variational` instead
integrates analytic total sensitivity equations with CVODES and combines the
fixed-time sensitivities with a supplied event gradient using the first-order
event-time and total event-state derivative formulas. It reports the
transversality denominator and rejects zero or cancellation-dominated roots.
This API relies on the caller supplying correct sensitivity equations and event
partials; CVODE tolerances control integration error but are not rigorous global
error bounds, and the API does not estimate modeling error. BASIC programs can call
the same bounded operation as `CVODEEVENTSENS`; its argument and result layout
are specified in the [language reference](LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md#terminal-event-parameter-sensitivities).
Editable BASIC programs can use `CVODEEVENTVAR` to supply those callbacks; see
the [language reference](LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md#terminal-event-parameter-sensitivities).

documents.title: Canonical sparse matrices
documents.html:
use modernbasic::{error::Error, NativeCsrMatrix};

fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
    let a = NativeCsrMatrix::new(
        2, 2,
        vec![0, 1, 2],
        vec![0, 1],
        vec![2.0, 3.0],
    )?;
    assert_eq!(a.multiply(&[4.0, 5.0])?, vec![8.0, 15.0]);
    assert_eq!(a.quadratic_form(&[4.0, 5.0])?, 107.0);
    assert_eq!(a.transposed()?.shape(), [2, 2]);
    Ok(())
}

new(rows, columns, row_pointers, column_indices, values) takes ownership of zero-based CSR vectors. Row pointers include the final entry offset, start at zero, are monotone and span all stored entries. Columns are strictly increasing within each row. Stored values are finite and nonzero; duplicates and both signs of stored zero are rejected. The logical limits are 100,000 rows/columns and 250,000 nonzero entries. shape, nnz, row_pointers, column_indices and values expose immutable views. A clone owns an independent copy.

NativeCsrMatrix::kronecker(&other) and BASIC SPKRON(A,B) form the sparse product A ⊗ B directly in canonical CSR. They preserve the matrix-product block ordering, omit coefficients that underflow to zero and reject nonfinite products. The output obeys the same axis, 250,000-entry and work limits, and can be passed directly to sparse products, iterative solvers and native sparse factorization APIs.

NativeCsrMatrix::kronecker_sum(&other) and BASIC SPKRONSUM(A,B) assemble A ⊗ I + I ⊗ B for square component matrices. The implementation coalesces overlapping diagonal entries exactly and returns canonical CSR under the same dimension, entry and work limits. This supports sparse multidimensional stencils without materializing dense intermediates.

NativeKroneckerSum::conjugate_gradient(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial) solves the same row-major I_n ⊗ A + B ⊗ I_m operator used by multiply. It returns NativeSparseSolveResult and shares the CG recurrence, fresh residual stopping, correction rebasing and cancellation/work accounting with sparse CG. Exactly symmetric factors and a finite positive combined diagonal are checked; positive definiteness remains the caller's requirement. Factors need not each be positive definite. The matrix-free adapter computes symmetric Jacobi-scaled products without allocating a full dense/CSR matrix or incomplete factors. BASIC exposes this as KRONSCG; its result and tolerance conventions match SPCG. Factor/vector limits are one million entries, maximum iterations 100000, and the shared solve work limit is 100 million units. This typed API does not require interpreter Values, external providers or a GPU.

NativeCsrMatrix::conjugate_gradient(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial) uses the same CPU preconditioned-CG kernel as BASIC SPCG, with Jacobi scaling by default. conjugate_gradient_with_preconditioner accepts NativeCgPreconditioner::Jacobi or ::IncompleteCholesky(level) for IC(0) through IC(8). The matrix must be square, exactly symmetric and have a positive diagonal; these checks do not prove positive definiteness. A nonpositive curvature encountered during iteration returns a non-converged report. Both methods use NativeSparseSolveResult, a 100,000-iteration ceiling, the shared 100-million-unit work/cancellation budget and a freshly recomputed residual for the original system. IC lower and upper factors share a one-million-entry cap.

NativeCsrMatrix::minres(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial) exposes the unpreconditioned CPU MINRES kernel. minres_with_preconditioner accepts the same arguments followed by NativeMinresPreconditioner::None, ::Jacobi, or ::IncompleteCholesky(level) for fill levels zero through eight. Incomplete Cholesky requires positive diagonal entries and positive pivots; it applies a symmetric triangular change of coordinates and can reject matrices for which the bounded incomplete factor is not positive definite. Both methods use the same CPU kernel as BASIC SPMINRES and return NativeSparseSolveResult with the best solution, status, completed iteration count, freshly computed original-system residual norm and stopping threshold. The input must be square and exactly symmetric; indefinite and consistent singular systems are supported. It uses short-recurrence O(n) working vectors, optionally applying symmetric Jacobi scaling from the absolute diagonal, and a 100,000-step ceiling, the shared 100-million-unit work budget and runtime cancellation. Status CONVERGED is based on the original residual. MAXITER and BREAKDOWN return the latest candidate and do not prove inconsistency.

NativeCsrMatrix::gmres(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial) solves a general real square sparse system with restarted CPU GMRES, row equilibration and the same automatic restart width used by BASIC. The explicit gmres_with_preconditioner method also accepts restart and NativeGmresPreconditioner::{RowEquilibration,None,Ilu(level)}; ILU levels 0 through 8 retain the BASIC factor-entry cap and report missing/zero pivots as errors. Both methods return the same NativeSparseSolveResult; CONVERGED requires a freshly computed original-system residual. The restart is limited to 128, total iterations to 100,000, basis storage to two million elements and the shared work budget to 100 million units. A finite residual is not a forward-error or conditioning guarantee. The matrix and vectors are borrowed for each call; no interpreter values or persistent solver object are required.

NativeCsrMatrix::bicgstab(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial) exposes the short-recurrence CPU solver for general nonsymmetric square systems. Its typed bicgstab_with_preconditioner variant accepts NativeBicgstabPreconditioner::{RowEquilibration,None,Ilu(level)} for ILU(0) through ILU(8). It reuses GMRES's bounded left-preconditioning and factor kernels, stores O(n) iteration vectors, and returns NativeSparseSolveResult with a fresh original-matrix residual. BiCGSTAB can break down even when a system is nonsingular; BREAKDOWN is not an inconsistency certificate. BASIC calls the same kernel with SPBICGSTAB.

NativeCsrMatrix::lsqr(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations) solves rectangular least-squares systems without forming AᵀA. It starts at zero and uses the Golub-Kahan CPU iteration, so rank-deficient and underdetermined problems target the ordinary Euclidean minimum-norm solution in exact arithmetic. Its NativeSparseLeastSquaresResult reports both ||b-Ax||₂ and a freshly recomputed stationarity norm; only the latter controls convergence. It is ||Aᵀ(b-Ax)||₂ by default and ||D Aᵀ(b-Ax)||₂ under column scaling, with matching threshold max(rtol*||D Aᵀb||₂,atol) (D=I by default). Column scaling also requires every stationarity component to meet its own relative and absolute tolerance, with a binary64 roundoff floor, so a large component cannot mask an unresolved small one. Thus an inconsistent fit can be CONVERGED while its ordinary residual remains positive. The operation shares the sparse axis, entry, iteration, work and cancellation limits. For ill-scaled columns, use NativeCsrMatrix::lsqr_with_preconditioner(...,NativeLsqrPreconditioner::ColumnNorm) or BASIC SPLSQR(...,"COLUMN") to normalize each nonzero column to unit 2-norm. The fit residual is always computed against the original matrix; the scaled mode applies D only to the stationarity test. This right scaling changes the minimum-norm metric for rank-deficient or underdetermined systems; use the default None mode to preserve the ordinary Euclidean choice. Scaling that would underflow a stored coefficient is rejected. BASIC calls the same kernel with SPLSQR.

Native zero axes retain shape: a 0 × n matrix multiplies an n-vector into an empty vector; its n × 0 transpose multiplies an empty vector into n zeros. The existing BASIC CSR1 format keeps positive dimensions and one-based indices. Physics Jacobians retain their separate positive-dimension requirement.

NativeCsrMatrix::weighted_lsqr(b,weights,rtol,atol,max_iterations) and weighted_lsqr_with_preconditioner solve min sum(wᵢ(bᵢ-Aᵢx)²) with the same bounded CPU iteration. Weights must be finite, nonnegative and not all zero; zero-weight rows are excluded. NativeSparseWeightedLeastSquaresResult reports residuals and threshold using weights normalized by the maximum weight, plus weight_scale for restoring original units. The fit norm scales by sqrt(weight_scale) and the normal residual by weight_scale. A stored coefficient that would underflow during row scaling is rejected. BASIC SPWLSQR uses this same typed kernel, and the optional column preconditioner applies after row weighting.

It returns `NativeSparseSolveResult` and shares the CG recurrence, fresh residual
stopping, correction rebasing and cancellation/work accounting with sparse CG.
Exactly symmetric factors and a finite positive combined diagonal are checked;
positive definiteness remains the caller's requirement. Factors need not each
be positive definite. The matrix-free adapter computes symmetric Jacobi-scaled
products without allocating a full dense/CSR matrix or incomplete factors.
BASIC exposes this as `KRONSCG`; its result and tolerance conventions match
`SPCG`. Factor/vector limits are one million entries, maximum iterations 100000,
and the shared solve work limit is 100 million units. This typed API does not
require interpreter `Value`s, external providers or a GPU.

`NativeCsrMatrix::conjugate_gradient(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial)` uses
the same CPU preconditioned-CG kernel as BASIC `SPCG`, with Jacobi scaling by
default. `conjugate_gradient_with_preconditioner` accepts
`NativeCgPreconditioner::Jacobi` or `::IncompleteCholesky(level)` for IC(0)
through IC(8). The matrix must be square, exactly symmetric and have a positive
diagonal; these checks do not prove positive definiteness. A nonpositive
curvature encountered during iteration returns a non-converged report. Both
methods use `NativeSparseSolveResult`, a 100,000-iteration ceiling, the shared
100-million-unit work/cancellation budget and a freshly recomputed residual for
the original system. IC lower and upper factors share a one-million-entry cap.

`NativeCsrMatrix::minres(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial)` exposes the
unpreconditioned CPU MINRES kernel. `minres_with_preconditioner` accepts the
same arguments followed by `NativeMinresPreconditioner::None`, `::Jacobi`, or
`::IncompleteCholesky(level)` for fill levels zero through eight. Incomplete
Cholesky requires positive diagonal entries and positive pivots; it applies a
symmetric triangular change of coordinates and can reject matrices for which
the bounded incomplete factor is not positive definite.
Both methods use the same CPU kernel as BASIC `SPMINRES` and return `NativeSparseSolveResult`
with the best solution, status, completed iteration count, freshly computed
original-system residual norm and stopping threshold. The input must be square
and exactly symmetric; indefinite and consistent singular systems are supported.
It uses short-recurrence O(n) working vectors, optionally applying symmetric
Jacobi scaling from the absolute diagonal, and a 100,000-step
ceiling, the shared 100-million-unit work budget and runtime cancellation.
Status `CONVERGED` is based on the original residual. `MAXITER` and `BREAKDOWN`
return the latest candidate and do not prove inconsistency.

`NativeCsrMatrix::gmres(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial)` solves a general
real square sparse system with restarted CPU GMRES, row equilibration and the
same automatic restart width used by BASIC. The explicit
`gmres_with_preconditioner` method also accepts `restart` and
`NativeGmresPreconditioner::{RowEquilibration,None,Ilu(level)}`; ILU levels 0
through 8 retain the BASIC factor-entry cap and report missing/zero pivots as
errors. Both methods return the same `NativeSparseSolveResult`; `CONVERGED`
requires a freshly computed original-system residual. The restart is limited to
128, total iterations to 100,000, basis storage to two million elements and the
shared work budget to 100 million units. A finite residual is not a forward-error
or conditioning guarantee. The matrix and vectors are borrowed for each call;
no interpreter values or persistent solver object are required.

`NativeCsrMatrix::bicgstab(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial)` exposes the
short-recurrence CPU solver for general nonsymmetric square systems. Its typed
`bicgstab_with_preconditioner` variant accepts
`NativeBicgstabPreconditioner::{RowEquilibration,None,Ilu(level)}` for ILU(0)
through ILU(8). It reuses GMRES's bounded left-preconditioning and factor
kernels, stores O(n) iteration vectors, and returns `NativeSparseSolveResult`
with a fresh original-matrix residual. BiCGSTAB can break down even when a
system is nonsingular; `BREAKDOWN` is not an inconsistency certificate. BASIC
calls the same kernel with `SPBICGSTAB`.

`NativeCsrMatrix::lsqr(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations)` solves rectangular
least-squares systems without forming `AᵀA`. It starts at zero and uses the
Golub-Kahan CPU iteration, so rank-deficient and underdetermined problems target
the ordinary Euclidean minimum-norm solution in exact arithmetic. Its
`NativeSparseLeastSquaresResult` reports both `||b-Ax||₂` and a freshly
recomputed stationarity norm; only the latter controls convergence. It is
`||Aᵀ(b-Ax)||₂` by default and `||D Aᵀ(b-Ax)||₂` under column scaling, with
matching threshold `max(rtol*||D Aᵀb||₂,atol)` (`D=I` by default). Column
scaling also requires every stationarity component to meet its own relative
and absolute tolerance, with a binary64 roundoff floor, so a large component
cannot mask an unresolved small one. Thus an inconsistent fit can be
`CONVERGED` while its ordinary residual remains positive. The operation shares the sparse axis,
entry, iteration, work and cancellation limits. For ill-scaled columns, use
`NativeCsrMatrix::lsqr_with_preconditioner(...,NativeLsqrPreconditioner::ColumnNorm)`
or BASIC `SPLSQR(...,"COLUMN")` to normalize each nonzero column to unit 2-norm.
The fit residual is always computed against the original matrix; the scaled
mode applies `D` only to the stationarity test. This right scaling changes the minimum-norm metric for rank-deficient or underdetermined
systems; use the default `None` mode to preserve the ordinary Euclidean choice.
Scaling that would underflow a stored coefficient is rejected. BASIC calls the
same kernel with `SPLSQR`.

Native zero axes retain shape: a `0 × n` matrix multiplies an `n`-vector into an
empty vector; its `n × 0` transpose multiplies an empty vector into `n` zeros.
The existing BASIC CSR1 format keeps positive dimensions and one-based indices.
Physics Jacobians retain their separate positive-dimension requirement.

NativeCsrMatrix::weighted_lsqr(b,weights,rtol,atol,max_iterations) and
weighted_lsqr_with_preconditioner solve min sum(wᵢ(bᵢ-Aᵢx)²) with the same
bounded CPU iteration. Weights must be finite, nonnegative and not all zero;
zero-weight rows are excluded. NativeSparseWeightedLeastSquaresResult reports
residuals and threshold using weights normalized by the maximum weight, plus
weight_scale for restoring original units. The fit norm scales by
sqrt(weight_scale) and the normal residual by weight_scale. A stored coefficient
that would underflow during row scaling is rejected. BASIC SPWLSQR uses this
same typed kernel, and the optional column preconditioner applies after row
weighting.

documents.title: Arithmetic, errors and recovery
documents.html:
multiply uses exact two-factor products per row and one final binary64 rounding. quadratic_form computes the supplied square matrix's complete x^T A x with exact triple products, then rounds once. It does not mirror a stored triangle, assume symmetry or certify positive definiteness. Input coefficients and vectors are binary64 values; these operations do not recover precision lost before those inputs were supplied.

Intermediate overflow/underflow and cancellation do not discard a representable final answer. Correct final binary64 underflow, including signed zero, is retained. A nonfinite final result is an error. Shape, invalid-data and interrupt errors return without changing the matrix or returning a partial vector/value. The BASIC SPQUAD(A,x) frontend shares this kernel and canonicalizes signed zero to positive zero, following the existing BASIC numeric contract. Native operations observe the runtime's interrupt mechanism. Logical input bounds do not impose process-wide memory isolation or constrain capacity already reserved by a native caller's input vectors.

documents.title: Bounded CPU complex Fourier transforms
documents.html:
NativeComplexFft exposes the same arbitrary-length CPU transform used by BASIC FFT and IFFT, without constructing interpreter Value lists:

use modernbasic::{error::Error, BasicComplex, NativeComplexFft};

fn spectrum(samples: &[f64]) -> Result<Vec<BasicComplex>, Error> {
    let input = samples
        .iter()
        .map(|sample| BasicComplex::new(*sample, 0.0))
        .collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()?;
    NativeComplexFft::forward(&input)
}

The forward convention uses a negative exponential and the inverse divides by the sample count. transform_in_place stages work and only replaces the input after a complete finite result is available; empty input, work-limit errors, interrupts and nonfinite outputs preserve the caller's buffer. Length is capped at one million elements, the internal convolution workspace at 2,097,152 elements, and estimated transform work at 160 million units. This allocating, staged interface is for bounded block analysis and scientific workloads, not a hard real-time audio callback. Rust and BASIC share the same checked kernel.

NativeSignalMath exposes the same bounded real convolution and correlation kernels as BASIC CONVOLVE, AUTOCORR and XCORR:

use modernbasic::{error::Error, NativeSignalMath};

fn analyze(samples: &[f64], impulse: &[f64]) -> Result<Vec<f64>, Error> {
    let filtered = NativeSignalMath::convolve(samples, impulse)?;
    let autocorrelation = NativeSignalMath::autocorrelation(&filtered, Some(256))?;
    Ok(autocorrelation)
}

Convolution and cross-correlation return the full linear result; cross-correlation uses BASIC's lag orientation. Autocorrelation returns symmetric negative-to-positive lags and accepts an optional maximum lag. Inputs and outputs are finite binary64, with exact product accumulation and one final rounding per result. Inputs and result lists are capped at one million elements, and each call is capped at ten million product operations with periodic interrupt checks. Empty-input and out-of-range lag behavior match the BASIC functions.

For workloads beyond the direct product budget, NativeSignalMath::convolve_fft and BASIC FFTCONVOLVE(left, right) compute full linear convolution with zero-padded radix-2 transforms. This path shares the bounded CPU FFT kernel and is binary64 approximate; floating-point transform error differs from the exact product-sum path. Inputs and outputs remain capped at one million elements, the padded transform obeys the FFT workspace/work limits, and calls observe interrupts. Use CONVOLVE when exact product accumulation is required and the operation count fits its ten-million-product cap.

The same type generates symmetric Hann, Hamming, Blackman, Blackman–Harris and Kaiser windows through NativeSignalMath::window(count, shape). Select a NativeSignalWindow variant; Kaiser takes a finite beta in [0,64] and shares BASIC's bounded modified-Bessel evaluation. Zero-length windows are empty and one-element windows contain 1. All windows cap the output at one million coefficients and observe interrupts; the Kaiser path also enforces the shared ten-million-operation budget.

documents.title: Stateful CPU sinc resampling
documents.html:
NativeSincResampler is a typed Rust block API for native audio consumers that need sample-rate conversion without allocating during processing. Construct it with input/output rates and the maximum input block size, then allocate the output slice once using max_output_frames_per_call():

use modernbasic::{error::Error, NativeSincResampler};

fn convert(input: &[f64]) -> Result<Vec<f64>, Error> {
    let mut resampler = NativeSincResampler::new(48_000, 44_100, 512)?;
    let mut output = vec![0.0; resampler.max_output_frames_per_call()];
    let count = resampler.output_frames_for_input(input.len())?;
    let written = resampler.process_into(input, &mut output[..count])?;
    let mut result = output[..written].to_vec();
    let tail_count = resampler.pending_flush_frames()?;
    let mut tail = vec![0.0; tail_count];
    let tail_written = resampler.flush_into(&mut tail)?;
    result.extend_from_slice(&tail[..tail_written]);
    Ok(result)
}

process_into consumes a complete block, emits only samples with sufficient lookahead, and uses a rational phase accumulator. output_frames_for_input reports the exact required slice length without changing state. flush_into emits the delayed end-of-stream tail with constant endpoint extension; processing after flush requires reset(). The lookahead is exposed in input frames through latency_input_frames(). Invalid samples, insufficient output space, work-limit exhaustion or interruption preserve converter state and leave the caller's output slice unchanged. Each call is bounded by the constructor's input-block size and the shared math work limit. Rate ratios requiring a radius above 32,768 frames are rejected.

The kernel is chunk-invariant and tested against passband, alias-rejection, DC, flush and recovery cases. Construction precomputes one coefficient row for each exact rational phase when the full table is at most 500,000 coefficients. Ratios whose phase table exceeds that cap retain the bounded per-output coefficient calculation. Both paths use the same rational phase and output contract. Live scheduler integration and hardware latency qualification remain separate work.

documents.title: Qualification and remaining work
documents.html:
The checkpoint passed 1,888 native Rust tests across 65 targets, strict application Clippy/Rustdoc, all ten exact-artifact phases and 68 math suites (188,351 checks). Each of ARM64 and RISC-V passed 72 affected-component/API tests under user emulation. The public quadratic API passed 264 independent exact-rational bit references on all three architectures, including finite cancellation, overflow rejection and signed-zero/subnormal cases. Source/test identities and executable hashes are in output/native-csr-2026-10-23/validation.json and the retained cross-component evidence. The BASIC frontend also passed 263 positive-dimension reference cases on each architecture and against the exact native executable. tools/check-native-csr.py --binary PATH --report REPORT.json retains this command-line regression suite; four success/failure/output-protection groups qualified the checker. It is additional to the 68-suite math gate.

The HiGHS Rust/BASIC optimizer adapter, broader independent cross-target application/reference gates, complete OS images and physical hardware acceptance remain open. A sparse matrix/quadratic kernel is a foundation for those tasks.

The subsequent registry checkpoint includes native-csr in the regular math qualification command: all 69 suites pass (188,614 checks), plus 467 Python regressions, on the same frozen executable. The earlier ten-phase acceptance record retains its original 68-suite scope. Evidence: output/native-csr-registry-2026-10-23/validation.json.

documents.title: Shared Rust LP/MIP models and worker execution
documents.html:
On Linux the crate exports NativeLinearModel, NativeOptimizationBounds, NativeVariableKind, NativeObjectiveSense, NativeOptimizationLimits and NativeOptimizationReport (including optional primal/dual data). They use the same NativeCsrMatrix, admission checks, exact primal kernels and worker protocol as BASIC LPSOLVE/MIPSOLVE. Bounds use Option<f64> endpoints; None is unbounded. NativeLinearModel::validate does not invoke native code.

solve_native_linear_model_with_worker(worker,provider,model,limits,checkpoint) accepts trusted executable/provider paths and a Rust cancellation callback. It starts a fresh resource-limited Linux worker and recomputes primal quality from the original model after admitting its bounded result. Native termination and dual values remain native claims. A candidate's independently_feasible flag means within the explicit absolute tolerance, not an exact certificate.

solve_native_linear_model(model,limits) uses the current executable and standard libhighs.so.1 lookup. Embedding applications using this convenience function must call dispatch_native_math_worker() before normal application/UI startup, returning its result when it is Some. The CLI and newly compiled BASIC applications perform this dispatch automatically. Applications can instead point the explicit-worker function at a verified ModernBASIC CLI executable.

Input and result frames are versioned and bounded; absent candidates remain None. Process failure, timeout or cancellation returns an error, never a made-up solver point. The trusted worker/provider are resource-contained native code, not a filesystem/network sandbox. Provider packaging/images and full cross-target/hardware acceptance remain open.

documents.title: Exact rational LP through optional QSopt_ex
documents.html:
The Linux crate exports NativeRational, NativeExactLinearProgram, NativeExactLpBounds, NativeExactLpCandidate and NativeExactLpStatus. Coefficients and bounds use reduced arbitrary-precision integer ratios. NativeExactLinearProgram::validate() checks dimensions, coefficient widths and bound ordering without starting a provider.

solve_native_exact_linear_program_with_worker(worker, provider, model, seconds, checkpoint) invokes a trusted QSopt_ex 2.5.10 esolver path through a fresh Rust worker process. The provider path is canonicalized before the worker changes to its private directory. solve_native_exact_linear_program(model, seconds) uses MODERNBASIC_QSOPT_EX_EXECUTABLE, defaulting to /usr/bin/esolver. Applications must call dispatch_native_math_worker() before UI or program startup. The provider inherits CPU, address-space, file-size and process-group limits; the worker uses private temporary files and deletes them on every exit path.

For an optimal status, the receiver parses exact rationals, restores omitted zero-valued variables, recomputes variable and row feasibility and the objective, then verifies exact reduced-cost stationarity, row-dual signs, and complementary slackness for every row and variable bound. An optimal status is returned only when these checks form an exact dual certificate. primal_verified reports the exact primal/objective checks. status_verified is true for an optimal result with the dual certificate, an infeasible result with a normalized exact Farkas witness, and an unbounded result with an exactly feasible base point and improving recession direction. The unboundedness check verifies every row and variable recession condition and strict objective improvement. Certificate construction shares the original solve deadline and bounded rational/model limits. The worker accepts only a bounded regular solution file from its private directory. It opens with Linux O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK|O_CLOEXEC, verifies the same regular-file device/inode and size after open, then caps reads at the protocol limit. A deterministic stale-check replacement test rejects a symlink and nonblocking FIFO; live concurrent races and broader flood tests remain open. Provider identity, cross-target execution, image packaging and release licensing/notice review remain open.

The real-provider independent reference suite includes eight seeded six- variable rational LPs with fractional data and duplicate-row degeneracy. The exact rational oracle enumerates all 74,613 six-row active sets per case, checks each candidate against every inequality and matches both objective senses and receiver-certified status. Eight models cover 596,904 active sets. Evidence: output/qsopt-ex-six-variable-2026-10-24/validation.json. Broader model families, provider identity, cross-target execution, image packaging and release licensing/notice review remain open.

Exact LP precision is tested through the Rust worker API and BASIC EXACTLPSOLVE. With D=2^13000+1, maximizing x+2y subject to 3x+4y<=1/D, x,y>=0 returns the exact optimum (0,1/(4D)) and objective 1/(2D), even though 1/D underflows binary64. A separate test passes 16,382-bit normalized numerator and denominator values through both APIs; the configured limits are 16,384 bits and 10,000 ASCII characters per rational. Serialized models are bounded at 2 MiB before text construction. The QSopt_ex CLI currently truncates extremely long solution lines near 4 KiB, and the exact receiver rejects those partial results. Evidence: output/qsopt-ex-rational-limit-2026-10-24/validation.json.

documents.title: Exact matrix curvature
documents.html:
NativeCsrMatrix::is_positive_semidefinite() and is_negative_semidefinite() prove curvature of an exactly symmetric square matrix using the same rational kernels as symbolic quadratic optimization and BASIC SPISPSD/SPISNSD. Native zero-by-zero matrices are semidefinite; the BASIC CSR1 format retains its positive-axis contract. Shape/symmetry errors and proof resource limits return errors, not false or approximate certificates.

documents.title: Native quadratic model and isolated candidate service (Linux)
documents.html:
NativeQuadraticModel { linear: NativeLinearModel, hessian: NativeCsrMatrix } represents x^T Q x / 2 + c^T x + offset. The full canonical CSR Hessian must match the number of variables and be exactly symmetric. validate() requires continuous variables and proves PSD for minimization or NSD for maximization using the shared exact curvature kernel. Nonconvex/wrong-sense objectives, mixed-integer QP, malformed dimensions and inconclusive resource-limited proofs return errors. Existing linear-model bounds and coefficient admission apply.

objective(&point) computes exact triple products and sums, divides by two, and rounds once to binary64. gradient(&point) computes Q*x+c with one exact accumulation per component. Nonfinite points/final values fail; overflowing intermediate products that cancel do not cause false overflow. These methods revalidate mutable model fields and support cooperative cancellation.

scaled_objective() returns (cost, hessian, exponent), with cost and Hessian multiplied exactly by 2^exponent. The largest nonzero coefficient is normalized to binary exponent 20 using integer significands/exponents, without constructing a possibly overflowing floating scaling factor. Any discarded bit, underflow, overflow, or nonzero scaled Hessian magnitude outside 1E-12 < ABS(Q) < 1E15 returns an error. An identically zero objective uses exponent zero. Constraints and bounds remain in the original model. The constant offset is deliberately excluded from solver scaling and must be included when reporting the original objective; no field in the original model is changed. This prepares objective scaling for the pinned provider but does not itself load or invoke that provider.

The isolated candidate service uses bounded versioned model and result frames. solve_native_quadratic_model_with_worker(worker,provider,model,limits,checkpoint) starts a fresh resource-limited worker; solve_native_quadratic_model(model,limits) uses the current executable and libhighs.so.1. Embedding applications using the convenience function must call dispatch_native_math_worker() before normal startup. The worker decodes and validates the bounded model before loading the provider, applies the exact power-of-two objective scaling and sends the exact symmetric Hessian as lower-triangular CSC. It confirms the provider retained the expected Hessian nonzeros.

NativeQuadraticCandidate carries native model/primal/dual statuses, an optional candidate point, the original-model objective recomputed by Rust, the native objective in its scaled units, and optional dual vectors. The receiver checks bounds and rows within the declared absolute tolerance and recalculates the original quadratic objective; unavailable candidates remain absent.

When both primal and dual vectors are available, the receiver independently recomputes relative primal-feasibility, stationarity, dual-sign and complementarity residuals. NativeQuadraticCandidate.kkt contains those values, and NativeQuadraticKktResiduals::satisfied() compares all four with limits.tolerance. The check uses exactly scaled objective coefficients and HiGHS dual values, with normalized floating-point residuals. A provider “optimal” status remains only a solver claim if kkt is absent or fails; passing residuals are numerical qualification, not an exact-arithmetic proof. BASIC QPSOLVE now exposes the checked candidate as a composable HIGHSQP1 record. Seeded CPU references cover 35 two-variable diagonal cases, 24 three-variable non-diagonal positive-definite cases, 12 five-variable cases, and eight six-variable and eight seven-variable cases with dependent active rows and non-unique duals. Callers must inspect the KKT fields alongside native status. Singular-Hessian models, broader conditioning, provider packaging and cross-target/hardware acceptance remain open. A seven-variable Rust API reference records stationarity near 1.998e-7: the default KKT threshold 1e-7 rejects it, while an explicit 1e-6 threshold passes. Five additional seven-variable models pass through the Rust API and BASIC with a positive-semidefinite singular Hessian: four bounded zero-curvature coordinates are selected by a linear objective, while one flat interval yields a non-unique primal optimum. A separate seven-variable model with a two-dimensional nullspace verifies the full bounded flat optimal face. Nullspaces above two dimensions remain open. The resource-limited worker contains crashes and resource use but is not a filesystem/network sandbox.

Evidence and exact qualification scope: output/quadratic-model-2026-10-23/basic-qp-checks-v4.log and output/native-backend-checks-Qln6Ug0J/. The earlier in-process-foundation receipt is output/quadratic-model-2026-10-23/validation-v2.json.

documents.title: Exact integer systems with optional 4ti2 (Linux)
documents.html:
The crate exports NativeIntegerSystem, NativeIntegerRelation, NativeIntegerSign, NativeIntegerSolutions and NativeIntegerLimits. solve_native_integer_system_with_worker(worker, model, limits, checkpoint) starts the current executable as a worker and dynamically loads the optional 4ti2 libzsolve/lib4ti2common C API. The convenience solve_native_integer_system(model, limits) uses the current executable and standard soname lookup; embedding applications must call dispatch_native_math_worker() before normal startup. The BASIC ZSOLVE frontend uses this same Rust API and returns its checked 4TI2Z1 record.

The model carries arbitrary-precision BigInt rows, RHS values, relations and variable-sign constraints. The provider runs in the existing resource-limited Linux worker, with a private temporary project directory and bounded input and result frames. Rust parses the provider's matrix files as exact decimal integers and independently verifies every returned inhomogeneous, homogeneous and free vector against the original constraints and signs. This does not independently prove that the provider returned a complete basis. The Markov CLI is admitted only when its bounded --version probe reports 4ti2 1.6.10 with arbitrary- precision integers. It retains at most 4096 output bytes; the private worker's existing 8 MiB file-size limit caps output written before validation. The qualified amd64 runtime checks GNU build IDs for the actual C API libzsolve/lib4ti2common files and direct GMP/GMPXX libraries before loading; the Markov path checks 4ti2gmp and its direct 4ti2/GMP libraries before use. Unadmitted builds are rejected. These checks do not authenticate package signatures or attest every transitively mapped object. Other architectures, complete package-image integration and GPL notices remain open; no 4ti2 library is bundled by this checkpoint. Evidence: output/4ti2-evaluation-2026-10-23/runtime-identity-v2.json.

NativeIntegerKernel { matrix }, NativeIntegerBasisKind::{Hilbert,Graver,Markov}, and NativeIntegerBasis { vectors } provide direct exact kernel-basis access. compute_native_integer_basis_with_worker(worker,kernel,kind,limits,checkpoint) uses the same isolated provider path. compute_native_integer_basis uses the current executable. The worker uses 4ti2's Hilbert or Graver C API state, and invokes 4ti2gmp markov for Markov calculations. Set MODERNBASIC_4TI2_MARKOV_EXECUTABLE when that executable is not on PATH; the process runs inside the same bounded worker group. Before solving, Rust requires the executable to report the tested 1.6.10 release and GMP arbitrary-precision mode; the probe has a five-second deadline, retains at most 4096 bytes, and inherits the worker's 8 MiB file-size bound and process-group cancellation. Rust validates exact kernel membership for every returned vector, enforces nonnegativity for Hilbert vectors, removes duplicate rows, and uses an owner-only temporary directory that is deleted after the operation. Vector checks do not certify basis completeness. BASIC exposes HBASIS(A[,seconds]), GRAVER(A[,seconds]) and MARKOV(A[,seconds]), returning composable 4TI2H1, 4TI2G1 and 4TI2M1 records.

Native-provider evidence: output/4ti2-evaluation-2026-10-23/validation-4ti2-bases-v4.json.

documents.title: One-sided power-density analysis
documents.html:
NativeSignalMath::periodogram(samples, sample_rate, window) accepts borrowed real sample and optional window slices, returning NativePeriodogram with frequencies_hz and power_density. BASIC PERIODOGRAM calls the same kernel. The estimator uses every supplied sample, no detrending or implicit padding, window-energy normalization and doubled interior bins; DC and even-length Nyquist are counted once. It reuses the CPU arbitrary-length FFT. Empty input, nonpositive/nonfinite sample rate, mismatched or zero-energy windows, nonfinite samples/weights and resource excess return errors. Input slices are unchanged on failure/cancellation. Scale normalization avoids many intermediate overflows; ordinary binary64 rounding, underflow and finite output range remain.

The input limit is one million samples, with the existing FFT scratch/work caps. This is an allocating analysis call, not a device-callback API. It neither records audio nor estimates a fundamental note. See programs/science/spectrum_analysis.bas for a two-tone example and tools/check-periodogram.py for independent SciPy power-density and Parseval comparisons.

documents.title: Matrix-free nonsymmetric separable solves
documents.html: NativeKroneckerSum::gmres(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial) and gmres_with_restart(...,restart) return NativeSparseSolveResult, sharing BASIC KRONSGMRES and the original sparse restarted GMRES recurrence. The operator is I_n ⊗ A + B ⊗ I_m on row-major fields. Its row-equilibrated action uses the two factors directly and freshly checks original-operator residuals. Unlike CG, nonsymmetric/indefinite factors are accepted; convergence is not promised for singular or ill-conditioned systems. Restart is 1–128, with a size-aware default up to 30 and at most two million retained basis elements. The existing million-element factor/vector and 100-million solve-work caps, finite checks and cancellation remain. No full grid matrix or ILU factor is built. Error, iteration exhaustion, breakdown and stagnation are explicit; inputs remain reusable. General callback operators use NativeLinearOperator, described below; other matrix-free preconditioners remain separate work.

## Matrix-free nonsymmetric separable solves

`NativeKroneckerSum::gmres(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial)` and
`gmres_with_restart(...,restart)` return `NativeSparseSolveResult`, sharing
BASIC `KRONSGMRES` and the original sparse restarted GMRES recurrence. The
operator is `I_n ⊗ A + B ⊗ I_m` on row-major fields. Its row-equilibrated action
uses the two factors directly and freshly checks original-operator residuals.
Unlike CG, nonsymmetric/indefinite factors are accepted; convergence is not
promised for singular or ill-conditioned systems. Restart is 1–128, with a
size-aware default up to 30 and at most two million retained basis elements.
The existing million-element factor/vector and 100-million solve-work caps,
finite checks and cancellation remain. No full grid matrix or ILU factor is
built. Error, iteration exhaustion, breakdown and stagnation are explicit;
inputs remain reusable. General callback operators use `NativeLinearOperator`,
described below; other matrix-free preconditioners remain separate work.

documents.title: Caller-supplied fixed linear operators
documents.html:
NativeLinearOperator::new(dimension, callback) owns a callable FnMut(&[f64], &mut [f64]) -> Result<(), Error>. It must fill every output slot with a finite value and implement a fixed linear map. dimension() reports the validated size (1 through one million). gmres(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial) returns NativeSparseSolveResult using the shared sparse GMRES recurrence, without an assembled matrix or interpreter data allocation. The callback may compose existing native kernels and caller-owned model data. This is an allocating analysis solve, not a hard-real-time audio callback API.

gmres_with_options(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial,restart,row_scales) adds an explicit restart (1–128) and optional positive finite row divisors. Left scaling follows callback evaluation; nonfinite raw output is rejected even if a later scaling could make it finite. Fresh original-callback residuals decide convergence. A callback's rounded products define that residual; this interface does not provide CSR's exact row-product accumulation inside arbitrary code. Default restart is size-aware up to 30, basis storage is at most two million elements, solver vector work is capped at 100 million charged operations, and there are at most 10000 callback applications per solve. Inputs and initial guess are borrowed and unchanged. Callback errors propagate without partial solution delivery, but caller side effects are not rolled back.

NativeCancellationToken checkpoints run around each callback and during solver vector work. They cannot interrupt a blocking native callback; caller code should cooperate with cancellation for expensive internal work. The resource limits bound the solver and callback count, not arbitrary callback allocations/work. Linearity, repeatability and useful conditioning remain caller obligations. BASIC MFGMRES uses the same implementation with a scoped DEF FN adapter.

gmres_with_preconditioner(b,rtol,atol,max_iterations,initial,restart,&mut callback) accepts a second FnMut(&[f64], &mut [f64]) -> Result<(), Error> computing a fixed left inverse action P^-1*r. It fills every output slot, with the same finite-output validation as the forward operator. Native LU or sparse factors can be retained by the closure and reused. Both maps must remain fixed and linear; the preconditioner must be nonsingular. This is ordinary GMRES, not flexible GMRES, and does not validate those mathematical properties. A bad preconditioner cannot bypass the original-residual convergence check. Zero projected residual with a nonzero original residual returns BREAKDOWN.

The combined operator/preconditioner application count is at most 10,000 per solve; vector work, basis storage and cancellation limits are shared. Validation precedes both callbacks, except mathematical breakdown/output errors that can only be discovered on invocation. The preconditioner is not invoked when an initial solution already satisfies tolerance; the forward operator still verifies that residual. Preconditioner errors propagate and inputs remain borrowed; side effects are not rolled back. Existing gmres and positive row-scaling APIs retain their behavior. BASIC accepts "FNPC" in place of the eighth row-divisor argument.

This inverse-action convention and original-residual stopping rule also appear in SciPy's GMRES documentation. Qualification uses independent dense LU and sparse SuperLU/Woodbury solutions, not SciPy GMRES as the sole reference. See preconditioned_transport.bas for 2048-state nonlocal transport with a reusable sparse LU preconditioner.
