Ebers–Moll. Diffusion uses transport current, and PNP mirrors the voltage and
charge signs. No native solver state or BASIC value is retained by a model.

`NativeCircuitElement::ChargeNpn {c,b,e,model}` and `ChargePnp` participate in
the same shared circuit analysis and checkpoint APIs. Their active BE/BC
branches contribute separate stored-voltage edges. Tied terminals and disabled
branches add no storage edge; exact common-mode differences survive retained
coordinates. The shared mass, full-rate Jacobian, source forcing and structural
sparse paths iterate both branches. Storage-export admission includes both
rows in the prescribed-storage map. Model tags 14/15 serialize all 14 parameters;
existing ordinary/switched record versions are unchanged.

BASIC NPNQ/PNPQ rows and DEVICE inspection expose the native model. Full units,
parameter ranges, tensor axes and physical omissions are documented in the
language reference. Independent laws, coupled AC, charge-balance trajectories,
source corners, sparse/fresh-process persistence and native/export workloads
are qualified in `output/bipolar-charge-2026-10-26/validation.json`. MOS models,
base-width/high-injection effects, non-quasistatic transport, general index
reduction and production/OS/hardware acceptance remain open.


### Native constant-slope MOS charge sheet

`NativeChargeSheetMosModel::new(threshold,beta,slope,kelvin,oxide_capacitance,body)`
validates the long-channel model above the shared native circuit engine. `body`
is a `NativeDynamicJunctionModel` at exactly the same actual temperature, with
positive zero-bias capacitance. `parameters()` returns the five core parameters;
`body_junction()` returns the exact bulk model. `evaluate([Vd,Vg,Vs,Vb],pmos)`
returns `NativeMosSample { currents, jacobian, charges, capacitance,
charge_hessian }`, with four signed terminal axes and analytic derivatives.
`NativeCircuitElement::Nmos/Pmos { d,g,s,b,model }` supplies direct Rust reuse;
BASIC NMOSQ/PMOSQ and DEVICE expose the same implementation.

The full law, units, charge-reference threshold and limitations are specified in
the language reference's Long-channel MOS terminal charge section. Implicit
endpoint charge avoids exponential overflow in strong inversion; exact scaled
ratios avoid intermediate slope/temperature overflow, with unrepresentable
normalization derivatives rejected. A differential
charge solve resolves small drain bias. Second derivatives produce the full
rate-dependent transient Jacobian. Terminal derivatives obey current/charge
conservation and reference-voltage invariance; the charge matrix is generally
nonreciprocal. Bulk junctions use the existing bounded depletion/diffusion law.

Four-terminal structural stamps enter shared dense/KLU patterns, storage maps,
source-rate loads, source-corner projection, switching and continuation.
Storage coordinates retain differences relative to source before evaluation;
this avoids reconstructing tiny gate/drain biases from rounded common-mode
voltages. New model identity tags 16/17 store all twelve parameters and four
nodes in ordinary/switched records. Earlier tags and record versions remain
valid. No provider, GPU dependency or separate runtime engine is introduced.

Qualification includes independent 90-digit Lambert-W/charge-integral derivative
references, CMOS inverter DC/AC/Radau charge balance, sparse and fresh-process
continuation, cancellation, finite-input overflow errors and standalone parity.
Evidence: `output/mos-charge-2026-10-26/validation.json`. Process fitting,
advanced short-channel/body models, noise/thermal/NQS, general index reduction
and physical hardware acceptance remain open.

Mathematical background: [EPFL EKV model equations](https://www.wrcad.com/xictools/docs/model_docs/ekv-2.6/ekv_v262.pdf) and [terminal charge integrals](https://ekvmodel.com/notebooks/Intrinsic%20capacitances/Intrinsic_capacitances.html). The implemented constant-slope approximation and its limits are specified above.


The CPU IDA bridge uses a Newton convergence coefficient of 0.03 for ordinary
integration, keeping the supplied relative/absolute integration tolerances and
algebraic error control intact. This addresses step stagnation observed in a
strict-tolerance CMOS restart with a correct reduced residual/Jacobian. The
variational-sensitivity API retains its explicit coefficient setting. Circuit
and general IDA dense/sparse/event/initialization references are checked together;
this solver setting is not an added physical effect in the MOS model. See
[SUNDIALS nonlinear convergence control](https://sundials.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ida/Usage/index.html).

documents.title: Native point projections and clearances
documents.html:
PROJECTLINE2D(p,origin,direction), PROJECTRAY2D(p,origin,direction) and PROJECTSEGMENT2D(p,a,b) have corresponding 3D forms. Points/directions are ordinary two- or three-element lists. PROJECTPLANE3D(p,origin,normal) uses the plane through origin with the supplied normal. Direction/normal need not have unit length. A line permits any real parameter; a ray starts at origin and extends in the positive direction; a segment includes both endpoints.

Each returns {closestPoint,offset,distance}. offset is input point minus the mathematical closest point, and distance is its unsigned Euclidean length in the same units as the coordinates. Offset is computed independently of the rounded closest point. Use the returned distance for clearance tests: subtracting the returned point can lose a small separation at large coordinates. Components are binary64, so a rounded point is not guaranteed to lie exactly on the primitive. There is no hidden positional tolerance or coordinate snapping.

10 R=PROJECTSEGMENT3D({3,4,0},{0,0,0},{2,0,0})
20 PRINT R(1): REM {2,0,0}, closest point
30 PRINT R(2): REM {1,4,0}, offset
40 PRINT R(3): REM SQR(17), distance

A segment whose endpoints coincide is a point. Zero line/ray direction and zero plane normal are errors. Inputs must be finite with the required dimension; nonfinite final coordinates, offsets or distance produce an overflow error and leave an assignment target unchanged. A huge line parameter alone is not an error: it is never needed to form the result. Distance rounds the square root of an exact squared-residual ratio using integer comparisons, so even individually underflowed offset components do not erase a representable distance. Point/offset components are rounded once from exact rational expressions in the represented inputs; distance is also correctly rounded for the represented inputs. Results are binary64 values, not exact symbolic distances or certified interval bounds.

The Rust NativeGeometry methods project_line, project_ray, project_segment accept [f64;N] for N=2 or 3 and return NativePointProjection<N> with public point, offset, distance fields. project_plane accepts 3D inputs. Native distance(a,b) shares the implementation used by BASIC DIST and DIST3D. All queries honor native cancellation and have constant bounded work and storage; small fixed-size accumulators/temporary vectors do not grow with scene size. These are individual point/primitive queries, not an acceleration index or a continuous collision solver. No external numerical provider is required.

documents.title: Exact-input spatial hit reports
documents.html:
Rust and BASIC share exact represented-input classification for closed box overlap, closed-ball overlap, forward ray/box intervals and isolated ray/triangle crossings. AABBHIT, SPHEREHIT, RAYAABB and RAYTRIANGLE retain their existing signatures and miss conventions. Touching counts as overlap. Zero-radius balls are points; zero-width box axes are allowed. Bounds must be ordered, radii nonnegative and directions nonzero. All coordinates and dimensions must be finite 3D values.

RAYBOXHIT3D(origin,direction,min,max) returns an empty list for a miss, otherwise {entryPoint,exitPoint,entryParameter,exitParameter}. Each point is a three-element list. Each parameter field is {t} if the parameter rounds to a finite binary64 value, or {} if it overflows. The interval is clipped to t>=0, so starting inside the box produces the original point and {0} at entry. The exit point remains available even when its parameter overflows. RAYAABB only needs the entry parameter; an unrepresentable exit no longer causes a spurious overflow error.

RAYTRIANGLEHIT3D(origin,direction,a,b,c) returns an empty list when there is no isolated forward-ray crossing within the closed triangle. A hit returns {point,barycentric,parameter}, with three weights for a,b,c and a parameter field using the same {t} / {} convention. The triangle is two-sided. Parallel, coplanar and degenerate triangles have no isolated crossing in this API and return an empty list; constructing coplanar overlap segments remains separate work. There is no near-parallel tolerance. A representable nonzero determinant is not required: exact product signs decide the hit before any coordinate is rounded.

10 H=RAYTRIANGLEHIT3D({.25,.25,1},{0,0,-1},{0,0,0},{1,0,0},{0,1,0})
20 IF LEN(H)=0 THEN END
30 PRINT H(1): REM {.25,.25,0}, hit point
40 PRINT H(2): REM {.5,.25,.25}, weights for a,b,c
50 T=H(3): IF LEN(T)>0 THEN PRINT T(1)

A ray uses origin+t*direction; t is physical distance only for a unit direction. Very small positive parameters may round to zero. Use the returned point instead of reconstructing it from a rounded parameter. Point, parameter and barycentric components are independently rounded once from exact rational expressions in the represented inputs. Rounded weights may not sum to exactly one, and a rounded hit point need not lie exactly on the mathematical surface. Classification uses the unrounded inputs, with no implicit snapping or positional tolerance.

The legacy RAYAABB and RAYTRIANGLE calls still report overflow when the required hit parameter does not fit; the detailed reports preserve the finite point in that case. Other invalid inputs produce errors before assignment, preserving targets. These constant-sized queries honor native cancellation and use bounded exact product/ratio kernels already shared by the math engine. They need no numerical provider and do not attach physics bodies or create a spatial acceleration index.

Native crate-root NativeGeometry exposes:

  • aabbs_intersect_3d(min_a,max_a,min_b,max_b) -> Result<bool,Error>.
  • spheres_intersect_3d(a,ra,b,rb) -> Result<bool,Error> for closed balls.
  • ray_box_3d(origin,direction,min,max) -> Result<Option<NativeRayBoxHit3>,Error>. The report has entry and exit, both NativeRayPoint3 {point,parameter}.
  • ray_triangle_3d(origin,direction,a,b,c) -> Result<Option<NativeRayTriangleHit3>,Error>. The report has point, barycentric, and parameter.

Points and weights are [f64;3]. Report parameters are Option<f64>: None means parameter overflow, while the outer None means no reported hit. General geometry, mesh-wide constructions, other primitive pairs, broader curve/path families and installed CAD/physics qualification remain open. Triangle point coordinates and linear closest pairs are described in their dedicated sections below.

Evidence: output/spatial-queries-2026-10-26/validation.json when accepted. The independent reference uses exact rational squared-distance and slab equations, plus an exact Gaussian-elimination solve of the ray/triangle affine system. programs/science/ray_picking.bas is an editable consumer, including the three reproduced defects and optional-parameter examples.

documents.title: Shared polynomial curves
documents.html:
BASIC accepts two, three or four control points, each consistently 2D or 3D, defining linear, quadratic or cubic Bezier curves on parameter 0 through 1. Coincident controls, closed curves, cusps and collinear reversals are valid. Nonfinite coordinates, inconsistent dimensions and parameters outside this interval are errors.

  • BEZIERPOINT(controls,t) returns the point.
  • BEZIERDERIV(controls,t[,order]) returns a parameter derivative. Order defaults to 1 and may be 0 through 3; orders above the degree return zero.
  • BEZIERSPLIT(controls,t) returns {leftControls,rightControls}. Each new curve uses parameter 0 through 1, so derivative magnitudes change with its span.
  • BEZIERSAMPLE(controls,tolerance[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]]) returns {parameters,points,{maximumDeviation},status}. An empty deviation list means the estimate exceeds binary64 range. The ordered polyline covers the whole curve, even when a limit prevents convergence. Status is CONVERGED, SEGMENT_LIMIT or RESOLUTION_LIMIT; only CONVERGED meets the tolerance. Defaults are 4096 segments and depth 40; hard limits are 65536 segments and depth 52. Tolerance is positive, finite and expressed in coordinate units.
  • BEZIERLENGTH(controls[,absTol[,relTol[,maxEvaluations[,maxIntervals]]]]) returns {length,estimatedAbsoluteError,evaluations,intervals,status}. Defaults/limits match shared quadrature: absolute tolerance 1E-9, zero relative tolerance, one million evaluations and 4096 intervals. Only CONVERGED meets the estimated tolerance. The error estimate is heuristic.

Crate-root NativeBezier<N>::new(&[[f64;N]]) exposes the same kernels for N=2/3: degree, control_points, point, derivative, split, sample_uniform, sample(NativeCurveSamplingOptions) and length(NativeQuadratureOptions). NativeCurveSamples<N> contains parameters, points, optional maximum_deviation and NativeCurveSamplingStatus. Uniform sampling takes 1..65536 segments. Native calls observe shared cancellation and allocate bounded storage. BASIC returns ordinary lists; user programs remain freely editable.

Curve components and derivatives accumulate exact products of original binary64 inputs and round once. Split controls independently round from their exact de Casteljau expressions; evaluating a rounded subcurve need not reproduce the unsplit curve bit for bit. Final derivative overflow is an error. Length normalizes speed by a power of two derived from exact control differences and rescales its report. This retains subnormal lengths and avoids unrepresentable intermediate speeds when the final length is finite. Numerical quadrature is not a certified length enclosure; cusp/resolution/work limits remain explicit.

Adaptive sampling splits the worst remaining interval. Its conservative displacement estimate uses h^2/8 times a componentwise bound on the original second derivative, plus endpoint rounding margins. It handles collinear reversals and coincident endpoints. Points are evaluated from the original curve, avoiding repeated subdivision drift. Coordinate tolerance does not imply screen-space accuracy after an arbitrary transform.

The preexisting BASIC BEZIER drawing statement and renderer C/Q paths now use this backend with adaptive sampling in local coordinates (0.25 units, at most 256 segments, depth 24), replacing private fixed-16-segment formulas. Rendering uses the complete approximation at these limits; its existing API does not report mathematical tolerance status. SVG output retains analytic paths. Screen-space transform-aware quality and sustained installed rendering remain separate qualification tasks.

Definitions follow the primary MIT evaluation/subdivision reference and Michigan Tech derivative notes. The chord estimate uses the linear interpolation remainder. No external curve code or dependency is incorporated.

Rational surfaces, broader curve families, composite continuity and arc-length parameterization and CAD/physics application qualification remain open. General triangle queries are now covered in the triangle section below. Evidence: output/bezier-curves-2026-10-26/validation.json once verified.

documents.title: Shared 3D transforms and camera math
documents.html:
Crate-root NativeTransform3 stores a finite row-major 4-by-4 matrix applied to column vectors. new(matrix) accepts singular matrices; identity() and matrix() construct/read the value. translation([x,y,z]), scaling([x,y,z]) and rotation(NativeQuaternion) build affine transforms. Zero scales are allowed. compose(right) applies right first, then self. inverse() returns the inverse of any nonsingular finite 4-by-4 input when its rounded coefficients fit binary64. It uses exact-input cofactors/determinants; exact singularity is an error, with no arbitrary small-pivot rejection threshold. This specialized inverse does not change general dense BASIC INVERSE.

BASIC adds TRANSFORMCOMPOSE(left,right) and TRANSFORMINVERSE(matrix). Existing TRANSLATE3D, SCALE3D, ROTATE3D, TRANSFORMPOINT, TRANSFORMVECTOR, LOOKAT, ORTHOGRAPHIC and PERSPECTIVEMAT use this same Rust implementation. Native point([x,y,z]) divides exact homogeneous row sums before rounding; exact W=0 is an error. Native vector([x,y,z]) uses only the upper-left 3-by-3 block, ignoring translation and the last row. It is not a projective tangent or surface-normal transform; normals have the separate NativeSurfaceMath::oriented_normal / NORMALTRANSFORM3D API.

NativeQuaternion::rotate_vector evaluates the original-input Hamilton sandwich divided by the exact squared norm. Tiny vector components are not scaled away. Rotation matrix entries and raw Hamilton product components also round once from original-input expressions. Zero quaternions cannot define rotations. A returned matrix rounds each coefficient before later application: direct quaternion rotation can therefore retain small effects that its rounded matrix cannot represent. Likewise an inverse matrix is rounded; ill-conditioned transforms can amplify rounding and an inverse round trip need not be exact.

look_at(eye,target,up) uses exact differences/cross products to detect degeneracy, then approximate normalization to build a right-handed view whose forward direction is -Z. Coincident eye/target and zero/parallel up are errors. Translation uses exact dot products with the final rounded basis. orthographic(left,right,bottom,top,near,far) accepts ordered x/y extents and 0<=near<far. perspective(fovY,aspect,near,far) accepts radians 0<fovY<PI, aspect>0 and 0<near<far. Both map near/far to normalized depth -1/+1. Projection depth/orthographic coefficients retain exact endpoint differences; perspective field-of-view coefficients use approximate trigonometry. Axis-angle construction, quaternion normalization and SLERP also remain floating approximations; these are not symbolic or interval-valued rotations.

Inputs and required outputs must be finite. Invalid shape, degeneracy, exact singularity, cancellation or final overflow raises an error before assignment. Underflow rounds to the nearest representable value, possibly zero. Exact arithmetic prevents avoidable intermediate overflow, not true output overflow. Work/storage are bounded per 4-by-4 operation, and native queries honor the shared cancellation token. No external math provider or GPU is required.

programs/science/camera_transforms.bas composes a camera, animates quaternion poses and checks model/inverse consistency. Independent qualification uses Fraction homogeneous arithmetic, a separate Gauss-Jordan inverse, exact Hamilton products and a 120-digit camera reference. Evidence is recorded in output/geometry-transforms-2026-10-26/validation.json when accepted. Mesh-wide constructions, other primitive closest pairs, broader curve/path families and sustained installed graphics/CAD/physics workloads remain open; this checkpoint does not complete general geometry.

upper-left 3-by-3 block, ignoring translation and the last row. It is not a

`NativeSurfaceMath::oriented_normal` / `NORMALTRANSFORM3D` API.

`NativeQuaternion::rotate_vector` evaluates the original-input Hamilton sandwich
divided by the exact squared norm. Tiny vector components are not scaled away.
Rotation matrix entries and raw Hamilton product components also round once
from original-input expressions. Zero quaternions cannot define rotations.
A returned matrix rounds each coefficient before later application: direct
quaternion rotation can therefore retain small effects that its rounded matrix
cannot represent. Likewise an inverse matrix is rounded; ill-conditioned
transforms can amplify rounding and an inverse round trip need not be exact.

`look_at(eye,target,up)` uses exact differences/cross products to detect
degeneracy, then approximate normalization to build a right-handed view whose
forward direction is -Z. Coincident eye/target and zero/parallel up are errors.
Translation uses exact dot products with the final rounded basis.
`orthographic(left,right,bottom,top,near,far)` accepts ordered x/y extents and
0<=near<far. `perspective(fovY,aspect,near,far)` accepts radians 0<fovY<PI,
aspect>0 and 0<near<far. Both map near/far to normalized depth -1/+1.
Projection depth/orthographic coefficients retain exact endpoint differences;
perspective field-of-view coefficients use approximate trigonometry.
Axis-angle construction, quaternion normalization and SLERP also remain
floating approximations; these are not symbolic or interval-valued rotations.

Inputs and required outputs must be finite. Invalid shape, degeneracy, exact
singularity, cancellation or final overflow raises an error before assignment.
Underflow rounds to the nearest representable value, possibly zero. Exact
arithmetic prevents avoidable intermediate overflow, not true output overflow.
Work/storage are bounded per 4-by-4 operation, and native queries honor the
shared cancellation token. No external math provider or GPU is required.

`programs/science/camera_transforms.bas` composes a camera, animates quaternion
poses and checks model/inverse consistency. Independent qualification uses
Fraction homogeneous arithmetic, a separate Gauss-Jordan inverse, exact
Hamilton products and a 120-digit camera reference. Evidence is recorded in
`output/geometry-transforms-2026-10-26/validation.json` when accepted.
Mesh-wide constructions, other primitive closest pairs, broader
curve/path families and sustained installed graphics/CAD/physics workloads
remain open; this checkpoint does not complete general geometry.

documents.title: Triangle coordinates and closest points
documents.html:
TRIANGLECOORDS2D(p,a,b,c) returns signed barycentric coordinates of p in the triangle's affine frame. Its 3D form first projects p orthogonally to the triangle plane. These coordinates may lie outside the triangle. PROJECTTRIANGLE2D(p,a,b,c) and PROJECTTRIANGLE3D instead find the closest point on the closed triangle, including its interior.

All four take ordinary 2D/3D point lists and return {point,offset,distance,weights,feature$,degenerate}. Offset is p minus the unrounded point; distance is its unsigned Euclidean length. Weights are ordered A, B, C. The feature string is "FACE", "AB", "BC", "CA", "A", "B", "C", or (coordinates only) "OUTSIDE". In 3D the feature classifies the projected point, not whether p lies in the plane.

10 R=PROJECTTRIANGLE3D({2,2,3},{0,0,0},{2,0,0},{0,2,0})
20 PRINT R(1): REM {1,1,0}
30 PRINT R(4): REM {0,0.5,0.5}
40 PRINT R(5): REM BC
50 PRINT R(3): REM SQR(11), actual clearance

A collinear or coincident triangle has no unique plane coordinates: TRIANGLECOORDS reports an illegal-quantity error. PROJECTTRIANGLE treats it as its segment/point convex hull and returns degenerate=-1 (otherwise 0). Degenerate weights still reconstruct the exact closest point before rounding, but are not unique. Ties select AB, BC, CA in that order, and a zero-length edge selects its first vertex. Relabelling degenerate vertices may change weights and feature without changing the point or distance.

Point/offset components and weights round once from exact rational expressions; distance uses a correctly rounded square root of the exact squared residual. Classification and candidate-distance comparisons occur before rounding, with no geometric tolerance. A weight that rounds to zero can still denote an exact positive contribution. Rounded weights need not sum to exactly one; subtracting the returned point need not reproduce the returned offset. Use distance directly for clearances. If an unbounded coordinate weight cannot fit binary64, weights is an empty list; finite point/offset/distance remain available. Closest-triangle weights always fit. Required nonfinite outputs produce overflow errors, and failed assignments leave their old value intact. All inputs must be finite and have the requested dimension. Native cancellation is honored.

Rust exports NativeTriangleProjection<N>, NativeTriangleFeature and NativeGeometry::triangle_coordinates/project_triangle for N=2 or 3. The report has point, offset, distance, barycentric: Option<[f64;3]>, feature, and degenerate fields. Feature has as_str(). These kernels use existing bounded integer arithmetic and shared final rounding, with no new dependency. There are only four input points, at most three edge candidates, and fixed binary64 exponent bounds; work/storage do not grow with a mesh. This exact path costs more than unchecked floating-point formulas; it is not a mesh acceleration structure or continuous collision engine.

Full geometry inventory, reference sources and qualification: GEOMETRY.md.

## Linear primitive closest pairs

`Ray {origin,direction}`, and `Segment {start,end}` variants.

first/second points, independently computed offset, distance,
`parameters:[Option<f64>;2]`, `features:[NativeLinearFeature;2]`,
parallel, unique, `degenerate:[bool;2]`, and intersects.
Feature variants are Interior, Start, End, Point and have `as_str()`.
Missing parameters mean overflow, not absent geometry. Unique describes the
geometric pair; intersects uses exact separation, even if distance underflows.
The fixed-dimension Rust implementation shares exact coordinates and rounding
with triangle queries. Full constraints, degeneracy/tie rules, BASIC examples,

documents.title: Linear and plane intersection sets
documents.html:
NativeGeometry::intersect_linear(first,second) accepts existing NativeLinearPrimitive<N> for N=2 or 3; intersect_plane(primitive,origin,normal) accepts 3D inputs. Both return NativeLinearIntersection<N> with public kind, points, optional direction, first_parameters and second_parameters fields. NativeIntersectionKind has Empty, Point, Segment, Ray, Line and as_str(). Reports contain at most two points; parameter vectors hold Option<f64> values for those points. None means parameter overflow, whereas a plane's absent second parameterization has zero entries. Classification uses exact represented inputs; output coordinates are rounded binary64 and are not symbolic objects. All constraints, orientation/degeneracy rules, BASIC access and evidence are in GEOMETRY.md.

Closed triangle intersection sets

NativeGeometry::intersect_triangle accepts a NativeLinearPrimitive<N> and three vertices (N=2 or 3), returning NativeTriangleIntersection<N> with kind, points, parameters, barycentric and degenerate fields. It includes full coplanar chords and degenerate convex hulls. See Geometry for ordering, exact-input classification, rounded output and cancellation.

Full triangle-pair intersections

NativeGeometry::intersect_triangles(first,second) accepts two [[f64;N];3] triangles (N=2 or 3). NativeTrianglePairIntersection exposes kind, points, first_barycentric, second_barycentric, degenerate and projection_axes. Results include coplanar polygons and collapsed hulls. Projection axes are zero-based in Rust. See Geometry for canonical ordering, precision, resource and cancellation contracts.

Plane systems and triangle/plane slices

NativePlane3 {origin:[f64;3],normal:[f64;3]} describes a finite plane with nonzero normal. NativeGeometry::intersect_planes(&[NativePlane3]) accepts 1..64 planes and returns NativePlaneIntersection3: kind (Empty/Point/Line/Plane), point, direction and normal, with each vector an Option<[f64;3]>. NativeGeometry::intersect_triangle_plane([[f64;3];3],NativePlane3) returns NativeTrianglePlaneIntersection3 with kind, points, barycentric, degenerate and zero-based projection_axes. NativeBoundedIntersectionKind is an alias of the existing NativeTrianglePairKind; old API names remain compatible. Exact classification, minimax line representatives, scaled direction/normal conventions, rounded output and resource bounds: Geometry.

Indexed mesh plane cuts

NativeMeshIntersectionIndex::slice_plane(NativePlane3,NativeMeshSliceLimits) reuses the existing immutable mesh BVH and returns NativeMeshPlaneSlice3 with points, sources, cells, work and tested_faces. NativeMeshSliceSource retains original Vertex or Edge identity. NativeMeshFaceSlice3 retains original face, kind, point indices, barycentric rows and projection axes, including coplanar triangles. NativeTriangleMesh3::slice_plane is a one-query convenience. Native indices are zero-based. Exact pruning, topology versus rounded output, bounds, cancellation and BASIC access: Geometry.

Mesh contour topology and shared batches

NativeMeshIntersectionIndex::section_plane/section_planes and the corresponding NativeTriangleMesh3 convenience methods construct NativeMeshSection3 and NativeMeshSections3. A section has slice and topology; a batch has sections, hits, work and tested_faces. NativeMeshContourTopology exposes edges, canonical paths, isolated points, junctions, coplanar patches, ambiguous edges, removed interior-edge count and topology work. Supporting records are NativeMeshContourEdge, NativeMeshContourPath and NativeMeshCoplanarPatch. NativeMeshSliceLimits apply cumulatively to 1..1024 planes, including contour work. Exact source IDs preserve topology despite rounded coordinate collisions. Branch, patch/seam, error and BASIC contracts: Geometry.

documents.title: Shared nonuniform cubic Hermite paths
documents.html:
HERMITE(knots,values,derivatives) creates an editable {"HERMITE1",knots,valueRows,derivativeRows} list. Knots are finite, strictly increasing coordinates; each has a finite value vector and first-derivative vector. Scalar lists are accepted and normalized into one-component rows. Derivatives use the original knot coordinate (for example seconds), rather than a normalized interval parameter. Supplied knot values and slopes are retained.

  • HERMITEPOINT(curve,x) returns a component list.
  • HERMITEDERIV(curve,x[,order]) defaults to first derivative; orders 0–3 evaluate the value or successive derivatives.
  • HERMITEBATCH(curve,queries[,order]) defaults to values and returns component rows in input order. Empty query lists are valid.
  • HERMITEINTEGRAL(curve,from,to) returns the componentwise definite integral of the represented piecewise cubic. Reversed bounds negate it; equal bounds return zeros. This is an integral of each component, not geometric arc length.

Every query/bound must lie in the closed knot range; there is no extrapolation. A cubic matches both endpoint values and first derivatives on each interval. The resulting path is C1. Second/third derivatives at an interior knot use the right interval; at the final knot they use the left interval. Higher derivatives need not be continuous. Orders zero and one at knots return the input values verbatim, including signed zero.

The native NativeHermiteSpline::new(knots,values,derivatives) takes owned Vec<f64> knots and Vec<Vec<f64>> rows. Its point, derivative, evaluate_many and integral methods provide the same contracts without BASIC values or interpreter callbacks; getters expose immutable inputs. A native object can be reused across queries. BASIC packets remain ordinary editable lists; each operation validates the current packet, and a batch converts it once. For example, C(3,2,1)=5 changes component one at knot two.

Rust forms exact rational weights from the original finite binary64 knots and data, then rounds each final component once to nearest-even binary64. It does not first round the interval width or normalized parameter. Definite integrals accumulate exact panel sums, preserving cancellation even when individual panels would overflow binary64. This is exact arithmetic for the represented input interpolant, not a guarantee about the unknown function between samples. Nonfinite inputs and unrepresentable final results are errors.

Limits are 2–65,536 knots, 1–4,096 components, one million elements in each value/derivative matrix, 65,536 queries and one million output batch components. Input copies, evaluation and integral traversal include cancellation checks. Exact rational numerators/denominators are capped at 65,536 bits after reduction. A contiguous integral has at most two partial panels; full panels use a closed formula to avoid denominator growth with the number of knots. Failure returns no partial batch or assigned BASIC result; the native object remains reusable. Bounds limit storage and work but do not promise real-time audio execution: wide exponent ranges require larger integer arithmetic.

ODE event dense interpolation uses this same original-coordinate Rust kernel, including reverse-time intervals; the implicit solver's linear interpolation uses the shared exact-coordinate helper. ODE trajectory tolerances, event detection limitations and callback/work budgets retain their documented meaning.

programs/science/hermite_motion.bas composes position, velocity, acceleration and integration through these backend calls. The exact endpoint-constraint reference checker tools/check-hermite.py also compares ordinary-scale cases with SciPy's independent interpolator. Evidence is retained at output/hermite-paths-2026-10-26/validation.json when accepted.

Rational surfaces, broader curve families, composite continuity, arc-length parameterization and installed graphics/physics/audio workloads remain separate open requirements. Caller-supplied slopes do not establish monotonicity or automatic smoothness beyond C1.

documents.title: Automatic cubic spline fitting
documents.html:
CUBICSPLINE(knots,values[,boundary]) fits slopes from finite samples and returns the same editable HERMITE1 packet used by the Hermite functions. SPLINEFIT(knots,values[,boundary]) returns {curve,maximumScaledResidual,workingPrecisionBits}. Use HERMITEPOINT, HERMITEDERIV, HERMITEBATCH and HERMITEINTEGRAL on the returned curve; the fitting and query engines are shared Rust code.

The default boundary is "NOTAKNOT". Supported whole-curve choices are:

  • "NOTAKNOT": the first two intervals, and the final two intervals, share their cubic polynomial. Two samples select a line; three samples select a parabola.
  • "NATURAL": zero second derivative at both endpoints.
  • "CLAMPED": zero first derivative at both endpoints.
  • "PERIODIC": equal endpoint first and second derivatives. The first/last value rows must match exactly as numbers; no tolerance silently changes data. Two samples give a constant. Three samples form the two-interval periodic interpolant.
  • {startCondition,endCondition}: each endpoint is "NOTAKNOT" or {order,derivativeValues}, with order 1 or 2 and one value per component. A scalar derivative is accepted for one-component data. For example, {{1,{0,0}},{2,{0,0}}} prescribes zero initial velocity and final curvature for a two-component path. A not-a-knot endpoint with two samples instead prescribes the secant slope at that endpoint.

Knots remain strictly increasing and in their original units. Values may be component rows or a scalar list. Periodicity is a fitting boundary condition: queries still stay inside the closed knot range, with no automatic wrapping or extrapolation. The Hermite higher-derivative side convention remains unchanged.

Native Rust calls NativeHermiteSpline::fit(knots,values,NativeSplineBoundary) and receives NativeSplineFit { curve, maximum_scaled_residual, working_precision_bits }. The boundary enum has NotAKnot, Natural, Clamped, Periodic and Endpoints { start: NativeSplineEnd, end: NativeSplineEnd } variants. An endpoint is NotAKnot, FirstDerivative(Vec<f64>) or SecondDerivative(Vec<f64>).

The fitter selects 192–16,384 bits of binary working precision from the interval-width range and each component's data/boundary-value range. Guard bits cover the span-ratio amplification in boundary elimination. This addresses uneven-grid forward error that a small residual alone can conceal. It uses a bounded wider exponent range, pivoted tridiagonal factors and a border solve for periodic systems. It factors the knot system once for all components, rather than building a dense matrix for each coordinate. Working mantissa exponents are limited to −32,768 through 32,768. Input/output limits are those of the Hermite constructor: 2–65,536 knots, 1–4,096 components, and one million value elements. Factors and per-component solve scratch have linear storage. A conservative 128 MiB numerical scratch estimate and the shared billion-unit work limit can reject a large, high-precision problem before factor allocation. The estimate is knots*18*(64+ceil(bits/8)) bytes; work is charged as 64*knots*components*ceil(bits/192)^2. Input/output matrix storage is bounded separately. Traversals check cancellation. Nonfinite inputs, inconsistent boundary dimensions, invalid periodic endpoints, unrepresentable fitted binary64 slopes, arithmetic limits and failed residual checks return errors without partial results.

Returned slopes are binary64. Fitting is numerical, so C2 and boundary equations hold to numerical precision, not as exact real-number identities. The diagnostic is the largest componentwise row residual of the assembled derivative system, abs(A*s-b)/(sum(abs(A_ij*s_j))+abs(b)), computed again after output rounding. A zero denominator with zero residual contributes zero. Residuals above 2E-12 are rejected. This is a backward-error diagnostic, not a condition estimate, certified error bound or guarantee about an unknown function between samples. Extreme knot spacing can magnify slope rounding in higher derivatives. The Hermite evaluator retains its exact represented-input arithmetic guarantee for the returned slopes; it does not undo fitting error.

Caller-supplied first derivatives are retained verbatim. Editing a returned packet freely changes its interpolant; it does not refit slopes, restore C2 continuity or update an earlier residual report. Call the fitter again to obtain a new constrained fit. These smooth cubic fits can overshoot data and do not guarantee monotonicity.

The independent checker tools/check-cubic-splines.py solves all local polynomial endpoint/continuity/boundary constraints with exact rationals, and also compares ordinary-scale cases with SciPy. The editable consumer programs/science/cubic_spline_motion.bas combines periodic fitting, batch positions/velocities and integrals. Qualification evidence: output/cubic-splines-2026-10-26/validation.json when accepted.

Rational curves/surfaces, composite continuity workflows, arc-length parameterization and installed application/OS/hardware acceptance remain open.

The default boundary is `"NOTAKNOT"`. Supported whole-curve choices are:

- `"NOTAKNOT"`: the first two intervals, and the final two intervals, share
  their cubic polynomial. Two samples select a line; three samples select a
  parabola.
- `"NATURAL"`: zero second derivative at both endpoints.
- `"CLAMPED"`: zero first derivative at both endpoints.
- `"PERIODIC"`: equal endpoint first and second derivatives. The first/last
  value rows must match exactly as numbers; no tolerance silently changes data.
  Two samples give a constant. Three samples form the two-interval periodic
  interpolant.
- `{startCondition,endCondition}`: each endpoint is `"NOTAKNOT"` or
  `{order,derivativeValues}`, with order 1 or 2 and one value per component.
  A scalar derivative is accepted for one-component data. For example,
  `{{1,{0,0}},{2,{0,0}}}` prescribes zero initial velocity and final curvature
  for a two-component path. A not-a-knot endpoint with two samples instead
  prescribes the secant slope at that endpoint.

Knots remain strictly increasing and in their original units. Values may be
component rows or a scalar list. Periodicity is a fitting boundary condition:
queries still stay inside the closed knot range, with no automatic wrapping or
extrapolation. The Hermite higher-derivative side convention remains unchanged.

Native Rust calls
`NativeHermiteSpline::fit(knots,values,NativeSplineBoundary)` and receives
`NativeSplineFit { curve, maximum_scaled_residual, working_precision_bits }`. The boundary enum has
`NotAKnot`, `Natural`, `Clamped`, `Periodic` and
`Endpoints { start: NativeSplineEnd, end: NativeSplineEnd }` variants.
An endpoint is `NotAKnot`, `FirstDerivative(Vec<f64>)` or
`SecondDerivative(Vec<f64>)`.

The fitter selects 192–16,384 bits of binary working precision from the
interval-width range and each component's data/boundary-value range. Guard bits
cover the span-ratio amplification in boundary elimination. This addresses
uneven-grid forward error that a small residual alone can conceal. It uses a
bounded wider exponent range, pivoted tridiagonal factors and a border solve
for periodic systems. It factors the knot system once for all components, rather than building
a dense matrix for each coordinate. Working mantissa exponents are limited to
−32,768 through 32,768. Input/output limits are those of the Hermite constructor:
2–65,536 knots, 1–4,096 components, and one million value elements.
Factors and per-component solve scratch have linear storage. A conservative
128 MiB numerical scratch estimate and the shared billion-unit work limit can
reject a large, high-precision problem before factor allocation. The estimate
is `knots*18*(64+ceil(bits/8))` bytes; work is charged as
`64*knots*components*ceil(bits/192)^2`. Input/output matrix storage is bounded
separately. Traversals check cancellation. Nonfinite inputs, inconsistent boundary dimensions, invalid
periodic endpoints, unrepresentable fitted binary64 slopes, arithmetic limits
and failed residual checks return errors without partial results.

Returned slopes are binary64. Fitting is numerical, so C2 and boundary equations
hold to numerical precision, not as exact real-number identities. The diagnostic
is the largest componentwise row residual of the assembled derivative system,
`abs(A*s-b)/(sum(abs(A_ij*s_j))+abs(b))`, computed again after output rounding.
A zero denominator with zero residual contributes zero. Residuals above `2E-12`
are rejected. This is a backward-error diagnostic, not a condition estimate,
certified error bound or guarantee about an unknown function between samples.
Extreme knot spacing can magnify slope rounding in higher derivatives.
The Hermite evaluator retains its exact represented-input arithmetic guarantee
for the returned slopes; it does not undo fitting error.

Caller-supplied first derivatives are retained verbatim. Editing a returned
packet freely changes its interpolant; it does not refit slopes, restore C2
continuity or update an earlier residual report. Call the fitter again to obtain
a new constrained fit. These smooth cubic fits can overshoot data and do not
guarantee monotonicity.

The independent checker `tools/check-cubic-splines.py` solves all local
polynomial endpoint/continuity/boundary constraints with exact rationals, and
also compares ordinary-scale cases with SciPy. The editable consumer
`programs/science/cubic_spline_motion.bas` combines periodic fitting, batch
positions/velocities and integrals. Qualification evidence:
`output/cubic-splines-2026-10-26/validation.json` when accepted.

Rational curves/surfaces, composite continuity
workflows, arc-length parameterization and installed application/OS/hardware
acceptance remain open.

documents.title: Shape-preserving cubic interpolation
documents.html:
PCHIP(knots,values) returns an editable HERMITE1 packet with slopes fitted by the shared Rust NativeHermiteSpline::fit_monotone(knots,values) method. The values may be a scalar list or equally sized component rows. Query the result with HERMITEPOINT, HERMITEDERIV, HERMITEBATCH and HERMITEINTEGRAL. There is no extrapolation or implicit periodic wrapping.

This fit is C1: values and first derivatives join continuously, while curvature may jump at knots. For each component, every segment is monotone in the direction of its two samples and stays between their values. Flat intervals stay constant; opposite-sign or zero adjacent secants give a zero interior derivative. Other interior derivatives are the nonuniform weighted harmonic mean of the two secants. Endpoint derivatives use a one-sided quadratic estimate, limited to the adjacent sample direction and three times the adjacent secant when directions change. Two samples use their common secant.

This is the local PCHIP convention described in the SciPy reference. Componentwise shape preservation does not imply spatial convexity, a straight line between vector samples, absence of self intersections, conservation of a physical quantity, smoothing of noisy measurements or a bound on an unknown function's interpolation error. Use CUBICSPLINE when C2 boundary fitting is needed; it has different continuity and overshoot behavior.

The Rust implementation computes local sample differences, ratios, sign decisions and limiting with exact rational arithmetic from the original finite binary64 inputs, using the shared Hermite rational core. This avoids intermediate width, difference and reciprocal overflow on extreme scales. Slopes round to nearest binary64; if that rounding crosses the exact three-times-secant bound, the value moves one representable step toward zero. Thus the returned slopes remain in the sufficient monotonicity box for each segment. Subnormal slopes may round to signed zero. A fitted slope that cannot round to finite binary64 returns RealOverflow. Shared exact Hermite evaluation rounds the represented polynomial only on output.

Constructor limits remain 2–65,536 strictly increasing finite knots, 1–4,096 components and one million value elements. Local arithmetic scratch does not grow with the number of knots; output derivatives have the same dimensions as the input values. The shared 65,536-bit rational limit bounds arithmetic; work is charged as 256*knots*components against the shared billion-unit limit. Traversal checks cancellation and errors return no partial curve. No new external dependency is required.

Editing a packet's values/slopes can remove its shape-preserving property. Call PCHIP again after changing the samples to refit it. User BASIC source remains freely editable. The consumer programs/science/monotone_envelope.bas composes gain/opacity samples, batch values/derivatives and integrated gain. tools/check-monotone-splines.py compares independent SciPy results and exact rational polynomials, and proves the derivative sign across each complete represented interval by examining its quadratic minimum. Evidence: output/monotone-splines-2026-10-26/validation.json when accepted.

Rational curves/surfaces, composite continuity, arc-length parameterization, application workloads and broader math/OS/hardware acceptance remain open.
