general math/application/OS/hardware qualification remain open.


### Certified adaptive NURBS pieces

`NURBSADAPT(curve[,tolerance[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]]])` samples every nonempty
closed active knot span. Defaults are `1e-3`, `4096` and `40`. It returns
`{"NSAMPLE1",status$,segments,{maximumDeviation},pieces}`. Each piece is
`{knotSpanIndex,{from,to},parameters,points,{maximumDeviation},status$}`.
Draw each piece separately. Even a continuous join retains two incident endpoints;
a discontinuous join never adds a fabricated connecting segment. Original knot
indices are one based in BASIC and zero based in Rust.

Native `NativeNurbs<N>::sample(NativeCurveSamplingOptions)` returns
`NativeNurbsSamples<N>` with `pieces`, `segments`, `maximum_deviation` and `status`.
Each `NativeNurbsSamplePiece<N>` has `span_index`, `interval` and
`samples:NativeCurveSamples<N>`. Piece parameters increase strictly and include
both closed-span endpoints. Sampling uses exact original homogeneous span
polynomials and exact Bernstein restrictions, never rounded refinement packets.

The deviation certificate bounds Euclidean distance from every point of the
original exact curve to its corresponding rounded output chord. Positive/common-
sign rational control hulls and exact projection give upward-rounded L1 bounds,
shared with rational Bezier sampling. Zero-weight/zero-numerator controls may be
omitted; mixed signs or a zero-weight direction may require subdivision before
a finite hull certificate exists. An empty bound means no finite certificate.
This is geometric distance, not same-parameter, tangent, length or inverse-
distance error. Repeated traversal can lie on a chord without increasing this
error; use a length operation for travel distance.

Only `CONVERGED` meets tolerance. `SEGMENT_LIMIT` and `RESOLUTION_LIMIT` retain
complete ordered output for every span, with honest per-piece/global bounds.
Blocked panels remain in the result while other refinable panels continue.
The global status prioritizes an unmet segment budget over blocked depth/float
resolution, and otherwise converges only when every piece meets tolerance.
Limits are global: `maxSegments` must be 1..65536 and at least the number of
nonempty spans. An insufficient initial budget is an error, not a partial path.
The output has at most segments+pieces points (131072 overall).

Finite tolerance must be positive. Depth is 1..2100; the larger cap covers the
full signed finite knot range down to subnormal spacings. Midpoints are formed
exactly before one final binary64 rounding, avoiding subtraction overflow.
Adjacent parameter values and depth limits cannot imply convergence by themselves.

Whole-span exact domain validation precedes output: raw zeros (even removable),
hidden one-sided poles and entirely undefined spans are errors. Domain analysis
keeps its 2,000,000-step cap. Sampling then has a separate 16,000,000-step budget,
the shared 65536-bit reduced-fraction cap, and at most one cached exact span.
Heap/output storage is O(maxSegments+spans), not an exact-coefficient cache for
every panel. Work/arithmetic/cancellation errors return no partial report.
A regular denominator does not guarantee finite point outputs; output overflow
also returns an error. Curve degree remains 0..16 and controls at most 65536.

### Certified NURBS path length

`NURBSLENGTH(curve[,absoluteTolerance[,relativeTolerance[,maxSegments[,maxDepth]]]])`
returns `{value,{absoluteError},lowerBound,{upperBound},segments,status$}`.
Defaults are `1e-6,1e-6,4096,1074`. Native Rust uses
`NativeNurbs::<2/3>::length(NativeCurveLengthOptions)` and the shared
`NativeCurveLengthReport` / `NativeCurveLengthStatus` types.

The result sums traversal length over **every nonempty closed knot span**.
Repeated travel counts; jumps between disconnected pieces do not. Degree-zero
pieces contribute zero. Each span uses its own endpoint continuations, including
both sides of repeated knots. This is curve length, not the length of sampled
chords, and does not depend on a rounded knot-refinement packet.

Exact original homogeneous span polynomials are restricted in Bernstein form.
Outward-rounded endpoint norms give lower bounds; positive-weight rational
control polygons give upper bounds. For arbitrary degree, the rational Bernstein
basis has monotone cumulative weights, so total variation is bounded by that
polygon. Ordered collinear controls reduce to endpoint distance; reversing
controls do not. Exact aggregate sums and intersections of earlier valid bounds
avoid losing certificates to floating-point addition or refinement roundoff.
Signed/zero weights are supported: mixed-sign restricted hulls may initially have
no finite upper certificate and refine until one becomes available.

`CONVERGED` means `absoluteError <= MAX(absoluteTolerance,relativeTolerance*value)`,
compared exactly. Both tolerances must be finite/nonnegative, at least one
positive. `SEGMENT_LIMIT` and `RESOLUTION_LIMIT` retain complete path bounds,
including unresolved spans. `{}` for upper bound/error means no finite upper
certificate has been established; the reported value then equals the lower
bound and is not a converged estimate. A blocked span does not prevent other
spans from refining. Parameter means are exact before rounding, including
intervals from `-MAX` to `+MAX`. Lack of a representable interior parameter can
yield `RESOLUTION_LIMIT` even though an exact real curve has interior motion.

Global segment cap: `1..65536`, at least one per nonempty span; an insufficient
budget is an error rather than partial coverage. Depth cap: `1..2100` per original
span. All existing degree/control limits apply. Exact domain preflight rejects
every raw denominator zero (including removable 0/0 and endpoints) and undefined
span. The separate domain work limit remains in force. Length adds a
16,000,000-step work cap and uses the existing 65,536-bit fraction limit,
cancellation checks, a bounded panel heap and one cached exact span. Work/bit
exhaustion, cancellation or certified lower-bound overflow returns an error
without a partial report. A loose polygon upper bound that overflows is unknown,
not evidence that the actual length overflows. Absolute point coordinates may
be unrepresentable while a finite length remains certifiable.

cutting segments with a feed-time calculation. Independent exact Cox span
polynomials and high-precision integrals qualify the bounds, including limits,
backtracking and extreme scales; native and exported consumers are also required.

### Tensor-product B-spline and NURBS surfaces

The Rust `NativeNurbsSurface<N>` engine supports 2D/3D coordinates, independent
U/V degrees `0..16`, nonuniform/repeated/nonclamped knots and at most **65536 total
controls**. Degree zero and discontinuous patches are valid. BASIC constructors:

- `BSPLINESURFACE({uDegree,vDegree},uKnots,vKnots,points)` uses unit weights.
- `NURBSSURFACE({uDegree,vDegree},uKnots,vKnots,points,weights[,mode$])` accepts
  `"WEIGHTED"` Euclidean points (default) or `"HOMOGENEOUS"` numerator controls.
- Points are a rectangular U-row/V-column grid of coordinate lists; weights
  have the same U/V shape. Native arrays are flattened U-major/V-fast:
  `index=u*vCount+v`. Each knot vector determines its axis control count.
- The freely editable packet is
  `{"NSURFACE1",{uDegree,vDegree},uKnots,vKnots,points,weights,mode$}`.

`NURBSSURFACEPOINT(S,u,v[,uSide$[,vSide$]])` returns a coordinate list.
`NURBSSURFACEDERIV(S,u,v,uOrder,vOrder[,uSide$[,vSide$]])` returns a mixed
partial, with orders independently `0..3` (including `(3,3)`).
`NURBSSURFACEBATCH(S,{{u,v},...}[,uOrder[,vOrder[,uSide$[,vSide$]]]])`
returns complete input-order results; both derivative orders default to zero.
Each side defaults to `"AUTO"`: the right continuation at interior knots,
the left continuation at the final active endpoint. `"LEFT"`/`"RIGHT"`
apply independently to U and V. A side pointing outside an active domain is
an error; no extrapolation or snapping occurs. Endpoint continuations are
computed from the selected nonempty knot spans.

Native constructors are `new([p,q],[&uKnots,&vKnots],&points,&weights)`,
`from_homogeneous(...)` and `polynomial([p,q],[&uKnots,&vKnots],&points)`.
Accessors expose `bases()`, `shape()`, `coordinates()`, `weights()` and
`is_homogeneous()`. Queries are `point([u,v])`,
`point_on([u,v],[uSide,vSide])`, `derivative([u,v],[du,dv])`,
`derivative_on([u,v],[du,dv],[uSide,vSide])` and
`evaluate_many(&parameters,[du,dv],[uSide,vSide])`. Sides use `NativeKnotSide`.

The backend reuses exact local Cox-de Boor basis jets. Numerator/denominator
products, mixed quotient differentiation and original-knot scaling stay exact
until each final component rounds once to binary64. Rational derivatives can
remain nonzero above the polynomial degree. Zero/signed weights are admitted
except an all-zero weight array; every query rejects a raw zero denominator,
including removable 0/0. Homogeneous input permits directions at infinity in
the control net. Weighted one-hot queries preserve the original control's
signed zeros after the denominator check.

Inputs, outputs and knots must be finite. Shape, degree, total control, query
and derivative limits are checked. Batches contain at most 65536 parameter
pairs and preflight all parameter domains before computing results. A shared
16,000,000 charged-step budget covers a complete query/batch, including local
basis and mixed-jet work; each query does not receive a fresh batch budget.
The existing reduced-fraction 65536-bit cap and cancellation checks also apply.
Exhaustion, cancellation, a zero denominator or final overflow returns an error
without partial output. A BASIC query revalidates the entire editable packet;
batching amortizes that cost. Native queries use only the local
`(uDegree+1)*(vDegree+1)` control neighborhood after construction.

This is a **pointwise surface foundation**, with exact original-data derivative
evaluation. It does not certify a whole patch free of denominator zeros or
provide tessellation error bounds, trimming/intersections, area integration or
a complete CAD system. Those and inverse arc-length traversal remain open.
`programs/science/nurbs_surface.bas` exercises a rational cylinder and its
tangents. Required qualification includes exact independent polynomial/series
references, SciPy comparisons where supported, analytic sphere/cylinder models,
large grids, cancellation, BASIC recovery and standalone export.
Evidence when accepted: `output/nurbs-surface-2026-10-27/validation.json`.
Broader math/application/OS/image/architecture/hardware gates remain open.

### Whole-patch NURBS surface denominator certificates

`NURBSSURFACEDOMAIN(surface[,maxCells[,maxDepth]])` examines **every nonempty
closed U/V knot rectangle**, with separate one-sided continuations at joins.
It returns
`{"NSDOMAIN1",{{uFrom,uTo},{vFrom,vTo}},status$,patches,refinements,zeroCells,unresolvedCells,cells}`.
Each cell is
`{{uSpan,vSpan},{{u0,u1},{v0,v1}},status$,{lowerW,upperW},witnesses}`.
Span indices are one-based in BASIC and zero-based in Rust. Cells are ordered
by original patch and rectangle coordinates. They cover every patch completely;
shared edges are included on both sides.

Native Rust uses `NativeNurbsSurface::domain(NativeNurbsSurfaceDomainOptions)`
and typed `NativeNurbsSurfaceDomainReport` / `NativeNurbsSurfaceDomainCell`
records. Report/cell status types are `NativeNurbsSurfaceDomainStatus` and
`NativeNurbsSurfaceDomainCellStatus`. Defaults are 4096 total cells and depth
40 per axis. Limits: cells `1..65536` and depth `1..2100`. At least one cell per
original knot rectangle is required; insufficient initial coverage is an error.

Cell meanings:

- `POSITIVE` / `NEGATIVE` certify a strictly nonzero denominator throughout
  the closed cell, including real parameter pairs between binary64 values.
- `IDENTICALLY_ZERO` certifies the denominator is zero everywhere in the cell.
- `ZERO_WITNESS` provides one parameter pair with an exact raw denominator zero.
- `SIGN_CHANGE` provides two parameter pairs with exact opposite denominator
  signs; continuity within that patch proves at least one zero between them.
- `CELL_LIMIT` / `RESOLUTION_LIMIT` mean unresolved. They never mean regular.
  Resolution covers per-axis depth or a lack of an interior binary64 midpoint.
  Parameter-independent directions are not pointlessly subdivided.

Witnesses belong to the cell's **selected patch continuation**, which can differ
from an automatic point query at a discontinuous join. Identically-zero and
regular/limited cells have no witness list. A cell containing proved zeros is
not subdivided further just to locate every zero. `zeroCells` counts cell
incidences, not distinct zeros, poles or connected zero-set components. Raw
removable zeros are included. `unresolvedCells` is reported even when zeros
have also been proved elsewhere.

Overall status is `REGULAR` only if every cell is Positive/Negative;
`ZERO_DENOMINATOR` if any cell proves a zero; otherwise `CELL_LIMIT` takes
precedence over `RESOLUTION_LIMIT`. A finite sampled grid alone never admits
a patch as regular. Different signs in disconnected patch continuations do not
imply a zero between those patches.

The shared Rust exact de Boor channel kernel produces original-data tensor
power coefficients, converted exactly to Bernstein controls. All restrictions
use that original net; no rounded child surface is used. Convex control bounds
are rounded outwards for `lowerW/upperW`. Strict same-sign original weights
provide an inexpensive valid certificate. For a nonnegative Bernstein net
whose corners are positive, the closed-cell lower bound also uses
`minCorner * 2^(-max(uDegree-1,0)-max(vDegree-1,0))`. This follows from the
minimum of the endpoint Bernstein basis sums; degree-zero axes contribute
one. Negative nets use the same argument after a sign flip. Thus interior
zero controls do not prevent a valid strict certificate. A strict lower
bound can round to zero at extreme scales; the Positive/Negative status
comes from the exact proof, not the rounded bound alone.

Subdivision has one global cell budget, breadth-first fairness, separate
per-axis depths, overflow-safe exact midpoints and one cached exact patch.
The domain operation has a 16,000,000 charged-step limit and the existing
65536-bit reduced-fraction cap. Work/bit exhaustion or cancellation is an
error without a partial report. Cell/depth/parameter limits instead retain
complete coverage and explicitly unresolved cells.

This certifies denominator regularity only. It does not establish finite
coordinate outputs, geometric continuity, injectivity, tessellation accuracy,
surface area, or complete algebraic classification of a bivariate zero set.
Tangent zeros at nonrepresentable parameters can remain unresolved. Those
limits, trimming/intersections, area, inverse arc-length traversal and broader
math/application/OS/image/hardware gates remain explicit follow-on work.
`programs/science/nurbs_surface_domain.bas` admits a regular cylinder and
rejects a hidden tangent-zero patch before tessellation.
Evidence when accepted: `output/nurbs-surface-domain-2026-10-27/validation.json`.

### Certified NURBS surface meshes

`NativeNurbsSurface<N>::tessellate(NativeNurbsSurfaceMeshOptions)` is the CPU
native counterpart of `NURBSSURFACEMESH`. Options contain
`absolute_tolerance` (default 1e-3), `max_triangles` (8192) and `max_depth`
(40). `NativeNurbsSurfaceMesh<N>` contains `interval`, `triangles`,
`maximum_deviation: Option<f64>`, `status` and `pieces`. Status is
`NativeNurbsSurfaceMeshStatus::{Converged,TriangleLimit,ResolutionLimit}`.

Each `NativeNurbsSurfaceMeshPiece<N>` contains original zero-based `spans`,
`interval`, `parameters: [Vec<f64>;2]`, U-major/V-fast `vertices`, local
zero-based `triangles`, optional `cell_deviation` bounds for pairs of triangles,
and `maximum_deviation`. Grids conform in parameter space across the complete
surface; patch seams retain independent indices and one-sided coordinates.
Degenerate geometric triangles retain their parameter coverage. The certificate
bounds same-parameter positional error against actual rounded vertices; it
does not certify normals, injectivity, a closed solid or seam welding.

See GEOMETRY.md for the exact proof, output ordering, admission and all limits.
Raw-denominator admission and meshing share one bounded operation; cancellation
or hard arithmetic/work/coordinate failures return no partial mesh. A
TriangleLimit/ResolutionLimit report still covers all original patches, but
must not be treated as satisfying the requested tolerance. None is an unknown
finite upper bound, never zero. Evidence when accepted:
`output/nurbs-surface-mesh-2026-10-27/validation.json`.

### Indexed NURBS surface consumers

`NativeNurbsSurface<3>::indexed_mesh(NativeNurbsIndexedMeshOptions)` returns
an immutable `NativeNurbsIndexedMesh`. Options contain `mesh:
NativeNurbsSurfaceMeshOptions`, `seam_policy:
NativeNurbsSeamPolicy::{Continuous,Separate}` (default Continuous), and explicit
`wrap_axes: [bool;2]` (default false/false). The triangle budget is capped at
100000 for compatibility with `NativeTriangleMesh3`.

Accessors: `mesh()`, `maximum_deviation()`, `patches()`, `source_vertices()`,
`joined_seams()`, `unjoined_seams()`, `wrap_axes()` and
`patch_vertex_indices()`. Native mesh faces/maps use zero-based indices.
`into_mesh(self)` consumes the result and returns the shared mesh.
The private fields prevent editing geometry while retaining a trusted
certificate. Cloning the result preserves the same immutable semantics.

Indexing requires converged tessellation and joins only proven identical
original rational boundaries. Wrapped boundaries must agree with the same
parameter orientation; internal nonidentical boundaries remain separate.
No global coordinate/epsilon welding occurs. See GEOMETRY.md for the exact
proof, packet correspondence, resource limits and failure behavior.
`NativeSolidDomain3` and `NativeStl` consume `result.mesh()` directly.
Topology validity, embedded solidity and format precision remain independent
checks; positional accuracy does not certify these properties.
Evidence when accepted: `output/nurbs-indexed-mesh-2026-10-27/validation.json`.

documents.title: Shared inverse arc-length traversal
documents.html:
NativeBezier<N>::travel, NativeRationalBezier<N>::travel and NativeNurbs<N>::travel take NativeCurveTravelTarget::{Distance(f64),Fraction(f64)} and NativeCurveTravelOptions { absolute_tolerance, max_segments, max_depth }. They return NativeCurveTravelReport<N> with parameter, zero-based original span_index, rounded point, optional absolute_distance_error, prefix_lower/prefix_upper, total_lower/total_upper, separate position_rounding_error, segments, range_certified and NativeCurveTravelStatus::{Converged,SegmentLimit,ResolutionLimit}.

A single clamped NURBS representation preserves original Bezier controls/weights without rounding conversions. The shared engine restricts original exact span polynomials and reuses certified chord/control-polygon length bounds. A balanced initial span tree stores additive prefix/suffix enclosures; refinement splits only an implicated leaf and updates ancestors. It does not repeatedly integrate the whole prefix or infer travel from sampled-point spacing. Fraction residuals use (1-q)*prefix - q*suffix, retaining correlation with total length.

See the language reference's distance-based traversal section for full limits, discontinuous/zero-length conventions and range semantics. Only Converged proves a target in range and the requested distance tolerance. Returned locations are original-span points; coordinate rounding has a separate Euclidean bound. This is a positional traversal primitive, not a feed-rate, acceleration, jerk, collision-clearance or machine-control planner. Repeated calls currently build separate bounded indexes; a reusable multi-query index remains future work.

Implementation: src/math_engine/curves/nurbs/travel.rs and the shared src/math_engine/curves/travel.rs contract/BASIC packet. Qualification evidence: output/curve-travel-2026-10-27/validation.json when accepted.

documents.html:
NativeTable::new(&[NativeTableField], &[Vec<NativeTableCell>]) admits explicit types into immutable column storage. NativeTableType has Integer, Real, Boolean and Text; NativeTableCell adds Null. Native inputs must match their declared types exactly. Reals are finite, with canonical zero. schema, row_count, column_count, checked zero-based cell, and rows inspect it. select(&[String]), filter(&[Option<bool>]) and group(&[String], &[NativeTableAggregate]) return new tables. An aggregate names column, output and a NativeTableReduction: Count (non-null), Sum, Mean, Min, Max, VariancePopulation, VarianceSample, StandardDeviationPopulation or StandardDeviationSample. Exact integer keys, checked integer sums, once-rounded real sums/means/moments and missingness share BASIC's numerical contracts. Sample moments with fewer than two present observations return Null; population moments with one observation return zero. Clones/projections share buffers. Calls observe NativeCancellationToken; caps and non-interruptible phases are documented in the language reference. See TABULAR_ANALYTICS.md for provenance and qualification limits.

NativeTable::join(&right, &left_keys, &right_keys, &options) returns a new table. NativeTableJoinOptions contains kind: NativeTableJoinKind (Inner, Left, Right, Full, Semi, Anti), nulls: NativeTableJoinNulls (Never or Equal), and right_prefix: String. Default is Inner/Never/"right.". Keys must be nonempty, distinct within each side, paired by position, and identically typed. Exact equality, deterministic ordering, unmatched null padding and prefix rules match TABLEJOIN. Both sets of key columns are retained; Semi/Anti retain only the left schema. Plan admission counts all duplicate matches and their repeated text payload before creating result indices/columns. The existing one-million row/cell, 256-field and 64 MiB cell-text limits apply to the result. Join planning uses Rust's hash index over borrowed typed keys and existing column gathers; no additional crate or native provider is required. Each column gather is a bounded, non-interruptible phase with checkpoints around it.

NativeTable::window(&keys, &aggregates, &options) appends reduction columns. NativeTableWindowOptions has preceding: Option<usize>, following: Option<usize> and min_periods: usize. None means unbounded; Some(0) means the current row on that side. Default is cumulative: preceding None, following Some(0), min_periods 1. Empty keys select a global partition; otherwise exact nullable keys define partitions. Frames count input-order rows within each partition, including nulls, while numeric reductions skip null observations. COUNT ignores min_periods; other reductions require max(1,min_periods), and sample variance/deviation require at least two. Original rows/columns retain their order; existing column buffers are shared. The language reference defines caps, atomic errors and cancellation boundaries. This row-frame interface does not imply timestamp/range frames, ranking, lag/lead or larger-than-memory execution. Evidence when qualified: output/table-windows-2026-10-27.

documents.title: Ordered table analytics and numeric range frames
documents.html:
NativeTableSortKey { column, descending, nulls_first } specifies a typed ordering key. table.sort(&order) returns a stable row permutation with the original schema. Null placement is independent of direction; exact integers, finite reals, Boolean values and UTF-8 byte ordering follow TABLESORT.

table.rank(&keys, &order, mode, output) appends a field in original row order. NativeTableRank provides RowNumber, Rank, DenseRank, PercentRank and CumulativeDistribution, with the BASIC peer/denominator contracts. An empty partition-key list means one global partition.

table.shift(&keys, column, offset, output) appends a typed positional lag (positive i64 offset), lead (negative) or copy (zero). Input partition order, null source observations and null out-of-range positions are preserved. Text payload amplification is admitted before the output gather.

table.range_window(&keys, order_column, &aggregates, &bounds, min_periods) reuses the checked reversible window reducers. NativeTableRangeBounds is either Integer { preceding: Option<i64>, following: Option<i64> } or Real { preceding: Option<f64>, following: Option<f64> }; None is unbounded. Bound variants must match the order column, finite/nonnegative values are required, and the order column must be present/nondecreasing within each partition. Both endpoints and all equal-order peers are included. Integer distance comparisons use i128 and real comparisons use the shared exact accumulator; no rounded subtraction/endpoint is used. Arbitrary time units can be supplied but calendar/time-zone semantics are not inferred.

All calls are immutable and observe NativeCancellationToken. Output uses the existing row/cell/field/text caps; sort/rank additionally admit at most 50 million field comparisons and 256 MiB of compared text prefixes. Column gathers remain bounded backend phases with checkpoints before/after. No partial table escapes an error/cancellation. Qualification when accepted: output/table-ordering-2026-10-27.

documents.title: Typed CSV streams
documents.html:
NativeTableCsvReader<R: BufRead>::new(reader,schema,options,limits) validates an explicit schema and consumes the optional header on its first read_batch. Positive batch sizes must satisfy the table cell/row bounds. Each result is independent; EOF returns an empty table with the original schema. bytes_read counts consumed bytes; is_finished becomes true when EOF is observed, possibly on the read following an exactly full batch. into_inner preserves the unread buffer/cursor. Invalid batch sizes consume nothing. Parsing, I/O and cancellation errors poison the reader; construct a new reader on a reopened source.

NativeTableCsvOptions contains delimiter: u8 and header: bool. NativeTableCsvLimits contains max_bytes (default/hard maximum 256 MiB) and max_field_bytes (default 1 MiB; hard maximum 64 MiB). The encoded-byte budget is cumulative across a native reader, not reset per batch. Per-batch table and per-record limits also apply. No asynchronous I/O or hard real-time cancellation is promised for an arbitrary caller-supplied blocking reader/writer.

NativeTable::from_csv requires a whole input to fit one table and never silently truncates. csv_size computes the checked exact encoded size. to_csv preflights that size before allocating. write_csv preflights limits before emitting bytes and streams without building a complete CSV string. An external writer can contain partial output after an I/O/cancellation error; the BASIC file adapter adds atomic replacement. All use the language reference's explicit quoting, null, schema and numeric contracts. CSV syntax follows the quoting/record conventions described in RFC 4180, with documented UTF-8, alternate-delimiter/newline and typed-null extensions.

documents.title: Bounded grouped streaming statistics
documents.html:
NativeTableAccumulator::new(schema,keys,aggregates,limits) creates an exact summary plan. NativeTableAccumulatorLimits exposes max_groups, max_state_bytes and max_rows with the language reference's defaults/hard caps. Empty keys mean one whole-stream group. update(&table) appends a batch; merge(&other) combines matching plans transactionally. merged(&other) returns a new combined state without changing inputs, including self-merge. The left state supplies limits and first-appearance order.

result() returns a typed table without discarding exact state. rows_seen(), group_count(), state_bytes() and limits() expose admission metadata; reset() restores the empty plan. Native callers budget their owned states, clones and input/output tables. BASIC adds shared reservations/lifetime rules. All submitted rows count toward the cap; reducers independently skip nulls.

The stream reuses table reducers, exact integer/dyadic sums and exact first/second moments. Merges add accumulator limbs/counts/integer sums before rounding; extrema use typed comparisons. The billion-row cap keeps i128 sums and fixed moment arrays within capacity. Numeric results are independent of batch partitioning and merge-tree rounding; group order follows left-first encounters. Cancellation/admission failures preserve state, and result overflow does not prevent later updates or reset.

Qualification: output/table-stream-2026-10-27. Streaming joins/sliding windows, persisted state recovery and installed/other-target qualification remain open.

documents.title: Reversible exact paired windows

NativeTable::window_with_aggregations(keys,specs,options) and range_window_with_aggregations(keys,order,specs,bounds,min_periods) extend the existing window methods to mixed NativeTableAggregation specifications. The original single-column methods remain compatible wrappers. Both use one shared frame traversal and the exact paired kernel used by scalar, grouped and streaming statistics. Numeric ranges retain exact type-matched axis bounds.

Minimum periods count complete pairs independently for each pair specification; Count always returns its count. Paired frame removal preserves all integer and binary64 residual bits. Column output is preflighted; cancellation/errors expose no partial table. Inputs remain immutable. The per-partition traversal admits bounded work and handles each entering/leaving row once per reducer, including monotone min/max queues for mixed single-column specifications.

No cross-batch history or persisted window state is introduced. Existing table/field/text/operation caps and NativeCancellationToken behavior apply. Host workload and independent reference evidence when accepted: output/table-pair-window-2026-10-27.

documents.title: Rolling statistics across input batches
documents.html:
TABLE ROLLCREATE name$,schema,keys,aggregates,preceding[,minPeriods[,maxGroups[,maxStateBytes[,maxRows]]]] creates a named trailing row-window state. A nonnegative INTEGER preceding value includes that many earlier rows of the same group and the current row. An empty list {} means the whole group prefix. Empty keys select one global group. Rows retain input order; interleaved groups retain independent history.

Aggregation entries are {"MEAN","x","average"} or paired entries such as {"SLOPE","x","y","gain"}, with the same operations, exact INTEGER handling, null rules and minPeriods behavior as TABLEWINDOW. minPeriods defaults to 1; COUNT and PAIRCOUNT always report their respective present counts.

TABLE ROLLADD name$,table,destination processes a batch and returns its original columns plus the requested aggregate columns. Later batches continue from the last successful update. The declared schema must match exactly. A failed update, output conversion, destination assignment or cancellation preserves the state. Each emitted row must have representable results; an overflow rejects the whole batch, even if a later row would have brought a sum back into range.

TABLE ROLLINFO name$,destination returns {rowsSeen,groupCount,accountedStateBytes,retainedRows}. TABLE ROLLRESET name$ discards observations and history, retaining the plan and limits. TABLE ROLLFREE name$ releases the state. CLEAR and runtime reset release all rolling states. There are at most 32 named rolling states, sharing the existing asset budget with other assets and table accumulators.

Limits default to 4,096 groups, 8 MiB accounted state and one billion lifetime rows. Hard limits are 65,536 groups, 64 MiB state and one billion rows. BASIC reserves twice maxStateBytes to cover retained state and one staged copy. These are conservative admission charges, not a measurement of process memory. Finite preceding and minPeriods bounds are at most one million; output tables still obey the one-million-cell and 256-field limits. Each update admits at most ten million key/reducer work units. Cancellation is cooperative.

Finite frames retain at most preceding+1 reducer observations per group, with memory charged before admission; unrelated input text/columns are not retained. Prefix windows use fixed-size reducers per group and retain no row history. Groups remain until RESET/FREE and still consume their group/key budget.

The native Rust interface is NativeTableRollingWindow::new for single-column plans or new_with_aggregations for mixed plans, using NativeTableWindowOptions with following=Some(0) and NativeTableAccumulatorLimits. update(&table) atomically returns a new table; updated(&table) returns a staged state and output without changing the original, allowing callers to validate output before committing. It also exposes rows_seen, group_count, state_bytes, retained_rows, limits, options and reset.

This is a causal row-window API. Lookahead, cross-batch numeric/calendar range frames, streaming joins and persisted state recovery remain open. Source/native qualification does not establish installed-OS or other-architecture availability. Example: programs/science/streaming_rolling.bas.

documents.title: Civil dates, business calendars and dated cash flows
documents.html:
Civil dates are INTEGER days relative to 1970-01-01. The supported proleptic Gregorian range is 0001-01-01 through 9999-12-31 (-719162 through 2932896). There are no timezones, daylight-saving transitions, locale guesses or fictitious 1900-02-29. Existing clock-oriented DATE$ behavior is unchanged.

FunctionContract
CIVILDATE(year,month,day)Construct a valid date; reject invalid fields.
CIVILPARSE(text$)Parse exactly ten ASCII characters in YYYY-MM-DD form.
CIVILFORMAT$(date)Format exactly YYYY-MM-DD.
CIVILPARTS(date)Return {year,month,day,weekday}, Monday=1 through Sunday=7.
CIVILADD(date,amount[,unit$[,preserveMonthEnd]])Signed INTEGER increment; units DAYS (default), MONTHS or YEARS. Missing target days clamp to month end. The optional 0/1 flag additionally preserves an original month end for MONTHS/YEARS.
DAYCOUNT(start,end[,basis$])Signed day count under the named convention.
YEARFRAC(start,end[,basis$])Fraction of a year, rounded once from an exact integer ratio.
YEARFRACRATIO(start,end[,basis$])Return {numerator,denominator}; denominator is positive, and the ratio need not be reduced.
BUSCAL(holidays[,weekendMask])Construct an editable {"BUSCAL1",mask,holidays} record. Holidays are date integers.
BUSISDAY(calendar,date)Return 1 for an open date, otherwise 0.
BUSCOUNT(calendar,start,end)Count open dates in [start,end); reverse endpoints negate the count.
BUSADD(calendar,date,amount)Advance by signed business days, excluding the start. Zero returns the start unchanged.
BUSADJUST(calendar,date,convention$)Apply the explicit adjustment convention below.
DATEDNPV(rate,amounts,dates,valuationDate[,basis$])Value dated cash flows using an annual effective rate and explicit valuation date.

Day-count basis defaults to ACT365F. Supported spellings are:

  • ACT365F: actual elapsed days divided by 365.
  • ACT360: actual elapsed days divided by 360.
  • ACTACTISDA: actual days in each calendar year divided by that year's 365/366 days. Whole intervening years contribute one each; integer arithmetic combines the two partial years before the single final division.
  • 30E360: European/Eurobond 30E/360; replace each day 31 by 30 and use 360*(endYear-startYear)+30*(endMonth-startMonth)+endDay-startDay. February keeps its actual day number. This is a separate convention from 30E/360 ISDA, US/NASD and coupon-schedule-dependent Actual/Actual methods.

All four day-count/year-fraction operations are signed and antisymmetric. Intervals with identical endpoints have zero length. ACTACTISDA day counts are actual elapsed days; its year-fraction denominator depends on the endpoint years.

Weekend mask bits 0..6 mean Monday..Sunday. The default 96 closes Saturday and Sunday. Masks 0..126 are accepted; all seven weekdays cannot be closed. BUSCAL admits at most 65,536 supplied holidays, removes duplicates and omits holidays already closed by the weekend mask. No national holidays, observed-day rules or exchange schedules are implicit. Every BASIC operation validates the calendar record; native callers can reuse its prepared Rust representation.

Business adjustment names are UNADJUSTED, FOLLOWING, PRECEDING, MODFOLLOWING and MODPRECEDING. Modified conventions switch direction if the first adjustment would cross a month boundary. At the supported calendar boundary they try the opposite direction. Open dates remain unchanged. If no valid date can be returned within the supported range, the operation reports an error. Counting uses whole weeks and sorted holiday ranges; advancing uses a bounded binary search rather than walking through every intervening day.

DATEDNPV uses: SUM(amount[i] * (1 + rate)^(-YEARFRAC(valuationDate, dates[i], basis))). The rate must be finite and greater than -1. Amount/date list lengths must match and are capped at one million. Empty lists return zero. Dates can be unsorted, repeated or before valuation; valuation-day flows are included without discount, and earlier flows compound forward. Monetary amounts/results use binary64, including conversion of BASIC INTEGER amounts; they are not fixed-decimal money.

Discount weights use log1p/exp. Finite weights and amounts are multiplied and summed with the existing exact product accumulator before final rounding, which preserves cancellation even when an individual product would overflow. A weight outside binary64 uses the existing scaled-principal fallback; an unrepresentable fallback term or final result raises overflow. Transcendental approximation and ill-conditioned cancellation remain relevant; this is not certified valuation or a correctly rounded transcendental sum. Cancellation is checked while preparing inputs and after the bounded exact accumulation phase. Native inputs are immutable; errors return no partial result.

Native exports: NativeCivilDate, NativeDayCount, NativeBusinessCalendar, NativeBusinessConvention and NativeDatedCashflow. NativeFinancialMath exposes dated_net_present_value(rate,flows,valuation,basis). Native date construction, parsing, formatting and arithmetic use checked values. Calendar operations share the same rules as BASIC. Example: programs/finance/dated_cashflows.bas.

This checkpoint adds no new registry package: Chrono 0.4.45 was already vendored and pinned through the table dependencies. Its direct dependency enables only the standard-library date support, with clock/timezone defaults disabled. Existing upstream license files and archive/file checksums remain intact. Chrono supplies checked Gregorian dates; ModernBASIC supplies the public bounds, business-calendar contract, exact day-count ratios and financial integration.

References inspected for date APIs and convention comparison: Chrono NaiveDate, QuantLib Actual/Actual implementations, QuantLib 30/360 implementations. QuantLib is a comparison reference, not a new runtime dependency or copied engine.

Remaining financial work includes schedule generation/stubs, additional day-count families, country/exchange calendar datasets, instrument-specific calibration and additional return models, currency/decimal rounding, portfolio risk and wider model qualification. Timezone timestamps, persisted calendar identities, typed DATE table columns, installed OS and other CPU architectures retain separate acceptance gates.

See DATE_SCHEDULES.md for complete signatures, defaults, indexing, limits, cancellation, stub/adjustment rules and remaining scope.

documents.html:
DISCOUNTCURVE constructs a positive log-linear discount curve with explicit day-count and extrapolation conventions. CURVEDF, CURVELOGDF and CURVEZERO accept a date or a batch; CURVEFORWARD returns interval rates and CURVENPV values dated flows with the shared exact finite-product accumulator.

The native exports NativeDiscountCurve, NativeDiscountKnot, NativeCurveExtrapolation and NativeRateCompounding share these kernels. See DISCOUNT_CURVES.md for complete signatures, data contracts, numerical and resource limits, recovery and remaining model scope.

documents.title: Bracketed dated returns
documents.html:
DATEDIRR and DATEDIRRINFO solve the dated annual-effective cash-flow equation within an explicit rate bracket. They share Rust calendar, exact-accumulation and safeguarded scalar-search kernels, expose convergence and work counts, and support the four named day-count bases. NativeFinancialMath exposes the same operation to Rust through NativeDatedIrrOptions and NativeDatedIrrReport.

See Dated internal rates of return for full signatures, report fields, multiple-root handling, precision and range limits. The editable example is programs/finance/dated_return.bas.

documents.title: Shared adaptive numerical Jacobians in physics
documents.html:
Backward-Euler and index-one DAE numerical Newton paths reuse the Rust adaptive Jacobian kernel with scaled coordinates, cached samples and cumulative budget checks. Numerical DAE initialization holds the differential prefix fixed during all probes. See Physics Jacobians for domain recovery, analytic/CSR behavior, limits and the previously failing boundary examples.

Complex elementary ranges and canonical branch cuts

Complex exponential/trigonometric scaling preserves small representable components near overflow/underflow. Native BasicComplex and BASIC use the same kernels. See trigonometry contracts for canonical cut sides, domain errors, independent references and remaining limits.

Shared angular coordinates and graphics phase

ROTATE2D, TOPOLAR, TORECT, ATAN2, RAD and DEG share checked Rust coordinate operations. Degree drawing paths reuse the same phase kernels. See angular coordinate contracts for native APIs, signed radius/zero conventions, numerical bounds and evidence.

Checked reciprocal trigonometry and source inventory

SEC, CSC, COT and COTH share NativeTrigonometry::sec, csc, cot and coth, completing typed native access to the six existing real reciprocal functions. See reciprocal contracts and the complete angle-operation inventory for radians, represented poles, overflow, complex-input restrictions, independent references and the separate installed/architecture/certification gates.

documents.title: Shared Rust error functions
documents.html:
The crate-root NativeErrorFunctions::erf(x) and ::erfc(x) accept finite binary64 inputs and return Result<f64, Error>. BASIC ERF(x) and ERFC(x) use these same kernels. Nonfinite native arguments return RealOverflow; BASIC retains ordinary real-only argument and arity rules, and failed assignments preserve their destination. Successful zero results are canonical.

The piecewise rational algorithm is adapted from Sun fdlibm s_erf.c 1.3 (1995-01-18). Its exact source, SHA-256 provenance, coefficient checks and permission notice are retained under src/math_engine/special/upstream/; the notice is also retained in the Rust port. No new Cargo dependency or foreign erf/erfc call is introduced. f64::exp remains the Rust platform exponential primitive, so this is a port of the error-function algorithm, not a replacement of the whole platform math library.

documents.title: Shared normal-distribution math
documents.html:
NativeNormalDistribution::new(mean, standard_deviation) creates an immutable, finite CPU Gaussian distribution with strictly positive standard deviation. Its pdf(x), cdf(x), survival(x), probability(lower,upper), quantile(p) and inverse_survival(p) methods return checked binary64 results.

BASIC preserves NORMALPDF(x[,mean[,sd]]), interval-valued NORMALCDF(lower,upper[,mean[,sd]]), and INVNORM(p[,mean[,sd]]). NORMALSF(x[,mean[,sd]]) supplies the direct upper tail; INVNORMSF(p[,mean[,sd]]) supplies its inverse without subtracting a small probability from one. These named functions retain ordinary list broadcasting. Native cdf(x) is the single lower tail; BASIC NORMALCDF continues to take both interval endpoints. Finite endpoints have zero Gaussian point mass.

The native and BASIC APIs share Rust kernels, as do the existing Poisson normal approximation and European-option normal probabilities. Parameters, samples and bounds must be finite; invalid standard deviations, reversed intervals and quantile probabilities outside 0<p<1 are errors. Mathematically unrepresentable densities or affine quantiles raise RealOverflow. Underflow may yield zero; successful zeros are canonical. Failed BASIC assignments preserve their destination.

Quantiles refine the existing Acklam seed with three bounded Newton steps. Near the center they compare the centered error function; in the tails they compare logarithmic probabilities. Large positive tails use the real-positive Mills expansion from DLMF 7.12.1, bounded to 64 terms. mean+sd*z uses the shared exact product accumulator and rounds that affine sum once. The standard quantile z remains an approximation: cancellation against a large mean can magnify its absolute error, and this is not an arbitrary-precision quantile.

Interval probabilities retain the original scaled width when transformed endpoints coincide. Narrow smooth intervals use fixed four-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature with the midpoint density factored out; wider tails use logarithmic differences. This avoids zero results from subtracting two nearly equal CDF values. Scalar calls have bounded work and no heap allocation or thread creation; long native loops manage their cancellation boundaries.

Qualification uses exact represented inputs with independent 400-digit references, including small/subnormal probabilities, adjacent endpoints, overflow/cancellation, failure recovery and direct/native/standalone consumers. It is sampled binary64 qualification, not a proof of correct rounding across every input or platform. Evidence: output/normal-distribution-2026-10-27; consumer: programs/science/normal_distribution.bas. Other target math libraries, installed OS acceptance and broader distribution/inference tasks remain open.

documents.title: Shared discrete count distributions
documents.html:
NativeBinomialDistribution, NativeGeometricDistribution and NativePoissonDistribution expose immutable CPU probability models with checked pmf, cdf and survival methods. Survival is the strict upper tail P(X > k); each model also returns lower/upper probabilities together. The binomial packet is [mass, lower_tail, upper_tail] and the other packets are [lower_tail, upper_tail].

BASIC preserves BINOMPDF(n,p[,k]), BINOMCDF(n,p[,k]), GEOMETPDF(p,k), GEOMETCDF(p,k), POISSONPDF(mean,k) and POISSONCDF(mean,k). New BINOMSF, GEOMETSF and POISSONSF return direct upper tails with the same arguments. These functions share the native Rust kernels and ordinary list broadcasting. Omitting binomial k returns the full table for counts zero through n; BASIC list indices start at one. Native pmf_table, cdf_table and survival_table provide the corresponding zero-based Rust vectors.

Binomial trials range from zero through one million. Scalar calls use constant storage; table calls accept at most one million entries, hence at most 999,999 trials. Larger workloads are rejected before allocation or iteration. Counts above the finite support return mass zero, CDF one and survival zero. Scaled mode-centered recurrence and compensated, separately accumulated tails avoid intermediate underflow and subtraction from a rounded CDF. A table temporarily uses an eight-byte mantissa and four-byte exponent per entry, returning one eight-byte probability per entry. Allocation failures are errors. Worst-case scalar work visits at most n+1 masses; tables add one linear pass. A decreasing tail stops early once its entire remaining relative mass is bounded below half the smallest representable probability. Cancellation is checked before work and at most 256 recurrence/table steps apart.

Geometric trials start at one and native callers retain the full u64 range; BASIC retains its nonnegative signed-integer range. The count product uses the shared exact product accumulator with high/low integer pieces. Logarithms of 1-p and expm1 preserve small probabilities. p=0 is the existing limiting convention: no success on any finite trial, CDF zero and survival one. p=1 places all mass on trial one.

Poisson means are finite and nonnegative. Counts through 2^53-1 keep count+1 exactly representable in the shared gamma distribution. This removes the former one-million-count ceiling and the rough normal approximation above mean 700. The gamma identity follows DLMF 8.4.7; the same bounded series, continued fractions and large-shape expansion supply the probabilities. A zero mean places all mass on zero. Scalar calls allocate no heap memory. Gamma iteration limits and cancellation rules also apply.

Parameters outside their stated domains, fractional/negative BASIC counts, and resource limits are errors. Nonfinite native parameters raise RealOverflow. Failed BASIC assignments preserve their destination. Distribution counts are not automatically rounded or interpreted as continuous endpoints.

Qualification uses exact represented inputs, independent high-precision masses and tails, scaled finite sums and gamma-density quadrature, extreme/tiny probabilities, native/BASIC/table parity, cancellation/recovery, measured CPU resources and standalone consumers. Sample checks do not certify every binary64 input or CPU math library. Native binomial work remains linear in its stated trial bound; larger binomial models, quantile/sampling/inference extensions and installed-OS acceptance remain separate tasks. Evidence: output/discrete-distributions-2026-10-27; consumer: programs/science/discrete_distributions.bas.

documents.title: Shared continuous probability laws
documents.html:
NativeExponentialDistribution::new(rate), NativeUniformDistribution::new(minimum,maximum) and NativeWeibullDistribution::new(shape,scale) are immutable, allocation-free CPU objects. Each exposes pdf, cdf, survival, probabilities (lower/upper pair), quantile and inverse_survival. BASIC calls exactly these Rust kernels.

LawBASIC functions and argument order
Exponential, rate parameterEXPPDF(x,rate), EXPCDF(x,rate), EXPSF(x,rate), EXPINV(p,rate), EXPINVSF(p,rate)
Uniform, finite ordered endpointsUNIFORMPDF(x,minimum,maximum), UNIFORMCDF(x,minimum,maximum), UNIFORMSF(x,minimum,maximum), UNIFORMINV(p,minimum,maximum), UNIFORMINVSF(p,minimum,maximum)
Weibull, shape and scale, zero locationWEIBULLPDF(x,shape,scale), WEIBULLCDF(x,shape,scale), WEIBULLSF(x,shape,scale), WEIBULLINV(p,shape,scale), WEIBULLINVSF(p,shape,scale)

Parameters and samples must be finite; rate, shape and scale must be strictly positive, and uniform minimum must be less than maximum. For exponential and Weibull lower inverses, 0 <= p < 1; upper inverses accept 0 < p <= 1. Their finite boundary returns zero. Uniform inverses include both 0 and 1. Infinite inverse endpoints are domain errors, rather than finite sentinels. Unrepresentable finite-input results and singular Weibull density at zero for shape below one return overflow. Uniform endpoint density retains the inclusive BASIC convention. Failed BASIC assignments preserve the previous destination. Invalid native parameters return IllegalQuantity, nonfinite inputs return RealOverflow. The old exponential/Weibull adapters used named MathDomain errors for nonpositive parameters; they now use this common parameter-error contract.

Lower tails use expm1 and upper tails are computed directly. Weibull evaluates near-scale displacements with log1p((x-scale)/scale) so a rounded division does not erase concentration-sensitive information. Inverses retain the displacement of the hazard around one using a split representation of exp(-1). Scaled inverse results and exponential densities reuse the shared exponent-reduced scaling kernel described below, retaining subnormal displacements and final overflow. Uniform inverses exactly accumulate their affine products before one rounding, avoiding overflowing interval widths and rounded 1-p complements.

These closed-form scalar operations do fixed work, create no threads or heap buffers and check cancellation at entry. They use platform binary64 logarithm and exponential primitives; sampled high-precision checks are not a certificate of correct rounding on every input or another CPU. Very concentrated laws may have adjacent representable samples with widely separated probabilities; a rounded quantile cannot promise a small probability round-trip error there. Underflow may correctly produce zero. RNG generation, fitting, inference, additional distributions and installed/other-target acceptance remain separate.

Formulas: NIST exponential, uniform and Weibull. The Rust implementation adapts mathematical formulas; no upstream engine code or dependency is imported. Evidence: output/continuous-distributions-2026-10-27; BASIC consumer: programs/science/continuous_distributions.bas.

documents.title: Shared exponential scaling
documents.html:
BASIC SCALEEXP(value,power) and crate-root scaled_exponential(value,power) -> Result<f64,Error> compute value*exp(power) with finite real inputs. The exponential alone need not fit in binary64: SCALEEXP(1E-300,1000) and SCALEEXP(1E300,-1000) both return finite nonzero results. Genuine final overflow and nonfinite arguments return RealOverflow; underflow rounds to a subnormal or canonical zero. A zero coefficient with any finite exponent returns zero. Failed BASIC assignments retain their destination.

The common Rust kernel is also used by financial compounding, present/future value, dated discounting, discount-curve interpolation/bootstrap, option-price consumers, exponential densities and Weibull inverses. It reduces the exponent as k*ln(2)+r using a high/low split of ln(2) and fused multiply-add. It keeps the expm1(r) correction separate: fused multiply-add performs the ordinary final rounding, and exact triple-product sums handle boundary scaling. Thus a small growth term cannot turn true overflow into a smaller finite result, and a subnormal halfway displacement is not lost in an intermediate multiplication. Near zero, value+value*expm1(power) uses one fused multiply-add, preserving that sum without the wider accumulator's overhead. Work and stack storage are fixed; the scaling kernel does not allocate or create threads, and its public entry checks cancellation.

One-period FV now uses exact product sums of the supplied cash flows and rate. One-period PV uses the exact finite-input rational formula before final rounding, retaining both cancellation and representable quotients with overflowing intermediate numerators. It reuses bounded integer accumulators; that rational division can allocate, so the allocation-free scaling claim does not apply to every financial operation. Near-unit multi-period annuities retain the separate capital-growth correction in their final accumulation.

Parameter conventions, payment timing and cash-flow signs are unchanged. Other multi-period financial results still include logarithm/exponential and annuity-factor approximation; ill-conditioned cancellation can amplify those errors. The kernel relies on platform expm1 accuracy and sampled binary64 qualification, not a correct-rounding certificate for every input or platform. Broader financial models, inference and installed/other-CPU acceptance remain open.

Mathematical identities: DLMF exponential definitions. Primitive contract: Rust fused multiply-add. No new dependency or toolchain is required. The independent reference checker uses 400-digit expressions and integer quantization at the final binary64 spacing to avoid double-rounding its own subnormal reference results. Evidence: output/exponential-scaling-2026-10-27; consumer: programs/science/exponential_scaling.bas.

documents.title: Shared beta distribution
documents.html:
NativeBetaDistribution::new(alpha,beta) exposes immutable CPU Rust pdf(x), cdf(x), survival(x), probabilities(x) (lower and upper tails), quantile(p) and inverse_survival(p). Both shapes must be finite and strictly positive. This is the beta law on [0,1], distinct from the beta special function.

BASIC functionResult
BETAPDF(x,alpha,beta)Probability density
BETACDF(x,alpha,beta)Lower cumulative probability
BETASF(x,alpha,beta)Direct upper-tail probability
BETAINV(p,alpha,beta)Lower inverse
BETAINVSF(p,alpha,beta)Inverse of a directly supplied upper tail

Finite samples outside [0,1] have zero density and saturated probabilities. Endpoint density is zero when the adjacent shape exceeds one, equals the other shape when it is one, and raises a real overflow error when it is below one. Nonfinite arguments/results raise real overflow; invalid shapes and probabilities raise illegal quantity. Inverse probabilities include both endpoints: lower inverse 0/1 returns 0/1; upper inverse 0/1 returns 1/0.

Selected MIT-licensed CDFLIB-rs 0.4.3 beta routines and required helpers are adapted locally. Exact upstream source, license, archive hash and adaptation notes are in src/math_engine/beta_distribution/upstream. No new Cargo dependency is added. Both BASIC and native Rust call these same kernels.

Each forward probability query permits at most 100,000 iterative work units; an inverse shares a one-million-unit budget across at most 62 binary64 coordinate bisections. Iterative kernels check cancellation at least every 64 units; native entry points and inverse steps also check it. Exhaustion or unresolved numerical convergence produces a math-domain error, preserving BASIC assignment destinations. An underflow bound qualifies zero extreme tails; a failed series is not silently accepted as a partial probability.

The implementation retains direct small tails, logarithmic inverse comparisons for subnormal probabilities, exact accumulated central displacements and stable density scaling. Results remain binary64 approximations with platform elementary functions; they are not certified interval enclosures. Inverses can round to support endpoints where interior quantiles are unrepresentable. Extremely ill-conditioned models cannot acquire precision beyond their represented inputs. Sampling, fitting and broader statistical inference are separate capabilities.

BASIC consumer: programs/science/beta_distribution.bas. Host qualification receipt: output/beta-distribution-2026-10-27/validation.json.

adapted locally. Exact upstream source, license, archive hash and adaptation
notes are in `src/math_engine/beta_distribution/upstream`. No new Cargo
dependency is added. Both BASIC and native Rust call these same kernels.

Each forward probability query permits at most 100,000 iterative work units;
an inverse shares a one-million-unit budget across at most 62 binary64
coordinate bisections. Iterative kernels check cancellation at least every
64 units; native entry points and inverse steps also check it. Exhaustion
or unresolved numerical convergence produces a math-domain error, preserving
BASIC assignment destinations. An underflow bound qualifies zero extreme
tails; a failed series is not silently accepted as a partial probability.

The implementation retains direct small tails, logarithmic inverse comparisons
for subnormal probabilities, exact accumulated central displacements and stable
density scaling. Results remain binary64 approximations with platform elementary
functions; they are not certified interval enclosures. Inverses can round to
support endpoints where interior quantiles are unrepresentable. Extremely
ill-conditioned models cannot acquire precision beyond their represented inputs.
Sampling, fitting and broader statistical inference are separate capabilities.

documents.html:
NativeFrame2D assembles and solves small-displacement, linear elastic, rigid-joint Euler–Bernoulli frames on the CPU. Each straight member has constant positive Young's modulus E, area A and second area moment I. Axial extension and in-plane bending share the existing Rust dense solve and exact accumulation kernels. No new dependency or external solver is required.

Native nodes are [x,y]; member and constraint indices are zero based. NativeFrame2DElement contains nodes:[start,end], young_modulus, area, second_moment and uniform_load:[qx,qy]. Local x runs from start to end; local y is 90 degrees counterclockwise from x. Global displacement/load DOFs are [ux,uy,theta] and [Fx,Fy,Mz], with counterclockwise angles/moments positive. Choose consistent units (for example m, N, Pa, m², m⁴, N/m, rad); the API does not attach or check physical unit dimensions.

new(nodes,elements) creates an immutable reusable model. stiffness() exposes the unconstrained global matrix; equivalent_loads() exposes the flattened global consistent nodal loads of all member loads. solve(nodal_loads,constraints) accepts one force/moment row per node and NativeFrame2DConstraint{node,dof,displacement} entries. Only constrained DOFs are prescribed; all others are free. Nonzero support settlements are supported. Disconnected frames are allowed when each component has independent restraints; isolated nodes and duplicate constraints are errors.

The result includes nodal displacements, reactions (zero on free DOFs), local member_end_forces in [Fx1,Fy1,M1,Fx2,Fy2,M2] order, nodal_strain_energy, and the maximum componentwise backward_error of the scaled free equations. End forces act on the member and include subtraction of its consistent loads. Nodal energy is 0.5*u^T*K*u of the finite-element interpolation, evaluated from nonnegative axial/curvature modes to avoid rigid-motion cancellation. Under distributed loads this excludes the additional within-element deformation energy; a fully fixed uniformly loaded member therefore has zero nodal energy despite nonzero end forces and continuum strain energy.

Bounds: 2–64 nodes, 1–1,024 members, at most three prescribed DOFs per node. All data and reported results must be finite binary64 values; material/length/ stiffness factors must remain positive and representable. Scaling that would erase a nonzero stiffness coefficient or free-equation load is rejected, as is underflow while unscaling a nonzero displacement. Assembly sums contributions before rounding, checks restraint rank of all three rigid-body modes per component, equilibrates the free equations symmetrically, and permits two refinement corrections to reach componentwise backward error at most 1e-12. This residual criterion is not a forward-error/conditioning guarantee. Cancellation is checked during assembly and between bounded solve stages.

This model excludes shear deformation, geometric/material nonlinearity, hinge releases, thermal loads, dynamics, buckling, plates/solids and 3D members. It implements no structural design standard. Section stress fields remain separate work; continuous member-field recovery is documented below.

Independent implementation uses the standard axial and cubic Hermite strain-energy formulation. Formula references: TU Delft, local element stiffness, coordinate transforms, and consistent element loads. Their illustrated rotation convention differs; ModernBASIC consistently uses theta = dv/dx (counterclockwise in local x/y). Host qualification passed: 37 independent model/error cases containing 12,158 scalar comparisons, 34 Rust regressions, native CPU/resource and interpreter/export checks. Evidence is in output/frame2d-2026-10-28. Installed systems and other CPU/hardware targets remain open.

documents.title: Planar frame continuum fields and total strain energy
documents.html:
NativeFrame2D::sample(displacements,queries) evaluates the continuous member solution using supplied global nodal [ux,uy,theta] rows and the model's original uniform local member loads. NativeFrame2DQuery{member,fraction} selects a zero-based member and normalized undeformed distance fraction in [0,1]. Queries may be repeated or unordered; an empty list is allowed. The operation validates the complete request and returns no partial result on errors or cancellation. It accepts at most 65,536 queries per call.

NativeFrame2DSample includes undeformed global position, global displacement, local_displacement:[u,v], rotation=dv/dx, axial_force=N=EA*du/dx, shear_force=V=-EI*d³v/dx³, bending_moment=M=EI*d²v/dx², axial_strain=du/dx and curvature=d²v/dx². Its to_array() uses the same twelve-column order as BASIC: [x,y,ux,uy,u,v,theta,N,V,M,epsilon,kappa]. The equilibrium signs satisfy dN/dx=-qx, dV/dx=-qy and dM/dx=-V. Section values at the start equal the negatives of the first three local member end forces, and values at the end equal the last three, within numerical error.

Field recovery solves the constant-property member equations exactly in the Euler–Bernoulli model before binary64 rounding: quadratic axial displacement and quartic transverse displacement under uniform loads. It includes the zero-end-displacement/slope particular solution inside each member. A beam fixed at both ends can therefore have nonzero interior deflection when every nodal displacement is zero. Positions refer to the undeformed geometry; add the global displacement when drawing a deformed shape. Endpoint global displacements are returned directly from the supplied nodal rows.

strain_energy(displacements) returns NativeFrame2DEnergy{nodal,member_load,total}. The existing solver's nodal_strain_energy retains its meaning. The additional member-load energy is integrated from the interior particular fields: qx²*L³/(24*EA) + qy²*L⁵/(1440*EI) per member. These fields are energy-orthogonal to the homogeneous nodal interpolation, so total energy is their sum. The shared nodal-energy helper integrates nonnegative strain modes.

The caller can supply solved or prescribed kinematics; field/energy evaluation does not assert global equilibrium, certify a load case, or bind the data to a previous solve. The caller must use the intended frame and load model. Forces, strains, curvature, energy and displacement have their usual different physical units; inputs must use a consistent unit system. Finite binary64 intermediate terms and outputs are required; unrepresentable evaluations return errors. Products/ratios retain exponent range to avoid premature overflow of EI or powers of member length. Numerical estimates are not certified error bounds.

All previous model limits remain: small displacement, linear elasticity, constant positive EA/EI, rigid joints, and uniform member loads. Interior concentrated loads require nodes at their locations. Section/fiber stress, varying properties, hinges, shear deformation, 3D, nonlinear/dynamic/buckling models and design standards remain separate work. Reference: TU Delft continuum field postprocessing and member-load differential equations. ModernBASIC retains its documented counterclockwise rotation convention. Host qualification passed: 59 field/error cases (6,642 scalar comparisons), 37 retained frame cases (12,158 comparisons), 46 Rust regressions, maximum-batch native resources/cancellation and interpreter/export parity. Evidence is in output/frame2d-fields-2026-10-28. Installed systems and other CPU/hardware targets remain open.

documents.title: Physical units and dimension-checked quantities
documents.html:
The shared CPU Rust backend provides exact rational unit definitions and finite binary64 quantities. Definitions follow the BIPM SI Brochure and NIST SP 811 conversion tables; the 2022 SI prefix extension is included. This is an independent implementation using the existing bounded Rust rational-arithmetic kernel; no new dependency or external engine is required.

Native API: NativeUnit::parse(text), dimensions(), scale(), offset(), is_affine(), convert(value, &target) and convert_values(&values, &target). Units are immutable and reusable. Dimensions are seven integer exponents in this order: length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity. Exact rational scales and offsets are retained internally; conversions combine the full source/target transform before rounding once. Extreme scales can cancel in direct conversion even when scale() would overflow or round to zero. Numeric results reject overflow/nonfinite values; underflow rounds to subnormal/zero, ties to even. Negative zero becomes zero.

NativeQuantity::new(value, &unit) constructs a linear quantity; temperature_point(value, &unit) explicitly constructs a temperature reading. from_si(value, dimensions, point_flag) validates native stored inputs. Getters are si_value(), dimensions(), is_temperature_point(). Operations are value_in(&unit), add, subtract, multiply, divide, powi(i16) and sqrt(). Binary operations take another quantity by reference and return a new quantity. Quantities store a rounded SI binary64 value at each construction/arithmetic boundary. They preserve dimensions, not arbitrary-precision measurement values or uncertainty. Conversion back from a quantity can therefore lose small differences relative to a large SI offset; direct UNITCONVERT avoids that intermediate rounding.

BASIC functionResult and contract
UNITINFO(unit$){scale,offset,{7 dimension exponents},affine_flag}; canonical SI coordinate = value * scale + offset.
UNITCONVERT(value,from$,to$)Scalar or nested numeric list conversion, preserving list shape; incompatible dimensions fail.
QTY(value,unit$)Linear quantity packet {SI_value,{7 dimension exponents},0}.
QPOINT(value,unit$)Temperature point packet with last entry 1; requires pure temperature dimensions.
QVALUE(quantity,unit$)Numeric coordinate in a compatible output unit.
QADD(a,b) / QSUB(a,b)Add/subtract matching dimensions, enforcing point/interval rules.
QMUL(a,b) / QDIV(a,b)Multiply/divide linear quantities, combining dimensions.
QPOW(quantity,n)Integer power -32..32; dimension bounds still apply. Zero to power zero is 1.
QSQRT(quantity)Nonnegative linear value with every dimension exponent even.

Packets are ordinary editable BASIC lists and are validated on every operation. Use the Q functions for checked arithmetic: ordinary BASIC list arithmetic does not understand or preserve quantity semantics. Existing numeric solvers still accept numeric arrays; convert/validate dimensions at their input/output boundary. See programs/science/unit_checked_engineering.bas for mechanical stress, electrical energy, thermal differences, a millimetre-based frame model and audio sample counts over the same backend.

Unit expressions use explicit *, /, integer ^ and parentheses. Products/divisions associate left to right: m/s/s means m/s^2; use m/(s/s) for a grouped denominator. Whitespace is permitted around operators, but implicit multiplication and Unicode symbols are not accepted. Symbols are case-sensitive: MPa is megapascal, mPa millipascal. Use ASCII u for micro, Ohm for resistance, deg for degrees, degC/degF for temperature coordinates. Prefixes apply before powers: mm^2 has scale 10^-6. Prefixes cannot stack and mass prefixes attach to g.

Supported symbols:

  • SI bases: m kg s A K mol cd; gram g.
  • Derived SI: rad sr Hz N Pa J W C V F Ohm S Wb T H lm lx Bq Gy Sv kat.
  • Additional units: L l min h d t in ft yd mi lb oz lbf psi bar atm eV deg % and dimensionless 1. Length/weight units use international definitions; lbf uses standard gravity. deg uses binary64 pi divided exactly by 180.
  • Temperature: degC degF deltaK deltaC deltaF. K also expresses intervals and temperature factors in compound units.
  • All 24 decimal SI prefixes: Q R Y Z E P T G M k h da d c m u n p f a z y r q. Prefixes apply to SI bases other than kg, derived SI units, g L l t bar eV. They do not apply to additional time/customary units, deg, % or temperature aliases. Full symbols take precedence over prefix splitting.

Temperature coordinates with an offset (degC and degF) must stand alone, possibly parenthesized; products/powers require K, deltaC or deltaF. A point minus a point produces an interval; point plus/minus interval produces a point; interval plus point produces a point. Point plus point, interval minus point, and multiplication/division/powers/roots of a point fail. QTY(20,"degC") fails: use QPOINT(20,"degC") for a reading or QTY(20,"deltaC") for a difference. Extract Kelvin with QVALUE(point,"K") when a model explicitly needs absolute temperature as a multiplicative scalar. Conversions do not enforce a particular model's thermodynamic domain.

Limits: unit strings 1..256 ASCII bytes, at most 32 symbol terms, parentheses depth 8, written powers -32..32, intermediate/final dimensions -128..128. Exact arithmetic shares the 4096-bit normalized coefficient limit and 32-million-work-unit budget per operation. Native batches admit at most one million values; BASIC conversions admit one million nested nodes plus the root, depth at most 32. Work exhaustion/cancellation/invalid entries fail atomically; caller inputs and failed BASIC assignment targets remain intact.

SI dimensional equality does not distinguish physical kinds with identical dimensions: torque/energy, frequency/radioactivity, radians/scalars, and luminous intensity/flux can coincide. Currency, logarithmic units (dB), calendar-dependent durations, fractional dimensions, user-defined unit registries, uncertainty propagation and automatic solver-wide quantity tracking are not supplied by this API. Those are explicit further integration requirements; this checkpoint does not complete engineering/CAD or analytics.

Host qualification passed: 895 independent reference/rejection cases, 43 Rust regressions, three million native conversions in million-value batches, mid-batch cancellation/recovery, 65,536-row BASIC conversion and exact interpreter/export stdout parity. Evidence: output/physical-units-2026-10-28. Installed OS, other targets and physical hardware acceptance remain separate gates.

documents.title: First-order multivariate measurement uncertainty
documents.html:
NativeUncertainty shares the sparse exact positive-semidefinite proof and finite triple-product accumulators. For an input covariance C and an output-by-input Jacobian J it evaluates Cout = J C J^T. This is the first-order propagation law described by JCGM 102:2011, section 6.2. It is exact for affine models apart from numeric output rounding. A nonlinear model uses the caller's Jacobian at its nominal point; derivative errors and higher-order/non-Gaussian effects are not automatically bounded. Existing NativeDifferentiation::jacobian reports can supply derivatives, after the caller verifies their completion/status and error estimates.

NativeUncertainty::new(covariance: NativeRealMatrix) validates and retains an immutable reusable covariance. It must be exactly symmetric and positive semidefinite for its stored binary64 entries. Zero-variance and singular correlated models are accepted when the exact proof succeeds; negative pivots, incompatible symmetry, or proof resource exhaustion fail. No floating tolerance, symmetrization, diagonal jitter or clipping silently changes the data. The proof reuses exact diagonal dominance or bounded rational Schur elimination. As in SPISPSD, a difficult valid matrix can exceed the exact proof's 4096-bit coefficient, retained-bit or work limits and return a resource error.

propagate(&jacobian) returns NativeUncertaintyReport with a NativeRealMatrix covariance and Vec<f64> standard_uncertainties. Each output covariance entry is accumulated from exact triple products and rounded once. Each standard uncertainty is the correctly rounded square root of the exact nonnegative variance, taken before rounding the variance. Consequently a reported covariance diagonal can underflow to zero while the standard uncertainty remains nonzero. Rounded covariance entries are not a certificate that the rounded output matrix remains exactly PSD; reusing nearly singular rounded results can fail strict admission.

standard_uncertainties(&jacobian) computes only the standard uncertainties, so it can return 1E200 when the corresponding 1E400 variance cannot be stored as binary64. The full report rejects an unrepresentable covariance entry; both paths reject an unrepresentable standard uncertainty or other invalid input. input_count() reports the model dimension. Output ordering follows Jacobian rows.

For unit-aware work, construct with from_quantities(&covariance_rows, &input_units), where entries are NativeQuantity values and units are NativeUnit values. Every covariance entry must be linear with dimensions input_i * input_j. Then propagate_quantities(&jacobian_rows, &output_units) returns NativeQuantityUncertaintyReport containing a matrix of covariance quantities and a vector of standard-uncertainty quantities. Every derivative must be linear with dimensions output_i / input_j. standard_uncertainties_quantities supplies the range-safe standard-only path. Unit declarations establish dimensions; quantity packets already carry SI values, so declarations do not rescale those values a second time. Use interval units K/deltaC/deltaF for temperature uncertainty; offset units and temperature points are rejected. Returned standard uncertainties are linear quantities.

UNCERTSTD(jacobian,covariance)Standard-uncertainty vector without storing output covariance.
QUNCERTPROP(jacobian_quantities,covariance_quantities,input_units$,output_units$)Same pair, containing quantity packets. Unit arguments are lists of strings.
QUNCERTSTD(jacobian_quantities,covariance_quantities,input_units$,output_units$)Vector of standard-uncertainty quantity packets.

For example, resistance V/I at 12 V and 0.5 A has Jacobian {2 /A,-48 V/A^2}. With voltage variance 0.01 V^2, current variance 0.000004 A^2 and covariance 0.00008 V*A, its first-order standard uncertainty is approximately 0.184 Ohm. The editable consumer is programs/science/measurement_uncertainty.bas.

Input/output axes are bounded to 0..256. Empty-input models represent constants; a native m x 0 Jacobian returns m zero uncertainties and an m x m zero covariance. Empty BASIC rows preserve these constant outputs. Each propagation admits at most 50 million nonzero-covariance triple-product terms, counting both covariance and standard-deviation evaluations for a full report. Partition output rows or use the standard-only path when the full work limit would be exceeded. Model construction has separate exact-proof limits. Quantity dimensions retain the physical-unit exponent limits. All loops are cancellable; inputs are borrowed/immutable and errors return no partial result or BASIC assignment. No external provider or new dependency is introduced.

This API does not produce a nonlinear error bound, a confidence/coverage interval, a Monte Carlo distribution, an uncertainty budget by source, or a guarantee that the supplied covariance/derivatives accurately describe measurements. first-order propagation law described by

caller verifies their completion/status and error estimates.

immutable reusable covariance. It must be exactly symmetric and positive

incompatible symmetry, or proof resource exhaustion fail. No floating
tolerance, symmetrization, diagonal jitter or clipping silently changes the data.

`NativeQuantity` values and units are `NativeUnit` values.

are rejected. Returned standard uncertainties are linear quantities.
