documents.title: Exact decimal arithmetic and explicit rounding
documents.html:
The crate exports NativeDecimal, NativeDecimalContext and NativeDecimalRounding. Parse ASCII decimal strings with NativeDecimal::parse or exact signed integers with from_integer. Strings retain decimal scale; arithmetic uses the existing exact Rust rational kernel, without a binary64 conversion. format() produces fixed decimal text; compare compares numerical values ignoring trailing zeros. to_f64 is an explicit rounded conversion: overflow fails, underflow may become zero.

NativeDecimalContext::new(places, mode) declares the output quantum 10^-places. Places range from -1024 through 1024: negative places round to tens/hundreds/etc. quantize, add, subtract, multiply, divide, multiply_add and powi round only the final exact expression. sum consumes up to one million borrowed decimals incrementally and rounds the final sum. Thus adding two 0.005 values at two places produces 0.01, whereas separately rounding the inputs first can produce 0.00. Integer powers range from -1024 through 1024; zero to power zero is one, and a negative power of zero fails.

Policies are HalfEven (nearest, ties to even), HalfUp (nearest, ties away from zero), HalfDown (nearest, ties toward zero), Up (away from zero), Down (toward zero), Ceiling (toward positive infinity), Floor (toward negative infinity), and Unnecessary (error unless exact). The string names accepted by NativeDecimalRounding::parse are the uppercase BASIC names below. Negative zero formats as positive zero. Nonnegative places retain trailing zeros; negative places produce expanded integer text.

Limits are explicit: at most 4096 ASCII input bytes, parsed scale -1024..1024, 4096 bits per normalized numerator/denominator and the shared 32-million-unit arithmetic budget per operation. Bounded intermediates can fail even if a later cancellation would make the final value small. No NaN/infinity or automatic currency conversion is admitted. Operations are cancellable; immutable inputs remain reusable after failure. Arithmetic and formatting can each reject a representation that exceeds these bounds.

Host qualification passed: 49 Rust tests, 766 independent decimal cases and 1,092 high-precision compatibility checks; million-entry native sums, a 65,536-entry BASIC sum, cancellation/recovery and interpreter/export parity. Evidence: output/decimal-arithmetic-2026-10-28. Currency identity, jurisdiction-specific rounding, allocation policies, financial model integration and installed/other-target acceptance remain separate work.

documents.title: Exact-moment mean inference
documents.html:
One-sample and Welch tests now accumulate the original observations exactly through the shared single/pair moment backend. The BASIC interfaces retain INTEGER bits; native slice interfaces consume the supplied finite binary64 values. Sample means, mean differences, variance ratios and Welch degrees of freedom stay exact until the final statistic or distribution argument is rounded. This prevents an already-rounded large sample mean from erasing a real shift.

NativeStudentT::paired_test(first,second,hypothesized_difference,confidence) returns NativePairedTTest, an alias of NativeOneSampleTTest. Pair observations by position; use the mean and variance of exact first-second differences. NativeStudentT::pooled_test(first,second,confidence) returns NativePooledTTest, an alias of NativeWelchTTest. Pooled testing explicitly assumes equal population variances; Welch retains its unequal-variance formula. All reports contain t_statistic, degrees_of_freedom, two_sided_p_value and a two-sided confidence_interval for the mean or mean difference. A hypothesized mean changes the statistic, not the reported mean interval.

At most one million total observations are admitted (500,000 pairs); each sample needs two values, paired lengths must match, and the variance relevant to the test must be nonzero. Undefined statistics, nonfinite input, or a final unrepresentable report fail; overflowing intermediate means/differences/standard deviations alone do not force failure. Summary storage is fixed per sample; input arrays remain caller-owned. Cancellation is checked during accumulation and distribution/interval evaluation.

Confidence is strictly between zero and one. Small central coverage is computed directly; below 1e-8, the inverse uses its linear term with relative cubic correction below 1e-16 for the admitted degrees of freedom, preserving the coverage as an exact factor. Interval endpoints use exact rational enclosures of center plus/minus the computed square-root width; matching rounded bounds decide each endpoint, with at most 8192 working root bits. This certifies endpoint rounding for the computed critical factor, not statistical coverage or the transcendental distribution approximation. Critical values and probabilities remain subject to the shared Student-t kernel's numerical accuracy.

BASIC adds TTESTPAIRED(a,b[,confidence[,null_difference]]) and TTESTPOOLED(a,b[,confidence]); all four tests return {t,df,p,lower,upper}. Confidence defaults to 0.95 and paired null difference to zero. Samples are flat lists of INTEGER/REAL observations, without automatic missing-value removal. Choose pairing, independence and variance assumptions from the study design; these calculations do not establish those assumptions or correct multiple tests. Host qualification passed: 55 Rust regressions and 364 independent reference cases (1,765 scalar comparisons), four million native observations, 65,536-observation BASIC samples, cancellation/recovery and interpreter/export parity. Indexed list-initialization performance is a separately recorded open runtime issue. Evidence: output/mean-inference-2026-10-28. Further inference/regression, domain/installed/other-target acceptance remain open.

documents.title: Fisher F probability distribution
documents.html:
NativeFisherF::new(numerator_degrees, denominator_degrees) constructs the central Fisher-Snedecor law. pdf, cdf, survival, probabilities, quantile and inverse_survival share the bounded CPU incomplete-beta engine with the BASIC functions below. probabilities returns both tails.

Degrees must be finite, positive and have exactly representable positive binary64 halves; unrepresentable subnormal halves are rejected explicitly. Samples and probabilities must be finite. Negative samples have zero density/CDF and unit survival. At zero the density is infinite for numerator degrees below two (reported as RealOverflow), one for two degrees, and zero above two. The lower inverse accepts 0 <= p < 1 and the upper inverse 0 < p <= 1; unbounded endpoints and finite critical values beyond binary64 raise overflow. A critical value below the first positive binary64 coordinate is returned as that first coordinate; exact zero-probability endpoints return zero.

Both beta coordinates are retained independently. Original F displacement is used near a concentrated distribution's center, and logarithmic tails preserve probabilities when transformed beta coordinates or tail probabilities underflow. Inverses search ordered positive binary64 coordinates in at most 63 bisections, with a shared one-million-step beta work budget. Scalar evaluation uses a 100,000-step budget and cooperatively checks interruption. Numerical exhaustion returns a domain error; this is not a certified enclosure or an arbitrary- precision probability distribution.

This is a central F law, with no noncentrality/location/scale parameter. Distribution functions alone do not implement ANOVA models or establish the assumptions for a statistical inference. A variance ratio from independent normal populations is one consumer. Mathematical definitions: NIST F distribution. Regression tests: tests/fisher_f_tests.rs. Independent numerical qualification: tools/check-fisher-f.py, registered in tools/qualify-math.py.

documents.title: Exact-moment variance and group inference
documents.html:
The public Rust NativeFisherF::variance_test(first, second, hypothesized_ratio, confidence_level) returns NativeVarianceRatioTest: f_statistic, numerator_degrees, denominator_degrees, two_sided_p_value, and the two-element confidence_interval for population variance(first)/variance(second). The positive null ratio scales the test statistic; it does not change that interval. Each sample needs at least two finite values and positive sample variance. Confidence is supported on [1e-6, 1); smaller central coverages are rejected because the tail-based F inverse has not been qualified at that resolution.

NativeFisherF::one_way_anova(&[&[f64]]) returns NativeOneWayAnova: f_statistic, between_degrees, within_degrees, p_value, and eta_squared (between/total variation). It requires at least two nonempty groups, more observations than groups, and positive combined within-group variation. Individual singleton/constant groups are allowed. Equal group means return F=0, p=1 and eta-squared=0. All-constant groups are rejected, including groups with different constants: an infinite F statistic is not a finite report.

Both procedures cap combined observations at 1,000,000, check cancellation, and use the existing exact Rust sample moments and private rational arithmetic. They retain offsets and cancel variance scales before binary64 rounding; BASIC also retains full signed INTEGER observations. ANOVA streams group summaries rather than copying samples or retaining per-group moment objects. Reported probabilities use the final rounded F statistic. A positive statistic or interval endpoint rounding to zero is a domain error; overflowing report fields return an overflow error. These are numerical estimates, not certified intervals, and raw sums of squares that might overflow are not report fields.

The variance test assumes independent samples from normal populations. Ordinary one-way ANOVA assumes independent, normal, common-variance group errors. The routines do not check the experimental design or those assumptions. Welch ANOVA is available through NativeFisherF::welch_anova below. Repeated measures, multi-factor models and post-hoc comparisons remain separate work. Formulas: NIST variance F test and NIST one-way ANOVA.

documents.title: Welch unequal-variance group inference
documents.html:
NativeFisherF::welch_anova(&[&[f64]]) returns NativeWelchAnova with f_statistic, numerator_degrees, denominator_degrees, and p_value. BASIC calls the same kernel through ANOVAWELCH. Each group requires at least two finite observations and positive sample variance; there must be at least two groups and at most one million observations total. Constant groups and singleton groups are explicit errors. Cancellation is supported.

The method tests equality of means for independent normal populations, using Welch's approximate F reference distribution and adjusted denominator degrees. It permits unequal variances and unequal group sizes. It does not validate normality or independence, supply post-hoc pair comparisons, or model repeated measurements or multiple factors. No equal-variance eta-squared is attached to this report. For two groups the statistic reduces to squared Welch t and uses the same denominator degrees. See Welch (1951), equations 29-30, and the SciPy reference procedure.

Exact existing sample moments retain large offsets and full BASIC INTEGER precision. Inverse-variance weights are rounded once to dyadic rationals with individual relative error at most 2^-127, retaining their exponents even outside binary64. Weighted moments and the degree correction are then summed exactly. This prevents unrelated sample-variance denominators from causing unbounded rational growth; remaining denominators come from bounded group sizes. No copy of observations or list of group summaries is retained. F and degrees are rounded to binary64 before the shared F survival calculation. Positive F that rounds to zero is rejected, and overflowing F raises overflow; exact zero between-group differences return F=0 and p=1. These are numerical estimates, not certified uncertainty enclosures.

NativeMultipleTesting::adjust_p_values(values, method, family_size) returns adjusted p-values in the original order. NativePAdjustMethod selects None, Bonferroni, Holm, Hochberg, Hommel, BenjaminiHochberg or BenjaminiYekutieli. The optional family size defaults to the input length. Every p-value must be finite and in [0,1]; empty input is valid. Family size must be an integer between the input length and 1,000,000. Inputs and outputs are bounded at one million values. Results are between their original p-value and one; tied p-values receive tied corrections, and signed zero becomes zero.

Bonferroni and Holm control family-wise error for valid input tests with arbitrary dependence. Hochberg and Hommel require independence or suitable positive dependence satisfying the Simes inequality. BH controls false discovery rate under independence or positive regression dependence; BY allows arbitrary dependence and includes the harmonic-family correction. None makes no correction. The caller chooses the family and method; this API does not validate the underlying tests, model assumptions, or a data-dependent selection of hypotheses. References: R multiple-testing documentation and SciPy FDR documentation.

An explicit larger family treats omitted hypotheses as p=1 for step-up/FDR/ Hommel methods and beyond observed ranks for Holm/Bonferroni. None ignores the correction count after validation. Hommel computes closed Simes tests: for each subset size, monotonicity means the maximal local p-value containing one hypothesis uses that hypothesis plus the largest other values. Missing p=1 members are folded algebraically instead of allocating a padded family. This independently expressed Rust procedure is checked against exhaustive closed-subset references; no R implementation is bundled.

Stable merge sorting, reductions, harmonic summation and BASIC result conversion observe cancellation. Hommel's estimated quadratic work is limited to 2*m*(m-1) <= 20,000,000 for m supplied p-values (at most 3,162); excess work returns an explicit work-limit error. Other methods accept one million values. Scaled products preserve subnormal probabilities; BY exactly accumulates rounded binary64 reciprocals before rounding the harmonic sum. These remain binary64 estimates, not certified enclosures. No caller-owned input is modified.

Tensor reduction and loss precision

NativeTensor::sum, mean, sum_axis and mean_axis use the same bounded exact accumulators as BASIC TSUM/TMEAN and the native tape. Each output uses one accumulator; means divide before rounding, preserving subnormal values and finite means whose unscaled sum would overflow. Tangent and higher-order reductions use the same rule.

NativeTensorTape::mean_squared_error and TMSE accumulate exact squared residuals before dividing; the reverse, tangent and higher-order paths avoid premature product overflow. Cross-entropy Taylor propagation consistently shifts both logits and their target-weighted sum, including parameter-dependent targets.

documents.html:
Civil dates are INTEGER days relative to 1970-01-01. The supported proleptic Gregorian range is 0001-01-01 through 9999-12-31 (-719162 through 2932896). There are no timezones, daylight-saving transitions, locale guesses or fictitious 1900-02-29. Existing clock-oriented DATE$ behavior is unchanged.

FunctionContract
CIVILDATE(year,month,day)Construct a valid date; reject invalid fields.
CIVILPARSE(text$)Parse exactly ten ASCII characters in YYYY-MM-DD form.
CIVILFORMAT$(date)Format exactly YYYY-MM-DD.
CIVILPARTS(date)Return {year,month,day,weekday}, Monday=1 through Sunday=7.
CIVILADD(date,amount[,unit$[,preserveMonthEnd]])Signed INTEGER increment; units DAYS (default), MONTHS or YEARS. Missing target days clamp to month end. The optional 0/1 flag additionally preserves an original month end for MONTHS/YEARS.
DAYCOUNT(start,end[,basis$])Signed day count under the named convention.
YEARFRAC(start,end[,basis$])Fraction of a year, rounded once from an exact integer ratio.
YEARFRACRATIO(start,end[,basis$])Return {numerator,denominator}; denominator is positive, and the ratio need not be reduced.
BUSCAL(holidays[,weekendMask])Construct an editable {"BUSCAL1",mask,holidays} record. Holidays are date integers.
BUSISDAY(calendar,date)Return 1 for an open date, otherwise 0.
BUSCOUNT(calendar,start,end)Count open dates in [start,end); reverse endpoints negate the count.
BUSADD(calendar,date,amount)Advance by signed business days, excluding the start. Zero returns the start unchanged.
BUSADJUST(calendar,date,convention$)Apply the explicit adjustment convention below.
DATEDNPV(rate,amounts,dates,valuationDate[,basis$])Value dated cash flows using an annual effective rate and explicit valuation date.

Day-count basis defaults to ACT365F. Supported spellings are:

  • ACT365F: actual elapsed days divided by 365.
  • ACT360: actual elapsed days divided by 360.
  • ACTACTISDA: actual days in each calendar year divided by that year's 365/366 days. Whole intervening years contribute one each; integer arithmetic combines the two partial years before the single final division.
  • 30E360: European/Eurobond 30E/360; replace each day 31 by 30 and use 360*(endYear-startYear)+30*(endMonth-startMonth)+endDay-startDay. February keeps its actual day number. This is a separate convention from 30E/360 ISDA, US/NASD and coupon-schedule-dependent Actual/Actual methods.

All four day-count/year-fraction operations are signed and antisymmetric. Intervals with identical endpoints have zero length. ACTACTISDA day counts are actual elapsed days; its year-fraction denominator depends on the endpoint years.

Weekend mask bits 0..6 mean Monday..Sunday. The default 96 closes Saturday and Sunday. Masks 0..126 are accepted; all seven weekdays cannot be closed. BUSCAL admits at most 65,536 supplied holidays, removes duplicates and omits holidays already closed by the weekend mask. No national holidays, observed-day rules or exchange schedules are implicit. Every BASIC operation validates the calendar record; native callers can reuse its prepared Rust representation.

Business adjustment names are UNADJUSTED, FOLLOWING, PRECEDING, MODFOLLOWING and MODPRECEDING. Modified conventions switch direction if the first adjustment would cross a month boundary. At the supported calendar boundary they try the opposite direction. Open dates remain unchanged. If no valid date can be returned within the supported range, the operation reports an error. Counting uses whole weeks and sorted holiday ranges; advancing uses a bounded binary search rather than walking through every intervening day.

DATEDNPV uses: SUM(amount[i] * (1 + rate)^(-YEARFRAC(valuationDate, dates[i], basis))). The rate must be finite and greater than -1. Amount/date list lengths must match and are capped at one million. Empty lists return zero. Dates can be unsorted, repeated or before valuation; valuation-day flows are included without discount, and earlier flows compound forward. Monetary amounts/results use binary64, including conversion of BASIC INTEGER amounts; they are not fixed-decimal money.

Discount weights use log1p/exp. Finite weights and amounts are multiplied and summed with the existing exact product accumulator before final rounding, which preserves cancellation even when an individual product would overflow. A weight outside binary64 uses the existing scaled-principal fallback; an unrepresentable fallback term or final result raises overflow. Transcendental approximation and ill-conditioned cancellation remain relevant; this is not certified valuation or a correctly rounded transcendental sum. Cancellation is checked while preparing inputs and after the bounded exact accumulation phase. Native inputs are immutable; errors return no partial result.

Native exports: NativeCivilDate, NativeDayCount, NativeBusinessCalendar, NativeBusinessConvention and NativeDatedCashflow. NativeFinancialMath exposes dated_net_present_value(rate,flows,valuation,basis). Native date construction, parsing, formatting and arithmetic use checked values. Calendar operations share the same rules as BASIC. Example: programs/finance/dated_cashflows.bas.

This checkpoint adds no new registry package: Chrono 0.4.45 was already vendored and pinned through the table dependencies. Its direct dependency enables only the standard-library date support, with clock/timezone defaults disabled. Existing upstream license files and archive/file checksums remain intact. Chrono supplies checked Gregorian dates; ModernBASIC supplies the public bounds, business-calendar contract, exact day-count ratios and financial integration.

References inspected for date APIs and convention comparison: Chrono NaiveDate, QuantLib Actual/Actual implementations, QuantLib 30/360 implementations. QuantLib is a comparison reference, not a new runtime dependency or copied engine.

Anchored civil schedules and explicit stubs are described in DATE_SCHEDULES.md. Remaining financial work includes additional schedule/roll conventions and day-count families, country/exchange calendar datasets, dated IRR and curve bootstrapping, currency/decimal rounding, portfolio risk and wider model qualification. Timezone timestamps, persisted calendar identities, typed DATE table columns, installed OS and other CPU architectures retain separate acceptance gates.

## Overview

documents.title: BASIC API
documents.html:
DATESCHEDULE(start,end,amount,unit$[,stub$[,endOfMonth[,firstRegular[,lastRegular]]]]) returns an editable list of strictly increasing contractual date integers. Dates use days since 1970-01-01, years 1..9999. Start must precede end. Amount is an INTEGER in 1..4294967295. Units are DAYS or MONTHS; use 12 MONTHS for years and 7 DAYS for weeks. There are at most 100,000 periods (100,001 dates).

All regular dates are computed directly from the original anchor at multiples of the interval. Monthly schedules do not drift after clamping February. The optional endOfMonth flag is 0 (default) or 1. With 1, an anchor that is a calendar month end rolls to each target month end. With 0, retain the anchor's day number, clamping only where absent. A non-month-end anchor keeps its day number even when the flag is 1. DAYS rejects endOfMonth=1.

Stub names:

NameAnchor and treatment of an incomplete period
SHORTBACK (default)Generate forward; keep the short final period.
LONGBACKGenerate forward; merge a short final period with the adjacent generated regular period.
SHORTFRONTGenerate backward; keep the short initial period.
LONGFRONTGenerate backward; merge a short initial period with the adjacent generated regular period.
EXACTGenerate forward; reject an automatically incomplete period.

A long policy changes nothing when the span divides exactly. If there is no adjacent generated regular period to merge, a single stub remains unchanged. A theoretical next date outside the supported year range counts as overshooting the in-range endpoint, so a valid short/long terminal stub can still be returned.

firstRegular explicitly ends an initial stub; lastRegular explicitly starts a final stub. Each supplied date must lie strictly between start and end, and firstRegular must not exceed lastRegular. Omit them or use an empty list {} to leave them unspecified. Equal first/last dates yield two explicit stubs without an intervening regular period.

With front rules the regular anchor is lastRegular, or end; with back/EXACT rules it is firstRegular, or start. An explicit boundary at the other end must be reached exactly by the regular grid. The engine rejects inconsistent dates rather than inserting an extra stub next to the explicit one. Long rules never remove an explicitly supplied boundary. EXACT permits explicitly supplied stubs but requires the regular span to divide exactly.

SCHEDULEPERIODS(dates,calendar[,accrualRule$[,paymentRule$[,paymentLag[,basis$[,accrualDates$[,terminationRule$]]]]]]) accepts generated or user-edited strictly increasing dates and a BUSCAL record. Each output row contains:

  1. Unadjusted start.
  2. Unadjusted end.
  3. Adjusted start.
  4. Adjusted end.
  5. Payment date.
  6. Exact year-fraction numerator.
  7. Exact positive year-fraction denominator.
  8. Binary64 year fraction, rounded once from the ratio.

Rows use BASIC's existing multidimensional list indexing: P(i,5) is the ith payment date. Defaults are MODFOLLOWING accrual adjustment, FOLLOWING payment adjustment, zero payment lag, ACT365F basis and UNADJUSTED accrual dates. Rules are the five BUSADJUST conventions. The optional terminationRule overrides only the final accrual boundary; otherwise it uses accrualRule.

Payment dates are computed independently: adjust the contractual period end using paymentRule, then advance by signed INTEGER business days using paymentLag. Zero lag leaves that adjusted date unchanged, including a closed date if the payment rule is UNADJUSTED. A negative lag supports payment in advance. Repeated payment dates are permitted; no automatic payment aggregation occurs.

accrualDates is UNADJUSTED or ADJUSTED. It selects which pair determines the day-count ratio. Supported bases are ACT365F, ACT360, ACTACTISDA and European 30E360. ACTACTISDA is not coupon-reference-period Actual/Actual ICMA. Ratios need not be reduced; 30E360 can legitimately give zero for distinct dates.

All adjusted accrual boundaries must remain strictly increasing. A collision or reversal raises an error, even when unadjusted dates were selected for interest. No period is silently removed. Inputs remain unchanged and no partial result is returned after an error or cancellation. Arithmetic is bounded by the admitted date range and output count; generation, adjustment and BASIC conversion include cooperative cancellation checkpoints. This does not promise hard real-time latency.

documents.title: Native Rust API
documents.html:
The crate exports NativeDateSchedule, NativeScheduleOptions, NativeScheduleInterval (Days/Months), NativeScheduleStub, NativeAccrualOptions and NativeAccrualPeriod.

NativeDateSchedule::generate(start,end,options) constructs anchored schedules; from_dates(&dates) validates externally supplied schedules; dates() exposes the immutable boundaries. accrual_periods(&calendar,options) returns typed period records using the same rules as BASIC. Options implement Default. Native callers can reuse a prepared NativeBusinessCalendar without rebuilding a BASIC record. Payment dates and year fractions compose with NativeDatedCashflow and NativeFinancialMath::dated_net_present_value.

Example: payment_schedule.bas.

documents.title: References and remaining scope
documents.html:
The public OpenGamma Strata periodic schedule description and QuantLib schedule source were inspected for established schedule concepts. The Rust implementation is independent; neither engine was copied or added as a dependency. The published Strata long-initial quarterly example is a regression fixture. The independent checker enumerates month/day grids, scans business days with Python datetime, and calculates accrual fractions with exact rational arithmetic.

This is an explicit civil schedule contract, not full compatibility with either reference engine. IMM/CDS/third-Wednesday rolls, smart stubs, business-month-end rolls, coupon-reference-period day counts, country/exchange datasets, additional return models, curve calibration/bootstrapping, fixed-decimal money and portfolio risk remain open. Timezone/intraday schedules, typed DATE tables, persisted calendar identities, installed OS and other CPU architectures remain separate qualification gates.

Dated discount-factor curves value payments using an explicit term structure and expose continuous/annual spot and forward rates.

Bracketed dated returns solve the annual-effective cash-flow equation through shared Rust/BASIC kernels with explicit convergence reports.

## Overview

The Rust curve engine shares [civil-date/day-count math](CALENDAR_MATH.md),

BASIC programs and native Rust callers use the same implementation. No provider,

documents.title: BASIC API
documents.html:
FunctionContract
DISCOUNTCURVE(reference,dates,factors[,basis$[,extrapolation$]])Construct an editable curve record from strictly ordered future knots.
CURVEDF(curve,dateOrDates)Positive discount factor, or a list of factors for a list of dates.
CURVELOGDF(curve,dateOrDates)Natural logarithm of the factor, including cases where the factor cannot fit in binary64.
CURVEZERO(curve,dateOrDates[,compounding$])Annualized zero/spot rates from the reference date.
CURVEFORWARD(curve,start,end[,compounding$])Annualized rate over the stated forward interval.
CURVENPV(curve,amounts,dates)Value dated flows at the curve reference date.

Dates are INTEGER civil days since 1970-01-01 in years 1..9999. Dates/factors must be matching nonempty lists of at most 100,000 future knots. Factors must be finite and strictly positive, including representable subnormals. The reference-date factor is implicitly exactly one and is not supplied as a knot. Knots must increase strictly by date and by elapsed time under the selected basis. Duplicate dates and zero-length time spans (possible under 30E360) are rejected.

The default basis is ACT365F. ACT360, ACTACTISDA and European 30E360 are also available, using the existing explicit conventions. BASIC factors and monetary amounts use binary64; INTEGER inputs convert to binary64 as documented for the financial APIs. This is not fixed-decimal currency arithmetic.

The returned record is: {"DFCURVE1",reference,basis$,extrapolation$,dates,factors}. It remains ordinary editable BASIC data. Each operation validates the entire record; native callers reuse the prepared Rust curve. Batch queries validate once, preserve the input order and allow repeated dates. Empty query lists return empty lists. Batch queries and cash flows are capped at one million entries. An error or cancellation returns no partial output and leaves inputs unchanged.

documents.title: Interpolation, rates and valuation
documents.html:
For an interval between positive factors D0 and D1, the interpolated factor is D0^(1-w) * D1^w, where w is elapsed time from the left knot divided by the interval's time. Time coordinates use the selected day-count convention. Exact integer day-count ratios are combined before one division, avoiding subtraction of nearly equal rounded absolute year coordinates.

The factor at a supplied knot is returned with the original binary64 bits. Interior calculations choose the nearer endpoint and use a local exponential change. Nearby factor ratios use log1p; wider ratios avoid overflow/underflow in the division before falling back to separate logarithms when necessary.

Extrapolation defaults to NONE: dates beyond the last knot raise an error. FLATFORWARD explicitly extends the final interval's log-factor slope; it does not keep the final zero rate or factor constant. Dates before the reference date are rejected under either policy. Negative interest rates and nonmonotone factor sequences are permitted; positivity is not a general no-arbitrage or market-data quality certificate.

Compounding is CONTINUOUS (default) or ANNUAL (annual effective). For elapsed years t and factor D: continuous zero rate = -ln(D)/t; annual zero rate = expm1(continuous rate). For a forward interval use ln(D(start)/D(end))/t. Zero-rate dates must have strictly positive elapsed time from reference. Forward intervals require start < end and strictly positive elapsed time.

Within one segment, forward rates use that segment's log ratio and the direct interval duration. They do not subtract two nearly equal absolute log factors. At two exact knots, use the original factor ratio directly. Other forward intervals combine two partial intervals and the intervening knot ratio with exact accumulation of the finite products. Transcendental values are still approximate; cancellation across differently sloped segments can lose relative accuracy. These results are not certified or correctly rounded transcendental calculations, and the implementation does not claim a complete yield-curve model.

CURVENPV computes SUM(amount[i] * CURVEDF(curve,date[i])). Reference-day flows are included; repeated and unsorted cash-flow dates are allowed. Empty matching lists return zero. Every date must be in the curve's domain, including dates attached to zero amounts. Finite amount/factor products are summed exactly before final binary64 rounding, preserving cancellation even when an individual multiplication would overflow.

A discount factor that would round to zero or infinity raises a range error; CURVELOGDF and continuous rates can remain usable. Annual rates that cannot be represented as a finite value strictly greater than -1 also raise a range error. CURVENPV requires representable positive factors and a finite final result; it does not rescue an unrepresentable factor using a compensating principal. Construction, queries and preparation include cooperative cancellation checks; the bounded exact valuation accumulation checks cancellation at its boundary. Measured host latency does not establish hard real-time behavior.

documents.title: References and remaining scope
documents.html:

documents.title: Dated return equation
documents.html:
DATEDIRR finds one annual-effective rate r in a caller-supplied bracket for:

sum(amount[i] * (1+r)^(-YEARFRAC(reference,date[i],basis))) = 0

Dates use the civil-date API and Gregorian years 1..9999. The reference is the earliest surviving nonzero cash-flow group. Moving that reference multiplies the equation by a positive factor and does not change its mathematical roots. Rates must exceed -1. This is a numerical root of the supplied cash flows, not a guarantee of investment performance or a unique return.

The implementation is Rust. BASIC and direct Rust consumers share the calendar, exact accumulator and safeguarded scalar-search kernels. No external solver, Python process or new dependency is required.

documents.title: BASIC calls
documents.html:
DATEDIRR(amounts,dates,lowerRate,upperRate [,basis$[,absoluteTolerance[,relativeTolerance [,maxEvaluations[,maxIterations[,maxCashflowEvaluations]]]]]])

DATEDIRRINFO has the same arguments. Amounts and dates are matching lists of at most 1,000,000 entries. Amounts must be finite. Input may be unsorted and dates may repeat; input lists are not modified. Zero payments are ignored in the equation but included in the reported input count. At least one positive and one negative nonzero grouped payment, at distinct day-count times, are required. An identically zero equation is rejected because it does not identify a return.

The basis defaults to ACT365F. ACT360, ACTACTISDA and 30E360 are also supported, with the definitions in Calendar math. Equal day-count times are grouped using exact rational comparisons, including January 30/31 aliases under European 30/360. Same-time payments are summed exactly as represented binary64 inputs. A finite expansion preserves small residuals and group totals that exceed the range of a single binary64 number.

The bracket must be finite, ordered and have lowerRate > -1. Both endpoints are evaluated. An endpoint numerical zero is accepted; otherwise opposite objective signs are required. A same-sign bracket is rejected even when it contains two roots. Select a separate bracket for each desired return. Automatic bracket discovery, root enumeration, uniqueness proofs and detection of non-sign-changing tangent roots are not provided.

Defaults are absoluteTolerance = 1E-12, relativeTolerance = 1E-12, maxEvaluations = 4096, maxIterations = 2048 and maxCashflowEvaluations = 10000000. Tolerances are finite and nonnegative, relativeTolerance is at most one, and at least one tolerance must be positive. Evaluation limits are 2..32771 and iteration limits 1..16384. The cash-flow work cap may not exceed ten million and must allow both endpoint evaluations of all prepared terms.

DATEDIRR returns a REAL only for ZERO_FOUND or INTERVAL_TOLERANCE. Otherwise it raises an error identifying the stopping reason and recommending DATEDIRRINFO. DATEDIRRINFO returns the diagnostic report for valid searches, including searches that reach a work, iteration or floating-point resolution limit.

documents.title: Diagnostic report
documents.html:
The first nine fields match ROOTFIND:

FieldMeaning
1Selected rate.
2Normalized signed objective at that rate.
3, 4Final lower and upper rate bounds.
5, 6Objective values at those bounds.
7Objective evaluations, including both original endpoints.
8Search iterations.
9Status string.
10Prepared cash-flow terms evaluated: field 7 times field 12.
11Original input cash-flow count, including zero amounts.
12Effective finite expansion terms after exact time grouping.
13Reference civil date, in the shared integer epoch.
14Exact sign (-1, 0 or 1) of the represented weighted sum at field 1.

ZERO_FOUND means the sum of the represented floating-point products is exactly zero. INTERVAL_TOLERANCE means the bracket width meets the absolute tolerance or the relative tolerance times the selected rate magnitude. These are numerical stopping criteria, not certificates of the exact transcendental equation.

EVALUATION_LIMIT, ITERATION_LIMIT and RESOLUTION_LIMIT do not establish convergence. The selected point is an evaluated endpoint with the smaller absolute normalized objective, except that an interior numerical zero is returned directly. A small objective alone is not used to claim convergence.

The objective removes a common positive exponential and divides the signed sum by the sum of absolute represented expansion-term products. It lies in [-1,1] and is dimensionless, not a currency NPV. For a nonzero ratio smaller than the least binary64 subnormal, field 2 uses a signed minimum-subnormal value so that underflow cannot falsely report ZERO_FOUND; field 14 preserves its exact sign. Expansion pieces may have opposing signs, so the denominator is a numerical normalization, not the sum of absolute economic payments.

documents.title: Precision, limits and cancellation
documents.html:
Amounts, rates, year fractions and exponential evaluations use binary64. Exact grouping and product accumulation avoid summation overflow, underflow and lost cancellation, but do not remove transcendental approximation or make currency decimal-exact. The implementation uses log1p for rates near zero.

When a discount factor would be subnormal, the exponential is split into three normal factors and their four-factor products with amounts are accumulated exactly. Queries requiring any split factor below the normal binary64 range raise a range error. Even valid date/rate inputs can therefore exceed the supported exponential range; a very wide bracket can fail before reaching a representable root. No tiny payment is silently discarded.

The work cap counts prepared term evaluations, not preparation, sorting or every machine operation. Grouping can substantially reduce repeated-date workloads. Preparation and objective loops have cancellation checkpoints. Sorting and the bounded exact accumulation run between checkpoints, so this is cooperative cancellation, not a hard real-time latency guarantee.

An error or cancellation leaves caller inputs intact. Changing a bracket or tolerance can select a different root when several exist. Results do not imply Excel XIRR compatibility: the explicit bracket, date support, basis choices, validation and stopping/reporting contracts are ModernBASIC's own.

documents.title: Model and scope
documents.html:
The shared Rust engine constructs a positive log-linear discount curve from dated cash flows and quoted present values. One instrument determines one new knot. Instruments are processed in strictly increasing maturity order; each equation is:

sum(cashflow[i] * discount(date[i])) - price = 0

Previously accepted knots stay fixed. Payments within the new segment use the same log-linear interpolation as CURVEDF, so off-knot coupons affect calibration. The result is directly usable by CURVEDF, CURVEZERO, CURVEFORWARD and CURVENPV. Both native Rust consumers and BASIC call the same implementation.

A quote is a present value at the explicitly supplied reference date, in the same units as its cash flows. It is not automatically a clean bond price, yield, deposit rate or swap spread. Programs must convert their conventions into dated fixed-payment equations, including settlement, accrued interest, notional and payment calendars. The existing schedule/calendar functions compose with this API. Curve-dependent floating payments, multi-curve calibration, least- squares fitting to inconsistent quotes and instrument convention catalogs remain separate work.

This follows the general sequential repricing approach described by QuantLib's PiecewiseYieldCurve documentation. No QuantLib source is copied or linked; the implementation reuses ModernBASIC's Rust curve, scalar-search and exact-accumulation kernels.

documents.html:
CURVEBOOTSTRAP(reference,instruments [,basis$[,extrapolation$[,absoluteLogTolerance[,relativeLogTolerance [,maxEvaluations[,maxIterations[,maxCashflowEvaluations [,normalizedPriceTolerance[,absolutePriceTolerance]]]]]]]]])

CURVEBOOTSTRAPINFO accepts the same arguments. Each instrument is an ordinary editable six-field BASIC list:

{maturity,price,lowerFactor,upperFactor,amounts,dates}

The amount/date lists must match. Supply 1..100000 instruments and at most one million cash flows across all instruments. Every amount and price is finite; prices and payments may have either sign. Cash-flow dates may repeat or be unsorted, but all must be within reference..maturity, including zero payments. The net coefficient at the maturity's exact day-count time must be nonzero. This rejects constant or unidentifiable equations after exact cancellation.

Maturities must increase strictly both by civil date and by elapsed time under the chosen basis. The four existing bases are ACT365F (default), ACT360, ACTACTISDA and 30E360. Extrapolation defaults to NONE; FLATFORWARD explicitly extends the finished curve's last segment. Calibration itself never relies on extrapolation. See Discount curves and Calendar math for their definitions.

Each factor bracket must be finite, positive and strictly ordered. It must contain an endpoint numerical zero or give opposite signs at its endpoints. Signed cash flows can produce several solutions; supply separate brackets to select them. Same-sign intervals, tangent roots, automatic bracket discovery, uniqueness proofs and inconsistent-quote reconciliation are not supplied.

CURVEBOOTSTRAP returns the existing DFCURVE1 curve record only when every instrument is accepted. ## BASIC interface

CURVEBOOTSTRAP(reference,instruments
        [,basis$[,extrapolation$[,absoluteLogTolerance[,relativeLogTolerance
        [,maxEvaluations[,maxIterations[,maxCashflowEvaluations
        [,normalizedPriceTolerance[,absolutePriceTolerance]]]]]]]]])

CURVEBOOTSTRAPINFO accepts the same arguments. Each instrument is an ordinary
editable six-field BASIC list:

    {maturity,price,lowerFactor,upperFactor,amounts,dates}

The amount/date lists must match. Supply 1..100000 instruments and at most one
million cash flows across all instruments. Every amount and price is finite;
prices and payments may have either sign. Cash-flow dates may repeat or be
unsorted, but all must be within reference..maturity, including zero payments.
The net coefficient at the maturity's exact day-count time must be nonzero.
This rejects constant or unidentifiable equations after exact cancellation.

Maturities must increase strictly both by civil date and by elapsed time under
the chosen basis. The four existing bases are ACT365F (default), ACT360,
ACTACTISDA and 30E360. Extrapolation defaults to NONE; FLATFORWARD explicitly
extends the finished curve's last segment. Calibration itself never relies on
extrapolation. See [Discount curves](DISCOUNT_CURVES.md) and
[Calendar math](CALENDAR_MATH.md) for their definitions.

Each factor bracket must be finite, positive and strictly ordered. It must
contain an endpoint numerical zero or give opposite signs at its endpoints.
Signed cash flows can produce several solutions; supply separate brackets to
select them. Same-sign intervals, tangent roots, automatic bracket discovery,
uniqueness proofs and inconsistent-quote reconciliation are not supplied.

CURVEBOOTSTRAP returns the existing DFCURVE1 curve record only when every
instrument is accepted. A work, search or price-fit limit raises an error naming
the status and recommending CURVEBOOTSTRAPINFO. Malformed input, cancellation,
unbracketed equations and numerical range errors also raise errors, leaving
caller data unchanged.

documents.title: Search and price-fit controls
documents.html:
Search operates on x = log(factor/lowerFactor), from zero to the stable log ratio of the bracket factors. Near either endpoint it scales that endpoint locally; exact endpoint factors retain their original binary64 bits. This avoids subtracting large rounded absolute logarithms for closely spaced factors.

Defaults: absoluteLogTolerance = 1E-12, relativeLogTolerance = 0, maxEvaluations = 4096 per instrument, maxIterations = 2048 per instrument, maxCashflowEvaluations = 10000000 across the entire calibration, and normalizedPriceTolerance = 1E-10. Absolute price tolerance is disabled when omitted. If supplied it is a finite nonnegative error bound in cash-flow units.

Search tolerances are finite/nonnegative, relative tolerance is at most one and at least one search tolerance is positive. Evaluation limits are 2..32771; iteration limits are 1..16384. The total cash-flow cap is 0..10000000. Normalized price tolerance is finite in [0,1]. Invalid controls are rejected even when the work cap is zero.

Each objective evaluates all the instrument's payments and uses the exact sum of represented amount/factor products minus the quote. Normalization divides by the exact sum of absolute represented payment products plus absolute quote. The reported normalized error is dimensionless and bounded by one. A nonzero ratio below the least binary64 subnormal uses a signed minimum-subnormal value; its exact represented numerator sign is reported separately. Underflow cannot silently produce a numerical zero.

Normalization is relative to gross discounted payments plus the quote, not just the quoted price. Large opposing payments can make it small despite a substantial currency error. Use absolutePriceTolerance when a currency-unit bound matters, and inspect both residuals. The absolute criterion compares the exact represented product-sum error against the tolerance before rounding. A rounded raw error may be zero while its exact represented sign is nonzero; zero absolute or normalized tolerance requires exact represented cancellation. This does not certify the exact transcendental equation.

A search interval meeting its tolerance alone does not accept a knot: the chosen factor is freshly revalued and must also meet normalized and any requested absolute price tolerance. This check costs one additional cash-flow evaluation per payment. The work cap includes it; three full valuations are reserved before starting a segment (two endpoints and one selected-point check). It does not count every machine operation, input validation or sorting/search overhead.

documents.title: Diagnostic packet
documents.html:
CURVEBOOTSTRAPINFO returns:

{"CURVEBOOT1",status$,acceptedCurveOrEmpty,steps,totalWork,completedKnots,requestedKnots}

CONVERGED means all requested knots met search and price-fit criteria. WORK_LIMIT means the shared payment-evaluation budget prevented completion. SEARCH_LIMIT means a per-instrument evaluation, iteration or floating-point resolution limit prevented convergence. PRICE_TOLERANCE means the search stopped successfully but the independent price-fit criterion failed.

Only accepted prefix knots appear in acceptedCurveOrEmpty; it is {} if none were accepted. Later instruments are not attempted after a limit. A rejected candidate is included in steps when a search was attempted; running out of work before an attempt adds no step. Always examine the top-level status before treating the packet as a complete calibration.

Each step contains:

FieldMeaning
1Instrument maturity.
2Candidate discount factor.
3Rounded raw price error, or {} if it exceeds finite binary64 range.
4Normalized price error at the freshly revalued candidate.
5Exact represented residual sign: -1, 0 or 1.
6Accepted flag: 1 or 0.
7, 8Selected log-growth search coordinate and normalized search objective.
9, 10Final lower and upper log-growth coordinates.
11, 12Objective values at those bounds.
13Search evaluations, excluding the extra final price check.
14Search iterations.
15Shared scalar-search status string.

The search status may be ZERO_FOUND or INTERVAL_TOLERANCE without acceptance if a price criterion fails. Numerical zeros describe represented products, and interval bounds describe the numerical search; neither proves a unique exact mathematical root.

documents.title: Native Rust API, precision and qualification
documents.html:
NativeCurveInstrument contains maturity, price, cashflows, lower_discount_factor and upper_discount_factor. Call NativeDiscountCurve::bootstrap(reference,&instruments,basis,extrapolation,options). NativeCurveBootstrapOptions contains shared NativeScalarSearchOptions, max_cashflow_evaluations, normalized_price_tolerance and optional absolute_price_tolerance.

NativeCurveBootstrapReport exposes curve (Option), steps, status, cashflow_evaluations and requested_knots. converged() and completed_knots() summarize acceptance. NativeCurveBootstrapStep exposes the same fields as the BASIC step, including NativeRootReport. The report owns its accepted curve; input instruments are never mutated.

The engine uses binary64 amounts, factors and transcendental evaluations, with exact represented product sums and day-count comparisons. It does not supply decimal currency, exact transcendental arithmetic, forward-error certificates or automatic conditioning diagnosis. A factor that cannot be represented as a positive finite number raises a range error. Accepted earlier prices retain their model equations because later knots do not change earlier segments.

Validation, preparation and valuation loops check cancellation; bounded exact accumulation checks at its boundary. This is cooperative cancellation, not a hard real-time guarantee. No new dependency, external solver process, network quote feed or GPU is required. The editable example is programs/finance/bootstrapped_curve.bas.

Further work includes instrument-specific rate helpers, floating/payment projection and multi-curve models, calibration sensitivities and risk, overdetermined/noisy fitting, decimal settlement rules and installed/hardware qualification. This milestone does not complete the general finance requirement.

documents.title: Gradients and Jacobians
documents.html:
NUMGRAD differentiates a scalar function of a numeric list. NUMJAC differentiates a vector function of a numeric list. Both execute the shared Rust adaptive finite-difference kernel. Users supply ordinary DEF FN functions; a tensor program is not required.

For an output vector with m components and an input with n components, the Jacobian has m rows and n columns: entry (i,j) is the derivative of output i with respect to input j. A gradient is returned as a flat n-element list. The INFO form represents a gradient as one Jacobian row.

10 DEF FNRHS(P)={P(2),-2*P(1)-.3*P(2)}
20 J=NUMJAC("FNRHS",{3,4})
30 PRINT J(1,1);J(1,2)
40 PRINT J(2,1);J(2,2)
50 DEF FNENERGY(P)=P(1)^2+.5*P(2)^2
60 G=NUMGRAD("FNENERGY",{3,4})
70 PRINT G(1);G(2)

The expected matrix is {{0,1},{-2,-.3}} and the energy gradient is {6,4}. See programs/science/linearized_motion.bas for a runnable diagnostic example.

documents.title: BASIC arguments
documents.html:
All four functions have the same positional arguments:

NUMGRAD(function$, point [, absTol [, relTol [, steps [, directions
  [, maxEntryEvaluations [, maxIterations [, maxCallbacks
  [, maxRequests [, maxCacheValues]]]]]]]]])
NUMGRADINFO(...)
NUMJAC(...)
NUMJACINFO(...)

The callback name includes FN. It receives one numeric list parameter and must return a finite scalar for NUMGRAD or a nonempty finite numeric list for NUMJAC. Its output length must remain constant. The input point is a nonempty finite numeric list. Each input/output dimension is at most 1,000, with at most 1,000,000 Jacobian entries.

ArgumentDefault and meaning
absTol1E-9, nonnegative absolute tolerance per entry
relTol1E-8, between zero and one; at least one tolerance must be positive
steps0 for automatic selection; positive scalar broadcast or one value per input axis; zeros in a list select automatic steps
directions0 central; 1 forward; -1 backward; scalar broadcast or one value per input axis
maxEntryEvaluations257 scalar sample requests per entry; allowed 5..4097
maxIterations64 adaptive iterations per entry; allowed 1..256
maxCallbacks100,000 actual callback invocations, including the center; allowed 1..1,000,000
maxRequests10,000,000 total scalar sample requests including cache hits; allowed 0..10,000,000
maxCacheValues262,144 retained vector elements; allowed 0..1,000,000; zero disables the off-center cache

An additional fixed limit allows at most 10,000,000 transported numeric values: actual callback invocations multiplied by (input dimension + output dimension). The center invocation counts toward this limit. The center value is always retained and is outside the off-center cache allowance. Cache metadata, the report matrix and transient callback values also require memory.

The actual work or allocation performed inside a user callback is not measured by these counters. Normal interpreter cancellation and resource limits still apply. A native callback must cooperate with cancellation during long work.

documents.title: Diagnostic reports and failure behavior
documents.html:
NUMGRAD and NUMJAC require every entry to converge; otherwise they raise an error suggesting the corresponding INFO function. INFO returns:

{"NUMDIFF1", overallStatus$, rows, columns, entryReports,
 valuesAtPoint, callbackCalls, sampleRequests, cacheHits,
 peakCacheValues, callbackValues}

Overall status is CONVERGED, NON_CONVERGED or WORK_LIMIT. Each entry report is:

{value, estimatedAbsoluteError, step, entryRequests, iterations, status$}

These fields and entry statuses follow the scalar DERIVATIVE contract. For example, R(5,2,1,6) reads the status of output 2 with respect to input 1. An unfinished entry is an empty list, never a fabricated zero. Entries are evaluated column by column, retaining complete earlier estimates if a global work limit stops evaluation. A partial current estimate is discarded when that limit interrupts its scalar solve.

A valid report satisfies: callbackCalls = sampleRequests - cacheHits + 1 and callbackValues = callbackCalls * (rows + columns). Requests include failed off-center domain probes; failed probes are not cached.

The center is evaluated once. A center error, changed output shape, invalid argument, non-domain callback failure or cancellation raises an error without publishing a partial result. Recoverable off-center domain errors use the scalar kernel's smaller-step retries. After a domain retry, an adequate first stencil is confirmed at a smaller radius before any attempted expansion. BASIC parameter scope is restored after each callback and a failed assignment leaves its previous target value intact.

documents.title: Cache and numerical assumptions
documents.html:
Callbacks must be deterministic: the same point must return the same values. The backend shares a bounded FIFO cache of vector samples across output rows, then clears it before the next input axis. This can greatly reduce callback invocations. It does not change an entry's scalar sampling decisions. Disabling the off-center cache preserves those numerical decisions while increasing work. Unused capacity from a native callback's returned vector is not retained.

Automatic steps, actual representable sample positions, one-sided boundary controls and per-entry stopping reports come from the scalar adaptive kernel. Estimated errors are heuristic, not certified mathematical bounds. Finite sampling can miss oscillations or discontinuities. Callback rounding and noisy data can prevent trustworthy derivatives; a reported convergence does not prove differentiability. Choose sensible units, domain directions and tolerances. No differentiability claim is made at a cusp.

documents.html:
The crate exports NativeMultivariateDerivativeOptions, NativeMultivariateDerivativeReport, and NativeMultivariateDerivativeStatus. Use NativeDifferentiation::gradient(function, &point, &options) with a FnMut(&[f64]) -> Result<f64, Error>, or jacobian with a callback returning Result<Vec<f64>, Error>.

Options contain the scalar NativeDerivativeOptions, optional per-axis initial_steps: Vec<Option<f64>> and directions, plus the three global limits. Empty override vectors use the common scalar setting; nonempty vectors must have exactly one element per input coordinate.

The native report contains the dimensions, center values, row-major Vec<Option<NativeDerivativeReport>>, status and work counters. entries[row * columns + column] is output-major. completed_entries() counts available estimates; converged() requires every entry to converge. Input slices are unchanged, including on failure.

documents.title: Curvature from ordinary BASIC functions
documents.html:
NUMHESS evaluates the Hessian of a deterministic scalar function of a numeric list. Entry (i,j) estimates the second partial derivative with respect to input coordinates i and j. Rust supplies the kernel; BASIC supplies the function and combines its result with the other math, graphics, simulation and analysis APIs.

10 DEF FNPOT(P)=3*P(1)^2+2*P(1)*P(2)+4*P(2)^2
20 H=NUMHESS("FNPOT",{1,2})
30 PRINT H(1,1);H(1,2)
40 PRINT H(2,1);H(2,2)

The expected matrix is {{6,2},{2,8}}. Hessians assume a twice continuously differentiable function in the sampled region. Symmetric entries share one solve; that symmetry does not establish smoothness or a positive-definite matrix.

documents.title: BASIC controls
documents.html:
NUMHESS and NUMHESSINFO accept the same 2..11 positional arguments as gradients and Jacobians:

NUMHESS(function$, point [, absTol [, relTol [, steps [, directions
  [, maxEntryEvaluations [, maxIterations [, maxCallbacks
  [, maxRequests [, maxCacheValues]]]]]]]]])
NUMHESSINFO(...)

The callback receives one numeric list and returns one finite scalar. There are 1..1000 input variables, at most one million matrix cells. Defaults are absTol=1E-9, relTol=1E-8, automatic steps, central differences, 257 requests per independently calculated entry, 64 iterations, 100000 actual callback invocations, 10000000 scalar sample requests and 262144 cached scalar values. At least one tolerance must be positive; relTol is at most one.

The per-entry request limit must be 25..4097. Other limits and validation follow the multivariable API. Steps may be a positive scalar or per-axis list; zero selects the automatic radius. Directions are 0 central, 1 forward or -1 backward, either a scalar broadcast or one value per axis. Automatic Hessian steps use a larger local radius than first derivatives while respecting representable spacing. Tolerances are in second-derivative units; large offsets, unfavorable units and one-sided calculations can require different steps or tolerances.

A fixed limit of 10000000 transported values counts actual callback calls multiplied by (input dimension+1). The center call counts. The kernel also caps all sample requests, including cached requests. Work performed inside callbacks is outside these counters. Native callbacks must cooperate with cancellation.

## BASIC controls

NUMHESS and NUMHESSINFO accept the same 2..11 positional arguments as
[gradients and Jacobians](MULTIVARIATE_DIFFERENTIATION.md):

```text
NUMHESS(function$, point [, absTol [, relTol [, steps [, directions
  [, maxEntryEvaluations [, maxIterations [, maxCallbacks
  [, maxRequests [, maxCacheValues]]]]]]]]])
NUMHESSINFO(...)
```

The callback receives one numeric list and returns one finite scalar.
There are 1..1000 input variables, at most one million matrix cells.
Defaults are absTol=1E-9, relTol=1E-8, automatic steps, central differences,
257 requests per independently calculated entry, 64 iterations, 100000 actual
callback invocations, 10000000 scalar sample requests and 262144 cached scalar
values. At least one tolerance must be positive; relTol is at most one.

The per-entry request limit must be 25..4097. Other limits and validation follow
the multivariable API. Steps may be a positive scalar or per-axis list; zero
selects the automatic radius. Directions are 0 central, 1 forward or -1 backward,
either a scalar broadcast or one value per axis. Automatic Hessian steps use a
larger local radius than first derivatives while respecting representable spacing.
Tolerances are in second-derivative units; large offsets, unfavorable units and
one-sided calculations can require different steps or tolerances.

A fixed limit of 10000000 transported values counts actual callback calls
multiplied by (input dimension+1). The center call counts. The kernel also caps
all sample requests, including cached requests. Work performed inside callbacks
is outside these counters. Native callbacks must cooperate with cancellation.

documents.title: Reports and failure behavior
documents.html:
NUMHESS returns a numeric square matrix only when every independent entry converges. Otherwise it raises an error suggesting NUMHESSINFO. INFO returns:

{"NUMHESS1", status$, dimension, entryReports, valueAtPoint,
 callbackCalls, sampleRequests, cacheHits, peakCacheValues, callbackValues}

Status is CONVERGED, NON_CONVERGED or WORK_LIMIT. Each available entry is:

{value, estimatedAbsoluteError, rowStep, columnStep,
 entryRequests, iterations, entryStatus$}

Entry statuses use the existing DERIVATIVE contract. For example, R(4,1,2,7) reads the status for the (1,2) mixed derivative. An unfinished entry is {}. A global work limit retains completed symmetric pairs and discards the unfinished solve. Upper-triangle entries are calculated in row order and copied to the lower triangle with step coordinates swapped. Mirrored work counters describe the same calculation and must not be added twice.

A valid report satisfies callbackCalls=sampleRequests-cacheHits+1 and callbackValues=callbackCalls*(dimension+1). Failed domain probes count as calls but are not cached. Per-entry request counts include cache hits. The center value is evaluated once and retained outside the cache allowance.

Invalid inputs, center errors, non-domain callback errors and cancellation raise an error without publishing a partial result. Recoverable off-center domain errors trigger smaller-step retries. BASIC restores callback parameter scope; failed assignments preserve their previous target value.

documents.title: Numerical method and limits
documents.html:
Diagonal entries use five-point interpolation at actual representable sample positions. Central entries also sample closer points to compare left and right second derivatives, accounting for their rounding uncertainty. Mixed entries use tensor products of first-derivative interpolation weights over a 5-by-5 sample grid. Axis-only and constant contributions are subtracted through exact binary product-sum accumulation before division by the represented step product. This prevents avoidable overflowing/underflowing intermediate step squares.

The adaptive controller compares successive estimates, estimates floating-point sample noise, and uses lower-order formulas to select its first refinement. It requires two complete stencils at distinct sample grids for convergence. A proposed reversal to an already tried radius is shortened to try intermediate radii before a roundoff stop. Estimated error is a heuristic, not a certified bound. The bilateral check rejects common cusps but cannot prove smoothness; finite samples can miss discontinuities or oscillations. Callback rounding or noise may make the requested tolerance unattainable. The algorithm adjusts a pair's two step radii together; this does not cover every poorly scaled or anisotropic case.

A bounded FIFO cache shares scalar samples across independent entries. Its keys store at most two changed coordinates, so keys do not copy the entire input vector. The cache allowance counts values; metadata, the result matrix, center and transient callback allocations require additional memory. Disabling the cache preserves numerical sampling decisions but increases actual callback work. Callbacks must be deterministic for cached reuse to be valid.

documents.title: Native Rust interface
documents.html:
Use NativeDifferentiation::hessian(function, &point, &options), where the callback is FnMut(&[f64]) -> Result<f64, Error> and options is NativeMultivariateDerivativeOptions. Existing scalar tolerance/iteration settings, per-axis steps/directions and global limits are shared with gradient/Jacobian APIs.

NativeHessianReport contains dimension, value_at_point, row-major optional NativeHessianEntryReport entries, global work/cache counters and status. Each entry has value, estimated_absolute_error, steps, evaluations, iterations and NativeDerivativeStatus. entries[i*dimension+j] addresses (i,j). completed_entries() counts matrix cells including mirrored entries; converged() requires every independent solve to converge. Input slices remain unchanged.

documents.title: Shared backend integration
documents.html:
The numerical path in IMPLICITSTEP, IMPLICITSOLVE and the related implicit event/hybrid and index-one DAE operations uses the shared Rust adaptive Jacobian kernel. NativePhysicsEquation uses the same implementation. Existing dense and CSR analytic callbacks retain their selection, matrix semantics and error behavior.

This replaces a fixed perturbation proportional to max(1,abs(state)). That old rule could move a small positive state outside a square-root or logarithmic domain. The shared kernel adapts local radii, reuses vector samples and reports whether each matrix entry met its estimated-error criterion.

10 DEF FNRHS(T,Y)={-SQR(Y(1))}
20 Y=IMPLICITSTEP("FNRHS",0,{1E-12},1E-9,1E-11,1E-23)
30 PRINT Y(1)

The formerly failing example now solves the backward-Euler equation y = 1E-12 - 1E-9*sqrt(y). Its nonlinear residual tolerance is distinct from time-integration error: a backward-Euler step remains first order.

documents.title: Coordinates and Newton correction
documents.html:
The numerical kernel differentiates the nonlinear residual, including the identity-minus-step-times-RHS structure of differential rows and the unmodified constraint function in algebraic rows.

Each free coordinate is represented as currentValue + unit*offset, centered at offset zero. unit is max(abs(currentValue),abs(initialValue)); when both are zero the unit is one. These are local numerical scales, not inferred physical units or supplied bounds. Sample positions use the shared exact binary dot accumulator, and a nonzero offset that cannot move its physical coordinate causes a solver-resolution failure.

Residual rows are normalized by max(abs(currentResidual),currentToleranceScale). The kernel solves the scaled Newton system, then maps its correction back to state units. This avoids constructing an unrepresentable unscaled Jacobian in some mixed-unit systems. The original residual criterion and backtracking still decide acceptance. Normalization does not certify conditioning or global convergence, and applications should still use coherent units and tolerances.

The current residual is reused for the center sample. RHS callbacks must be deterministic at the same time and state, as required for cached finite differences. The internal Jacobian uses relative tolerance 1E-7 and the shared kernel's remaining default tolerances and bounds. This inexact-Newton derivative target allows for rounding of physical probe coordinates in narrow domains; it does not relax the caller's nonlinear residual tolerance. Every entry must report convergence before its matrix is used. A work-limited or nonconverged derivative matrix is treated as a failed nonlinear attempt, allowing the existing adaptive integrator to reduce the time step. A single-step call reports nonconvergence. Actual equation budget exhaustion remains fatal.

documents.title: DAE initialization
documents.html:
DAEINIT holds the differential prefix exactly fixed. Its numerical Jacobian differentiates only the algebraic variables and solves the reduced algebraic block; it does not probe the frozen differential coordinates. This is equivalent to zero differential correction in the full Newton system.

10 DEF FNMODEL(T,Y)={-SQR(Y(1)),Y(2)-1}
20 Y=DAEINIT("FNMODEL",1,0,{0,0})
30 PRINT Y(1);Y(2)

The result is {0,1}. The differential value is preserved, including native signed-zero bits. The full callback must still return finite values, including its unused differential outputs, at every actual guess and trial. Analytic dense/CSR initialization continues to use identity differential rows and the supplied algebraic derivatives. A regular, nonsingular algebraic block and a suitable initial guess remain necessary.

## DAE initialization

DAEINIT holds the differential prefix exactly fixed. Its numerical Jacobian
differentiates only the algebraic variables and solves the reduced algebraic
block; it does not probe the frozen differential coordinates. This is equivalent
to zero differential correction in the full Newton system.


documents.title: Errors, budgets and cancellation
documents.html:
A recoverable domain, division-by-zero or nonfinite result at a numerical derivative probe may be retried at a smaller radius. Errors at the current Newton state or a backtracking trial remain fatal. Explicit analytic callback errors also remain fatal; they never trigger a numerical fallback. Invalid shape, user errors and cancellation propagate without a partial result.

The existing limits remain: 24 Newton iterations, 12 backtracking trials, 64 dense/numerical states, 4096 states with CSR callbacks, 200000 cumulative equation/Jacobian callback evaluations and 50000000 component-work units. The numerical path additionally charges matrix entries, probe-coordinate/ normalization work and completed scalar sample requests. Failed probes still consume the equation callback/work budget. Cached requests count as derivative work even though they do not invoke the RHS again. The shared derivative kernel also enforces its per-entry, global sample/transport and cache caps.

Input state slices are unchanged. BASIC callback parameter scope is restored; an error does not replace the target assignment. No partial trajectory is published on failure. Native cancellation can interrupt the shared Jacobian and a reset cancellation token permits a subsequent solve with the remaining equation budget.

documents.title: Qualification and remaining limits
documents.html:
Acceptance evidence is output/physics-jacobian-2026-10-27/validation.json. The retained baseline reproduces the original square-root failures. Qualification covers small-domain steps and DAE initialization, mixed units, large/small scales, independent closed-form/high-precision roots, existing nonlinear/adaptive/DAE reference suites, analytic/CSR behavior, work limits, cancellation, and native/ interpreted/exported consumers.

Finite differences give heuristic error estimates, not certified derivatives. This change does not add automatic state bounds, arbitrary one-sided Newton derivatives, general DAE index reduction or global root discovery. A callback without a usable neighborhood in the free variables, a singular system, a poor Newton starting point or an out-of-domain backtracking trial can still fail. Installed image, hardware and the broader physics/math requirements remain open.

documents.title: Overview
documents.html:
ModernBASIC has one audio engine with two sound sources:

  • a built-in oscillator for tones, sweeps, custom waves, and ordinary PLAY;
  • a sampled General MIDI SoundFont device selected by SOUNDFONT and INSTRUMENT.

No vintage chip, ROM, or hardware register map is emulated.

Each graphical program task owns a separate instance of that engine and a separate playback stream. Music in one program therefore continues while other programs draw, accept input, run games, or play their own music. Within one program, voices 1 through 16 have independent score cursors and may carry simultaneous songs or parts. Across program windows, the host audio server mixes the independent streams; crowded output may clip or sound noisy, but no program replaces another program's queue.

## Overview

ModernBASIC has one audio engine with two sound sources:

- a built-in oscillator for tones, sweeps, custom waves, and ordinary `PLAY`;
- a sampled General MIDI SoundFont device selected by `SOUNDFONT` and `INSTRUMENT`.

No vintage chip, ROM, or hardware register map is emulated.

Each graphical program task owns a separate instance of that engine and a
separate playback stream. Music in one program therefore continues while other
programs draw, accept input, run games, or play their own music. Within one
program, voices 1 through 16 have independent score cursors and may carry
simultaneous songs or parts. Across program windows, the host audio server mixes
the independent streams; crowded output may clip or sound noisy, but no program
replaces another program's queue.

The engine has a bounded maximum of 16 voices; the active count comes from the current synthesis profile or VOICES. VOICE n selects an active implicit voice used by the one-argument WAVE, four-argument ADSR, one-argument PULSEWIDTH, PAN, BEEP, and PLAY sequence$ forms.

VOL level sets the master output level; VOL voice,level sets one voice's level within that master. Both accept normalized values from 0 through 1.

The three explicit media subcommands extend the classic verb without changing note parsing. PLAY AUDIO decodes a local WAV, MP3, FLAC, Ogg, Opus, M4A, or AAC asset or a direct HTTP(S) audio stream. PLAY VIDEO decodes a local MP4, WebM, Matroska, MOV, AVI, or M4V or a direct HTTP(S) video stream, then projects its complete frames while playing its audio track when present. Local paths remain inside the file/output sandbox; URLs require the explicit --network capability. PLAY FLIPBOOK consumes an ordered retained still sequence.

PLAY is a media decoder, not a browser or DRM bypass. Open ordinary YouTube, Netflix, and other site pages with WEB OPEN; the Linux browser handles their JavaScript, accounts, and licensed playback. See the networking section of the language reference.

documents.title: PLAY notation
documents.html:
PLAY uses whitespace-separated tokens. Each note contains a letter, optional accidental, and required octave:

C4       middle C using default length
F#3      F sharp in octave 3
Db4      D flat in octave 4
C4:0.5   half a beat
C4/4     quarter note, one beat
C4/8     eighth note, half a beat
C4/8.    dotted eighth, three-quarters of a beat
C4/4@96 quarter note at MIDI velocity 96 (1 through 127)
R:2      two-beat rest
REST/4   one-beat rest
V2       use voice 2 for following tokens

Examples:

10 PLAY "C4/4@72 E4/4@84 G4/2@104"
20 PLAY 2,"C3:1 R:1 G3:2"
30 PLAY "V1 C4:1 V2 E4:2 V1 G4:1"

Every voice has an independent position. Switching with Vn resumes at that voice's own cursor; it does not accidentally continue on the previous voice's MIDI channel.

documents.title: Synthesis arrangements
documents.html:
The host-scanned default is AUTO, which selects a conservative arrangement from the available logical CPUs and memory. Programs that need a fixed render profile can select a named arrangement before creating audio:

10 CLEAR
20 SYNTHPROFILE "EXTENDED"
30 VOICES 12
40 OSCILLATORS 6

## Synthesis arrangements

The host-scanned default is `AUTO`, which selects a conservative arrangement
from the available logical CPUs and memory. Programs that need a fixed render
profile can select a named arrangement before creating audio:

```basic
10 CLEAR
20 SYNTHPROFILE "EXTENDED"
30 VOICES 12
40 OSCILLATORS 6
```

Profiles are `COMPACT` (8 x 2), `STANDARD` (16 x 3), `EXTENDED`
(16 x 6), and `MAXIMUM` (16 x 8). `SYNTHPROFILE "AUTO"` inspects available
logical CPUs, system memory, and the `paplay`/`aplay` playback command, then
selects a conservative profile. Playback availability does not limit WAV export:
the native engine renders software PCM before sending it to the audio device.

`VOICES count` selects 1 through 16 active voices. `OSCILLATORS count` selects
1 through 8 active oscillator slots in every native voice and can override a
profile. Put the profile first and exact overrides after it. Configure the
arrangement after `CLEAR` and before notes so reducing the active voice count
