documents.title: Oscillator controls
documents.html:
Every native voice contains the configured number of oscillator slots (selected by the host by default). WAVE is the direct waveform control for oscillator 1 and accepts SINE, TRIANGLE, SAW, PULSE, NOISE, BANJO, GUITAR, BASS, or a custom table containing 2 through 65,536 finite real values in the range -1 through 1. A table may be a numeric list, a numeric DIM-array snapshot, or a quoted comma/space-separated string. The expression is evaluated once and the synthesizer owns a copy:

10 S={-1,0,1,0}
20 WAVE S
30 WAVE 2,REVERSE(S)
40 OPTION BASE 1:DIM TABLE(4):TABLE()=S:WAVE TABLE()

WAVE TVALUE(t) works when the tensor value is a flat list. For a batched 1D filter result, first select one batch and channel: R=TVALUE(TCONV1D(signal,kernel)):WAVE R(1,1). Nested lists, complex values and out-of-range samples are rejected. The stored wavetable uses the synthesizer's existing binary32 sample format; changing the source list later does not change an installed waveform. Bare waveform names retain their named-wave meaning; parenthesize a same-named variable if its value is intended. String variables and numeric waveform-ID expressions are also accepted.

10 VOICE 1
20 WAVE "PULSE",.35
30 ADSR 8,80,.72,120
40 VOL .8
50 FILTER 1,"LOWPASS",2400,.2
60 PLAY "C4/4 E4/4 G4/2"
70 WAVEFILE "oscillator.wav"
80 END

programs/examples/tensor_music.bas constructs symbolic harmonics, applies a periodic five-tap filter, inspects its FFT, and writes a playable WAV using this list-to-synthesizer connection.

Numeric waveform identifiers remain accepted by WAVE/WAVEFORM:

ValueWaveform
0Triangle
1Saw
2Pulse
3Sine
4Noise

Attack, decay, and release are milliseconds. Sustain, volume, pulse width, and resonance are normalized 0 through 1. Stereo position is -1 through 1.

OSCILLATOR builds a layered native voice. Slots are 1 through the configured count, with a bounded maximum of 8; ratio is 0.0625 through 16 relative to the written or SOUND frequency; detune is -2400 through 2400 cents; and level is 0 through 1. Oscillator 1 starts as a full-level pulse wave, while oscillators 2 and 3 start silent. The physical BANJO, GUITAR, and BASS models occupy oscillator 1. PULSEWIDTH voice,oscillator,width controls any pulse slot.

FILTER is per voice. Its modes are OFF, LOWPASS, HIGHPASS, BANDPASS, and NOTCH. Cutoff is 20 Hz through the audio Nyquist limit, resonance is 0 through 1, and optional key tracking is 0 through 1. FILTERADSR supplies a separate cutoff contour; amount is -8 through 8 octaves. LFO independently configures the PITCH, LEVEL, FILTER, or PULSEWIDTH target. Its waveforms are SINE, TRIANGLE, SAW, PULSE, and SAMPLEHOLD; rate is 0 through 100 Hz. Pitch depth is in semitones, filter depth in octaves, and level/pulse-width depths are normalized. Each target retains its own LFO, so several modulations can run together. GLIDE sets 0 through 60,000 milliseconds of portamento. DRIVE adds normalized oscillator saturation before the filter.

10 TEMPO 104
20 MIXER 1,1,0
30 OSCILLATOR 1,1,"SAW",1,-7,.70
40 OSCILLATOR 1,2,"PULSE",.5,5,.35
50 OSCILLATOR 1,3,"TRIANGLE",2,0,.18
60 PULSEWIDTH 1,2,.32
70 ADSR 1,4,130,.55,180
80 FILTER 1,"LOWPASS",850,.68,.45
90 FILTERADSR 1,5,180,.25,120,3.2
100 LFO 1,"PITCH","TRIANGLE",5.2,.10
110 GLIDE 1,75
120 DRIVE 1,.28
130 PLAY 1,"C3/8 G3/8 Bb3/8 C4/4 G3/8 C4/2"
140 END

SOUND generates a tone at the supplied frequency; it does not parse musical notes or use PLAY notation. When the frequency is that of a musical note, the generated tone can be used as that note. Its required arguments are frequency in hertz, voice number, and duration in milliseconds. The voice keeps its complete native patch: oscillators, ADSR, pulse widths, filter and filter contour, LFOs, glide, drive, VOL, and STEREO. SOUND produces a steady tone when end-hz is omitted and a logarithmic sweep when it is present. A positive steps value makes the sweep discrete. The optional normalized level applies only to that tone. PLAY remains the separate statement for named-note notation, rests, and beat-based sequencing.

If SOUND returns an error, its temporary level and waveform cannot change the voice's saved patch or the later notes. Failed native tone/sweep/sequence operations also restore the prior score lengths, note queues, cursors and glide history. This applies to immediate Rust rendering and deferred native scores; an interrupted operation returns BREAK without publishing partial native audio. Recovery checkpoints store bounded metadata rather than copying the existing audio. Already played sound cannot be undone. This native contract does not imply an atomic rollback of an entire mixed SoundFont or speech program.

10 WAVE 1,"TRIANGLE":ADSR 1,8,80,.7,140
20 SOUND 261.63,1,500
30 SOUND 329.63,1,500
40 SOUND 392,1,1000,.65
50 SOUND RESUME
60 END

documents.title: Sampled SoundFont instruments
documents.html:
SOUNDFONT loads an uncompressed SoundFont 2 bank. Paths beginning with soundfont/ address the dedicated root-level backend hardware directory and remain stable when BASIC uses CD. Other paths resolve beneath the current BASIC file root. Use it before INSTRUMENT and PLAY:

10 CLEAR
20 SOUNDFONT "soundfont/MuseScore_General.sf2"
30 TEMPO 88
40 INSTRUMENT 1,"ACOUSTIC GRAND PIANO"
50 INSTRUMENT 2,"VIOLIN"
60 INSTRUMENT 3,"STANDARD DRUM KIT"
70 VOL 1,.8
80 STEREO 2,-.2
90 EXPRESSION 2,.86
100 MODULATION 2,.14
110 SUSTAIN 1,.7
120 PITCHBEND 2,.02
130 REVERB 1,.24
140 CHORUS 2,.12
150 PLAY 1,"C4/4@76 E4/4@86 G4/4@98 C5/2@108"
160 PLAY 2,"E4/4@68 G4/4@76 C5/4@86 E5/2@96"
170 PLAY 3,"C2/4@116 F#2/8@72 F#2/8@68 D2/4@108"
180 PRINT "PLAYBACK STARTING"
190 END

SOUNDFONT path$ selects one global bank. SOUNDFONT voice,path$ binds a bank to one BASIC voice, and SOUNDFONT first-voice,last-voice,path$ binds it to an inclusive range. This lets guitars, acoustic drums, bass, keyboards, and other banks play together from one program and one sample-accurate PLAY timeline. A later binding replaces an earlier binding for the affected voices.

For multiple operating-system users, keep programs and output files in a different --file-root for each account and select one administrator-owned, read-only bank directory with --soundfont-root. Instrument selection and audio queues are task-local (and process-local across separate launches), so concurrent users and program windows do not alter one another's sound controls.

The path must end in .sf2 and is limited to 512 MiB. Both the backend and user-bank paths reject traversal and symlinks. All SOUNDFONT statements must occur before sampled notes have been queued. Compressed .sf3, SFZ, VST, and Audio Unit instruments are not loaded by the built-in engine.

SOUNDFONT loads and parses a bank when the statement executes. Its voice numbers and path may be expressions; an unreachable statement does not load a bank. A missing or invalid bank reports an execution error. Successful banks are retained for repeated use until the program is replaced or closed. Relative user-bank paths resolve from the loaded program's directory. The reserved soundfont/ prefix selects the configured read-only backend bank directory. INSTRUMENT loads the default sampled bank when first needed.

INSTRUMENT selects a General MIDI program for one BASIC voice. Names are case-insensitive; PIANO is shorthand for program 0, and numeric programs range from 0 through 127. Drum-kit names explicitly route only the selected voice to MIDI percussion. Common drum notes include C2 (bass drum), D2 (snare), and F#2 (closed hi-hat), depending on the selected kit.

SoundFont pan combines the BASIC channel control with pan offsets stored in the bank's instrument regions. A bank with an intrinsic offset can therefore retain a small signal in the opposite channel even at a BASIC pan endpoint; this differs from hard-left/right routing of native oscillators. Bank authors control those region offsets. Test isolated channels when exact channel separation matters.

Sampled-instrument controls are programmed directly in BASIC. VOL and STEREO set per-voice level and pan. An explicit ADSR shapes the sampled voice's attack, decay, sustain, and release; without it, the bank's natural envelope is preserved. EXPRESSION, MODULATION, SUSTAIN, REVERB, and CHORUS take a voice and a normalized value from 0 through 1. PITCHBEND takes a voice and a position from -1 through 1; the standard range is two semitones down or up. A note suffix such as C4/4@96 sets its MIDI attack velocity from 1 through 127. These controller values are channel-wide settings for the queued render; this release does not provide DAW-style timed automation curves or plug-in hosting.

DSP voice,drive,tone,presence,compression,gate configures one sampled instrument after SoundFont rendering and before voices are mixed. All five settings are normalized from 0 through 1. drive provides soft amplifier saturation, tone controls the cabinet low-pass range, presence emphasizes pick and strike detail, compression controls peaks, and gate selects the fraction of each written note held before the SoundFont release begins. DSP is opt-in and isolated per BASIC voice. A drive value of zero uses a transparent clean path and does not apply the saturation curve.

100 DSP 1,.55,.48,.70,.30,.48
110 DSP 2,.28,.40,.72,.48,.64

documents.title: Selecting synth, MIDI, or both
documents.html:
MIXER voice,synth-level,midi-level routes subsequent PLAY notes for one voice. Each level is 0 through 1:

10 MIXER 1,1,0       ' computer synthesizer only
20 MIXER 2,0,1       ' MIDI/SoundFont instrument only
30 MIXER 3,.65,1     ' both sources layered

Zero disables that destination; its notes are not scheduled there. Nonzero values set the source balance. VOL voice,level is the overall voice level, after that balance. Without MIXER, automatic routing remains: PLAY uses the native generator when no SoundFont device is active and the MIDI/SoundFont device when one is active. An explicit nonzero MIDI level makes PLAY connect the configured or default SoundFont device if necessary. Use SOUNDFONT and INSTRUMENT first when a specific bank and instrument are required.

This MIDI layer is the built-in sample-accurate General MIDI/SoundFont renderer; it does not send events to an external hardware MIDI port. SOUND always addresses the computer sound generator and never becomes PLAY or a MIDI note command. When both queues contain music, live playback and WAVEFILE overlay them on one timeline and preserve the programmed balance.

When SOUNDFONT is omitted, the engine searches for soundfont/MuseScore_General.sf2 in the root-level backend and then common Linux locations for MuseScore General, FluidR3 GM, and TimGM6mb. The source release does not bundle a default root-level GM bank.

For the recommended lossless MuseScore General bank, run:

./install-soundfont.sh
cargo run --release -- run programs/examples/soundfont.bas

The installer downloads the approximately 206 MiB SF2 and its MIT license from MuseScore’s official mirror. On Debian or Ubuntu, sudo apt install fluid-soundfont-gm installs the MIT-licensed FluidR3 GM alternative, which ModernBASIC discovers automatically. Keep a bank’s license with redistributed copies and check its terms before publishing or selling rendered audio.

documents.title: Queue and playback controls
documents.html:
• SOUND OFF stops live music and speech, discards queued notes, and mutes later output.
  • SOUND ON re-enables output.
  • SOUND WAIT leaves queued audio pending.
  • SOUND RESUME starts the current queue in the background.
  • END and STOP start queued audio when necessary and wait for playback to finish, so a BASIC program does not exit ahead of its music.
  • CLEAR stops playback, clears speech, discards notes, resets instruments, restores oscillator defaults, and clears ordinary program state.
  • PLAY, SOUND RESUME, END, and STOP never create an audio file.
  • Export is an option, not a standard live-runtime process. Only an explicit WAVEFILE statement writes a file. It writes the native mix, the SoundFont score, retained SING vocals, or their layered combination as programmed.
  • A generated WAV can be muxed into program-driven MP4 or WebM output with VIDEO START path$,fps,wav-path$; both paths remain inside the output sandbox.

Live playback uses paplay when available and falls back to aplay. MIDI-only sampled scores are rendered and written in bounded 2,048-frame chunks, so the first audio does not wait for the complete song to render. Chunk boundaries preserve ADSR, cabinet/filter, presence, drive, and compressor state. Deterministic WAVEFILE export and live playback use the same sampled-score chunk renderer and fixed-gain PCM encoder. Quiet passages are never normalized upward, and chunk boundaries never change gain. Native-plus-MIDI playback combines the sources in matching bounded chunks, preserving sample alignment and programmed balance until the final ceiling. Output is 44.1 kHz, signed 16-bit stereo PCM.

On Linux, a live player that accepts no PCM data for five seconds reports an error and is terminated and reaped. Producer errors and unwinding panics also clean up the player. After end-of-stream, playback allows the remaining PCM playing time plus five seconds for draining; a player that then remains alive reports an error. This preserves the full duration when a player reads ahead. SOUND OFF and task closure can stop the stream while its pipe is full. Errors remain available to the task's playback wait or next playback request, and an older stopped/replaced producer cannot overwrite a newer session's state. These are process/pipe recovery guarantees; they do not measure physical audio latency or establish a device-callback scheduling contract.

Run ./audio-test.sh for a generated-WAV check followed by a four-note live speaker test. ./audio-test.sh --no-play performs only the deterministic WAV check, which is suitable for a headless machine.

- `PLAY`, `SOUND RESUME`, `END`, and `STOP` never create an audio file.
- Export is an option, not a standard live-runtime process. Only an explicit
  `WAVEFILE` statement writes a file. It writes the native
  mix, the SoundFont score, retained `SING` vocals, or their layered combination
  as programmed.
- A generated WAV can be muxed into program-driven MP4 or WebM output with
  `VIDEO START path$,fps,wav-path$`; both paths remain inside the output sandbox.

Live playback uses `paplay` when available and falls back to `aplay`. MIDI-only
sampled scores are rendered and written in bounded 2,048-frame chunks, so the first
audio does not wait for the complete song to render. Chunk boundaries preserve
ADSR, cabinet/filter, presence, drive, and compressor state. Deterministic
`WAVEFILE` export and live playback use the same sampled-score chunk renderer
and fixed-gain PCM encoder. Quiet passages are never normalized upward, and
chunk boundaries never change gain. Native-plus-MIDI playback combines the
sources in matching bounded chunks, preserving sample alignment and programmed
balance until the final ceiling.
Output is 44.1 kHz, signed 16-bit stereo PCM.

On Linux, a live player that accepts no PCM data for five seconds reports an
error and is terminated and reaped. Producer errors and unwinding panics also
clean up the player. After end-of-stream, playback allows the remaining PCM
playing time plus five seconds for draining; a player that then remains alive
reports an error. This preserves the full duration when a player reads ahead.
`SOUND OFF` and task closure can stop the stream while its pipe is full. Errors
remain available to the task's playback wait or next playback request, and an
older stopped/replaced producer cannot overwrite a newer session's state.
These are process/pipe recovery guarantees; they do not measure physical audio
latency or establish a device-callback scheduling contract.

Run `./audio-test.sh` for a generated-WAV check followed by a four-note live
speaker test. `./audio-test.sh --no-play` performs only the deterministic WAV
check, which is suitable for a headless machine.

documents.title: Speech
documents.html:
SAY calls eSpeak NG or eSpeak directly without a shell. The defaults are 150 words per minute, 110 Hz, level 1, voice en-us, and mode QUEUE.

Modes are:

  • QUEUE: speak after earlier queued requests;
  • INTERRUPT: stop active and queued speech, then speak;
  • WAIT: block the BASIC statement until speech finishes.

Rate is 40 through 450 words per minute, pitch is 65 through 320 Hz, and level is 0 through 1.

Timed singing

SING gives the eSpeak voice a musical contour by assigning one lyric syllable to every non-rest note. Separate syllables with hyphens; whitespace also starts a new syllable. The note string uses PLAY pitch, duration, dotted-note, rest, and velocity notation. Rests consume time without consuming a syllable. The current TEMPO converts beats to time, and an optional default-beats replaces the normal one-beat default.

10 TEMPO 112
20 SING "Hap-py birth-day to you","G4/8 G4/8 A4/4 G4/4 C5/4 B4/2"

The optional level is 0 through 1. A note's @velocity scales that level. Voice names and QUEUE, INTERRUPT, or WAIT modes match SAY; WAIT is the SING default so a batch program cannot exit before its vocal completes. Every note and rest still occupies its written time.

The vocal renderer removes device-start gaps by converting the complete line to one continuous 44.1 kHz stereo PCM stream. It automatically applies an 8 ms attack, a release of up to 24 ms, as much as 15 ms of adjacent-note crossfade, and restrained stereo room reflections. Written rests prevent a dry crossfade but let the room decay continue naturally. A short syllable leaves a shaped tail inside its note; a long syllable is released at the note boundary instead of being cut off abruptly. These smoothing effects are deliberately subtle and do not require extra BASIC arguments.

One statement accepts at most 4,096 combined notes and rests and at most 30 minutes. Notes must lie in the practical C2-through-C6 vocal range and must last at least 20 milliseconds. The number of lyric syllables must exactly equal the number of non-rest notes; Vn voice switches are rejected because the selected eSpeak voice applies to the complete vocal line.

This is an intentionally synthetic singer, not a studio vocal model. The eSpeak pitch control follows the written melody but is not sample-accurate equal-tempered synthesis. Each validated SING statement is retained for an optional WAVEFILE: the first vocal starts at frame zero, later vocals append on the vocal timeline, and the result is mixed sample-accurately with queued native and SoundFont music. INTERRUPT replaces earlier retained vocals just as it replaces the live speech queue. Live SING still runs when its statement executes; export re-renders the retained score. Both paths require eSpeak NG or eSpeak, and live playback additionally requires paplay or aplay.

documents.title: Removed 0.7-era spellings
documents.html:
The current source restores VOICES as a bounded native-synthesis arrangement control and adds OSCILLATORS plus SYNTHPROFILE. It intentionally does not expose VOLUME, MUSIC CLEAR/SCORE/PLAY/SAVE, STRUM, or HIT. Use the bounded statements documented above. REVERB, CHORUS, EXPRESSION, and MODULATION are voice-local controls applied with standard General MIDI controller semantics to that voice's sampled track; voices that reuse a MIDI channel do not overwrite one another's queued score settings.

SoundFont selection and queued dynamics

INSTRUMENT voice,program,bank selects an exact preset (program 0–127, bank 0–255; banks 128–255 are percussion). The two-argument numeric form selects bank 0. A string may be an exact preset name in the loaded SoundFont, such as INSTRUMENT 1,"Church Bell", or a supported General MIDI alias. A missing preset reports an error instead of silently playing another instrument.

Sampled PLAY notes retain the voice volume, stereo position, controllers, pitch bend, explicit ADSR and DSP settings in effect when queued. Later changes affect later notes. Streaming and WAVEFILE use the same state. A score may contain at most 256 distinct voice/control combinations.

The appliance player defaults to unity gain (65536 in PulseAudio units), so playback does not add a hidden boost over WAVEFILE. An explicit MODERNBASIC_PLAYER_VOLUME override is still supported. Player startup checks for asynchronous connection failures before consuming score PCM, then tries ALSA if PulseAudio fails. Errors include up to 4096 bytes of player diagnostics.

documents.title: Shared numerical filter core
documents.html: Native FILTER playback and mathematical SVFILTER processing now reuse one Rust topology-preserving state-variable recurrence. This extraction preserves the synth's existing cutoff clamp, resonance mapping and modulation behavior. SVFILTER operates on program sample lists with explicit continuation state; it does not start playback or replace SoundFont processing. Native callers use NativeStateVariableFilter for allocation-free sample/caller-buffer processing. The shared-SVF checkpoint records PCM parity for 15 existing native synth configurations, changing-control references and allocation tests. Device-rate negotiation, live scheduling and physical listening acceptance remain separate.
documents.text:
## Shared numerical filter core

Native `FILTER` playback and mathematical `SVFILTER` processing now reuse one
Rust topology-preserving state-variable recurrence. This extraction preserves
the synth's existing cutoff clamp, resonance mapping and modulation behavior.
`SVFILTER` operates on program sample lists with explicit continuation state;
it does not start playback or replace SoundFont processing. Native callers use
`NativeStateVariableFilter` for allocation-free sample/caller-buffer processing.
The shared-SVF checkpoint records PCM parity for 15 existing native synth
configurations, changing-control references and allocation tests. Device-rate
negotiation, live scheduling and physical listening acceptance remain separate.

documents.title: BASIC desktop application
documents.html:
applications/desktop/desktop.bas implements a graphical desktop, file browser, optional BASIC editor, program launcher and application menu in BASIC. Microsoft Edit is the default system text editor. Build and launch it from the project root. The desktop is optional; each user chooses whether to run its binary or start BASIC directly without the desktop:

./tools/build-desktop.sh
./run.sh                                  # interactive environment choice
./run.sh --desktop /path/to/writable/workspace
./run.sh --no-desktop                      # direct BASIC graphical environment
./run.sh repl                              # text-only terminal READY prompt

A bare run.sh requires an interactive terminal and never chooses a mode on the user's behalf. Scripts and launch shortcuts must pass a mode or a BASIC command. The choice applies to that launch, so users can switch on their next launch. tools/run-desktop.sh remains a direct desktop-only launcher. Choosing direct BASIC does not require the desktop binary or its browser dependencies. Choosing Desktop without a built binary reports the build instruction; it does not silently switch environments.

The default workspace is ~/ModernBASIC. The build needs the Rust toolchain; the resulting target/desktop/modernbasic-desktop is an ELF executable with the tokenized BASIC program and interpreter linked into it. This is native packaging, not direct BASIC-to-machine-code translation. Launch does not need the BASIC source or compiler. X11 is required; the browser also needs Python GTK and an installed Chromium-compatible engine (see Browser). The launcher enables the network capability and retains Chromium's sandbox. Linux and the existing host runtime provide platform services; Chromium renders web content. The desktop interface and application decisions are BASIC code.

Files presents a dedicated BASIC files area containing the user's programs, documents and supporting assets. Launchers create Programs, Binaries, Applications and Components folders without moving or replacing existing work. The bundled desktop, Office and browser binaries also default to ~/ModernBASIC when run directly; their working directory is never used as an accidental workspace. An administrator or launch script can explicitly choose another area with --file-root.

Files cannot navigate above this area or open Linux absolute paths. The runtime rejects parent traversal and symbolic links for file operations; child programs inherit the same boundary. This is a confined area backed by the Linux filesystem, not a separate disk format or an OS-wide sandbox for arbitrary host processes. Browser profile internals are replaced in Files by a Browser downloads shortcut. Its Up action returns to BASIC files. Existing files remain in place.

The browser opens a separate BASIC-drawn application window with an embedded page, tabs, bookmarks, history, downloads and explicit upload prompts. See Browser for storage, shortcuts and current limitations.

On the installed appliance, BASIC Console in the desktop menu opens the interactive BASIC programming prompt beside Microsoft Edit. Both use the same Programs folder in the selected desktop workspace (normally ~/ModernBASIC). The console inherits an explicit desktop workspace and rejects linked workspace or Programs directories. Save hello.bas there in the editor, then enter LOAD "hello.bas" and RUN in the console. You can also enter numbered lines directly, use LIST, EDIT, STEP, INSPECT, CONT, and SAVE, or build a native executable with COMPILE. HELP lists commands. Saving in the editor does not automatically replace a program already loaded in the console; use LOAD again when you want those saved changes.

Select text and press Ctrl+Shift+C to copy; use Ctrl+Shift+V to paste between the console and Microsoft Edit. Multiline BASIC source uses the same system clipboard. Select the numbered source lines from LIST when copying back to the editor. Switch environment in the desktop menu or Alt+F11 opens the full-session chooser; BASIC mode is the separate interactive BASIC programming environment, rather than another text editor.

The desktop surface uses wallpaper and unlabeled application icons. The grid icon at the left of the dock opens the application menu; menu labels appear only while it is open. Hover or use Up/Down to select an entry, then click or press Enter to activate it. F10 toggles the menu; Escape or a click outside dismisses it. The menu launches Files, Microsoft Edit, Web Browser and Office in separate windows. Office opens in Writer mode; its controls open Sheet and Slides in their own windows while preserving the current document. Programs shows tasks launched by this desktop and its apps. Each application has independent focus, resizing, minimize/maximize and close handling through the shared runtime and Linux window manager. Closing the desktop leaves its open applications running. Editor and Office close requests confirm unsaved work. Dock launchers focus an existing app launched there; opening a text file from Files creates a separate editor document window.

The live taskbar tracks BASIC application windows and, when launched with --linux-apps (the desktop launcher's default), native Linux X11 windows, including applications already running. Click an icon to restore and focus its window. Hover shows the current title and window state; the resting desktop remains free of text labels. The active window is highlighted, and minimized windows have an amber indicator. Right-click an icon for Restore, Minimize, Maximize / restore, and Close. Close uses the application's normal window close request, preserving unsaved-work confirmations.

The taskbar pages through eight windows at a time using its arrow buttons. Press F6 to select a window, then Left/Right, Home/End or Page Up/Down; Enter restores it, M minimizes, X toggles maximization, and Delete requests close. Up/Down opens its action menu; Escape dismisses the menu or keyboard selection. Titles and open/closed/minimized states refresh twice a second. The taskbar supports up to 256 windows, omits docks and windows marked skip-taskbar, and retains selection by window ID when the list changes. The Programs manager continues to show BASIC runtime tasks separately. Native Wayland-only windows are outside this X11 implementation.

The file browser supports directory navigation, folder creation, rename, and confirmed file deletion. Double-click a file or select it and press Enter: .bas and tokenized .m64b programs run in independent BASIC windows; other text files open in the editor. Select Edit source to edit a .bas file. Run BASIC or F5 runs the selected file. Delete does not remove directories recursively.

Microsoft Edit opens in a separate GTK/VTE terminal window, with the desktop's code font, foreground and background preferences. Its File/Edit/View menus, keyboard commands, mouse support and document handling come from the actual Microsoft editor. Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+O opens, Ctrl+F finds, and Ctrl+Q quits. Ctrl+Shift+C/V provides terminal clipboard copy/paste. Closing the window or using taskbar Close sends Edit its quit command, preserving its Save / Don't Save / Cancel prompt. Edit runs as the user; its own Open/Save dialogs have native Linux filesystem access. Files still validates paths inside BASIC files before handing a document to Edit.

The desktop launcher finds msedit, or uses the locally installed official binary from tools/install-microsoft-edit.py. That installer verifies a pinned release checksum and stores the executable under target/microsoft-edit. MODERNBASIC_EDIT_BINARY explicitly selects another Microsoft Edit executable. A Linux /usr/bin/edit command is accepted only if it identifies itself as Microsoft Edit; Debian's unrelated run-mailcap alias is not used. The terminal window requires system Python, PyGObject, GTK 3 and VTE 2.91. The Debian appliance already packages Microsoft Edit from its bundled source.

In Files, New BASIC program opens Programs/untitled.bas (or a chosen name) in Microsoft Edit. Save there with Ctrl+S. Select saved source in Files for Run BASIC, Build / install, or Review with Ollama. The new editor does not add BASIC-specific compiler commands to Microsoft's own menus. Keep BASIC source in Programs; Edit's native Save As can choose other paths.

Settings includes an Editor: Microsoft / BASIC button. Microsoft is the default; the optional built-in BASIC editor remains available for its integrated Run/F5 and editing workflow. The preference is text_editor=microsoft or text_editor=basic in editor.cfg, also writable with TASK PREFSAVE. The separate file keeps older standalone applications compatible with the theme file. Theme presets retain this choice. TASK EDIT path$ opens the selected system editor; an empty path opens a blank document. TASK APP "editor" explicitly opens the built-in BASIC editor for existing BASIC programs.

Save your source, then select it in Files and choose Build / install. Choose a binary name and one of these destinations:

ChoiceLocationBehavior
Build onlyBinaries/nameKeeps the compiled executable without installing it.
Software applicationApplications/nameInstalls a private executable for this user.
BASIC system componentComponents/nameInstalls a BASIC environment component; startup is separately opt-in.

Build binary (F5) and Install selected (F6) each require typing YES; Escape cancels. Installation is a separate step after a successful build. A failed build leaves the previous binary intact. Replacements are atomic, including updates while the previous executable is running. Sources remain in Programs; rebuild files and compiler cache remain in Binaries/name.build. Components start manually by default. Use Installed software → Component startup to explicitly enable desktop startup. They do not install Linux services or privileged files.

Use Run binary, or open an executable in these three folders from Files, to launch the actual native binary. These are separate native processes and are managed by the Linux window manager and appear in the native-window taskbar when --linux-apps is enabled. Graphical programs provide their own BASIC interface. Console-only binaries launched this way inherit the launcher's output and have no interactive stdin; run them from a terminal when they require input. The workspace is passed explicitly to launched binaries. Builds need Cargo, the runtime source and a working systemd user session; each build is limited to one CPU, 4 GiB RAM and 1 GiB swap. Closing the build window cancels its compiler scope. Only one build per workspace can run at once.

The desktop and Files launchers enable the --native-compile capability. When starting their binary directly, pass that flag to use build, install or native launch. The BASIC API is TASK WORKSPACE, TASK BUILD source$, name$, TASK INSTALL name$, "application" (or "component"), and TASK EXEC path$. These commands are also available to direct BASIC sessions with an explicit workspace and --native-compile; the GUI is optional. Low-level SAVE and COMPILE retain their explicit-path behavior for existing scripts.

The optional built-in BASIC editor's Run / F5 executes a snapshot of its current BASIC text, including unsaved changes. It does not save, replace the document, or consume the desktop session. Each program receives its own variables, input, graphics, errors and window. Program consoles use antialiased system monospace with the desktop colors; BASIC COLOR commands still control their own palette. Text programs support interactive INPUT and retain output at READY; graphical programs can continue running while you use the desktop. Use F5 in a READY program window to rerun it, or Ctrl+Escape to interrupt execution.

Open Programs from the menu or the fourth desktop icon to see READY, RUNNING, STOPPED and ERROR states. Select a program to switch to it, stop it, or close its window with confirmation. Up/Down and Page Up/Down scroll the list. Closing a child window leaves the desktop and editor intact. Closing the desktop leaves any remaining program windows open until you close them too. The session supports 32 BASIC windows total, including the desktop. Child programs inherit the caller's workspace and capabilities; static assets resolve relative to the source file (or the editor document's path). Running programs uses the runtime already linked into the desktop binary, with no compiler or separate modernbasic executable required.

The desktop uses Noto Sans for controls and menus and Noto Sans Mono for document text, with installed-font fallback. Vector interfaces render at the window’s physical pixel size so smaller windows keep sharp letters. Pango supplies Unicode shaping; fractional text measurements keep cursor and selection widths aligned. The following limits apply to the optional built-in BASIC editor, not Microsoft Edit: Tab inserts a tab character; documents preserve UTF-8 text. Editing positions count Unicode characters, not grapheme clusters; complex-script and bidirectional caret navigation still require further work. Documents are limited to 65,536 characters and 8,192 lines. This first editor has no syntax highlighting.

Paste into running programs is delivered in order through the bounded keyboard queue, with up to 65,536 pending characters. Graphics programs receive Tab as TAB, taskbar selection as F6, and the editor shortcuts as CTRL+A, CTRL+C, CTRL+X, CTRL+N, CTRL+O, CTRL+S, CTRL+F, CTRL+Z, and CTRL+Y from INKEY$. Navigation keys retain held Ctrl/Shift modifiers, for example SHIFT+LEFT and CTRL+SHIFT+HOME. Ctrl+Escape still interrupts execution.

Compiled programs accept --file-root path, --output-root path, --network, and -- followed by arguments exposed through COMMAND$. Compiled graphics programs also accept --headless. Their normal graphical launch opens only the application window, runs without an instruction-count timeout, and exits when the application ends; headless checks retain the normal execution limit. The desktop opts into SCREENCONTROL 4,1 to confirm a window-manager Close request when text is unsaved; other compiled programs keep ordinary close behavior. For the desktop's deterministic editor/file self-test, use a disposable root:

target/desktop/modernbasic-desktop --headless --file-root /tmp/desktop-test -- SELFTEST

Create that directory first. The self-test creates and removes desktop-check.txt; do not run it in a workspace containing that filename. The build script runs it in a new temporary directory automatically.

Appliance packaging must offer the same user choice between the desktop binary and direct BASIC without the desktop. Installing or updating the optional desktop must not switch an existing user's environment automatically. The current boot session still starts direct BASIC; the image-level chooser and both startup paths remain to be packaged and accepted. Desktop image acceptance must also cover window management, browser sandbox permissions, display scaling, keyboard layouts and sustained use on target hardware.

retains selection by window ID when the list changes. The Programs manager
continues to show BASIC runtime tasks separately. Native Wayland-only windows
are outside this X11 implementation.

The file browser supports directory
navigation, folder creation, rename, and confirmed file deletion. Double-click
a file or select it and press Enter: `.bas` and tokenized `.m64b` programs run
in independent BASIC windows; other text files open in the editor. Select
**Edit source** to edit a `.bas` file. **Run BASIC** or F5 runs the selected file. Delete does not remove
directories recursively.

Microsoft Edit opens in a separate GTK/VTE terminal window, with the desktop's
code font, foreground and background preferences. Its File/Edit/View menus,
keyboard commands, mouse support and document handling come from the actual
Microsoft editor. Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+O opens, Ctrl+F finds, and Ctrl+Q quits.
Ctrl+Shift+C/V provides terminal clipboard copy/paste. Closing the window or
using taskbar Close sends Edit its quit command, preserving its Save / Don't
Save / Cancel prompt. Edit runs as the user; its own Open/Save dialogs have
native Linux filesystem access. Files still validates paths inside BASIC files
before handing a document to Edit.

The desktop launcher finds `msedit`, or uses the locally installed official
binary from `tools/install-microsoft-edit.py`. That installer verifies a pinned
release checksum and stores the executable under `target/microsoft-edit`.
`MODERNBASIC_EDIT_BINARY` explicitly selects another Microsoft Edit executable.
A Linux `/usr/bin/edit` command is accepted only if it identifies itself as
Microsoft Edit; Debian's unrelated `run-mailcap` alias is not used. The terminal
window requires system Python, PyGObject, GTK 3 and VTE 2.91. The Debian appliance
already packages Microsoft Edit from its bundled source.

In Files, **New BASIC program** opens `Programs/untitled.bas` (or a chosen name)
in Microsoft Edit. Save there with Ctrl+S. Select saved source in Files for
**Run BASIC**, **Build / install**, or **Review with Ollama**. The new editor
does not add BASIC-specific compiler commands to Microsoft's own menus.
Keep BASIC source in `Programs`; Edit's native Save As can choose other paths.

Settings includes an **Editor: Microsoft / BASIC** button. Microsoft is the
default; the optional built-in BASIC editor remains available for its integrated
Run/F5 and editing workflow. The preference is `text_editor=microsoft` or
`text_editor=basic` in `editor.cfg`, also writable with `TASK PREFSAVE`.
The separate file keeps older standalone applications compatible with the theme
file. Theme presets retain this choice. `TASK EDIT path$` opens the selected system
editor; an empty path opens a blank document. `TASK APP "editor"` explicitly
opens the built-in BASIC editor for existing BASIC programs.

Save your source, then select it in Files and choose **Build / install**.
Choose a binary name and one of these destinations:

| Choice | Location | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build only | `Binaries/name` | Keeps the compiled executable without installing it. |
| Software application | `Applications/name` | Installs a private executable for this user. |
| BASIC system component | `Components/name` | Installs a BASIC environment component; startup is separately opt-in. |

**Build binary** (F5) and **Install selected** (F6) each require typing YES;
Escape cancels. Installation is a separate step after a successful build.
A failed build leaves the previous binary intact. Replacements are atomic,
including updates while the previous executable is running. Sources remain
in `Programs`; rebuild files and compiler cache remain in `Binaries/name.build`.
Components start manually by default. Use **Installed software → Component startup** to explicitly enable desktop startup. They do not install Linux services or privileged files.

Use **Run binary**, or open an executable in these three folders from Files,
to launch the actual native binary. These are separate native processes and
are managed by the Linux window manager and appear in the native-window taskbar
when `--linux-apps` is enabled. Graphical programs provide their own BASIC interface.
Console-only binaries launched this way inherit the launcher's output and have
no interactive stdin; run them from a terminal when they require input.
The workspace is passed explicitly to launched binaries. Builds need Cargo,
the runtime source and a working systemd user session; each build is limited
to one CPU, 4 GiB RAM and 1 GiB swap. Closing the build window cancels its compiler
scope. Only one build per workspace can run at once.

The desktop and Files launchers enable the `--native-compile` capability.
When starting their binary directly, pass that flag to use build, install or
native launch. The BASIC API is `TASK WORKSPACE`, `TASK BUILD source$, name$`,
`TASK INSTALL name$, "application"` (or `"component"`), and `TASK EXEC path$`.
These commands are also available to direct BASIC sessions with an explicit
workspace and `--native-compile`; the GUI is optional. Low-level `SAVE` and
`COMPILE` retain their explicit-path behavior for existing scripts.

The optional built-in BASIC editor's **Run / F5** executes a snapshot of its current BASIC text, including
unsaved changes. It does not save, replace the document, or consume the desktop
session. Each program receives its own variables, input, graphics, errors and
window. Program consoles use antialiased system monospace with the desktop
colors; BASIC `COLOR` commands still control their own palette. Text programs
support interactive `INPUT` and retain output at READY;
graphical programs can continue running while you use the desktop. Use F5 in
a READY program window to rerun it, or Ctrl+Escape to interrupt execution.

Open **Programs** from the menu or the fourth desktop icon to see READY,
RUNNING, STOPPED and ERROR states. Select a program to switch to it, stop it,
or close its window with confirmation. Up/Down and Page Up/Down scroll the
list. Closing a child window leaves the desktop and editor intact. Closing the
desktop leaves any remaining program windows open until you close them too.
The session supports 32 BASIC windows total, including the desktop. Child
programs inherit the caller's workspace and capabilities; static assets resolve
relative to the source file (or the editor document's path). Running programs
uses the runtime already linked into the desktop binary, with no compiler or
separate `modernbasic` executable required.

The desktop uses Noto Sans for controls and menus and Noto Sans Mono for document
text, with installed-font fallback. Vector interfaces render at the window’s
physical pixel size so smaller windows keep sharp letters. Pango supplies Unicode
shaping; fractional text measurements keep cursor and selection widths aligned.
The following limits apply to the optional built-in BASIC editor, not Microsoft
Edit: Tab inserts a tab character; documents preserve UTF-8 text. Editing positions
count Unicode characters, not grapheme clusters; complex-script and bidirectional
caret navigation still require further work. Documents are limited to 65,536
characters and 8,192 lines. This first editor has no syntax highlighting.

Paste into running programs is delivered in order through the bounded keyboard
queue, with up to 65,536 pending characters. Graphics programs receive Tab as
`TAB`, taskbar selection as `F6`, and the editor shortcuts as `CTRL+A`, `CTRL+C`, `CTRL+X`, `CTRL+N`,
`CTRL+O`, `CTRL+S`, `CTRL+F`, `CTRL+Z`, and `CTRL+Y` from `INKEY$`. Navigation
keys retain held Ctrl/Shift modifiers, for example `SHIFT+LEFT` and
`CTRL+SHIFT+HOME`. Ctrl+Escape still interrupts execution.

Compiled programs accept `--file-root path`, `--output-root path`, `--network`,
and `--` followed by arguments exposed through `COMMAND$`. Compiled graphics
programs also accept `--headless`. Their normal graphical launch opens only
the application window, runs without an instruction-count timeout, and exits
when the application ends; headless checks retain the normal execution limit.
The desktop opts into `SCREENCONTROL 4,1` to confirm a window-manager Close
request when text is unsaved; other compiled programs keep ordinary close behavior.
For the desktop's deterministic editor/file self-test, use a disposable root:

```sh
target/desktop/modernbasic-desktop --headless --file-root /tmp/desktop-test -- SELFTEST
```

Create that directory first. The self-test creates and removes
`desktop-check.txt`; do not run it in a workspace containing that filename.
The build script runs it in a new temporary directory automatically.

Appliance packaging must offer the same user choice between the desktop binary
and direct BASIC without the desktop. Installing or updating the optional desktop
must not switch an existing user's environment automatically. The current boot
session still starts direct BASIC; the image-level chooser and both startup paths
remain to be packaged and accepted. Desktop image acceptance must also cover
window management, browser sandbox permissions, display scaling, keyboard layouts
and sustained use on target hardware.

documents.title: Default directory
documents.html:
When ModernBASIC is started without --file-root, it searches for the installed programs directory and uses it as the BASIC user root. The launcher changes to the project directory before starting the executable, so the normal command is enough:

./run.sh

At READY.:

PWD
DIR
CD "examples"
DIR
DIR "*.dat"
DIR *
TREE /
CD /

The visible BASIC root is simply programs; no /home/... host prefix is shown. PWD and CD therefore report programs at the root and paths such as programs/examples or programs/music below it. These displayed paths can be typed back into CD, DIR, LOAD, and the other file commands. Plain DIR, and DIR with a directory path, show all user entries without exposing their host paths. Listings are divided into DIRECTORY FOLDERS, BASIC PROGRAMS, and OTHER FILES, in that order. This keeps .bas programs prominent while retaining access to their data and support files at the bottom. Use a pattern such as DIR *.dat to narrow the listing under MATCHING FILES. Listings report totals for the visible entries. TREE [path] and DIR /S [path] recursively browse nested directories with fixed entry and depth limits. CD / and CD \ return to programs; CD .. and compact CD.. move to the parent but remain at the root when already there. Forward and backslashes are both accepted as BASIC separators.

Paths cannot escape the user root. Symbolic links are displayed but recursive browsing does not follow them, and canonical path checks still reject a link that would leave the root. An explicit --file-root still overrides the default.

Existing files and directory components are resolved case-insensitively within that root. These therefore select the same packaged directory even while the graphical shell is in uppercase-input mode:

CD examples
CD EXAMPLES
CD "examples"

Listings retain each file or subfolder's real spelling beneath programs, but never print the absolute host prefix. A new output file keeps the spelling typed by the BASIC program, while an existing file is reused case-insensitively instead of creating a second name that differs only by case.

documents.title: Editing a listed program
documents.html:
1. Load or enter a program containing at least one numbered line.
  2. Press F2 to execute LIST, or press Ctrl+Up/Ctrl+Down directly. Direct program navigation automatically lists and captures a loaded program; an empty program leaves navigation inactive.
  3. Press Ctrl+Up or Ctrl+Down to select a numbered line. The complete canonical line is copied into the editable input row.
  4. Use Left, Right, Home, End, Backspace, and Delete to edit the line.
  5. Press Enter to replace the stored line.
  6. Continue with Ctrl+Up or Ctrl+Down, or press Escape to leave list-edit mode.

Page Up and Page Down scroll a long listing. Entering a line number without a body deletes that line, following classic BASIC rules.

Ordinary Up and Down browse the shared READY history. That history contains commands such as RUN and numbered statements such as 20 PRINT "HELLO". History navigation remains available while list-edit mode is active. Submitting a non-numbered command, pressing Escape, or using NEW/LOAD/RUN leaves list-edit mode so stale lines cannot be selected.

Ctrl+Left and Ctrl+Right move the character cursor safely and cannot be mistaken for control-letter shortcuts.

Ctrl+U toggles the graphical input mode between CAPS:ON and CAPS:OFF. The status line displays this shortcut. Lowercase typed inside a quoted string or path is preserved even while the general input mode is uppercase.

The controls have deliberately different lifecycle effects:

ActionExecutionProgram windowBASIC RAM and loaded program
Ctrl+Escape (BREAK)StopsRemains open at READY.Retained
Window X or shell CLOSETerminatesCloses immediatelyReleased when the task is reaped
Plain EscapeContinuesRemains openRetained

BREAK also stops task-owned audio, speech, decoder, and encoder processes while retaining variables, arrays, prepared assets, and queued synthesis data. Plain Escape only cancels current shell input or exits a graphics/list-edit view.

When RUN or CONT returns control after completion, STOP, BREAK, or a runtime error, the text screen prints the classic READY. line before accepting the next command. A program ending with a semicolon is moved to a fresh line before that prompt is printed.

The terminal environment retains the command form:

EDIT 120

It prints line 120 and asks for a replacement body. Unfinished structured blocks remain in the editor while you enter their closing lines. CHECK validates their structure without running them. RUN refuses an invalid draft without discarding it or running an older copy. EDIT "draft.bas" opens saved source for repair even when a block is incomplete. Lexical errors still need correction in a text editor. Use INSPECT A or INSPECT A(1) to examine values at STOP/STEP without losing continuation; CONT resumes. The embedded programming guide covers the complete edit/save/debug/compile workflow.

3. Press **Ctrl+Up** or **Ctrl+Down** to select a numbered line. The complete
   canonical line is copied into the editable input row.
4. Use **Left**, **Right**, **Home**, **End**, **Backspace**, and **Delete** to
   edit the line.
5. Press **Enter** to replace the stored line.
6. Continue with **Ctrl+Up** or **Ctrl+Down**, or press **Escape** to leave
   list-edit mode.

body deletes that line, following classic BASIC rules.

contains commands such as `RUN` and numbered statements such as
`20 PRINT "HELLO"`. History navigation remains available while list-edit mode
is active. Submitting a non-numbered command, pressing Escape, or using
`NEW`/`LOAD`/`RUN` leaves list-edit mode so stale lines cannot be selected.

mistaken for control-letter shortcuts.

The status line displays this shortcut. Lowercase typed inside a quoted string
or path is preserved even while the general input mode is uppercase.

The controls have deliberately different lifecycle effects:

| Action | Execution | Program window | BASIC RAM and loaded program |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Ctrl+Escape** (BREAK) | Stops | Remains open at `READY.` | Retained |
| Window **X** or shell `CLOSE` | Terminates | Closes immediately | Released when the task is reaped |
| Plain **Escape** | Continues | Remains open | Retained |

BREAK also stops task-owned audio, speech, decoder, and encoder processes while
retaining variables, arrays, prepared assets, and queued synthesis data. Plain
Escape only cancels current shell input or exits a graphics/list-edit view.

runtime error, the text screen prints the classic `READY.` line before accepting
the next command. A program ending with a semicolon is moved to a fresh line
before that prompt is printed.

The terminal environment retains the command form:

```basic
EDIT 120
```

It prints line 120 and asks for a replacement body. Unfinished structured blocks
remain in the editor while you enter their closing lines. CHECK validates their
structure without running them. RUN refuses an invalid draft without discarding
it or running an older copy. EDIT "draft.bas" opens saved source for repair even
when a block is incomplete. Lexical errors still need correction in a text editor.
Use INSPECT A or INSPECT A(1) to examine values at STOP/STEP without losing
continuation; CONT resumes. The embedded [programming guide](PROGRAMMING_GUIDE.md)
covers the complete edit/save/debug/compile workflow.

documents.title: Office and standalone editor windows
documents.html:
Files and the selected system editor can run without the desktop surface. The editor launcher defaults to Microsoft Edit and respects the editor choice saved in Settings:

./tools/run-files.sh /path/to/workspace
./tools/run-editor.sh /path/to/workspace
./tools/build-office.sh
./tools/run-office.sh writer /path/to/workspace
./tools/run-office.sh sheet /path/to/workspace
./tools/run-office.sh slides /path/to/workspace

Writer, Sheet and Slides are bundled BASIC interfaces, packaged into the target/office/modernbasic-office ELF with the shared runtime. Their navigation buttons launch another application window and preserve the current document. Office uses Noto Sans with measured carets, cell alignment and slide wrapping; text is drawn again at the current window resolution after resizing.

Office currently supports plain-text Writer documents, an 8-column by 20-row spreadsheet with simple formulas, and up to 50 slides. Native saves use .mbo; exports use TXT, CSV and HTML. DOCX, XLSX and PPTX are not supported.

Validate document behavior with tools/test-office.py --binary PATH_TO_MODERNBASIC. tools/check-office-windows.py --binary PATH_TO_OFFICE --report REPORT.json checks real window behavior and document isolation on an isolated Xvfb display.

Shared desktop settings and management

The desktop menu opens separate Settings, System Information, Programs, and Installed software windows. Left/Right switches menu columns. Settings stores desktop.cfg inside the BASIC workspace. Dark, light and high-contrast presets cover background, panels, buttons, editor, text, muted text, accents, borders, selections, wallpaper, warnings, Office paper and document ink. Interface and code fonts are independent; the desktop clock and gradient can be turned on or off. Bundled BASIC apps refresh shared colors and fonts while open. Document paper and ink are separate from application chrome. Third-party BASIC apps can read the same values with TASK PREFS key$,value$ or TASK PREFSALL text$.

TASK PREFSAVE key$,value$, TASK PREFRESET "dark" (also "light" or "contrast"), and TASK PREFSTATUS text$ expose the settings service. A corrupt configuration falls back to defaults without overwriting the bad file; an explicit preset reset repairs it. System Information uses TASK INFO text$ for read-only host/runtime details, without exposing the host filesystem in Files.

Programs manages BASIC windows in its own desktop session. The runtime grants only this bundled manager permission to focus, stop and close sibling tasks; ordinary programs retain control only of their descendants. Native installed executables are tracked separately in Installed software. It offers run, stop, uninstall and component startup controls, with confirmation before stop, uninstall or startup changes. Uninstall preserves source and build files. Stopping a native process is forceful and discards its unsaved state.

TASK SOFTWARE list$ returns tab-separated kind/name/state/startup rows. TASK STOPBINARY path$, TASK UNINSTALL name$,kind$, and TASK STARTUP name$,0|1 require --native-compile. TASK AUTOSTART report$ starts enabled components when the desktop opens. Status and duplicate-launch prevention cover children launched by the current host process. They are not a persistent Linux service manager: a new desktop session cannot recover tracking of binaries left alive by an older session. Avoid starting concurrent desktop sessions with the same auto-start components. Native graphical binaries have normal Linux windows; terminal programs requiring INPUT should run in a terminal.

Local Ollama code review

Save a .bas document and click Review with Ollama. A separate BASIC window lets you choose an installed local model (click its name or use Left/Right), then Review saved source. Up/Down/Page keys scroll the suggestions. The editor's source is never rewritten. The review uses a snapshot of that saved file, capped at 16 KiB, plus brief ModernBASIC dialect guidance. It does not send other documents or grant tools to the model. Reopen the review to capture newer edits. Reviews can be wrong; they do not substitute for execution or tests.

Desktop, editor and Files launchers enable --local-ai, a distinct capability that permits only the local Ollama endpoint at 127.0.0.1:11434. It does not grant WEB or general network access. Python 3 and a running Ollama installation with an already installed text model are required. Cloud/remote models are excluded, redirects and proxies are not used, and no model is downloaded automatically. The local Ollama service itself must be trusted. Requests are bounded to 190 seconds and 256 KiB of output; closing the review cancels its helper connection. The model/context settings also limit answer length.

BASIC programs can use the same local API without a desktop:

10 TASK AIMODELS MODELS$:PRINT MODELS$
20 TASK AICHAT "your-local-model", "Explain a FOR loop", ANSWER$
30 PRINT ANSWER$

TASK AIREVIEW model$,source$,review$ applies the review prompt; TASK AICHAT accepts a single prompt of up to 65,536 UTF-8 bytes (the model's context limit still applies). Both require --local-ai, including when running a compiled binary. The native launcher forwards only permissions already granted to the calling BASIC session. See programs/ai/local_chat.bas and programs/ai/basic_chatbot.bas for the two AI programming paths.

Installed Linux applications

Open Installed software, then Linux apps (or press Tab). The BASIC window lists registered Linux desktop applications by their localized display names, with descriptions and the selected desktop ID. Up/Down, Home/End and Page keys select entries; Enter or Run requests a launch. BASIC apps or Tab returns to workspace applications and components. F5/Refresh updates the list immediately; the Linux view also checks for changes every ten seconds.

The desktop launcher grants --linux-apps. Other BASIC hosts must explicitly grant it before TASK LINUXAPPS list$ or TASK LINUXLAUNCH desktopId$ can run. Listing returns newline-separated rows of desktop ID<TAB>name<TAB>description. The capability only resolves registered, visible desktop IDs; it accepts no arbitrary command or desktop-file path. BASIC windows opened within the same host inherit its capability. Separately launched compiled binaries require an explicit --linux-apps option; the workspace binary launcher does not add this new option to older executables.

The embedded helper uses system /usr/bin/python3 and PyGObject/GIO (Debian packages python3-gi and gir1.2-glib-2.0). GIO applies XDG directory precedence, localization, Hidden/NoDisplay, OnlyShowIn/NotShowIn and TryExec rules, and handles Exec arguments, terminal applications and D-Bus activation. Flatpak/Snap entries are included when exported into the current session's XDG application locations. Applications without registered desktop entries do not appear.

Linux applications keep their own windows and filesystem permissions. BASIC's Files view stays confined to the workspace. The Linux list does not claim running status, stop processes or uninstall packages. A successful launch request does not guarantee that the application completes its own startup. Taskbar integration and control of arbitrary Linux windows remain separate work.

seconds and 256 KiB of output; closing the review cancels its helper connection.
The model/context settings also limit answer length.

BASIC programs can use the same local API without a desktop:

```basic
10 TASK AIMODELS MODELS$:PRINT MODELS$
20 TASK AICHAT "your-local-model", "Explain a FOR loop", ANSWER$
30 PRINT ANSWER$
```

`TASK AIREVIEW model$,source$,review$` applies the review prompt; `TASK AICHAT`
accepts a single prompt of up to 65,536 UTF-8 bytes (the model's context limit
still applies). Both require `--local-ai`, including when running a compiled
binary. The native launcher forwards only permissions already granted to the
calling BASIC session. See `programs/ai/local_chat.bas` and
`programs/ai/basic_chatbot.bas` for the two AI programming paths.


### Installed Linux applications

Open **Installed software**, then **Linux apps** (or press Tab). The BASIC window
lists registered Linux desktop applications by their localized display names,
with descriptions and the selected desktop ID. Up/Down, Home/End and Page keys
select entries; Enter or Run requests a launch. **BASIC apps** or Tab returns to
workspace applications and components. F5/Refresh updates the list immediately;
the Linux view also checks for changes every ten seconds.

The desktop launcher grants `--linux-apps`. Other BASIC hosts must explicitly
grant it before `TASK LINUXAPPS list$` or `TASK LINUXLAUNCH desktopId$` can run.
Listing returns newline-separated rows of `desktop ID<TAB>name<TAB>description`.
The capability only resolves registered, visible desktop IDs; it accepts no
arbitrary command or desktop-file path. BASIC windows opened within the same host inherit its capability. Separately
launched compiled binaries require an explicit `--linux-apps` option; the workspace
binary launcher does not add this new option to older executables.

The embedded helper uses system `/usr/bin/python3` and PyGObject/GIO (Debian
packages `python3-gi` and `gir1.2-glib-2.0`). GIO applies XDG directory precedence,
localization, Hidden/NoDisplay, OnlyShowIn/NotShowIn and TryExec rules, and handles
Exec arguments, terminal applications and D-Bus activation. Flatpak/Snap entries
are included when exported into the current session's XDG application locations.
Applications without registered desktop entries do not appear.

Linux applications keep their own windows and filesystem permissions. BASIC's
Files view stays confined to the workspace. The Linux list does not claim running
status, stop processes or uninstall packages. A successful launch request does
not guarantee that the application completes its own startup. Taskbar integration
and control of arbitrary Linux windows remain separate work.
